readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's budget for 2021 — ₱75,628,681,748.26, drawn from the annual block grant, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected inside its territory, and projected collections on its own regional taxes and fees.

It is the first Bangsamoro budget that says what it adds up to. The FY 2020 act appropriated “the following sums, or so much thereof as may be necessary… out of any available funds” without a total and without naming a single revenue source. This one opens with a figure to the centavo and a list of where the money comes from, and every budget since has followed that form.

The money is organized by agency across 17 ministries, 6 other executive offices and 3 special purpose funds. 5 of those 6 offices — the Planning and Development Authority, the Attorney-General's Office, the Human Rights Commission, the Women Commission and the Youth Commission — exist because acts passed since the last budget created them, and this is where they first get funded. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱3,707,969,000, about 4.9% of the total.

The pandemic is in the numbers. The Ministry of Health carries a COVID Response line of ₱379,968,484, and the ₱5.44 billion Contingent Fund may be spent on “supplies and materials needed in response to the effect of the COVID19 pandemic including vaccines, health protective gears, and other paraphernalia not otherwise considered in budget allocation”.

The last 16 pages carry 70 sections of general provisions. Personnel Services across government may not exceed 45% of total revenue. At least 5% of every ministry's budget must go to a Gender and Development Plan. Deductions may never reduce an employee's monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000. Rainwater collection systems are required in public markets, school sites and government buildings. Infrastructure contracts, winning bidders and final costs must be published within 30 days, and officials who miss their quarterly reports have their salaries suspended automatically until they comply.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Government needs an annual appropriations act to function. This one was written in the first pandemic year, and its Introduction says so plainly: the government “has charged through turbulent times”, took “cognizance of the changes brought about by the ‘New Normal’”, and expects to keep operating “in an increasingly volatile, complex and uncertain environment”. It was passed and approved on the same day, 23 December 2020, a week before it took effect.
whoIsAffected: Everyone in the region served by a Bangsamoro Government program.
Patients and health workers, through the COVID Response appropriation.
All government personnel, whose allowances, bonuses and pay floor this fixes.
The 5 new commissions and offices funded here for the first time.
Contractors and suppliers, through procurement and disclosure rules.
Women's programs, guaranteed a 5% share of every ministry budget.
implementedBy: All 17 ministries, the 6 other executive offices and the special purpose funds
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, administering releases and issuing guidelines
Ministry of Health, on the COVID Response Plan
Office of the Chief Minister, clearing foreign travel and releasing the Contingent Fund
Bangsamoro Women Commission, on gender and development plans
Commission on Audit, as external auditor

funding.detail: ₱75,628,681,748.26 for fiscal year 2021, from the annual block grant from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territorial jurisdiction, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources.

whatChanges: ₱75.63 billion is appropriated for 2021 — the first regional budget to state a total.
5 commissions and offices created since the last budget are funded for the first time.
₱379,968,484 is set aside for the Ministry of Health's COVID Response Plan.
Personnel costs are held to 45% of revenue and gender programs floored at 5% of every budget.
Officials and employees are to be issued personal computers and essential electronic devices.
Spending deadlines tighten: construction paid by 30 June 2022, other deliveries by 31 March 2022.
readings.insight:
The interesting change here is not the amount but the form. The FY 2020 act appropriated “the following sums, or so much thereof as may be necessary… out of any available funds in the Bangsamoro Treasury Office… not otherwise appropriated” — no total, no revenue sources. A year later Section 1 names ₱75,628,681,748.26 and lists 3 sources: the block grant, the region's share of national taxes collected in its territory, and projected collections on its own taxes and fees. A government that could not state its revenue base in 2019 could state it in 2020, and the appropriations law changed shape accordingly. Every budget since has kept that shape, and each has added a source to the list — “other subsidies” in FY 2022, “unused/unutilized appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury” the same year, “unutilized prior years' allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury” by FY 2024.

This is also the first budget written after the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, and it shows. Where the FY 2020 act set out its own rule for remitting agency income, this one simply points at Section 3, Chapter I, Book VII of BAA 13. The FY 2020 act had asked for that code in its own Section 70; here the code is doing the work.

The pandemic appears in the line items rather than the general provisions — a ₱379,968,484 COVID Response appropriation in the Ministry of Health and a Contingent Fund authorisation for vaccines and protective gear — but not one of the 70 general provisions mentions COVID-19. The rules for spending did not change; only what was bought did.

The ₱5.44 billion Contingent Fund is also the first sign of a long retreat from lump-sum budgeting. A year earlier it had been ₱13.2 billion — 20% of the whole budget — and the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund alongside it another ₱9.28 billion. Here they are ₱5.44 billion and ₱1.78 billion, 9.6% of the budget between them against 34% the year before. The Contingent Fund keeps falling every year after this, reaching ₱666.8 million by FY 2025.

It carries the same quiet line the FY 2020 fund carried: “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs”. It appears again in FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024, FY 2025 and FY 2026 — 7 consecutive budgets making room for the same purchase.

Section 47 gave the money 1 year. BAA 24, passed a year later, extended it to 31 December 2022; BAA 38, passed in June 2023, was still authorising the release of unpaid obligations from this budget. Money appropriated for 2021 was still being disbursed in 2023.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament gives itself a seal. Circular, bordered by 2 green lines, with its name arched across the top on white and '20 BARMM 19' across the bottom on red. At the center sits the Bangsamoro flag shaped as a shield, and around it 80 boxes in a horseshoe — the shape of a debating chamber, and the number of its members.

Above the shield, an open book on a brown stand. The act says what it means: the living adherence of the Parliament to the rule of law.

The seal may be used on all official acts, communications and documents of the Parliament *and its members*, alongside the region's own seal, with the detail left to the Parliamentary Rules.
readings.whyProposed: The policy section is about standing rather than administration: adopting the seal establishes the Parliament as the legislative authority of the region, in recognition of the justness and legitimacy of the Bangsamoro cause. A body created by someone else's law marking itself as an institution in its own right.
whoIsAffected: Anyone receiving an official document from the Parliament or from a Member.
Members of Parliament, who may use the seal on their own official communications.
implementedBy: No implementing body is named; usage detail is left to the Parliamentary Rules, Procedures and Practices.
whatChanges: Parliament acquires a mark distinct from the region's own seal.
Members may use it, not only the institution.
The number of members and the chamber's form are written into the region's iconography.
deliberation: 19 January 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan noted that the bill's co-authors were missing from Committee Report No. 31; the Chair directed the Secretariat to include them in the record.

19 January 2021: MP Don Mustapha A. Loong asked how the seal's colors are defined to avoid future confusion; MP Lanang T. Ali, Jr. said they come from the BARMM flag and the book is brown, and welcomed defining them by amendment.

19 January 2021: MP Ali B. Sangki asked whether the 7-pointed star should become 8 now that Cotabato City has joined; MP Lanang T. Ali, Jr. said the 7 points stand for the 5 provinces, Cotabato City and the 63 barangays in North Cotabato.
19 January 2021: MP Romeo C. Saliga moved to include the year 2019 in the seal; accepted.
19 January 2021: MP Don Mustapha A. Loong moved to state the flag's red, green and yellow in the bill and to define the brown and gray; accepted.
19 January 2021: Explaining his yes vote, MP Ali B. Sangki said it was understood that the 7-pointed star would be adjusted if more provinces and cities join.
19 January 2021: Nominal vote: 49 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Third and Final Reading, 19 January 2021; 6 MPs explained their votes.
19 January 2021: Certified urgent by the Chief Minister and approved on third and final reading by nominal voting, 49 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions; it became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 16.
readings.insight:
Put this beside BAA 2 and the contrast is instructive. The Bangsamoro Seal — the mark that authenticates the region's official acts, where forgery would matter most — was specified in color names: golden yellow, slightly red, green. Parliament's own seal, adopted a year and a half later, is specified in hex codes throughout, down to 2 shades of grey for an open book and 2 browns for the stand it rests on. The institution was noticeably more exacting about its own emblem than about the region's.

The 80 boxes are the detail worth keeping. They fix the size of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority in the Parliament's own seal — which is a curious choice for a body whose membership is set by the transition arrangements and which is meant to be replaced by an elected Parliament. A seal that counts the current members is a seal that may 1 day count wrongly.

As with every other symbols act except the hymn, there is no offence for forging or misusing it.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's civil service code — 311 articles covering how the Bangsamoro Government hires, promotes, disciplines and separates its people, applying to the ministries, the component LGUs, the state universities and the chartered corporations.

Most of it deliberately mirrors national practice, and Article 2 says so outright: where the Code conflicts with the Constitution or national civil service law, the national rules prevail. What sits on top of that framework is what makes it a Bangsamoro code.

Working hours are the most visible example. The standard 8-to-5 day is written in, and then qualified: on Fridays, office hours for Muslim employees may run 7:00 to 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 to 6:00 p.m., leaving the middle of the day clear for congregational prayer. During Ramadan, employees may work 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. with no noon break, and the Code states plainly that the 2-hour difference is not counted as undertime. Employees may also elect to work Sundays and take Friday off instead.

Other openings run the same way. Passing the Shari'ah Bar is a civil service eligibility. Degrees from foreign institutions, expressly including Islamic ones, can be certified as equivalent. Human resource development may include Islamic values formation. Special civil service examinations are held for indigenous peoples. Bona fide residents get preference in appointment. And the norms of conduct require civil servants not to act contrary to law, “Adat or the Moro or non-Moro indigenous people's customary law”.

Then there is Article 305, buried in the transitory provisions and more consequential than anything around it.
readings.whyProposed: The new government needed its own civil service rules to replace the ARMM's, which Article 310 repeals wholesale. It also needed something the ARMM never had to provide: a lawful route into public employment for the combatants the peace process was decommissioning.
whoIsAffected: Everyone employed by the Bangsamoro Government, its LGUs, state universities and chartered corporations.
Former MILF and MNLF combatants seeking entry-level government work.
Muslim employees, whose Friday and Ramadan hours are set by statute.
Shari'ah Bar passers, madrasah teachers and graduates of Islamic institutions.
Indigenous peoples, through special examinations.
Employees facing reorganization, protected by a statutory order of removal.
implementedBy: Civil Service Commission for BARMM
Office of the Chief Minister, holding jurisdiction over cases at Salary Grade 25 and above
Bangsamoro Attorney-General's Office, conducting formal investigations in those cases
Development Academy of the Bangsamoro, on onboarding and on training for former combatants
Agency Promotion and Selection Boards, including elected rank-and-file representatives

funding.detail: The Code carries no appropriation. It prescribes the rules under which the government employs people rather than funding a program; the costs sit in agency personnel budgets under the annual appropriations act.

whatChanges: The region gains its own civil service code, repealing the ARMM's.
Friday and Ramadan working hours become statutory entitlements.
Shari'ah Bar passage and foreign Islamic degrees are recognized for appointment.
Special civil service examinations open for indigenous peoples.
Up to 30% of entry-level government posts are allocated to former MILF and MNLF combatants.
readings.insight:
Article 305 is why this Code matters beyond the personnel office. It permits Mujahideen and Mujahidat to be hired as temporary appointees to first-level positions “regardless of the presence of applicants who are civil service eligible”, and allocates up to 30% of the government's entire entry-level plantilla to them. That is the normalization track of the peace agreement expressed as employment law — the point at which decommissioning stops being a security arrangement and becomes a payroll.

The design is careful about its own limits. The route reaches only Salary Grade 9 and below. The appointments are temporary, running 12 months and renewable 3 times, so roughly 4 years to convert into something permanent — and conversion requires actually acquiring eligibility, with the Development Academy of the Bangsamoro directed to build the training that makes that possible. Hiring is confined to “the transition period”, a term the Code leaves undefined. So it is a door, held open for a while, at the bottom of the structure, with a staircase attached and a clock running.

What is striking is who holds the list. “It shall be the responsibility of the Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF to determine the mujahideen/mujahidat in the roster of their organic members who shall be considered for hiring under this provision.” A government statute delegates to 2 non-state organizations the power to certify who qualifies for a reserved share of public employment. There is no obvious alternative — nobody else knows who the combatants were — and the peace agreement is built on exactly this kind of recognition. But it is worth stating plainly, because it is the sort of arrangement that reads as unremarkable inside a transition and unusual outside one.

The Friday and Ramadan hours in Article 198 deserve a note of their own, because they do something the national civil service rules have never had reason to do: they change the shape of the working week around religious obligation rather than accommodating it around the edges. The Ramadan clause is the tell — employees work 8:00 fewer hours across the month and the Code declares in terms that this “is not counted as undertime”. That is not a permission to take leave; it is a redefinition of the working day.

One inconsistency across the registry is worth flagging. Article 2 here subordinates the Code to national civil service law in case of conflict. 4 years later, BAA 82's Section 271 asserted the opposite for labour — that the regional Code prevails over the national Labor Code within BARMM. Same government, same devolved-authority question, opposite answers. Nothing in either act explains the difference, and it will matter whenever the 2 regimes meet.
deliberation: 27 January 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan asked for a printed copy of the bill behind Committee Report No. 53 so MPs could check it with their lawyers; the Majority Floor Leader said copies would be distributed that day.

16 February 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan flagged inconsistent terms for the Civil Service Commission and agencies, undefined acronyms, and strong reservations on the Bangsamoro director-general and the non-application of Career Executive Service eligibility; MP Raissa H. Jajurie agreed to make terms consistent and said third-level references were left in by inadvertence.

16 February 2021: MP Raissa H. Jajurie said there are no third-level positions in the BARMM because these require presidential appointment, so the code instead creates second-level positions exercising executive or managerial functions.

16 February 2021: MP Paisalin P. Tago argued the BOL lets BARMM set its own qualification standards and said he would amend the code so Shari'ah bar passers before 2014 and Mujahidin are not limited to first-level positions up to Salary Grade 9.

16 February 2021: MP Maisara D. Latiph argued the BOL lets Parliament create its own third-level eligibility and proposed a Bangsamoro Executive Service Board for Bangsamoro third-level positions; MP Anna Tarhata S. Basman said the CES Board decree still limits that power.

16 February 2021: MP Laisa M. Alamia asked whether current permanent third-level occupants would get new appointment papers as second-level positions; MP Basman said in practical terms yes, and noted the appeal for later consideration.

16 February 2021: MP Laisa M. Alamia also challenged the nepotism rule's limit to the 3rd degree, the 3-month pre-election ban on reassignments, and the undefined offense of disloyalty to the Bangsamoro people; MP Basman said these were lifted from EO 292 and the 2017 RACCS and invited amendments.

24 February 2021: MP Ampatuan voted yes 'with strong reservation' because the Code drops the Career Executive Service eligibility requirement for third-level positions, saying the BARMM should not be lesser than the ARMM.
24 February 2021: MP Mawallil voted yes with reservations over the removed third-level standards, noting the committee accepted 12 of the 20 points in his position paper.

24 February 2021: MP Dipatuan said his amendment for the mujahideen and their families was not accepted but he yielded to a better proposition, and MP Macaraya hoped for an amendment qualifying mujahideen college graduates for salary grade 15 and up.

24 February 2021: Nominal vote: 65 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third reading; the journal lists 65 names in favor and states 'sixty-five (65) votes in favor, none against and no abstention'.
24 February 2021: Approved on third and final reading by nominal voting, 65 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions, as a bill certified urgent by the Chief Minister.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's education code, and the sentence that carries it is Section 54: the Bangsamoro Government “shall provide 2 parallel formal systems in delivering quality basic education – the ‘Public School System' and the ‘Public Madrasah System'”, both governed by common standards on curriculum, assessment, teachers, textbooks, infrastructure, management and quality assurance.

That is a real structural departure. Nationally, madrasah education reaches public schools as an enrichment program bolted onto the ordinary curriculum. Here it is a complete formal pathway with its own grade levels — Tahderiyah, Lower and Upper Ibtidaiyyah, Mutawassitah, Thanawiyyah — its own curriculum specifications, its own certificates and its own Thanawiyyah Diploma, overseen by a Director-General for Madaris Education sitting alongside the Directors-General for Basic, Higher and Technical Education. A child can go all the way through and come out with a recognized credential.

The code does other things worth noting. Islamic subjects and Arabic are taught to Muslim learners inside the public school system too. Mother tongue is the medium through Grade 3 in both systems. Bangsamoro history, culture and identity are integrated at every level, and made an express right of the learner. Peace education is a core component across all levels and delivery systems with its own dedicated funding. Corporal and humiliating punishment is prohibited. Schools must be allowed prayer spaces. Section 105 opens a civil service route for madrasah teachers who could not previously qualify.

And it takes over higher education. CHED-ARMM's powers, budgets, personnel and assets transfer to the Ministry, which now accredits, sanctions and can close institutions in the region — while the Minister sits ex-officio on the national Commission on Higher Education.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law obliges the Bangsamoro Government to establish and support a complete and integrated education system as a subsystem of the national one. Beyond the mandate, the code answers a long-standing problem: a large share of the region's children were being educated in madaris whose credentials led nowhere in the formal system, and a large share of their teachers held Arabic and Islamic Studies degrees that could not convert into civil service eligibility.
whoIsAffected: Every learner in the region, in either system.
Madrasah teachers, offered a special eligibility route.
Higher education institutions, now regulated regionally.
Indigenous learners, through IPEd and a Tribal University System.
Out-of-school youth and adults, through ALS and community learning centers.
Private and sectarian schools, supervised but protected from discrimination.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
4 Bangsamoro Directors-General — Basic, Higher, Technical and Madaris Education
Schools Division Offices and higher education provincial offices across the region
Bureaus for Basic Education, Alternative Learning Systems, Indigenous Peoples' Education, Physical Education and Sports, and Special Education
Civil Service Commission for BARMM, on Mudarris eligibility and teacher appointments

funding.detail: No amount is appropriated. Section 196 provides only that “the funding necessary for the implementation of this Act shall be included in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act”. The Code separately directs the Ministry to establish a waqf endowment fund for advanced education, faculty development and research, to adopt resource generation initiatives, and to guide the collection and use of the Special Education Fund with the local government ministry.

whatChanges: The madrasah becomes a full parallel formal school system with its own diploma.
Higher education regulation moves from CHED-ARMM to the regional ministry.
Bangsamoro history and peace education enter the curriculum at every level.
Corporal punishment is prohibited and prayer spaces must be allowed.
Madrasah teachers gain a route to permanent appointment.
An Alternative Learning System pathway recognizes Tahfidz Al-Quran and requires a learning center in every municipality.
readings.insight:
The 2-system design in Section 54 is the most consequential thing this Code does, and its promise rests entirely on the phrase “common standards”. On paper the 2 systems are equals — same standards for curriculum and competency, assessment, teachers, textbooks, infrastructure, management and quality assurance. In practice the Code's own text shows where the alignment breaks. The Public School System runs Junior High across Grades 7 to 10 and Senior High across 11 to 12. The Madrasah System runs Mutawassitah across Grades 7 to 9 and Thanawiyyah across 10 to 12. Those are different stage boundaries, which means a learner moving between the systems at Grade 10 is crossing a key stage in one and sitting mid-stage in the other — and the Code, for all its detail on curriculum content per level, says nothing about how transfers between the 2 parallel tracks work. For a design whose whole point is that families should be able to choose either without penalty, that is the gap most worth watching.

Section 105 is the other provision to read closely, because it gives and withholds in the same breath. Madrasah teachers had long been stuck: an Arabic or Islamic Studies degree, however distinguished, did not produce civil service eligibility, so permanent appointment was closed. The Code creates a special qualifying examination, grants a special license to those who pass, and exempts honor graduates from sitting it at all — a genuine and overdue opening. Then it adds that the eligibility “shall only qualify the appointee to permanent appointment to Mudarris and shall not be considered as a substitute to second level eligibility unless authorized by the Civil Service Commission”. So the door opens into one room. A Mudarris made permanent under this provision cannot move laterally into the wider bureaucracy on that credential. Whether that is a sensible boundary around a specialised qualification or a ceiling on a career is a judgement the Code does not make, but it is the kind of detail that decides whether parity is real.

What is missing is money. This is a 199-section code that establishes 2 parallel school systems, absorbs a national commission's regional functions, mandates a Community Learning Center in every municipality and city, requires regular funding lines for indigenous peoples' education and for peace education, and directs the creation of a Tribal University System — and Section 196 appropriates nothing, leaving it all to the annual budget. The Tribal University makes the point: mandated here in 2021, mandated again in BAA 64 in 2024, and still without a charter. The Code was passed and signed on the same day, 18 May 2021, which suggests broad agreement on the design. Building it was always going to be the harder part.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's overseas workers law, and it starts from an unusual premise. Section 2(d) recognizes what remittances do for the economy and then says outright that “the Bangsamoro government does not promote overseas employment as a means to sustain economic growth and achieve development” — the program exists only on the assurance that workers' dignity and rights will not be compromised, and the government commits instead to creating local jobs. Very few migration statutes in this country say that.

What follows is a set of floors. An employment contract must pay at least the host country's minimum wage or Metro Manila's, whichever is higher. The employer pays the visa, the airfare, the processing fee and the welfare bureau contribution. The worker pays a short closed list of document costs and, Section 13 says, nothing else in any amount, form, manner or purpose. Insurance is compulsory and must cost the worker nothing.

Then a set of gates. No deployment permit may issue for a country that lacks protective labour laws, has not ratified the relevant conventions, and has no bilateral agreement — and the official who issues one anyway is dismissed and barred from appointive office for 5 years. Companies with a record of discriminating against migrants “on account of religious affiliation and cultural diversity” are off-limits. 21 is the minimum age, and an agency that breaches it loses its license automatically, pays a fine, and must refund every peso within 30 days without being asked.

And a set of funds and services: an Emergency Repatriation Fund that may never fall below ₱10 million, a Legal Assistance Fund never below ₱5 million, a help desk in every Philippine labour office where the region's workers are, free legal aid including Shari'ah counselling, a reintegration program, and a mental health and psychosocial support program.
readings.whyProposed: Overseas work carries a great many households in this region, and the people who go are disproportionately exposed to illegal recruitment, placement-fee debt and abuse in the workplace. The act builds a regional layer on top of RA 8042 and RA 10022 — and adds protections the national framework has no reason to contain, particularly around Islamic financing and religious discrimination.
whoIsAffected: Overseas Bangsamoro Workers and their families.
Recruitment and manning agencies recruiting from or operating in the region.
Medical clinics conducting overseas employment examinations.
Insurance companies and lending institutions serving migrant workers.
Labour ministry officials and their relatives, barred from the recruitment business.
Local government units, made responsible for information dissemination.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment, with a Migration Affairs Unit
Bureau of Employment Promotion Welfare — accreditation, licensing, deployment permits
Overseas Workers Welfare Bureau — welfare, orientation, reintegration
Overseas Bangsamoro Workers Help Desks in Philippine Overseas Labor Offices
Ministry of Social Services and Development, on reintegration and counselling
Ministry of Health, regulating examination clinics
Local government units, on information and pre-employment orientation

funding.detail: 2 dedicated funds under the labour ministry, both initially drawn from the block grant and thereafter carried in the Bangsamoro Expenditure Program: an Emergency Repatriation Fund of ₱10,000,000 and a Legal Assistance Fund of ₱5,000,000. Each carries the same floor — the amount appropriated “shall in no case be less” than the stated figure, inclusive of outstanding balances.

whatChanges: Overseas contracts gain a wage floor pegged to Metro Manila.
Deployment costs shift decisively onto employers and agencies.
Countries and companies must clear protective tests before workers may be sent.
Placement-fee lending that violates Islamic financing becomes a prohibited act.
2 funds with statutory minimums back repatriation and legal aid.
readings.insight:
The most important thing about this act is how it became law. Parliament passed it on 17 June 2021, and it lapsed into force on 2 August 2021 *without the Chief Minister's signature*, under Article VII, Section 25(c) of the Organic Law. Of every act this registry has read, it is the only one that took effect that way. Nothing in the text explains why, and it would be wrong to guess — but the fact itself is worth recording, because it is the one visible instance of the executive declining to put its name to something Parliament had passed while also declining to send it back.

That has a small, strange consequence. Section 46 declares that “the day of signing by the Chief Minister of this Act shall be designated as 'Overseas Bangsamoro Workers Day'”. There was no signing. The act creates a commemoration and then anchors it to an event that never occurred.

On substance, 2 provisions stand out as genuinely regional rather than borrowed. The first is the treatment of debt. Placement-fee loans are the mechanism by which overseas work turns into indenture, and this act attacks them from 3 directions: granting such a loan “in violation of Islamic Financing” is a prohibited act, imposing a compulsory exclusive lender is a prohibited act, and refusing to condone or renegotiate the loan after the worker's contract collapses through no fault of their own is a prohibited act. Each carries 6 to 12 years and a fine up to ₱1 million. The second is the screen on employers: a company may not receive workers from this region if it has “a record of discriminating migrants on account of religious affiliation and cultural diversity”. For a workforce that prays 5 times a day, fasts for a month, and wears clothing that employers in some destination countries have treated as a problem, that is not an abstraction.

The act is also unusually willing to put officials at risk. Issuing a deployment permit for a country that has not cleared the guarantee test carries dismissal and 5 years' disqualification. So does violating the health examination rules. And officials of the ministry — along with their relatives to the fourth civil degree — are flatly barred from the recruitment business. In a sector where the boundary between regulator and recruiter has historically been porous, those are the clauses with teeth.

What it borrows is the punishment. Section 32 states the penalties conform to RA 10022 and adds, with unusual candour, that “should there be any amendment to the afore-cited national law, the Parliament may amend this Act”. A regional statute that must watch Manila to know what its own offences are worth is telling you something about the limits it is working inside. The same limits show in Sections 43 and 44, which purport to exempt workers from travel tax and airport fees and their remittances from documentary stamp tax — all national levies. And Sections 12 and 21 simply contradict each other on who pays the document costs, which will have to be resolved by whoever administers it.

readings.whatItDoes:
This puts 2 dates on every official document in the region, and it says which one goes first.

Memoranda, office orders and formal correspondence must carry both the Hijri and the Gregorian year, month and date — and the Hijri date leads. The reach is wider than most acts of this kind: every BARMM ministry, bureau, board, commission and corporation; every local government unit down to the barangay; and every school, private as well as public, across basic, higher and technical education.

Because a Hijri month begins when a new moon is actually sighted, someone has to look. The act gives that job to the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', which performs moon-sighting on the 29th day of each Hijri month and exchanges observations with nearby Southeast Asian Muslim countries. It gets ₱10 million to start, and a wider remit alongside — issuing fatwa, advising the Chief Minister on religious affairs, and leading intrareligious and interreligious dialogue.
readings.whyProposed: The stated policy is cultural self-governance under the Organic Law: recognizing the primacy of the predominant way of life in the region, while — the same sentence is careful about this — encouraging all-inclusive understanding, coexistence and harmony at every level of governance. Among its objectives is fulfilling equally the declaration of Islamic holidays already recognized under the national Code on Muslim Personal Laws.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, bureau, office, commission, administration, board, committee, institute and corporation of the BARMM, whether it performs a governmental or a proprietary function.
Every provincial, city, municipal and barangay local government unit in the region.
Every school in the region — private ones expressly included — across basic, higher and technical education.
Anyone who files, receives or reads official correspondence in the region.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, which implements the law
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', through which the OCM acts, and which performs the monthly moon-sighting

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 initial funding for the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', drawn from any available funds of the Bangsamoro Government, with subsequent years carried in the agency's regular budget subject to the usual accounting and audit rules.

whatChanges: Official documents carry 2 calendars instead of one, with the Hijri date first.
The duty reaches private schools — unusual for a Bangsamoro act, most of which bind government only.
The Hijri date becomes an administrative fact with an office responsible for determining it, rather than a matter of local practice.
The Darul-Ifta' is funded and given a defined role in regional governance, not only in religious affairs.
readings.insight:
The ordering is the substance. Requiring both calendars is a gesture toward plurality; requiring the Hijri first is a statement about whose reckoning of time is primary in the region. The act says as much in its policy section — the primacy of the predominant way of life — and then, in the same sentence, reaches the other way toward coexistence and inclusiveness. Both claims are in the law, and the sequence of the dates is where the first one is actually enforced.

The reach into private schools is the sleeper provision. Most Bangsamoro legislation binds government to itself. Section 4 names private basic, higher and technical education alongside public, which makes this one of the few regional acts that lands directly on institutions the government does not run.

And there is no penalty anywhere in it. A mandate on thousands of offices and schools, with no sanction for ignoring it and no prescribed format for complying — which makes uptake a matter of administrative habit rather than legal risk. The most concrete thing the act actually funds is the moon-sighting: ₱10 million, and someone looking at the sky on the 29th of every month so the date on the paperwork is right.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 20, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
7 short sections that buy oxygen.

₱50 million is authorised from the 2021 Quick Response Fund on Health — the standing emergency pot, so no new appropriation was needed — and it may be spent on one thing: additional oxygen tanks. The Ministry of Finance releases it to the Ministry of Health under the usual accounting and audit rules. The tanks are to be distributed equitably among the different provinces of the BARMM, so that health facilities across the Region have a sufficient supply.

And then a section that does not usually appear in a purchase authorisation: the Ministry of Health must include the details of the fund's distribution in what it posts on its transparency seal. The act obliges the spender to publish where the money went.

It took effect immediately on publication rather than after the usual 15 days.
readings.whyProposed: The date is the reason. It passed on 24 August 2021, in the middle of the pandemic's most lethal wave, when oxygen — not beds, not staff — was the constraint that decided whether critically ill patients survived. The short title says what it is: a buffer stock.
whoIsAffected: Anyone who needed medical oxygen in a Bangsamoro health facility from late 2021 onward.
Hospitals and health facilities in every province of the region, since distribution is required to be equitable across provinces.
The Ministry of Health, which receives, spends and must publish.
Taxpayers, whose emergency health reserve funded it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health (MOH), which acquires and distributes the tanks and publishes the distribution
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management (MFBM), which releases the fund

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 charged against the 2021 Quick Response Fund on Health of the Bangsamoro Government. No new appropriation was made — the money came from the emergency reserve, which is why the act could move as fast as it did.

whatChanges: Health facilities across the region gained a stock of oxygen tanks during the worst of the pandemic.
Distribution was required to reach every province rather than concentrate where the largest hospitals are.
The spending ministry was placed under an express duty to publish how the money was divided.
readings.insight:
Section 5 is the part worth noticing, because it is the part that did not have to be there. An emergency purchase authorisation can simply hand over the money; this one requires the Ministry of Health to post the distribution details on its transparency seal. In a ₱50 million buy of a scarce commodity during a crisis — precisely the conditions under which procurement goes wrong — Parliament wrote the disclosure into the authorising act rather than leaving it to general audit rules.

The weakness sits 1 section earlier. 'Equitably distributed' carries the whole distributive policy of the act and is left undefined: no formula, no per-province allocation, no weighting by population or case load, and no requirement to publish the basis on which equity was judged. Combined with Section 5, that produces a law that requires you to be told where the tanks went but not why they went there.

And, as with much emergency legislation, there is no deadline and no report-back. The act authorises a purchase, names a disclosure, and stops — leaving the question of whether the buffer stock still exists, or was ever fully bought, outside the reach of the document itself.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 21, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the largest single appropriation in the registry: ₱10 billion, ₱5 billion from the 2020 Special Development Fund and ₱5 billion from the 2021, for the rebuilding, rehabilitation and development of conflict-affected communities in the Bangsamoro. Spending has to follow the Bangsamoro Development Plan 2020–2022, and money is released by the finance ministry direct to implementing ministries on the Chief Minister's approval.

What is remarkable is everything the act attaches to the money.

Section 4 controls where and how you may build: not in critical geo-hazard areas or no-build zones; to construction standards that account for structural strength and climate resilience; and inside protected areas, major infrastructure only if the project is intended to enhance biodiversity.

Section 5 controls what the public is told. Within 30 days of signing a contract, the implementing ministry must post on its website the project title and description, the detailed estimates behind the approved budget, the winning contractor and the bid as awarded. Within 30 days of a completion certificate, the detailed actual cost and every variation order. Ministers, heads of office and web administrators are named as responsible for compliance.

Section 6 controls the reporting: quarterly financial and physical accomplishment reports, monthly financial reports by the tenth of the following month, through 3 channels each — and failure suspends the responsible official's salary until they comply.

And Section 8 puts the chairperson of the Bangsamoro Women Commission on the fund's Technical Working Group as of right, to keep the program gender-responsive.
readings.whyProposed: Section 2, Article XIV of the Organic Law provides the region a Special Development Fund. This act turns 2 years of that entitlement into an appropriation and points it at the communities the conflict damaged most.
whoIsAffected: Conflict-affected communities across the region — the fund's stated beneficiaries.
Contractors, whose winning bids, final costs and variation orders become public documents.
Ministers, heads of office and web administrators, personally named as responsible for the postings.
Women in those communities, through the Women Commission's guaranteed seat on the programming group.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which releases funds and issues guidelines
Implementing ministries and offices, which build, post and report
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, which reviews the program against the Development Plan and serves as TWG Secretariat
Special Development Fund Technical Working Group, chaired by the Senior Minister
Bangsamoro Women Commission, ex officio on the TWG
Ministries of Environment and of Public Works, on siting and construction standards

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000,000 in total — ₱5 billion as the 2020 Special Development Fund and ₱5 billion as the 2021 fund, under Section 2, Article XIV of the Organic Law. Releases go directly to implementing ministries on a Special Budget Request approved by the Chief Minister.

whatChanges: ₱10 billion is committed to conflict-affected communities under a published development plan.
Infrastructure siting is constrained by hazard, climate and biodiversity conditions.
Contract awards and final costs become mandatory website disclosures with named officials responsible.
Monthly and quarterly reporting is imposed, backed by salary suspension.
Gender-responsiveness is built into the programming body rather than left to policy.
readings.insight:
This act deserves to be read before any of the region's later budget legislation, because most of the accountability machinery that appears elsewhere starts here. The quarterly reports with automatic salary suspension that make BAA 33 notable in December 2022 are already in Section 6 of this act in October 2021, alongside a monthly reporting duty that BAA 33 does not carry. The lesson is that the region's transparency instruments were written early and attached first to its largest pot of money.

Section 5 is the strongest procurement disclosure requirement found anywhere in this registry, and it is worth being precise about why. It does not merely require a project list. It requires the estimates behind the approved budget, the winning contractor, the bid as awarded, the detailed *actual* cost, and every variation order — which is to say, exactly the 4 documents you would need to see whether a contract was padded, whether the winner was cheap, and whether the price rose after award. Variation orders in particular are where infrastructure spending quietly inflates, and this act puts them on the internet within 30 days of completion.

2 cautions belong alongside that. Section 7 permits changes to project scope, location, beneficiaries and implementation period after approval, subject to endorsement and the Chief Minister's approval — so the disclosed project and the delivered project need not be the same thing. And the spending discipline in Section 3 did not hold: BAA 34 extended it, and BAA 51 removed the disbursement deadline for this fund altogether. The obligations to publish and report were written to run alongside a hard cash-budgeting deadline that no longer exists.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 22, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's budget for 2022 — ₱79,862,015,000.00 — and the first one to say out loud that part of it is money the government already had and did not spend.

Section 1 draws on the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes collected inside its territory, projected collections on its own taxes and fees, and “unused/unutilized appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury”. That last phrase is new, and every budget after this one keeps a version of it.

The government has grown. There are now 11 other executive offices funded alongside the 17 ministries, up from 6 the year before — the Sports Commission, the Pilgrimage Authority, the Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Cooperatives and Social Enterprise Authority and the Development Academy of the Bangsamoro all appear for the first time. So do 2 special purpose funds that matter to anyone outside the bureaucracy: a Special Development Fund of ₱5,000,000,000 for conflict-affected communities, and a Local Government Support Fund of ₱1,394,016,000.

The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱3,558,163,162, about 4.5% of the total.

The last 19 pages carry 71 sections of general provisions. Personnel Services across government may not exceed 45% of total revenue. At least 5% of every ministry's budget must go to a Gender and Development Plan. Deductions may never reduce an employee's monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000. Rainwater collection systems are required in public markets, schools and government buildings — and may never be built on private lots. Infrastructure contracts, winning bidders and final costs must be published within 30 days, and officials who miss their quarterly reports have their salaries suspended automatically.

One provision is entirely new. Section 27 directs every ministry and office to work toward “the full integration and mainstreaming of Islamic or Shari'ah compliant finance within their services and activities”, and tells the Chief Minister to issue guidelines and stand up a body to check that products and services actually comply. It has appeared in every Bangsamoro budget since.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Government needs an annual appropriations act to function. This was the last budget of the first Bangsamoro Transition Authority, whose term the National Government had extended to 2025, and it was passed and signed on the same day — 28 December 2021 — 3 days before it took effect.
whoIsAffected: Everyone in the region served by a Bangsamoro Government program.
Constituent local government units, through the new ₱1.39 billion support fund and their income tax share.
Conflict-affected communities, through the ₱5 billion Special Development Fund.
All government personnel, whose allowances, bonuses and pay floor this fixes.
The 5 commissions and offices funded here for the first time.
Women's programs, guaranteed a 5% share of every ministry budget.
implementedBy: All 17 ministries, the 11 other executive offices and the special purpose funds
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, administering releases and issuing guidelines
Office of the Chief Minister, clearing foreign travel and issuing Islamic finance guidelines
Technical Working Group on Islamic Finance, recommending those guidelines
Bangsamoro Women Commission, on gender and development plans
Commission on Audit, as external auditor

funding.detail: ₱79,862,015,000.00 for fiscal year 2022, from the annual block grant and other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territorial jurisdiction, unused or unutilized appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources.

whatChanges: ₱79.86 billion is appropriated for 2022, partly from unused appropriations sitting in the Treasury.
A ₱5 billion Special Development Fund and a ₱1.39 billion Local Government Support Fund appear as budget lines for the first time.
5 more commissions and offices are funded, taking the count from 6 to 11.
Every ministry is directed to mainstream Islamic and Shari'ah-compliant finance.
The constituent LGUs' share of income taxes gets a year longer to be spent than anything else.
Personnel costs are held to 45% of revenue and gender programs floored at 5% of every budget.
readings.insight:
The phrase to notice in Section 1 is “unused/unutilized appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury”. Until this act, the region's budgets were funded from money it expected to receive. From here on they are funded partly from money it already received and did not manage to spend. The wording broadens again in FY 2023 to “unutilized prior years' appropriations”, and again in FY 2024 to add “unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury”. Read alongside the extension acts — BAA 14, BAA 24, BAA 33, BAA 52, each of which pushed an expiring budget's validity out by a year — and alongside the supplemental acts of 2024, 2025 and 2026, which re-appropriate ₱36.57 billion of previously unspent money between them, the pattern is consistent: the Bangsamoro Government has been appropriating faster than it can disburse for its entire existence, and its budget laws have gradually been rewritten to make that legal rather than exceptional.

Section 48 shows the same thing in miniature. Everything in this act expires on 31 December 2022 — except the constituent LGUs' share of income taxes, which gets until 31 December 2023. It is the first time a Bangsamoro budget carves out a class of money that outlives the rest, and the carve-out grows each year afterward until, in FY 2025, the LGU share stops lapsing altogether.

Section 49 is worth reading twice. It is headed “Retention or Deduction of Funds” and consists of a single sentence saying that fund releases shall be transmitted to the ministry concerned. The FY 2020 and FY 2021 acts headed the same section “Prohibition Against Retention or Deduction of Funds”, with the same single sentence and no actual prohibition; here even the word “Prohibition” is dropped. A sentence forbidding retention or deduction as reserves or overhead does not appear in any Bangsamoro budget until FY 2025.

The Contingent Fund keeps its familiar contents — ₱2.4 billion earmarked for a Transitional Development Impact Fund, money for COVID-19 vaccines and protective gear, and once again a “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs”, the third consecutive budget to make room for that purchase. Section 27, mainstreaming Islamic finance across the whole government, arrives in the same act. The 2 sit oddly together: an ambitious policy direction in the general provisions, and a line in a contingency fund for a bank the government has been trying to buy since 2020.

readings.whatItDoes:
This extends 2 budgets at once. Money appropriated in the 2020 Bangsamoro budget and money appropriated in the 2021 budget both stayed usable until 31 December 2022, for the purposes they were granted for and under the same conditions.

Infrastructure gets a longer tail. Capital outlays from either year could be obligated to the end of 2022 and then delivered, inspected and paid up to 30 June 2023 — recognizing that a road contracted in December is not finished in December.

Personnel Services is excluded from both, exactly as in the earlier extension: 2020 salary money died at the end of 2020, 2021 salary money at the end of 2021.
readings.whyProposed: 2 budget years were about to lapse with work still unfinished, in a government whose delivery machinery was still being assembled. The act was passed on 28 December 2021, 3 days before the 2021 money expired.
whoIsAffected: Communities with projects funded in either year, which did not have to be cancelled and re-appropriated.
Contractors delivering infrastructure, who gained 6 months beyond the obligation deadline to complete and be paid.
Ministries and offices holding unspent operating and capital funds.
Government employees, for whom nothing changed.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management (MFBM), authorised to issue implementing guidelines under both amended sections

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amount stated. The act extends the availability of money already granted by BAA 3 for FY2020 and BAA 15 for FY2021.

whatChanges: 2 budget years stayed obligable through 2022 instead of lapsing.
Infrastructure gained a payment window to 30 June 2023.
Salary appropriations expired on their original dates in both years.
readings.insight:
The significant fact is that this is the 2020 budget's second extension. BAA 14, passed in December 2020, had already carried it to the end of 2021; this act carries it again to the end of 2022, and lets infrastructure payments run to mid-2023. Money appropriated for the region's first full budget year was still being spent nearly 3 years later.

That is not necessarily waste — a new government building roads and health centers from a standing start will miss annual deadlines, and repeated extension is more honest than a fictional lapse followed by fresh appropriation. But it does mean the annual budget was not, in practice, an annual limit, and a reader trying to work out what the region actually spent in a given year cannot do it from that year's appropriations act alone.

The constant across every act in the series is the treatment of salaries. Personnel Services is never extended. Unfilled posts are the easiest surplus in any government budget, and refusing to let that money roll forward is the one piece of budget discipline these extension acts consistently keep.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 24, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes a 10-bed district hospital and authorises it to become a 100-bed one, moving it from Level I to Level II under the national standards the Department of Health's Bureau of Health Facilities and Services sets.

The upgrade is not only the beds. Section 3 sweeps in the existing buildings and their landscaping, the medical and office equipment, the other facilities, the operating funds and the personnel — all of them upgraded to include whatever construction and procurement is needed to reach the prescribed standard. The hospital must also integrate the national Universal Health Care Act into how it operates, and it sits under the administrative supervision of the Ministry of Health, which sets its organizational structure.

Funding comes from the Bangsamoro General Appropriations, and the Ministry of Health had 60 days from enactment to issue implementing rules.
readings.whyProposed: Section 22, Article IX of the Organic Law requires the region to provide comprehensive and integrated health service delivery and to establish a general hospital system by law. The policy section puts the purpose plainly: the individual's basic right to life should be attainable through prompt intervention of excellent and affordable medical services — which a 10-bed facility cannot deliver.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Datu Blah Sinsuat and the surrounding parts of Maguindanao.
Patients previously referred out of the area for services a Level II hospital can provide.
Hospital staff, whose establishment and funding are upgraded with the facility.
PhilHealth members, through the required integration of the Universal Health Care Act.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health – BARMM, which supervises the hospital, approves its organizational structure and was to issue implementing rules within 60 days
Bureau of Health Facilities and Services, Department of Health, whose national standards define what Level II requires

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Funding is appropriated from the Bangsamoro General Appropriations for construction, medical and office equipment, and the annual budget for personnel services, maintenance and operations — and thereafter 'such amount as may be needed' for continued operations. The cost of a tenfold capacity increase is left to the annual budget process.

whatChanges: A 10-bed facility is authorised at 100 beds.
Level I becomes Level II, which is a change in what can be treated rather than only in scale.
Staff, equipment and operating funds are upgraded alongside the building.
Universal Health Care provisions are pulled into the hospital's operations.
readings.insight:
The gap between authorisation and delivery is the thing to watch. This act does not build a hospital; it makes it lawful to have one, and then sends the cost to a general appropriations line with no figure, no schedule and no completion date. A tenfold increase in capacity — 10 beds to 100, plus the construction, equipment and staff that Level II standards require — is a substantial capital program, and the act commits to it in the words 'such amount as may be needed'.

That is not unusual drafting, and it may be the only practicable way for a transition government to legislate a hospital network. But it means the operative question for a resident is not what this act says; it is what appears in each year's budget afterwards. The act creates the entitlement to ask.

One small marker of where the region came from: the repealing clause reaches back to laws passed under the defunct ARMM governing this same hospital. The building predates the government now upgrading it.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 25, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This doubles the Wao District Hospital in Lanao del Sur from 25 authorised beds to 50, and upgrades the building, its landscaping, the medical and office equipment, the operating funds and the personnel to match — including whatever construction and procurement the national standards require at the larger size.

What it does not do is change the level. Wao stays a Level 1 hospital. It is the one act in the June 2022 hospital cluster that adds capacity without adding capability.
readings.whyProposed: The same clause of the Organic Law that carries the rest of the region's hospital legislation — Section 22, Article IX, on comprehensive and integrated health service delivery and a general hospital system established by law.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Wao and the surrounding parts of Lanao del Sur.
Patients turned away or held for want of a bed.
Hospital staff, whose establishment and funding are upgraded with the facility.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health – BARMM, which supervises the hospital and was to issue implementing rules within 60 days
Bureau of Health Facilities and Services, Department of Health, whose standards define Level 1 requirements

funding.detail: No amount stated. Funding is appropriated from the Bangsamoro General Appropriations for infrastructure, medical and office equipment, and the annual budget for personnel services, maintenance and operations.

whatChanges: Authorised capacity doubles from 25 beds to 50.
Staff, equipment and operating funds are upgraded alongside.
Universal Health Care provisions are integrated into operations.
The service level is unchanged — Level 1 before and after.
readings.insight:
Read against its siblings, this act is the modest one. Datu Blah Sinsuat went from 10 beds to 100 and from Level I to Level II on the same day; Wao goes from 25 to 50 and stays where it is. Whether that reflects a considered judgement about what Wao's catchment needs, or simply what was asked for, the act does not say — none of these hospital acts carries a needs assessment or a population figure.

That is the structural weakness of legislating a hospital network one building at a time. Each act is drafted around a single facility, names no amount, sets no deadline, and is silent on how its target capacity was arrived at. The result is a network shaped by which measures were filed rather than by where the beds are most needed — and nothing in the text lets a reader test that either way.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 26, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a hospital where there was none: a Level II district hospital with 100 beds in the municipality of Maimbung, Sulu.

It is run differently from the region's other new hospitals. Rather than reporting to the regional Ministry of Health, it sits under the direct administrative and technical supervision of the Integrated Provincial Health Office of Sulu. The regional ministry's role is narrower — its Regulation and Licensing Enforcement Division must bring the operational guidelines for a 100-bed Level II facility into the ministry's program, and it receives an annual operational plan from the hospital chief setting out programs, projects, activities and budgetary needs.

Growth is put on a planning footing too: any future increase in beds or upgrade of services has to rest on an annual hospital development plan prepared with IPHO-Sulu. Salaries and running costs go into the Bangsamoro's annual appropriations act.
readings.whyProposed: To put Level II services inside Maimbung rather than at the end of a journey, and to do it through Sulu's existing provincial health structure.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Maimbung and the surrounding municipalities of Sulu.
Patients who would otherwise travel for services a Level II hospital provides.
The Integrated Provincial Health Office – Sulu, which takes on supervision of a new 100-bed facility.
MOH-BARMM, which sets guidelines and receives annual plans.
implementedBy: Integrated Provincial Health Office – Sulu, with direct administrative and technical supervision
Ministry of Health – BARMM, through the Regulation and Licensing Enforcement Division
The Chief of Maimbung District Hospital, who submits the annual operational plan

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Personnel Services and Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses are to be included in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. The act funds the running of the hospital and is silent on the capital cost of building it.

whatChanges: A Level II hospital with 100 beds exists in law in Maimbung.
Supervision runs through the provincial health office rather than the regional ministry.
The hospital must produce an annual operational plan and, for any expansion, a hospital development plan.
Level II operational guidelines enter the regional ministry's program.
readings.insight:
The supervision arrangement is what distinguishes this from the rest of the June 2022 cluster. Datu Blah Sinsuat and Wao were placed under the regional Ministry of Health; Maimbung is placed under Sulu's own provincial health office, with the ministry keeping only the licensing standard and the annual plan. That is a meaningfully different model of health governance — provincial delivery with regional standard-setting — enacted without any statement in the act about why this facility takes that route and the others do not.

The planning requirements are the strongest feature. Most of these hospital acts simply authorise a capacity and stop; this one requires an annual operational plan naming programs, projects, activities and budgetary needs, and makes any future expansion contingent on a development plan. That is a document trail a citizen or a journalist can actually ask for.

What is missing is the building. Section 3 funds salaries and operating expenses. Nothing in the act appropriates construction, sets a completion date, or says what happens in the interval between the hospital existing in law and existing in Maimbung.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 27, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This doubles Sulu's provincial hospital — 100 beds to 200 — and lifts it to Level II, with the professional services, staffing complements and facilities upgraded to the national Department of Health standard behind it.

2 things set it apart from the other hospital acts passed the same week. First, Section 3 does not merely say personnel are upgraded; it directs the health ministry's Regulation and Licensing Enforcement Division, working with the finance ministry, to determine the additional plantilla positions to be created and filled — actual permanent posts, on the hospital administration's own recommendation.

Second, Section 5 sets a schedule. The budget is apportioned in 3 tranches starting in calendar year 2022: 40%, then 30%, then 30%. That is a delivery timetable, and almost none of these acts have one.
readings.whyProposed: Sulu's provincial hospital is the referral point for an island province where onward travel is a sea journey. Raising it to Level II keeps care that would otherwise leave the province inside it.
whoIsAffected: Residents across Sulu, for whom this is the main hospital.
Patients who would otherwise travel off-island for Level II services.
Health workers, through the additional plantilla positions the act requires to be determined and filled.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health – BARMM, with direct supervision and control, and whose Minister issues implementing orders in consultation with hospital management
Regulation and Licensing Enforcement Division, MOH-BARMM, with the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, on operational guidelines and plantilla positions
Sulu Provincial Hospital administration, which recommends the positions

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Personnel Services and MOOE go into the annual General Appropriations Act, apportioned in 3 tranches from calendar year 2022 at 40%, 30% and 30%. The percentages are precise; the sum they are percentages of is not given.

whatChanges: Bed capacity doubles to 200 at Level II classification.
New permanent health posts are to be determined and filled, not merely promised.
Funding follows a stated 3-year schedule rather than an open-ended appropriation.
The Minister must consult hospital management when issuing implementing rules.
readings.insight:
The tranche schedule is the most useful sentence in the whole June 2022 hospital cluster, and it is worth understanding exactly what it does and does not give you. It answers the question these acts otherwise leave hanging — when? — by committing to 3 years starting in 2022, front-loaded at 40%. Against a set of laws that mostly say 'such amount as may be needed', that is a real advance in accountability.

But the percentages float free of any number. 40% of an unstated total is not a figure anyone can hold the government to; it becomes one only when the first Bangsamoro appropriations act after 2022 puts a peso value on the line. So the schedule tells you the shape of the commitment and the budget tells you its size, and you need both documents to know whether the hospital is being built.

The plantilla clause is the other thing to watch. A hospital doubling its beds needs staff more than it needs walls, and this act is one of the few that treats posts as something to be created by name rather than assumed to follow.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 28, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
Buluan's district hospital goes from Level I to Level II and from 75 beds to 150. The facilities and professional services are upgraded to be commensurate with that, and the act says plainly that the number of medical personnel shall be correspondingly increased.

What makes this the most operationally serious of the June 2022 hospital acts is where it puts the money. Like the Sulu act, it sets 3 tranches from calendar year 2022 — 40%, 30%, 30%. But it goes one step further: Section 5 directs the Ministry of Health to include the initial implementation in its 2022 programs straight away, with that funding chargeable to available appropriations under the Contingent Funds.

Construction and upgrading sit under the direct supervision and control of the regional health ministry.
readings.whyProposed: The same Organic Law duty to build a general hospital system, applied to a district facility whose catchment had outgrown a 75-bed Level I.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Buluan and the surrounding parts of Maguindanao.
Patients referred elsewhere for services a Level II hospital can provide.
Medical personnel, whose numbers the act requires to be increased.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health – BARMM, which supervises and controls both the hospital and the construction, and must program the initial implementation for 2022

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Personnel Services and MOOE go into the annual General Appropriations Act in 3 tranches from 2022 at 40%, 30% and 30%. Initial implementation may be charged to available appropriations under the Contingent Funds — a source that exists now rather than a line in a future budget.

whatChanges: Level I becomes Level II; 75 beds become 150.
Medical personnel are required to increase alongside.
A funding schedule and an immediate funding source are both named.
Construction is placed under direct ministry supervision rather than left unassigned.
readings.insight:
Compare the 3 Maguindanao and Sulu hospital acts passed within a week of each other and you can watch the drafting improve in real time. Datu Blah Sinsuat (BAA 25) authorises a tenfold expansion against 'such amount as may be needed'. Sulu Provincial (BAA 28) adds a 3-tranche schedule. This one adds the schedule and then answers the question the schedule leaves open — what happens before the first budget cycle — by pointing at the Contingent Funds.

That is the difference between a law that permits a hospital to grow and a law that starts it growing. It is still permissive: funding 'may be charged' to Contingent Funds, not must. But naming an existing pot rather than a future appropriation is what lets work begin in the year the act passes.

What none of them do is say when it is finished. There is no completion date anywhere in the cluster, no reporting duty, and no consequence for a tranche that goes unreleased — so the schedule tells a citizen what to ask about, and the annual budget documents remain the only place the answer can be found.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 29, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes a 10-bed municipal hospital in Binidayan and makes it a 50-bed district hospital, renamed the Unayan District Hospital. The reclassification matters as much as the beds: a district hospital answers for a catchment wider than the municipality it sits in.

As with the other upgrading acts in this cluster, the whole facility comes with it — buildings and their landscaping, medical and office equipment, other facilities, operating funds and personnel, all upgraded to include the construction and procurement needed to meet the prescribed standard. The hospital must integrate the national Universal Health Care Act, sits under the Ministry of Health's administrative supervision, and the Ministry had 60 days to issue implementing rules.
readings.whyProposed: Section 22, Article IX of the Organic Law: comprehensive and integrated health service delivery, a general hospital system established by law, and the basic right to life made attainable through prompt intervention of excellent and affordable medical services.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Binidayan and the wider Unayan area of Lanao del Sur.
Patients whose local option was a 10-bed facility.
Hospital staff, whose establishment and funding are upgraded.
PhilHealth members, through the required Universal Health Care integration.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health – BARMM, which supervises the hospital, approves its organizational structure, and was to issue implementing rules within 60 days

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Funding is appropriated from the Bangsamoro General Appropriations for infrastructure, medical and office equipment and the annual operating budget, and thereafter 'such amount as may be needed'.

whatChanges: 10 authorised beds become 50.
Municipal classification becomes district classification, widening the catchment it serves.
The facility is renamed the Unayan District Hospital.
Staff, equipment and operating funds are upgraded alongside.
readings.insight:
This act closes the June 2022 hospital cluster and, oddly, closes it by reverting. Passed 5 days after Sulu Provincial and Buluan — both of which carried 3-tranche funding schedules, and Buluan a named Contingent Fund source — Unayan goes back to 'such amount as may be needed', with no schedule, no starting source and no deadline.

So within a single week Parliament produced 2 versions of the same instrument: one that says when the money arrives and one that does not. Nothing in either text explains the difference. For a reader trying to judge which of these hospitals is likely to be built, that drafting choice is more informative than any of the capacity figures.

The renaming is worth noting for a practical reason. Records, referrals and signage under 'Unayan Municipal Hospital' refer to a facility the law now calls the Unayan District Hospital, and the act sets no transition arrangements for the change of name.
