readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a board to decide how the region uses what is under its ground and in its waters — and, unusually, it is a joint body. The Senior Minister chairs it; a National Government official co-chairs it; up to 6 national representatives sit alongside the regional environment, interior and finance ministers, the planning authority, the chair of Parliament's environment committee, and one representative elected by recognized NGOs.

Section 3 sets out the framework it must formulate, and the drafting there is unlike anything else in the registry. The governing principle is Moral Governance, defined in the text as rules and processes 'completely devoid of all the evils of graft and corruption'. Beneath it sit 4 principles, the first of which is Environmental Vicegerency — invoking *Khalifa*, the trusteeship and stewardship of the earth — alongside Social Justice and Well-Being, Respect to Culture, Belief and Heritage, and Economic Progress with Equity.

And Section 10 does something concrete. Not less than 1% of all revenues collected from the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources in the Bangsamoro is allocated to run the Board — and that amount shall not be deducted from the block grant the region receives under the Organic Law.

Section 11 requires the Board to review the act's own implementation after 5 years and every 5 years after, with Parliament part of the process.
readings.whyProposed: To put economic, social and environmental considerations into a single framework before the region's resources are developed, rather than after — and to do it jointly with the National Government, which retains substantial authority over natural resources.
whoIsAffected: Communities where natural resources are explored, developed or extracted.
Women and marginalised groups, whose climate vulnerability the Board must address by name.
Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, whose rights the policy section recognizes within the framework of the Constitution and national laws.
Recognized NGOs, which elect a member of the Board.
Settler communities, children and youth, all named in the framework's social justice principle.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sustainable Development Board
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, which serves as the regional secretariat
National Government, which organizes and funds its own secretariat and representation
Bangsamoro Parliament, part of the mandatory 5-year review

funding.detail: Initial funding from the Contingent Fund of the 2022 budget, then the MENRE's regular budget, plus not less than 1% of revenues collected from natural resource exploration, development and utilization in the region — expressly excluded from the amount deducted from the block grant under Section 21, Article XII of the Organic Law. The National Government bears its own secretariat costs. No peso figure is stated.

whatChanges: The region gains a framework for sustainable development, formulated jointly with the National Government.
Environmental governance acquires a dedicated funding stream tied to resource revenues.
Women's and marginalised groups' climate vulnerability becomes an express duty of the Board.
Civil society gains an elected seat.
The act builds in its own 5-yearly review, with Parliament involved.
readings.insight:
The clause worth reading twice is the one about the block grant. Earmarking 1% of resource revenues for environmental governance is a reasonable idea that could be entirely undone by arithmetic: the region funds the Board from resource revenue, and the National Government reduces the block grant by the same amount, leaving the Bangsamoro exactly where it started and the Board funded out of its own pocket. Section 10 forecloses that in a single proviso. Whoever drafted it understood that in a fiscal relationship as intricate as this one, the money matters less than where it is counted.

The framework in Section 3 is the other thing that sets this act apart. Most legislation states its principles in the vocabulary of administration; this one states them in the vocabulary of trusteeship, and grounds environmental duty in *Khalifa* — stewardship of the earth on behalf of God. That is a genuine attempt to write a development framework in terms the region's own population would recognize as binding, rather than in borrowed language from an international convention. It sits beside Moral Governance, which is defined as the absence of graft — an anti-corruption principle stated as the compass for everything else.

What the act does not give the Board is teeth. It formulates, promotes, calls upon, monitors and reviews. It does not license, does not inspect, does not sanction. So the 1% funds a body whose influence over an actual extraction project runs entirely through the policies it writes and the ministries that apply them — and, as with the flag and the calendar acts, the duty is stated without a consequence attached. One small marker of the same looseness: the signed copy carries the Chief Minister's signature above a blank date line, the second act in this registry found in that condition.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region's budget for 2023 — ₱85,359,315,687.00, drawn from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes collected inside its territory, unutilized prior years' appropriations sitting in the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on its own taxes and fees. The published volume carries a theme on its cover: “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”.

It funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 5 special purpose funds. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱3,939,145,853, about 4.6% of the total. The Special Development Fund holds steady at ₱5,000,000,000, the Local Government Support Fund grows to ₱2,297,491,000, and the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund jumps to ₱2,615,269,253 — nearly 4 times what it was the year before.

The last 24 pages carry 73 sections of general provisions, and 3 of them are new and genuinely consequential.

Section 18 requires every ministry to buy its common-use supplies through the Procurement Service rather than on its own. Section 21 caps engineering and administrative overhead at 1% of project funds, and only for infrastructure costing more than ₱1,000,000. And Section 50 closes a gap that had been open since the first budget: money transferred from one agency to another, or out to a local government, is no longer “disbursed” at the moment of transfer. It counts only when it has “actually been utilized to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period”.

The familiar rules carry over. Personnel Services across government may not exceed 45% of total revenue. At least 5% of every ministry's budget goes to a Gender and Development Plan. Deductions may never reduce an employee's monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000. Infrastructure contracts, winning bidders and final costs must be published within 30 days, and officials who miss their quarterly reports have their salaries suspended automatically until they comply.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Government needs an annual appropriations act to function. This was the first budget of the Parliament reconstituted after the transition period was extended, sitting in a First Regular Session begun on 15 September 2022. It was passed on 20 December 2022 and signed by the Chief Minister on 22 December, 9 days before it took effect.
whoIsAffected: Everyone in the region served by a Bangsamoro Government program.
Constituent local government units, through a ₱2.30 billion support fund.
Conflict-affected communities, through the ₱5 billion Special Development Fund.
All government personnel, whose allowances, honoraria and pay floor this fixes.
Contractors, through the 1% overhead cap and the tightened definition of disbursement.
Women's programs, guaranteed a 5% share of every ministry budget.
implementedBy: All 17 ministries, the 11 other executive offices and the special purpose funds
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, administering releases and issuing guidelines
Procurement Service, supplying common-use goods to all ministries
Ministry of Public Works, setting infrastructure standards
Bangsamoro Women Commission, on gender and development plans
Commission on Audit, as external auditor

funding.detail: ₱85,359,315,687.00 for fiscal year 2023, from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territorial jurisdiction, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources.

whatChanges: ₱85.36 billion is appropriated for 2023 under the theme “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”.
Transferring money to another agency or a local government no longer counts as spending it.
Engineering and administrative overhead is capped at 1% on projects over ₱1,000,000.
Common-use supplies must be bought through the Procurement Service.
Honoraria are limited to a defined list, capped at 25% of annual basic salary for special projects.
The Local Government Support Fund rises to ₱2.30 billion and the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund to ₱2.62 billion.
readings.insight:
The theme printed on the cover is “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”, and for once the general provisions bear the slogan out — but the optimisation is aimed inward, at the government's own accounting.

Section 50 is the change that matters. Since the first budget, a ministry could move money to another agency or to a local government and treat it as disbursed. From this act on it cannot: the transfer counts only when the money has “actually been utilized to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period”. That single sentence turns a paper transfer into a real one, and it is the sort of provision that only gets written after somebody has noticed the reported disbursement rate and the delivered-project rate diverging. Section 21's new 1% ceiling on engineering and administrative overhead, and Section 18's requirement to buy common-use supplies through the Procurement Service rather than agency by agency, point the same way.

Parliament's own line is where the tension sits. Of the ₱3,093,405,532 in its Operations budget, the act itemises ₱1,026,816,000 for Representations/Constituency Building, ₱267,840,000 for Special Legislature Activities, ₱120,000,000 for Community Upliftment and ₱104,544,000 for Oversight, against ₱364,640,000 labeled Legislation — with ₱1,159,565,532 of Personnel Services left undistributed across all of them. The categories that are not lawmaking outweigh the one that is, in the itemised portion, by roughly 4 to 1. Constituency service is real work and every legislature funds it, but a budget themed on optimisation itemising its own representation line 4 times larger than its legislation line is a proportion worth stating plainly.

The Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund nearly quadruples, from ₱663,300,922.35 to ₱2,615,269,253 — a fund for salary deficiencies and positions in offices not yet filled, growing much faster than the budget as a whole. And Section 51, headed “Retention or Deduction of Funds”, still contains no sentence forbidding retention or deduction; that sentence does not enter a Bangsamoro budget until FY 2025.

Section 44 keeps the provision that has run unchanged since the first budget: hazard duty pay only for personnel in “strife-torn or embattled areas as may be determined and certified by the Secretary of National Defense”. This is the last budget to carry it. From FY 2024 the provision simply disappears, with no repealing clause and no explanation.
deliberation: 20 December 2022: MP Jose I. Lorena asked whether ₱85,000,000,000 was the whole fiscal space; sponsor MP Ubaida C. Pacasem said it covers the block grant, tax shares, local taxes and 2020 and 2021 savings, but not projected 2022 savings.

20 December 2022: MP Jose I. Lorena worried that extending older appropriations prolongs projects and asked about the organic law’s preference for local residents; MP Ubaida C. Pacasem pointed to procurement-law provisions in the budget since 2020.

20 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan argued Section 58 lets ministries modify allotments the Parliament approved; MP Ubaida C. Pacasem replied the rule was taken from the national budget and only shifts activities within a program.

20 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan noted ministries’ accomplishment stood at 30% from January to October and sought a mid-year review by the finance committee; MP Ubaida C. Pacasem said oversight needs no special provision and cited election, plebiscite and reappointment bans.

20 December 2022: MP Benjamin T. Loong asked to insert ₱100,000,000 for tractors from the ₱2,000,000,000 Special Purpose Fund or ₱6,000,000,000 Contingent Fund; MP Ubaida C. Pacasem declined, saying those funds are earmarked.

20 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan called the MOOE-to-Capital Outlay modification a technical malversation and moved to delete it and add semi-annual review; on division of the house it lost, 17 in favor, 22 against, 3 abstentions.
20 December 2022: Nominal vote: 45 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third and final reading, 20 December 2022; 45 in favor, none against, no abstention.

20 December 2022: Nominal vote: 17 in favor, 22 against, 3 abstentions. Division of the house by show of hands on MP Baintan A. Ampatuan’s proposed amendment during the period of amendments; not approved. No names recorded.
20 December 2022: Certified urgent by the Chief Minister, approved on third and final reading the same day by nominal voting, 45 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions.

readings.whatItDoes:
2 acts in one. The first half is a budget extension of the familiar kind: most 2022 appropriations stay obligable to the end of 2023, infrastructure can be completed and paid up to 30 June 2024, other items to 31 March 2024, and Personnel Services expires on schedule at the end of 2022. It adds a clause the earlier extensions lacked — unreleased appropriations lapse, and unexpended money reverts to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation, with ministries told to strictly observe both.

The second half is about disclosure, and it is the part worth reading. Every ministry and office must file quarterly reports on its financial *and physical* accomplishments — what was spent and what was actually built — within 30 days of each quarter. Not to one place but to 4: the Unified Reporting System, a hard copy to the finance ministry, the ministry's own website, and a copy to Parliament and to the Chair of the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management.

And then a sanction that is rare in this body of law. Failure to comply results in the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they comply. Repeated refusal without justifiable cause can become an administrative disciplinary matter. The Minister or Head of Office is made personally responsible for enforcing it.
readings.whyProposed: The immediate reason is the lapse of the 2022 appropriations. But the act was passed by the second Bangsamoro Transition Authority in its first regular session, 3 months into a new mandate, and it uses the extension as the vehicle for tightening how the region accounts for money — reversion rules on one side, publication and sanction on the other.
whoIsAffected: Anyone trying to find out what the Bangsamoro Government spent and built — the reports must be posted publicly.
Every ministry and office, which acquires a 4-channel quarterly filing duty.
Ministers and heads of office, who are personally responsible for enforcing the penalty.
Officials and employees who miss a report, whose salaries stop until they file.
Constituent LGUs, whose share of income taxes collected in the region had its own extended window.
Communities and contractors with 2022-funded infrastructure.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which receives hard copies and issues implementing guidelines
Each ministry and office, which files and publishes
The Minister or Head of Office, responsible for ensuring compliance with the penalty provision
Parliament's Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, which must be furnished copies

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amount stated. The act extends money already granted by BAA 23 for FY2022 and adds reporting duties.

whatChanges: The 2022 budget runs a year longer, with staged deadlines for delivery and payment.
Unspent money now expressly lapses and reverts to a Special Fund rather than drifting.
Quarterly financial and physical reports must be published on ministry websites, not just filed.
Parliament and its finance committee must receive copies.
Missing a report suspends the responsible official's salary.
deliberation: 21 December 2022: MP Eduard U. Guerra said election-year restrictions, the reappointment of Members and the Maguindanao plebiscite cost about 5 months, and the national 2022 budget already had 2-year validity.
21 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan explained her vote by citing the 2022 elections, the Maguindanao plebiscite and the national government’s own extension of its 2022 budget.
21 December 2022: MP Abdulraof A. Macacua said he hesitated because of the many extensions already granted but voted yes in deference to the Body.

21 December 2022: Nominal vote: 54 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third reading, held on 22 December 2022 after the session resumed; 54 named in favor, none against, no abstention.
21 December 2022: Certified urgent; approved on third reading by nominal voting, 54 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions.
readings.insight:
This is the act that carries the pattern-breaking provision into the general budget. The mechanism itself is older: BAA 22, appropriating the ₱10 billion Special Development Fund in October 2021, already imposed quarterly reporting with automatic salary suspension, and a monthly financial report besides. What this act does is take that machinery, written for one large fund, and make it a general provision of the region's whole appropriations act.

Against the rest of the region's legislation the recurring weakness is the duty without a sanction — flags that must be flown, calendars that must be used, appointments that must be merit-based, all stated as obligations with nothing attached to breach. Section 67 as rewritten here does the opposite: it names the report, names the deadline, names 4 places it must go, and then stops the responsible official's pay until it arrives.

It is also the rare provision that requires *physical* accomplishment reporting alongside financial. Spending figures alone tell you money moved; a physical accomplishment report is what lets someone ask whether the road exists. Requiring both, quarterly, on a public website, is the single most useful transparency mechanism found anywhere in the acts read so far.

2 cautions. The salary suspension operates 'pursuant to Section 57, Chapter 6, Book VI of E.O. 292, as may be applicable' — so its real force depends on the national civil service framework rather than on this act standing alone. And compliance is dated from the ministry's own written notice that it has filed or posted, which makes the ministry the timekeeper of its own deadline.

readings.whatItDoes:
This keeps ₱10 billion alive. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 22 had appropriated that sum from the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund; this act rewrites its cash budgeting section so the money stayed releasable and disbursable to the end of 2023.

The deadlines are staged the way capital spending actually works: infrastructure could be obligated to 31 December 2023, with construction completed, inspected and paid by 30 June 2024; other items obligated to the same date with delivery and payment by 31 March 2024.

Unlike the general appropriations extensions, there is no carve-out for Personnel Services here — the Special Development Fund is a development pot rather than an operating budget, so there is no payroll in it to protect.
readings.whyProposed: A very large development program, appropriated across 2 budget years in a government still building its delivery capacity, was about to lapse with works unfinished.
whoIsAffected: Communities whose roads, buildings and facilities were funded from the Special Development Fund.
Contractors mid-delivery.
Ministries and offices administering the fund.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, given the size of the sum.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue guidelines for the cash budgeting system

funding.detail: No new appropriation. It extends the ₱10,000,000,000 already appropriated by BAA 22 from the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund.

whatChanges: ₱10 billion of development money stayed usable through 2023 instead of lapsing.
Infrastructure gained a completion and payment window to 30 June 2024.
Other capital and operating items gained a window to 31 March 2024.
deliberation: 21 December 2022: MP Ubaida C. Pacasem said the ₱5,000,000,000 yearly Special Development Fund reached ministries late, in the second half of 2021 for 2020 funds and the second quarter of 2022 for 2021 funds, and was further slowed by the pandemic.
21 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan explained that SDF approval came only in October 2021 and actual implementation of the 2020 and 2021 funds would begin in January 2023.

21 December 2022: MP Susana S. Anayatin said they had proposed ₱10,000,000 but Congress approved ₱5,000,000 for 10 years (figures as recorded), and recounted giving capital to 100 war widows in Datu Piang and South Upi.

21 December 2022: Nominal vote: 53 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third and final reading, 22 December 2022; the journal states 53 in favor but prints 54 names, none against, no abstention.
21 December 2022: Certified urgent; approved on third and final reading by nominal voting, stated as 53 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions, although 54 names are printed in favor.
readings.insight:
The Special Development Fund is the largest single pot of money encountered anywhere in this registry, and it is worth understanding why it keeps needing rescue. ₱10 billion appropriated across 2020 and 2021 — a period covering the pandemic and the earliest years of a government still assembling its procurement and engineering capacity — was never going to be spent on an annual cash budgeting cycle. Extension was the realiztic alternative to mass lapse and re-appropriation.

What makes this act worth reading alongside its successor is what came next. This one still sets outer limits: obligate by the end of 2023, pay by mid-2024. A year later BAA 51 extended the same fund again and dropped the payment deadline altogether, making the money disbursable 'until fully expended'. The chain from BAA 22 to 34 to 51 is a fair record of how a hard budget constraint became a soft one, one act at a time.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 34, enacted text as signed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the rulebook for how the Bangsamoro elects its own parliament. Before it, the region had no election law of its own — the Bangsamoro Organic Law required one, and this Code is it.

It sets the shape of an 80-member Parliament: half the seats go to party representatives elected region-wide, 40% to district representatives elected by their own districts, and 10% — at least 8 seats — are reserved for sectors. Those reserved seats are named: 2 each for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples and for settler communities, and one each for women, youth, traditional leaders, and the 'Ulama. A voter who belongs to more than one of those sectors may register in up to 3 of them.

It also builds the machinery around the vote. It establishes the Bangsamoro Electoral Office as COMELEC's arm in the region, and a Bangsamoro Registration and Accreditation Committee to register and accredit regional political parties, subject to COMELEC en banc approval. Parties must meet standards to register, and candidates for the reserved seats must be certified by the relevant ministry on the basis of a track record of advocacy for that sector, then declare their sector under oath.

The Code is written to push politics away from personalities and towards parties: it says so directly, instructing that where a provision is ambiguous, the reading that strengthens party-based parliamentary politics wins.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Organic Law obliges the region to enact its own electoral code, and no parliamentary election could be held without one. Members debating it framed it as more than compliance: the first election law written for a parliamentary system in the Philippines, and the instrument that would let the first Bangsamoro parliamentary election proceed.
whoIsAffected: Every registered voter in the BARMM, who will vote for party, district, and sectoral representatives under a system that did not exist before.
Regional political parties, which must register and be accredited, and meet the Code's standards to field candidates.
Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, settler communities, women, youth, traditional leaders, and the 'Ulama — the 6 groups holding reserved seats.
Anyone seeking a seat: district candidates face a 1-year residency requirement, and sectoral nominees must be certified and must swear to their sector.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections (COMELEC), which retains authority over the conduct of elections and approves party accreditation en banc
Bangsamoro Electoral Office (BEO), COMELEC's office in the region, whose organizational structure and staffing COMELEC determines
Bangsamoro Registration and Accreditation Committee (BRAC), which registers and accredits regional political parties
The ministries and regional agencies that certify sectoral candidates, which were given 120 days from promulgation to issue their certification guidelines
Local governments, which continue to fund election boards, canvassing, forms, and voting centers

funding.detail: The Code carries no appropriation of its own. The BEO's budget forms part of COMELEC's yearly budget, and the Bangsamoro Parliament may add to it — the Code provides for an election reserve fund in an election year, including for the assemblies that elect sectoral representatives. Local governments keep paying for election boards, forms, paraphernalia, and voting centers.

whatChanges: The region gains an election law of its own, making a Bangsamoro parliamentary election legally possible for the first time.
8 seats are set aside for sectors that would otherwise have to win an ordinary contest to be represented.
Half of Parliament is elected by party rather than by locality, which shifts campaigning towards platforms and party lists.
Regional parties acquire a registration and accreditation process, and a body to run it.
Ministries acquire a new duty: certifying that a sectoral candidate genuinely represents that sector.
deliberation: MP Alamia voted yes but said she would keep pressing for wider inclusion of women and marginalised sectors inside regional political parties.
MP Maglangit voted yes while recording a reservation: she believes in wider and bigger representation of women in Parliament than the Code provides.
MP Arnado gave 4 reasons for her vote, singling out the anti-political-dynasty provision as the first of its kind in the country, and a provision discouraging non-biodegradable campaign materials.
MP Basman argued the Code cements women's participation in practical terms, noting it requires a concrete women's agenda before a party can register.
MP Ali, Jr. noted the Code went through a series of consultations with COMELEC, and that it would enable the first parliamentary election in the region in 2025.

MP Alih framed it as asymmetry made real — a system built for the region rather than copied from the national one — and cited the 30% women requirement in party representation and the anti-dynasty provision.
Passed on Third and Final Reading by nominal voting, 64 in favor, none against, no abstentions (Journal No. 21, 7 March 2023).
readings.insight: The reserved seats are the part to watch. 8 seats out of 80 is a floor, not a ceiling, and the Code hands the ministries a gatekeeping role — a sectoral candidate needs a certification of advocacy before standing. That makes the certification guidelines, due within 120 days of promulgation, as consequential as the seat count itself: they decide who is allowed to claim a sector. The other thing to watch is that the Code says out loud which way to resolve ambiguity — towards party-based politics — which is unusual, and tells you what its drafters expected to be argued about.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 35, enacted text

readings.whatItDoes:
This solves a specific and very ordinary injustice: a worker doing a job in the Bangsamoro, on a program paid for by the national government, going unpaid because the money has not yet come down from Manila.

The act puts ₱1 billion in a revolving fund. When a national transfer is delayed, the Bangsamoro ministry supervising the program asks the finance ministry to release from the Fund, and the worker is paid on time. When the national agency eventually transfers the money, the Fund is reimbursed immediately and stands ready for the next delay.

2 guardrails come with it. Section 5 says plainly that none of this makes the Bangsamoro Government responsible for the National Government's obligations — the Fund covers timing, not liability, and ministries must still do whatever is needed to get the national funds released. And Section 9 requires a quarterly report on every release, obligation and disbursement, going to Parliament through the Speaker.
readings.whyProposed: The policy section frames it as protecting workers' welfare, and names the gap exactly: personnel deployed in the region under nationally funded programs, needing a mechanism that ensures timely payment for services already rendered.
whoIsAffected: Workers and personnel on nationally-funded programs directly supervised by Bangsamoro ministries, agencies or offices.
Those ministries, which request releases and must pursue the national downloading.
The Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which administers the Fund and reports on it.
Parliament, through quarterly reports and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which administers the Fund, releases on request, operates the reimbursement mechanism, issues the rules and reports quarterly
BARMM ministries, agencies and offices implementing nationally-funded programs

funding.detail: ₱1,000,000,000 appropriated as a revolving fund, chargeable against the Contingent Fund. Because it is reimbursed whenever national funds arrive, the ₱1 billion is a working balance rather than an annual cost.

whatChanges: Delayed national transfers no longer mean delayed wages for workers in the region.
A standing ₱1 billion facility exists for the purpose, replenished by reimbursement.
Parliament receives quarterly accounts of its use.
The Fund cannot be quietly wound up — it survives program discontinuance and dissolves only after 2 fiscal years of disuse.
readings.insight:
This is a devolution act disguised as a budget mechanism. The Bangsamoro cannot make the national government pay on time; what it can do is stand between the delay and the worker, and then get its money back. That is a modest legal idea with a large practical effect, and it is aimed at exactly the people least able to absorb a late paycheque.

The drafting is unusually careful in 3 places. Section 5 forecloses the obvious risk — that a bridging fund becomes a permanent subsidy, with national agencies content to let the region carry their payroll — by stating in terms that the Bangsamoro Government assumes none of the National Government's responsibilities. Section 6 forecloses the opposite risk, that the Fund is dissolved the moment a program pauses, by requiring 2 full fiscal years of no requests before reversion, reported to Parliament. And Section 9 requires quarterly reporting on every release and disbursement, which for a ₱1 billion fund operating on ministry requests is the difference between a facility and a slush fund.

What the act cannot do is make reimbursement happen. It requires the MFBM to provide a mechanism for immediate reimbursement once national funds arrive, but nothing here reaches the national agency that is late in the first place. If the delays became permanent rather than occasional, the ₱1 billion would drain and the act gives no answer to that.

readings.whatItDoes:
This moves the capital. The seat of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region is established at Parang in Maguindanao del Norte, where a new government center is to be built to house the Office of the Wali, the Office of the Chief Minister, the Parliament, the ministries and agencies.

It is deliberately unhurried. A Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government — chaired by the Senior Minister, with the finance, public works, environment and transport ministers, the cultural heritage commission and the planning authority, and civil society organizations invited as observers — identifies the site, subject to Parliament's approval, and prepares the master plan and timetable. The physical transfer from Cotabato City proceeds gradually, only as office buildings, roads, light and power, water and communications are completed.

2 provisions deserve separate attention. Section 4 places the government center outside local policies, measures and issuances that would run counter to the primacy of uninterrupted government service. And Section 7 requires the existing center in Cotabato City to be improved rather than abandoned, preserved for its historical value, and renamed once the move is complete.

₱50 million funds the first year, with foreign grants and donations permitted alongside the regional budget. The Committee dissolves when the job is done, and in any event within 10 years unless Parliament extends it.
readings.whyProposed: The act says only that the region has power to organize its own bureaucracy in the exercise of self-governance. It offers no stated reason for moving, and none for choosing Parang — which, for a decision of this magnitude, is a conspicuous silence.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Parang, whose municipality becomes the regional capital.
Cotabato City, which loses the seat of government it currently hosts.
Every government employee who would eventually relocate.
Anyone who travels to the regional government for services.
Local government units along the way, whom the Committee must consult.
implementedBy: Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government, chaired by the Senior Minister
Bangsamoro Parliament, which must approve the specific site
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority and the ministries seated on the Committee

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 for the Committee's first year, including the master plan, with later amounts through the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. Foreign grants, aid and donations may also be used, subject to Inter-Governmental Fiscal Policy Board guidelines. The act appropriates planning money; the cost of building a capital is nowhere estimated.

whatChanges: The region's seat of government moves from Cotabato City to Parang.
A planning committee with a 10-year life is created, with Parliament approving the site.
The new government center sits partly outside local government authority.
The existing Cotabato City center is preserved, improved and eventually renamed.
Foreign grants become an express funding channel.
readings.insight:
Cotabato City is the fact this act does not mention. It is not part of Maguindanao — it is a chartered city that voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro, and it has hosted the regional government ever since. Moving the seat to Parang relocates the capital out of that city and into the province. The act frames the whole thing as bureaucratic organization and offers no reasoning, but the geography carries an argument the text declines to make.

Section 4 is the provision to watch. Excluding the government center from local policies 'that would run counter to the primacy of uninterrupted government service' is drafted broadly enough to cover a great deal, and it creates an enclave of regional authority inside a municipality that is simultaneously promised consultation and dialogue. Which of those prevails in a real dispute is not answered here.

The design is otherwise careful in ways worth crediting. The transfer is conditioned on infrastructure actually existing rather than on a date, which avoids the standard failure of capital-moving projects — ministers decanted into a building site. Parliament must approve the site, so the choice of ground is not the executive's alone. Civil society is written in, if only as observers. And the old capital is to be preserved rather than left to decay, with its renaming treated as a matter for consultation. What is missing is a cost: ₱50 million plans a capital, it does not build one, and the act never says what the real figure might be.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is about unpaid bills. Across 3 budget years the region had obligated money — committed it to contracts, to buildings, to goods delivered — and had not yet paid it out before the appropriations were due to die.

The act deals with each year in turn. For 2020 and 2021, infrastructure, capital outlays and continuing operating programs could be obligated up to 31 December 2022; for 2022, up to 31 December 2023. And then, in each case, the same sentence: the appropriation shall continue to be effective until fully released and disbursed.

Personnel Services is excluded from all 3, as in every act in this series — 2020 salary money died at the end of 2020, 2021's at the end of 2021, 2022's at the end of 2022. And the constituent LGUs' share of income taxes collected in the region is protected, available until fully expended or disbursed.
readings.whyProposed: To avoid leaving contractors and suppliers unpaid for work already done and accepted. An appropriation that lapses does not cancel the debt; it removes the legal authority to settle it, which is a worse outcome than an extension.
whoIsAffected: Contractors and suppliers owed for completed work under any of the 3 budgets.
Communities whose projects were funded and built but not yet paid for.
Constituent local government units, whose tax shares are protected.
Ministries and offices carrying unpaid obligations.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue implementing guidelines for each amended provision

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amount stated. It keeps effective money already granted by BAA 3, BAA 15 and BAA 23.

whatChanges: Obligated amounts from 2020, 2021 and 2022 remain payable with no closing date.
New commitments were still bounded by the stated obligation cut-offs.
LGU income tax shares stay available until fully expended.
Salaries continue to expire on their original dates.
readings.insight:
This is the act that starts the shift, and it is worth being precise about the sequence. Read on its own it is unobjectionable — paying for work already delivered is the least controversial thing a budget law can do, and the alternative is stiffing contractors on a technicality. But the mechanism chosen was not another dated extension. It was the phrase 'shall continue to be effective until fully released and disbursed', applied to 3 budget years at once, in June 2023.

6 months later BAA 51 used comparable wording — 'until fully expended' — for the Special Development Fund, and BAA 52 carried it into the 2023 general appropriations. So the removal of disbursement deadlines was not a single decision about one pot of money; it began here, with unpaid obligations, and became the standing approach within half a year.

The distinction that keeps it defensible is one this act observes and the later ones partly relax: the open-ended wording applies to *disbursement of already-obligated amounts*, while the power to make new commitments still ends on a stated date. That is a meaningful line. An appropriation that can still pay old debts is not the same as one that can still be spent on new things. Anyone reading the region's budget legislation should check, in each act, which side of that line the open-ended clause sits on.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the region deciding which days it stops for, and it distinguishes carefully between 3 kinds.

4 days are regular non-working holidays: Bangsamoro Foundation Day on 21 January, Eid'l Fit'r, Eid'l Adha, and the Day of Shuhada on 18 March. 2 more are special non-working — the Day of Arafah and the first Day of Tashriq, both falling around the Hajj. Everything else is a special *working* holiday: commemorated, marked, funded, but not a day off.

That third category is where the region's history sits. Bud Daho on 6 March, Bayang on 2 May, Shariff Kabunsuan on 19 December, the signing of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro on 27 March, and the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the MNLF alongside the 1976 Tripoli Agreement on 2 September. Ministries, agencies and local governments must allocate funds and hold commemorative activities for them.

Because the Islamic dates move, Section 6 routes them through the Grand Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', who recommends the actual dates to the Chief Minister — and Section 11 requires the Chief Minister to publish the whole of next year's calendar by 31 December.

And Section 12 does the practical work: pending a Bangsamoro Labor Code, the holiday pay rules of the national Labor Code apply to private sector employees in the region.
readings.whyProposed: To replace Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 17, the ARMM-era law, with the region's own. The policy section names 3 things at once: preserving the heritage of the Bangsamoro *and other peoples* in the region, upholding the rights and well-being of workers, and keeping the regional economy competitive — which is a fair description of the tension every holiday law has to resolve.
whoIsAffected: Every private sector worker and employer in the region — the act binds the private sector expressly.
All regional government branches, agencies and instrumentalities, and constituent LGUs.
BARMM offices located outside the region, which are covered too.
Local governments wanting their own founding anniversary recognized.
Anyone whose legal deadline falls on a holiday.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, which proclaims holidays and issues the annual calendar by 31 December
Grand Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', who recommends Islamic dates on the Hijri calendar
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which recommends localized proclamations and formulates guidelines
Ministries, agencies and LGUs, which must fund and conduct commemorative activities

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Section 8 requires every ministry, agency, office and LGU to allocate funds from their own budgets for activities commemorating the holidays.

whatChanges: The region has its own holiday law in place of the ARMM's.
4 regular and 2 special non-working holidays are fixed, with 9 working commemorations.
An annual proclamation must publish next year's dates by 31 December.
Islamic dates are set through the Grand Mufti rather than administratively.
Private sector holiday compensation is expressly governed by the national Labor Code pending a regional one.
A deadline falling on a holiday moves to the next business day.
readings.insight:
The division between non-working and working holidays is where the act's real judgement lies, and it cuts in a particular direction. The days off are religious — the 2 Eids, Arafah, Tashriq — plus the region's founding and its martyrs. The battles, the treaties and the peace agreements are working holidays: commemorated with funded activities, but not at the cost of a day's production. The policy section's reference to the vibrance and competitiveness of the regional economy is doing visible work in that choice.

Section 12 is the quietly important one. A regional government can declare holidays; whether a worker is paid for them is labour law, and the Bangsamoro has not yet written its own. Rather than leave that gap open — which would have made the holidays worthless to exactly the workers least able to insist on them — the act plugs it by applying the national Labor Code's compensation rules in the meantime. It is a small clause that determines whether the rest of the act means anything in a private workplace.

One inclusion worth noticing: Bangsamoro Indigenous Peoples' Thanksgiving Day, set for the day the IP Code is enacted. A holiday whose date does not yet exist, held open for a law not yet passed — the calendar equivalent of a reserved seat.

readings.whatItDoes:
This builds the region its own science high school system, and pegs it explicitly to the Philippine Science High School — the national specialist schools that are among the hardest places in the country to get into. Education in it is free to qualified Bangsamoro learners, and the Board may add scholarships, stipends and allowances on top.

The curriculum carries one element the national model does not: Values Education, defined in the act as a subject aimed at strengthening the foundations of faith among learners as they are trained in science and technology. The Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta' sits on the Board of Trustees alongside the science and education ministers, the President of the Mindanao State University System, the chair of Parliament's science committee, 2 private sector representatives, and the president of the alumni association.

Money given to the System stays with it. Legacies and gifts are exempt from Bangsamoro taxes, and all revenues and donations go into a dedicated BSHS Fund used exclusively for the System's purposes.

And 2 provisions rarely found together in this registry: Section 15 requires gender equity and a non-discriminatory policy to address disparities so students and faculty of both genders can thrive in science education, and Section 17 requires feedback and grievance mechanisms that let students, faculty and staff report misconduct fairly and confidentially.
readings.whyProposed: The policy section makes 2 claims at once — that the region will run a complete education system conforming to national standards, and that it will do so within a framework relevant to the needs, ideals and aspirations of the Bangsamoro people. This act is where those 2 commitments meet.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro learners with talent in science and mathematics, particularly those whose families could never fund specialist schooling.
Families, for whom the school is free.
Faculty and staff, covered by the gender equity and grievance provisions.
Alumni, who hold a permanent seat on the governing board.
Communities near a campus, who may be consulted through the citizen's arm a Campus Director can convene.
implementedBy: Ministry of Science and Technology, which has administrative control and supervision and issues the implementing rules
Board of Trustees, which approves admission criteria, curricula, scholarships and graduation
Executive Committee, which screens and selects students and scholarship recipients
Campus Directors, each the administrative and academic head of a campus

funding.detail: ₱55,000,000 to support initial implementation, with such sums as needed thereafter in the annual General Appropriations Act. The System also holds its own BSHS Fund of revenues and donations, and gifts to it are exempt from Bangsamoro taxes.

whatChanges: Free, specialist science secondary education becomes available in the region rather than only outside it.
Admission, curriculum, scholarships and graduation are governed by a single Board.
Faith formation is written into a science curriculum as a named subject.
Gender equity and a confidential grievance route are required across the System.
Donations to the schools are tax-exempt and ring-fenced.
readings.insight:
The decision to peg the System to Philippine Science High School standards is the load-bearing one, and it cuts both ways. It sets a real benchmark — the national schools are genuinely selective and well-resourced, and matching them is a demanding commitment rather than a rhetorical one. It also means the region has chosen to compete on the national scale rather than define its own, which is a confident thing for a young education system to do.

The Values Education provision is where the act does something the national model does not, and it is worth reading precisely. It is not framed as a constraint on science teaching; the definition says it strengthens the foundations of faith *as* learners are trained in science and technology, and Section 4 calls it a way of strengthening the foundation of science education and faith together. Whether that works in practice depends entirely on the curriculum the Board approves — the act sets the intention and leaves the substance open.

The practical limit is scale. Section 10 provides expressly for the case where the System 'only has one campus', which tells you what was expected at the outset, and ₱55 million establishes a school rather than a network. The provision that will decide how far this reaches is Section 8's enrolment quota policy — free education for those admitted is a real benefit, but the number admitted is a Board decision the act does not constrain.

readings.whatItDoes:
12 barangays of Pigcawayan in North Cotabato become the Municipality of Pahamuddin, seated at Libungan Torreta, inside the Special Geographic Area of the Bangsamoro.

Section 2 carries the fact that explains the whole act: these barangays *petitioned and voted to be included in the BARMM in the 2019 plebiscite*. They chose the region 4 years earlier and had been sitting inside it while still administratively attached to a municipality outside it. This act resolves that.

The boundary work is the most thorough in the registry. The signed copy carries a political boundary map and a full surveyed technical description — bearings, distances, metes and bounds, an area of 6,253.7231 hectares, prepared by a geodetic engineer and approved by the Minister.

As with every creation act, nothing happens without a plebiscite, held within 60 days and run by COMELEC through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office. The Chief Minister then appoints the first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 councillors — and Section 7 adds a requirement absent from the Maguindanao creations: those appointments must be made with due regard to the representation of women of the Bangsamoro.
readings.whyProposed: The 2019 plebiscite left the region with an unusual inheritance: 63 barangays scattered across North Cotabato that had voted to join, but which belonged to municipalities that had not. Governing them from a distance through mother municipalities outside the region was never a permanent arrangement. This act, and its 6 siblings, turn those barangays into municipalities of the Bangsamoro.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 12 named barangays, who voted to join the region in 2019 and now vote on their own municipality.
Pigcawayan, North Cotabato, which loses 12 barangays — and which sits outside the BARMM entirely.
Women of the Bangsamoro, whose representation must be considered in the first appointments.
Incumbent Pigcawayan councillors resident in the new municipality.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which conducts the plebiscite
Office of the Chief Minister, which appoints the first municipal officials
Bangsamoro Government, which provides the monthly financial assistance

funding.detail: The act requires monthly financial assistance until the municipality receives its national tax allotment share but states no amount — a notable difference from the Maguindanao creation acts of December 2023, which each specify not less than ₱2.5 million a month. Plebiscite costs come from the current fiscal year appropriations.

whatChanges: 12 barangays that voted into the region in 2019 gain a municipality of their own inside it.
A surveyed boundary is fixed by map and technical description.
Women's representation becomes a stated consideration in the first appointments.
The municipality becomes entitled to a share of national taxes.
readings.insight:
This act is the administrative completion of a vote taken 4 years earlier, and that is what distinguishes it from the region's other municipality creations. The Maguindanao acts carve new units out of existing Bangsamoro municipalities — a redrawing of internal lines. This one takes territory that chose the region in a plebiscite and had no proper place in it, and gives it one. The mother municipality here is not a Bangsamoro unit at all; it is Pigcawayan, in a province outside the region.

2 drafting details repay attention. The boundary documentation is the best in the registry — a map and a full geodetic survey with metes and bounds, rather than the bare reference to 'existing barangay boundaries' that the Maguindanao acts mostly rely on. For territory transferred between regions, that thoroughness is not decorative; it is the difference between a settled border and a future dispute.

The second is Section 7's instruction that the first appointments be made with due regard to the representation of women of the Bangsamoro. The 3 Maguindanao creation acts passed 4 months later contain no such clause. It is a soft obligation — 'due regard', with no quota and no remedy — but it is present here and absent there, and nothing explains the difference.

What this act does not say is how much money the new municipality gets. It promises monthly assistance and names no figure, where the later acts name ₱2.5 million. For a municipality with no tax base and no revenue allotment yet, that is the most practically important number in the law, and it is missing.

readings.whatItDoes:
This act creates a new municipality, Ligawasan, out of 7 barangays that used to belong to Pikit in North Cotabato — Bagoinged, Barungis, Bulol, Buliok, Gli-Gli, Kabasalan, and Rajamuda. All 7 voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro, and they sit in what the region calls its Special Geographic Areas. The act separates them from Pikit and constitutes them as a municipality in their own right, with its seat of government at Barangay Bagoinged and its boundary following the existing lines of the 7 barangays.

Becoming a municipality is not automatic. The act requires a plebiscite in those barangays within 60 days of approval, run by the Commission on Elections through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, and Ligawasan acquires corporate existence only if a majority of the votes cast approve. Until an election is held, the first mayor, vice-mayor, and council are appointed rather than elected.

A new municipality has no share of national tax revenue until it is entered into the allocation, so the act commits the Bangsamoro Government to pay monthly financial assistance for the new local government's administration and operation until that share arrives, subject to ordinary accounting and audit rules.
readings.whyProposed: The 7 barangays voted in 2019 to leave North Cotabato for the Bangsamoro, which left them inside the region but still attached to a municipality outside it. The Bangsamoro Government has the power under the Organic Law to create municipalities, and this act uses it to give those barangays a local government of their own.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 7 barangays — about 29,800 people across roughly 112 square kilometers, by the figures annexed to the bill.
The Municipality of Pikit, North Cotabato, which loses the 7 barangays and the revenue attached to them.
Elected officials of Pikit who live in the separated barangays: the bill addressed how their existing terms are handled.
The Bangsamoro Government, which carries the new municipality's operating cost until national tax allotment begins.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which conducts and supervises the plebiscite
The Bangsamoro Government, which appropriates the monthly financial assistance
The appointed first set of municipal officials, who run Ligawasan until an election is held

funding.detail: The bill as filed named a figure: not less than ₱2,500,000 every month until the municipality received its share of national tax revenue. The enacted act keeps the monthly commitment but drops the amount, promising financial assistance "every month" subject to usual accounting and auditing rules. Plebiscite costs come out of existing COMELEC funds.

whatChanges: 7 barangays stop being part of Pikit and become a municipality, if the plebiscite approves.
Ligawasan gains its own local government, seated at Bagoinged, initially by appointment rather than election.
The Bangsamoro Government takes on a recurring monthly cost until national tax allotment reaches the new municipality.
North Cotabato's Pikit is reduced by 7 barangays, about 112 square kilometers.
readings.insight: The interesting difference is between the bill and the law. The filed copy guaranteed at least ₱2.5 million a month; the enacted text promises monthly assistance without saying how much. That converts a floor into a budget decision, and it is the kind of change that is invisible unless you read both documents. Worth tracking alongside it: the plebiscite had to happen within 60 days of approval, and a new municipality's finances stay dependent on the regional government until the national tax allotment catches up — which is a slower process than 60 days.

readings.whatItDoes:
This replaces the ARMM's local government code with the region's own, running to 605 sections across 4 Books and governing every province, city, municipality and barangay in the BARMM.

The structural commitment is devolution: ministries must gradually transfer basic services and facilities to LGUs within 5 years, supervised by a Devolution Committee chaired by the Senior Minister, which had 6 months to assess whether LGUs could actually carry them and 3 months more to produce a plan. Marawi City, Cotabato City and Basilan keep the full devolution status they already held.

On accountability, the Code does several things the national Local Government Code does not. Newly elected officials must complete 8 hours of onboarding and a 32-hour continuing program that includes conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding, with disqualification from the next election for those who deliberately skip it. Sanggunian members must disclose in writing any relationship within the 4th civil degree with anyone affected by a measure, before they take part in the debate. Sessions may be conducted in a local language. The interior ministry must maintain a Bangsamoro Register of Ordinances that is digital, online and public. A local treasurer who fails to publish monthly collections and disbursements faces a fine of ₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000, suspension or up to a year in prison.

And then Section 45(g), which is the provision everything else in this Code will be remembered alongside: anyone related within the 2nd civil degree to an incumbent local official running for office — parents, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, and spouses — is disqualified from running in the same election in that same province, city, municipality or barangay. Every candidate must swear in their certificate of candidacy that no such relationship exists.
readings.whyProposed: The region had inherited the ARMM's 1990s code and needed one built for a parliamentary regional government with 15 ministries and a devolution timetable. The accountability provisions answer a more specific problem, one the Code's own transitory section is candid about: local office in this region has tended to stay in a small number of families.
whoIsAffected: Every voter and every candidate for local office in the region.
All constituent provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays.
Ratepayers and taxpayers, through the local taxation Book.
Residents of the Special Geographic Area, now organized into 8 municipalities.
Barangay officials, tanods and peacekeeping teams, newly covered by insurance.
Communities in the path of regional projects, protected by consultation and relocation requirements.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, through its Local Government Operations Officers
Devolution Committee, chaired by the Senior Minister, with parliamentary and LGU representation
Office of the Chief Minister, exercising general supervision and disciplinary jurisdiction over senior local officials
Bangsamoro Local Government Academy, delivering the mandatory training
Bangsamoro Electoral Office of the COMELEC, on plebiscites, recall and candidate eligibility
Special Geographic Area Development Authority, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 initially, charged against the appropriations of the Office of the Chief Minister, for the Devolution Committee's work including an information campaign on the Code. LGU operations are funded from their share of national taxes and their own revenue-raising powers under Book II, with the Bangsamoro Government providing assistance and augmentation at no extra cost to the LGU.

whatChanges: The ARMM's local government code is repealed and replaced.
Basic services devolve from regional ministries to LGUs over 5 years.
Elected officials must be trained, and can be disqualified for refusing.
Close relatives of incumbents are barred from the same ballot, from 2028.
A public digital register of every local ordinance is created.
The 63 Special Geographic Area barangays become 8 municipalities with their own taxing powers.
readings.insight:
Section 45(g) is the most ambitious thing this Code attempts, and Section 595 is the sentence that determines what it will actually mean. The Philippines has had an anti-dynasty clause in its Constitution since 1987 and no enabling law in the 4 decades since; Congress has never passed one. A regional legislature enacting one for its own local offices is genuinely without precedent in the country. And then the transitory provision defers it — along with the training disqualification — to the May 2028 elections, 5 years after the Code took effect and a full local election cycle away.

There are defensible reasons to phase in a rule that reshapes who may stand for office: candidates and families need notice, and the electoral machinery needs time to administer a relationship test. But the effect is that the officials who passed the Code did not have to run under it, and the 2025 local elections proceeded on the old rules. Whether the provision survives to 2028 is a live question — Section 586 says the Code may only be amended after the mandatory review, but that review falls 10 years after enactment, in 2033, which either entrenches Section 45(g) against early repeal or will simply be worked around.

The scope is also worth reading carefully rather than from the headline. The bar reaches the 2nd civil degree — parents, children, siblings, spouses — and only relatives of an *incumbent running in the same election*, in the *same* LGU. A family can still hold the governorship and a mayoralty in different municipalities. A relative can run once the incumbent steps back. Cousins, nephews and in-laws beyond the second degree are untouched. Paragraphs (h) and (i) close 2 adjacent doors — an incumbent cannot decamp to run in a neighbouring LGU, and a chief executive cannot step down to the next office below — which suggests the drafters were thinking about the actual manoeuvres, not just the principle.

What the Code does immediately, and without deferral, is smaller but real: disclosure of conflicts before a sanggunian member debates a measure; a digital public register of ordinances; criminal liability for a treasurer who stops publishing the monthly numbers; sessions in a local language with minutes translated; insurance for the barangay tanod. Those are the provisions a resident might actually use next week, and they arrived in 2023.

One quiet asymmetry runs through the whole Code, as it does through the Administrative Code. Section 33 governs local chief executives' supervision over the police, fire and jail personnel in their jurisdiction by referring the question entirely to “applicable national law and the BOL”. The region wrote 605 sections about local government and left the one about who controls the police at a cross-reference.

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes the ARMM-era Regional Madrasah Graduate Academy at Buluan, abolishes its 2003 charter, and rebuilds it as a chartered regional institution of higher learning — the Bangsamoro Kulliyyah for Islamic Studies — offering baccalaureate and postgraduate degrees in Islamic studies and Arabic.

The governance is the notable part. A Board of Trustees chaired by the education Minister holds the highest policy-making power, and its membership reaches well beyond officialdom: the president of the faculty association, the president of the Student Government Organization, the president of the Alumni Association, a representative of private Islamic institutions recognized by the ministry, and the Bangsamoro Mufti all sit on it as members.

Financially it is given something most attached agencies are not: its own money. Tuition, fees, government subsidies and income from auxiliary services and land grants become special trust funds that the Kulliyyah retains and the Board disburses, with interest staying in the fund. Donations to it are exempt from all taxes and deductible from the donor's income tax. Against that, the Board must run a socialised tuition scheme for poor but deserving students.

And Section 19, in a single sentence, says the Kulliyyah shall not discriminate on the basis of color, race, religion, sex or disability in admissions, employment or any program.
readings.whyProposed: The academy was operating under a 20-year-old ARMM statute. A region committed to an educational system that is “a subsystem of the national education system” needed an institution that could actually award recognized degrees in Islamic and Arabic studies, rather than an academy whose graduates' credentials sat awkwardly against the national framework.
whoIsAffected: Madrasah graduates seeking degree-level study.
Students, faculty and alumni, each with a seat on the governing board.
Private Islamic institutions recognized by the education ministry.
Personnel of the defunct REMAcademy, transitioned within 90 days.
Communities elsewhere in the region, where branches may be opened.
implementedBy: Board of Trustees, chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, meeting at least quarterly
Office of the President of the Kulliyyah, appointed by the Chief Minister from at least 3 Board-endorsed nominees for a 4-year term renewable once
Academic Council, chaired by the President and composed of academic staff at Assistant Professor rank and above
MBHTE, holding direct supervision, regulatory powers, the staffing pattern and the implementing rules

funding.detail: No peso figure is appropriated. Initial implementation is charged against the current year's appropriations, and continued operation and maintenance is carried in the education ministry's budget under the annual appropriations act. The institution's own tuition, fees, subsidies, auxiliary service income and land grant income are retained as special trust funds it may disburse itself.

whatChanges: The region gains a chartered institution awarding degrees in Islamic studies and Arabic.
Students, faculty and alumni take seats on its governing board.
The institution keeps and spends its own tuition and income.
Socialised tuition becomes a requirement, and discrimination on religion or disability is barred.
The Regional Madrasah Graduate Education Act of 2003 is repealed and the academy absorbed.
readings.insight:
Section 19 is the sentence to notice, because of where it appears. An institution created specifically for Islamic studies, with the Bangsamoro Mufti on its board, is told in plain terms that it may not discriminate on the basis of religion in admissions, employment or any program. Read alongside BAA 64's direction that the Tribal University shall be open to all “regardless of religion, ethnicity or nationality” while prioritizing indigenous learners, a consistent drafting instinct shows through: the region builds institutions rooted in a particular community and then writes the door open. Whether that reflects conviction or a careful eye on the constitutional limits of a subsystem of the national education system, the effect is the same.

The financial design is the other thing worth pulling out, and it is unusually generous by the standards of this registry. Most bodies created by these acts get a peso figure and then depend on the annual budget. This one gets no figure at all — but it gets to keep its own money. Tuition, fees, subsidies, auxiliary income, land grant income, and the interest on all of it, become special trust funds the Board disburses “any provision of existing laws, rules, and regulations to the contrary notwithstanding”. Donations come in tax-free and leave the donor's income tax lighter. For an institution expected to build itself up, that combination is worth more than a one-off appropriation — provided it can attract enough students and donors to make the retention meaningful, which for a specialised institution in Buluan is not a small proviso.

Where the autonomy stops is equally clear. The education ministry chairs the Board, holds direct supervision and regulatory powers, and determines the complete staffing pattern. The Chief Minister appoints the President — from the Board's shortlist, but the choice is not the Board's — and appoints everyone at Salary Grade 25 and above. The President sits at Salary Grade 26, below the head of any of the region's commissions, and below several division chiefs elsewhere in the bureaucracy. An institution can be given its own money and its own board and still be quite firmly held; this one is.

readings.whatItDoes:
This does 2 things, and the second matters far more than the first.

The first is routine: it moves deadlines. Special Development Fund money from 2020, 2021 and 2022 can be released and obligated until 31 December 2024; money from the 2023 fund until 31 December 2025. 4 budget years of development spending, extended in one act.

The second is a change of kind rather than degree. Each of the 3 provisions ends with the same phrase — the appropriations 'shall continue to be available for disbursement until fully expended'. That removes the payment deadline altogether. Under a cash budgeting system an appropriation dies on a date whether or not it has been spent; under this wording, the money for these 4 funds does not die at all. It ends when it runs out.
readings.whyProposed: Projects funded from 4 successive Special Development Funds were unfinished, and the earlier extension in BAA 34 was itself expiring. Rather than return year after year for another date, Parliament removed the date.
whoIsAffected: Communities whose development projects draw on any Special Development Fund from 2020 onward.
Contractors, for whom payment is no longer bounded by a statutory deadline.
Ministries and offices administering the funds.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, whose money is now held under a materially weaker time constraint.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, authorised to issue guidelines for the cash budgeting system

funding.detail: No new appropriation and no amounts stated. It extends funds appropriated by BAA 22 (₱10 billion for 2020–2021), BAA 23 (2022) and BAA 32 (2023).

whatChanges: Release and obligation windows extended to end-2024, and to end-2025 for the 2023 fund.
The disbursement deadline is removed for all 4 years — the money is available until fully expended.
The underlying appropriations acts otherwise remain in force.
readings.insight:
Follow the chain and the shape of it is clear. BAA 22 appropriated ₱10 billion under a cash budgeting rule with hard dates. BAA 14 and 24 extended the general budgets, always keeping outer limits. BAA 34 extended this fund with staged deadlines — obligate by end-2023, pay by mid-2024. And this act extends it again and takes the payment deadline away entirely.

The wording did not originate here. BAA 38, 6 months earlier, had already made the 2020–2022 general appropriations 'effective until fully released and disbursed' — but only for amounts already obligated, to settle unpaid bills. This act goes further: it removes the limit on the fund's availability itself, not merely on paying debts already incurred.

'Until fully expended' is 4 words that undo the central discipline of the system the region wrote for itself. A deadline is what forces an agency either to spend money on the thing it was voted for or to give it back to be voted again; without one, an appropriation can sit obligated indefinitely, and the question of whether the project was ever delivered stops having a date attached to it. Note also what is not here: no reporting duty, no progress requirement, no review — none of the quarterly publication machinery that BAA 33 imposed on the general budget a year earlier reaches these funds.

There is a real argument on the other side, and the registry should state it. A post-conflict government building roads and clinics from nothing, through a pandemic, with procurement capacity it was still constructing, cannot deliver on an annual cash cycle — and repeated short extensions are their own kind of waste, consuming parliamentary time and leaving contractors uncertain. Removing the deadline is the honest version of what the previous 3 acts were doing anyway.

But it is a decision about accountability, made in a sentence at the end of 3 subsections, in an act whose title says only that it continues validity. Anyone tracking where the region's development money actually goes should treat this as one of the most consequential provisions in the registry.
