readings.whatItDoes:
This is the second supplemental budget in this registry funded the same way as the first — “out of the unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury”. Where the 2024 supplemental redistributed ₱8.44 billion of unspent money, this one redistributes ₱16.83 billion.

The composition has shifted decisively. In 2024 agriculture led at 43.6%. Here the Ministry of Labor and Employment takes ₱6.67 billion — 39.6% of the entire act — in a single program line called Employment Facilitation and Promotion. Broken down by object, ₱4.15 billion of it is labour and wages and ₱2.38 billion is financial assistance and subsidy. The same ministry received ₱148 million in the 2024 supplemental.

Agriculture follows at ₱2.75 billion, environment and energy at ₱1.32 billion, and the Office of the Chief Minister at ₱1.08 billion — ₱720 million of that for the TABANG assistance program and ₱360 million for internet connectivity, booked as subscription expenses.

Then 2 special purpose funds. A ₱1 billion Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund covers salary deficiencies, newly created positions and compensation adjustments. And a ₱2 billion Contingent Fund whose stated uses include digitalising the bureaucracy, a Transitional Development Impact Fund, Islamic finance programs, customs duties on foreign assistance, infrastructure for a new Bangsamoro Government Center — and “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs”.

The general provisions are tighter than the 2024 version: procurement is routed through PhilGEPS under the New Government Procurement Act, and the validity window runs to 30 June 2028 with Personnel Services expiring earlier, on 31 December 2027.
readings.whyProposed: Because ₱16.83 billion of previously appropriated money remained unspent. As with the 2024 supplemental, the act exists to recover spending capacity rather than to distribute new revenue.
whoIsAffected: Workers and jobseekers, the intended recipients of the largest allocation by far.
Farmers, fisherfolk and agrarian reform beneficiaries.
Households receiving TABANG assistance and communities gaining connectivity.
Hajj pilgrims and cooperatives.
Bangsamoro Government personnel, through the personnel benefit fund.
The regional financial system, if the Al-Amanah acquisition proceeds.
implementedBy: 19 ministries, offices and agencies receiving direct releases
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, issuing release orders and recommending Contingent Fund releases
Office of the Chief Minister, approving every Contingent Fund release and every motor vehicle purchase
Commission on Audit, whose findings agencies must answer within 60 days

funding.detail: ₱16,830,171,595, appropriated entirely out of unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury. Releasable and obligable until 30 June 2028, except Personnel Services which expire on 31 December 2027 with payment extendable to 31 March 2028. Unreleased appropriations, unobligated allotments and obligated allotments for undelivered goods or incomplete works revert to the Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation.

whatChanges: ₱16.83 billion of previously unspent money is returned to service — roughly double the 2024 supplemental.
Employment facilitation becomes the region's single largest program line at ₱6.67 billion.
A ₱2 billion Contingent Fund is created covering Islamic finance and bank acquisition.
Procurement is routed through PhilGEPS under the New Government Procurement Act.
Spending authority extends to 2028, well beyond the Transition Authority's own life.
readings.insight:
2 things about this act deserve to be stated plainly, without inference beyond what the text shows.

The first is the concentration. ₱6.67 billion — 39.6% of the whole act — sits in one program, at one ministry, and ₱4.15 billion of it is classified as labour and wages. In the 2024 supplemental the labour ministry received ₱148 million; this is roughly 45 times that. Large emergency employment programs are a legitimate and common instrument, particularly in a region with the country's highest poverty incidence, and the money is drawn from funds that would otherwise have lapsed. But a wages line of that size, in a single ministry, is the largest single commitment this registry has recorded in any act, and it is worth knowing it exists.

The second is the timing. Parliament passed this on 20 May 2026 and the Chief Minister approved it the following day — in the closing period of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, the appointed body that has governed since 2019, ahead of the region's first elected Parliament. The spending authority it creates runs to 30 June 2028, and for infrastructure completion to 31 December 2028. In other words, an outgoing appointed legislature has committed ₱16.83 billion of spending authority extending roughly 2 years past its own existence, including a ₱2 billion Contingent Fund releasable at the Chief Minister's discretion for purposes that expressly include “unforeseen initiatives not covered by this Act”. Nothing in that is unlawful — supplementals routinely outlive the sessions that pass them, and the cash budgeting rules force reversion of anything unused. It is simply a fact about who decided, when, and for how long.

The Al-Amanah line is the most consequential item hidden in a special provision. Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines is the country's only Islamic bank, and Section 32, Article XII of the Organic Law directs the Bangsamoro Government to develop an Islamic banking and finance system. Acquiring the institution rather than chartering a new one would be the fastest route to that, and it is authorised here in a single clause inside a contingency fund rather than by a dedicated act. Whether the acquisition proceeds, and on what terms, is not something this act settles.

readings.whatItDoes:
This constitutes a Bangsamoro Parliament's Council as an advisory and consultative body of 19, sitting alongside the executive rather than inside it.

The Chief Minister chairs it. The members are the 2 Deputy Chief Ministers, the Senior Minister, the Speaker of the Parliament, 6 cabinet members designated by the Chairman, 6 members of Parliament designated by the Speaker, a representative of local government units and a representative of the private sector. Legislators' membership is described as "an extension of their legislative functions"; cabinet members sit ex officio; and no government official on the Council receives any additional emolument, allowance or pay for it.

Its purpose is to advise the Chief Minister in his capacity as chairman of the Bangsamoro Economic Development Council, and its 8 functions are all about aligning 2 plans that are made separately. It reviews the consistency of Parliament's legislative agenda with regional development to ensure the 2 are integrated; recommends socio-economic development goals to guide the Bangsamoro Development Plan; advises on vital issues; studies how to integrate the regional plan into the national development plan as the Organic Law requires; studies the coordination of official development assistance from multilateral and bilateral institutions; monitors the effectiveness of the Development Plan and Investment Programs; integrates ecological and environmental principles into the plan; and recommends sources of revenue and ways to cut unnecessary expenditure.

The Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority serves as secretariat, assisted by the Office of the Chief Minister and Parliament's planning staff. The Council meets at least quarterly, first within 45 days of effectivity, and reports after every meeting to all members of Parliament. ₱5,000,000 is authorised from the Bangsamoro Treasury for fiscal year 2022.
readings.whyProposed:
The problem the bill addresses is a real one in a young government: Parliament writes a legislative agenda and the executive writes a development plan, and nothing obliges either to look at the other. A bill establishing a hospital is passed in one place while the investment programme that would build it is drafted in another.

The Council's answer is a standing table where the 2 agendas are compared — chaired by the head of government, seating the Speaker and 6 legislators, and serviced by the planning authority that actually drafts the Development Plan.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, 6 of whom would sit on an executive advisory body designated by the Speaker.
The cabinet, 6 of whom sit at the Chief Minister's designation.
Local government units, holding 1 seat of 19.
The private sector, also holding 1 seat.
The Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, which becomes the Council's secretariat on top of its own work.
All members of Parliament, who receive a report after every meeting whether or not they sit on it.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Parliament's Council — 19 members chaired by the Chief Minister, meeting at least quarterly
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority as secretariat, assisted by the Office of the Chief Minister and Parliament's planning staff

funding.detail: ₱5,000,000 authorised out of unappropriated funds of the Bangsamoro Treasury Office for the Council's operating and capital expenditures in fiscal year 2022, with later appropriations in the regional budget. No member who is a government official receives any additional emolument, allowance or pay for serving.

whatChanges: Parliament's legislative agenda and the Bangsamoro Development Plan get a standing body to compare them.
6 legislators sit on a body advising the Chief Minister, as an extension of their legislative functions.
Local government and the private sector each gain a seat at regional development planning.
Official development assistance from multilateral and bilateral institutions gets a coordinating study function.
All members of Parliament receive a report after every meeting.
readings.insight:
The composition is the thing to weigh, and it cuts against the bill's own framing. A Council chaired by the Chief Minister, seating 6 cabinet members he designates himself, plus the Senior Minister and 2 Deputy Chief Ministers, gives the executive 10 of 19 seats before the Speaker's 6 legislators are counted. Calling the legislators' membership "an extension of their legislative functions" does not change the arithmetic: on any question the government's own members can carry the Council, and its advice is addressed to the person who chairs it.

In a parliamentary system that objection is weaker than it first appears — the Chief Minister is a member of Parliament and the cabinet is drawn from it, so the separation this would blur is already blurred by design. The sharper question is what an advisory body tells the head of government that his own cabinet cannot. The answer in the text is the 2 seats that are not officials: local government and the private sector. Those are the only voices in the room that do not already report to the Chairman, and they hold 2 seats of 19.

The reporting duty is the provision that does the most for Parliament. A Council that must report to *all* members after every meeting means the 13 legislators who are not on it still see what was discussed, which turns a consultative body into a source of information for the whole chamber. For a Parliament trying to hold an executive to a development plan, a quarterly written record of what the planning conversation actually was is worth more than a seat at it.

The ₱5 million is appropriated for fiscal year 2022, which dates the bill precisely and is now 4 budget cycles in the past. A measure still at Committee Stage carrying an appropriation for a closed fiscal year would need that clause rewritten before it could take effect at all — a small mechanical consequence of a bill sitting for 4 years.

readings.whatItDoes:
This provides a framework for volunteerism in the region and builds 2 bodies to run it.

Section 5 names 6 modalities, each defined. Volunteerism in disasters — consistent participation in preparedness and response, whether organised by government or by non-government organisations. Volunteerism in community activities, covering work that benefits vulnerable and disadvantaged sectors, with women, children, the elderly, differently-abled persons, orphans and indigenous peoples named. Volunteerism in agriculture and aquaculture, to promote productivity and improve the income of farmers and fisherfolk. Volunteerism in health, on activities that help save lives and reduce malnutrition and maternal and child mortality and morbidity. Volunteerism in education, improving access for less fortunate children especially in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. And volunteerism in non-government organisations advancing the rights, welfare and protection of vulnerable sectors.

A Bangsamoro Volunteers Advisory Body is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary of the Office of the Chief Minister, co-chaired by the Director General of the planning authority, and seats the director generals of the finance, education, interior, social services and health ministries together with a representative each of civil society organisations, the academe and the business sector. Those 3 non-government members are appointed by the Chief Minister for 3-year terms and receive a per diem for every meeting. The Body meets at least twice a year, once each semester, and adopts its own rules.

Beneath it, Section 8 creates a Bangsamoro Volunteer's Coordinating Bureau. The framework is based on Republic Act No. 9418, the national Volunteer Act.
readings.whyProposed:
Volunteers already do a great deal of the work the bill describes — disaster response, community health, teaching in remote barangays — and they do it without legal standing, insurance, recognition or coordination. A framework act gives the state a way to recognise, deploy and support them rather than relying on them informally.

In a region with recurrent displacement, flooding and a thin public service, that is not a civic nicety. Volunteers are often the first and sometimes the only response, and the 6 modalities track the places where that is true.
whoIsAffected: Volunteers across the 6 named modalities, who gain recognition and a coordinating structure.
Non-government organisations, whose volunteers the framework covers and which hold a seat on the advisory body.
Communities in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, named as the beneficiaries of education volunteering.
Farmers and fisherfolk, whose productivity and income agricultural volunteering is meant to raise.
The academe and the business sector, each holding an appointed seat with a per diem.
The Office of the Chief Minister, whose Cabinet Secretary chairs the body.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Volunteers Advisory Body — chaired by the Cabinet Secretary of the Office of the Chief Minister, co-chaired by the planning authority, meeting at least twice a year
Bangsamoro Volunteer's Coordinating Bureau, created under Section 8
6 ministries represented at Director General level

funding.detail: No amount is named; the funds necessary for operationalisation go into the annual appropriations of the region. The only cost the Act states specifically is the per diem for the 3 appointed non-government members of the advisory body.

whatChanges: Volunteerism acquires a statutory framework with 6 defined modalities.
An advisory body and a coordinating bureau are created to deploy and support volunteers.
Civil society, the academe and the business sector gain appointed seats with 3-year terms.
Volunteer work in disasters, health, education, agriculture and community welfare is recognised in regional law.
readings.insight:
Twice a year is the problem with this design. The advisory body meets once each semester, and 3 of the 6 modalities it oversees — disasters, health, and work with displaced and vulnerable communities — operate on timescales of days. A body that convenes in, say, June and November cannot coordinate a flood response, and the bill's answer is presumably the Coordinating Bureau beneath it, which is where the operational capacity would have to sit. The Act creates the bureau and gives the schedule to the body above it, so the division of labour between deliberation and response is left to implementing rules.

The composition is unusually senior and unusually broad at once. 6 ministries at Director General level is heavy representation, and seating civil society, the academe and business with 3-year terms and a per diem gives the non-government members a real stake rather than an observer's chair. Volunteerism in this region runs largely through non-government organisations and religious institutions, so a body where they hold 3 of 10 seats is closer to the ground than most of the councils in this registry.

Building on Republic Act No. 9418 is the right method and the bill's main limitation. The national Volunteer Act already provides the architecture — a coordinating agency, accreditation, recognition — so the region is localising rather than inventing, which is faster and keeps regional volunteers within a national framework that other agencies recognise. It also means the bill inherits whatever the national act does not do, and the national act is notably silent on the thing volunteers in a conflict-affected region most need: insurance and protection when the work is dangerous.

That gap is visible by comparison. The enacted Local Governance Code provides insurance for the barangay tanod; this bill provides a per diem for a business representative attending a meeting twice a year and nothing for a volunteer entering a flooded barangay. Naming the modalities is the bill's contribution; protecting the people in them is the part it leaves out.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 4, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Special Geographic Area Sub-District Engineering Office under the Ministry of Public Works, located at Pikit and covering the 63 barangays that voted to join the region.

It assumes jurisdiction over all infrastructure and public works in the Special Geographic Area, responsible for highways, flood control, water resources development and other public works. Its functions are the ordinary engineering-office set: implementing construction and maintenance policy; inspecting, verifying, monitoring, supervising and evaluating projects against existing standards; implementing projects in its jurisdiction; assessing the condition of roads and bridges and reporting to the ministry; preparing and evaluating plans, programs of work and estimates; preparing and endorsing funding requests for infrastructure damaged by calamities; and managing and maintaining construction property, plant and equipment.

It is headed by an Assistant District Engineer. Section 6 provides for staff pending approval of the plantilla and appointments, and Section 7 addresses the transfer of construction and maintenance equipment, assets and liabilities.
readings.whyProposed:
The Special Geographic Area is 63 barangays that voted in 2019 to leave North Cotabato for the Bangsamoro, scattered across 6 mother municipalities. Public works in that territory were the responsibility of engineering offices in a province the barangays had voted to leave, and the region's own public works ministry had no field office there.

An engineering office at Pikit — the mother municipality contributing the largest share of the area's population — gives the region an operational arm inside the territory it is now responsible for.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 63 barangays of the Special Geographic Area.
The Ministry of Public Works, which gains a field office and the jurisdiction that comes with it.
North Cotabato's engineering offices, which would cease to be responsible for these barangays' public works.
Communities needing calamity repairs, for which the office prepares and endorses funding requests.
An Assistant District Engineer and the staff appointed pending the plantilla.
implementedBy: Special Geographic Area Sub-District Engineering Office (SGA-SDEO) at Pikit, under the Ministry of Public Works, headed by an Assistant District Engineer
Ministry of Public Works, which supervises it and receives its reports and funding requests

funding.detail: Section 8 provides for the regular budget of the new office without naming an amount, and Section 7 contemplates the transfer of construction and maintenance equipment, assets and liabilities — so part of the capitalisation is intended to come from existing holdings rather than new money.

whatChanges: The Special Geographic Area gains a regional engineering office inside its own territory.
Jurisdiction over its roads, flood control and water works moves to the Bangsamoro public works ministry.
Calamity repair funding requests originate from an office in the area rather than outside it.
readings.insight:
This is the most practical of the measures in this registry addressed to the Special Geographic Area, and it is worth reading against the ones that are not. In December 2022 Parliament received 8 bills constituting the area's barangays as municipalities, all 8 of which became law in August 2023. This bill, filed 3 months earlier, would have given the area the engineering office that actually builds and repairs its roads — and it is still at Committee Stage.

The sequencing matters because of what municipalities need. The 8 new municipalities each carry a ₱2.5 million monthly bridging subsidy because they have no revenue base, and what they conspicuously do not have is capacity to plan or supervise infrastructure. A sub-district engineering office is the institution that supplies that, and the region created the municipalities without it.

Siting the office at Pikit is the right call on the bill's own logic and worth noting for a reason the bill does not give. Of the 6 mother municipalities contributing barangays to the area, Pikit contributes about 90,000 people — close to half the area's population — and it is also where BAA 48 created the Municipality of Ligawasan and BAA 46 the Municipality of Malidegao. Putting the engineering office where the population and the new municipalities concentrate is sensible, and it does mean the barangays taken from Aleosan and Carmen are the furthest from it.

The assets provision is the quietly important one. Equipment, plant and liabilities have to come from somewhere, and in practice that means from North Cotabato's district engineering offices. The bill contemplates the transfer and does not say how it is agreed — which is the same gap the Special Geographic Area arrangements have everywhere: the region legislates what it will take over, and the province it is taking from is not a party.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 5, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This constitutes 32 parliamentary districts for the region, filed on the opening filing day of the Second Parliament — 15 months before the cabinet's own districting bill, which became BAA 58.

The criteria are the same ones the enacted act uses: apportionment based on population and geographic area, each district comprising as far as practicable contiguous, compact and adjacent territory, each with a population of at least 100,000, and equitable representation as the underlying principle.

The apportionment is not the same. This bill groups the districts under 8 headings, listing the municipalities in each: Northern Maguindanao 4 districts, Southern Maguindanao 5, the City of Cotabato 2, the Special Geographic Areas in Cotabato Province a single Lone District covering the 63 barangays in Pigcawayan, Aleosan, Midsayap, Pikit, Kabacan and Carmen, Lanao del Sur 6, Basilan 3, Sulu 6, and Tawi-Tawi 3.

Annexes give the detail, with municipality and barangay-level population figures and a population total per district — including the Special Geographic Areas table showing the population drawn from each of the 6 North Cotabato mother municipalities, from 5,060 in Aleosan to 90,319 in Pikit.
readings.whyProposed:
The Organic Law fixes the shape of the Parliament — Section 7(b) allocating the seats and Section 10 of Article VII requiring districts apportioned on population and geographic area — and leaves the districts themselves to be legislated. Without them the 40% of seats elected by district cannot be filled.

Filing on 19 September 2022 put this bill in front of Parliament before the Electoral Code itself was enacted in March 2023. It is the earliest attempt in the registry to answer a question the region had to answer before it could hold its own election.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region, whose district this bill would have defined.
Lanao del Sur and Sulu, which receive fewer districts here than in the act Parliament eventually passed.
Maguindanao del Sur, which receives more here than in the enacted act.
The Special Geographic Areas, given a single Lone District in both this bill and the enacted act.
Cotabato City, given 2 districts in both versions.
implementedBy: The Act is self-executing as to the boundaries; elections within them are run by the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and COMELEC under the Bangsamoro Electoral Code

funding.detail: Section 4 provides for the funds necessary for implementation but names no amount. The measure draws boundaries and creates no office, so the cost is the plebiscite-free administrative work of applying them.

whatChanges: The region would acquire 32 named parliamentary districts.
The 40% district share of an 80-member Parliament becomes electable.
The Special Geographic Areas become a single Lone District.
Districts are defined by lists of municipalities, with population annexes down to barangay level.
readings.insight:
2 bills districted this region and the allocation differs where it matters most. This one gives Lanao del Sur 6 districts and Sulu 6; BAA 58, enacted from the cabinet's Bill No. 267, gives them 8 and 7. Going the other way, this bill gives Maguindanao del Sur 5 where the act gives 4. Same 32 seats, same stated criteria, and 4 seats moved between provinces between the member's bill and the government's — which is the whole substance of a districting dispute, and no published committee record explains the shift.

There is a defect in the enumeration that is worth recording because I checked it twice. Section 3 declares 32 districts. Counting the districts the bill actually enumerates gives 30, and Lanao del Sur's numbering runs First, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh — there is no Second Parliamentary District for the province. I re-read those pages at 400 dpi with a different page-segmentation mode to rule out a scanning artefact, and the gap is in the document. A districting bill that declares a number it does not enumerate cannot be applied as written.

The Special Geographic Areas table is the bill's most useful contribution and it survives in the enacted act's arithmetic. Breaking the 63 barangays down by mother municipality — Pikit 90,319, Midsayap 39,965, Carmen 24,645, Pigcawayan 17,885, Kabacan 14,450, Aleosan 5,060 — shows that nearly half the Special Geographic Area population comes from Pikit alone. That matters for the question BAA 58 leaves open: a single Lone District for an area that size under-represents it, and the internal concentration means the district's politics will be Pikit's.

One dating detail. This bill calls the provinces Northern and Southern Maguindanao; by the time BAA 58 was enacted they were Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur. The province was divided by a plebiscite days after this bill was filed, so the naming marks the document as written at the moment the split was happening.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 6, copy as filed, with population annexes
Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 58, the enacted districting act

readings.whatItDoes:
This proposes that all 63 barangays of the Special Geographic Area become 1 municipality, named the Hashim Salamat Municipality after the founding chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

Section 4 lists the component barangays by mother municipality: 22 from Pikit, 13 from Midsayap, 12 from Pigcawayan, 7 from Carmen, 7 from Kabacan and 2 from Aleosan. The seat of government goes to Manaulanan in Pikit — chosen, the bill says, for its strategic location and because it has the biggest population of all 63 barangays.

The environment ministry conducts the survey to identify the metes and bounds of the 63 barangays, since boundaries drawn barangay by barangay in a 2019 plebiscite had never been surveyed as a single territory.

And then Section 6, which is where this bill departs from every other municipality measure in the registry. Corporate existence depends on ratification by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite conducted in the constituent barangays **and in the municipalities from which those barangays came** — Pikit, Pigcawayan, Carmen, Kabacan, Midsayap and Aleosan — held within 120 days of approval. The interior ministry coordinates with COMELEC, and the cost is borne by the Bangsamoro Government from its own Contingent Fund.

On ratification the Chief Minister appoints the mayor, vice-mayor and Sangguniang Bayan until officials are elected at the next local elections.
readings.whyProposed:
The 63 barangays voted in 2019 to leave North Cotabato for the Bangsamoro and then sat inside the region while still administratively attached to municipalities outside it. Something had to be done, and this bill was filed on the opening filing day of the Second Parliament — 3 months before the cabinet's own answer.

Its answer is consolidation. One municipality of 63 barangays, with a single mayor, a single council and a single budget, is an administratively coherent unit in a way that scattered fragments of 6 North Cotabato towns are not. And naming it for Hashim Salamat makes the political claim explicit: this territory is Bangsamoro because its people chose to be.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 192,000 residents of the 63 barangays, who would live in 1 municipality rather than 8.
Pikit, Pigcawayan, Carmen, Kabacan, Midsayap and Aleosan — which under this bill would vote on losing the barangays.
Manaulanan in Pikit, which would become the seat of a municipality of 63 barangays.
The Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, which must survey the metes and bounds.
The Bangsamoro Contingent Fund, which pays for the plebiscite.
The Chief Minister, who appoints the first municipal government.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy — the survey identifying the metes and bounds of the 63 barangays
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, coordinating with COMELEC on the plebiscite
Commission on Elections, conducting and supervising it
The Chief Minister, appointing the first mayor, vice-mayor and Sangguniang Bayan

funding.detail: The plebiscite is charged to the Contingent Fund of the Bangsamoro Government — the region paying for its own referendum, where the 8 bills that were enacted charged it to COMELEC's appropriations. The bill sets out the Local Government Code principles for local budget preparation rather than naming a bridging subsidy; the 8 enacted acts each carry a floor of not less than ₱2.5 million a month.

whatChanges: The Special Geographic Area becomes 1 municipality instead of remaining fragments of 6 North Cotabato towns.
The mother municipalities get a vote on losing the barangays.
The 63 barangays are surveyed as a single territory for the first time.
A municipality is named for the MILF's founding chairman.
readings.insight:
Section 6 is the most important provision in any municipality bill in this registry, and it is the one Parliament did not adopt. This bill would hold the plebiscite in the departing barangays *and* in the 6 municipalities losing them. Every other creation measure here — the 8 Special Geographic Area bills enacted as BAA 41 to 48, the Nuling, Datu Sinsuat Balabaran and Sheik Abas Hamza acts, the Pilintangan and Bayantol bills — polls only the barangays that are leaving. The Organic Law conditions creation on approval "in the political units directly affected", and the question of whether a municipality losing a third of its barangays is directly affected is answered one way here and the other way in everything that passed.

The structural choice is the other half. 63 barangays became 8 municipalities in August 2023; this bill would have made them one. 8 municipalities mean 8 mayors, 8 councils, 8 sets of offices and — on the enacted acts' own figures — at least ₱20 million a month in bridging subsidy, since each carries a floor of ₱2.5 million until its national revenue share arrives. One municipality would have carried 1 such subsidy. Against that, 8 municipalities put a local government within reach of communities scattered across 6 former towns, which a single municipality seated at Manaulanan would not.

That trade-off is the substance of the decision, and neither this bill nor the 8 that passed discusses it. The registry records that the cabinet's approach prevailed and that this measure, filed first, never left First Reading.

The survey provision is worth keeping for what it reveals. Directing the environment ministry to establish the metes and bounds of the 63 barangays concedes that nobody knew exactly where this territory was — the 2019 vote was taken barangay by barangay against boundaries drawn for a different province. Of the 8 acts that followed, only BAA 41 carries a full surveyed technical description.

The name is a political statement and should be read as one. Hashim Salamat founded the MILF and died in 2003; the region has also declared his burial site a memorial under BAA 60 and seats his family's representative on the board that governs it. Naming the territory that chose the Bangsamoro after the man who led the movement for it is the clearest version of the argument this bill makes.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 9, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires every Muslim restaurant and food establishment in the region to hold a halal certificate, renewed annually.

Anyone covered — sole proprietor, partnership, cooperative, association, corporation or other juridical entity, franchised or not, running a Muslim restaurant or eatery — must secure certification from an accrediting body before the end of January each year. The accrediting bodies are those recognised by the Department of Trade and Industry's Philippine Accreditation Bureau, the Islamic Da'wah Council of the Philippines and the Halal Development Institute of the Philippines among them. An application must be evaluated within 15 days, the result is a pass or a fail, and it holds for 1 year. The certificate must be posted where customers can see it and indicated in the menu. The application fee is capped at ₱500.

Section 7 sets the substantive standard: the food must contain no component of animals prohibited under Shariah or not slaughtered according to it, no ingredient considered haram, no preparation on equipment contaminated with haram ingredients, and complete separation from haram food throughout preparation, processing, storage and transport. Those requirements sit alongside the existing Philippine standards, and accrediting bodies may impose stricter ones.

The penalties reach into national criminal law. Violations ground cancellation of the certificate and may lead to suspension of operations for up to 6 months or cancellation of business permits. Falsely claiming halal status constitutes false description or representation under Article 189 of the Revised Penal Code; falsifying a certificate constitutes falsification by a private individual under Article 172, carrying prisión correccional in its medium and maximum periods and a fine of up to ₱1,000,000. Operating without any certificate at all draws ₱500 a day until compliance. Existing certificates may be used until December of the year the Act takes effect.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues from the region's character — as a Muslim region, the Bangsamoro Government regulates the business establishments within it, and restaurants are among them — and cites research on halal principles as a food safety measure rather than only a religious one.

The bill also records where it came from, in a footnote on its own face. It began as an entry by Ibrahim D. Pendatu, Santanina D. Datu-Imam and Farhaida H. Datu-Imam in a bill and resolution drafting contest run by the offices of MP Ampatuan and MP Mawallil to engage youth and communities in producing legislative measures, with revisions by MP Ampatuan's office.
whoIsAffected: Every Muslim restaurant and eatery in the region, which must certify annually and display the result.
Consumers, who would be able to see a current pass or fail certificate before ordering.
The Islamic Da'wah Council of the Philippines, the Halal Development Institute of the Philippines and other accredited bodies, which do the inspecting and certifying.
Establishment owners and, for corporate entities, their directors and officers, exposed to criminal liability under the Revised Penal Code.
Operators without certification, liable at ₱500 a day until they comply.
The Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, which administers the Act and monitors fee collection.
implementedBy: Halal accrediting bodies recognised by the DTI Philippine Accreditation Bureau — inspection, evaluation within 15 days, and issue of a pass or fail certificate valid 1 year
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism (BARMM) — administration of the Act and monitoring of fee collection
Local government units, to which suspension of operations or cancellation of permits may be recommended
Courts applying Articles 172 and 189 of the Revised Penal Code to false claims and falsified certificates

funding.detail: No appropriation. The scheme is fee-funded: an application fee capped at ₱500, collected by the accrediting bodies and monitored by the trade ministry. Non-compliance carries ₱500 a day, and falsification of a certificate exposes the offender to a fine of up to ₱1,000,000 under the Revised Penal Code.

whatChanges: Halal certification becomes compulsory and annual for Muslim restaurants rather than voluntary.
A pass or fail result must be displayed to customers and stated in the menu.
Falsely claiming halal status becomes a crime under the Revised Penal Code, not merely a regulatory breach.
Operating uncertified costs ₱500 a day.
A ₱500 ceiling on the application fee keeps the requirement affordable for small eateries.
readings.insight:
The pass-or-fail design is the cleverest thing in this bill and also its hardest edge. An establishment does not merely obtain a certificate or fail to; it receives a result, valid for a year, which it must post where customers can see it and state in its menu. A failed certificate displayed in the window is a far stronger sanction than a fine, and the bill reaches it without any enforcement machinery of its own. Whether a small eatery in a rural municipality survives publishing its own failure is the question the drafting does not ask.

The ₱500 fee cap is the provision that shows the bill was written for the economy it applies to. Halal certification in commercial practice is expensive, and a mandatory scheme priced at market rates would close small establishments rather than improve them. Capping the fee at ₱500 makes the requirement survivable; it also means the accrediting bodies must inspect within 15 days for a sum that will not cover a serious inspection, which is a tension the bill leaves unresolved.

Routing the penalties through the Revised Penal Code rather than creating regional offences is an efficient piece of drafting and a fragile one. Articles 172 and 189 are national provisions on falsification and false representation, and invoking them gives the bill real teeth — up to ₱1,000,000 and imprisonment — without the region legislating new crimes. It also makes enforcement depend on national prosecutors taking up a regional regulatory breach.

The footnote crediting 3 named citizens is worth pausing on. Legislatures rarely record where a text came from, and a filed bill that names the contest entrants who drafted it — and says the sponsoring office revised it — documents a form of public participation that is otherwise invisible. 2 other bills in this registry carry the same kind of footnote: Bill No. 155 on Lake Lanao and Bill No. 94 on the welfare of minors.

3 bills in this registry regulate what the region eats, and they pick 3 different instruments for the same problem. Bill No. 10 licenses: every Muslim restaurant must hold an annual halal certificate. Bill No. 60 polices the lie: no certificate is required, but misrepresenting food as halal becomes an offence with a long schedule of prohibited acts. Bill No. 164 discloses: it does not regulate halal at all, instead requiring named fast food chains to label anything containing pork. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none of the 3 has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 10, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This lifts agrarian reform out of MAFAR and makes it a ministry of its own — the Ministry of Agrarian Reform — as the principal agency assisting in the region's agrarian reform programme.

The structure runs from a Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister down through ministry services to Provincial Offices in every province and as many Municipal Offices as required. Section 12 keeps the chain of command explicit: until and unless a law devolves these powers to local government units, the Minister exercises technical and administrative control and supervision over the provincial and municipal offices.

The provision that matters most is Section 9, which places the Bangsamoro Agrarian Reform Adjudication Board inside the new ministry. Agrarian reform is not primarily a service-delivery function — it is an adjudicative one, deciding competing claims to land — and the Board is the body that does the deciding.

The transition mechanics are identical in all 3 and unusually careful for a reorganisation. The relevant MAFAR units and the corresponding Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General are abolished, with their powers, funds, appropriations, records, equipment, property and personnel transferred across. The whole transfer — including the new internal structure, staffing pattern, operating system and revised budget — must be completed within 6 months, and existing staff hold their posts in holdover capacity until new appointments issue. In filling the new positions, preference goes to personnel of the abolished office, provided they meet Civil Service qualification standards, with seniority breaking ties between equally qualified candidates.
readings.whyProposed:
Agrarian reform sits awkwardly inside a ministry whose other 2 mandates are production. Agriculture and fisheries are about output; agrarian reform is about who owns the land that produces it, and it works through claims, awards and adjudication rather than through extension and inputs.

The bill does not argue this at length, but the inclusion of the Adjudication Board makes the case structurally. A quasi-judicial body determining land rights is a different kind of institution from an office distributing seed, and folding both into 1 ministry means the adjudication competes for attention with the planting season.
whoIsAffected: Agrarian reform beneficiaries and claimants, whose cases would be decided by a board inside a dedicated ministry.
Landowners facing agrarian claims, on the other side of the same adjudication.
Staff of MAFAR's agrarian reform units and the Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General for Agrarian Reform, whose offices are abolished and who get preference for the new posts.
Every province in the region, which gains a provincial agrarian reform office.
MAFAR itself, which loses a third of its mandate and the corresponding budget line.
implementedBy: Ministry of Agrarian Reform, headed by a Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Agrarian Reform Adjudication Board (BARAB), placed within the new ministry
Provincial Offices in each province and Municipal Offices as required, under the Minister's technical and administrative control
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which approves the organizational framework and staffing pattern
The ministry's Legal Affairs Office with MFBM and the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office — implementing rules within 60 days

funding.detail: No new money at the point of separation. Initial implementation is taken from the current fiscal year's appropriation for agrarian reform under MAFAR — the existing line, moved — with sufficient funds appropriated in each subsequent Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Agrarian reform gets a ministry, a Minister and a budget line of its own.
The Agrarian Reform Adjudication Board sits inside a ministry whose only subject is agrarian reform.
Provincial and municipal agrarian reform offices are established under regional control.
MAFAR's agrarian reform units and director-general's office are abolished, with staff given preference for the successor posts.
readings.insight:
Putting the Adjudication Board inside the new ministry is the decision worth arguing about, and the bill does not acknowledge that there is an argument. A board that adjudicates land claims sits better at arm's length from the ministry that implements the programme those claims arise under — otherwise the body deciding whether an award was correctly made reports, through the same hierarchy, to the office that made it. Against that, an adjudication board with no ministry behind it has no capacity, and the bill's structure at least gives the Board a home whose whole attention is the subject. The filed copy chooses institutional capacity over separation and says nothing about the trade.

The staffing provisions are the most humane thing in the package, and they are easy to overlook. A reorganisation abolishes offices, which in practice means people losing posts; this bill requires preference for the personnel of the abolished office, subject only to Civil Service qualification standards, and then makes seniority the tiebreaker between equally qualified applicants. Those 2 provisos are what stop a restructuring from becoming a rehiring exercise, and they appear in all 3 bills of the package.

2 drafting artefacts show the template these bills were cut from. Section 15 says existing personnel keep their posts "at MAF" — a ministry that does not exist under either the old or the proposed name — and refers to the abolition of offices "as specified in Section 16", when Section 16 is the appropriations clause and the abolition is in Section 13. And Section 12, in a bill about agrarian reform, speaks of devolving powers "over agriculture" and of carrying out "agriculture, fisheries, and agrarian reform programs". The 3 bills were plainly drafted from 1 pattern, and the substitutions were not finished.

These 3 bills are one proposal filed as 3. MP Mawallil lodged Bill No. 11, Bill No. 12 and Bill No. 15 together in September 2022, and read in sequence they take the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform apart: Bill 11 lifts agrarian reform into a ministry of its own, Bill 12 does the same for fisheries and aquatic resources, and Bill 15 renames what is left the Ministry of Agriculture and reorganises it around that narrower mandate. Each bill draws its start-up money from the corresponding line in MAFAR's existing appropriation, so the package is designed to be budget-neutral at the point of separation. All 3 remain at Second Reading, Committee Stage; MAFAR is still 1 ministry.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 11, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources as the principal agency responsible for the region's fisheries and aquatic resources, taking those functions out of MAFAR.

A Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister head it, with ministry services beneath them and — the detail that distinguishes this bill from its 2 siblings — Provincial, Municipal *and City* Fisheries Offices. Neither the agrarian reform bill nor the agriculture bill establishes city-level offices; the fisheries bill does, which follows from where fishing communities actually are.

Section 10 attaches the Philippine Fisheries Development Authority in the BARMM to the new ministry, bringing the national body's regional presence under regional supervision.

The transition mechanics are identical in all 3 and unusually careful for a reorganisation. The relevant MAFAR units and the corresponding Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General are abolished, with their powers, funds, appropriations, records, equipment, property and personnel transferred across. The whole transfer — including the new internal structure, staffing pattern, operating system and revised budget — must be completed within 6 months, and existing staff hold their posts in holdover capacity until new appointments issue. In filling the new positions, preference goes to personnel of the abolished office, provided they meet Civil Service qualification standards, with seniority breaking ties between equally qualified candidates.
readings.whyProposed:
The region's geography is the argument. The Bangsamoro includes Sulu, Tawi-Tawi and Basilan — island provinces whose economies are built on fishing and seaweed — alongside the inland lake and river systems of Lanao del Sur and the Maguindanao provinces. Fisheries is not a subsidiary of agriculture here; for a large share of the population it is the primary livelihood.

The city offices and the attachment of the Philippine Fisheries Development Authority both follow from treating fisheries as a sector in its own right rather than a division of an agriculture ministry.
whoIsAffected: Fisherfolk across the island provinces and the inland waters, who gain a ministry whose only subject is their livelihood.
Seaweed farmers, a mainstay of the Tawi-Tawi and Sulu economies.
The Philippine Fisheries Development Authority's regional operations, attached to the new ministry.
Staff of MAFAR's fisheries units and the Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General for Fisheries, whose offices are abolished and who get preference for the new posts.
Cities in the region, which gain fisheries offices that the companion bills do not provide for their sectors.
implementedBy: Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, headed by a Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister
Provincial, Municipal and City Fisheries Offices
Philippine Fisheries Development Authority in the BARMM, attached to the ministry
MAFAR, MFBM and the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office — implementing rules within 60 days

funding.detail: No new money at separation. Initial implementation comes from the current fiscal year's appropriation for fisheries under MAFAR, with sufficient funds appropriated in each subsequent Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Fisheries and aquatic resources get a ministry of their own.
City-level fisheries offices are established alongside provincial and municipal ones.
The Philippine Fisheries Development Authority's regional arm comes under the new ministry.
MAFAR's fisheries units and director-general's office are abolished, with staff given preference for successor posts.
readings.insight:
Of the 3 bills in this package, this is the one with the strongest independent case, and the reason is demographic rather than administrative. A region containing Sulu, Tawi-Tawi and Basilan has a fishing population large enough that folding it into an agriculture ministry structurally subordinates it — and the region's own legislation bears that out, since the agriculture and fisheries training institute created by BAA 59 had to write in a Training Officer for every island province precisely because the mainland tends to absorb the attention.

The city offices are the quiet evidence that the drafting was thought through rather than copied. The companion bills give their ministries provincial and municipal offices; this one adds cities, which is where fish landings, cold storage and markets concentrate. Where the template was followed mechanically elsewhere in the package, here it was adapted.

Attaching the Philippine Fisheries Development Authority is the provision whose effect is hardest to predict. It brings a national body's regional operations under a regional ministry, which is what meaningful autonomy over fisheries would require — and it is the same assertion of regional supremacy over a national agency's regional presence that runs through the indigenous peoples act and the electoral code. The bill states it in 1 sentence and does not address how it sits against the national charter of the body being attached.

These 3 bills are one proposal filed as 3. MP Mawallil lodged Bill No. 11, Bill No. 12 and Bill No. 15 together in September 2022, and read in sequence they take the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform apart: Bill 11 lifts agrarian reform into a ministry of its own, Bill 12 does the same for fisheries and aquatic resources, and Bill 15 renames what is left the Ministry of Agriculture and reorganises it around that narrower mandate. Each bill draws its start-up money from the corresponding line in MAFAR's existing appropriation, so the package is designed to be budget-neutral at the point of separation. All 3 remain at Second Reading, Committee Stage; MAFAR is still 1 ministry.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 12, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Ministry of Tourism as the region's primary government agency for tourism, with powers and functions, a structural organization, a Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister, ministry services, and Tourism Provincial Field Units it is authorised to establish.

Section 10 does the transfer: the existing Bureau of Tourism and its officers and personnel are absorbed into the new ministry.

The pattern is the one MP Mawallil used across his reorganisation bills — lift an existing bureau out of the ministry that houses it, give it ministry rank, and move the staff with it.
readings.whyProposed:
Tourism in the region currently sits as a bureau inside the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, which is to say it competes for attention with trade and investment promotion. The argument for a ministry is that a region with Lake Lanao, the Sulu and Tawi-Tawi seas, a distinct material culture and a long coastline has a tourism proposition that a bureau cannot develop.

The counter-argument the bill does not address is security. Tourism depends on travel advisories, and the region's are not favourable — which is a constraint no change of organisational rank affects.
whoIsAffected: Staff of the existing Bureau of Tourism, whose office is absorbed into the new ministry.
The Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, which loses a third of its name and mandate.
Provinces, which would gain Tourism Provincial Field Units.
Tourism operators and communities with heritage or natural sites.
implementedBy: Ministry of Tourism, headed by a Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister
Tourism Provincial Field Units, which the Ministry is authorised to establish

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act. As with the author's other reorganisation bills, the starting point is the budget of the bureau being absorbed.

whatChanges: Tourism gains ministry rank and a budget line of its own.
The Bureau of Tourism is abolished and its staff transferred.
Provincial tourism field units become possible.
readings.insight:
This belongs to a pattern worth seeing whole. The same member filed bills creating a Ministry of Agrarian Reform and a Ministry of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources and renaming MAFAR the Ministry of Agriculture; another member filed bills splitting the education ministry into 4 agencies and the environment ministry into 2. Add this one and the First Regular Session received proposals to turn 4 existing ministries into 10.

None of them passed, and the reason is probably arithmetic rather than principle. Each new ministry needs a Minister, a Deputy Minister, ministry services and field units, and the region's own Administrative Code fixes the cabinet it has. A Parliament that approved all of these would have roughly doubled its executive overhead in a single term.

Where this bill is weaker than its siblings is in the case for separation. Agrarian reform has an adjudicative function that sits oddly beside agricultural extension; fisheries serves island provinces that mainland-led ministries tend to overlook. Tourism and trade, by contrast, are complementary — both are about attracting outside money — and the bill does not explain what the bureau cannot do that a ministry could.

Like most of the measures still at First Reading, this one has never been referred to a committee. The registry shows what that means in practice: of the bills filed in the Second Parliament, the ones that became law were overwhelmingly referred within months, while a measure left at First Reading can sit for years — MP Alamia's transitional justice bill waited 2 years and 9 months there before moving, and then passed in 3.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 13, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the third part of the package and the one that does the subtraction. The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform is renamed the Ministry of Agriculture and reorganised, structurally and functionally, around the narrower mandate that remains once agrarian reform and fisheries have been lifted out by the companion bills.

The new mandate is production economics: promoting agricultural development by providing the policy framework, public investments and support services needed for domestic and export-oriented business. A Minister and Deputy Minister appointed by the Chief Minister head it, with Provincial and City Agricultural Offices beneath.

Section 10 attaches the Philippine Coconut Authority in the BARMM to the ministry — the companion fisheries bill makes the equivalent move with the Philippine Fisheries Development Authority.

The transition mechanics are identical in all 3 and unusually careful for a reorganisation. The relevant MAFAR units and the corresponding Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General are abolished, with their powers, funds, appropriations, records, equipment, property and personnel transferred across. The whole transfer — including the new internal structure, staffing pattern, operating system and revised budget — must be completed within 6 months, and existing staff hold their posts in holdover capacity until new appointments issue. In filling the new positions, preference goes to personnel of the abolished office, provided they meet Civil Service qualification standards, with seniority breaking ties between equally qualified candidates.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill's premise is that a ministry carrying 3 mandates carries none of them well, and that agriculture defined narrowly — inputs, extension, investment, market access — is a coherent portfolio in a way that agriculture plus fisheries plus land adjudication is not.

Attaching the Philippine Coconut Authority points at what the narrower ministry is for. Coconut is among the region's major crops and the national authority's regional operations sit outside regional control; bringing them in is the kind of thing an agriculture ministry with a single subject has the capacity to pursue.
whoIsAffected: Farmers across the region, whose ministry would have agriculture as its only subject.
Coconut growers, through the attachment of the Philippine Coconut Authority's regional operations.
Staff of MAFAR's agriculture units and the Office of the Bangsamoro Director-General for Agriculture, whose offices are abolished and who get preference for successor posts.
The existing MAFAR, which loses its name, 2 of its 3 mandates and the corresponding budget lines.
Provinces and cities, which gain agricultural offices under the reorganised ministry.
implementedBy: Ministry of Agriculture — MAFAR renamed and reorganised, headed by a Minister and Deputy Minister
Provincial and City Agricultural Offices
Philippine Coconut Authority in the BARMM, attached to the ministry
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, approving the organizational framework and staffing pattern
MAFAR, MFBM and the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office — implementing rules within 60 days

funding.detail: Initial implementation is taken from the current fiscal year's appropriation under MAFAR, with sufficient funds appropriated in each subsequent Bangsamoro appropriations act. Because this bill keeps the residual institution rather than creating a new one, it inherits whatever the 2 companion bills do not carve away.

whatChanges: MAFAR becomes the Ministry of Agriculture, with a mandate limited to agricultural development.
The Philippine Coconut Authority's regional arm comes under the ministry.
Provincial and City Agricultural Offices are established.
The agriculture director-general's office is abolished and its functions absorbed.
readings.insight:
This bill only makes sense alongside the other 2, and that is the package's structural weakness. Bill 15 renames MAFAR the Ministry of Agriculture and reorganises it around a mandate that assumes agrarian reform and fisheries have gone elsewhere — but if Bill 11 and Bill 12 do not pass, this bill strips the ministry's name of 2 functions it still performs. 3 bills that must move together, filed as 3 separate measures, is a drafting choice that gives a committee 3 chances to break the design, and all 3 have now sat at Committee Stage since 2022.

The reorganisation is also the only 1 of the 3 that abolishes offices without creating a new institution to receive them, which makes its transition provision the most delicate. Existing personnel hold over at a ministry that has been renamed under them, waiting on a staffing pattern the finance ministry must approve, with preference for the abolished office's staff and seniority as the tiebreaker. 6 months is a short window for that, and the bill's own cross-references suggest the drafting was not finished: Section 13 refers to "the abolition of offices as specified in Section 13", which is Section 13 itself, when the abolition is in Section 11.

What the package as a whole would settle, if it moved, is a question the region has not answered: whether agriculture, fisheries and land are 1 subject or 3. The Organic Law gives the region the power to organise its own bureaucracy, and 3 bills filed on 1 day in 2022 are the only attempt in this registry to use it on the ministry that touches most people's livelihoods.

These 3 bills are one proposal filed as 3. MP Mawallil lodged Bill No. 11, Bill No. 12 and Bill No. 15 together in September 2022, and read in sequence they take the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform apart: Bill 11 lifts agrarian reform into a ministry of its own, Bill 12 does the same for fisheries and aquatic resources, and Bill 15 renames what is left the Ministry of Agriculture and reorganises it around that narrower mandate. Each bill draws its start-up money from the corresponding line in MAFAR's existing appropriation, so the package is designed to be budget-neutral at the point of separation. All 3 remain at Second Reading, Committee Stage; MAFAR is still 1 ministry.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 15, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is MP Alamia's bill on internal displacement, filed the same day as the cabinet's own Bill No. 32 on the same subject, and it takes a different route to the same problem.

The architecture is a Bangsamoro Internal Displacement Management Council with its own composition and powers, supported by a Bangsamoro Internal Displacement Coordination and Monitoring Office, running an Internal Displacement Regional Program. Section 7 addresses intergovernmental relations — the question of how a regional displacement body deals with national agencies, which is unavoidable when displacement is caused by armed conflict involving national forces.

Section 11 sets out rights during and after displacement. Section 12 is the provision that distinguishes this bill: it covers return, local integration *or resettlement elsewhere* — the 3 durable solutions recognised in international displacement law, named as alternatives rather than collapsed into an assumption that people go home. Section 14 provides for Bangsamoro rehabilitation and transition, and Section 15 builds mechanisms for international humanitarian assistance.

The funding clause is the most concrete in the package. Implementation draws on the appropriations of the ministries and constituent local governments, and expressly taps the Special Development Fund — the ₱50 billion the National Government committed to the region at ₱5 billion a year over 10 years — as a source, with later requirements in the regional appropriations law.
readings.whyProposed:
The region's displacement problem is chronic rather than episodic: the 2017 Marawi siege, the recurrent flooding of the Maguindanao lowlands, and clan feuding all displace communities, and the national bill on internally displaced persons has repeatedly failed to pass in Congress.

What this bill adds to that case is a funding answer. Naming the Special Development Fund as a source is an argument that displacement is a consequence of the conflict the peace agreement was meant to settle, and therefore properly charged to the money that agreement produced rather than to the ordinary social services budget.
whoIsAffected: Internally displaced people across the region, whether displaced by armed conflict, disaster or clan feuding.
Communities facing a choice between returning home, integrating locally, or resettling elsewhere — all 3 recognised here as durable solutions.
Constituent local government units, whose own appropriations are named as a funding source.
International humanitarian organisations, for whom the bill builds entry mechanisms.
National agencies, addressed through the intergovernmental relations provision.
The Special Development Fund, tapped for a purpose beyond infrastructure and livelihoods.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Internal Displacement Management Council
Bangsamoro Internal Displacement Coordination and Monitoring Office
Ministry of Social Services, which issues the implementing rules within 60 days
Ministries and constituent local government units, through their own appropriations

funding.detail: No single appropriation. Implementation is funded from the appropriations of the ministries and of constituent local governments through their own appropriations ordinances, and expressly from the Special Development Fund provided by the National Government — ₱50,000,000,000 over 10 years at ₱5,000,000,000 a year — with later requirements in the general appropriations law of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Displacement gets a standing regional council, a monitoring office and a regional programme.
Return, local integration and resettlement elsewhere are all recognised as durable solutions.
The Special Development Fund becomes a named source for displacement response.
Local governments carry part of the cost through their own appropriations ordinances.
International humanitarian assistance gains a statutory entry mechanism.
readings.insight:
2 bills on internal displacement were filed on the same day by 2 different authors, and the difference between them is instructive. The cabinet's Bill No. 32 is the more substantial document: it writes the UN Guiding Principles into regional law, enumerates entitlements in detail, names clan war and development-driven displacement as causes, and builds a coordinating council seating more than 20 bodies. This bill is leaner and answers 2 questions Bill 32 leaves open — where the money comes from, and what happens when people cannot go home.

Section 12 is the better provision of the 2. Displacement policy fails in a predictable way: it assumes return, treats camps as temporary, and has nothing to say to a community whose land is now a firing range, a flood plain or somebody else's title. Naming local integration and resettlement elsewhere as alternatives on the same footing as return is the settled international standard, and it is the difference between a policy that manages evacuation centres and one that ends displacement.

Tapping the Special Development Fund is the bolder move and the one most likely to be contested. That fund is the peace agreement's money, ₱5 billion a year, and it is heavily spoken for — the registry contains 5 separate acts extending the validity of appropriations against it because the region could not spend it fast enough. Directing part of it at displacement is defensible on principle and competes with every road, school and hospital already queued against the same source.

MP Alamia filed 9 bills on 19 September 2022, the first filing day of the Second Parliament, and 5 of them are a transitional justice programme rather than 5 separate measures. Bill No. 20 protects internally displaced persons; Bill No. 21 documents the human rights violations of the conflict and recognises its victims; Bill No. 22 pensions the ageing combatants; Bill No. 23 compensates the orphans of war; and Bill No. 25 creates the commission to run the whole thing. readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 20, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the most specific document in the registry about what happened during the conflict, and it is specific because it names things.

The period is fixed exactly: 18 March 1968 to 6 February 2019 — from the Jabidah massacre to the ratification of the Organic Law. Within that window the Act covers violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law committed by State actors and State-affiliated armed groups. Victims are defined to include persons killed, tortured, raped or sexually assaulted, mutilated or injured; internally displaced persons; widows and orphans of war; and persons whose property was destroyed or forcibly taken.

The definition of State-affiliated armed groups names them: the Ilaga, the Blackshirts, the Barracudas, the Civilian Armed Force Geographical Unit, the Civilian Volunteer Forces and the Special CAFGU Armed Auxiliary, alongside the former Philippine Constabulary, the Integrated National Police, the AFP, the PNP and the Civilian Home Defense Group — and any group organised, funded, equipped, indoctrinated, controlled or supervised by a person acting in an official capacity.

Section 6 then lists the emblematic cases the documentation must focus on, drawn from the 2016 Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission report. Disproportionate force and mass atrocity by State actors: the Jabidah massacre, the burning of Jolo in February 1974, the Malisbong massacre. Violations by State-affiliated groups: the Ilaga campaign of 1970 to 1972, the Manlili massacre, massacres in Lamitan City, Tuburan and Bagumbayan in Sultan Kudarat, the Maguindanao/Ampatuan massacre, killings by the Special CAFGU Armed Auxiliary employed by David M. Consunji, Inc. from 1986 to 1990, the Tingin-Tingin massacre and the Pata massacre. And 5 named displacement events, from the fighting in Upi and Cotabato in 1970 to the clashes of February 2003 and August 2008.

The work goes to the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, which must establish the facts, assess them against international law, reach conclusions on whether a violation occurred and where possible identify victims and alleged perpetrators, issue narrative reports with reparation recommendations, and build a database with a registry and sectoral mapping of victims. A special office inside the Commission does the work, headed by a Director at Salary Grade 28 or above with a named minimum staff — 5 legal officers, 5 researchers, 5 investigators, 5 administrative staff, a security officer and a data officer.

Section 7 requires a public narrative report within 3 years. Section 8 then dissolves the office: 2 months after publication it transfers its documents and becomes functus officio.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration grounds itself in the Constitution's adoption of international law and its guarantee of human rights, in the ICCPR and ICESCR, and in the March 2015 report of the interim Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission.

Its own argument is about sequence. Acknowledgement comes first: the Bangsamoro Government is obliged to acknowledge the violations committed during the decades of conflict, including those by State actors and State-affiliated groups, through a systematic and permanent mechanism of documentation. Recognition of individual victims follows, so that they or their families can benefit from social protection and the monetary and non-monetary reparations in the transitional justice packages. And the whole exercise is to form part of the construction of the Bangsamoro Historical Memory — the same phrase Bill No. 25 uses to name one of its sub-commissions.
whoIsAffected: Victims of violations between 18 March 1968 and 6 February 2019, and their families, who may apply for recognition.
Survivors and descendants in the named cases — Jabidah, Jolo, Malisbong, Manlili, Tingin-Tingin, Pata, Ampatuan and the rest.
The Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, which takes on the documentation, the database and the reparation recommendations.
State actors and members of the named paramilitary groups, whose identities the Commission is to establish where possible.
David M. Consunji, Inc., named in the statute in connection with killings by armed auxiliaries it employed from 1986 to 1990.
The national Commission on Human Rights and the Human Rights Violations Victims' Memorial Commission, potential parties to information-sharing agreements.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, under BAA 4, which establishes facts, reaches conclusions, reports and builds the victims database
A Special Office for the Documentation and Investigation of Past Human Rights Violations inside the Commission, headed by a Salary Grade 28 Director with a statutory minimum staff of 18
Memorandums of Agreement with the Commission on Human Rights, the Human Rights Violations Victims' Memorial Commission and the former ARMM Regional Human Rights Commission

funding.detail: No new appropriation. The amount necessary is to be sourced from the regular budget of the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission — which means a documentation exercise covering 51 years and 10 named mass-casualty events, with a statutory minimum staff of 18, is to be absorbed within an existing commission's budget. Contractual staff and service providers, including interpreters, translators and verbatim note takers, are capped at 15% of the office's annual operating budget.

whatChanges: The conflict's violations acquire a legal definition, a fixed 51-year window, and a named list of cases to be investigated.
Paramilitary groups of the conflict are named in regional law.
A victims register and sectoral mapping become the basis for later reparations.
A public narrative report is due within 3 years, after which the investigating office dissolves.
Recognition as a victim becomes something an individual can apply for.
readings.insight:
Naming the cases is what makes this bill different from every other transitional justice measure in the registry, including the act that passed. BAA 89 documents violations from the American period onward and traces land dispossession to 1898, which is a wider mandate and a vaguer one. This bill picks 10 events and 5 displacement episodes and says: start here. A commission given 51 years of history and no priorities produces a literature review; one given the Malisbong massacre and the Ilaga campaign produces findings that a family can point to.

The naming goes further than most statutes would. Listing the Ilaga, the Blackshirts and the Barracudas in a definition, and identifying killings by armed auxiliaries employed by a named private construction company between 1986 and 1990, puts specific allegations against specific actors into the text of a proposed law. That is a deliberate choice about the function of legislation — the list itself is a form of acknowledgement, and it survives whether or not the Commission ever reports.

The asymmetry in the mandate is the thing to state plainly, because the bill does not. It documents violations by State actors and State-affiliated armed groups. Violations by the Moro fronts are outside its scope. There is a coherent rationale — this is a regional government legislating about what was done to the people it now governs, and the fronts' conduct was addressed through the peace process — and it is also the reason the resulting record will be a partial one. The companion Bill No. 22 shows the author was not unaware of the question: it disqualifies from a veteran's pension anyone found guilty by final judgment of a gross human rights violation while in the service.

The funding clause is where the bill is weakest, and it is a familiar weakness in this registry. A 3-year investigation of 10 mass-casualty events, with 18 statutory staff, is to come out of the Human Rights Commission's regular budget. The sunset clause compounds the risk: the office dissolves 2 months after publishing, which is clean institutional design and leaves no one to act on the findings, since the reparations it recommends are the business of the other bills in this package — none of which has passed either.
