whatChanges: The region gains a corporation able to explore and develop its own energy resources.
That corporation may import, refine, store, distribute and sell petroleum products.
Energy development moves from a ministerial function to a commercial one.
deliberation: 22 November 2022: MP Eduard U. Guerra said he was disappointed the bill had not moved despite the Chief Minister certifying it as urgent and asked the Body to fast-track it.

22 November 2022: MP Randolph C. Parcasio recalled that the MNLF peace pact shares energy revenues 50-50 and lodges license applications with the autonomous government, which recommends approval to the Department of Energy.
readings.insight:
The corporation this charter creates has no ministry to report to. Section 4 places the EDCB under the supervision of the Ministry of Energy — and there is no Ministry of Energy in the region. It would be created by Bill No. 48, which splits the environment ministry in 2, and that bill is also sitting at Committee Stage. So 2 measures filed in September 2022 by 2 different proponents depend on each other, and neither mentions the other. If this one passed alone, its supervising authority would not exist.

The petroleum purposes are the provision that deserves the most scrutiny, because they reach a long way. Importation, exportation, refining, storage, supply, sale and distribution of crude oil and refined products is the full downstream and midstream chain, and it is a capital-intensive, price-volatile business in which government corporations across the region's own country have a poor record. A charter granting those powers without a stated capitalisation, a debt limit or a mandate to justify entry into any particular line is an authorisation to lose public money at scale — and the companion development corporation charter, filed the same month, shows the drafters knew how to specify capital when they chose to.

What the charter does not mention is the thing a reader would most expect. The Agus hydroelectric complex is the region's principal energy asset and is operated nationally; the drawdown of Lake Lanao for generation is the central energy-and-environment conflict in the region, contested in 2 separate authority bills in this registry. A corporation chartered to develop all the region's energy resources is silent on the one that already exists, which leaves its most important question — what the region's relationship to Agus is to be — unaddressed.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 33, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This charters a Bangsamoro Development Corporation — a government-owned corporation with the region and its local governments as shareholders.

The capital structure is the heart of it. Capital stock of ₱50,000,000, divided into 500,000 shares with a par value of ₱100 each, and no stock may be issued below par or for anything but cash. At least 51% must be subscribed by the Bangsamoro Government; the remainder may be offered to the provincial, municipal and city governments within the region. 10% of the value of all subscribed stock is paid at subscription, and the balance is callable on a vote of 3 fifths of the Board with the approval of the finance minister.

Voting power follows ownership: the region's stock is voted by the Chief Minister or his designee, and a local government's stock by that government's chief executive. So a province or city that subscribes gets a vote proportionate to its money, exercised by its own governor or mayor.

The corporation is subject to the existing corporation laws and holds the general powers of a corporation plus what it needs for its mandate, managed by a Board of Trustees with enumerated functions and responsibilities.
readings.whyProposed:
A regional government that wants to invest — in infrastructure, in enterprises, in joint ventures — cannot easily do it through a ministry. Ministries spend appropriations within a fiscal year, cannot hold equity, and cannot borrow. A chartered corporation can do all 3, and the registry shows the region reaching for that instrument repeatedly: an electrification corporation in Bill No. 263, an energy corporation in Bill No. 33, and this general-purpose one.

Offering the minority stake to local governments is the design choice that distinguishes it. It gives provinces, cities and municipalities a way to co-invest in regional projects and a seat, through their own chief executives, in deciding what the corporation does.
whoIsAffected: The Bangsamoro Government, which must subscribe at least 51% of the stock.
Provincial, city and municipal governments, which may subscribe the remainder and vote their own shares.
Governors and mayors, in whom the voting power of their government's stock is vested personally.
The Minister of Finance, Budget and Management, whose approval is needed to call the unpaid balance.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, who provide the region's majority subscription.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Development Corporation (BDC), subject to the existing corporation laws
A Board of Trustees with enumerated functions and responsibilities
The Chief Minister or his designee, voting the Bangsamoro Government's stock
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, approving calls on the unpaid balance

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 authorised capital in 500,000 shares at ₱100 par. At least 51% is subscribed by the Bangsamoro Government, with 10% of all subscriptions paid in at the time of subscription and the balance callable on a 3-fifths Board vote with the finance minister's approval — so the region's immediate cash outlay is a fraction of its subscription, with the rest a contingent liability.

whatChanges: The region gains a general-purpose development corporation able to hold equity and act commercially.
Local governments may become shareholders in a regional corporation.
A governor or mayor votes their government's shares personally.
Only 10% of subscriptions is paid up front, with the rest callable later.
readings.insight:
The 10% paid-in requirement is the provision that makes this charter workable and also the one that carries the risk. Paying a tenth at subscription means the region can charter the corporation for about ₱2.5 million of actual cash against a ₱25.5 million subscription, which is how a government with a cash-based budget can capitalise an entity at all. It also means 90% of the capital is a liability that can be called by a 3-fifths Board vote — and while the finance minister must approve, the call falls on a government whose appropriations expire annually. The registry's 5 budget-extension acts are evidence that this region struggles to spend money inside its fiscal year, let alone produce an unbudgeted call.

Letting local governments subscribe is the more interesting half, and the bill does not follow it through. A province that buys shares gets a vote exercised by its governor, which creates a corporation whose board answers partly to local chief executives with their own constituencies and projects. That could be a genuine mechanism for co-financing regional infrastructure, or a vehicle for directing corporate activity toward particular municipalities. The charter says nothing about conflict of interest, related-party transactions, or what happens when the corporation's commercial judgement and a shareholder-mayor's interest diverge.

Set beside the other corporate charters in this registry, the pattern is of a region building commercial instruments faster than it is building the oversight for them. Bill No. 263's electrification corporation carries a ₱100 million capitalisation, a provision that no court below the Court of Appeals may enjoin its orders, and a rule deeming transactions approved after 30 days of ministerial silence. This charter is more conventional, and like the others it has not moved past Committee Stage — so the region has legislated none of them.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 34, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the cabinet's bill for a memorial to the dead of the Bangsamoro struggle, sited at Camp Abubakar in Barira.

The marker itself is defined in one sentence: it carries a list of the names of the shuhada who were martyred as a result of their service in the protracted war for the right to self-determination and freedom of the Bangsamoro people. It stands inside a park, and the park gets the longer treatment — constructed, properly landscaped, and designed with structures and ornaments reflective of Bangsamoro culture and art, with a multi-purpose hall, parking, comfort rooms and wash areas, and access roads.

The body that builds it is a Bangsamoro Memorial Council: the chairperson of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, plus 5 provincial focal persons appointed by the Chief Minister, one each for Maguindanao including Cotabato City and the 63 barangays, Lanao del Sur, Basilan including Lamitan City, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi. The Council sets the eligibility criteria for whose names go on the marker, submits the final list to the Office of the Chief Minister, and monitors construction against its own standards and designs. When the marker and park are finished and turned over to the heritage commission, the Council dissolves automatically and its members are discharged.

Maintenance afterwards falls to the heritage commission, and the heritage commission has 90 days from effectivity to issue implementing rules.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note is signed by the Chief Minister and argues from obligation rather than policy. The Bangsamoro Government is a product of almost 5 decades of armed struggle and peace negotiations; many shed their sweat, blood, tears and even their lives for the right to self-determination. The shuhada should not only be written in history books, and remembrance should not be limited to memoirs, holidays or speeches.

The note is explicit that a marker cannot hold what it commemorates — "while the creation of a memorial marker will not be able to encapsulate the sacrifice of our shuhada, it is a way for us to immortalize this distinct part of our history" — and it closes on a sentence that is unusual in a legislative document: "We cannot let our people down."
whoIsAffected: The families of those killed in the struggle, whose relatives' names may or may not appear on the marker depending on criteria this bill leaves to a council.
Barira, Maguindanao, which hosts the park and the construction that comes with it.
Each of the region's 5 provinces, which gets a focal person on the council — with Cotabato City and the 63 barangays folded into the Maguindanao seat.
The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which chairs the build and maintains the site indefinitely afterwards.
Visitors to Camp Abubakar, which becomes a public park with a hall, parking and access roads rather than only a former camp.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Memorial Council (BMC) — chaired by the chairperson of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, with 5 provincial focal persons appointed by the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage (BCPCH), which maintains the site after turnover and issues the implementing rules within 90 days
Office of the Chief Minister, which receives the final list of names

funding.detail: No amount is named. Implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government, and maintenance after turnover goes into the annual budget of the heritage commission. The enacted act later fixed a figure: BAA 61 appropriates ₱15 million to start.

whatChanges: Camp Abubakar gains a memorial marker and a public eco-park built around it.
A list of the shuhada becomes an official document, with criteria set by a council and the final list approved through the Office of the Chief Minister.
The heritage commission takes on a permanent maintenance obligation.
A temporary council exists only until the work is turned over, then dissolves by operation of the act.
readings.insight:
The bill's hardest question is the one it hands to somebody else. Who counts as shuhada decides whose family is recognised by the region and whose is not, and the bill answers it in a single clause — martyred as a result of their service in the protracted war — and then assigns the eligibility criteria to a council it creates for the purpose. The enacted act widened the definition rather than narrowing it: BAA 61 covers those who gave and devoted their lives "directly or indirectly", which takes in people who were not combatants.

The council changed shape between filing and enactment, and the direction of the change is consistent. This bill seats 6 people, 5 of them provincial appointees of the Chief Minister. BAA 61 replaced that with a Memorial Management Board seating the public works, trade and tourism, education and environment ministries, the Darul-Ifta’, the local government of Barira, and a representative from every province — and added 2 obligations this bill does not carry: a functioning grievance mechanism, and a duty to consult and actively involve local communities. Given that the contested question is whose names appear, a grievance mechanism is the provision that matters most, and it was not in the bill.

2 smaller things. The bill places Camp Abubakar in "Maguindanao"; by the time the act was ratified in August 2024 the province had been split, and the enacted title reads Maguindanao del Norte. And the park specification gained a children's playground somewhere between the filed copy and the law — which is a small decision about whether the site is a place of mourning or a place people bring their families.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 35, copy as filed, with explanatory note
Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 61, enacted text

readings.whatItDoes:
5 sections and 2 pages. This declares the burial site of Sheikh Salamat Hashim, founding chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, and of Alim Abdul Aziz Mimbantas, its vice chairman and vice chairman for military affairs, at Camp Bushra Somiorang in Butig, Lanao del Sur, a Bangsamoro Historical Shrine to be known as the Hashim and Mimbantas Memorial Site.

The site is to be preserved and, where necessary, reconstructed as much as possible in its original form. The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage exercises supervision and control over that work and issues the rules to carry it out. Funds come from the annual appropriations for public works, with disbursements made by the heritage commission. The act takes effect on approval.

That is the whole bill. It fixes no boundary for the site, names no management body, sets no amount, and gives no role to anyone outside the heritage commission.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note attached to the filed copy, and the operative text argues nothing — it declares. What the bill treats as self-evident is that the graves of the MILF's founding chairman and its vice chairman for military affairs are a matter for regional heritage law.

It was filed on the same day as Bill No. 35, the Camp Abubakar memorial, and the 2 moved through Parliament together under one committee report. Read as a pair, they are the Government of the Day legislating the physical sites of its own movement's history in the first week it could.
whoIsAffected: The families of Sheikh Salamat Hashim and Alim Abdul Aziz Mimbantas, who are given no role at all in this version.
Butig, Lanao del Sur, and the community around Camp Bushra Somiorang.
The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which receives supervision and control over the site and the disbursements for it.
Anyone visiting or maintaining the graves, whose legal status changes from a burial place to a declared regional shrine.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage — supervision and control over preservation and reconstruction, the rules to effectuate the act, and the disbursements

funding.detail: No amount is named. Necessary funds are to be provided in the annual appropriations for public works, with disbursements made by the heritage commission. The enacted act fixed a figure: BAA 60 appropriates ₱5 million.

whatChanges: A burial site becomes a declared Bangsamoro Historical Shrine with a statutory name.
Preservation and reconstruction become the heritage commission's responsibility rather than anyone's private undertaking.
Public works appropriations become the funding channel for it.
readings.insight:
What this bill leaves out is the whole of what the enacted act added. BAA 60 sets aside at least 1,000 square meters, creates a management board seating the education, public works and tourism ministries and the Darul-Ifta’, brings the site into the region's recognised tourism and heritage network, and appropriates ₱5 million. None of that is here. The filed copy declares a shrine and hands it to one commission.

The single most consequential addition is Section 5(f) of the act, which seats a representative of each family as a full member of the board. This bill gives the families nothing — not a seat, not consultation, not notice. A measure about 2 men's graves, drafted without them in it, became a law in which their descendants sit on the body that governs the site. That is the kind of change that happens in committee and leaves no trace in the published record.

One registry note. Parliament's bills index stops this measure at "Approved on Second Reading – 7/23/2024" and records no act. BAA 60 was ratified on 23 July 2024 — the same day. The index is recording the sitting, not the outcome, and a reader trusting it would conclude the bill never became law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 36, copy as filed
Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 60, enacted text

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Science High School System: a secondary school offering scholarships to deserving Bangsamoro learners, admitted and trained under a curriculum designed to prepare them for careers in science and technology. Education is free to qualified learners.

The first campus goes to Parang, Maguindanao, with authority to add campuses elsewhere in the region later, all forming one System. Management sits with the Ministry of Science and Technology rather than the education ministry — an unusual placement, and a deliberate one, since the bill's declaration of policy leads with research and development, invention, innovation and their utilization.

The Board of Trustees runs to 11 or more: the science Minister as ex-officio chairperson, the education Minister as ex-officio vice-chairperson, the President of the Mindanao State University System, the campus director, the president of the alumni association, the president of the parents-teachers association, and one private sector representative each for higher education, education for the gifted, industry, agriculture, and new and emerging technologies. The private sector seats are staggered: of the first 5 appointments, 3 serve 4 years and 2 serve 2, and every appointment after that is a fixed 4-year term.

Below the Board, a Campus Director appointed by search for a fixed 6-year term, removable only for cause, and an Executive Committee of the director and the heads of department that screens and selects students, picks scholarship recipients, and develops the curriculum subject to the Board.

The money is ring-fenced. All revenues and donations go into a Bangsamoro Science High School Fund spent by the Board exclusively on this Act; legacies and gifts are tax-exempt and deductible for the donor; and the System itself is exempt from all taxes, fees, assessments and other charges of the Government.

One subject is written into the statute by name. Values education is defined as a subject aimed at strengthening the foundations of faith among learners as they are trained in science and technology, and Section 3 requires the System to integrate it as a way of strengthening the foundations of science education and faith together.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is 3 sentences and makes a resourcing argument rather than an educational one: the Bangsamoro Government prioritizes research and development, invention, innovation and their utilization, along with education, training and services in science and technology, and maintains a comprehensive, adequate and integrated high school science education system tailored to the needs of learners in the Bangsamoro.

No explanatory note is attached to the filed copy. The measure is a cabinet bill filed on the first filing day of the Second Parliament.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro learners with aptitude in science and mathematics, who gain a free specialist secondary school with scholarships, stipends and allowances available on top.
Parang, Maguindanao, which hosts the first campus.
The Ministry of Science and Technology, which takes on running a school system.
Parents, through a PTA president seated on the Board of Trustees.
The private sector, which holds 5 of the Board's seats across higher education, gifted education, industry, agriculture and emerging technologies.
Donors, whose gifts to the System are tax-exempt and deductible.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Science High School System, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, first campus in Parang, Maguindanao
A Board of Trustees chaired ex officio by the science Minister, with the education Minister as vice-chairperson
A Campus Director appointed by search for a fixed 6-year term, removable only for cause
An Executive Committee of the Campus Director and heads of department, for admissions, scholarships and curriculum
Bangsamoro Science High School Fund, holding all revenues and donations

funding.detail: No amount is named. Implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. Separately, all revenues and donations to the System go into a dedicated Bangsamoro Science High School Fund, spent by the Board exclusively on this Act; gifts and legacies are tax-exempt and deductible from the donor's gross income, and the System is exempt from all taxes, fees, assessments and other charges of the Government.

whatChanges: The region gets a specialist science high school with free tuition for qualified Bangsamoro learners.
Science education is placed under the science ministry rather than the education ministry.
A dedicated fund keeps the System's own revenue and donations out of the general budget.
Values education becomes a statutory subject in a science curriculum.
Campus leadership gets a 6-year term and protection from removal except for cause.
deliberation: 16 January 2023: MP Aida M. Silongan said BARMM had the lowest number of passers in the 2020 DOST scholarship report, only 1.15% of 4,397, and is the only Mindanao region without a Philippine Science High School campus.
readings.insight:
The benchmark is the difference between this bill and the law it became. This version says the System "shall be at par with the standards of other science high schools in the country" — a general aspiration. BAA 40 pegs it explicitly to the Philippine Science High School, which is a specific, demanding and measurable commitment: the national campuses are among the hardest schools in the country to enter. Turning a comparison into a named standard is the single most consequential edit made to this measure.

The Board was restructured in the same direction. This bill gives the private sector 5 seats and seats the PTA president; the enacted act cut the private sector to 2, dropped the PTA seat, and added the Mufti of the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta’ and the chair of Parliament's science committee. The effect is to move the board away from stakeholder representation and toward oversight — a legislator to answer to, and a religious authority to sit alongside the values education mandate that this bill writes in but leaves entirely undefined in practice.

The act also picked up 2 provisions with no ancestor here: a gender equity and non-discrimination requirement aimed at disparities in science education, and feedback and grievance mechanisms for students, faculty and staff to report misconduct. A bill that is otherwise carefully drafted about corporate powers, tax exemptions and board terms says nothing about what happens to a student who is mistreated.

The placement under the science ministry is worth one more note. Putting a school system outside the education ministry means its budget competes with research programs rather than with other schools, and its head of agency is not the region's education authority. It is a defensible choice for a specialist institution, and it is the kind of choice that is easy to make at charter stage and hard to revisit.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Bangsamoro Agriculture and Fisheries Training Institute — a body whose purpose is teaching farmers and fisherfolk, and teaching the people who train them, rather than subsidising or lending to them.

BAFTI leads the formulation of the regional agriculture and fisheries extension agenda and its budget, prepares an integrated plan for publicly funded training programs, and issues the guidelines for planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating extension programs. Its operational job is to prop up the local government extension system — the workers who actually reach villages — through capability building, technical assistance, training of LGU personnel, improvement of physical facilities, extension-cum-research, and information support, in coordination with state universities and colleges.

At least 3 BAFTI offices are established in key areas of the Bangsamoro territory, each headed by a Director I, all attached to the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and reporting directly to the Office of the Minister.

3 sections carry the substance. Farmers' and fisherfolk's cooperatives are named the cornerstone for training development and dissemination, with the Cooperative and Social Enterprise Authority as a key partner. A training needs assessment run jointly by BAFTI, the ministry and the local government must precede delivery, so that training is correct, culturally appropriate and relevant — and information, education and communication materials must be delivered in the language most appropriate to the end-user. And halal development is prioritized, with halal standards and their incentives required in all training modules.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy states the case directly: agriculture is a means to alleviate poverty and achieve food sufficiency in the region, so the Bangsamoro Government gives priority to science and technology training and innovation for all Bangsamoro farmers and fisherfolk, and commits to an extensive information campaign promoting modern techniques, innovations and knowledge.

No explanatory note is attached to the filed copy. It is a cabinet bill, filed on the first filing day of the Second Parliament.
whoIsAffected: Farmers and fisherfolk across the region, as the intended recipients of the training.
Farmers' and fisherfolk's cooperatives, named as the cornerstone of how training is developed and disseminated.
Local government extension workers, whose capability, facilities and support the Institute is built to improve.
State universities and colleges, which partner on training modules and research.
Halal producers and certifiers, whose standards enter every training module.
The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, which gains at least 3 attached offices reporting directly to the Minister.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Agriculture and Fisheries Training Institute (BAFTI), attached to the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform
At least 3 BAFTI offices in key areas of the region, each headed by a Director I, reporting directly to the Office of the Minister
Cooperative and Social Enterprise Authority, as key partner for dissemination and needs assessment
State universities and colleges, for training modules and research
The Technical Education arm of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, for agriculture and fisheries short courses

funding.detail: No amount is named. Implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. The enacted act took the funding question more seriously than the filed copy did — BAA 59 carries "appropriating funds therefor" in its own title, which this bill does not.

whatChanges: Agricultural extension in the region gets a lead agency, an agenda and a budget of its own.
At least 3 training offices are established across the territory.
Training must be preceded by a needs assessment done with the local government.
Materials must be delivered in the language most appropriate to the end-user.
Halal standards become a required component of every training module.
Cooperatives become the designated channel for reaching farmers and fisherfolk.
deliberation: 17 January 2023: MP Mohammad S. Yacob said many Bangsamoro farmers do not even use basic crop calendars and the proposed institute would lead training with TESDA, state universities and local governments.
readings.insight:
Section 9 of this bill is the sentence that makes it more than a routine training statute, and it survived into the law intact. Requiring a training needs assessment conducted with the local government, and materials "in the language most appropriate to the end-user", is a direct answer to the way agricultural extension usually fails: material designed centrally, delivered in a language the farmer half-follows, about conditions that are not theirs. In a region with several major languages and the Special Geographic Area's own communities, that is not a formality.

The coverage promise got much more specific between filing and enactment. This bill says "at least 3" offices in "key areas". BAA 59 puts a Training Officer in every island and mainland province and in the Special Geographic Areas, expressly to serve far-flung communities. The difference between 3 offices somewhere and a named officer everywhere is the difference between a headquarters function and a service, and it is the single largest change the measure underwent.

The halal provision was also expanded rather than trimmed. Here it is one section requiring halal standards in training modules; in the act it grows into an industrial policy in miniature, with a definition of the halal industry reaching beyond food into cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, tourism, logistics, Islamic financing and more. The region has a structural advantage in that sector that no other Philippine region can claim, and the enacted version is the one that treats it as such.

A drafting note for anyone reading the filed copy: it has no Section 5. The numbering runs 4, then 6, and nothing appears to be missing from the substance — the offices section simply absorbed whatever was going to sit between them.

readings.whatItDoes:
4 sections. This declares 2 May of every year the "Battle of Bayang Day", in commemoration of the heroic sacrifices made there.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, the Bangsamoro Commission on the Preservation of Cultural Heritage and other concerned agencies ensure its proper observance. The heritage commission, with the education ministry, monitors the annual activities prepared and implemented by regional government agencies, schools, colleges and universities. The Act takes effect 15 days after publication.

It declares no holiday, creates no body and appropriates nothing.
readings.whyProposed:
The Battle of Bayang was fought in May 1902 in Lanao del Sur, when Maranao defenders resisted United States forces during the American campaign in Mindanao. It is among the earliest set-piece engagements of Moro resistance to American rule, and it ended in heavy Maranao losses.

Commemorating it is a claim about when the Bangsamoro struggle began — well before the movements of the 1970s, and against a colonial power rather than the Philippine state.
whoIsAffected: Communities in Bayang and Lanao del Sur, whose history the day commemorates.
Regional government agencies, schools, colleges and universities, which must prepare and implement annual activities.
The Bangsamoro Commission on the Preservation of Cultural Heritage and the education ministry, which monitor those activities.
The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, named first among the agencies ensuring observance.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety, the Bangsamoro Commission on the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, and other concerned agencies — observance
The heritage commission with the Ministry of Basic, Technical and Higher Education — monitoring the annual activities of agencies and schools

funding.detail: No appropriation. Agencies and schools absorb the cost of the commemorative activities within their own budgets.

whatChanges: 2 May becomes a commemorative day across the region.
Schools and agencies must mount annual activities, monitored by the heritage commission.
readings.insight:
The day already exists in law, and this bill does not know it. BAA 39, the Bangsamoro Legal Holidays Act, was enacted in July 2023 and lists Bayang on 2 May among the region's special *working* holidays — commemorated with funded activities, with nobody getting the day off. That act came from Bill No. 192, filed by the Government of the Day in June 2023. This bill, also a Government of the Day measure, was filed in September 2022 and is still listed at Second Reading, Committee Stage.

So the region's own cabinet filed 2 measures about the same date 9 months apart, and the later one — which handled the whole calendar rather than a single day — overtook the earlier. That is the most economical illustration in the registry of what the absence of a coordinating mechanism inside Parliament costs: not a policy dispute, just 2 bills doing the same thing with no visible awareness of each other.

What this bill would have added, had it moved first, is the monitoring. BAA 39 requires ministries, agencies and local governments to allocate funds and hold commemorative activities for working holidays; this bill goes further by naming the heritage commission and the education ministry as the bodies that monitor what schools and agencies actually do. A commemoration nobody checks tends to become a memorandum, and that is the gap the enacted act leaves.

The choice of 1902 is the substantive point and worth stating plainly. The region's commemorative legislation otherwise centres on the modern conflict — the memorial marker at Camp Abubakar, the burial site of the MILF founders, the Mujahideen memorial wall, the Day of Shuhada for the 1968 Jabidah killings. Bayang reaches back 2 generations further, to resistance against the Americans, and locates the struggle in a longer history than the peace agreement's own timeline.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Bangsamoro Buffer Fund for a specific and unglamorous problem: paying people whose salaries the national government has not yet transferred.

The Fund exists to defray the timely payment of salaries and other remuneration of nationally-funded workers or personnel directly supervised by Bangsamoro ministries or offices, and to offset the effects of delay in the transfer or downloading of funds by the national agencies responsible. The finance ministry administers it under its cash management and disbursement system, releasing money only for that purpose and only on request from the ministry or office concerned.

Section 5 protects the Fund from being wound up prematurely. It is not automatically dissolved when nationally-funded programmes in the region stop, when the appropriation lapses from the regional budget, or when the hiring or renewal of deployed workers ceases — it continues to be available for its purpose, expressly to safeguard the workers' interest and welfare. It is dissolved and reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury only where it has completely stopped operating for 2 years, and the finance ministry must report that transfer to the Chief Minister.
readings.whyProposed:
A substantial number of people working under Bangsamoro ministries are paid from national programme funds, and those funds arrive late. When they do, the person who goes unpaid is a teacher, a health worker or a project employee, not the agency that delayed the transfer.

A buffer fund is the standard remedy — the region pays on time out of its own money and is made whole when the national transfer arrives. The bill's contribution is to make that a standing facility rather than an improvisation each time it happens.
whoIsAffected: Nationally-funded workers and personnel supervised by Bangsamoro ministries and offices, who would be paid on time.
The Bangsamoro ministries and offices that employ them, which must request the release.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which administers the Fund.
National agencies whose late transfers the Fund is designed to absorb.
The Bangsamoro Treasury, to which the Fund reverts after 2 years of inactivity.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — administration, management, release on request, implementing rules, and the report to the Chief Minister on any reversion

funding.detail: Section 6 appropriates the Fund, and the figure in the filed copy is internally inconsistent — see the note below. The words read ₱500 million; the numerals read ₱500,000.00.

whatChanges: Workers paid from national programme funds get paid on time out of a regional buffer.
The Fund survives the end of the programmes that gave rise to it, and lapses only after 2 years of inactivity.
Releases are controlled by the finance ministry on request from the employing ministry.
readings.insight:
The appropriation clause does not agree with itself. Section 6 reads: "The amount of Five Hundred Million Pesos (Php 500,000.00) is hereby appropriated as Bangsamoro Buffer Fund." The words say ₱500 million; the figures say ₱500,000 — a thousandfold difference in the only number in the bill. I re-read that page at 400 dpi under 2 different page-segmentation settings and the text is the same both times, so this is the filed document rather than a scanning artefact. Philippine practice on construing a conflict between words and figures would generally favour the words, but a fund whose size is uncertain by 3 orders of magnitude cannot be administered, and the defect would have to be cured before enactment.

The difference is not academic. ₱500,000 would cover the monthly salaries of perhaps 12 people; ₱500 million would carry a substantial payroll across a delayed transfer cycle. Which the drafters meant is answerable from the bill's own purpose — a buffer that absorbs national transfer delays for an entire category of workers needs the larger figure — but the statute does not say so.

Section 5 is the provision that shows real thought about how funds like this die. The ordinary fate of a buffer is that the programme it supported ends, the appropriation is not renewed, and the balance is swept up while workers from the tail end of the programme are still owed. This bill blocks each of those routes expressly, keeps the Fund alive on its purpose rather than on its programme, and sets a 2-year inactivity test before reversion — with a report to the Chief Minister so the reversion is visible.

It is worth reading against the 5 budget-extension acts in this registry. Those exist because the region could not spend its appropriations inside the fiscal year; this bill addresses the opposite failure, where money the region is entitled to has not arrived at all. Both are symptoms of a government whose cash flow depends on transfers it does not control, and this is the only measure here that tries to insulate workers from that.

readings.whatItDoes:
This builds the region's irrigation institutions and sets their priorities.

Section 3 applies the Act to all irrigable agricultural land in the region, with priority to Small Scale Irrigation Projects and to farmers holding 8 hectares or less — and it provides that institutional arrangements on nationally funded projects, which remain under the sole authority of the National Irrigation Administration, are to be defined in the Act.

Section 4 creates a Bangsamoro Irrigation Board as the policy-making body on irrigation, supported by a Bangsamoro Irrigation Office as its operational arm, with the Board attached to the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform.

The Board is chaired by the agriculture ministry and seats the environment, public works and interior ministries, a representative of the National Irrigation Board, and representatives of the local government unit concerned and its provincial or municipal agriculture officer. It convenes at least quarterly. An Executive Director carries the functions and responsibilities set out in Section 9.
readings.whyProposed:
Irrigation decides whether land that could grow rice does. The region's agriculture is concentrated in the Maguindanao lowlands and the river systems around the Liguasan marsh, where water is abundant and the infrastructure to move it is not — and irrigation in the Philippines has historically been built and operated nationally, by an agency answering to Manila.

The bill's answer is to build regional institutions for the part of the sector the region can reach — small-scale projects and smallholders — while expressly leaving nationally funded systems with the national agency.
whoIsAffected: Farmers holding 8 hectares or less, given express priority.
Communities dependent on small-scale irrigation rather than national systems.
The National Irrigation Administration, whose sole authority over nationally funded projects the Act preserves.
Local government units and their provincial and municipal agriculture officers, seated on the Board.
The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, which chairs the Board and hosts it.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Irrigation Board — policy-making, chaired by the agriculture ministry, convening at least quarterly
Bangsamoro Irrigation Office — the Board's operational arm, headed by an Executive Director
National Irrigation Administration, retaining sole authority over nationally funded projects

funding.detail: No amount is named. Implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government "without prejudice to the nationally-funded projects" — which keeps the national programme's money separate rather than folding it into the regional budget.

whatChanges: The region gains an irrigation board and an operational office of its own.
Smallholders with 8 hectares or less and small-scale projects become the stated priority.
Local governments and their agriculture officers sit on the body setting irrigation policy.
The division of authority with the national irrigation agency is written into regional law.
readings.insight:
The 8-hectare priority is the substantive policy choice and it is the right one for the region's agriculture. Irrigation investment tends to flow to large contiguous service areas because they are cheaper per hectare to command, which systematically favours bigger holdings; naming smallholders and small-scale projects as the priority reverses that default. In a region where land tenure is contested and where the indigenous peoples act had to legislate against dispossession by ostensibly lawful means, directing water infrastructure at small farmers rather than large ones has consequences beyond yield.

Seating the local government and its own agriculture officer on the Board is the other design decision worth noting. Irrigation fails on maintenance more than on construction — a canal silts up, a gate breaks, and nobody local owns the problem. A board that includes the municipal agriculture officer who will have to deal with that is better placed than one composed only of ministers in Cotabato City.

Expressly preserving the National Irrigation Administration's sole authority over nationally funded projects is unusual restraint in this registry. The pattern elsewhere — in the indigenous peoples act's certification requirement, the electoral code's arrangements with COMELEC, the energy corporation's silence on the Agus complex — is for regional statutes to assert over national ones and leave the collision unaddressed. This bill does the opposite, drawing the line itself. That makes it more likely to work and it also concedes the larger half of the sector: the systems that irrigate the most land stay national.

What the bill does not do is address water rights. Irrigation presupposes an entitlement to divert water, and in this region that question runs into Lake Lanao, the Agus drawdown, and the ancestral domain provisions of BAA 64, which give indigenous communities priority rights over resources in their domains and require consent before projects proceed. An irrigation statute silent on all of that leaves its Board to discover the conflict in practice.

readings.whatItDoes:
This moves the capital. The administrative capital of the Bangsamoro Government is established in Parang, Maguindanao, where a Bangsamoro Government Administrative Center is to be built to house the Office of the Chief Minister, the Parliament, and the ministries, offices and agencies.

Section 3 is the provision with teeth. Invoking Parliament's power to create, divide, merge, abolish or substantially alter the boundaries of municipalities and barangays, it declares the Government Center within Parang "autonomous from the local government unit" and places it directly under the control and supervision of the regional government. Consultations and dialogues with the local governments concerned and other stakeholders are to be conducted to ensure a smooth transition.

The work is given to a Committee on the Establishment of Administrative Capital: the Senior Minister as chair plus 4 members — the Minister of Finance, Budget and Management, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, and the Director-General of the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Office. It leads the preparation of masterplans, strategies, processes and a timetable, convenes immediately on approval, and ceases to exist when the objectives are fully implemented — which shall not exceed 10 years unless Parliament extends it.

Funding is charged against annual appropriations, with no amount stated. The Committee has 90 days from effectivity to issue implementing rules in consultation with agencies and stakeholders.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is a claim of competence rather than an argument for Parang. In the exercise of its right to self-governance the region is free to pursue its political, economic, social and cultural development, and it has the power to create offices and organize its own bureaucracy to ensure efficient and effective delivery of government programs and services.

No explanatory note is attached, and the bill offers no reason for choosing Parang over anywhere else — including over Cotabato City, which had hosted the regional government since 2019 and which the bill never mentions.
whoIsAffected: Cotabato City, which loses the seat of government and is not named anywhere in the bill.
Parang, Maguindanao, which gains the administrative capital and simultaneously loses jurisdiction over the land it sits on.
Every ministry, office and agency of the Bangsamoro Government, and the Parliament itself, all of which relocate.
Regional government employees, who would move with their offices.
The local government of Parang and its residents, promised consultation and dialogue but not consent.
implementedBy: Committee on the Establishment of Administrative Capital (CEAC) — chaired by the Senior Minister, with the Ministers of Finance, Budget and Management; Public Works; and Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, and the Director-General of the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Office
The Committee issues the implementing rules within 90 days and dissolves on completion, in any case within 10 years unless Parliament extends it

funding.detail: No amount is named. Implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. The enacted act put a figure on it: BAA 37 funds the first year with ₱50 million and permits foreign grants and donations alongside the regional budget.

whatChanges: The seat of the Bangsamoro Government moves from Cotabato City to Parang, Maguindanao.
The land the Government Center occupies is declared autonomous from the municipality and placed under regional control and supervision.
A 5-member cabinet committee holds the masterplan, the timetable and the implementing rules.
A 10-year outer limit is set on the transition, extendable only by Parliament.
readings.insight:
The carve-out was narrowed on the way to enactment, and that is the change to read first. This bill declares the Government Center "autonomous from the local government unit" and "directly under the control and supervision of the regional government" — a wholesale exclusion of Parang's jurisdiction over the site. BAA 37 replaced that with a test: the center sits outside local policies, measures and issuances that would run counter to the primacy of uninterrupted government service. Still broad, but it is a standard a dispute can be argued against, where the filed version simply removed the municipality from the picture.

The committee was widened and the decision taken back. This bill lets a 5-member cabinet committee prepare the masterplan with no external check; the enacted act adds the transport minister and the cultural heritage commission, invites civil society organizations as observers, and makes the choice of site subject to Parliament's approval. A cabinet bill that would have settled the region's capital inside the cabinet came out of Parliament requiring Parliament's own sign-off.

The act also filled 2 silences. This version never mentions Cotabato City; BAA 37 requires the existing center there to be improved rather than abandoned, preserved for its historical value, and renamed once the move is complete. And this version sets no pace, while the act requires the physical transfer to proceed gradually, only as buildings, roads, light and power, water and communications are finished — which converts a relocation into a condition-based sequence.

There is a loose end the bill left and the act tied off. The seat of government was already named in the Bangsamoro Administrative Code — Book 1, Chapter 2, Section 9 of BAA 13 — and this bill relocates the capital without touching it, relying on its general repealing clause to resolve the conflict. BAA 37 amends that section by name. It is the difference between leaving 2 provisions to argue and deciding which one governs.

One more thing changed, in the title rather than the text. This bill establishes an "administrative capital"; the act establishes "the seat of government of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region", and adds the Office of the Wali to the offices being housed. The difference between an administrative center and a seat of government is not decorative — one is where the paperwork is done, the other is where the region is.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 37 (Seat of Government Act of 2023), enacted text — the signed copy is headed "BILL NO. 43"

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Veteran Mujahideen Affairs Office and pays a monthly allowance to ageing fighters of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and the Moro National Liberation Front.

A Veteran Mujahideen is defined precisely: a member of the MILF or MNLF who actually rendered revolutionary services in the protracted wars for self-determination for at least 20 years between 1969 and 2014, and who is at least 55 years old when the Act takes effect. The benefit goes to the underprivileged among them — those with no opportunity for employment because of old age, lack of the required education, or other requirements for employment.

What distinguishes this version is that it prices service by role. Revolutionary service is sorted into 4 categories, each with its own monthly allowance. Category A, combatants who had actual engagement in military combat, receives ₱10,000. Category B, first aiders who provided medical support during combat, ₱8,000. Category C, the support group who provided food and non-food supplies to combatants, ₱6,000. Category D, the peace mechanism — those who contributed to the peace process through official platforms or back-door negotiations — ₱5,000.

Beyond the cash: free medical assistance at any health facility supervised by the regional health ministry, and exemption from taxes, fees and other charges imposed by the Bangsamoro Government. On a veteran's death, the monthly allowance continues to the spouse and children for 5 years.

The office sits inside the Ministry of Public Order and Safety as a component division, headed by a Director II, with 3 divisions — processing and validation, benefit availment, and monitoring and evaluation. And Section 13 says where the names come from: the ministry coordinates with the Central Committee of the MILF and of the MNLF for the list of qualified and validated beneficiaries.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is general — the Bangsamoro Government protects the interests of its people, ensures basic necessities and equal opportunities, and puts in place economic mechanisms tailored to their needs. Section 3 is more specific: the purpose is to assist veterans who are underprivileged and have no opportunity for employment because of their old age, lack of education, or other employment requirements.

The unstated logic is in the exclusion. Section 10 withholds the benefits from veterans who receive benefits and privileges under the decommissioning process as part of normalization. The peace agreement provides for combatants who are formally decommissioned; this bill is for the ones who are not in that process and have nothing — men and women who spent 20 years or more in an armed movement and reached their mid-50s without a pension, a qualification or a job.
whoIsAffected: MILF and MNLF veterans aged 55 or over with at least 20 years of service between 1969 and 2014, who are underprivileged.
Veterans already receiving decommissioning benefits under normalization, who are expressly excluded.
Spouses and children of qualified veterans, who continue receiving the allowance for 5 years after a death.
The Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF, which supply the validated list of beneficiaries.
The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, which houses and runs the office.
Health facilities under the regional health ministry, which provide free medical assistance to beneficiaries.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Veteran Mujahideen Affairs Office (BVMAO), a component division of the Ministry of Public Order and Safety, headed by a Director II
3 divisions — Processing and Validation, Benefit Availment, and Monitoring and Evaluation — each headed by a Development Management Officer V
An inter-agency working group drawn from the social services, health, trade, agriculture, education and human settlements ministries
Central Committees of the MILF and the MNLF, consulted for the list of qualified and validated beneficiaries
Ministry of Public Order and Safety with the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office — implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No amount is named; implementation is charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. The enacted act named one: BAA 57 appropriates ₱500 million for initial implementation, with continuing costs in the annual budget under the Office of the Chief Minister.

whatChanges: Ageing MILF and MNLF veterans outside the decommissioning process receive a monthly allowance for the first time.
Revolutionary service is graded into 4 categories with different rates of payment.
Beneficiaries receive free medical assistance and exemption from Bangsamoro taxes, fees and charges.
A surviving spouse and children keep the allowance for 5 years.
The former armed movements' own central committees become the source of the official beneficiary list.
readings.insight:
The 4 categories are the most revealing thing in this bill, and Parliament removed them. As filed, a combatant receives ₱10,000 a month and someone who worked on back-door negotiations receives ₱5,000 — the state putting a price on kinds of contribution to an armed struggle, with fighting at the top and peacemaking at the bottom. BAA 57 pays everyone ₱7,000. Whatever was said in committee is not published, but the decision to flatten the scale is the single largest change the measure underwent, and it declines to rank the ways people served.

The eligibility test was rebuilt in the same pass. This bill turns on age — 55 — and on a soft description of being underprivileged. The act turns on being a senior citizen or permanently disabled and on an income below ₱250,000 a year. Replacing a description with a means test makes the benefit administrable and also narrows it: a 56-year-old in reasonable health earning above the threshold qualifies here and not there.

The act took something away as well. This version continues the allowance to a spouse and children for 5 years after the veteran dies; BAA 57 makes the pension lifetime and non-transferrable, ending at death. For a benefit aimed at households with no other income, that is the provision a family would feel.

And there is the sentence in Section 13 that no summary of this measure should skip. The list of qualified beneficiaries is to be assembled in coordination with the Central Committee of the MILF and of the MNLF. Determining who fought, for how long, in a war with no personnel files means asking the organisations that fought it — which is administratively unavoidable and constitutionally striking, since it gives 2 non-state bodies a hand in deciding who receives public money.

One drafting slip in the filed copy: Section 7 puts a Director II at the head of the office, while Section 8 provides for the appointment of an "Executive Director I" with a 3-year term under the interim Chief Minister and a non-renewable 6-year term thereafter. The 2 sections do not name the same post.
