readings.whatItDoes:
This requires the region to analyse conflict before it plans, and it attaches that requirement to the planning documents local governments already have to produce.

The scope covers all provincial, city, municipal and barangay governments, the interior ministry, and every ministry and agency involved in preparing a Comprehensive Development Plan, a Contingency Plan or a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan. Where practicable, conflict sensitivity and the Do No Harm principle apply to other planning processes too.

At the regional level, the Bangsamoro Regional Peace and Order Council must produce a Bangsamoro Peace and Order Status Report within 12 months of the implementing rules — an annual conflict analysis assessing ongoing armed or violent conflicts, evaluating the capacity of the regional government and its ministries to prevent, manage, resolve and transform conflict, and identifying 3 categories of area: those with ongoing or active protracted armed conflict, those conflict-affected, and those vulnerable to armed conflict or violence. The Report is revised twice a year to account for changing conflict factors and presented to Parliament.

Beneath it, every local government conducts its own conflict analysis, integrated into existing planning rather than added alongside it, and indispensable for any area the regional Report has identified. Barangays may do a lighter conflict assessment. The Act specifies the key elements an analysis must contain while leaving the framework to be designed or adopted from existing practice.

The consequences are built into approval and money. Section 12 requires local governments to prioritise policies based on robust conflict analysis, and programmes and projects resulting from conflict analyses conducted in advance are to be given priority in approval and resource allocation. Comprehensive Development Plans must be based on the Report and the local analyses, with the sectoral issues of vulnerable groups highlighted throughout. Local Development Council members must undergo conflict sensitivity capacity development, and planning teams must complete training on the Do No Harm Action and Relationship Frameworks.

The Regional Peace and Order Council leads; anything not expressly assigned falls to the interior ministry. A Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System and a capacity development programme support it, with assistance from peace partners expressly contemplated.
readings.whyProposed:
The premise is that development spending in a conflict-affected region is never neutral. A road, a school or a water system allocates something scarce between communities that may be in dispute, and a project designed without reference to that can deepen the conflict it was meant to relieve — which is what the Do No Harm framework exists to prevent.

The region is the obvious place to legislate it. Most of its territory falls into 1 of the 3 categories the Report is required to identify, its development budget is large relative to its institutions, and its own peace agreement commits it to conflict transformation rather than only to service delivery.
whoIsAffected: Every provincial, city, municipal and barangay government in the region, which must analyse conflict before planning.
Communities in areas identified as conflict-affected or vulnerable, for whom analysis becomes indispensable rather than optional.
Vulnerable sectors, whose participation in local planning is guaranteed and whose sectoral issues must be highlighted.
Local Development Council members and planning teams, who must complete conflict sensitivity and Do No Harm training.
The Bangsamoro Regional Peace and Order Council, which leads and must report to Parliament twice a year.
Peace partners — the civil society and international organizations whose assistance the Act contemplates.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Regional Peace and Order Council (BRPOC) — the Peace and Order Status Report, revised bi-annually and presented to Parliament, and lead responsibility for compliance
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, carrying any authority not expressly assigned
Constituent local government units, conducting their own conflict analyses and integrating them into planning
Local Development Councils, whose members undergo conflict sensitivity capacity development
A Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System and a Conflict Sensitivity Capacity Development Program

funding.detail: No amount is named. The Act works by attaching requirements to planning processes that local governments already fund, and contemplates assistance from peace partners for capacity development — which is realistic, since the substantial costs here are training and analysis rather than construction.

whatChanges: Conflict analysis becomes a required step before local development planning, not an optional add-on.
An annual regional conflict analysis goes to Parliament and is revised twice a year.
Areas are formally classified as having active conflict, being conflict-affected, or being vulnerable.
Projects grounded in advance conflict analysis get priority for approval and funding.
Local planners must be trained in Do No Harm frameworks.
Vulnerable sectors gain guaranteed participation in local planning.
readings.insight:
Section 12 is what separates this from a reporting requirement. Analysis obligations are easy to enact and easy to satisfy on paper; what makes them bite is attaching them to money, and this bill does — programmes and projects that come out of conflict analyses conducted beforehand get priority in approval and in resource allocation. That gives a mayor a reason to do the analysis properly rather than to commission it after the project is chosen.

The 3-category classification is the provision with the most consequences the bill does not discuss. Designating an area as having active protracted armed conflict, or as conflict-affected, or as vulnerable, is a determination with effects well beyond planning — on investment, on insurance, on how a community is policed and perceived. The bill requires the classification, revises it twice a year, and says nothing about whether a local government may contest its designation. For something revised that often, and presented to Parliament, that is a gap worth closing.

Making the analysis indispensable only in already-identified areas is a sensible rationing of effort and carries a predictable failure. Conflict in this region is often latent before it is active, and the places that most need a Do No Harm analysis may be the ones the Report has not yet flagged. The bill's answer is that analysis is integrated into ordinary planning everywhere and merely indispensable in the identified areas, which is the right structure if the ordinary requirement is enforced and a loophole if it is not.

Read against the enacted Local Governance Code, this bill is the missing piece. BAA 49 requires newly elected local officials to undergo continuing training that includes conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding — a provision Parliament added in committee and which takes effect immediately. That trains the officials; this bill would have conditioned their plans and their budgets. Half of the design is law and the half with the money attached has sat in committee since October 2022.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 63, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is a Bangsamoro Human Rights Defenders Act: 52 sections across 6 chapters, enumerating what a human rights defender may do, what the state must do about it, and what happens when the state does the opposite.

The definition is deliberately wide. A human rights defender is any person who, alone or with others, acts or seeks to act to protect, promote or strive for human rights and fundamental freedoms at local, national, regional or international level — and any bona fide member of a human rights organization is one by definition. A human rights organization may be formal or informal. A human rights violation is defined to cover acts by State actors and by non-State actors acting under their orders or with their acquiescence.

Chapter II enumerates the rights: to promote and protect human rights; to form groups and associations; to solicit, receive and use resources; to seek, receive and disseminate information; to develop and advocate human rights ideas; to communicate with non-governmental and governmental bodies; to access and cooperate with international bodies; to participate in public affairs; to peaceful assembly; to represent and advocate; to freedom of movement; to privacy; against intimidation or reprisal; against defamation, stigmatization and vilification; to exercise cultural rights; to an effective remedy and full reparation; and to establish a sanctuary for human rights victims and their families. Section 23 then sets the limits on those rights.

Chapter III is the half that binds the government, and it reads as a list of the things that go wrong. Obligations to respect, promote, protect and fulfil defenders' rights; to facilitate their work; to provide free access to human rights materials; not to disclose confidential sources; to prevent and protect against intimidation or reprisal, and to penalize it; to refrain from derogatory and unfounded labeling; to protect against arbitrary or unlawful intrusion; not to participate in violations; to investigate whenever there is reasonable ground; to ensure effective remedy and full reparation; to ensure non-recurrence; to enforce and institutionalize command responsibility; to adopt human rights-based governance; to strengthen the protection programme of the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission; and to promote human rights education.

Chapter IV creates a Human Rights Defenders Protection Committee with stated qualifications, terms of office and functions, and requires training and vetting of everyone involved in it. Chapter V penalises violations and makes any violation of the Act an aggravating circumstance, with the Revised Penal Code applying suppletorily.

Section 3 sets the interpretive rule: all provisions are to be construed in favour of human rights defenders.
readings.whyProposed:
Human rights work in the Philippines carries a documented occupational risk, and the particular mechanisms are what the bill's obligations track one by one. Defenders are labelled as fronts for armed movements, surveilled, sued, refused access to detainees, and in the worst cases killed — and the people who order it are rarely the people who do it.

Congress has repeatedly considered a national Human Rights Defenders Act and never passed one. A region with its own legislative power, its own human rights commission under BAA 4, and a recent history in which both State forces and armed groups committed violations, is the one jurisdiction in the country positioned to enact one for itself.
whoIsAffected: Anyone who acts to protect or promote human rights, including members of informal organizations, who are defenders by definition under this Act.
Public authorities, bound by 16 enumerated obligations and penalised for intimidation or reprisal.
Commanders and superiors, reached through the obligation to enforce and institutionalize command responsibility.
Journalists and researchers relying on confidential sources, protected by the non-disclosure obligation.
Victims of human rights violations and their families, for whom defenders may establish a sanctuary.
The Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, whose protection programme the Act requires be strengthened.
implementedBy: A Human Rights Defenders Protection Committee created by the Act, with statutory qualifications, fixed terms, enumerated functions, and mandatory training and vetting of all persons involved in it
The Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, whose protection programme the Act strengthens
All public authorities, bound by the Chapter III obligations
Courts, applying the penalties and treating violations as aggravating circumstances, with the Revised Penal Code applying suppletorily

funding.detail: No amount is named. Section 49 provides that upon effectivity such sum as may be necessary is to be appropriated, with later requirements in the regular budget — the standard formulation, and a thin basis for a protection committee with vetting and training obligations and a strengthened commission programme.

whatChanges: Human rights defenders acquire enumerated statutory rights rather than relying on general constitutional guarantees.
Derogatory and unfounded labeling of defenders becomes a breach of a statutory obligation.
Command responsibility becomes something public authorities are obliged to enforce and institutionalize.
Intimidation or reprisal against a defender is penalised, and any violation of the Act aggravates another offence.
Confidential sources may not be disclosed by public authorities.
A protection committee is created, with its members vetted and trained.
Ambiguities in the Act are resolved in the defender's favour.
readings.insight:
Section 30 is the provision that would matter most in practice, and its plain words are worth keeping: an obligation on public authorities to refrain from derogatory and unfounded labeling. In the Philippines that practice has a name — red-tagging, the public identification of activists, lawyers, journalists and aid workers as fronts for armed movements — and its consequence is that the people named become targets for someone else. No national statute prohibits it. A regional act that makes it a breach of a defined obligation, with violations serving as an aggravating circumstance under Section 46, is the most concrete legal response to it anywhere in Philippine law.

Command responsibility in Section 36 is the other provision of real consequence. The pattern in the documented cases is that the person who pulls the trigger is unidentifiable and the person who created the conditions is untouchable; a duty to enforce and institutionalize command responsibility is aimed squarely at the second. Whether a regional statute can impose that on national uniformed services is the same question this registry raises about the indigenous peoples act and national permits, and the bill asserts past it rather than addressing it.

The definitional breadth is a deliberate choice with a real trade-off. Making any bona fide member of a human rights organization a defender, and recognising informal organizations, means protection does not depend on accreditation by the state that may be the threat — which is the right instinct. It also means the category is wide, and a government inclined to resist the Act has an obvious argument about who qualifies. Section 3's rule that everything is construed in favour of defenders is the answer the drafters chose.

The context makes this bill more notable, not less. The region's own transitional justice measures — Bill No. 21's documentation of violations by State actors and State-affiliated armed groups, and Bill No. 22's disqualification of veterans convicted of gross violations — are about what was done in the past. This one is about what is being done now, and it binds the region's own authorities rather than the national government's. Filed in October 2022, it has not moved past Committee Stage in 4 years, which is itself a datum about the appetite for it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 66, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires every local government in the region to set aside land for a public cemetery, and it sets the ratio.

The allocation is a minimum of 2,000 square meters per 1,000 population, to be incorporated into the local government's Comprehensive Land Use Plan or zoning ordinance and approved by its Sanggunian. And 20% of the land allocated must be set aside for use by non-Muslims.

Design is not left open. Registration requirements and the mandated design parameters and road specifications — burial plot sizes, access to plots, the circulation system, service utilities, buffer strip, facilities and amenities, and the perimeter fence — must comply with HLURB Board Resolution No. 681, Series of 2002, and other pertinent rules.

Local governments establish, maintain and operate the cemeteries and ensure compliance with design, sanitation and safety standards, while control and supervision of construction, operations and maintenance rests with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. The appropriation covers capital outlay, maintenance, operating expenses and personnel services.
readings.whyProposed:
Burial is a religious obligation with a short deadline. Islamic practice requires interment as soon as possible after death, which means a family cannot wait while a plot is found or a fee negotiated — and in a region where public cemetery provision is uneven, that pressure falls hardest on those who cannot pay for a private plot.

Setting a population-based ratio turns an intermittent local decision into a planning requirement, and putting it in the Comprehensive Land Use Plan means the land is reserved before it is built on.
whoIsAffected: Families burying relatives, who gain a public cemetery sized to the population.
Non-Muslims in the region, for whom 20% of every allocation must be set aside.
All constituent local government units, which must allocate the land and operate the cemeteries.
Local Sanggunians, which must approve the allocation through the land use plan or a zoning ordinance.
The Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, which controls and supervises construction and operation.
implementedBy: Constituent local government units — land allocation through the Comprehensive Land Use Plan or zoning ordinance, and the establishment, maintenance and operation of the cemeteries
Local Sanggunians, approving the allocation
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — control and supervision of construction, operations and maintenance

funding.detail: No amount is named. Upon effectivity, such sum as may be necessary for capital outlay, maintenance, operating and other expenses and personnel services is to be provided — notably including personnel, since a cemetery needs staff, which most measures of this kind forget.

whatChanges: Every local government must reserve at least 2,000 square meters of cemetery land per 1,000 people.
That reservation enters the Comprehensive Land Use Plan rather than depending on a later decision.
A fifth of every public cemetery is set aside for non-Muslims.
National design standards for cemeteries become binding on plot sizes, access, drainage and fencing.
readings.insight:
The 20% set-aside for non-Muslims is the provision that matters most and the one that will be read in 2 ways. On its face it guarantees burial space to Christians, indigenous peoples and others in a Muslim-majority region where a public cemetery would otherwise follow Islamic practice — which is a real protection, and consistent with the instinct that runs through this registry, where the Kulliyyah for Islamic Studies is told it may not discriminate on religion and the tribal university must be open to all. Read the other way, a fixed fifth is a quota that could be above or below the actual need in any given municipality, and the bill applies the same proportion to a town that is 2% non-Muslim and one that is 40%.

Adopting the HLURB design standards is the unglamorous decision that makes the Act work. Cemetery design is a public health matter — plot depth and spacing, drainage, the buffer strip between graves and groundwater — and a statute that required cemeteries without specifying standards would produce burial grounds that contaminate wells. Incorporating an existing national resolution rather than drafting fresh parameters is also the right method: the standards already exist and have been applied.

The ratio is the provision a planner would question. 2,000 square meters per 1,000 people, allocated once, is a stock being drawn down by a flow — a municipality's cemetery need accumulates every year while the land allocation does not. The bill ties the allocation to the Comprehensive Land Use Plan, which is periodically revised, so the mechanism for topping it up exists; nothing in the Act requires the revision to do so.

Including personnel services in the appropriation is worth noting because so few bills here do. A cemetery requires someone to dig, record and maintain, and a capital outlay that buys land and a fence without funding a caretaker produces exactly the neglected ground the bill is trying to prevent.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires solar energy systems in every regional housing project the Bangsamoro Government implements, current and future, and then connects them to the national renewable energy regime so the households actually benefit.

Section 5 integrates solar as an accessory use in all such projects, to provide secure, clean power in urban and rural areas — and names the intended beneficiaries: the disadvantaged, the homeless, victims of conflicts and atrocities, and internally displaced persons. The sum allocated must include installation, upkeep and maintenance, not just the panels. And every end-user must be told, on their monthly electric bill, how much of their consumption and generation charge the solar system supplied.

The mechanisms come from national law. The finance ministry applies the general incentives in Chapter VII of Republic Act No. 9513, the Renewable Energy Act of 2008. Beneficiaries enjoy the privileges granted to qualified end-users under Sections 10 and 12 of that Act, as certified by the Department of Energy's Renewable Energy Management Bureau. Section 7 requires the government to ensure distribution utilities enter net-metering agreements with all end-users, implemented under Section 10 of the same Act. And Section 8 exempts power generated for the homeowner's own consumption from the universal charge under Section 34 of Republic Act No. 9136.

The human settlements ministry writes the guidelines within 90 days, with the science ministry, the environment ministry and renewable energy stakeholders.
readings.whyProposed:
Socialized housing is built for people with no money, and the recurring cost that defeats them is not the amortisation but the utility bill. A housing project in an unelectrified or underserved area either has no power or has power its occupants cannot pay for.

Solar with net metering answers both: the household generates its own supply, and under the Renewable Energy Act the surplus it exports is credited against what it draws. That is the difference between a panel on a roof and a bill that goes down.
whoIsAffected: Beneficiaries of regional socialized housing — expressly the disadvantaged, the homeless, victims of conflict and atrocities, and internally displaced persons.
Distribution utilities, which must enter net-metering agreements with every end-user.
The Ministry of Human Settlements and Development, which writes the guidelines within 90 days.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which must apply the national renewable energy incentives.
The Department of Energy's Renewable Energy Management Bureau, which certifies qualified end-users.
implementedBy: Ministry of Human Settlements and Development, with the science and environment ministries and renewable energy stakeholders — guidelines within 90 days
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, applying the incentives under the Renewable Energy Act
Distribution utilities, through net-metering agreements
Department of Energy Renewable Energy Management Bureau, certifying qualified end-users

funding.detail: No amount is named, but the Act requires that whatever is allocated cover installation, upkeep and maintenance — which is the provision that distinguishes a funded system from an abandoned one. The national incentives under Republic Act No. 9513 and the universal charge exemption under Republic Act No. 9136 reduce the cost to the household rather than to the government.

whatChanges: Solar becomes mandatory in all regional housing projects rather than optional.
Funding must cover maintenance, not only installation.
Households see on their bill how much of their power the solar system provided.
Net-metering agreements become an obligation on distribution utilities.
Self-consumed solar power is exempt from the universal charge.
readings.insight:
Requiring the allocation to include upkeep and maintenance is the sentence that separates this from the usual solar mandate. Installed panels across the Philippines fail for want of a replaced inverter or a cleaned array, because the capital budget bought the hardware and no operating budget maintains it. A statute that makes maintenance part of the sum allocated is legislating against the predictable failure mode, and it costs nothing to write.

The transparency requirement is the other provision doing real work. Telling the household, on the monthly bill, how much of its consumption and generation charge the solar system supplied turns an invisible benefit into a visible one — which matters politically, because a household that cannot see what the panels save has no reason to protect them, and matters practically, because a bill showing zero solar contribution is the first evidence that the system has stopped working.

Building on the national Renewable Energy Act rather than inventing a regional scheme is the right instinct and the bill's main dependency. Net metering, the qualified end-user privileges and the universal charge exemption all come from national statutes administered by national bodies — the Department of Energy's Renewable Energy Management Bureau certifies, and the distribution utilities must agree. A regional act can require its own government to install the systems; whether a national bureau certifies and a utility signs is not within its gift, and the bill asserts the obligation on utilities without addressing that.

Naming internally displaced persons and victims of conflict among the beneficiaries ties this to the rest of the registry. The region has 2 competing bills on internal displacement, neither enacted, and a transitional justice package largely stalled. This measure would reach the same population through the thing they most immediately need after a roof, which is light.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 68, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants recognition and cash incentives to Bangsamoro who place from Top 1 to Top 10 in board, bar and other national licensure examinations — and it is the only one of the 8 competing incentive bills that names no amount.

Coverage is all Bangsamoro individuals and other inhabitants of the region who rank in the top 10 of any national licensure examination, including the professional examinations given by the Professional Regulation Commission and the Bar examination administered by the Supreme Court. A topnotcher must hold the corresponding certification from the administering agency.

Section 5 is where the money question goes. A Committee is created under the Office of the Chief Minister with 3 tasks: write a procedural manual for granting the recognition and incentives, assess the documents required to verify a claimant's authenticity and rank, and determine "the amount of incentives that the topnotchers will receive". The appropriation clause then funds whatever that committee decides, out of the Office of the Chief Minister's budget in the annual appropriations act.

The implementing rules fall to the education ministry, within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues from the cost of the attempt rather than the value of the result. Every board or bar candidate has been through "a staggering test of mettle through a gauntlet of hardships, adversities, and pressures", made worse by the COVID-19 pandemic, and the burden is mental, economic and spiritual. Placing in the top 10 after that is "an impressive feat worthy of emulation and public acknowledgment".

The policy section adds the regional argument: promoting self-reliant capabilities, optimum proficiency and improved aptitude, and recognising those who bring honour and distinction to the region.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro and other residents of the region who place Top 1 to Top 10 in any national licensure examination.
Bar examinees, whose examination is named specifically alongside the PRC's.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which houses the committee and carries the appropriation.
A committee of unnamed composition, which would decide how much each topnotcher actually receives.
The Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, which writes the implementing rules.
implementedBy: A Committee created under the Office of the Chief Minister — procedural manual, verification of documents and rank, and determination of the incentive amounts
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education — implementing rules within 90 days of approval

funding.detail: No amount is named anywhere in the bill, and no scale is set. Section 5(c) gives a committee under the Office of the Chief Minister the power to determine the amount of incentives, and Section 6 funds whatever that comes to through the Office of the Chief Minister's line in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Placing in the top 10 of a national licensure examination becomes a statutory basis for a cash incentive.
A committee under the Office of the Chief Minister gains the power to set the amounts.
Verification of rank runs through documents certified by the administering national agency.
readings.insight:
The design choice that distinguishes this bill is the one most readers would call a gap. Section 5(c) delegates the amount of the incentive to a committee, which means the entitlement this Act creates has no value fixed in law — an incoming administration could set it at ₱1,000 without amending anything. Against that, none of the rival bills can adjust to a bad year without going back to Parliament, and 7 of them lock in figures that were chosen in 2022 and 2023 and would be worth measurably less by the time they were paid.

There is a second asymmetry worth naming. The committee sits under the Office of the Chief Minister and also writes the procedural manual and verifies the claims, while the implementing rules are written by the education ministry. 2 offices hold parts of the same process and the bill does not say how they settle a disagreement.

8 bills in this registry do this same job, and reading them together is the point. Bill No. 69 and Bill No. 200 are MP Mawallil's; Bill No. 207 and Bill No. 208 are MP Loong's; Bill No. 198 is MP Dilangalen's, Bill No. 201 MP Ampatuan's, Bill No. 202 MP Ramos's, and Bill No. 222 MP Hashim's. 7 of the 8 were filed between 16 and 23 June 2023 — 1 week — and all 8 were referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management on the same day, 16 October 2024. Parliament took more than a year to notice they were one subject, and then noticed all at once.

The spread on the same achievement is the substantive finding. A Bar topnotcher placing first would receive ₱100,000 under Bill 207, ₱100,000 under Bill 202, ₱150,000 under Bill 198, and ₱500,000 under Bill 222 — a fivefold range for an identical result, with no published committee record reconciling them. Bill 69 and Bill 200 name no figure at all and hand the amount to an administrative body.

This is also 1 of 2 bills the same member filed on this subject — the other, Bill No. 200, does the same thing for athletes and likewise leaves the amount to an agency. Whatever the drafting office's view, it was applied consistently.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 69, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the most ambitious of the 3 dialysis bills: within 5 years of effectivity, a dialysis unit in every government hospital in the region.

Section 3 specifies what a unit means rather than leaving it to rules. Sufficient machines, equipment, paraphernalia and supplies, and appropriate numbers of medical and other personnel — naming nephrologists, dialysis nurses, dialysis technicians and operating room nurses, in both peritoneal and hemodialysis. Every hospital in the region, including stand-alone dialysis facilities, must have a dialysis service area compliant with the licensing and accreditation requirements of the national Department of Health and PhilHealth.

Section 4 makes treatment free for indigent patients in all government hospitals, and defines who that is: a patient with no visible means of income, compensation or financial assistance from relatives to support basic needs, or whose income is insufficient for the family's subsistence, as identified by the Ministry of Social Services and Development.

Section 6 is the part no other dialysis bill has. Every government hospital and stand-alone centre must run chronic kidney disease prevention and health promotion — advocacy aimed at the relatives of dialysis patients, who are themselves at risk; instructional materials and regular education on symptoms, risk factors, diet and lifestyle, the diagnostic tests and the common causes of kidney failure; and advisories on diagnostic protocols. Patients and relatives must be told that medicines for diabetes and hypertension are available from government health centres, and about the importance of taking them regularly and monitoring kidney function.

Quality and safety standards are monitored by the health ministry, rules are due within 90 days, and funding comes from the ministry's current appropriations and then the annual budget.
readings.whyProposed:
Kidney failure is among the leading causes of disease-related death in the Philippines, and dialysis is the treatment that keeps a patient alive — 2 or 3 sessions a week, indefinitely, at a cost no ordinary household absorbs. A region whose government hospitals cannot provide it forces patients to travel for every session or to stop.

The bill's structural argument is in Section 6. Dialysis is the most expensive possible point at which to intervene in kidney disease, and the diseases that cause most of it — diabetes and hypertension — are treatable at a health centre for a fraction of the cost. A dialysis statute that also mandates prevention is trying to reduce the number of people who reach the machine.
whoIsAffected: Patients with kidney failure anywhere in the region, who would have a unit in their local government hospital.
Indigent patients, entitled to free treatment once identified by the social services ministry.
Relatives of dialysis patients, expressly targeted by the prevention advocacy because they share the risk factors.
Every government hospital in the region, which must build, staff and license a unit within 5 years.
Stand-alone private dialysis facilities, also required to meet the service-area standard.
Nephrologists, dialysis nurses and technicians, whose posts the Act would create across the region.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — ensuring free treatment for indigents, monitoring safety and quality standards, and issuing rules within 90 days
All government hospitals in the region, which must establish and staff the units and run the prevention programmes
Ministry of Social Services and Development, which identifies indigent patients
National Department of Health and PhilHealth, whose licensing and accreditation standards the service areas must meet

funding.detail: No amount is named. Initial implementation is taken from the Ministry of Health's current appropriations, with later requirements in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act. For a mandate to build, equip and staff dialysis units in every government hospital in the region within 5 years, that is the bill's central weakness — the cost is real, recurring and unestimated.

whatChanges: Every government hospital in the region must have a dialysis unit within 5 years.
Units must be staffed with named specialists and offer both peritoneal and hemodialysis.
Indigent patients receive dialysis free, on identification by the social services ministry.
Hospitals must run kidney disease prevention and education, including for patients' relatives.
Service areas must meet national licensing and PhilHealth accreditation standards.
readings.insight:
Section 6 is why this bill is worth more than its 2 rivals put together. Dialysis is where kidney disease ends up, and a region that builds machines without touching the causes will fill them. Requiring every hospital to run prevention — and specifically to target the relatives of the patients already on dialysis, who share the household diet, the genetics and the untreated hypertension — is the cheapest intervention in the whole document and the only one that reduces future demand. It also names the practical link that gets missed: telling patients and families that the diabetes and hypertension medicines are available free at a government health centre.

Naming the staff is the other thing this bill does that the others do not. A dialysis unit is not a room with machines; it needs a nephrologist, dialysis nurses and trained technicians, and specifying both peritoneal and hemodialysis matters because peritoneal dialysis can be done at home and is often the only realistic option for a patient on an island. A mandate that lists the posts is a mandate the finance ministry has to cost.

Which is where the bill is exposed. Every government hospital in the region within 5 years, equipped, licensed and staffed with nephrologists — funded from "the current appropriations of the Ministry of Health". There are not enough nephrologists in the region to staff that, and the bill contains no training pipeline, no salary premium and no figure. Bill No. 279 reaches the opposite conclusion from the same problem, confining the duty to provincial tertiary hospitals, and Bill No. 145 confines it to 1 hospital and puts ₱20 million behind it. Read together, the 3 bills are an argument about whether to promise everything and fund nothing, or promise 1 thing and build it.

3 bills in this registry address dialysis and they pick 3 different scales. Bill No. 88, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022, requires a dialysis unit in every government hospital in the region within 5 years. Bill No. 145, filed by MP Sema in February 2023, builds 1 centre at 1 named hospital with ₱20 million behind it. Bill No. 279, filed by MP Dilangalen in February 2024, requires provincial tertiary hospitals to have a unit within 1 year. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 88, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This imposes a region-wide curfew on minors from 10:00 pm to 4:00 am, and it is the most heavily researched bill in the registry — 15 pages carrying more than 50 footnotes.

2 things are prohibited: a minor roaming, loitering, wandering, staying, meandering or remaining in any public place during curfew hours without lawful purpose or justifiable reason; and a parent or guardian knowingly permitting that, or allowing it through insufficient control.

The exceptions run to 8 paragraphs and are lifted, with attribution, from the Quezon City ordinance the Supreme Court upheld in G.R. No. 225442. A minor is outside the Act when accompanied or authorised in writing by a parent to run lawful errands; travelling to or from a lawful activity, graduation, religious observance or school-sanctioned extra-curricular activity, or unable to get home early for reasons beyond their control; attending or experiencing an emergency such as a fire, earthquake, hospitalisation, road accident or an encounter involving law enforcers; in authorised employment or travelling directly to or from it; in a vehicle accompanied by an adult; involved in an emergency; attending or returning from an official school, religious, recreational, educational, social or community activity sponsored and supervised by a recognised body; or able to produce papers showing they are a student dismissed from an evening class or a working student.

Section 12 is where the bill's legal care shows. Following Section 57-A of Republic Act No. 9344, the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, it provides that no penalty is imposed on the child for a curfew violation — a status offence — while the parent or guardian may be fined or penalised. The consequences are graduated: on a first offence the child is brought home or to a barangay official, their name recorded in the barangay logbook, and the Barangay Council for the Protection of Children counsels the child with the parents before release, with both admonished about what follows a second violation.

Each local government writes the implementing rules, the Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children enforce, and each council keeps a Barangay Curfew for Minors Logbook. Age may be established by birth certificate, baptismal certificate or other documents.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill's own footnote records where it came from: it was inspired by the entry of Ms. Firdaus S. Abdullah in the Office of MP Ampatuan's Online Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest, under the same title.

The case it builds is about exposure rather than delinquency — children out at night are more likely to be harmed, recruited or exploited, and the note cites the child protection statutes to that effect: Republic Act No. 7610 on child abuse and exploitation, Republic Act No. 9775 on child pornography, and Article 139 of the Child and Youth Welfare Code, which already lets city and municipal councils set curfew hours. The argument for a regional act is uniformity: a curfew that exists in some municipalities and not others protects children unevenly.
whoIsAffected: Every minor in the region, subject to a curfew between 10:00 pm and 4:00 am.
Working students and students dismissed from evening classes, expressly excepted on production of papers.
Minors in authorised employment, travelling directly to or from work.
Parents and guardians, who may be fined or penalised where the child may not be.
Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children, which enforce, counsel and keep the logbook.
Local government units, each of which writes its own implementing rules.
implementedBy: Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children (BCPC) — enforcement, counselling, and the Barangay Curfew for Minors Logbook
Each local government unit, which promulgates the implementing rules
Barangay officials, to whom an apprehended child is brought

funding.detail: No appropriation. Enforcement rests on existing barangay structures, and the only money in the Act is the fine a parent or guardian may be made to pay.

whatChanges: A uniform curfew applies to minors across the whole region rather than municipality by municipality.
No penalty may be imposed on a child for violating it; the parent or guardian bears the consequence.
First offences route to counselling with the parents rather than to custody.
Barangays keep a logbook of children apprehended.
8 categories of exception protect students, workers and those caught by emergencies.
readings.insight:
Section 12 is the reason this bill deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as a curfew. Section 57-A of the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act provides that juvenile status offences — being out late, truancy — carry no penalty for the child, because the point is protection rather than punishment. Curfew ordinances across the Philippines have repeatedly been struck down or criticised for ignoring that. This bill applies it correctly, puts the liability on the parent, and routes a first offence to counselling conducted with the family rather than to a cell. A drafter who knew only that curfews are popular would not have written that.

The citation practice is what makes the bill unusual. It lifts its exceptions from the Quezon City ordinance *and says so in a footnote*, noting that the Supreme Court upheld that ordinance in G.R. No. 225442 as sufficiently safeguarding minors' constitutional rights. Copying the text that survived judicial review, and showing the reader that is what you are doing, is a better method than drafting fresh language that has not been tested — and the bill does the same with its definition of admonition, citing the Court's own gloss.

The gap is in the hours. Section 4 imposes 10:00 pm to 4:00 am. The model the bill relies on, and the ordinance the Supreme Court upheld, runs 10:00 pm to 5:00 am, and the note discusses that version. Shortening the curfew by an hour is a choice the bill does not explain, and it matters for the constitutional argument the footnotes are built to support: the narrower the restriction, the easier it is to defend, so the change is probably in the bill's favour — but a measure resting this heavily on a precedent should say where it departs from it.

Some drafting untidiness survives from the sources. The section numbering carries 2 provisions numbered 8 and 2 numbered 12, a stray Section 21, and an unnumbered section on determination of age; and exception (e) refers to "this Ordinance" rather than this Act, which is the Quezon City text showing through. None of that affects the substance, and all of it would need cleaning before enactment.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires social preparation before a development project is built — a preliminary engagement with the community that will host it, conducted on a stated timetable before construction begins.

The periods are set by project type. At least 1 month of community engagement for education ministry vertical projects — school buildings, madaris buildings, water and sanitation. At least 1 month for public works and agriculture ministry horizontal infrastructure: roads, bridges, shore protection, drainage. At least 2 months for public works and interior ministry vertical infrastructure: multi-purpose buildings, gymnasiums, covered courts, government buildings and housing.

Around that sit objectives, expected outcomes, and a set of key strategies and activities for the social preparation phase. Section 8 requires each agency to maintain a database, feeding a Bangsamoro Government database. Section 10 sets a mandatory review after 10 years, and Section 11 provides for parliamentary oversight of implementation.

Section 12 carves out 2 exceptions: projects covered by emergency initiatives, and conditional cash transfers.
readings.whyProposed:
The premise is that infrastructure fails in this region for social reasons more often than technical ones. A school built where a community did not want it, a road crossing contested land, a housing project allocated without consultation — each becomes an abandoned structure or a grievance, and the money is spent either way.

Social preparation is the standard remedy in development practice: engage before you build, so that the project has a community behind it and the disputes surface while they can still be addressed. The bill's contribution is to make it mandatory and to put a minimum duration on it, which is what stops it becoming a signature gathered the week before groundbreaking.
whoIsAffected: Communities hosting development projects, who gain a guaranteed engagement period before construction.
The education, public works, agriculture and interior ministries, whose projects carry 1 or 2 month engagement requirements.
Contractors and implementing offices, whose project timelines lengthen by the engagement period.
Communities affected by emergency projects and recipients of conditional cash transfers, both expressly outside the Act.
Parliament, which gains an oversight function over implementation.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Government through the implementing rules, with each agency conducting the social preparation for its own projects
Each agency maintaining a database, consolidated into a Bangsamoro Government database
The Bangsamoro Parliament, exercising oversight under Section 11

funding.detail: No appropriation. The cost is staff time and travel inside existing project budgets, which is the realistic way to fund a process requirement — and also the reason it can be skipped if nobody checks.

whatChanges: Community engagement becomes a mandatory phase before construction rather than good practice.
Minimum engagement periods are fixed by project type, from 1 to 2 months.
Agencies must keep records of the engagement, consolidated regionally.
Emergency projects and cash transfers are exempt.
Parliament acquires oversight and a 10-year mandatory review.
readings.insight:
Putting a minimum duration on consultation is what makes this bill more than a statement of intent. Every development agency in the world claims to consult; the question is always whether the consultation happened before the decision or after it. 1 month for a school building and 2 for a gymnasium are short periods, but they are periods — a project that cannot show them has not complied, which is a test an auditor can apply.

The graduated timetable also shows the drafter thought about which projects are contentious. Roads and bridges get 1 month; multi-purpose buildings, gymnasiums, covered courts, government buildings and housing get 2. That is the right way round: a road's route is contested but its benefit is diffuse, whereas a covered court or a housing allocation is a discrete good sited in 1 barangay rather than another, and that is what communities actually fight about.

The exceptions are correctly drawn and worth noting for what they imply. Emergency initiatives cannot wait a month, and a conditional cash transfer has no site to prepare. Carving out exactly those 2 and nothing else means the Act bites on the ordinary construction programme, which is where the money is.

Read against Bill No. 63, the conflict sensitivity bill filed by another member a month later, the 2 measures are halves of a single idea — analyse the conflict before you plan, and engage the community before you build. Neither has moved past Committee Stage, while the provision that did become law is the one in BAA 49 requiring newly elected local officials to be trained in conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding. The region has legislated the training and not the process.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes an Annex Bangsamoro Government Center within Cotabato City, to decongest the existing one.

Section 4 sets 6 criteria for choosing the site, each defined. It must be sparsely populated, and must not cause displacement of the people living in the target area. It must be within Cotabato City and within a 10-kilometer radius of the existing centre. It must have minimal exposure to natural and human-induced hazards. It must be accessible — connected to the city's main roads, reachable by the public once operational, and accessible to banks and the main commercial areas. It must be within reach of existing internet service provider towers or have the potential for one. And it must be within the service areas of the Cotabato Light and Power Company and the Metro Cotabato Water District, so that power and water supply are stable.

The centre is to be not less than 5 hectares, with a stated minimum of office buildings and facilities, and Section 7 identifies the target users.
readings.whyProposed:
The stated objective is decongestion: the existing Bangsamoro Government Center is full, and offices spread across rented premises deliver worse service than offices in one place.

The criteria are the substance of the argument, and they are written by someone who had watched government buildings go up in the wrong places — in flood-prone ground, beyond the reach of a reliable power line, or where people had to be moved to make room.
whoIsAffected: Constituents dealing with regional government offices, who would find them consolidated rather than dispersed.
Residents of any candidate site, protected by the requirement that the centre cause no displacement.
Regional government employees and the offices identified as target users.
Cotabato City, which would host a second government complex of at least 5 hectares.
The Cotabato Light and Power Company and the Metro Cotabato Water District, whose service areas bound the site.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Government, applying the 6 statutory site criteria and building to the stated minimum facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. A government complex of not less than 5 hectares with a specified minimum of office buildings is a major capital project, and the bill leaves the figure to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: A second government centre is established in Cotabato City, at least 5 hectares.
Site selection becomes governed by 6 defined statutory criteria rather than discretion.
No site may be chosen that would displace the people living on it.
Hazard exposure, internet, power and water availability become legal conditions of the choice.
readings.insight:
This bill and the act that moved the capital point in opposite directions, and they were before the same Parliament within weeks of each other. Bill No. 43, filed in September 2022, establishes the seat of government at Parang and was enacted as BAA 37 in June 2023. This bill, filed in October 2022, builds a second government centre in Cotabato City. One measure leaves the city; the other invests in it.

They are not strictly incompatible, and BAA 37 is the reason. Its Section 7 requires the existing centre in Cotabato City to be improved rather than abandoned, preserved for its historical value and renamed once the move is complete. An annex consistent with that could be read as the improvement the act contemplates. But BAA 37 also provides that the transfer to Parang proceeds gradually as buildings and utilities are completed, so a region building a new 5-hectare complex in the city it is leaving would be funding 2 capitals at once — and neither document acknowledges the other.

The site criteria are the part worth keeping regardless of what happens to the capital. 6 conditions, each defined, including a bar on displacement and a requirement that power and water be available from the named utilities, is a better procurement standard than most public buildings in the region are held to — and the registry supplies the evidence for why it is needed, in the hospital bill that documents a facility whose structure was built for 10 beds while its designation said 50.

The displacement criterion deserves separate credit. "Shall not be a cause of displacements of the population residing in the target area" is a single clause, and in a region where displacement is the defining social fact and where the indigenous peoples act had to legislate against development-driven removal, writing it into the siting rule for a government building is the kind of consistency that is easy to omit.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 96, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the Bangsamoro Revenue Sharing Act of 2022, and it is not the measure Parliament's index says it is. The filed copy is MP Baintan Ampatuan's bill detailing how the region's share of national taxes is divided with its local governments — see the note at the end of this reading on the indexing.

The Organic Law splits the national taxes, fees and charges collected inside the region: 25% to the National Government, accruing to the Bangsamoro Government for the first 10 years and extendable on petition, and 75% to the Bangsamoro Government inclusive of the shares of its constituent local governments. Section 13 of Article XII then requires Parliament to enact a law detailing what those local shares are. This bill is the attempt to do that.

Section 4 counts the region for the purpose: 5 provinces, 3 cities, 116 municipalities and 2,590 barangays, including the 37 barangays of Cotabato City and the 63 barangays of North Cotabato that voted to join.

Section 5 then sets the distribution of the 75% share — 30% to the Bangsamoro Government, 20% to the provinces, 20% to the cities, 20% to the municipalities and 20% to the barangays.

The mechanics are direct. Section 6 requires the National Government, through the Department of Budget and Management, to transfer the 75% share to the Bangsamoro Treasury Office starting with fiscal year 2021 "without need of any further action". Section 7 makes the Treasury Office the principal custodian and requires it, on the Chief Minister's approval, to release the local shares on a regular basis. The finance ministry writes rules for a simplified disbursement scheme designed for speedy and effective enforcement.
readings.whyProposed:
The Organic Law requires this law to exist. Section 13 of Article XII directs Parliament to enact a statute detailing the constituent local governments' shares in the region's 75%, and until it does, the local governments' entitlement is a figure in a national transfer with no regional rule allocating it.

The declaration builds the case from both directions — the national policy of local autonomy and adequate resourcing under the Local Government Code, and the region's own right to fiscal autonomy under the Organic Law, with the principles named: equalization, equity, accountability, administrative simplicity, harmonization, economic efficiency and fiscal autonomy. Section 3 adds the practical argument that local governments cannot discharge devolved responsibilities without resources to match.
whoIsAffected: All 5 provinces, 3 cities, 116 municipalities and 2,590 barangays of the region, whose share of regional revenue this bill would fix.
Cotabato City's 37 barangays and the 63 barangays from North Cotabato, expressly counted in.
The Bangsamoro Treasury Office, made principal custodian and responsible for regular release.
The Office of the Chief Minister, whose approval conditions each release.
The national Department of Budget and Management, directed to transfer the 75% share without further action from fiscal year 2021.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which must design a simplified disbursement scheme.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Treasury Office — principal custodian of the funds and the office that releases local shares
Office of the Chief Minister, approving releases
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — rules for a simplified disbursement scheme
National Department of Budget and Management, transferring the 75% share to the Bangsamoro Treasury

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing; it allocates an existing revenue stream. The sums involved are nonetheless the largest in the registry — the 75% share of all national taxes, fees and charges collected in the region, which the bill directs be transferred to the Bangsamoro Treasury from fiscal year 2021 onward, separate and distinct from the annual block grant.

whatChanges: Local governments get a stated share of regional revenue rather than an unallocated entitlement.
The Bangsamoro Treasury Office becomes the custodian and the release point for local shares.
The national budget department is directed to transfer the 75% share without further action, backdated to fiscal year 2021.
A simplified disbursement scheme must be designed for speed.
readings.insight:
The distribution in Section 5 does not add up. 30% to the Bangsamoro Government plus 20% each to provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays is 110% of a 75% share. The words and the numerals agree on every line, and re-reading the page at higher resolution with a different segmentation returns the same 5 figures, so this is the filed text rather than a scanning artefact. A revenue-sharing statute whose formula exceeds the fund it divides cannot be implemented as written — whichever body is paid last receives nothing, and the bill does not say who that is.

That matters more than an ordinary drafting slip would, because of what this bill is. The Organic Law obliges Parliament to enact a law detailing local shares; this is the measure filed to discharge that obligation, and it has been at Committee Stage since October 2022. The consequence is not academic. Until the law exists, the 75% share reaches the region as a single sum and the local governments' portion of it rests on administrative practice rather than on the statutory entitlement the Organic Law contemplates — which is the same gap that the ₱2.5 and ₱3 million monthly bridging subsidies for new municipalities elsewhere in this registry are improvising around.

The allocation's shape is worth reading even though its arithmetic fails, because it shows the intended priority. Under this formula the regional government keeps the largest single share and the 4 tiers of local government are treated identically — a barangay tier of 2,590 units and a city tier of 3 receive the same 20%. Whether that is equalisation or its opposite depends on facts about population and revenue the bill does not supply, and the Organic Law's own list of principles includes both equalization and equity as things the allocation is meant to serve.

Section 6's instruction to the national budget department is the provision most likely to be contested. A regional statute directing a national department to transfer funds "without need of any further action", backdated to a fiscal year already closed when the bill was filed, asserts more than a regional legislature can straightforwardly command — the same pattern as the indigenous peoples act's certification requirement on national agencies and the electoral code's arrangements with COMELEC.

**A note on the indexing, because it matters for anyone looking this measure up.** Parliament's bills index lists Bill No. 97 under the title of a hospital upgrade — the Datu Alawaddin T. Bandon, Sr. Memorial Hospital in Sibutu — and attributes it to MP Eddie Alih. The filed PDF under that number is this revenue-sharing bill by MP Ampatuan, and the index's own URL for the entry points at a page slugged "an-act-detailing-the-shares-of-local-government-units-in-the-seventy-five-percent-75-share". So the index's title and author fields are crossed: they belong to the Sibutu hospital measure, which is Bill No. 100, filed by MP Alih and enacted as BAA 76. This reading is of the document the number actually carries.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Evacuation Center Act of 2022 requires the Bangsamoro Government to build a standard evacuation center in every municipality and city in the region.

The Ministry of Public Works prepares the standard design and the construction, working from the Philippine building code. Each center must stand in a safe and accessible place in the town and accommodate at least 100 to 200 internally displaced people. It must have proper ventilation, a kitchen, water, plumbing and sanitation, and facilities for women — breastfeeding mothers are named — for the elderly and for people with special needs.

Management sits with the Ministry of Social Services and Development, delivered on the ground by the Municipal or City Social Welfare and Development Officer, who gets a designated office inside the center that doubles as their municipal office. The local government complements MSSD’s manpower through the municipal disaster risk reduction officer.

The centers are also meant to work between disasters: the objectives include giving each local government a designated place for prepositioning, stocking, repacking and piling relief goods, so supplies are staged before an emergency rather than moved during one.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is a single line about safety and general welfare in crisis and disaster situations. The explanatory note is more specific: the Philippines is disaster-prone and the Bangsamoro carries typhoons, floods, landslides, earthquakes and drought, along with fires and displacement caused by armed groups. It opens with a hadith on relieving a believer of the hardships of this world.

The practical problem it addresses is one every disaster in this region exposes. In the absence of purpose-built centers, displaced families are housed in schools and covered courts — which closes the schools, provides no sanitation for the numbers involved, and gives no privacy at all.
whoIsAffected: Displaced families across the region, who currently shelter in schools and covered courts.
Women and breastfeeding mothers, the elderly and people with special needs, named for specific facilities.
Every municipality and city in BARMM, each of which would host a center.
Municipal and City Social Welfare and Development Officers, who would manage the centers and be based in them.
Schools, which would stop being the default shelter.
Basilan and Marawi City, where social welfare services are already devolved and which the Act only encourages rather than binds.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW), for the standard design and construction
Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD), which supervises the centers
Municipal and City Social Welfare and Development Officers, who manage them
Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officers, who complement MSSD manpower

funding.detail: No figure. Construction, operation and maintenance are to be included in the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region. A purpose-built center in each of the region’s municipalities and cities is a large capital program, and the bill states neither a total nor a per-unit cost.

whatChanges: Every municipality and city in the region is to have a standard evacuation center.
A standard design exists, drawn by MPW against the national building code.
Centers must hold at least 100 to 200 people and carry kitchen, water, sanitation and facilities for women, the elderly and people with special needs.
MSSD supervises and the municipal or city social welfare officer manages, from an office inside the center.
Local governments gain a designated place to preposition and repack relief goods.
readings.insight:
The capacity figure is the thing to look at hardest. A center built for 100 to 200 people is the right size for a barangay-scale flood and nowhere near the right size for what this region actually experiences. The 2017 Marawi siege displaced roughly 200,000 people; a single bad flood season in the Maguindanao lowlands displaces tens of thousands. One center per municipality at 200 heads is a floor worth having and should not be mistaken for a plan that meets the region’s largest events.

Section 8 contains an odd carve-out. The Act covers all municipalities and cities in the region, but where social welfare has already been devolved to the local government — the bill names Basilan province and Marawi City — those LGUs are merely "encouraged" to implement it. Marawi is the site of the largest displacement in the region’s recent history, and it is the one place the Act does not bind.

The office-inside-the-center provision is quietly clever and easy to miss. Putting the social welfare officer’s permanent municipal office in the evacuation center means the building is occupied, staffed and maintained between emergencies rather than standing empty and deteriorating, which is how most single-purpose emergency structures fail.

On its progress: filed September 2022, First Reading January 2023, and then referred to the Committee on Local Government in July 2025 — 2.5 years between reading and referral.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Level 1 general hospital of 50 beds in South Ubian, Tawi-Tawi, to be known as the South Ubian Municipal Hospital.

The operative text is 6 sections and holds no surprises: the Ministry of Health determines which units and services the hospital needs, integrates the Universal Health Care Act into how it runs, and holds direct supervision including the organizational structure and the plantilla positions. The finance ministry funds the plantilla and the maintenance and operating expenses through the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. No construction budget is named, and no amount appears anywhere in the bill.

What carries the measure is the explanatory note, which is unusually concrete. South Ubian is a 3rd class coastal municipality of roughly 29,583 people across about 27,204 hectares, with a poverty incidence of 25.27%. Its entire health provision is one health center on Tabawan island headed by a nurse, plus 5 barangay health stations headed by midwives — no doctor. Anyone needing hospital care travels 96 km by motor launch to Bongao, a trip of 8 to 10 hours on a boat that sails 3 times a week, usually in a condition not fit for travel. The note states plainly that there have been many fatalities in transit and on arrival.
readings.whyProposed:
The note builds its case on 3 provisions of the Organic Law rather than on general principle: Article IX Section 8, requiring the Bangsamoro Government to deliver basic and responsive health programs; Article IX Section 22, requiring it to establish a general hospital system by law; and Article XII Section 19, requiring Parliament to assign the highest budgetary priority to education, health and social services.

The argument it makes from them is a geographic one. A region that has committed to a hospital system and to funding it first has an obligation that reaches the islands, and the note closes on it: "a torch of hope lit in a small island in Tawi-Tawi... This time, nobody will be left behind."
whoIsAffected: The roughly 29,583 residents of South Ubian, and the neighbouring islands the bill names as part of the hospital's purpose.
Patients who currently make the 96 km crossing to Bongao, and those who cannot.
The nurse-led health center on Tabawan and the 5 midwife-led barangay health stations, whose referral destination changes.
Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital in Bongao, which carries this catchment today.
The Ministry of Health, which supervises the hospital and sets its structure and plantilla.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — direct supervision, organizational structure, plantilla positions, and the units and services the hospital will carry
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — annual funding for plantilla and operating expenses through the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act

funding.detail: No amount is named. The finance ministry is to provide annual funding for plantilla positions and for maintenance and other operating expenses through the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. Construction is not separately funded in the bill. The enacted act supplied the figure: BAA 66 appropriates ₱50 million from the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund of the 2025 Bangsamoro budget.

whatChanges: South Ubian gets a hospital rather than a health center headed by a nurse.
A 96 km sea crossing stops being the nearest route to hospital care for the municipality.
The Ministry of Health takes direct supervision, including the creation of permanent plantilla posts.
Universal Health Care Act provisions are folded into the hospital's operations.
readings.insight:
The bill asked for 50 beds. BAA 66 established 25.

That halving is the single most important fact about this measure, and it is not unique to South Ubian — the Sibutu bill filed the same day by the same principal author asked to upgrade a 10-bed hospital to Level II with 50 beds, and BAA 76 delivered Level I with 25. 2 bills, same author, same province, same reduction. Whatever the reasoning, Parliament applied it consistently, and the published record does not contain it.

What the act added is worth setting against what it took away. BAA 66 names ₱50 million and charges it to a specific fund in a specific year's budget, where this bill names no figure at all and leaves construction unfunded. A bill that asks for twice the beds and no money is, in practice, asking for less than a law that gives half the beds and pays for them. The act also wrote the neighbouring islands into the catchment, which is the bill's own framing carried into the statute.

The explanatory note deserves to be read on its own terms. Most bills in this registry argue from policy; this one argues from a boat schedule. 3 sailings a week, 8 to 10 hours, 96 km, and deaths in transit — the case is made in facts a constituent could check, and the drafting that follows is almost an afterthought by comparison.

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Datu Alawaddin T. Bandon, Sr. Memorial Hospital in Sibutu, Tawi-Tawi, from a Level I facility of 10 beds to a Level II general hospital of 50 beds.

It also fixes a 32-year-old error of geography. The hospital was created by Republic Act No. 6853 in 1990 as a 10-bed municipal hospital in Sitangkai. Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 197 later carved Sibutu out of Sitangkai, and the hospital ended up in the new municipality while the national law still says otherwise. Section 2 of this bill simply declares the location to be Sibutu.

Beyond the upgrade, 2 provisions do more than the genre requires. Section 4 upgrades existing facilities and professional manpower to Level II standards and requires the operating systems to keep up with advances in science and technology. It then asks for something specific: the hospital's information system is to be streamlined into a complete patient record in a simplified, easily comprehensible format, able to sync and share the inputs of doctors and authorised personnel across departments and offices, generating clear and instantaneous communication. That is a health records mandate written into a hospital charter, and it is rare in this registry.

Supervision goes to the Ministry of Health with the finance ministry, which together approve the structure and plantilla and monitor the administration of the hospital.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues from occupancy. Sibutu is a municipality of roughly 34,243 people — mostly boat builders and seaweed farmers — on 109 square kilometers, about 14 km from the coast of Sabah. Its only hospital is Level I with 10 beds, and the management reported average bed occupancy of 95.89% in 2019, 85.44% in 2020 and 73% in 2021. Poverty incidence is 26.26%.

The referral chain is the rest of the case. The next facility is Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital in Bongao, 51.7 km away, reachable only by a motor launch scheduled 3 times a week, 3 hours at sea. Sakilan is itself a Level I hospital running at 150 to 200% occupancy, so in most cases patients continue to Zamboanga City. The note says this has caused numerous fatalities.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 34,243 residents of Sibutu, whose only hospital runs at or near capacity.
Patients currently referred onward to Bongao and then to Zamboanga City.
The staff of the existing 10-bed hospital, whose facilities and professional complement are to be upgraded.
Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital in Bongao, already operating at 150 to 200% occupancy.
The Ministry of Health and the finance ministry, which jointly determine the upgraded structure and plantilla.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — organizational structure, plantilla positions, and supervision and monitoring of the hospital
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — annual funding through the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act

funding.detail: No amount is named. The finance ministry is to provide annual funding for plantilla positions and for maintenance and other operating expenses in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. The enacted act supplied a figure: BAA 76 appropriates ₱50 million charged against the 2025 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: A 10-bed Level I hospital becomes a Level II general hospital of 50 beds.
The hospital's legal location moves from Sitangkai to Sibutu, catching the statute up with a municipal boundary drawn after it.
Facilities and professional manpower are upgraded to Level II standards.
The hospital is required to run a unified, shareable patient information system.
Universal Health Care Act provisions are integrated into its operations.
readings.insight:
Parliament granted half of what this bill asked for. The bill sought Level II with 50 beds; BAA 76 established Level I with 25. The same author's South Ubian bill, filed the same day, asked for 50 beds and got 25 as well. Whatever standard Parliament was applying to island hospitals, it applied it twice, and no published committee record explains it.

The records provision survived, which is the more interesting outcome. Section 4's requirement for a streamlined, shareable patient information system is the kind of clause that usually gets cut as administrative detail, and BAA 76 kept it. The act then went further than the bill in a direction the bill did not anticipate: it requires the hospital administrator to file an annual report on operations, performance, financial expenditure and service delivery outcomes, copied to the local governments and — the words that matter — made publicly accessible. A hospital in Sibutu now has a statutory transparency duty that most regional agencies do not.

Section 2 is worth a moment on its own. A national law of 1990 placed this hospital in Sitangkai; a regional law of 2006 created Sibutu out of Sitangkai and left the hospital sitting in a municipality its own charter does not name. The bill resolves it in 2 sentences. Small statutory housekeeping of this kind rarely gets filed at all, and the gap had stood for 16 years.
