readings.whatItDoes:
One amendment, in one section, to one line of a budget law. This rewrites Section 3 of BAA 22 — the Special Development Fund appropriations for 2020 and 2021 — to keep that money alive until 31 December 2023.

The extension is graded by what the money buys. Everything stays available for release and disbursement until the end of 2023. Infrastructure capital outlays may be obligated until then, with construction, inspection and payment allowed to run on to 30 June 2024. Maintenance and other operating expenses and other capital outlays may also be obligated until the end of 2023, with delivery, inspection and payment permitted until 31 March 2024.

The finance ministry issues the guidelines. That is the entire bill: 3 sections, 1 page, no appropriation of its own.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note on the filed copy. The Special Development Fund is the money the national government committed to the region under the peace agreement, appropriated regionally for 2020 and 2021, and a cash-based budget makes an appropriation expire at the end of its year.

The unstated premise is that the money had not been spent. An extension bill is only ever filed because the alternative — letting the appropriation lapse and reverting the balance — would mean the projects it was meant to build do not get built.
whoIsAffected: Communities waiting on Special Development Fund projects from the 2020 and 2021 programs.
Ministries and offices holding unobligated or undisbursed balances from those years.
Contractors on infrastructure whose completion, inspection and payment window moves to mid-2024.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which writes the guidelines and administers the cash budgeting system.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management (MFBM) — guidelines for the cash budgeting system as amended

funding.detail: No new money. The bill extends the life of appropriations already made under BAA 22 rather than adding to them.

whatChanges: The 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund stays spendable through 2023 instead of lapsing.
Infrastructure work funded from it may be completed and paid up to 30 June 2024.
Operating and other capital items may be delivered and paid up to 31 March 2024.
deliberation: 21 December 2022: MP Ubaida C. Pacasem said the ₱5,000,000,000 yearly Special Development Fund reached ministries late, in the second half of 2021 for 2020 funds and the second quarter of 2022 for 2021 funds, and was further slowed by the pandemic.
21 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan explained that SDF approval came only in October 2021 and actual implementation of the 2020 and 2021 funds would begin in January 2023.

21 December 2022: MP Susana S. Anayatin said they had proposed ₱10,000,000 but Congress approved ₱5,000,000 for 10 years (figures as recorded), and recounted giving capital to 100 war widows in Datu Piang and South Upi.

21 December 2022: Nominal vote: 53 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third and final reading, 22 December 2022; the journal states 53 in favor but prints 54 names, none against, no abstention.
21 December 2022: Certified urgent; approved on third and final reading by nominal voting, stated as 53 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions, although 54 names are printed in favor.
readings.insight:
The interest in this bill is not in the text, which is 1 page, but in the sequence it belongs to. The same fund is extended again 11 months later by Bill No. 265, which pushes the 2020 to 2022 Special Development Fund to 31 December 2024 and then adds the phrase that matters more than any date: the money is to remain available "until fully expended or disbursed". A deadline replaced by a condition is a different instrument altogether.

Enacted as BAA 34 on 22 December 2022 — 9 days before the appropriations it rescues would have lapsed. Its companion, Bill No. 128, became BAA 33 on the same day. Budget extension bills in this registry are consistently passed in the last weeks of December, which tells you they are not planned instruments but responses to a year ending with money unspent.

What no document in this sequence contains is the amount. The bill moves a date; it does not say how much of the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund was still sitting there when the year ran out. That figure would answer the question the extension raises, and it is not in the law, the bill, or the index.

readings.whatItDoes:
This rewrites Section 48 of BAA 23, the 2022 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, to keep the year's budget alive through 2023 — with personnel services carved out.

Everything except personnel services stays available for release and disbursement, under the same general and special provisions, until 31 December 2023, as does the constituent local governments' share of income taxes collected within the region. Infrastructure capital outlays may be obligated to the end of 2023 with construction, inspection and payment running to 30 June 2024; operating expenses and other capital outlays may be obligated to the end of 2023 with delivery, inspection and payment to 31 March 2024. Personnel services, by contrast, stay valid only until 31 December 2022 — salaries do not get extended.

The provision also states what happens at the end. Unreleased appropriations lapse. Unexpended or undisbursed funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of the Organic Law. Ministries and offices are directed to observe both rules strictly.
readings.whyProposed:
No explanatory note is attached. The structure of the amendment says what happened: a budget written on a cash basis, to be spent within its own year, reached the end of that year with a substantial part of it unspent.

The carve-out for personnel services is the tell that this is about delivery rather than payroll. Salaries were paid; the projects, goods and services were not.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry and office holding unspent 2022 appropriations.
Constituent local government units, whose share of income taxes collected in the region stays available through 2023.
Contractors and suppliers on 2022 procurements, whose delivery and payment windows extend into 2024.
Bangsamoro government employees, who are expressly excluded — personnel services expire on schedule.
The Bangsamoro Treasury, which receives whatever is still unspent when the extension runs out.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management (MFBM) — guidelines for implementing the amended cash budgeting provision
Ministries and offices, directed to observe the validity of appropriations and the reversion of funds

funding.detail: No new money. The bill extends the availability of appropriations already made in BAA 23, and expressly does not extend personnel services.

whatChanges: The 2022 regional budget, except salaries, stays spendable through 2023.
Local governments' share of income taxes collected in the region stays disbursable through 2023.
Infrastructure may be completed and paid to 30 June 2024; goods and operating items to 31 March 2024.
Personnel services expire on 31 December 2022 regardless.
Whatever is left after the extension reverts to a Special Fund in the Treasury for reappropriation.
deliberation: 21 December 2022: MP Eduard U. Guerra said election-year restrictions, the reappointment of Members and the Maguindanao plebiscite cost about 5 months, and the national 2022 budget already had 2-year validity.
21 December 2022: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan explained her vote by citing the 2022 elections, the Maguindanao plebiscite and the national government’s own extension of its 2022 budget.
21 December 2022: MP Abdulraof A. Macacua said he hesitated because of the many extensions already granted but voted yes in deference to the Body.

21 December 2022: Nominal vote: 54 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Nominal voting on third reading, held on 22 December 2022 after the session resumed; 54 named in favor, none against, no abstention.
21 December 2022: Certified urgent; approved on third reading by nominal voting, 54 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions.
readings.insight:
The reversion clause is the part worth reading closely, because it is the only place in this short bill where the region says what it does with money it could not spend. Unreleased appropriations lapse; unexpended balances go back to the Treasury into a Special Fund, to be reappropriated under Section 19, Article XII of the Organic Law. That is a proper fiscal loop rather than a quiet rollover — and it is precisely the loop that each successive extension act defers by another year.

Which is what happened here. This bill extended the 2022 budget to the end of 2023; Bill No. 265, filed in November 2023, amends the very same Section 48 again, exempting General Administration and Support under operating expenses as well and letting appropriations under the Special Development Fund run until fully expended. Section 48 of BAA 23 has now been rewritten twice by 2 separate acts, each time enlarging what stays alive.

The exclusion of personnel services is the clearest signal in the sequence. Salaries are spent on time; capital and operating budgets are not. Whatever is slowing the region's spending, it is not the payroll — it is procurement, construction and delivery, which is what every date in this bill is written to accommodate.

Enacted as BAA 33 on 22 December 2022, 9 days before the budget it extends would have expired.

readings.whatItDoes:
This constitutes the Municipality of Pahamudin in the Special Geographic Areas, out of 12 barangays of Pigcawayan, North Cotabato, with its seat of government at Barangay Libungan Torreta.

The annex is the substance. It lists every constituent barangay with its land area, population and annual income as of 2020, totalling about 50.13 square kilometers, 19,627 residents and roughly ₱62.8 million in combined annual income. The territorial boundary follows the existing barangay lines.

The machinery is identical across all 8. Corporate existence arrives only on ratification by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite in the constituent barangays within 60 days of approval, conducted by COMELEC through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and charged to COMELEC's own appropriations for the year. The first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members are appointed by the Chief Minister and hold office until successors are elected at the next general local elections, while incumbent councillors of the mother municipality who live in the new one serve out their terms there. And because a new municipality has no revenue share until the national allotment reaches it, the Bangsamoro Government must provide not less than ₱2,500,000 every month to run it in the meantime.
readings.whyProposed: Section 2 of every bill in this set carries the fact that explains all of them: these barangays petitioned and voted to be included in the Bangsamoro in the 2019 plebiscite. They chose the region, and then spent years inside it while still administratively attached to a municipality outside it — paying taxes to, and receiving services from, a local government in North Cotabato that they had voted to leave. These bills resolve that anomaly by giving the barangays municipalities of their own.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 19,627 residents of the constituent barangays, who vote on whether the municipality exists.
Pigcawayan, which loses the barangays and does not itself vote.
Incumbent Sangguniang Bayan members of the mother municipality who live in the new one, who finish their terms in the mother municipality.
The Chief Minister, who appoints the entire first municipal government.
COMELEC, which runs the plebiscite and, under this bill, pays for it from its own appropriations.
The Bangsamoro budget, committed to at least ₱2.5 million a month until the revenue allotment arrives.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite
The Chief Minister — appointment of the first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members
The Bangsamoro Government — monthly financial assistance pending entitlement to the internal revenue allotment

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the administration and operation of the new municipal government until it is allocated its share in the internal revenue allotment — at that floor, at least ₱30 million a year, for an unstated period. Against that, the annex records the constituent barangays' own combined annual income at about ₱62.8 million. The plebiscite is charged to COMELEC's available funds under the current fiscal year appropriations.

whatChanges: 12 barangays of Pigcawayan, North Cotabato become a municipality of their own inside the Bangsamoro.
Barangays that voted to join the region in 2019 stop being administered from outside it.
The first municipal government is appointed by the Chief Minister rather than elected.
The regional budget takes on a monthly floor of at least ₱2.5 million.
readings.insight:
The name did not survive. This bill creates the Municipality of Pahamudin; what Parliament enacted on 17 August 2023 is BAA 41, the Municipality of Pahamuddin. The identification is not a guess — the mother municipality, the barangay list and the annexed population total of 19,627 are the same in both, and 19,627 is also the figure the Parliamentary Districts Act later prints for Pahamuddin. Only the spelling changed, from Pahamudin to Pahamuddin. This is also the largest of the 8 by barangay count and, at about 50 square kilometers for nearly 20,000 people, the most densely settled — and the only one whose signed act carries a full surveyed technical description and a political boundary map rather than a reference to existing barangay lines.

One figure in the annex deserves a second look. The combined annual income of the 12 barangays is recorded at about ₱62.8 million, which is the highest in the set and more than twice what several of the others record. Set against the ₱2.5 million monthly floor the Bangsamoro Government commits to, this municipality begins closer to viability on its own revenue than any of its siblings.

8 cabinet bills were filed together in December 2022 to constitute the Special Geographic Areas as municipalities — Bills 129 through 136 — and all 8 became law on 17 August 2023 as BAA 41 through 48. Parliament's bills index records that outcome for Bill No. 136 alone. The other 7, this one among them, are still listed as sitting at Second Reading, Committee Stage, 3 years after they were enacted.

The plebiscite question is the same across the set and cuts the same way. The vote is held only in the barangays being constituted, so the North Cotabato municipality losing them has no say — which is defensible here in a way it is not elsewhere in the registry, because these barangays had already voted in 2019 to leave that province altogether. What the design does not address is the mother municipality's own position: it loses territory, population and revenue by a regional law it cannot vote on, under a national allotment formula nobody in this Parliament controls.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Level 1 general hospital in Northern Kabuntalan, Maguindanao del Norte, to be known as the Northern Kabuntalan Municipal Hospital.

The operative text is short and conventional for the genre: a hospital, under the health ministry, funded through the Bangsamoro appropriations. What carries the bill is the explanatory note, and in particular 1 sentence of it about how people actually get to a hospital.

Northern Kabuntalan is a 5th class municipality of around 26,000 residents whose only health facility is a Rural Health Unit limited to checkups, basic treatment and pregnancy deliveries. Anything beyond that — cancer patients needing management, dengue patients needing further treatment, first-time or difficult deliveries, anyone needing monitoring, observation or laboratory testing — is referred out to Midsayap, Libungan or Dalikan, and some go as far as Cotabato City.

The municipality provides an ambulance for selected cases. Most residents travel by habal-habal, the single-motorcycle transport that serves rural Mindanao. Those living on the riverside of Northern Kabuntalan take a boat first and continue by land.
readings.whyProposed:
The note grounds the bill in Section 22, Article IX of the Organic Law — the mandate to establish a general hospital system by law — and in the constitutional duty to make health services available at affordable cost.

Its own argument is narrower and better. A rural health unit that can deliver a straightforward baby and treat a straightforward fever is not a hospital, and the gap between those 2 things is measured here in habal-habal rides and boat crossings. The note also notes the hospital would serve the neighbouring municipalities of Mother Kabuntalan and Datu Piang, so the catchment is wider than the 26,000 the bill is filed for.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 26,000 residents of Northern Kabuntalan, whose only facility handles checkups, basic treatment and deliveries.
Patients needing cancer management, dengue treatment, difficult deliveries, monitoring or laboratory work, all currently referred out of the municipality.
Residents of the riverside barangays, who reach a hospital by boat and then by land.
The neighbouring municipalities of Mother Kabuntalan and Datu Piang, named in the note as likely users.
Hospitals in Midsayap, Libungan, Dalikan and Cotabato City, which carry this catchment now.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — supervision of the hospital and its organizational structure

funding.detail: The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" but the filed copy names no amount. The enacted act did: BAA 68 appropriates ₱50 million from the Miscellaneous and Personnel Benefit Fund of the 2025 Bangsamoro budget, and separately directs the Ministry to ensure funding for the building, infrastructure, equipment, maintenance and personnel.

whatChanges: Northern Kabuntalan gains a Level 1 hospital where it had a rural health unit.
Referrals out of the municipality — to Midsayap, Libungan, Dalikan or Cotabato City — stop being the only option.
2 neighbouring municipalities gain a nearer facility.
readings.insight:
What Parliament added to this bill is the most interesting devolution scheme in the hospital series. BAA 68 has the Ministry of Health take *full* responsibility for the hospital's financial management at the start — budget allocation, procurement, expenditures — and then transfer it to the municipality in phases, against benchmarks, with the Ministry evaluating whether the local government has shown sufficient capacity, including compliance with accounting standards and efficient procurement.

Set that beside the Basilan pair. Bills 104 and 105 proposed provincial control from day one and the enacted acts reversed them into regional control with a later handover. Here the bill said nothing about who manages the money and the act supplied a staged answer keyed to demonstrated capacity. Across 3 hospitals, Parliament reached the same conclusion each time: the region runs it until the local government can prove it is ready — and, in this one, defined what proof looks like.

The explanatory note is worth keeping for the word habal-habal. Health access papers are usually written in kilometers and travel times; this one names the vehicle, which is a single motorcycle carrying a patient who may be in labour or bleeding, over roads that a 5th class municipality maintains. A bill that says its constituents reach hospital care by motorcycle and boat has made the case more effectively than any statistic in the document.

Parliament Bill No. 142, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets up a Madaris Education Fund Assistance — a fund for private Islamic schools covering infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation.

The assistance is awarded against criteria the bill lists: continuous teacher training, infrastructure facilities, scholarship grants, the socio-economic needs of students with priority to the poorest, the school’s overall performance, and the academic qualifications and financial needs of both students and teachers.

What the fund pays for is set out as 10 items: a nutrition and feeding program for young children; classroom facilities down to desks, tables and chalkboards; textbook assistance at a ratio of one book per student per subject; an in-service training fund for teachers; scholarship grants to children of teachers; scholarship grants to qualified students; funding for training and seminars for Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education teachers; an increase in ALIVE teachers’ salaries; funding for madaris registration and accreditation; and madrasah infrastructure development.

MBHTE issues the rules, in coordination with other agencies.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions and the contribution madaris make to educating the region’s children, and commits to a fund system for their infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation, with subsidies aimed particularly at the underprivileged. It also commits the government to encouraging non-formal, informal and indigenous learning systems.

The underlying problem is the same one Bills 167 and 168 address: madaris teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, sit outside the public funding system, and have no standing route to regional money.
whoIsAffected: Madaris across the region, for infrastructure, textbooks, classroom furniture and accreditation costs.
ALIVE teachers — Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education — who would receive training funds and a salary increase.
Teachers in madaris generally, through an in-service training fund and scholarships for their children.
Students, through scholarships, textbooks at one book per subject, and a feeding program for the young ones.
MBHTE’s Bureau of Madaris, which would administer the fund out of its own current appropriation.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education (MBHTE), which issues the rules
MBHTE Bureau of Madaris, against whose current appropriations the fund is charged

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 for initial implementation, provided in the Bangsamoro Appropriation Act and charged under the current appropriations of the MBHTE Bureau of Madaris. It is one of the few bills in this group to carry a figure at all — and it is a small one against a list of 10 funded items that includes region-wide infrastructure development, one textbook per student per subject, and a salary increase for a whole category of teachers.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists for madaris, covering infrastructure, textbooks, training, scholarships and accreditation.
ALIVE teachers get a training fund and a salary increase.
Textbook assistance is set at a ratio of 1 book per student per subject.
Children of madrasah teachers become eligible for scholarships.
The cost of madaris registration and accreditation is funded.
₱10 million is charged against the Bureau of Madaris’ current appropriations.
readings.insight:
Read this next to Bills 167 and 168 and the picture changes. 3 separate bills in this Parliament propose to fund madrasah education: this one from MPs Matalam, Ismael and Alih, Bill 167 from MPs Ampatuan and Mitmug, and Bill 168 from MP Antao. All 3 were filed within 4 months of each other in 2023. Bill 167 and this bill overlap substantially — both fund student assistance, teacher support, classroom facilities and textbooks — and their forms of assistance are close enough to read as variations on one draft. Whether they are consolidated is a decision for the committee, and Parliament’s index shows all 3 sitting in the Committee on Basic, Higher and Technical Education or with Finance alongside it.

The ₱10 million is the number to weigh. It is charged not as new money but against the Bureau of Madaris’ existing appropriations, and it is asked to cover 10 categories including madrasah infrastructure development region-wide and a salary increase for ALIVE teachers. Either the figure is a token first tranche or the list is aspirational; the bill does not say which.

The most concrete thing in it is the textbook ratio. One book per student per subject sounds unremarkable until you have been in a classroom where a book is shared between 4 children, which in this region is not a rare sight.

readings.whatItDoes:
This directs the Bangsamoro Government to establish orphanages in every province and builds the system around them.

An orphaned minor is defined as a child under 18 left without care or guardian by the death of the father, or without proper parental care through the death, disappearance or abandonment by both parents for at least 6 continuous months.

Section 5 creates a monitoring and evaluating system whose membership reaches from the regional ministry down to the barangay: the Ministry of Social Services and Development, the provincial, municipal and city social welfare offices, the interior ministry, and provincial, local and barangay local government units — and then traditional leaders and the religious sector, the Ulama or Imam of each province. Its job is to identify and select qualified beneficiaries by a transparent and cost-efficient method, to keep updated data on the number, location and personal profile of orphaned minors in each community, to develop the appropriate model of orphanage for that community, and to monitor the children once they are in one.

A Comprehensive Support Program is institutionalised covering 6 named needs: basic needs, physical safety and security, socio-economic needs, educational needs, emotional and spiritual needs, and access to justice. A Managing Committee runs each orphanage and trains its staff, and is responsible for every child admitted until that child turns 18.

Section 10 sets the timetable, and it is the only hard target in the bill: the social services ministry is to begin accreditation immediately, with at least 2 accredited orphanages in every province by the end of the transition period and an accredited orphanage in every local government unit by 2025. The ministry may adopt the national department's accreditation standards or write entirely new ones.

Local governments must monitor the orphanages in their jurisdiction and help them toward accreditation, funded from their own appropriations.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note rests on one finding, from The Asia Foundation's 2020 study *Children of War: A Rapid Needs Assessment of Orphans in Muslim Mindanao*: there are no orphanages or shelters accredited by the national social welfare department anywhere in the Bangsamoro region.

What follows from that is the rest of the case. Muslim orphans processed in Mindanao are often sent to orphanages in Manila, and the facilities that do serve Bangsamoro children have grown up in the diaspora instead — Maharlika Village in Taguig, Culiat in Quezon City, Quiapo, and Baguio City. A region with its own government, emerging from a conflict that produced the orphans in question, was sending them 900 kilometres away to be cared for.
whoIsAffected: Orphaned children under 18 across the region, for whom no accredited facility currently exists.
Children currently sent to orphanages in Manila or cared for in diaspora-run facilities in Taguig, Quezon City, Quiapo and Baguio.
The Ministry of Social Services and Development, which must accredit institutions and may write its own standards.
Every province, required to have at least 2 accredited orphanages by the end of the transition period.
Every local government unit, required to have an accredited orphanage by 2025 and to fund monitoring from its own appropriations.
Traditional leaders and the Ulama or Imam of each province, seated on the monitoring system.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD) — lead ministry, accreditation, and central planning and monitoring
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government (MILG), coordinating and co-drafting the implementing rules within 3 months
A monitoring and evaluating system seating regional, provincial, municipal, city and barangay bodies together with traditional leaders and the Ulama or Imam of each province
A Managing Committee for each orphanage, responsible for every child until age 18
Constituent local government units, monitoring orphanages in their jurisdiction from their own appropriations

funding.detail: No amount is named. The financial requirements are met through the implementing ministries' appropriations, with local governments funding monitoring and accreditation assistance from their own appropriations. Identical to the funding clause in Bill No. 112.

whatChanges: The region commits to having accredited orphanages of its own rather than sending children to Manila.
At least 2 accredited orphanages per province by the end of the transition period, and 1 per local government unit by 2025.
A single system holds the data on who and where the region's orphaned children are.
Traditional and religious leaders sit in the body that identifies beneficiaries.
Care covers 6 defined needs including emotional and spiritual needs and access to justice.
readings.insight:
This is the clearest case of duplicate legislation in the registry, and it is worth being exact about the evidence rather than calling the 2 bills similar. Normalise both operative texts and they contain the same number of words — 1,255 — and match to better than 95%, with the residual differences traceable to scan noise and page furniture. 17 sections, same headings, same order, same definitions, same 2025 deadline, same 6 categories of need.

What that tells you is not that anybody acted improperly. Model bills circulate, civil society organisations draft text and offer it to whoever will file it, and the Asia Foundation study both versions rely on was published for exactly that purpose. 2 members filing the same text 3 months apart is what happens when a subject has an obvious champion text and no coordinating mechanism inside Parliament to notice it has already been filed.

The cost of that is visible in the outcome. Both bills went to committee and both stopped. The same thing happened, on a larger scale, to the 8 competing topnotcher and athlete incentive bills — filed within 1 week of each other, referred to the same 2 committees on the same day 16 months later, none enacted. Duplication does not merely waste drafting effort; it splits the sponsorship of a subject so that no single measure carries the weight of a member's reputation, and committees receive 2 identical papers instead of 1 with 2 names on it.

The substance deserves better than that. The finding underneath both bills — that the region had no accredited orphanage and sent its orphans to Manila — is among the sharpest facts in the registry, and the deadline both bills set for fixing it has now passed.

Bill No. 112 and Bill No. 143 are the same bill. Both carry the title "An Act Institutionalizing Support to the Welfare and Care for Orphans by Establishing Bangsamoro Orphanages", both run to 17 sections with identical headings in identical order, and set side by side the operative texts run to 1,255 words each and match almost word for word — the few differences being scan artefacts rather than drafting. MP Ramos filed hers on 17 October 2022; MP Anayatin filed the same text on 17 January 2023, 3 months later. Both were referred to committee and both are still there.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 143, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Bangsamoro Convention Center as a government-owned and controlled corporation with its own legal personality, and puts it in the Municipality of Parang, Maguindanao del Norte.

The Center is to host local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events, and to provide the facilities for them — the text names meeting rooms, exhibition halls, auditoriums and accommodation. It may set and collect its own fees and charges, enter contracts, market itself, and form partnerships with private and public entities.

It is run by a board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, sitting with the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism, the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and 2 private sector representatives appointed by the Chief Minister. The board sets policy and appoints a chief executive officer for day-to-day operations, and must issue implementing rules within 60 days. The Center reports annually to the Bangsamoro Government and the relevant committees of Parliament, and is subject to audit.
readings.whyProposed: The declaration of policy is the whole argument: to provide a venue for local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events in order to promote economic growth and cultural exchange, and to establish the Bangsamoro as a leading destination for events and gatherings. The region currently has no purpose-built facility at that scale, and hosts its larger gatherings in hotel function rooms, university halls and government buildings.
whoIsAffected: The Municipality of Parang and Maguindanao del Norte, which would host the facility and whose Governor sits on its board.
The regional events, tourism and hospitality trade, which gains a venue and a competitor at the same time.
The Bangsamoro Government, which would carry the cost of building and standing up a corporation.
Organizers of regional gatherings, who currently work around the absence of a large purpose-built venue.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Convention Center, as a government-owned and controlled corporation under the management and supervision of the Bangsamoro Government

A board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, with the Ministers of Trade, Investments and Tourism and of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and 2 private sector appointees
A chief executive officer appointed by the board

funding.detail: No figure appears anywhere in the bill. The amount necessary for initial implementation is to be included in the annual general appropriations act, and the Center is expected to generate funds of its own through fees, charges and partnerships. For a measure whose entire purpose is to build a building, the absence of any construction estimate is the most conspicuous thing in the text.

whatChanges: A Bangsamoro Convention Center exists as a corporation with its own legal personality.
It is sited at Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, rather than at the seat of government.
It can set and keep its own fees and charges and enter its own contracts and partnerships.
The Chief Minister chairs its board and appoints 2 private sector trustees.
It reports annually to Parliament’s relevant committees and is subject to audit.
readings.insight:
The siting is the decision worth arguing about, and the bill does not argue it. Parang is not the seat of government — Cotabato City is, half an hour away — but Parang holds Polloc port and the region’s freeport, and putting a convention center next to a deepwater harbour rather than next to the ministries is a bet on trade traffic over government traffic. The text states the location in a single clause and gives no reasoning for it.

The second thing is the board. 4 of its 7 seats are held ex officio by the Chief Minister and ministers, one by a provincial governor, and 2 by private sector appointees the Chief Minister chooses. A corporation meant to compete for international events is governed almost entirely by people whose day job is something else, and the trade it serves has no seat that is not in the Chief Minister’s gift.

Third, and most practically: the bill authorises a corporation to build and run a convention center and never says what that costs. Every other creation measure of this size in the registry carries at least an initial figure. This one leaves the whole question to the annual appropriations act, which means the decision that matters — how big, and how much — is made after the law rather than in it.

It has moved further than most. The index has it at Second Reading, deferred in July and again in August 2025, which puts it among the handful of bills in this batch past the committee stage.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes 1 dialysis centre, at the Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital in Pinaring, Sultan Kudarat, and it is the only 1 of the 3 dialysis bills that says how it will be paid for.

Section 10 appropriates ₱20,000,000 for the facilities, equipment, machines and supplies needed to open. The hospital provides the building and the space and hires or designates the physicians, nurses and administrative staff, charged against its own budget. All purchased equipment is owned and maintained by the hospital, with deeds of transfer executed as needed.

The pricing rule is the distinctive provision. Section 7 caps the service fee at no more than 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment, and charges nothing at all to indigent patients. Section 8 then lets the collections accrue to the centre's own income, to be used primarily for its operation — so the 10% margin above supplier cost is what funds the centre's running expenses.

Section 9 adds bridging support: the Ministry of Health, through its Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government programme, allocates funds to augment the centre's expenses during its first year.

A Joint Technical Working Group of the health ministry and the hospital writes the implementing rules, covering hiring, procurement, construction under the national Department of Health's administrative orders, and the centre's licensing and regulation.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note gives a figure rather than a principle. Renal disease is among the major causes of disease-related death in the country, and at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital alone there were 162 patients in 2022 needing dialysis.

That is the argument: a specific hospital, a counted caseload, and a facility sized to it. The bill does not claim to solve the region's kidney disease problem; it claims that 162 patients at 1 hospital justify a centre there.
whoIsAffected: The 162 patients the note counts at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital in 2022, and those who follow them.
Indigent patients, who pay no service fee at all.
Paying patients, whose fee is capped at 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment.
Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital, which provides the building, hires the staff from its own budget and owns the equipment.
The Ministry of Health, which augments the first year through its AMBaG medical assistance programme.
implementedBy: Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital — building, space, staffing, ownership and maintenance of equipment
Ministry of Health, through the Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government (AMBaG) Programme, for first-year assistance
A Joint Technical Working Group of the Ministry of Health and the hospital, writing the implementing rules

funding.detail: ₱20,000,000 appropriated for facilities, equipment, machines and supplies for initial operation. The building, space and staff costs fall on the hospital's own budget. Thereafter the centre funds itself: fees capped at 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment accrue to the centre as income and pay primarily for its operation, with free treatment for indigents and first-year augmentation from the health ministry's AMBaG programme.

whatChanges: A dialysis centre opens at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital with ₱20 million of equipment.
Dialysis is free for indigent patients and capped at 110% of supplier cost for everyone else.
The centre keeps its own fee income and runs on it.
The health ministry's medical assistance programme covers the first year's shortfall.
readings.insight:
The 110% cap is the most interesting mechanism in any of the 3 dialysis bills, and it is doing 2 jobs at once. It protects the patient — a session cannot be priced at more than a tenth above what the consumables actually cost, which forecloses the margins that make private dialysis unaffordable. And because Section 8 lets the collections stay with the centre, that same 10% is the centre's operating budget. It is a self-financing design, and its weakness is visible on the face of it: 10% of consumable cost will not cover staff, maintenance and machine replacement, which is presumably why the hospital carries the salaries and the health ministry has to bridge year one.

The bill's real virtue is that it is the only 1 of the 3 that is costed and therefore buildable. Bill No. 88 requires a unit in every government hospital in the region and funds it from "current appropriations"; Bill No. 279 requires one in every provincial tertiary hospital within a year and does the same. This bill names ₱20 million, names the hospital, names who owns the equipment afterwards and names the programme that covers the first year. A single facility that opens is worth more to a patient than a regional mandate that does not.

The counted caseload is the other thing to credit. "162 patients for the year 2022" at a named hospital is the kind of number almost no bill in this registry supplies, and it makes the measure checkable — a reader can ask whether a centre sized for 162 patients is enough, which is a question the other 2 bills give no way of asking.

What the bill does not address is everyone outside Sultan Kudarat. A dialysis patient needs treatment 2 or 3 times a week for life, so a centre serves only the people who can reach it that often. For Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, a facility at Pinaring is not a service, and the island provinces are exactly where Bill 88's regionwide mandate was aimed.

3 bills in this registry address dialysis and they pick 3 different scales. Bill No. 88, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022, requires a dialysis unit in every government hospital in the region within 5 years. Bill No. 145, filed by MP Sema in February 2023, builds 1 centre at 1 named hospital with ₱20 million behind it. Bill No. 279, filed by MP Dilangalen in February 2024, requires provincial tertiary hospitals to have a unit within 1 year. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 145, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital from 50 beds to 100, with its facilities and professional complement raised with it.

The bill's real subject is a gap between 2 laws and a building. Republic Act No. 11330 converted the facility into a 50-bed district hospital; the note says the funds released to it have remained at the level of a 10-bed budget since that adoption, and the hospital's physical structure was built for Level I status at 10 beds. So the 50-bed designation exists on paper, the money is for 10 beds, and the building is for 10 beds.
readings.whyProposed:
The note's argument is about implementation rather than need. A national statute gave the hospital a 50-bed designation and neither the budget nor the building followed, so the institution has spent years carrying a status it was never resourced to hold.

Asking for 100 beds in that context is asking for the whole thing to be done properly once — a structure, a budget and a staffing complement matched to a designation — rather than for a second unfunded upgrade on top of the first.
whoIsAffected: Patients of Datu Odin Sinsuat, the largest municipality in Maguindanao del Norte by population.
The hospital's staff, working in a building designed for a 10-bed Level I facility.
Anyone relying on a hospital whose funding has remained at 10-bed levels despite a 50-bed designation.
The Ministry of Health and the finance ministry, which would have to fund the structure as well as the beds.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: A 50-bed designation that was never funded becomes a 100-bed hospital with the budget and building to match.
The facility's physical structure is upgraded beyond the Level I, 10-bed design it was built to.
Professional and medical staffing rises with the capacity.
readings.insight:
This is the only hospital bill in the registry whose complaint is that an existing law was never implemented, and that makes it the most useful of the set for understanding why the others may not work either. Republic Act No. 11330 designated this hospital at 50 beds. The designation arrived; the construction budget did not, and the operating budget stayed at the 10-bed level. A decade of bills in this registry create and upgrade hospitals by statute on the assumption that the designation is the hard part — this one is evidence that it is the easy part.

Read against the enacted acts, the pattern holds. BAA 73 converted the Iranun District Hospital to 200 beds with ₱50 million; BAA 74 made the Maguindanao Provincial Hospital a 350-bed Level III facility with the same ₱50 million. Those figures buy neither a building nor a staff at that scale, which is precisely the position this bill describes Datu Odin Sinsuat as already being in.

Asking for 100 beds when the funded reality is 10 is therefore a calculated move rather than an overreach. The bill is not requesting a doubling of an operating 50-bed hospital; it is requesting that a facility be built and funded for the first time, and choosing a number that reflects the municipality's size rather than the paper status it already has. Whether Parliament reads it that way is the question, and the registry's habit of converging on smaller figures suggests the risk.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 146, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes: This establishes and constructs a Level I municipal hospital with 50 beds in Datu Piang, Maguindanao del Sur, to be known as the Datu Piang Municipal Hospital, appropriating funds for its facilities and professional health care and medical personnel.
readings.whyProposed:
Datu Piang had a population of 28,380 at the 2020 census and no hospital of its own.

The measure is 1 of 2 hospital bills MP Anayatin filed on the same day — the other upgrades the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital — and both are framed around the same problem: a municipality's population measured against provision that does not exist or was never funded.
whoIsAffected: The 28,380 residents of Datu Piang recorded at the 2020 census.
Patients currently travelling out of the municipality for any hospital care.
Neighbouring facilities that absorb the catchment.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: Datu Piang gains a 50-bed Level I municipal hospital.
Funds are appropriated for facilities and for professional and medical personnel, not only for the building.
A municipality of over 28,000 stops depending on hospitals elsewhere.
readings.insight:
50 beds for 28,380 people is nearly twice the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 that other bills in this registry invoke, and the bill does not explain the margin. There are defensible reasons — Datu Piang sits in the Liguasan marsh area, among the most flood-prone and historically conflict-affected parts of the region, where a hospital serves a wider catchment than its own municipality in an emergency — but the note does not make that argument, and a committee comparing this bill against the Ambolodto measures, which size hospitals precisely to population, would have to supply it.

The title's specificity about what the money is for is the bill's better feature. It appropriates funds "for its facilities and professional health care, medical personnel" rather than simply for the hospital. Nearly every hospital measure in this registry funds a building and leaves the staffing to be found inside an existing ministry line, and the companion bill by the same author documents exactly what that produces: a 50-bed designation running on a 10-bed budget for years. Naming personnel in the appropriation is the lesson of that experience written into the next bill.

Datu Piang is also the mother municipality of several units created in this registry's own pages, including barangays that appear in the parliamentary districts schedule. A hospital there serves a population that has been administratively rearranged more than once, and the bill's decision to size it above the municipality's own count reads better against that than against a ratio.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 147, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a BARMM Badjao Development Project, and it is the only measure in the registry addressed to a single ethnic community.

Section 2 states the premise without hedging: the Badjao community is "arguably the most marginalized, disenfranchised, vulnerable, disadvantaged and isolated indigenous ethnic group in the region and falling behind all human development indicators, at individual, familial and communal levels". The policy covers their basic political and human rights — including birth and citizenship registration — and the promotion and protection of their marine ecology and lifestyle.

The project is built on the United Nations Human Security framework, and its 7 objectives follow that framework's categories. Political security: supporting ancestral domain claims and the establishment of their own kampung, and ensuring participation in BARMM decision-making. Economic security: livelihoods in fishing, agriculture and handicrafts, support for traditional economic practices, and a route into the global creative economy and eco- and cultural tourism. Food security, including support for traditional food practices. Health security, including traditional health practices. Environmental security: protecting their marine ecology and lifestyle, and awarding ancestral domain claims "where they can begin communal life anew". Personal security: education, housing, cultural identity and heritage. And community security: social cohesion, disaster preparedness, and representation in local legislative bodies through the Indigenous People's Mandatory Representation system and in bodies requiring civil society participation.

Section 3 names what the kampung is to be protected from: commercial fishery encroachment, high sea robbery and similar insecurities.

A Project Management Office under the Office of the Chief Minister implements it, with Community Development Officers assigned to clusters of Badjao communities as focal person, facilitator, organizer and conduit, and Provincial Supervisors above them doing quality assurance. A Project Consultative Body of Badjao male and female elders and youth leaders convenes before each annual budget cycle to give inputs on policies and programmes affecting them.
readings.whyProposed:
Birth and citizenship registration appearing in the declaration of policy is the tell. The Badjao are a seafaring people whose communities live on boats and in stilt villages across the Sulu archipelago and whose members frequently hold no birth certificate — which means no school enrolment, no PhilHealth, no bank account, no passport and, in the most serious cases, no demonstrable citizenship in any of the 3 countries whose waters they move through.

The bill's answer is to treat that as a security problem rather than a welfare one, which is why it reaches for the Human Security framework. A community that can be moved off a shoreline, fished out by commercial fleets, robbed at sea and left undocumented is insecure in several distinct ways at once, and the framework gives the bill a way to name all 7 of them in a single programme.
whoIsAffected: The Badjao communities of the region, including those living on boats and in stilt settlements.
Badjao without birth or citizenship registration, for whom the bill makes documentation a policy objective.
Badjao fishing households competing with commercial fishery encroachment.
Badjao elders and youth leaders, male and female, seated on the Project Consultative Body before each budget cycle.
Local legislative councils, which would seat Badjao representation through the Indigenous People's Mandatory Representation system.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which would house the Project Management Office.
implementedBy: A Project Management Office under the Office of the Chief Minister — supervision, implementation, resource mobilisation and the implementing rules
A Project Consultative Body of Badjao male and female elders and youth leaders, convening before each annual budget cycle
Community Development Officers assigned to clusters of Badjao communities
Provincial Supervisors, serving as quality assurance and compliance officers

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is charged against the BARMM budget for the year, and the government may accept donations or grants from external sources. For a programme spanning documentation, livelihoods, housing, health and ancestral domain claims across scattered communities, the absence of a figure is the bill's main structural weakness.

whatChanges: The Badjao become the subject of a dedicated government programme rather than a line in a general one.
Birth and citizenship registration becomes a stated objective of regional policy.
Ancestral domain claims extend to a seafaring people and their kampung.
Commercial fishery encroachment and high sea robbery are named as threats the state will act against.
Badjao elders and youth advise on the budget before it is drafted, not after.
Community Development Officers are placed with clusters of Badjao communities.
readings.insight:
Putting birth registration in a development statute is the most consequential thing this bill does, and it is easy to read past because it sounds administrative. A person with no birth certificate cannot enrol in school, hold a formal job, open an account, claim health insurance or prove citizenship — so every other objective in the bill, from livelihoods to education to housing, is gated behind a document many Badjao do not have. A programme that funds boats and training without fixing registration would reach the people who are already least excluded.

The Human Security framework earns its place here rather than decorating the bill. Most measures in this registry pick 1 instrument — a facility, a subsidy, an office. The Badjao's situation is simultaneously about land they have no title to, seas being fished by others, robbery they cannot report, documents they do not hold and representation they do not have, and a framework with 7 named dimensions is a way of holding all of that in one programme without pretending any single intervention solves it.

The consultative body's timing is the detail that shows real drafting care. It convenes "before the onset of the annual budget cycle" — not after the budget is drafted, when consultation is ratification, but before, when inputs can still shape allocations. Several bodies created elsewhere in this registry are required to consult and none of them says when.

What the bill cannot resolve is its relationship to the enacted indigenous peoples act. BAA 64 brought the Badjao and the Sama peoples expressly within the coverage of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the ancestral domain machinery, which is most of what this bill's political and environmental security objectives were reaching for. This measure would sit alongside that as a dedicated programme with its own office and field staff, and the case for it after BAA 64 is the gap between having rights recognised in a statute and having a community development officer in the kampung — which, on the bill's own account of where the Badjao stand on every human development indicator, is a real gap.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Level I general hospital with 50 beds in Talipao, Sulu.

Talipao is a 1st class rural municipality in Sulu's first district — 52 barangays and a population of 100,088 — and it is among the largest municipalities in the province. It is reachable from the nearest major city, Zamboanga, only by sea or air.

The municipality has no hospital. Its only health facilities are barangay health stations and rural health units.
readings.whyProposed:
The note sets out 2 arguments and the first is historical. In the 1970s, at the height of the war between the MNLF and the Armed Forces, and again during the more recent fighting with the Abu Sayyaf, Talipao was among the most brutally affected areas, enduring tremendous human suffering and loss of life and property.

The second is the referral chain as it now stands. Patients needing emergency care travel to Jolo; and the note is candid that Jolo is not the answer either — the Sulu Provincial Hospital cannot sufficiently provide for severe conditions, so patients continue to Zamboanga City. The note attributes a high mortality rate in the municipality to the absence of healthcare facilities.
whoIsAffected: The 100,088 residents of Talipao across 52 barangays, who have no hospital.
Emergency patients travelling first to Jolo and then, if necessary, to Zamboanga City.
Communities that bore the heaviest fighting in the 1970s and again more recently.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital in Jolo, which the note says cannot sufficiently handle severe cases.
The Ministry of Health, which would establish and supervise the hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: A municipality of over 100,000 people gains its first hospital.
Barangay health stations and rural health units stop being the only provision for 52 barangays.
The referral chain to Jolo and onward to Zamboanga City stops being the only option.
readings.insight:
100,000 people and no hospital is the plainest statement of need in this registry. Talipao is larger than several municipalities for which the region has enacted hospital acts — South Ubian has about 29,500 people and received a 25-bed Level I hospital under BAA 66 — and it has 52 barangays, which is more than 1 of the Special Geographic Area municipalities created in 2023. The bill asks for 50 beds, which on the Department of Health ratio its companion bills invoke is exactly half what the municipality's population implies.

The note's admission about Jolo is what distinguishes it. Most hospital bills in this registry argue that patients must travel to a provincial hospital; this one says the provincial hospital cannot handle severe cases either, so the real destination is Zamboanga City — across water, in another region. That makes the measure about more than convenience: a province of 1 million people whose referral endpoint is outside it does not have a hospital system, which is the conclusion Bill No. 161's bed arithmetic reaches from the other direction.

The conflict history is included for a reason the bill leaves implicit. A municipality that absorbed heavy fighting in the 1970s and again recently has a population with untreated injury, displacement and the chronic conditions that follow both — and it is precisely the sort of place from which health infrastructure withdraws during a conflict and does not return. Read with MP Alamia's health care subsidy bill, which would give conflict-affected people a card entitling them to subsidised care, the 2 measures address the same population from opposite ends: 1 funds the patient, this one builds the place to treat them.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities in every government office and every local government unit in the region.

The desk is where a senior citizen or a person with a disability may make inquiries, ask for assistance and lodge complaints, and it must attend to and address what is brought to it. The bill defines both groups by reference to national law — Republic Act 9994 for senior citizens, any resident citizen at least 60 years old, and Republic Act 10754 for persons with disabilities, using the long-term impairment and barriers formulation.

Section 5 puts the duty on local chief executives by name. Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors must fill the gap in protecting and overseeing the welfare of senior citizens and persons with disabilities in their areas, and all local governments must advocate their rights and take a proactive stance in disseminating information about the benefits and privileges they are entitled to.

The implementing rules are for MSSD to prepare in consultation with MILG within 60 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is about dignity and access: valuing the dignity of senior citizens and persons with disabilities, guaranteeing full respect for their human rights, and integrating them into mainstream society through programs that ensure easy access to government services.

The practical problem is that the benefits already exist under national law and the barrier is the counter. A person who cannot find out where to go, or who is sent between offices, does not receive an entitlement they legally hold.
whoIsAffected: Senior citizens and persons with disabilities across the region, who gain a named point of contact in every government office.
Every government office and local government unit in BARMM, each of which must staff a desk.
Provincial governors and city and municipal mayors, on whom Section 5 places the duty by name.
MSSD and MILG, which write the implementing rules.
implementedBy: All government offices and local government units in the Bangsamoro, which host the desks
Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors
Ministry of Social Services and Development, with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for the implementing rules

funding.detail: No figure. Funds for establishing the desks in all government offices and LGUs are to be included in the annual appropriations of the region and submitted to Parliament for approval. A desk in every office in the region is mostly a staffing cost, and the bill does not estimate it or say whether existing personnel are to be redesignated.

whatChanges: Every government office and LGU in the region must run a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities.
The desk handles inquiries, assistance and complaints.
Local chief executives carry a named duty to oversee the welfare of both groups.
Local governments must proactively publicise the benefits and privileges available.
MSSD and MILG must issue implementing rules within 60 days.
readings.insight:
This is a small bill and it is aimed at the right thing. Senior citizen and PWD benefits in the Philippines are generous on paper and unevenly delivered in practice, and the failure is almost always at the counter rather than in the statute. A named desk with a duty to take complaints is a cheap intervention against exactly that failure.

What it lacks is a consequence. There is no penalty, no reporting requirement, no obligation to record what the desk receives, and no one designated to check that the desks exist. A duty to establish a desk, with nobody counting them, is likely to produce a sign on a wall in the offices that were already helpful and nothing at all in the ones that were not. A single annual report from MSSD on how many desks are operating and what they handled would change the character of the bill entirely.

The drafting also leaves the desks unstaffed in the literal sense: the Act says a desk is established, not who sits at it. In a small municipal office that will mean a person already doing something else, which is workable — but it should be said, because the appropriation is meant to pay for it.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred in July 2025 to 3 committees at once — Social Services, Women Youth Children and PWDs, and Finance.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Free Lunch Act of 2023 institutionalises a free lunch for students in public schools, served 5 days a week for the whole school year, beginning when classes open.

Schools in 3 situations are given priority: those with reported severe malnutrition, those in areas of armed conflict, and those in highly congested areas.

A Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council supervises. It is chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education with the Minister of Health as co-chair, and seats the Ministers of Social Services and Development, of Agriculture, and of the Interior and Local Government. The Council writes the framework that serves as the blueprint — the integrated package of nutrition services, an information database, and the operational detail. MBHTE has primary responsibility for administering the program, working to nutritional standards the Act requires, and a School Lunch Committee operates at school level with duties set out for its members.

The program reports annually to Parliament.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section runs from the right to health and access to essential goods and social services to the specific problem of malnutrition among students, and frames the program as protection for children who by reason of their family’s economic circumstances do not get the nutrition their development requires.

The objectives put the educational case alongside the health one: a child who has not eaten does not learn, so mitigating malnourishment is presented as support for the learning process rather than as welfare attached to a school.
whoIsAffected: Students in public schools across the region, who would receive one free meal on every school day.
Schools in areas of severe malnutrition, armed conflict and congestion, given explicit priority.
Families, for whom a guaranteed school meal is a real reduction in household food cost.
MBHTE, which administers the program, and the 4 other ministries on the Council.
Local suppliers and producers, through a program feeding public school students 5 days a week — the Minister of Agriculture sits on the Council.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council — MBHTE as chair, Health as co-chair, with Social Services and Development, Agriculture, and the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, with primary responsibility for administration
School Lunch Committees at school level

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are to be included in the annual General Appropriations of the Bangsamoro and submitted to Parliament for approval. This is the most expensive recurring commitment in this group of bills by a wide margin — a hot meal for every public school student in the region, 5 days a week, every week of the school year — and it is the one where the absence of a costing is hardest to defend.

whatChanges: Public school students receive one free lunch on every school day of the year.
The meal is served 5 days a week for the full duration of the school year.
Schools with severe malnutrition, in armed conflict areas, or in congested areas are prioritized.
A 5-minister Council supervises and writes the nutrition framework.
Each school runs a School Lunch Committee.
The program reports to Parliament annually.
readings.insight:
The coverage does not match itself, and a committee needs to fix it before anything else. Section 3 institutionalises the program "in all kindergarten and elementary students enrolled in all public schools". Section 11 says the Act covers all public schools in the region and every eligible student enrolled, then defines public schools as "primary and secondary educational institutions". So one section limits the program to kindergarten and elementary, and the other pulls in secondary. The difference is a very large number of students and a very large amount of money.

That matters because the bill carries no figure at all. A daily hot meal for every public school student in BARMM is among the largest recurring programs the region could adopt, and whether it covers elementary only or elementary and secondary changes the cost by a multiple. Leaving both the scope and the price to be settled later leaves nothing to scrutinise.

The Minister of Agriculture’s seat on the Council is the quiet good idea. A guaranteed daily purchase of food for every public school in the region is agricultural demand as much as it is nutrition policy, and putting agriculture on the supervising body is how a feeding program becomes a market for local producers rather than a procurement contract.

The priority list is well chosen and worth noting for what it names: schools in areas of armed conflict, alongside malnutrition and congestion. Few feeding bills anywhere would need that category.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority as a body attached to the Office of the Chief Minister, responsible for the overall policy-making, planning, coordination and management of the lake's rehabilitation and development, with regulatory and supervisory authority over programs and projects in the Lake Lanao area.

The board is assembled at the top of government. A Chairman appointed by the Chief Minister chairs it; the Minister of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy is Co-Chair; and the Ministers of Agriculture, Public Works, Trade, Transportation, and Finance sit as members, alongside the Director General of the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, a representative of the Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, and 2 representatives of non-government organisations appointed by the Chief Minister from nominations.

The instrument at the centre of the Act is a 30-year Master Plan, and Section 16 specifies what it must contain: an assessment of the physical and natural resources and potential of the Lake Lanao area, its social and economic conditions, hydrological characteristics and power potential; the development of scenic and tourist spots and conservation of water resources; and proposed rehabilitation projects including watershed protection and management, flood control, the revival and restoration of the lake's biodiversity, maintenance of desirable water quality, and socio-economic projects using local raw materials. Everything from provincial to local level must be anchored on that plan, and it must be reviewed regularly against its targets.

Section 18 requires an independent review every 10 years by a panel of experts appointed by the Chief Minister, reporting to the Chief Minister and to Parliament. Section 20 provides that any doubt in interpreting the Act is to be construed liberally in favour of fulfilling its objectives.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill argues from the ecology, with footnotes — to the Australian Museum on biodiversity and to WWF on ecological balance — and from the physical fact that Lake Lanao drains through only one outlet, the Agus River in Lanao del Norte.

That single outlet is why the lake is both ecologically fragile and economically valuable, and the bill's answer is a plan rather than a prohibition: a 30-year horizon covering water quality, biodiversity, watershed, flood control and the livelihoods that depend on all of them, with everything else required to align to it.

The bill also records where it came from. A footnote on its first page states that it was inspired by the entry of Najib A. Haron in the Online Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of MP Ampatuan and MP Mitmug, under the title "An Act Creating Lake Lanao Rehabilitation Program to Preserve, Beautify, Improve, Restore and Utilize the like for Socio-Economic Purposes".
whoIsAffected: Communities in the Lake Lanao area, whose local programs must align with the Master Plan.
The Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, which holds 1 seat on a board of 10.
Non-government organisations, which hold 2 board seats filled by the Chief Minister from nominations.
7 ministries whose ministers sit on the board in person.
Fisherfolk and shoreline residents, as the intended beneficiaries of biodiversity revival and water quality provisions.
Parliament, which receives an independent expert review of the Authority every 10 years.
implementedBy: Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister

An LLRDA Board of 10 — a Chairman appointed by the Chief Minister, the environment Minister as Co-Chair, 5 further ministers, the planning authority's Director General, a provincial government representative and 2 NGO representatives
An Executive Office under the Board, with the LLRDA Board writing the implementing rules
An independent review panel of experts appointed by the Chief Minister every 10 years, reporting to the Chief Minister and Parliament

funding.detail: No amount is named. Initial operations are charged against the Contingent Fund of the 2023 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, and annual expenditures including capital outlays go into the Bangsamoro appropriations act thereafter. The bill gives the Authority no revenue-raising power of its own.

whatChanges: Lake Lanao gains a single body responsible for its rehabilitation, chaired at cabinet level.
A 30-year Master Plan becomes the instrument every program in the lake area must align to.
Non-government organisations hold seats on the governing board.
An independent expert panel reviews the Authority every decade and reports to Parliament.
Doubts about the Act are resolved in favour of its objectives rather than narrowly.
readings.insight:
The 30-year Master Plan is this bill's real instrument, and it is a better fit for the problem than a regulatory body alone would be. Lake Lanao's difficulties — siltation, water quality, biodiversity loss, a shoreline that moves with the drawdown — are cumulative and slow, and none of them is solved inside a political term. Writing a 30-year horizon into the statute, requiring provincial and local activity to anchor on it, and specifying its contents down to hydrological characteristics and power potential, commits successive governments to a single document rather than to a sequence of projects.

What the bill conspicuously does not do is name the National Power Corporation. The Agus River appears once, as the lake's single outlet; the Master Plan must assess the lake's "power potentials"; and the entity that actually operates the hydroelectric complex on that outlet has no seat, no obligation and no mention. Bill No. 111, covering the same lake, seats NAPOCOR on its board. A plan that assesses power potential without binding the power operator is a plan that can be written and then contradicted by the drawdown, and this is the gap a committee comparing the 2 bills would have to close.

The board composition is the other half of the comparison. 7 ministers in person, a chair appointed by the Chief Minister and 2 NGO seats is a heavyweight regional body — it can requisition attention across government in a way Bill 111's board of provincial directors cannot. The cost is distance: 1 seat for the Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, no seat for Marawi City, none for the municipal or barangay leagues, and no consultative assembly. The lake is governed for the province rather than by it.

The independent review in Section 18 is the provision most worth keeping from either bill. A panel of experts, appointed outside the Authority, reviewing its policies and programs every 10 years and reporting to Parliament as well as the Chief Minister, is the only external check on a 30-year plan in either document — and 30 years is 3 of those reviews, which is roughly the right cadence for a body whose results cannot be judged in less.

One thing about this bill's provenance deserves recording, because it is rare. The measure began as a citizen's entry in a drafting contest and says so on its own first page, naming the entrant. 3 bills in this registry carry that footnote — this one, the Halal Food Certification bill and the bill on the safety and welfare of minors — all traceable to contests run by MP Ampatuan's office with MP Mawallil and MP Mitmug. A parliament that takes legislative text from the public and credits the author by name in the filed copy is doing something most legislatures do not, and the practice is visible only in the footnotes.

2 bills in this registry create an authority for Lake Lanao and they are not versions of each other. Bill No. 111, filed by MP Ramos in October 2022, creates a Ranaw Development Authority run by provincial officials and covering the whole of Lanao del Sur. Bill No. 155, filed by MP Ampatuan in March 2023, creates a Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority run by ministers and confined to the lake area. Both are still at Second Reading, Committee Stage. Neither has become law, and the lake has no authority of any kind.
