readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes and constructs a Level I municipal hospital with 50 beds in Talayan, Maguindanao, to be known as the Talayan Municipal Hospital, appropriating funds for its facilities, professional health care and medical personnel.

Its declaration of policy carries the wider formulation used in a handful of the region's hospital measures: beyond comprehensive and integrated health service delivery and the basic right to life, the Bangsamoro Government is to act "in order to adequately respond to emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases".
readings.whyProposed:
The bill is short and its case rests on the absence of a facility in the municipality rather than on a documented caseload.

The emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases clause is the one substantive addition to the standard policy language, and it is the same sentence that appears in the Masiu hospital bill which became BAA 69 — drafted in the years after both the Marawi siege and the pandemic, in a province where displacement and flooding are recurrent.
whoIsAffected: The residents of Talayan, Maguindanao, who have no hospital in the municipality.
Patients travelling to facilities in neighbouring municipalities.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital.
Communities affected by flooding and displacement, addressed through the emergencies and disasters clause.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: Talayan gains a 50-bed Level I municipal hospital.
Funds are appropriated for personnel as well as facilities.
The hospital's mandate expressly covers emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases.
readings.insight:
This is the thinnest of the hospital bills on evidence and it is worth saying so. Where the Ambolodto measures compute a bed deficiency from census data and a published ratio, and the South Upi bill cites 5 years of occupancy rates, this one asserts the need without measuring it. That is not a reason to doubt the need — Talayan appears in the parliamentary districts schedule with 34,156 people and the province's hospital provision is documented as thin throughout this registry — but a committee choosing among 12 competing hospital bills has nothing here to weigh.

The emergencies and disasters clause is the provision to keep, and its history in this registry is instructive. The same sentence appears in the bill that became BAA 69, where it survived into the enacted act. A hospital whose statutory purpose expressly includes disaster response has a basis for stockpiling, for surge planning and for claiming calamity funds that a hospital established only for ordinary care does not — and in the Maguindanao lowlands, where flooding displaces communities most years, that is a practical difference rather than a rhetorical one.

The appropriation language matters for the same reason it does in the companion bills filed that season: funding "its facilities and professional health care, medical personnel" rather than the hospital in the abstract. Several members converged on that formulation in early 2023, which suggests a shared diagnosis that the region's problem was never the designation but the staffing that failed to follow it.

Section 4 integrates the Universal Health Care Act into the hospital's system of operations. The declaration of policy carries the wider formulation used in a handful of the region's hospital measures: beyond comprehensive and integrated health service delivery and the basic right to life, the Bangsamoro Government is to act "in order to adequately respond to emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases".
readings.whyProposed:
The bill is short and rests its case on the absence of a hospital in the municipality rather than on a documented caseload or travel time.

The emergencies and disasters clause is the 1 substantive addition to the standard policy language, and it is the same sentence that appears in the Masiu hospital bill which became BAA 69 — drafted after both the Marawi siege and the pandemic, in provinces where flooding and displacement are recurrent.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Datu Anggal Midtimbang, recorded at about 28,224 in the Parliamentary Districts Act schedule, who have no hospital in the municipality.
Patients travelling to facilities in neighbouring municipalities or to the provincial hospital.
Communities affected by flooding and displacement, addressed through the emergencies and disasters clause.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title appropriates funds for facilities and for professional health care and medical personnel — naming staffing alongside construction, which is the lesson several members drew in early 2023 from hospitals designated at a level they were never staffed for.

whatChanges: Datu Anggal Midtimbang gains a 50-bed Level I municipal hospital.
Funds are appropriated for personnel as well as facilities.
The hospital's mandate expressly covers emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases.
readings.insight:
The name is worth noting plainly, because the registry rewards attention to it. The municipality is Datu Anggal Midtimbang and the bill's author is MP Tawakal B. Midtimbang. A member filing to build a hospital in the municipality that carries their family name is unremarkable in Philippine local politics and worth recording in a reading whose purpose is to show what the documents say — particularly since the measure appropriates for a facility twice the size the municipality's population supports.

Against that, the need is real on the registry's own evidence. Datu Anggal Midtimbang sits in the first district of Maguindanao del Sur, alongside South Upi, Talayan, Guindulungan, Datu Unsay and Datu Hoffer Ampatuan — a district of roughly 170,000 people in which this registry records no hospital act at all, while the neighbouring northern district of Maguindanao del Norte has 2 hospitals and 4 further bills seeking more. The question a committee would have to answer is not whether the municipality needs a facility but whether 50 beds there is a better use of the money than 25 beds there and 25 somewhere else.

All 3 municipalities are small. The Parliamentary Districts Act prints Talayan at 34,156, Guindulungan at 24,933 and Datu Anggal Midtimbang at 28,224. On the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 that other bills in this registry invoke, each supports about 25 to 34 beds — so a 50-bed request is roughly double what the municipality's own population implies, and the bills do not explain the margin.

MP Midtimbang filed 3 hospital bills on the same template. Bill No. 156 establishes a 50-bed Level I hospital at Talayan, Bill No. 157 at Datu Anggal Midtimbang and Bill No. 158 at Guindulungan — all in the Maguindanao provinces, all 50 beds, all with the same declaration of policy and the same Universal Health Care integration clause. The Talayan bill reached Second Reading; these 2 are still at First Reading.

Guindulungan is the smallest of the 3 municipalities in this set, at under 25,000 people, and it is asking for the same 50 beds as the other 2. That is the clearest illustration in the registry of what happens when hospital bills are drafted from a template rather than from a catchment: the bed count is a constant where the populations vary by a third.

The contrast with the Ambolodto bills filed 4 months later is instructive. Funding "its facilities and professional health care, medical personnel" rather than the hospital in the abstract is the formulation several members converged on in early 2023, and the registry shows why: Bill No. 146 documents a 50-bed designation that ran on a 10-bed budget for years, and Bill No. 264 a hospital still operating at 25 beds 31 years after a national law raised it to 50.

readings.whatItDoes:
This institutionalises a community dispute-resolution system called PASAD — the People’s Alternative System in Addressing Disputes — and builds an office to run it in every province and municipality of the region.

The purpose section states the aim plainly: that people take genuine steps to resolve disputes before certain court actions are begun, and that parties keep the autonomy to settle their differences by a process they agree on. Parties may agree that a dispute is resolved by PASAD; the Ministry of Public Order and Safety then facilitates the constitution of the PASAD Provider the parties choose, and appoints one itself if the parties cannot agree. Providers must be neutral, preferably accredited by MPOS, at least 30 years old, and unrelated by blood or marriage to either party within the third degree.

The process is bounded by confidentiality, with stated exceptions and a waiver mechanism, and by a right of recusal. Where it succeeds, the parties sign a written settlement agreement, the Provider authenticates it and gives them copies, and they may deposit it with the appropriate office where one of them resides. If it has to be enforced, a party may petition a court and may ask the Ministry for help enforcing it.

Section 19 is the section that makes this a Bangsamoro law rather than a generic mediation statute. The Ministry must ensure the PASAD procedure on conciliation, peacemaking and amicable settlement accords with Islamic law — sulh, the tradition of reconciliation — and must also promote the traditional methods used by non-Moro indigenous peoples.

The structure is a Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with a secretariat under an Executive Director and 3 departments: Finance and Administration; Training, Accreditation and Promotion; and Policy, Compliance and Monitoring. Below it sits a Provincial Office under a Provincial Administrator in every BARMM province including the Special Geographic Area, and a Municipal Coordinating Office in every cluster or municipality.
readings.whyProposed:
The stated purpose is speedy, impartial and inexpensive justice through early dispute resolution, and — in the bill’s own phrase — justpeace and sustainable development in the region.

The unstated context is what makes it serious. Formal courts are distant, slow and expensive for most of this region, and disputes that go unresolved here do not simply persist: they escalate into rido, the clan feuding that is among the largest causes of violence and displacement in the Bangsamoro. Sulh and traditional settlement are how most disputes have always actually been resolved. The bill is an attempt to give that a statutory footing, a trained and accredited cadre, and an office structure reaching down to the municipality.
whoIsAffected: Parties to disputes across the region, who gain a settlement route that is faster and cheaper than a court.
Communities affected by rido, where an unsettled dispute is the first step in a feud.
Non-Moro indigenous peoples, whose traditional dispute processes the Ministry is required to promote.
PASAD Providers, a new accredited role with stated qualifications and a recusal duty.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, which would carry a regional office, a provincial office in every province and the Special Geographic Area, and a municipal coordinating office in every municipality or cluster.
The courts, which the system is designed to keep certain disputes out of.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety (MPOS), which accredits and where necessary appoints Providers
Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with an Executive Director and 3 service departments
PASAD Provincial Offices under Provincial Administrators, in every province and in the Special Geographic Area
Municipal Coordinating Offices for PASAD in every municipality or cluster
A Technical Working Group organized by the Chief Minister within 1 month of approval, to draft the implementing rules, with an Oversight Committee

funding.detail: No figure. The amount necessary is to be included in the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act of the year following enactment and thereafter — which means, unusually, the Act carries no first-year money at all and the whole structure waits for the next budget cycle. For a bill that creates a regional office, a provincial office in every province and a coordinating office in every municipality, that is a substantial standing cost with no stated size and a 1-year delay built into the text.

whatChanges: PASAD becomes a recognized route to settling a dispute, agreed to by the parties.
A settlement reached through it is a written, authenticated agreement that a court can be asked to enforce.
The procedure must be aligned with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and traditional non-Moro indigenous methods must be promoted.
Providers become an accredited role with stated qualifications, a recusal right and a confidentiality duty.
MPOS gains a PASAD office structure reaching from the region to the municipality.
The Office may recommend statutory changes on dispute resolution directly to Parliament.
readings.insight:
The most consequential thing in this bill is Section 19, and it is one paragraph long. It requires that the whole procedure accord with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and separately that traditional methods among non-Moro indigenous peoples be promoted. That is the difference between a mediation statute and a Bangsamoro one — it takes sulh, which is how disputes here have in practice always been settled, and gives it a place inside the formal system rather than beside it.

What the bill does not do is make PASAD compulsory. The purpose section says people should take genuine steps to resolve disputes "before certain court actions are instituted", but the operative provision begins with the parties agreeing. No category of dispute is required to go through PASAD first, and no court is directed to send anything to it. Compared with the barangay justice system under national law, which does bar certain suits until conciliation has been attempted, this is an invitation rather than a gate — and the gap between the aspiration in Section 2 and the mechanism in Section 8 is where the bill will be tested.

The funding clause is the practical worry. An office in every province and every municipality is a real payroll, and the Act deliberately takes no money in its first year, deferring everything to the following budget. A dispute-resolution system that exists in law and not yet in the municipalities is worse than none, because parties will have been told to use something that has no one to staff it.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred to the Committees on the Bangsamoro Justice System and on Finance in October 2024, where the index leaves it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 159, copy as filed
Parliament Bill No. 160, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This proposes to integrate zakat — the obligatory almsgiving of Islam — with the individual income tax paid by Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government.

The mechanism is set out plainly. An employee’s income tax is reduced by an amount equal to the zakat they pay. The finance officer of the office deducts both, remits the income tax to the Bureau of Internal Revenue, and remits the zakat to the Office of the Lujnatul Uliya of the place, or to its authorised collector. Zakat is computed at 2.5% of net — not gross — income, following the majority Sunni position, which the bill states.

Coverage is confined to government service under BARMM: regular and semi-regular employees, permanent or contractual, and holders of political and appointive positions.

The bill knows it has a problem, and says so. Section 9 requires a representative of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit together and settle the issues. Section 10 then provides that, pending that settlement and national approval, ₱25,000,000 shall be appropriated annually as a subsidy to cover the income tax not remitted to the BIR — the region paying the Bureau the difference, so that no national revenue is lost while the question is unresolved.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section frames it as moral governance: merging what it treats as 2 obligations of the same character — both, in the bill’s reasoning, levies for public use and public purpose — into a single obligation, so a Muslim employee is not paying twice. The justification section calls the present arrangement a duplicity of obligation and argues that removing it is consistent with the Philippine law of taxation being progressive, regressive and uniform.

Underneath is a real situation. Observant Muslim employees in the region pay income tax to the state and zakat to their community, and for many the combined burden is the reason zakat goes unpaid or is paid without record.
whoIsAffected: Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government — regular, semi-regular, permanent, contractual, political and appointive.
The Office of the Lujnatul Uliya and its authorised zakat collectors, who would receive remitted zakat through a government payroll.
Finance officers in every Bangsamoro government office, who would deduct and remit both.
The Bureau of Internal Revenue, whose collection from these employees would be made whole by a regional subsidy rather than by the taxpayer.
Non-Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government, who are outside the scheme.
The national government, whose agreement Section 9 requires.
implementedBy: Finance officers of Bangsamoro government offices, who deduct and remit
Office of the Lujnatul Uliya, and its authorised collectors of zakat
Bureau of Internal Revenue, which continues to receive the tax — via the subsidy, pending settlement
A joint discussion of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government, required by Section 9

funding.detail: ₱25,000,000 annually, appropriated as a subsidy to pay the Bureau of Internal Revenue the income tax that employees do not remit because they have paid zakat instead. The subsidy is expressly a holding arrangement — it runs "pending settlement of the issues and approval thereof by the National Government". It is one of the few precise figures in this batch and it buys time rather than a service.

whatChanges: A Muslim employee’s income tax is reduced by the zakat they pay, at 2.5% of net income.
Zakat is deducted at payroll and remitted to the Lujnatul Uliya by the employing office.
The Bangsamoro Government appropriates ₱25 million a year to make the BIR whole in the meantime.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government are required to meet and settle the legal question.
readings.insight:
This is the most legally exposed bill in this batch, and the striking thing is that its drafters clearly knew it.

Individual income tax is a national tax, imposed by the National Internal Revenue Code and collected by the BIR. A regional parliament cannot reduce a national tax liability, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law does not give the region that power. The bill does not pretend otherwise. Section 9 requires the region, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit down over it, and Section 10 provides ₱25 million a year so that until they do, the national treasury loses nothing and the employee’s zakat still reaches the Lujnatul Uliya. That is an unusually honest structure: it converts a jurisdictional claim the region cannot yet make into a subsidy the region can pay, and it leaves the constitutional question open on the face of the statute.

The second question is one the bill does not address. The scheme routes a payroll deduction from a government office to a religious body, and confers a fiscal benefit that depends on the employee’s religion. Those raise establishment and equal protection questions under the Constitution that Section 9’s discussion would have to reach.

A drafting point that matters practically: the bill repeatedly says "individual income tax return" where it means the tax itself. A return is a form. The distinction would need fixing before enactment, because the operative sections deduct and remit something that, as written, is a document.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, deferred in July 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This increases the bed capacity of the Luuk District Hospital at Tubig Putih in Luuk, Sulu, with the facilities and professional complement raised commensurately and future growth tied to the hospital development plan.

The bill is the most quantitatively argued hospital measure in the registry. It works from Department of Health Administrative Order 2006-0004, the guidelines for issuing a certificate of need to establish a new hospital, which set the ratio at no more than 1 bed per 1,000 population.

Against that standard: Sulu has 1,000,108 people and 320 beds — a deficit of 680. Counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the establishment of the Maimbung District Hospital still leaves 480 missing. And the eastern part of the island is served by a 25-bed infirmary and a 25-bed Level I district hospital for 4 municipalities — Luuk, Old Panamao, Kalingalan Caluang and the coastal municipality of Omar — holding more than 155,000 people across over 900 square kilometers.
readings.whyProposed:
The note makes its case through a single event. A patient must travel more than an hour to reach the Provincial Hospital in Jolo when the Luuk District Hospital is overwhelmed and cannot transfer them to the Panamao infirmary — "just like what happened during the onslaught of the COVID-19 Pandemic". In emergent situations, the note says, that travel time can mean life and death.

The argument for upgrading rather than building is practical. As a Level I district hospital, Luuk already provides major and minor surgery, emergency care, obstetric and neonatal care, laboratory testing, outpatient and even dental services. The capability exists; the beds, staff and equipment do not.
whoIsAffected: The 155,000 people of Luuk, Old Panamao, Kalingalan Caluang and Omar, across more than 900 square kilometers.
Patients travelling over an hour to Jolo when the district hospital is full.
The 25-bed infirmary at Panamao, which cannot absorb overflow.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital in Jolo, which receives what eastern Sulu cannot handle.
The Ministry of Health, which would fund the additional beds, staff and equipment.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: Eastern Sulu's district hospital gains beds, staff and equipment.
A facility already capable of surgery and obstetrics gets the capacity to use those services.
Growth is tied to a hospital development plan rather than to further legislation.
readings.insight:
Upgrading a hospital that already has the clinical capability is the most efficient hospital proposal in this registry, and the bill makes the argument explicitly. Luuk can already perform major and minor surgery, deliver babies, run a laboratory and see outpatients — it simply cannot admit enough people. Adding beds to an existing Level I facility buys clinical capacity that building a new 25-bed hospital elsewhere would not, because the new hospital would need the theatre, the laboratory and the staff from scratch.

The COVID example is the most concrete failure documented in any of these bills. The note does not argue hypothetically about overcrowding; it records that the district hospital was overwhelmed, that the Panamao infirmary could not take the transfers, and that the alternative was more than an hour to Jolo. That is a referral chain breaking under load, witnessed, and it is the strongest evidence a hospital bill in this registry offers.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

What the bill does not say is how many beds it asks for. It increases capacity, raises facilities and staffing commensurately, and ties future growth to the development plan — without naming a number. Against the Ambolodto bills, which compute a deficit and state the beds sought, that is a gap: a measure this well argued on the arithmetic leaves its own ask unquantified.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 161, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Parang District Hospital in Parang, Sulu, increasing its authorised bed capacity for general care services to 50 — from the 10 it currently holds.

A district hospital authorised for 10 beds is, in practice, an infirmary with a district hospital's name, and the bill's purpose is to bring the authorisation up to the number a Level I facility serving a municipality needs.
readings.whyProposed:
Parang is a municipality of Sulu — not to be confused with the Parang in Maguindanao del Norte where the region's seat of government is to be established — and its district hospital carries an authorised capacity of 10 beds.

The case is the same arithmetic its companion bill sets out for the province as a whole: Sulu has about 320 beds for over 1 million people, and a district hospital authorised for 10 of them contributes almost nothing to closing that gap.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Parang, Sulu, served by a district hospital authorised for 10 beds.
Patients referred to Jolo because the district hospital cannot admit them.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital, which absorbs what the district hospitals cannot.
The Ministry of Health, which would fund a fivefold increase in capacity.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: A district hospital's authorised capacity rises from 10 beds to 50.
General care services gain the capacity to admit patients rather than refer them.
readings.insight:
10 beds is the number to hold onto, because it shows what "district hospital" can mean in this region. A district hospital is meant to be the referral facility for a cluster of municipalities; authorised at 10 beds it cannot be the referral facility for one. The same member filed Bill No. 161 for the Luuk District Hospital in the same province on the same subject, and together the 2 describe a provincial hospital system in which the district tier barely exists.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

The jump from 10 to 50 is the largest proportional increase sought by any hospital bill in this registry — fivefold — and it is also the one most likely to be reduced. The pattern in the enacted acts is convergence on 25 beds to national minimum standards: the South Ubian and Sibutu bills each asked 50 and received 25, while the Pura bill asked 10 to 15 and received 25. On that record a 10-bed hospital asking for 50 would most likely come out at 25, which would still be a substantial gain.

One point of care for anyone searching the registry: there are 2 Parangs. This bill concerns Parang in Sulu. The Parang in Maguindanao del Norte is where BAA 37 establishes the region's seat of government, where the Iranon District Hospital was converted to a 200-bed provincial hospital by BAA 73, and where Bongo Island lies — the subject of Bill No. 269. 4 separate measures in this registry turn on the 2 names.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 162, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a district hospital in Languyan, Tawi-Tawi, to be known as the Languyan District Hospital — a Level 1 facility of 50 beds.

What distinguishes the drafting is that it works from the standard rather than asserting a level. The note sets out what the Department of Health requires a Level 1 district hospital to have by way of clinical services, and the bill is written to that specification.
readings.whyProposed:
Languyan covers 581.20 square kilometers — 224.40 square miles — which is 16.03% of the province's land area, with a population of 37,096 at the 2020 census.

The case is the familiar island-province one: a municipality holding a sixth of Tawi-Tawi's territory and more than 37,000 people, whose patients must reach the provincial hospital at Bongo for anything a health unit cannot handle. The bill is presented as the answer to that gap, sized and specified to the national standard for the level it claims.
whoIsAffected: The 37,096 residents of Languyan, across 16.03% of Tawi-Tawi's land area.
Patients currently travelling to the provincial hospital in Bongao.
The Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital, already documented elsewhere in this registry as running at 150 to 200% occupancy.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and staff it to Level 1 clinical standards.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the facility and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Languyan gains a 50-bed Level 1 district hospital.
The facility is specified against the Department of Health's own clinical service requirements for the level.
Pressure eases on the overloaded provincial hospital at Bongao.
readings.insight:
Setting out the Department of Health's clinical service requirements in the note is the practice that ought to be standard and almost never is. A bill that says "Level 1 district hospital" is asking for a label; a bill that lists the clinical services the label requires is asking for a facility, and it gives the health ministry and the finance ministry something to cost. Of the 23 hospital bills in this registry, this is 1 of only 2 that engage with what a level actually means — the other being the Maguindanao Provincial Hospital upgrade, which reproduces the administrative order.

The land-area figure is the argument that a population count alone would miss. Languyan is 16% of Tawi-Tawi spread across a province of islands, so the distance a patient travels is not from Languyan to Bongao but from wherever in Languyan they live to the sea, and then across it. A single district hospital in the municipality does not solve that for the furthest barangays, and no bill in this registry addresses intra-municipal distance in an island setting.

The co-authorship is worth a note: 5 principal authors and 13 co-authors, including most of the members who filed the island hospital bills separately. A measure with that much of the chamber's name on it and 3 years at Committee Stage says something about the difference between signing a bill and moving it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 163, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the Bangsamoro Fast Food Labeling Act, and it does something none of the other food bills does: it names the companies.

Section 3 applies the Act to fast food restaurants "including but not limited to Jollibee, McDonalds, Chowking, Greenwich Pizza, Mang Inasal, KFC, Goldilocks, Red Ribbon, Pizza Hut, and Shakeys", whether inside or outside malls, operating anywhere in the region. A fast food restaurant is then defined by 6 characteristics — quick service, food already prepared or quickly preparable, disposable wrappings and utensils, preparation encouraging consumption off the premises, orders not taken at the table, and an asset size of ₱5,000,000 or above.

The labelling rule has 2 halves and the first is the important one. Food items and condiments are *presumed not to contain* pork, lard or any by-product unless labelled otherwise, and the bill states the consequence expressly: "The lack of label is equivalent to a claim on the absence of the aforementioned ingredients." Anything that does contain pork must be labelled "WITH PORK" or words to that effect — on advertisements and on promotional and marketing materials distributed anywhere in the region, in the menus in every branch, and in the eMenus of online food platforms, with GrabFood and foodpanda named. Management is responsible for ensuring the label is printed or shown conspicuously enough to be read and understood by an ordinary person.

Prohibited acts are failing to label a pork-containing item in advertisements, materials, menus or eMenus; falsely claiming a food item or condiment contains no pork; and violating the implementing rules. Penalties escalate: ₱10,000 to ₱20,000 for a first offence, ₱20,000 to ₱50,000 for a second, ₱50,000 to ₱100,000 for a third, imposed on the owner or, for a corporate entity, on the directors, officers, employees or persons responsible. On a third or later offence the Council may recommend suspension of operations for up to 6 months, or cancellation of licences or permits, to the local government concerned.

A Fast Food Labeling Council enforces it, chaired by the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism with the Minister of Health as vice-chair and the interior ministry among its members.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy is consumer education and protection, and the mechanism chosen is disclosure rather than prohibition: the Act regulates the labelling, display and advertisement of food products and condiments by popular fast food chains in the region.

The practical problem is specific. National fast food chains operate standard menus across the Philippines, and a Muslim customer in Cotabato City ordering from the same board as a customer in Manila has no way of knowing which items contain pork or lard. The bill does not ask the chains to change what they sell; it asks them to say what is in it, in every place a customer might look — including the delivery apps.
whoIsAffected: Muslim consumers in the region ordering from national fast food chains.
The 10 named chains and any other quick-service restaurant with assets of ₱5,000,000 or more.
Owners and, for corporate operators, directors, officers and responsible employees, who bear the penalties personally.
Online food platforms including GrabFood and foodpanda, whose eMenus must carry the labels.
Advertisers and marketers distributing promotional material in the region.
Small eateries below the ₱5,000,000 asset threshold, which fall outside the Act.
implementedBy: Fast Food Labeling Council, chaired by the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism with the Minister of Health as Vice Chairperson and the interior ministry among its members
Local government units, to which the Council may recommend suspension of operations or cancellation of permits
Fast food management, expressly made responsible for the conspicuousness of the labelling

funding.detail: No appropriation. The scheme is funded by nothing and enforced by escalating fines — ₱10,000 to ₱20,000, then ₱20,000 to ₱50,000, then ₱50,000 to ₱100,000 — with suspension of operations for up to 6 months or cancellation of permits available on a third or later offence.

whatChanges: Pork-containing items must be labelled "WITH PORK" in menus, eMenus, advertisements and marketing materials in the region.
An unlabelled item legally represents itself as pork-free.
Delivery platform listings come within the labelling duty.
Named national chains are brought under a regional labelling regime enforced by a ministerial council.
Repeat offenders risk suspension or loss of their business permits.
readings.insight:
The default presumption is the legally interesting move and it is easy to read past. Most labelling statutes require a disclosure and punish its absence. This one goes further: it declares that the absence of a label is itself a positive claim that the food contains no pork. That converts every unlabelled item on every menu into a representation the chain has made, which means a mislabelled item is not merely an omission but a false claim — and it is what allows the second prohibited act, falsely claiming an item contains no pork, to bite without anyone having to prove the chain said anything at all.

Naming the 10 companies in the statute is unusual and cuts 2 ways. It removes any argument about coverage — Jollibee cannot contend it is not a fast food restaurant within the meaning of the Act — and it dates the law to the brands trading in 2023, while the "including but not limited to" and the 6-characteristic definition are what carry it forward. The ₱5,000,000 asset threshold is the real line, and it deliberately exempts the small local eatery, which is the sensible half of the design: a family carinderia cannot maintain compliant eMenu labelling across delivery platforms.

Extending the duty to eMenus and naming GrabFood and foodpanda is the provision that makes this bill current rather than a decade behind the market. A consumer ordering through an app never sees the in-store menu board, and a labelling law confined to premises would have missed the fastest-growing way food is sold. Few statutes in this registry engage with the platform economy at all.

What the bill does not do is address halal more broadly, and that is a deliberate narrowing. Pork is the clearest case and the easiest to label; the harder questions — slaughter method, cross-contamination, gelatine and other derivatives — are exactly what Bill No. 10's certification scheme and Bill No. 60's prohibited acts are built for. Read together the 3 bills are close to a complete scheme, and taken one at a time each has an obvious gap.

3 bills in this registry regulate what the region eats, and they pick 3 different instruments for the same problem. Bill No. 10 licenses: every Muslim restaurant must hold an annual halal certificate. Bill No. 60 polices the lie: no certificate is required, but misrepresenting food as halal becomes an offence with a long schedule of prohibited acts. Bill No. 164 discloses: it does not regulate halal at all, instead requiring named fast food chains to label anything containing pork. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none of the 3 has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 164, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This gives Bangsamoro voters the power to make regional law themselves, and sets out every step of how.

The power covers propositions to enact, amend or repeal regional legislation, and is exercised by registered voters of the region. 5 things are off limits, among them propositions embracing more than one subject and propositions outside the powers of the Bangsamoro Government or inside the reserved powers of the national government.

The procedure runs like this. Proponents first send the proposed text to the Bangsamoro Attorney General and ask for a circulating title and summary and a unique numerical identifier. Once issued, they have 180 days to gather signatures. The petition is filed with the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies whether it is sufficient and whether the signatures are authentic. An Initiatives Coordinator is provided for.

The threshold is the heart of it: a proposition qualifies as a ballot measure if signed by at least 10% of all registered voters of the region, reckoned from the immediately preceding election, and — for propositions affecting the whole region — every parliamentary district must be represented by at least 3%. A plebiscite follows.

The bill then does something a plain initiative statute would not. Section 18 limits Parliament: a proposition approved by initiative cannot be repealed, modified or amended within 6 months, may only be repealed by Parliament within 3 years, and any law seeking to repeal a law enacted by initiative is itself subject to a referendum. Section 19 provides a separate, gentler route — a people-initiated bill, filed by petition with Parliament for it to consider in the ordinary way.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Organic Law contemplates a system of initiative and referendum for the region, and until it is legislated the power exists on paper and cannot be exercised. This bill supplies the machinery: who may propose, what may be proposed, how a petition is titled and circulated, how many signatures are needed and from where, who certifies them, and what happens after a proposition passes.
whoIsAffected: Every registered voter in the Bangsamoro, who gains a route to legislate directly.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, whose power to amend or repeal a successful initiative is expressly restricted for 3 years.
The Bangsamoro Attorney General, given the gatekeeping function of issuing the circulating title and summary.
The Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which must verify signatures at region-wide scale and run the plebiscites.
Civil society and advocacy groups, for whom this is the mechanism to put a measure Parliament will not take up to a vote.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies sufficiency and authenticity and conducts the plebiscite
Office of the Bangsamoro Attorney General, which issues the circulating title, the summary and the numerical identifier
An Initiatives Coordinator provided for in the Act
The Bangsamoro Parliament, for the people-initiated bill route and for the adoption provision

funding.detail: No figure. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s appropriations of the agencies named in the Act, and later years go into the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act. Verifying signatures from 10% of the region’s registered voters and running a region-wide plebiscite are both expensive, and the cost falls first on the Bangsamoro Electoral Office out of a budget already set.

whatChanges: Registered voters can propose regional legislation directly and put it to a plebiscite.
A proposition needs 10% of the region’s registered voters, with at least 3% from every parliamentary district for region-wide measures.
Proponents get 180 days to gather signatures after the Attorney General issues the circulating title.
Parliament cannot touch a successful initiative for 6 months and can only repeal it within 3 years — and a repealing law must itself go to a referendum.
A separate route lets voters file a bill with Parliament by petition.
Propositions embracing more than one subject, or outside Bangsamoro competence, are barred.
readings.insight:
The district floor is the design decision that will decide whether this power is ever used. Requiring 10% of all registered voters region-wide is a high bar on its own; requiring in addition that every parliamentary district supply at least 3% means an initiative cannot be carried by a concentrated majority in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao alone. It has to reach into the island districts and into every constituency. That is a deliberate protection for the smaller and more distant parts of the region against a mainland majority, and it is also, in a region with this geography and these transport costs, a very hard signature drive to run.

Section 18 is the more unusual provision and it is genuinely strong. Most initiative statutes let the legislature amend what the people pass; this one bars Parliament from touching it for 6 months, restricts repeal to a 3-year window, and then requires any repealing law to go to a referendum of its own. That makes a successful initiative harder to undo than an ordinary act of Parliament, which is a real transfer of power away from the chamber that would be passing this bill.

Worth noting what it does not cover. Section 4 confines the power to regional legislation and leaves initiatives on all other legislative acts to existing law, so this is not a route to amending the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which is national legislation.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading June 2023, deferred in August 2024 and referred to the Committee on Rules that same month, where it sits.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 165, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is MP Froilyn Mendoza's indigenous peoples code — 14 chapters recognising the rights of non-Moro indigenous peoples and creating a Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs to administer them.

The ministry is the structural choice the whole bill turns on. Section 51 creates the MNMIPA as the primary government agency responsible for policies, plans and programmes for non-Moro indigenous peoples specifically — a ministry of their own, not a bureau inside a larger one.

The chapters run from ancestral domains and the indigenous concept of ownership, through self-governance and empowerment, the traditional or tribal justice system, social justice and human rights, cultural integrity and identity, the ministry itself, delineation and recognition of domains, enforcement, the Ancestral Domains Fund, penalties, intergovernmental relations and final provisions.

2 figures carry most of the bill's weight. Section 11 gives non-Moro indigenous peoples and communities an equitable share of revenue from the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources within their titled territories of "no less than 50%", determined by the new ministry. And Section 78 creates an Ancestral Domain Fund with an initial ₱200,000,000 for compensation for expropriated lands, delineation and development — expressly to be taken from the Bangsamoro Government's Block Grant.

The penalties run from 9 months to 15 years' imprisonment, or a fine of ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000, or both, with customary law applied first subject to bars on cruel or degrading punishment, the death penalty and excessive fines. Officers of a juridical offender are personally liable and their certificates and licences cancellable.

Chapter XIII builds a channel the bill calls intergovernmental relations: a Council or Consultative Body for each non-Moro tribe, members selected under their own customary laws, advising the Minister — and expressly able to lobby the Chief Minister where a policy violates their rights, with the ministry funding the convening.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration reaffirms the 1987 Constitution, the national Indigenous Peoples Rights Act, Muslim Mindanao Act 241 — the ARMM-era Tribal Peoples Rights Act — the Organic Law, and international instruments including International Labour Organization Convention No. 169 and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Its operative claim is about identity rather than services: non-Moro indigenous peoples are to have the freedom to retain their distinct indigenous and ethnic identity *in addition to* their Bangsamoro political identity, with no discrimination on the basis of identity, religion or ethnicity.

That sentence is the bill. The Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo, Erumanun ne Menuvu, Higaonon and B'laan are not Muslim and were not party to the conflict the region was created to settle, and the fear the bill addresses is that a Bangsamoro government will serve them as a minority within a Moro framework rather than as peoples with their own standing.
whoIsAffected: The non-Moro indigenous peoples of the region — Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo, Erumanun ne Menuvu, Higaonon and B'laan.
Companies extracting natural resources in ancestral domains, who would owe no less than half the revenue.
Each non-Moro tribe, which gains a council selected under its own customary law with a channel to the Chief Minister.
The existing Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, whose non-Moro mandate would move to a new ministry.
Marginalized Moro communities — Sama Dilaut, Jama Mapun and others — who are outside this bill's coverage.
The Bangsamoro Block Grant, from which the ₱200 million domain fund would be taken.
implementedBy: Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs (MNMIPA), created by the Act as the primary agency for non-Moro indigenous peoples
Councils or Consultative Bodies for each non-Moro tribe, selected under customary law, advising the Minister and able to lobby the Chief Minister
Traditional or tribal justice systems, applying customary law in the first instance
An Ancestral Domain Fund of ₱200 million drawn from the Block Grant

funding.detail: An Ancestral Domain Fund with an initial ₱200,000,000 for compensation for expropriated lands, delineation and development of domains, expressly charged to the Bangsamoro Government's Block Grant. Separately, communities are to receive no less than 50% of revenue from natural resources extracted in their titled territories, determined by the new ministry — a transfer rather than an appropriation, and much the larger sum.

whatChanges: Non-Moro indigenous peoples gain a ministry of their own rather than a share of an existing one.
Communities receive at least half the revenue from resources taken from their domains.
Each tribe gains a council chosen under its own customary law, funded to meet and able to lobby the Chief Minister.
Penalties for intrusion on ancestral domains reach 15 years and ₱1 million.
ILO Convention 169 enters the region's policy framework alongside UNDRIP.
readings.insight:
50% against 10% is the difference that matters most, and it is the clearest measurable gap between any 2 competing bills in this registry. This bill gives communities no less than half the revenue from resources extracted in their ancestral domains. The cabinet's Bill No. 273, filed 9 months later, set the floor at 10% — and that is the version Parliament enacted as BAA 64 in December 2024. On the single question of what an indigenous community is owed for what is taken from its land, the enacted law delivers a fifth of what the indigenous members' own bill proposed.

The ministry is the deeper disagreement. This bill creates a Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs, on the premise that non-Moro peoples need an institution answerable to them alone. BAA 64 took the opposite path: it strengthens the single Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and widens its coverage to include Badjao, Sama Dilaut, Jama Mapun, Sama Banguingui and Sama Pangutaran alongside the non-Moro groups, declaring the whole territory the shared ancestral domain of all peoples with pre-colonial ties. That is a defensible and generous architecture, and it is also precisely the subsuming this bill was written to prevent.

Which reading is right is a political question this registry cannot settle. What it can record is who proposed what. MP Mendoza holds 1 of the 2 parliamentary seats reserved for non-Moro indigenous peoples under the Organic Law, and she filed this in April 2023. The Government of the Day filed its own version in January 2024 and had it enacted inside 11 months. The reserved-seat mechanism gave non-Moro peoples a voice that produced a complete legislative text, and the text that became law was the cabinet's.

Chapter XIII deserves attention as the provision most likely to have survived scrutiny on its merits. Councils constituted per tribe under each tribe's own customary law, funded by the ministry to convene, advising the Minister and expressly entitled to lobby the Chief Minister when a policy violates their rights, is a more robust consultation design than a seat on a board — it keeps the selection inside the community and routes the grievance above the ministry that might be the problem. Nothing equivalent appears in the enacted act.

One point of continuity worth noting: this bill cites Muslim Mindanao Act 241, the ARMM's Tribal Peoples Rights Act, which BAA 64 repealed and replaced. Both measures understood themselves as succeeding that statute. They disagreed about what should succeed it.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Madaris Education Assistance Act of 2023 puts money into private Islamic schools — madaris — by paying 3 different recipients directly.

Students get tuition of not less than ₱1,000 a year, reading materials, and a nutrition and feeding program for the young ones. Teachers — gurus, the bill uses the Arabic term and defines it — get an allowance of not less than ₱2,000 a month plus a faculty education development program. The madrasah itself gets classroom facilities, named down to desks, tables and chalkboards, and textbook assistance.

The faculty program is the most substantial piece: scholarships for master’s and doctorate degrees, in the country and outside it, plus seminars and training. Anyone who qualifies to study abroad must sign an undertaking to return and serve for a period set against the length of the scholarship.

Eligibility is narrow and stated. Priority goes to students whose family income is not more than ₱40,000 a year. Assistance runs only to Muslim students who are Filipino citizens and residents of the Bangsamoro, who are not already receiving another government scholarship, who are enrolled in a madrasah, and who have not transferred to one outside the region. MBHTE, through the Bureau of Madaris Education, sets the criteria, accredits which madaris qualify, and assesses whether the schools receiving the money are still teaching well.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section grounds it in Section 16, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law — the mandate to establish and maintain a complete and adequate system of education responsive to the needs and aspirations of the Bangsamoro people — and says the way to improve quality in the madaris is to assist the teachers and the students directly.

The unstated premise is that madaris are community-based and privately operated. They sit outside the public school funding system, they teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, and until something like this passes there is no standing mechanism for regional money to reach them.
whoIsAffected: Students in madaris across the region, with priority to those whose family income is ₱40,000 a year or less.
Gurus, who would receive a monthly allowance and access to postgraduate scholarships abroad.
Madaris as institutions, which would receive classroom furniture and textbooks.
Students already holding another government scholarship, who are expressly excluded.
Non-Muslim students, who are outside the stated coverage.
MBHTE and the Bureau of Madaris Education, which would have to build an accreditation system to run any of it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education (MBHTE), for policy guidance, monitoring and the implementing rules
Bureau of Madaris Education (BME), which delivers the assistance and, with MBHTE, sets the income criterion

funding.detail: No total is stated. MBHTE determines the amount necessary for initial implementation, and later years go into the annual Bangsamoro appropriations. The only hard figures in the bill are the floors on individual benefits — not less than ₱1,000 per student per year and not less than ₱2,000 per guru per month — and the ₱40,000 annual family income mark that sets priority.

whatChanges: Regional money reaches privately operated madaris for the first time through a standing mechanism.
Gurus gain a monthly allowance with a floor of ₱2,000 and access to postgraduate scholarships.
Students in madaris gain a tuition subsidy, reading materials and a feeding program.
MBHTE must build an accreditation policy to determine which madaris qualify.
Assistance is conditioned on continued quality, which MBHTE is required to assess.
readings.insight:
Every benefit in this bill is a floor rather than a figure. Not less than ₱1,000 a year, not less than ₱2,000 a month: generous drafting in one sense, because nothing caps what MBHTE may pay, and empty in another, because the bill sets no total and MBHTE decides the initial appropriation itself. What the law guarantees is a minimum per head; what it costs is settled somewhere else entirely.

The floors themselves are worth reading against the region. ₱1,000 a year in tuition and ₱2,000 a month for a teacher are modest sums, and the ₱40,000 annual family income that triggers priority is well under the national poverty threshold for a family of 5 — which means the priority mark will catch a very large share of the households the bill is aimed at rather than distinguishing between them.

The scholarship clause is the quiet ambition in it. Master’s and doctorate study abroad for madrasah teachers, with a return-service undertaking, is a serious investment in a teaching corps that has largely had no route to formal postgraduate credentials.

The coverage clause runs to Muslim students only. In a region with substantial non-Muslim indigenous communities that is a real limit, though it follows from what a madrasah is; it is stated here because the bill states it and a reader should not have to infer it.

readings.whatItDoes:
Where Bill 167 pays for madrasah education as it exists, this one proposes to rebuild the curriculum underneath it.

The bill creates a Special Madrasah Fund to review, redesign, pilot test and then implement a balanced basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School. "Balanced" is the operative word and the text defines it at length: curricula that are interactively balanced for the spiritual and worldly development of the learner, that integrate the core subjects of mainstream basic education in deeply contextualised form, and that guarantee parallelism with — the text says if not superiority to — what DepEd prescribes for standard madaris.

The method is set out as a sequence. Existing curricula and textbooks are reviewed and redesigned; a Project Management Team merges related subjects to cut what the bill calls information overload; the result is field-tested in at least 2 qualified madaris for elementary and 2 for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area; it is enhanced on the results, adopted in transition elsewhere for terminal validation, packaged, and then implemented by at least one madrasah for each level in every municipality and city in the region.

Governance sits with a Special Madrasah Fund Board chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education, with the Directorate Generals for Basic and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, and members drawn from the most prominent regional madaris association, the dominant registered ulama federation, and the regional offices of DepEd, TESDA, the Commission on Muslim Filipinos and the finance ministry. The Chief Minister appoints them for 3 years and may revoke an appointment for disgraceful or immoral conduct or corrupt practice. Board membership must be balanced across expertise in Islamic scholarship, curriculum development, school management, and fund administration.

The destination is accreditation. The bill’s stated ultimate goal is that DepEd recognize the madrasah as a Standard Muslim Education Institution and issue Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificates, so a madrasah completer can transfer into the state system, enrol at the next level, or present the certificate as an educational qualification for a job.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes an argument few filed bills bother with. It says the balanced madrasah is idealised and does not exist: the madaris DepEd accredits as Standard Private Madrasah are balanced only in the sense that 5 core subjects have been added on top of the Qur’an, Seerah, Hadith, Aqeedah, Fiqh and Arabic, which produces information overload rather than integration. It cites the Constitution’s education article and Section 16 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and it argues its theological case from Surah Al-Qasas 28:77 and a hadith on not surrendering either world for the other.

The practical driver is the Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate. Without it, years spent in a madrasah convert into nothing a state school or an employer will count.
whoIsAffected: Madrasah learners from Grade 1 to Senior High School, whose curriculum and textbooks would be rewritten.
Madrasah completers, for whom the accreditation certificate would convert years of study into a recognized qualification.
The madaris selected for pilot testing — at least 2 for elementary and 2 for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area — and eventually at least one per municipality or city.
Gurus, who would teach a merged and rewritten subject set.
DepEd and TESDA, whose recognition the whole design depends on and who sit on the board.
The regional madaris association and the ulama federation, given seats on the board that governs the fund.
implementedBy: Special Madrasah Fund Board, chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education with the Directorate Generals for Basic Education and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, appointed by the Chief Minister for 3 years
A Project Management Team, recruited by the Board and approved by the MBHTE Minister, which prepares a 10-year development and operational plan and runs the review, rewriting and pilot testing
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Department of Education, whose accreditation and equivalency certificate is the stated end point, in collaboration with MBHTE

funding.detail: No total is stated. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s Bangsamoro appropriations and later years go into the annual General Appropriations Act. The bill does itemise what the money is for, which is more than most: curriculum and textbook review and development, reproduction of new textbooks, pilot testing in each province and the Special Geographic Area, and construction of pilot testing building units, specified as a 7-room unit of one office and 6 classrooms.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists to redesign the basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School.
Subjects are merged to reduce overload, and mainstream core subjects are integrated in contextualised form.
A board seating madaris and ulama organizations alongside DepEd, TESDA and the finance ministry governs the fund.
A 10-year development and operational plan is required, with budget allocations attached.
Curricula are pilot tested province by province before general adoption, then rolled out to at least one madrasah per level per municipality or city.
Buildings are funded for the pilot sites, at a specified 7-room configuration.
readings.insight:
The whole design turns on something the Bangsamoro Parliament cannot legislate. The Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate is issued by DepEd, a national department, and the bill can fund the curriculum, staff the board and run the pilots but cannot make DepEd recognize the result. The text is careful about this — it says the measure creates the "potentiality" that DepEd would accredit, and that the mechanics are for the Department to set in collaboration with MBHTE. That is honest drafting, and it also means the bill’s stated ultimate goal is an outcome it can only make more likely.

The appropriations clause has aged. It names the provinces where pilot testing is to happen and the list includes Sulu, which the Supreme Court removed from the Bangsamoro in 2024, after this bill was filed in May 2023. Section 5, which sets out the same pilot design, refers instead to "every province of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region" and the Special Geographic Area — wording that survives the change. The 2 clauses now describe different maps.

One more thing worth noticing: the board seats are drawn from the "most prominent" regional madaris association and the "most dominant" registered ulama federation. Neither superlative is defined, and in a region with several competing ulama bodies, deciding which one is dominant is a political act the bill hands to whoever makes the appointment.
