readings.whatItDoes:
This creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city of the region.

The interior ministry develops the criteria, qualifications and disqualifications. The award is called the "Best Lupong Tagapamayapa", and it carries 3 things: a commemorative plaque or medal; a monetary grant of ₱30,000, which may be increased as circumstances warrant; and an invitation to regional events that salute the importance of the barangay justice system.

There is 1 recipient in each municipality and city, annually. The ministry has 90 days to develop the programme and the rules governing selection.
readings.whyProposed:
A Lupong Tagapamayapa is unpaid. Its members mediate neighbours' disputes, land quarrels and family conflicts in their own time, and the measure of their success is a case that never becomes a court docket — which is invisible by definition.

Recognition and a modest grant are the only levers available for work that cannot be compensated as employment, and the bill's premise is that a Lupon that knows its work is noticed does it better.
whoIsAffected: Members of the Lupong Tagapamayapa in every barangay, who do this work unpaid.
The winning Lupon in each municipality and city, which receives ₱30,000 a year.
Communities whose disputes are mediated rather than litigated.
The Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, which sets the criteria and runs the selection.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — criteria, qualifications and disqualifications, the programme, and the rules governing selection within 90 days

funding.detail: ₱30,000 per award, 1 in each municipality and city annually. With 116 municipalities and 3 cities in the region, the annual commitment at that rate is roughly ₱3.6 million — one of the few measures in this registry whose cost can be calculated from its own text.

whatChanges: The best Lupon in every municipality and city receives recognition and ₱30,000 a year.
The interior ministry must define what good barangay mediation looks like, in published criteria.
Lupon members are invited to regional events rather than remaining invisible.
readings.insight:
The criteria are the whole bill, and the bill delegates them. Deciding what makes a Lupong Tagapamayapa the best in its municipality means deciding what barangay justice is for — the number of disputes settled, the proportion that stay settled, the speed, the absence of complaints, or the willingness of parties to come back. Each of those rewards different behaviour, and a Lupon chasing settlement counts has an incentive to pressure a weaker party into agreeing. The interior ministry will write those criteria, and the published result will say more about the region's justice policy than this bill does.

The ₱30,000 is well calibrated for what it is. Too small to attract people who want money, large enough to matter to an unpaid panel in a rural barangay — it buys a filing cabinet, a meeting space, transport to hearings. The bill's provision that the grant may be increased as circumstances warrant is sensible drafting for a figure that will erode.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

What the award scheme cannot do is address capacity, and the companion bills are the author's acknowledgment of that. A Lupon that does not know the law cannot apply it well no matter how it is incentivised, which is what Bill No. 172's handbook is for; and a Lupon with no standing in the local power structure cannot enforce a settlement, which is what Bill No. 173's federation and peace-and-order-council seats are for. Read alone this is a prize. Read as 1 of 3, it is the recognition layer of a capacity programme.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 170, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires the interior ministry to formulate, develop and publish a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook, translated into the major languages of the region.

Section 5 sets the standard the handbook must meet, and it is written in plain terms: the material must communicate the ideas clearly to the officials concerned, make the task of following the procedure as effortless as possible, and include annotations of the relevant laws — the Katarungang Pambarangay law, the jurisdictional rules, and special laws. It may be republished every 5 years to keep pace with new measures.

Section 6 handles distribution. The ministry provides an electronic and a hard copy to every barangay in the region, and requires each to keep a hard copy available in its office.

The implementing rules are drawn up in consultation with government agencies, experts, teachers, historians, linguists, legal luminaries and other stakeholders. The Act is titled the "Alay sa Lupon Act" — an offering to the Lupon.
readings.whyProposed:
The barangay justice system runs on unpaid volunteers applying procedural rules about jurisdiction, mediation, conciliation and the certification that allows a case to proceed to court. Getting those rules wrong means a settlement that will not hold or a case dismissed for want of the right certificate.

The handbook is the cheapest intervention available. It does not change the law, create a body or appropriate a facility — it puts the procedure in the hands of the people expected to follow it, in a language they read.
whoIsAffected: Lupong Tagapamayapa members in every barangay, who must apply procedural rules without legal training.
Parties to barangay disputes, whose settlements depend on the procedure being followed correctly.
Speakers of the region's major languages, into which the handbook must be translated.
Barangay offices, each required to keep a hard copy available.
Linguists, teachers and legal practitioners consulted on the implementing rules.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — formulating, publishing, translating and distributing the handbook, and the implementing rules within 90 days in consultation with experts, teachers, historians, linguists and legal practitioners

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is translation, publication and distribution of a hard and electronic copy to every barangay in the region — a one-off with a 5-year republication cycle, and among the smallest price tags attached to any measure in this registry.

whatChanges: Every barangay receives a handbook on the justice system it is required to operate.
That handbook exists in the region's major languages, not only in English or Filipino.
A hard copy must be kept available in each barangay office.
The text is annotated with the relevant laws and republished every 5 years.
readings.insight:
Translation into the major languages is the provision that makes this bill worth more than its cost. The region's barangay officials work in Maranao, Maguindanaon, Tausug, Yakan, Sama and several others; the Katarungang Pambarangay law and its jurisprudence exist in English. A volunteer mediator reading procedural rules in a second or third language applies them approximately, and the resulting defect surfaces later as a settlement that will not stand or a case thrown out. This is the same instinct as the enacted BAA 59's requirement that agricultural training materials be delivered "in the language most appropriate to the end-user", and the Local Governance Code's provision for sessions in a local language with translated minutes — the region keeps returning to the point that a rule nobody can read is not in force.

Requiring both an electronic and a hard copy, with the hard copy kept available in the office, is unglamorous and correct. Barangay offices in much of this region have intermittent power and no reliable connection, and an electronic-only handbook would be a handbook nobody opens.

The 5-year republication cycle is the provision most likely to lapse. Statutes requiring periodic revision are routinely complied with once; the registry's own evidence is the Bangsamoro Register of Ordinances, which BAA 49 requires to be digital, online and public, and whose maintenance depends on the same ministry this bill relies on.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

What makes the handbook harder than it looks is that in this region the barangay panel is not the only forum. A dispute between Muslims may belong before a Shari'ah court; one involving an indigenous community is governed, under BAA 64, by that community's customary law, with ambiguity resolved in its favour. A handbook on jurisdiction has to explain when the Lupon should not take a case at all, and the bill's instruction to include "jurisdictions" among the annotations is where that work would have to be done.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 172, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the structural measure of the 3 — it federates the region's Lupong Tagapamayapa members and gives them a seat at the table where local security is decided.

A Federation of Lupong Tagapamayapa Members is created, with every barangay represented and chapters organised at municipal, city and provincial level, topped by a Regional Council. The interior ministry facilitates the election of the federation heads at each level.

Section 7 is the provision with real consequence. The elected presidents of the Federation at municipal, city and provincial level, and the chairperson of the Regional Council, serve as ex-officio members of the corresponding Peace and Order Council — municipal, city, provincial and regional. They hold those seats only while they hold the federation office, and in no case beyond the term of the government head who convened the council.

Section 9 funds the Federations from contributions by member local government units, from the regional government, and from their own fund-raising, with fund-raising proceeds tied to the projects they were raised for. Section 10 requires a Barangay Justice Summit within 6 months of the Federation being constituted. The Act is titled the "Enhanced Bangsamoro Barangay Justice" measure, and it cites Section 411 of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code on the composition of the Lupong Tagapamayapa.
readings.whyProposed:
The barangay justice system handles an enormous share of the region's disputes and has no voice above the barangay. Lupon members are appointed locally, serve unpaid, and have no standing body through which to raise a problem, share practice or be consulted on policy that affects them.

Federating them creates that voice. Seating their presidents on the peace and order councils then connects the people who mediate disputes to the bodies that handle the consequences when mediation fails — which in this region means the councils that deal with rido, with armed incidents and with displacement.
whoIsAffected: Lupong Tagapamayapa members in every barangay, who gain a federation and representation above the barangay.
Municipal, city, provincial and regional Peace and Order Councils, which gain an ex-officio member from the barangay justice system.
Local government units, asked to contribute to the Federations' funds.
Communities affected by clan feuding, where mediation and peace-and-order responses meet.
The Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, which facilitates the federation elections.
implementedBy: A Federation of Lupong Tagapamayapa Members, with municipal, city and provincial chapters and a Regional Council
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, facilitating the election of federation heads at each level
Peace and Order Councils at municipal, city, provincial and regional level, which seat the federation presidents ex officio
A Barangay Justice Summit, within 6 months of the Federation being constituted

funding.detail: The Federations derive funds from contributions of member local government units, from the regional government, and from their own fund-raising, with fund-raising proceeds restricted to the projects they were raised for. No amount is named from any of the 3 sources, which leaves the Federation's capacity dependent on voluntary local contributions.

whatChanges: Lupon members are federated from barangay to regional level.
Federation presidents sit ex officio on the Peace and Order Councils at every level.
A Barangay Justice Summit convenes within 6 months.
The Federations may raise their own funds, restricted to the purposes raised for.
readings.insight:
Section 7 is the reason this is the most consequential of the 3 bills. Peace and Order Councils in this region are where armed incidents, clan feuding and displacement are handled, and their membership is officials and uniformed services. Putting the president of the barangay mediators' federation in the room as of right brings the one body that deals with disputes before they become violence into the body that deals with them after. For a region whose own legislation repeatedly identifies rido as a cause of displacement on a par with armed conflict, that is a structural connection worth making.

The term limitation attached to it is careful drafting. The seat lasts only while the person holds the federation office and in no case beyond the term of the government head who convened the council, which prevents a federation president outlasting the body they sit on and keeps the seat institutional rather than personal.

The funding is the weakness, and it is the familiar one. A federation funded by contributions from member local governments, an unquantified share from the regional government, and its own fund-raising has no assured income — and a body of unpaid volunteers running fund-raising projects to finance its own representation is a thin foundation for something the Act seats on 4 tiers of peace and order council. Compare the registry's other federated structure: the Local Governance Code enacted as BAA 49 provides insurance for the barangay tanod, a named benefit funded through the ordinary budget.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

Citing Section 411 of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code is worth noting because of the timing. That Code was enacted as BAA 49 in November 2023, and this bill was filed in April 2023 — so the citation is to a bill that had not yet become law when this measure was written. The 2 moved at very different speeds: the Code passed inside a year and this bill has never left First Reading.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

Parliament Bill No. 174, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates, in every barangay of every city and municipality, a Barangay Justice System Multi-Sectoral Traditional and Customary Laws Advisory Council — a body to advise the barangay justice system on the customary law of the community it is settling disputes in.

The Council is chaired by the city or municipal mayor and seats a representative of the city or municipal police office, a purok leader, a traditional leader, a religious leader, an indigenous people’s leader, a tribal leader, and representatives of women, youth and persons with disabilities, each drawn from the barangay concerned.

Its functions are advisory and expressly without prejudice to the Katarungang Pambarangay Law, the national barangay justice statute. It provides specialised information, skills and experience on the community’s existing traditional and customary laws to aid the people running the barangay justice system; provides guidance and technical advice in areas outside the Lupon members’ usual expertise; encourages retirees from government and the private sector to join the barangay justice system; supplies customary and traditional laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice; and acts as the system’s advocate in the barangay.

Mayors must convene the Councils within 6 months of approval. Members receive no remuneration.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is short and states the aim: that the customs, beliefs and traditions of the Bangsamoro people are recognized, respected and guaranteed, and that disputes are resolved justly and peacefully.

The practical case is that the Lupong Tagapamayapa — the barangay conciliation panel under national law — applies a national framework in communities whose disputes are actually governed by customary law, whether Moro or indigenous. The Council is meant to put that knowledge at the panel’s disposal rather than leave it to whichever member happens to have it.
whoIsAffected: Parties to barangay-level disputes, whose settlement would draw on customary law explicitly.
Lupong Tagapamayapa members, who gain an advisory body for matters outside their expertise.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders, given a formal role in the barangay justice system.
Women, youth and persons with disabilities, each given a seat.
City and municipal mayors, who chair every one of these Councils in their jurisdiction and must convene them within 6 months.
implementedBy: City and municipal mayors, as chairs and as the officials required to convene the Councils
The Councils themselves, in every barangay
City and municipal police offices, which supply a representative to each

funding.detail: The bill makes no appropriation and states that members receive no remuneration for their duties. It is designed to cost nothing, which is a defensible choice for an advisory body — and also the reason to ask how often bodies with no budget and no paid members actually meet.

whatChanges: Every barangay in the region gains a customary law advisory council for its justice system.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders acquire a formal advisory role.
Women, youth and PWD representatives sit on the council by right.
Customary laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice are to be supplied back to the system.
Mayors must convene the councils within 6 months of approval.
The Katarungang Pambarangay Law is expressly unaffected.
readings.insight:
The chairmanship does not scale, and it is the first thing a committee should look at. The Council exists in every barangay, and the chair of every one of them is the city or municipal mayor. Lanao del Sur has municipalities with dozens of barangays; a mayor there would chair dozens of separate councils. The bill gives no provision for a designated representative, no quorum rule, and no meeting schedule. As drafted, the person who must sit at the head of each council is the one person in the municipality who cannot be in all of them.

The function about disused customary law is the most interesting line in the bill and the least noticed. Providing the barangay justice system with "customary and traditional laws that may not have been in use for reasons of non-practice" is a revival mandate, not merely an advisory one — it invites councils to bring back rules that fell out of use. Whether that is restoration or invention will depend entirely on who sits on the council, which is why the composition matters as much as it does.

The seats for women, youth and persons with disabilities are worth noting for what they do in this context. Customary dispute resolution in the region is, in practice, largely conducted by senior men. Writing those 3 seats into the statute is a deliberate correction, and it sits in tension with the traditional and tribal leadership seats beside it in a way the bill leaves unresolved.

Read alongside Bill 159, which builds a whole PASAD office structure for alternative dispute resolution, this is the same instinct at a fraction of the cost — and both are before the Committee on the Bangsamoro Justice System.

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets out how to behave while the Bangsamoro Hymn is played, and then declines to punish anyone who does not.

The code has 7 rules. Stand at attention, upright, facing the Bangsamoro flag if one is displayed. Face the flag, or the direction of the sound if the hymn is pre-recorded, or the singer if the singer is visible. Place the right hand as a **closed fist** across the chest — and the bill is explicit that this applies to everyone, including those who cannot stand unaided, and that a person walking when the hymn begins must stop, stand at attention and hold the gesture until it ends. Remove the hat with the right hand and hold it against the chest, a protocol applying to men, women, children and the elderly — but expressly excluding any religious or culture-related headwear. Men in uniform salute from the first note and hold it to the last. Put away technological devices and give the hymn full attention. And do not applaud afterwards.

Coverage extends to all citizens and guests present, with ministries, government offices, agencies, educational institutions public and private, local government units and government corporations in the region "highly enjoined" to observe it.

Section 5 then states the consequence of breach: no punishment will be enforced for breaching the flag or hymn code of decorum, but it is imperative to respect the Mujahideen and Mujahidat who fought for the aspirations of the Bangsamoro people and to honour the region's symbols by observing it. The interior ministry and the education ministry write the rules within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill grounds itself in Article II Section 2 of the Organic Law, the provision under which the region adopts its own flag, anthem and other symbols — the same authority BAA 1 used to adopt the flag.

What it is for is the gap that follows. A region that has legislated a flag and a hymn has said nothing about how either is to be treated, and in the absence of a rule, practice drifts toward whatever people remember of national anthem etiquette. Writing the code down fixes it, and Section 5 explains why the bill declines to enforce it: the reason for standing is respect for the people who fought, and respect compelled by penalty is a different thing.
whoIsAffected: Everyone present when the hymn is played, citizens and guests alike.
All ministries, government offices, agencies, local government units and government corporations in the region.
Public and private educational institutions, where the hymn is most often sung.
People who cannot stand unaided, expressly covered by the hand gesture rather than excused from the code.
Anyone wearing religious or cultural headwear, expressly exempted from the removal protocol.
Men in uniform, required to salute for the hymn's full duration.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, in coordination with the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education — implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No appropriation and no penalty. The Act creates duties of observance and expressly provides that no punishment will be enforced for breaching them.

whatChanges: The region acquires a written code of decorum for its own hymn.
The gesture is a closed fist over the chest, and it applies to those who cannot stand as well as those who can.
Religious and cultural headwear is exempt from the requirement to uncover.
Applause after the hymn is declared improper.
Observance is required of every government office and school, and enforced against nobody.
readings.insight:
The closed fist is the whole bill in one gesture. Philippine national anthem etiquette, set by the national flag and heraldic code, is an open right palm over the heart; this bill specifies a closed fist. Nothing in the text explains the change, and none is needed — a clenched hand over the chest is the posture of a movement rather than of a citizenry, and the region is legislating decorum for a hymn about, as Section 4.7 puts it, "the Bangsamoro people's number one core value: the right to self-determination". 2 symbols, 2 gestures, and the difference between them is the point.

The headwear exemption is the most carefully considered line in the document. A general rule requiring hats to be removed would collide immediately with the hijab, the kufi and the tubao, and a code drafted without noticing that would have made observance impossible for most of the people expected to observe it. Excluding religious and culture-related headwear from the protocol, while keeping it for ordinary hats, resolves that in a single clause.

So does the provision on people who cannot stand. Rather than excusing them, the bill extends the hand gesture to them expressly — "applies to everyone including those who cannot stand on their own". That is a small piece of drafting with a clear instinct behind it: a code of respect that writes disabled people out of the act of respect would be a worse code.

Section 5 is the bill's real argument and the reason it is not a trivial measure. It sets out obligations in detail and then states that no punishment will be enforced for breaching them, resting instead on what is owed to the people who fought. Anthem laws elsewhere commonly carry fines, and several countries prosecute people for sitting down. A region emerging from armed conflict, writing its first code of decorum for its own hymn, choosing to make it unenforceable is a deliberate decision about what its symbols are for — and it is the opposite of the choice most governments make.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires all signage in the Bangsamoro, in both public and private institutions and establishments, to be in English and Arabic.

The 2 must appear together — written side by side, or English above and Arabic below. Signage is defined broadly: any written announcement installed, posted, hung, painted or otherwise displayed in a public place, and generally any graphic display intended to convey information to an audience. The Ministry of Public Works is to provide a list of all appropriate and lawful signages and other devices and instruments.

Funds come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act. The Act takes effect 15 days after publication in at least 2 newspapers of regional circulation.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy states it as inclusivity: the Bangsamoro Government respects and promotes inclusivity within the region, and to that end mandates English-Arabic signage in public and private establishments.

Arabic is the liturgical language of Islam and the language of madrasah instruction across the region, and its visible presence in public space is a marker of the Bangsamoro identity the autonomy arrangement exists to express.
whoIsAffected: Every private establishment in the region — shops, restaurants, offices, clinics — which would have to replace or supplement its signage.
Every public institution and government office in the region.
The Ministry of Public Works, which must issue the list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Readers of Arabic, for whom public information becomes accessible.
Speakers of the region’s own languages — Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan, Iranun — and of Filipino, none of which the bill provides for.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW), which provides the list of appropriate and lawful signages, devices and instruments

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are charged against the General Appropriation Act of the Bangsamoro. The appropriation would cover government signage; the bill also binds every private establishment in the region and says nothing about who pays for theirs, which is the larger cost by far and falls on the businesses.

whatChanges: All signage in the region, public and private, must be in English and Arabic.
The 2 languages must appear together — side by side, or English above Arabic.
MPW must publish a list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Government signage costs come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act.
readings.insight:
Section 4 defines "Official Language" as "English-Arabic, to be used in signages" — and that definition is where the difficulty is. Under the Constitution the national language is Filipino, and the official languages are Filipino and English. The Bangsamoro Organic Law treats Arabic as an official language of the region alongside Filipino and English, so Arabic on public signage is on solid ground; what is not is a signage rule that requires English and Arabic and leaves Filipino out entirely.

The compliance cost is the second thing, and it is not small. The bill binds every private establishment in the region and provides money only through the regional appropriations act, which will not be paying for the signage of shops in Bongao or Marawi. Nor is there a transition period, a threshold exempting small businesses, or a penalty — so the Act takes effect 15 days after publication and every non-compliant sign in the region is immediately non-compliant with no stated consequence, which is a strange combination.

Third, and most substantively: the region has 6 or more living languages of its own. A signage law justified by inclusivity that mandates Arabic and English while making no provision for Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan or Iranun is making a particular argument about what Bangsamoro identity consists of. That is a legitimate argument to make and the bill should be read as making it.

It carries 9 principal authors, among the most in this batch, which suggests the argument is widely shared.

readings.whatItDoes:
8 articles and 2 pages. This directs the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage to establish a Mujahideen Memorial Wall in the region, carrying a list of the names of certified Moro Islamic Liberation Front and Moro National Liberation Front members who died in the struggle for the right to self-determination.

Article 4 creates a Committee of 5 members appointed by the Chief Minister, whose single task is to establish the eligibility criteria for standard verification in identifying the Mujahideen, and to give the heritage commission the final list of names for inclusion.

Funds come from the general appropriations of the Bangsamoro. The bill names no site, no dimensions, no design and no deadline.
readings.whyProposed:
The authority cited is Section 24 of Article IX of the Organic Law — the Bangsamoro Government's duty to preserve the history, culture, arts, traditions and rich cultural heritage of the Bangsamoro people.

The measure's purpose is to put the dead of both fronts on a single wall. The MNLF and the MILF fought the same war in different decades and signed separate agreements with the national government, and a memorial that names members of both is a statement that the struggle was one struggle.
whoIsAffected: Families of MNLF and MILF members who died in the conflict, whose relatives' names may appear.
Families whose relatives are not certified, who have no route to inclusion that the bill describes.
The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which must build and hold the Wall.
A 5-member Committee appointed by the Chief Minister, which sets who counts as Mujahideen.
Both former fronts, whose dead are commemorated together on one monument.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which establishes the Wall
A Committee of 5 appointed by the Chief Minister, which sets the eligibility criteria and supplies the final list of names

funding.detail: No amount is named; the funds necessary are charged against the general appropriations of the Bangsamoro. For comparison, the 2 commemorative measures that became law in this registry carry figures — BAA 61 appropriates ₱15 million for the Camp Abubakar memorial and eco-park, and BAA 60 ₱5 million for the Hashim and Mimbantas memorial site.

whatChanges: The region would acquire a single memorial naming the dead of both the MNLF and the MILF.
A committee would fix, for the first time, the criteria for who counts as a Mujahideen who died in the struggle.
The heritage commission takes on a third commemorative site.
readings.insight:
The committee is the whole bill, and the bill does not notice it. 5 people appointed by the Chief Minister would decide the eligibility criteria for who counts among the dead of a 5-decade armed struggle, and then supply the final list of names. There is no appeal, no grievance mechanism, no requirement to consult the families, and no standard the criteria must meet — the Act delegates the question entirely and says nothing about how it should be answered.

That gap is the more striking because Parliament had already addressed it. BAA 61, the Camp Abubakar memorial act, requires its management board to keep a functioning grievance mechanism and to consult and actively involve local communities, precisely because the hardest question in a memorial is whose names go on it. BAA 60 seats a representative of each family on the board governing the site where their relatives are buried. This bill, filed in May 2023 between those 2 measures, carries neither.

The word "certified" is where the difficulty concentrates. Certification implies a record, and the registry shows what records exist: the veteran mujahideen bills establish that determining who served, and for how long, requires asking the MILF and MNLF Central Committees, because the fronts kept the only lists there are. So the committee's criteria will in practice be applied to names supplied by the organisations whose dead are being commemorated — which is unavoidable and worth stating, since it means the state is ratifying a list rather than compiling one.

Commemorating both fronts on 1 wall is the bill's substantive contribution and it is not a small one. The MNLF signed in 1996 and the MILF in 2014, and the relationship between them has not always been easy. A monument that does not distinguish between their dead is a political act in the direction of a single Bangsamoro history, and it is the only measure in this registry that treats the 2 movements as one.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 177, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This authorises the continued use of funds to settle unpaid obligations from fiscal years 2020 and 2021, and extends the validity of the 2022 and 2023 appropriations.

What makes it the document to read in this sequence is not the operative text but the explanatory note, which is the only place in the registry where the region sets out, in order, why its budgets keep needing rescue.

The note begins with Executive Order No. 91 of 2019, which moved the whole country from obligation-based budgeting to a Cash Budgeting System — appropriations to be spent within their own year, so that programs move faster and goods reach people sooner. Then the pandemic, which interrupted the functions of every agency, including the spending of their budgets. The note then lists what the national government did about it: Republic Act No. 11464 extending the 2019 appropriations into 2020, RA 11520 extending 2020 into 2021, and RA 11640 extending 2021 into 2022 — after which the 2022 and 2023 national budgets were simply written with 2-year availability from the start.

The region's own chain follows: BAA 24 extending 2020 and 2021 funds, BAA 33 extending 2022, and BAA 32, the 2023 budget, with its own graded deadlines for infrastructure and for operating expenses.

And then the note makes an argument against the reform itself. Citing the Philippine Institute for Development Studies, it observes that cash-based budgeting can pose major problems for developing countries and transition economies, which "may not have the administrative capacity or other pre-requisites needed for the effective introduction" of such a reform. It names the region's own causes of delay: a government in transition, an area undergoing major reforms as it emerges from decades of violent conflict, natural calamities, right-of-way problems, and the prohibitions that apply during electoral exercises.
readings.whyProposed:
The note's case is that the mismatch is structural rather than administrative. A cash budgeting system assumes an agency can plan, procure, build and pay inside 12 months. A region rebuilding its entire government while recovering from conflict, on ground where right-of-way disputes and calamities are ordinary and where election periods freeze public works, cannot reliably do that — and the national government, facing a milder version of the same problem, responded by legislating 2-year availability into its own budgets.

So the bill is not asking for an indulgence. It is arguing that the deadline was set by a reform designed for a different kind of administration, and that the region should be measured against what it can actually execute.
whoIsAffected: Creditors of the regional government holding unpaid obligations from 2020 and 2021.
Ministries and offices carrying unspent balances across 4 fiscal years.
Contractors and suppliers whose delivery and payment windows are extended.
Communities waiting on projects funded in 2020 and 2021 and not yet built.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which administers the cash budgeting system throughout.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management (MFBM) — guidelines and administration of the extended validity periods
Ministries, offices and agencies, which must observe the validity of appropriations and the reversion rules

funding.detail: No new money. The bill keeps appropriations already made in earlier years available for release, obligation and disbursement rather than letting them lapse.

whatChanges: Unpaid obligations from 2020 and 2021 can still be settled from the original appropriations.
The 2022 and 2023 appropriations stay valid longer than their own acts provided.
The region's budget cycle formally stops being a single year for everything but salaries.
readings.insight:
This is the explanatory note that explains the other 4. Bills 127, 128, 265 and 266 each move a date in a budget law and say nothing about why; this one lays out the whole chain — EO 91, the pandemic, 3 national extension statutes, the region's BAA 24, 32 and 33 — and then does something unusual for a government bill. It cites research against the policy its own government is implementing. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies warning that cash-based budgeting may not suit developing and transition economies lacking administrative capacity is, in a cabinet bill, an admission dressed as a citation.

The list of causes is worth keeping, because it is specific where such lists are usually generic: a government still being built, an area emerging from decades of violent conflict, natural calamities, right-of-way problems, and the prohibitions that attach to election periods. Every one of those is a reason a project cannot be completed in the calendar year it was funded in, and none of them is the kind of thing a budget reform designed in Manila would have priced in.

Enacted as BAA 38. What the sequence shows, read end to end, is a region that adopted a national fiscal reform, could not meet it, and legislated its way around it 5 times — and, in this one document, said clearly that the reform was the wrong fit rather than that the government had failed.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Integrated Coastal Management Act of 2023 makes integrated coastal management the region’s official policy framework for its coasts and seas, and builds a council to run it.

Section 3 is the substance: integrated coastal management and related approaches, coastal resource management among them, become the regional management policy framework for the sustainable development of the region’s coastal and marine environment — aimed at food security, sustainable livelihood, poverty alleviation and reduced vulnerability to natural hazards, while preserving ecological integrity. The Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy is then to issue guidelines for coastal zoning: delineating coastal areas, identifying land uses, and regulating activity in the coastal zone.

The Integrated Coastal Management Council is chaired by the MENRE Minister and seats the Ministers of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and of Trade, Investments and Tourism, the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, the Directors-General for Environment and Natural Resources and for Fisheries, 2 representatives of accredited civil society organizations, and representatives from coastal communities in every province.

The Council oversees implementation, develops and implements a Coastal Management Plan, provides measures to protect mangroves, coral reefs and seagrasses, coordinates with law enforcement against destructive fishing and pollution, works with the trade ministry on ecotourism and sustainable fisheries, and works with the interior ministry to bring local governments and coastal communities into the process through consultations, capacity building and awareness work.

Costs are charged against MENRE’s existing budget and thereafter to the annual appropriations act. The Act would take effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation in the region.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note is unusually specific for a framework bill. BARMM holds mangroves, seagrass beds and coral reefs that carry ecological, economic and cultural weight; fisheries and aquaculture are the primary income for many communities and depend directly on the health of those systems; and the coast is also the region’s transport network. Against that it sets overfishing, pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change through sea level rise and warming water — and adds that conflict in coastal areas compounds the degradation. The remedy it proposes is regulation of fishing practice, pollution reduction, marine protected areas, and education.
whoIsAffected: Coastal and fishing communities across the region, who would gain named representation on the Council — one or more from every province — and whose fishing practices the framework is meant to regulate.
The island provinces above all, where the coast is not a margin but the entire economy.
Local government units with coastal jurisdiction, brought into the process through MILG.
Accredited civil society organizations, given 2 seats.
Operators in ecotourism, aquaculture and commercial fishing, whose activities the coastal zoning guidelines would regulate.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy (MENRE), which chairs the Council and issues the coastal zoning guidelines
Integrated Coastal Management Council (ICMC)
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Agrarian Reform, and Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for local government and community participation
Directors-General for Environment and Natural Resources and for Fisheries
Law enforcement agencies, with which the Council is to coordinate rather than direct

funding.detail: No sum is stated and no new money is created. The amount necessary is charged against MENRE’s current budget and thereafter included in the annual appropriations act — which means, in the first year, the Council and the Coastal Management Plan are funded by MENRE finding room for them inside a budget already committed.

whatChanges: Integrated coastal management becomes the region’s stated policy framework rather than a project approach.
MENRE must issue coastal zoning guidelines delineating coastal areas and regulating activity within them.
A standing Council exists with ministers, directors-general, civil society and coastal community representation.
A Coastal Management Plan is required, developed and implemented by the Council.
Mangroves, coral reefs and seagrasses acquire a named body responsible for measures to protect them.
Coastal communities gain seats at the table where their fisheries are regulated.
readings.insight:
This is a coordination bill, and reading it as anything stronger would misread it. The Council oversees, develops, provides measures and coordinates; it does not license, penalise or enforce. There are no penalties anywhere in the text. Enforcement against destructive fishing stays with the law enforcement agencies the Council coordinates with, and the operative regulatory instrument — the coastal zoning guidelines — is MENRE’s to write after the fact. What the bill actually delivers on the day it takes effect is a policy declaration, a council, and an obligation to produce a plan.

The funding clause is the constraint that matters. Charging a new regional framework to a ministry’s current budget, with no additional appropriation in the first year, is how coordination bodies end up meeting rarely and producing plans slowly.

One structural gap is worth flagging because it will be the first thing the Council fights about. The membership includes 2 civil society representatives and "representatives from coastal communities in every province" — unnumbered — and Section 5 leaves the mechanism for selecting both to the Council’s own first regular meeting. So the size of the Council and the question of who speaks for a coastal community are settled by the Council itself, after it has already been convened by the ministers and directors-general who are on it by office.

The bill is among the furthest advanced in this batch, sitting at Second Reading since October 2025.
