Parliament Bill No. 219, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Regional Infrastructure Geo-tagging Act of 2023 requires every infrastructure project the Bangsamoro Government builds to be geo-tagged at every stage and published on a public portal.

Geo-tagging is defined as attaching location metadata — latitude and longitude — to the physical site of a project and uploading it, together with the project name, the location and the cost, so that government, citizens and other stakeholders can check progress in real time. The projects covered are listed and the list is broad: roads, bridges, ports, flood control, water supply, schools, multipurpose buildings, government buildings, hospitals and health facilities, barangay and municipal halls, centers, housing, and other horizontal and vertical works.

On effectivity, all such projects must be geo-tagged at every stage using a GPS-enabled phone or other GPS and image-capture device, and uploaded to a regional online portal the Act creates. Every implementing agency must also carry a portal on its own official website where information for a specific project location can be found, feeding the regional one.

Around that sit implementing guidelines, an information and education campaign, rules on access and the regional portal, a requirement for regular data updates with cybersecurity measures, and capacity building.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section runs from the constitutional policy of full public disclosure and the role of information in nation-building to the Bangsamoro Government’s own principle of Moral Governance — and states the aim in unusually blunt terms: improving accountability for the physical and financial outcomes of government infrastructure projects, eliminating corruption, and ensuring multi-stakeholder participation.

The method is the national geo-tagging practice used in agriculture and public works, applied region-wide and made statutory rather than administrative.
whoIsAffected: Every implementing agency of the Bangsamoro Government that builds anything.
Contractors, whose work becomes photographically and geographically documented at each stage.
Citizens and civil society, who gain project name, location and cost on a public portal.
The Ministry of Public Works and the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office, which build the portal and run capacity building.
Communities in remote areas, where a project’s existence is hardest to verify from the capital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW) and the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology office (BICT), which establish the Regional Infrastructure Portal
All implementing agencies, which geo-tag their projects and host agency portals

funding.detail: ₱20,000,000 initial appropriation, made available to MPW, BICT and the other ministries to establish the online Regional Infrastructure Portal and to assist and train agencies in setting up portals on their own websites. Thereafter each implementing agency carries the cost in its regular budget. It is one of the few precise appropriations in this batch and it is a modest one for a region-wide system.

whatChanges: Every Bangsamoro infrastructure project must be geo-tagged at every stage of implementation.
Project name, location and cost go on a public portal, updated as work proceeds.
Each implementing agency must host its own project portal, feeding the regional one.
Data updates are periodic and subject to cybersecurity measures.
Agencies receive capacity building to do it.
₱20 million is appropriated to build the system.
readings.insight:
This is the most straightforwardly useful bill in the batch and one of the cheapest. Publishing a photograph, a coordinate and a cost for every project at every stage is the single most effective check there is against the project that is paid for and never built, or built at a fraction of the specification. It requires no new agency, no commission and no council — 3 things almost every other bill here creates.

It carries 17 principal authors, far more than anything else in this group, which is a fair indication of how uncontroversial the proposition is.

The question a committee should press is what happens when an agency does not comply. There is no penalty, no consequence for a project that appears on no portal, and no provision making disbursement conditional on the geo-tag being uploaded. The obvious fix is the one used elsewhere: tie the release of a progress payment to the upload. Without something of that kind, the register will be complete for the agencies that were already transparent.

The ₱20 million is for the portal, the training and the assistance; thereafter each agency funds its own compliance from its regular budget. That is the right structure, and it also means the recurring cost is invisible in this bill.

On its progress: filed June 2023, First Reading July 2023, and referred to the Committees on Public Works and on Finance in May 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This pays the highest rates in the cluster, and it is the only bill that requires the topnotcher to have been educated in the region and the only one that pays their school.

For Bar and Physician licensure topnotchers: ₱500,000 for Top 1, ₱300,000 each for Top 2 to 5, ₱200,000 each for Top 6 to 10. For all other national licensure examinations: ₱250,000, ₱150,000 and ₱100,000 on the same bands.

The eligibility condition is in the definition of a resident Bangsamoro topnotcher: the degree that was the prerequisite for sitting the licensure examination must have been finished at a learning institution in the Bangsamoro region. A Bangsamoro who took their degree in Manila and topped the Bar does not qualify.

That condition explains the second payment. Learning institutions are entitled to a grant, in the form of a project to improve their academic standards, of ₱100,000 — available once a year regardless of how many topnotchers the institution produced.

Section 6 forbids any memorandum, order or issuance from diminishing the prescribed incentives, and provides that donations and gifts from individuals, institutions or groups are separate from and additional to them. The Office of the Chief Minister carries the appropriation and writes the implementing rules within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The logic is visible in the structure rather than stated in a note. Paying only those who studied in the region, and paying their institution as well, turns an award for individual achievement into a subsidy for regional higher education — the money follows the school that produced the result, not merely the person who achieved it.

The rates follow from the same reasoning. If the point is to make a Bangsamoro university a place where a serious candidate chooses to study rather than a fallback, the incentive has to be large enough to be part of that decision, which is what distinguishes ₱500,000 from the ₱100,000 most of the rival bills offer.
whoIsAffected: Bar and Physician topnotchers who took their qualifying degree at an institution in the region, at ₱500,000 for first place.
Bangsamoro who studied outside the region and topped an examination, who are excluded entirely.
Topnotchers in other professions, on a scale roughly half the Bar and medicine rates.
Learning institutions in the region, each eligible for a ₱100,000 improvement grant once a year.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which carries the appropriation and writes the rules.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister — the appropriation and the implementing rules within 90 days of approval
Learning institutions in the region, which receive and spend the academic standards grant

funding.detail: Bar and Physician examinations: ₱500,000 for Top 1, ₱300,000 each for Top 2-5, ₱200,000 each for Top 6-10. Other national licensure examinations: ₱250,000, ₱150,000, ₱100,000. Learning institutions: ₱100,000 a year each, as a project grant, regardless of the number of topnotchers produced. No total appropriation is stated. Section 6 bars any issuance from reducing these amounts.

whatChanges: The largest incentives in the cluster — up to ₱500,000 for a single result.
Eligibility turns on having studied in the region, not on being Bangsamoro.
Schools that produce topnotchers receive money of their own.
No administrative issuance may reduce the amounts, and private gifts are additional to them.
readings.insight:
The residency condition is what makes this bill different in kind rather than degree. Every other bill in the cluster asks who achieved something; this one asks where they were taught. A Bangsamoro who studied in Manila and placed first in the Bar receives ₱500,000 under nobody’s reading of this bill and ₱150,000 under Bill 198. That is a deliberate redirection of the subsidy from the individual to the regional education system, and it is reinforced by the ₱100,000 institutional grant.

Whether it works depends on something the bill cannot control. The condition rewards a student for staying, but it also excludes exactly the person whose success would most obviously reflect on the region — and in a region whose universities are still being built, the number of Bar topnotchers who took their law degree inside it may be very small. An incentive scheme with a narrow eligibility gate can be generous on paper and rarely paid.

Section 6 is the provision to note for the long term. Barring any memorandum, order or issuance from diminishing the prescribed incentives protects the amounts from being quietly reduced by administrative circular, which is the ordinary fate of statutory benefits whose cost turns out to be inconvenient. None of the other 7 bills carries that protection, and it matters most here because these are the amounts most likely to be found inconvenient.

A drafting slip in the filed copy: there are 2 sections numbered 5, one granting incentives for other topnotchers and one granting the institutional grant. The numbering then continues from 6, so the bill has no Section 5 uniquely identifying either provision.

8 bills in this registry do this same job, and reading them together is the point. Bill No. 69 and Bill No. 200 are MP Mawallil's; Bill No. 207 and Bill No. 208 are MP Loong's; Bill No. 198 is MP Dilangalen's, Bill No. 201 MP Ampatuan's, Bill No. 202 MP Ramos's, and Bill No. 222 MP Hashim's. 7 of the 8 were filed between 16 and 23 June 2023 — 1 week — and all 8 were referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management on the same day, 16 October 2024. Parliament took more than a year to notice they were one subject, and then noticed all at once.

The spread on the same achievement is the substantive finding. A Bar topnotcher placing first would receive ₱100,000 under Bill 207, ₱100,000 under Bill 202, ₱150,000 under Bill 198, and ₱500,000 under Bill 222 — a fivefold range for an identical result, with no published committee record reconciling them. Bill 69 and Bill 200 name no figure at all and hand the amount to an administrative body.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 222, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This separates 18 barangays from Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte — Matengen, Ladia, Pigcalagan, Alamada, Raguisi, Pinaring, Damaniog, Ibotegen, Banatin, Nara, Kakar, Katidtuan, Maidapa, Kapimpilan, Bulibod, Kabuntalan, Nalinan and Katamlangan — and constitutes them as the Municipality of Nuling, seated at Barangay Pinaring, which becomes the Poblacion.

Unlike the 2 Datu Odin Sinsuat bills, this one states no land area and attaches no technical description: the territorial boundary simply follows the existing boundaries of the constituent barangays. What it does attach is a population table, barangay by barangay.

The machinery is the same template. Corporate existence on ratification by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite in those barangays within 60 days of approval, run by COMELEC through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and paid out of COMELEC's available funds. On ratification, the Chief Minister appoints a mayor, a vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members who hold office until the next regular election, while incumbent Sultan Kudarat councillors resident in the new municipality serve out their terms in the mother municipality. And not less than ₱2,500,000 a month from the Bangsamoro Government until the revenue allotment arrives.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note attached to the filed copy. The declaration of policy states the power rather than the reason: in the exercise of genuine autonomy and self-governance the Bangsamoro Government may create, divide, merge, abolish or substantially alter the boundaries of municipalities and barangays by a law of Parliament, and the units affected are entitled to their share of national taxes, provided a majority in a plebiscite approves.

So the case for this particular municipality is not made in the document. What the bill supplies is the list of barangays, the seat, and the money.
whoIsAffected: The residents of the 18 barangays leaving Sultan Kudarat, who vote on the creation.
Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, which loses them and does not vote.
Incumbent Sultan Kudarat Sangguniang Bayan members living in the new municipality, who finish their terms in the mother municipality.
The Chief Minister, who appoints the first municipal government in full.
The Bangsamoro budget, carrying at least ₱2.5 million a month until the revenue allotment arrives.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite
The Chief Minister — appointment of the first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members
The Bangsamoro Government — monthly financial assistance pending the internal revenue allotment

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the administration and operation of the new municipal government until it is allocated its share in the revenue allotment — at that floor, at least ₱30 million a year. The plebiscite is charged to COMELEC's available funds under the current fiscal year appropriations in this version; the enacted act charged it to the BARMM Contingent Fund under the 2024 budget.

whatChanges: Sultan Kudarat loses 18 barangays, on a vote held only among them.
Nuling comes into existence as a municipality of Maguindanao del Norte, seated at Pinaring.
Its first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 councillors are appointed rather than elected.
The regional budget takes on a third monthly floor of ₱2.5 million from the same season's bills.
readings.insight:
The municipality grew by one barangay between filing and enactment. Section 2 of this bill lists 18; BAA 53 creates Nuling out of 19. Nothing in the published record says which barangay was added or why, and a barangay is not a rounding error — it is a population, a boundary, and a vote in the plebiscite that decides whether the municipality exists at all.

The plebiscite bill also changed hands. This version charges the cost to COMELEC's own available funds; the enacted act charges it to the BARMM Contingent Fund under the 2024 budget. That is the region declining to spend a national agency's money on a regional decision, and it applies across all 3 creations passed that day.

What this bill has that its 2 companions do not is a population table. Attaching barangay-by-barangay figures is the closest any of the 3 comes to showing the viability arithmetic — how many people the new municipality will have, and therefore what the ₱2.5 million monthly floor is buying per head and how long the bridge to a revenue allotment might need to be. It is also the only one of the 3 that leaves the boundary undescribed, so between them the Nuling bill counts its people and the Datu Odin Sinsuat bills survey their ground, and no bill does both.

The plebiscite question is the same here and cuts the same way. Sultan Kudarat loses 18 barangays and does not vote on it, because Section 5 reads "the political units directly affected" as the departing barangays alone.

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Maguindanao Provincial Hospital to Level III with 350 beds — the largest hospital measure in the registry.

What makes the bill unusual is that it does not simply assert a classification. Section 4 defines what the levels mean, by reference to Department of Health Administrative Order No. 2012-0012 and its 2015 amendment, and then sets out the required services level by level: for Level I, qualified medical, allied medical and administrative staff headed by a licensed physician; bed space meeting DOH planning and design guidelines; an operating room with standard equipment and sterilisation provision built to the DOH reference plan; a post-operative recovery room; and maternity facilities with wards, rooms and a delivery room exclusively for maternity patients and newborns — and so upward through the levels.

The objectives in Section 3 are equally concrete: integrate the Universal Health Care Act into operations; improve facilities for residents of Maguindanao del Sur and nearby areas; provide essential and quality services especially to the sick, the poor and the marginalized; and improve the morale and the social and economic well-being of the hospital's health workers.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is the standard constitutional formula — protect and promote the right to health, instill health consciousness, adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach making essential goods, health and social services available at affordable cost.

The real case is in what Maguindanao Provincial Hospital already is. It is the referral destination for a province, sitting at the top of a system in which the other bills in this registry are creating 25-bed municipal hospitals. A region building Level I facilities across its municipalities needs somewhere for those facilities to refer to, and this is the bill that builds it.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Maguindanao del Sur and nearby areas, who gain a Level III referral hospital.
Patients currently travelling out of the region for tertiary care — oncology, dialysis, interventional imaging, trauma and stroke.
The 25-bed Level I hospitals being created elsewhere in the registry, which need a tertiary facility to refer into.
Medical graduates and trainees, since Level III requires accredited residency programs.
The hospital's existing health workers, whose morale and economic well-being the bill names as an objective.
The Ministry of Health, which must staff and equip a 350-bed teaching hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — supervision, structure, and the upgrade to Level III standards under the Department of Health administrative orders the bill cites

funding.detail: The filed copy names no amount. The enacted act appropriates ₱50 million initially from the 2025 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro — the same initial figure given to the 25-bed hospitals in the same series.

whatChanges: The region acquires a Level III tertiary hospital of 350 beds.
Teaching and training with accredited residency programs become part of the regional health system.
Oncology, dialysis, trauma and stroke care, rehabilitation and tertiary imaging enter the public system in the region.
The municipal hospitals being created elsewhere gain a referral destination inside the region.
readings.insight:
The definitions are the bill's real contribution, and Parliament kept them. Most hospital measures in this registry name a level and leave the content to the health ministry; this one spells out, by reference to the national administrative order, what each level actually requires — an operating room built to a stated reference plan, a recovery room, maternity facilities exclusively for maternity patients and newborns. That converts a classification into a checklist. BAA 74 carries the Level III list through: residency programs in Medicine, Pediatrics, Obstetrics and Gynecology and Surgery, trauma and stroke care, oncology, rehabilitation, an ambulatory surgical clinic, dialysis, a blood bank, a tertiary laboratory with histopathology, and Level III imaging with interventional radiology.

The money is where the arithmetic stops working. The enacted act appropriates ₱50 million initially — the identical figure appropriated for 25-bed Level I hospitals in South Ubian, Tipo-Tipo, Maluso and Northern Kabuntalan in the same series. A blood bank, a dialysis facility and interventional radiology do not cost what a 25-bed municipal hospital costs, and nothing in the act explains the equivalence. Either the ₱50 million is a standard seed figure with the real cost deferred to the annual budget, or the upgrade is underfunded by an order of magnitude. The documents do not say which.

The objective about health workers is worth a separate note because it is rare. Section 3(d) lists improving the morale and the social and economic well-being of the hospital's own staff as an aim of the Act, on the same footing as patient care. Hospital laws generally treat staff as an input; this one treats them as a constituency.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 225, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes: This establishes the Buldon General Hospital with 25 beds in Buldon, Maguindanao del Norte, to serve primarily but not only the patients of that municipality.
readings.whyProposed:
The note builds a catchment and then measures it. The northern part of the first district of Maguindanao holds 6 municipalities, with 2020 census populations given for each: Sultan Kudarat 105,121, Parang 102,914, Buldon 39,684, Barira 36,143, Matanog 36,034 and Sultan Mastura 25,331 — 345,227 people in total.

Those 6 municipalities are served by 2 hospitals: the Cotabato Sanitarium at Barangay Pinaring in Sultan Kudarat with 250 beds, and the Iranun District Hospital at Parang with 25, making 275 beds between them.

The Department of Health standard, the note says, is 1 bed per 1,000 population. On that measure 275 beds serve 275,000 people, against a catchment of 345,227 — a deficiency of at least 70 beds. The bill asks for 25 of them.
whoIsAffected: The 39,684 residents of Buldon, and the wider catchment of 345,227 across 6 municipalities.
Patients currently travelling to the Cotabato Sanitarium at Pinaring or the Iranun District Hospital at Parang.
Those 2 hospitals, which between them carry a catchment 70,000 people larger than their bed count supports.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and set its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the operative text leaves the sum to the appropriations act. The comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of bed count.

whatChanges: Buldon gains a 25-bed general hospital.
The northern first district's bed count rises from 275 toward the 345 its population implies.
Patients from neighbouring municipalities gain a nearer facility, since the hospital serves beyond Buldon.
readings.insight:
The method is what makes this bill worth reading, and it is also where the bill undersells itself. Having established a shortfall of at least 70 beds across the catchment, the measure asks for 25 — about a third of the gap it has just documented. That is either modesty about what the region can fund or an acknowledgment that 3 more bills would be needed, and the companion measures filed the same week for Sultan Mastura, Kabuntalan and Cotabato City suggest the second.

The arithmetic has since been overtaken, and in a way that vindicates it. One of the 2 hospitals the note counts is the Iranun District Hospital at Parang, credited with 25 beds. In May 2025 BAA 73 converted that hospital into the Iranun Provincial Hospital with an authorised capacity of 200 beds — which, on this bill's own ratio, adds 175,000 people's worth of provision to the same catchment and closes the 70-bed deficiency several times over. The bill that did it, Bill No. 246, was filed a month after this one by a different member, and neither document mentions the other.

That is the substantive point about this cluster. 4 bills arguing from a bed ratio and a fifth converting a district hospital to provincial scale were all before the same Parliament in the same period, and there is no sign in any of them that the cumulative effect on a shared catchment was ever computed. The method Ambolodto brought is exactly the method that would have caught it.

MP Ambolodto filed 4 hospital bills over 2 days in July 2023 — Buldon, Sultan Mastura, Kabuntalan and Cotabato City — and all 4 argue from the same method rather than from hardship. Each names the catchment, counts its population from the 2020 census, lists the hospitals serving it with their bed capacities, applies the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 people, and states the resulting shortfall. No other hospital bills in this registry do the arithmetic. All 4 remain at Second Reading, Committee Stage.

A drafting note common to the set: the constitutional citations are unreliable. 3 of the 4 bills cite the right to health as "Section 15, Article III" when it is Article II, and 1 cites the integrated-approach provision as "Section 11, Article XII" when it is Article XIII. Each bill has at least 1 wrong reference and they are not wrong in the same way, which is what happens when a shared preamble is retyped rather than copied.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 233, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes: This establishes a general hospital with 25 beds in Sultan Mastura, Maguindanao del Norte.
readings.whyProposed:
The note uses the same frame as its companions: the 6 municipalities of the northern first district of Maguindanao, 345,227 people between them, served by the Cotabato Sanitarium at Pinaring and the Iranun District Hospital at Parang.

Sultan Mastura is the smallest of the 6, with 25,331 people at the 2020 census. Applying the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000, the district's 275 beds fall short of its 345,227 population, and the bill proposes 25 beds in the municipality that has none.
whoIsAffected: The 25,331 residents of Sultan Mastura, the smallest of the district's 6 municipalities.
Patients travelling to Pinaring or Parang for hospital care.
The Cotabato Sanitarium and the Iranun District Hospital, which carry the district.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and set its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the operative text leaves the sum to the appropriations act. The comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of bed count.

whatChanges: Sultan Mastura gains a 25-bed general hospital.
A municipality of 25,331 people stops depending entirely on facilities in other municipalities.
readings.insight:
On the bill's own ratio, 25 beds for 25,331 people is exactly right — the Department of Health standard of 1 bed per 1,000 produces 25 beds for this municipality almost to the person. Of the 4 bills in this set it is the one whose ask matches its arithmetic, which is worth noting because the Buldon bill documents a 70-bed district shortfall and asks for 25, and the Cotabato City bill documents a far larger one.

That precision cuts against the bill as well as for it. A hospital sized exactly to a municipality's own population has no capacity for the neighbouring catchment, and the companion Buldon bill expressly contemplates its hospital serving beyond its own municipality. 2 25-bed hospitals 1 municipality apart, each sized for its own residents, is a different plan from 1 50-bed hospital serving both, and nothing in either bill addresses which is better.

There is a cross-reference worth carrying. Bill No. 284, filed in February 2024 by another member, proposes renaming Sultan Mastura to the Municipality of Subpangen, subject to a plebiscite. If both measures ever moved, the hospital this bill establishes would open in a municipality with a different name from the one in its own enacting text — the kind of collision that follows from measures on the same place travelling separately.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 234, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes: This establishes the Tumbao General Hospital with 25 beds in Kabuntalan, Maguindanao del Norte.
readings.whyProposed:
Kabuntalan has 17 barangays and roughly 25,000 people, and there is no hospital in the municipality at all.

The note is specific about where its patients go instead: when the need arises they have no option but to reach hospitals in Cotabato City or in Midsayap, North Cotabato — the second of which is outside the Bangsamoro region entirely.

Applying the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 population, a municipality of about 25,000 requires about 25 beds, which is what the bill proposes.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 25,000 residents of Kabuntalan across 17 barangays, who have no hospital.
Patients currently travelling to Cotabato City or to Midsayap in North Cotabato.
Hospitals in Midsayap, outside the region, which absorb part of this catchment.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and set its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the operative text leaves the sum to the appropriations act. The comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of bed count.

whatChanges: A municipality of about 25,000 with no hospital gains one.
Patients stop having to leave the region to reach hospital care.
Bed provision matches the Department of Health ratio for the municipality's population.
readings.insight:
Midsayap is the detail that distinguishes this bill from its 3 companions. Kabuntalan's patients go to Cotabato City or to Midsayap in North Cotabato — and Midsayap is outside the Bangsamoro. So part of a Bangsamoro municipality's hospital care is currently delivered by a province the region does not govern, funded by a local government the region does not fund, under a referral pattern no regional plan controls.

That is a more consequential fact than a travel time. It means the region's own health statistics understate what its population uses, and that the cost of serving Kabuntalan currently falls partly on North Cotabato. It is also the mirror image of the Special Geographic Area problem elsewhere in this registry, where barangays that voted to join the Bangsamoro were still administered from North Cotabato — here the administration is regional and the hospital care is not.

The name is worth a note. The bill establishes the "Tumbao General Hospital" in the Municipality of Kabuntalan, Tumbao being the older name by which the municipality has been known — the same pattern as the Special Geographic Area acts, where Kabuntalan appears in the parliamentary districts schedule as "Kabuntalan (Tumbao)". A hospital named for the place rather than the current municipal designation is a small choice about which name the institution carries forward.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 235, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a general hospital with 50 beds in Cotabato City, to be known as the Ghazali Jaafar General Hospital.

It is the largest of the 4 bills in the set by bed count and the only 1 sited in a city.
readings.whyProposed:
The note counts Cotabato City at 37 barangays and 325,079 people, and lists the 4 hospitals in it with their capacities: the Cotabato Puericulture Center and General Hospital Foundation with 30 beds, Notre Dame Hospital with 40, the Cotabato Regional and Medical Center with 600, and the Eros Medical Clinic and Hospital with 18.

Then it makes the deduction that carries the bill. The Cotabato Regional and Medical Center serves not only the city but patients from the adjacent provinces of Maguindanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte, so its 600 beds cannot be counted against the city's population alone. Setting CRMC aside, only 3 hospitals effectively serve the city, with an aggregate capacity of 88 beds.

On the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000, a population of 325,079 requires about 325 beds. The bill proposes 50 of them.
whoIsAffected: The 325,079 residents of Cotabato City across 37 barangays.
Patients relying on the 3 smaller city hospitals with 88 beds between them.
The Cotabato Regional and Medical Center, whose 600 beds serve the city and 2 adjacent provinces.
Patients from Maguindanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte who travel to CRMC, competing for the same beds.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and set its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the operative text leaves the sum to the appropriations act. The comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of bed count.

whatChanges: Cotabato City gains a 50-bed public general hospital.
The city's effective bed provision rises from 88 toward the 325 its population implies.
Pressure eases on the regional medical centre that also serves 2 provinces.
readings.insight:
Setting aside the 600-bed regional medical centre is the analytical move that makes this the strongest of the 4 bills. On paper Cotabato City has 688 hospital beds for 325,079 people — comfortably above the 1-per-1,000 standard. The note's point is that the arithmetic is an illusion, because CRMC is the end-referral hospital for 2 whole provinces as well as the city, so counting its beds against the city's population double-counts them. Remove it and the city has 88 beds, which is about a quarter of what the standard requires.

That is a real and frequently missed distinction, and it applies well beyond this bill. Several measures in this registry establish municipal hospitals on the basis that a provincial or regional facility is nearby; this note is the only place in the registry where anyone observes that a referral hospital's capacity is not available to its host city in the ordinary way.

The naming is the other thing to record. Ghazali Jaafar was vice chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and chaired the Bangsamoro Transition Commission that drafted the Organic Law, dying in 2019. Naming a hospital for him puts a figure from the peace process onto a working public institution in the region's largest city — the same instinct as the Aleem Abdulazis Mimbantas Memorial Hospital in Masiu and the Hashim and Mimbantas memorial site, and the third such naming in this registry.

What the bill does not resolve is whether 50 beds is the right answer to an 88-against-325 shortfall. It is a 57% increase on the city's effective public and private provision outside CRMC, and it is still 235 beds short of the standard the note itself invokes. As with the Buldon bill, the measure documents a large gap and asks for a fraction of it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 236, copy as filed, with explanatory note
Parliament Bill No. 240, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Budget Reform Act of 2023 fixes when the executive must give Parliament its budget, and what has to be in it.

The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management must submit the Proposed Bangsamoro Expenditure Program to Parliament not later than 30 days from the fourth Monday of July each year, and that document is the basis of the General Appropriations Bill. The Minister may also transmit supplemental or deficiency appropriations where laws enacted after transmission require it or the public interest otherwise needs it.

The form and content are prescribed. The Program must include a Minister’s Budget Message previewing the principles, objectives, policy framework and spending priorities; a Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing carrying the macroeconomic parameters, a 3-year expenditure, revenue, financing and outstanding debt picture, an overview of the financial position of Bangsamoro government-owned corporations and of public-private partnership projects, and a list of new multi-year projects with their duration, total project cost and contractual authorities issued; and a Bangsamoro Expenditure Program setting out strategic objectives, the detail of the 3-year expenditure program, performance information including key strategies, outputs and outcomes for each agency against its budget, and a staffing summary.

The finance ministry issues implementing rules within 90 days, in coordination with relevant agencies and stakeholders.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy is about results rather than timing: a budget oriented towards explicit objectives and expected results, so funds are used and operations conducted effectively, economically and efficiently — and, in the bill’s own words, to enforce the power of Parliament to hold every ministry, bureau, office and agency responsible for proposing, executing and delivering committed results in a timely, predictable and economic manner.

The timing provision serves that end. A Parliament handed the budget late cannot scrutinise it, and a budget that arrives without performance information cannot be scrutinised at all.
whoIsAffected: The Bangsamoro Parliament, which gains a fixed date and a prescribed document to work from.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which must produce all of it on schedule.
Every ministry, bureau, office and agency, whose outputs, outcomes and staffing appear against their budget.
Bangsamoro government-owned and controlled corporations, whose financial position must be disclosed.
Anyone tracking multi-year projects, whose duration, total cost and contractual authorities become a published list.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which submits the Program and writes the implementing rules
The Bangsamoro Parliament, which receives and acts on it

funding.detail: The filed bill has no appropriations section. It is a process reform carried out by an existing ministry using existing staff, and no additional money is asked for.

whatChanges: The budget must reach Parliament within 30 days of the fourth Monday of July every year.
The Proposed Bangsamoro Expenditure Program becomes the formal basis of the appropriations bill.
A 3-year expenditure, revenue, financing and debt picture is required, not just next year’s.
GOCC financial positions and PPP projects must be disclosed in the budget documents.
Multi-year projects are listed with duration, total cost and contractual authorities issued.
Every agency’s budget arrives with its outputs, outcomes and staffing summary attached.
readings.insight:
The performance information is the reform, not the calendar. Requiring that each agency’s budget arrive with its key strategies, outputs and outcomes and a staffing summary is the difference between a legislature approving line items and a legislature approving results — and the 3-year forward view, the debt position, the GOCC financial picture and the multi-year project list with total costs and contractual authorities are the 4 things that most often hide the real fiscal position of a government from the body voting on it.

The title promises more than the text delivers in one respect. It says the Act increases "budget transparency and participation". Transparency is amply provided for by the disclosure requirements. Participation is not: there is no public consultation mechanism, no civil society role, and no published document requirement beyond submission to Parliament. The only place stakeholders appear is in Section 5, where the finance ministry coordinates with them in writing the implementing rules. A committee could supply the missing half easily — a requirement that the Program be published when transmitted would do most of it.

What the bill does not carry is a consequence for late submission. The date is stated; nothing follows from missing it.

It was filed August 2023, given First Reading a month later, and referred to the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management in September 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is a full public-private partnership code for the region — 49 sections covering how the Bangsamoro Government may partner with private capital, and, unusually for a PPP law, mostly concerned with what happens after the contract is signed.

The front of the bill sets policy and 10 operative principles, running through local and fiscal autonomy, transparency and social accountability, the delineation between the government as regulator and as proprietor, the recognition of the private sector as prime mover of trade and industry, the right to information, and the guaranteed participation of civil society organizations in regulating and managing PPP projects. The Bangsamoro may provide equity, subsidy or guarantee, and its funds used in a PPP are declared to be for public use and purpose.

The body of the Act creates a PPP Regulatory Authority to perform contract management for every PPP the Bangsamoro enters: partnership management, performance and service delivery management, contract administration, and — the 2 with teeth — setting and monitoring the tariff and administering the subsidy. It is chaired by the Chief Minister or a designated Deputy, with the Deputy Chief Minister as vice-chair and 2 members of Parliament from 2 distinct registered political parties the Chief Minister does not belong to, chosen by proportional representation.

From there the Act is a contract-management manual in statutory form: post-award conference, personnel and training requirements, partnership management, service delivery, contract administration, closeout procedures, post-contract review, document control, a code of conduct with disciplinary action attached, liability, social accountability, transparency and right to information, capability building, and a monitoring and governance audit program. Every PPP contract must carry an alternative dispute resolution clause. Component local governments keep their own authority to pass PPP ordinances and run their own projects.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that the region is at a developmental juncture with untapped potential, that PPPs have elsewhere delivered better and more timely services, and that the Bangsamoro Organic Law itself recognizes the private sector as the prime mover of trade, commerce and industry. The specific fiscal argument is the interesting one: PPPs would let the region redirect capital budgets to other pressing sectors by avoiding the cost of public borrowing, and would bring technology transfer and private-sector expertise into local governance.
whoIsAffected: Private firms and financiers considering infrastructure and service projects in the region.
Users of any service delivered under a PPP, whose tariff the Regulatory Authority sets and monitors.
Component local government units, whose own PPP authority the Act expressly preserves.
Civil society organizations, given a guaranteed participation role in regulating and managing projects.
Opposition parties in Parliament, who are given 2 seats on the Regulatory Authority by design.
The Bangsamoro Government, which may put up equity, subsidies and guarantees.
implementedBy: PPP Regulatory Authority (PPP-RA), chaired by the Chief Minister or a designated Deputy Chief Minister, with the Deputy Chief Minister as vice-chair and 2 Members of Parliament from parties the Chief Minister does not belong to
The Bangsamoro Legal Officer, in preparing the contract management manual
Office of the Government Corporate Counsel and other bodies named for technical and financial assistance
Component local government units, for their own projects and ordinances

funding.detail: The appropriations section of the filed copy is blank. Section 41 reads that "the amount of (amount) Pesos (P [figures]) shall be appropriated" — the placeholder is in the document as filed, never replaced with a number. Thereafter such sums as may be necessary go into the annual Bangsamoro budget. So the bill as filed appropriates nothing, and the figure was left to be supplied later.

whatChanges: The region gains a statutory framework for entering public-private partnerships.
A PPP Regulatory Authority manages every Bangsamoro PPP contract and sets and monitors tariffs.
2 seats on that Authority go to parties the Chief Minister does not belong to.
Every PPP contract must carry an alternative dispute resolution clause.
Contract management — post-award, performance, closeout, post-contract review — is prescribed by statute rather than left to practice.
Civil society participation in regulating and managing projects is written into the operative principles.
Component LGUs’ own PPP authority is expressly recognized.
deliberation: Parliament’s index records the bill filed 15 August 2023, First Reading 19 September 2023, consolidated with Bill No. 329, and referred to the Committee on Ways and Means on 24 July 2025.
The consolidation means the measure that emerges from committee will not be this text alone. Bill 329 has not been read for this registry.
readings.insight:
The blank in Section 41 is the thing to know. The copy Parliament published carries an unfilled placeholder where the appropriation should be — "(amount) Pesos (P [figures])" — which means the bill as filed authorises a regulatory authority, a contract management regime and a tariff-setting power without appropriating anything at all. It is a drafting artefact rather than a policy choice, but it is in the filed document and anyone quoting the funding of this measure should quote the placeholder rather than a number.

The second thing is that parts of the text describe a government that does not exist. The operative principles refer to the "Regional Assembly" approving annual work programs, to the Regional Governor ensuring their implementation, and to the Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council as the region’s planning and coordinating agency. BARMM has a Parliament, a Chief Minister and the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority. Those are ARMM-era institutions, and their presence in the principles section indicates the passage was carried over from older model text rather than written for this government. The rest of the bill uses Chief Minister and Parliament correctly, which makes the inconsistency internal rather than pervasive — but a court reading Section 3 would be reading about bodies that were abolished.

What the bill gets genuinely right is the half most PPP laws neglect. Procurement is where PPP statutes usually stop; this one spends most of its length on contract management — post-award conference, performance monitoring, variation management, closeout, post-contract review, document control, a code of conduct with disciplinary consequences. Projects of this kind fail after signature far more often than at tender, and the drafting reflects that.

The composition of the Regulatory Authority deserves a note too. Reserving 2 seats for members from parties the Chief Minister does not belong to, allocated by proportional representation, builds an opposition presence into the body that sets tariffs and administers subsidies. That is a real check, and an unusual one to find in a bill of this kind.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Council on Autism under the Office of the Chief Minister and directs it to build a regional program for children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.

The Council is chaired by the Minister of Health with the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education as vice-chair, and seats the Ministers of Social Services and Development and of the Interior and Local Government, a representative of the Autism Society of the Philippines, and 2 representatives from non-governmental organizations working in the field.

Its functions are to formulate an integrated and comprehensive program, to create the framework that serves as its blueprint, to increase public awareness, education and information, and to establish family support networks and other programs for families, encouraging them to seek psycho-social support.

The program itself must include early screening and detection, and the bill goes on to provide for a secretariat, research and reports on autism spectrum disorder, an annual report to Parliament, implementation arrangements and an appropriation.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section commits the Bangsamoro Government to the total well-being of those diagnosed with autism — physical, mental, moral, intellectual and social — so they can be productive members of society, and to creating conditions in which they become independent, self-reliant and socially accepted.

The unstated problem is diagnosis. Specialist developmental assessment in this region is scarce to non-existent outside the cities, which means most autistic children here are never formally identified, and services that depend on a diagnosis therefore never reach them.
whoIsAffected: Children with autism spectrum disorder in the region, most of whom are currently undiagnosed.
Their families, for whom the bill provides support networks and psycho-social support.
Schools, through MBHTE’s vice-chairmanship and the early screening the program requires.
Health workers, who would carry out early screening and detection.
The Autism Society of the Philippines and NGOs in the field, given seats on the Council.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Council on Autism, under the Office of the Chief Minister, chaired by the Minister of Health with MBHTE as vice-chair
A secretariat provided for in the Act
Ministries of Social Services and Development and of the Interior and Local Government, as members

funding.detail: The bill has an appropriations section and the title says it appropriates funds; no amount is fixed in the operative text of the filed copy. Early screening at regional scale is the expensive part of what the Council is asked to build, and it is the part a figure would have told us most about.

whatChanges: The region gains a standing council on autism under the Office of the Chief Minister.
An integrated regional program and framework must be formulated, with early screening and detection in it.
Family support networks are to be established, with psycho-social support for families.
Public awareness, education and information become a named function.
Research and reports on ASD are required, and the Council reports to Parliament annually.
The Autism Society of the Philippines and 2 NGOs sit on the body.
readings.insight:
Early screening and detection is the right first provision and the one that will determine whether any of the rest happens. In most of this region a child is not assessed by a developmental specialist because there is no developmental specialist to assess them, so the number of diagnosed autistic children is a measure of service availability rather than of prevalence. A program built on early screening at least starts where the gap is.

The language in Section 3 has not aged well and a committee should look at it. 2 of the 7 seats go to NGOs "involved in the advocacy for the prevention, cure and rehabilitation of persons with ASD". Prevention and cure describe a way of thinking about autism that clinical practice and autistic people’s own organizations have largely moved away from — autism is a developmental difference to be supported, not a disease to be cured — and the choice of NGO seats will follow the words used to describe them. The rest of the bill, which talks about support, acceptance and family networks, does not read the same way, which suggests the phrase was carried in from older model text rather than chosen.

The body it creates is a council with a secretariat and a reporting duty, which is the modest end of what could have been done. There is no entitlement, no service standard and no obligation on any ministry to deliver anything specific — the Council formulates a program, and whether it exists in a municipality depends on what the framework says and what the budget provides.

It carries 9 principal authors, and was referred to the Committees on Health and on Women, Youth, Children and Persons with Disability in February 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This converts the Iranon District Hospital in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, into the Iranon Provincial Hospital with 200 beds, under the direct supervision and control of the Ministry of Health.

Where most hospital bills stop at declaring a capacity, this one legislates the things that make a capacity real. Section 4 requires existing professional health care services and facilities to be upgraded commensurate with the increase in beds. Section 5 requires the existing workforce — doctors, nurses and support personnel — to be increased correspondingly, with the additional plantilla positions determined by the health ministry together with the finance ministry and the Civil Service Commission, in consultation with the hospital's own management. Section 6 puts a deadline on the whole upgrade: 3 years from approval.

And Section 9 requires the Ministry of Health to report annually to the Chief Minister and to Parliament, through the Committee on Health and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, on the outcome and progress of the conversion.

The implementing rules are due within 60 days, made in consultation with the Provincial Government of Maguindanao del Norte and other stakeholders.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill carries no separate explanatory note, and its own text supplies the logic. An existing district hospital already serving the area is being asked to carry a provincial load, and converting it is cheaper and faster than building new.

The drafting suggests the authors had seen what happens when a hospital is upgraded on paper. Beds without staff, staff without plantilla positions, and upgrades with no deadline are the 3 standard ways a conversion stalls, and Sections 5, 6 and 9 are written against each of them.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Parang and the surrounding area of Maguindanao del Norte, served by a district hospital being raised to provincial scale.
The hospital's existing doctors, nurses and support personnel, whose complement must grow with the bed count.
Applicants for the new plantilla positions the health, finance and civil service bodies must determine.
The Provincial Government of Maguindanao del Norte, consulted on the implementing rules.
Parliament's Committee on Health and Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, which receive an annual progress report.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — direct supervision and control, implementing rules within 60 days, and the annual report
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management and the Civil Service Commission, with the Ministry of Health and hospital management — determining the additional plantilla positions
The Chief of Hospital, who prepares the hospital development plan governing further growth

funding.detail: No amount is named. The Ministry of Health provides initial funding through its approved annual budget, and the hospital's full operating and upgrading requirements go into the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act for the year following enactment. The enacted act appropriates ₱50 million initially from the 2025 budget.

whatChanges: A district hospital becomes a provincial hospital of 200 beds.
The workforce must grow with the bed count, with new plantilla positions created for it.
The upgrade carries a 3-year statutory deadline.
Parliament receives an annual report on whether the conversion is actually happening.
readings.insight:
Sections 5, 6 and 9 are what every other hospital measure in this registry is missing, and they survived into BAA 73 intact. Requiring the workforce to grow with the beds, setting a 3-year deadline for the upgrade, and obliging the health ministry to report to 2 parliamentary committees each year turns a declaration into something with a due date and an audience. 12 acts in this registry create or upgrade hospitals; this is the one that arranged to be checked.

The number that does not fit is the money. 200 beds, an upgraded workforce and upgraded facilities, funded initially with ₱50 million — the same initial appropriation the enacted acts give to 25-bed Level I hospitals in South Ubian, Tipo-Tipo, Maluso and Northern Kabuntalan, and to the 350-bed Level III regional medical center. A single figure applied across facilities that differ by a factor of 14 in bed count is a budgeting convention rather than a costing, and the annual report Section 9 requires is the mechanism most likely to expose the gap.

There is also a quiet drafting redundancy worth noting for anyone reading the filed copy. Section 2 converts the hospital to 200-bed capacity, and Section 3 then states that the authorized capacity "shall be increased to 200 beds" before going on to govern future increases. The 200 beds are legislated twice, and the section meant to handle growth spends its first sentence restating the starting point.

readings.whatItDoes:
This institutes a free marriage counselling programme for the region, delivered in 3 distinct interventions.

Pre-Marriage Counselling gives couples intending to marry a basis for making an informed and responsible decision about marriage. Marriage Enrichment Counselling helps married couples renew and enhance their marital relationship and intimacy and deepen their marital morality and spirituality. And Marital Crisis Counselling helps couples through emotional and psychological healing, gaining an objective perspective on their situation, identifying areas for behavioural change and strengths to reinforce, and acquiring techniques for effective communication and conflict resolution.

The Ministry of Social Services and Development leads. It must develop the policies, guidelines and programmes, including a Marriage Counselling Framework aligned with the cultural and religious values of the Bangsamoro people; conduct training, workshops and seminars to build the competency of counsellors and other service providers, in coordination with the interior ministry, the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta' and the health ministry; and establish partnerships with government agencies, non-government organisations and religious institutions.

The implementing rules are issued within 90 days by the social services ministry in consultation with the interior ministry, the Darul Ifta', the indigenous peoples ministry, the health ministry and non-government organisations.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy recognises the family as the foundation of society and marriage counselling as the intervention that keeps it functioning. The 3-stage design is the argument: counselling before marriage prevents what counselling in crisis has to repair, and most public provision anywhere offers only the last of the 3.

The requirement that the Framework align with the cultural and religious values of the Bangsamoro people, and the seat given to the Darul Ifta' in building counsellor competency, reflect what marriage is in this region — a contract under the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, in which religious authority has a defined role.
whoIsAffected: Couples intending to marry, entitled to pre-marriage counselling free of charge.
Married couples, through enrichment counselling and crisis counselling.
The Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', brought into the training of counsellors and the design of the framework.
The Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, consulted on the implementing rules — so the framework must accommodate non-Muslim and indigenous marriage practice.
Counsellors and service providers, who receive capacity-building and must meet competency standards.
Religious institutions and non-government organisations, as partners in delivery.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development — the Marriage Counselling Framework, policies, guidelines, counsellor training and partnerships
Bangsamoro Darul Ifta', the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government and the Ministry of Health, coordinating on counsellor competency
Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and non-government organisations, consulted on the implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No amount is named; the requirement goes into the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. The real cost is counsellors — a programme offering 3 kinds of counselling free across the region needs trained people in every municipality, and the Act funds their training without naming a figure for their employment.

whatChanges: Marriage counselling becomes free and publicly provided across the region.
Provision covers the period before marriage, during it, and in crisis.
A Marriage Counselling Framework must align with Bangsamoro cultural and religious values.
The Darul Ifta' is brought into the competency standards for counsellors.
Indigenous peoples' practice is accounted for through consultation on the rules.
readings.insight:
Including the indigenous peoples ministry in the consultation is the detail that saves this bill from a predictable failure. A marriage counselling framework built on the Code of Muslim Personal Laws and designed with the Darul Ifta' would be the natural product of this region's institutions, and it would fit the Teduray, Lambangian and other non-Moro communities badly — their marriage customs are governed by their own customary law, which BAA 64 expressly recognises for family relations. Consulting the indigenous peoples ministry on the rules is the mechanism by which 1 framework can serve several bodies of family law.

Marital Crisis Counselling is the component that does the most and carries the most risk. Teaching couples techniques for conflict resolution is useful; it is also the intervention most likely to be applied where one spouse is being harmed, and the bill says nothing about screening for abuse or about when counselling is the wrong answer. Couples counselling in the presence of violence is understood in practice to be unsafe, and a statute that mandates the service without addressing that leaves it to the framework.

The pre-marriage component is the one with the clearest public benefit and the easiest delivery. The region already has a point of contact with every couple intending to marry — the registration of the marriage — and attaching counselling to that reaches everyone rather than only those who seek help. The bill does not make the connection, and the implementing rules would have to.

This also sits oddly against the rest of what the region has legislated about family. The registry contains bereavement leave bills, moral recovery and pilgrimage leave bills, orphanage bills, and a measure for the welfare of minors — and the Labor and Employment Code enacted as BAA 82. Marriage counselling is the only one addressed to the relationship at the centre of all of them, and it is the only one of that group still in committee alongside the leave bills.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a 50-bed general hospital in Masiu, Lanao del Sur, under the direct control and supervision of the Ministry of Health, named the Aleem Abdulazis S. Mimbantas Memorial Hospital.

The operative text is 7 sections. Further increases in bed capacity and upgrades of services and facilities rest on a hospital development plan prepared by the Ministry of Health. Funding goes into the Ministry's own program and then the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act, and the implementing rules are due within 60 days.

The declaration of policy is slightly wider than the standard formula the region's hospital bills use. Alongside the usual language about a comprehensive and integrated health service and the basic right to life, it adds a purpose the others omit: to adequately respond to emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes a travel-time argument. Patients in Lanao del Sur, including those from Masiu and neighbouring municipalities, travel to Marawi City for consultation or hospitalization — about an hour and a half from Masiu, longer from remote barangays, and longer still when road construction on the highway delays the trip. The note's conclusion is the one that matters: because of the distance and the cost, some patients choose not to seek care at all.

The second reason is commemorative and stated openly. The hospital is to be named for Aleem Abdulazis S. Mimbantas, vice chairman for military affairs of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, whose contribution to the struggle for self-determination the note credits, and who it says untiringly advocated the signing of the peace agreement between the MILF and the national government.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Masiu and neighbouring municipalities in Lanao del Sur, currently 90 minutes or more from a hospital.
Patients who forgo care altogether because of distance and cost, whom the note names directly.
Marawi City's hospitals, which carry this catchment now.
The Ministry of Health, which controls and supervises the hospital and prepares its development plan.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — direct control and supervision, the hospital development plan governing future growth, and implementing rules within 60 days

funding.detail: No amount is named; the Ministry of Health includes implementation in its program and the funding goes into the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. The enacted act appropriates ₱50 million from the Miscellaneous and Personnel Benefit Fund of the 2025 Bangsamoro budget.

whatChanges: Masiu gains a 50-bed general hospital.
A 90-minute journey to Marawi City stops being the nearest route to hospital care.
A hospital in Lanao del Sur carries the name of an MILF vice chairman.
readings.insight:
The name links this bill to another one in the registry. Alim Abdul Aziz Mimbantas is the same man whose burial site at Camp Bushra Somiorang in Butig was declared a Bangsamoro memorial site by BAA 60, which began life as Bill No. 36 — filed by the Government of the Day in September 2022 and enacted in July 2024. This measure, filed by a private member in October 2023, gives his name to a working hospital in the same province. Within roughly a year the region commemorated the same figure twice, once with a shrine and once with 50 beds, and the 2 measures came from opposite ends of the chamber.

That is worth stating without editorialising, because it is how a post-conflict polity settles its own canon. Naming decisions made in the first years after a peace agreement determine whose names appear on buildings for decades, and here the choice is made in the explanatory note of a hospital bill rather than in any dedicated process.

The bed count survived unchanged — 50 beds asked, 50 beds enacted — which is not the pattern elsewhere in this series. The South Ubian and Sibutu bills each asked for 50 and received 25. What distinguishes this one is not obvious from the documents, and the published record offers no committee reasoning for any of the 3 decisions.

The policy addition is the small thing worth keeping. Writing emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases into the purpose clause, in a bill drafted in the years after both the Marawi siege and the pandemic, gives the hospital a mandate its siblings lack — and BAA 69 kept that sentence.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Bangsamoro Teachers' Continuing Education Program and makes it a condition of promotion.

Every Bangsamoro public school teacher must complete at least 18 hours of approved continuing education every 3 years, and the Act allocates those hours rather than leaving them open. At least 8 hours on refresher courses in the subjects they actually teach. At least 3 hours on the Code of Professional Conduct for Public School Teachers. At least 4 hours on innovative teaching methods, technologies and educational tools. And at least 3 hours on conflict resolution, peace education, cultural sensitivity and diversity.

Completion forms part of the qualification standards for promotional appointments. Credit units equal credit hours, computed by the time spent in an activity rounded to the nearest quarter hour and reported in decimal form.

The Bangsamoro Education Board constituted under the Administrative Code administers the programme, writes the implementing rules within 3 months including the guidelines for computing credit units, and hires the personnel needed for record-keeping, auditing, reporting and approval.
readings.whyProposed:
The stated purpose is to keep teachers abreast of a changing field and to give them opportunities to refresh their knowledge, particularly where advances are frequent.

The allocation of the hours is the substantive argument. A continuing education requirement that simply demands 18 hours gets filled with whatever is cheapest to deliver; specifying subject-matter refreshers, professional conduct, teaching technology and — distinctively — conflict resolution and peace education fixes what teachers will actually be trained in.
whoIsAffected: Every public school teacher in the region, who must complete 18 hours every 3 years.
Teachers seeking promotion, for whom completion becomes a qualification standard.
The Bangsamoro Education Board, which administers, approves activities, and must hire staff for record-keeping and auditing.
Providers of continuing education activities, which must be approved by the Board.
Students, as the intended beneficiaries of refreshed subject knowledge and new teaching methods.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Education Board, constituted under the Bangsamoro Administrative Code — administration, approval of activities, implementing rules within 3 months, and credit-unit guidelines
Board personnel hired for record-keeping, auditing, reporting and approval

funding.detail: No amount is named; the requirement goes into the annual Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act. The Act does oblige the Board to hire the personnel needed to run the credit system, so there is a recurring administrative cost, and it is silent on whether teachers or the government pay for the courses themselves.

whatChanges: Public school teachers must complete 18 hours of continuing education every 3 years.
The hours are allocated by subject rather than left to the teacher or the provider.
3 of every 18 hours go to conflict resolution, peace education, cultural sensitivity and diversity.
Completion becomes a qualification standard for promotion.
A credit-unit system with auditing and record-keeping is established.
readings.insight:
The 3 hours on conflict resolution and peace education are the reason this is a Bangsamoro bill rather than a transposed national one. Teachers in this region work with children who have been displaced, who have lost family members, and who sit in the same classroom as the children of people on the other side of a decades-long conflict. Making that a required component of every teacher's continuing education — a sixth of the mandated hours, recurring every 3 years — treats it as a permanent professional competence rather than a response to an incident.

It also lines up with what Parliament has actually enacted elsewhere. BAA 49 requires newly elected local officials to undergo continuing training that includes conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding. The region has legislated that for politicians and not for the teachers who see children every day, and this bill is the measure that would close the gap.

Tying completion to promotion is the enforcement mechanism, and it is the right one for a workforce this size. A requirement with no consequence is advisory; a fine on a teacher is punitive and unaffordable; making it a qualification standard for promotional appointments means the consequence falls on advancement rather than on income, and it falls only on those who seek it.

The unanswered question is who pays. The bill specifies the hours, the subjects, the credit computation and the audit trail, and it says nothing about the cost of the courses. Philippine teachers commonly fund their own professional development, and 18 hours every 3 years is a real expense in a region where teaching salaries are the household income. A mandate that is silent on cost defaults to the teacher paying, and the Act's own appropriation clause covers only its administration.
