This grants employees in both the private and public sectors 5 working days of bereavement leave at full pay on the death of an immediate family member — expressly "to grieve, attend to or make arrangements for the funeral".

Immediate family covers the employee's spouse, parents, child, brother or sister. The employer may request reasonable documentation, such as a death certificate or an obituary, to support the request.

3 provisions give the entitlement force. Section 4 provides that nothing in the Act reduces existing benefits under any law, order, contract, agreement or policy. Section 5 guarantees security of tenure: taking the leave may not be used as a reason for misconduct, demotion or termination, or treated as unsatisfactory performance. Section 6 sets a penalty — any person, corporation, trust, firm, partnership, association or entity violating the Act or its rules is fined up to ₱15,000, and where a corporate body is the violator, imprisonment falls on its responsible officers, including the president, vice president, chief officer, general manager, managing director or partner directly responsible.

The Ministry of Labor and Employment writes the rules for the private sector and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission for the public sector, each within 30 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section makes the welfare case directly: the region's duty is to support employees at the point where a family death and the demands of work collide, and to make the time to grieve and to bury a relative an entitlement rather than a concession.

The drafting suggests a second concern. Naming security of tenure and attaching a penalty means the author expected the entitlement to be refused — which is the realistic expectation for a new leave benefit in an economy of small employers, and the reason the bill spends 3 of its 10 sections on making the leave safe to take.
whoIsAffected: All employees in the region, private and public sector.
Employees whose spouse dies, covered here and not in the companion bill.
Employers, who may ask for a death certificate or obituary but face a fine of up to ₱15,000 for refusing the leave.
Company officers — presidents, general managers, managing directors and partners — who face imprisonment where a corporate employer violates the Act.
Employees who fear retaliation, protected by an express security of tenure clause.
The Ministry of Labor and Employment and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission, writing rules for their respective sectors.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment — implementing rules for the private sector within 30 days
Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission — implementing rules for the public sector within 30 days

funding.detail: No appropriation. The cost falls on employers as 5 working days of full pay per bereavement, and on the regional and local governments as employers of their own staff. The bill raises revenue only incidentally, through fines of up to ₱15,000 on employers who refuse.

whatChanges: Employees gain 5 working days of fully paid leave on the death of a spouse, parent, child or sibling.
Taking the leave cannot be treated as misconduct or grounds for demotion or dismissal.
Refusing the leave becomes an offence punishable by a fine, with imprisonment for responsible corporate officers.
Employers may require a death certificate or obituary but not more.
readings.insight:
Section 5 is the provision that makes this bill work, and it is the one its companion lacks. A statutory right to 5 days' leave means nothing to a contractual worker who believes taking it will cost them the job; saying in the Act that availment cannot be used as a reason for misconduct, demotion, termination or an unsatisfactory performance rating is what converts the entitlement into something a person will actually claim. Bill No. 270 grants the leave and says nothing about what happens to the employee who takes it.

The penalty structure is the other half of the same thought, and it is drafted with more care than the cash figure suggests. A fine capped at ₱15,000 is small against a large employer's payroll. But Section 6 also reaches the individuals — president, vice president, chief officer, general manager, managing director or the partner directly responsible — and personal exposure of named officers is a materially different deterrent from a corporate fine. The drafting does leave an oddity: the section states a fine as the penalty and then provides for imprisonment of officers where the violator is a corporation, without stating an imprisonment term anywhere.

Full pay for 5 working days, against the companion bill's 5 days at half pay, is the substantive policy difference, and this bill is the more expensive and the more coherent of the 2. Bereavement leave exists because a grieving employee cannot work; paying half of it asks them to absorb part of the cost of their own bereavement. Whether the region's small establishments can carry the full version is a real question, and neither bill contains any estimate of what it would cost.

Requiring documentation is the small provision worth keeping from this version. A death certificate or an obituary is proof an employee can produce without difficulty, and naming those 2 examples in the statute forecloses an employer demanding something harder — while the companion bill's 2-day availment deadline achieves verification by making the benefit difficult to claim at all.

2 bereavement leave bills sit in this registry, filed 2 weeks apart in early 2024. Bill No. 270 is MP Sema's, granting 5 days at half pay; Bill No. 281 is MP Hashim's, granting 5 working days at full pay with a penalty for employers who refuse. Both are still at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and the region has no bereavement leave.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 281, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants Bangsamoro officials and employees 30 calendar days of paid leave to perform a pilgrimage, once in a lifetime.

Eligibility turns on service: an aggregate of 2 years with the Bangsamoro government qualifies, and the leave may be taken only once regardless of which office in the region the employee works in at the time of application. Pilgrimage is defined broadly — visiting a place of religious or spiritual importance to perform acts of worship or a spiritual journey — without naming any faith.

The approval chain is where this bill does its real work, and it runs to the top. The Chief Minister approves applications on the favorable recommendation of the head of office. Parliament's own staff go to the Speaker instead. Local government employees are recommended by their local chief executive and then sent to the Chief Minister through the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. Every application reaches the Office of the Chief Minister, which keeps the record of everyone in the region who has taken the leave, local governments included. A head of office may refuse to recommend an application if granting it would seriously hamper operations.

2 provisions have no counterpart in the competing bill. Section 7 requires anyone who takes the leave to submit a written report on the pilgrimage they performed, within 30 days of returning to work. Section 8 makes an employee who deliberately did not perform the pilgrimage despite taking the leave subject to administrative sanctions and penalties.

The money goes in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister, and that office and the Civil Service Commission jointly write the rules within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note attached to the filed copy. Section 2 states the policy in 2 sentences: the Bangsamoro Government exercises its powers to promote the general welfare, and it "realizes the role of a strong and contented workforce in achieving a developed Bangsamoro region".

That is a workforce argument rather than a religious one, and it is the only case the document makes for itself. The bill carries 29 co-authors on its face, which is the other thing it offers in place of a note.
whoIsAffected: Every Bangsamoro government official and employee with at least 2 years of aggregate service, including in local government units.
Employees with under 2 years of service, who do not qualify.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which approves every application in the region and keeps the central record.
The Speaker, who approves for Parliament's own officials and employees.
Local chief executives, who must recommend before an application can proceed.
Heads of office, who may refuse to recommend where the absence would seriously hamper operations.
Anyone who takes the leave, who must file a written report and may face sanctions for not making the pilgrimage.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister — approval of every application, central record-keeping, receipt of post-leave reports, and the budget line
Office of the Parliament Speaker — approval for Parliament's own officials and employees
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — the route by which local government applications reach the Chief Minister
Civil Service Commission for BARMM, jointly with the Office of the Chief Minister — implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is carried in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister, with later requirements in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. Because the leave is paid and runs 30 calendar days, the appropriation is in substance a salary continuation for everyone who takes it.

whatChanges: Government employees with 2 years of service gain 30 calendar days of paid leave for pilgrimage, once in a lifetime.
The Chief Minister personally approves every such application in the region, including from local governments.
A central register of everyone who has taken the leave is kept in the Office of the Chief Minister.
Taking the leave creates a duty to report on the pilgrimage within 30 days of returning.
Not performing the pilgrimage after taking the leave becomes an administrative offense.
readings.insight:
Sections 7 and 8 are what distinguish this bill, and they are worth stating plainly: an employee who takes this leave must afterwards file a written account of their pilgrimage with the Office of the Chief Minister, and one who deliberately did not perform it faces administrative sanctions. The state is verifying an act of worship. There is a defensible reason — 30 days of paid absence is public money, and a benefit without a check invites the obvious abuse — but the check chosen puts a government office in the position of assessing whether someone's devotional journey really happened. The competing bill, which grants half the days and says nothing about pay, needs no such apparatus.

The approval chain compounds it. Every application in the region, from every ministry and every local government unit, lands on the Chief Minister's desk. For a benefit of this kind the natural approver is the employee's own agency head, and this bill makes that person a recommender only. What the design produces is a single regional register of which public servants have made a pilgrimage and when — a document that does not otherwise exist and that the bill does not say who may see.

Set against Bill No. 276, the 2 measures differ in nearly every parameter: 30 days against 15, paid against unstated, 2 years of service against none, a named approval chain against none, and a sanction against nothing. What they share is the vocabulary of accommodation, and where 276 writes religious neutrality into its operative text by naming both Muslim and Christian destinations, this one achieves neutrality by naming nothing at all — a pilgrimage is any journey to a place of religious or spiritual importance.

The path through Parliament was the same for both. Filed 5 February 2024, First Reading on 29 February, referred to the Committee on Rules in June 2024, and then nothing until Committee Report No. 176 took this bill and 276 together on 19 November 2025. 17 deferrals followed across 20 months before Third and Final Reading on 16 July 2026.

A note on the act number, because the registry does not agree with itself. Parliament's bills index records this measure as becoming BAA 94. Parliament's acts index gives BAA 94 a completely different title — the Special Geographic Area Development Authority act — word for word identical to its own entry for BAA 93, both dated 16 July 2026. One of those 2 entries is wrong, and since the leave measure passed Third and Final Reading on that same date, the likeliest reading is that the acts index duplicated BAA 93 into the BAA 94 slot and lost the leave act. No PDF has been published for BAA 92, 93 or 94, so the enacted text cannot be checked against either index. What follows is the bill as filed, not the law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 282, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates and establishes an infirmary hospital in Tipo-Tipo, Basilan.

The municipality has 25,531 people across 4,195 households at the 2020 census. The nearest hospital is the Lamitan District Hospital, 22.2 kilometers away by the Basilan Circumferential Road, and patients travel long hours to reach it.
readings.whyProposed:
The note's case is distance and the inadequacy of what lies at the end of it. Tipo-Tipo's patients travel 22.2 kilometers to Lamitan, to a district hospital that another bill in this registry documents as a 25-bed Level I facility with 4 permanent physicians serving a catchment of 100,150 people across 8 municipalities.

So the journey ends at a hospital that is itself over capacity, which is the argument for a facility in the municipality rather than a better road to the existing one.
whoIsAffected: The 25,531 residents of Tipo-Tipo across 4,195 households.
Patients travelling 22.2 kilometers to Lamitan District Hospital.
Lamitan District Hospital, whose catchment already covers 8 municipalities on 25 beds.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the infirmary.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the facility and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Tipo-Tipo gains an infirmary hospital.
A 22.2-kilometer journey stops being the route to the nearest facility.
Pressure eases on an over-subscribed district hospital in Lamitan.
readings.insight:
This bill needs reading against an act that already exists, and the registry does not connect them. In August 2025 BAA 78 established a 25-bed Level I general hospital in Tipo-Tipo, with ₱50 million from the 2025 budget and a scheme for transferring management to Basilan province once the province can show the capacity to run it. That act began as Bill No. 104, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022.

This bill was filed in February 2024 — after Bill 104 had been filed and before it was enacted — and proposes an infirmary in the same municipality. It is still listed at Second Reading, Committee Stage, while the measure it overlaps became law. So Tipo-Tipo is the subject of 2 hospital measures from 2 different members, 1 of which is now an act, and neither document refers to the other.

Whether that is duplication or complement depends on a distinction the bills do not draw. An infirmary and a 25-bed Level I general hospital are different facilities — an infirmary is smaller, cheaper and aimed at stabilisation and short stays — and a municipality could sensibly have both, or could have wanted the infirmary as an interim step while the hospital was built. But nothing in this bill positions it that way, and with BAA 78 enacted the practical question is whether this measure now has any work left to do.

That is the recurring cost of the pattern this registry documents: 23 hospital bills from 10 members, converging on the same municipalities without visible coordination, with no mechanism inside Parliament for noticing that a subject is already taken. The Tipo-Tipo pair and the 2 identical orphanage bills are the clearest instances.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 283, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
3 sections and one page. This renames the Municipality of Sultan Mastura in Maguindanao del Norte to the Municipality of Subpangen.

Section 2 makes the change conditional: the renaming takes effect only on ratification by a majority of the votes cast by qualified voters in a plebiscite conducted and supervised by COMELEC in the present Municipality of Sultan Mastura. The expenses of that plebiscite are to be borne by the Bangsamoro Government.

The Act takes effect 15 days after publication. There is nothing else in it — no transitional provision for records, seals, signage or contracts held in the old name.
readings.whyProposed:
No explanatory note is attached and the bill offers no reason. Sultan Mastura is named for a historical figure; Subpangen is a place name.

What the bill does say, by requiring a plebiscite, is that the author treated the name of a municipality as belonging to the people who live in it rather than to Parliament. Renaming is within the region's power to legislate over its own political subdivisions, and the choice to put it to a vote anyway is the substantive decision in the document.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Sultan Mastura, who would vote on their municipality's name.
The municipal government, whose records, seal, signage and contracts all carry the existing name.
The Bangsamoro Government, which pays for the plebiscite.
COMELEC, which conducts and supervises it.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite in the present Municipality of Sultan Mastura
The Bangsamoro Government, which bears the plebiscite expenses

funding.detail: No amount is named. The expenses of the plebiscite are borne by the Bangsamoro Government — a departure from the municipality creation bills in this registry, which charge the plebiscite to COMELEC's own appropriations.

whatChanges: Sultan Mastura would become Subpangen, if its voters approve.
The region pays for the plebiscite rather than passing the cost to COMELEC.
readings.insight:
Requiring a plebiscite to change a name is the choice worth noting, and it turns out to be the region's settled practice rather than this bill's innovation. BAA 90, which renamed Datu Blah T. Sinsuat to West Upi in May 2026, does the same thing: it conditions the change on ratification by a majority of the municipality's own voters, in a plebiscite run by COMELEC under the Local Government Code's procedure for changes of name. So on the central question this bill is in line with what Parliament went on to enact.

Who pays is also consistent, and it runs the more principled way. Every municipality *creation* bill in this registry charges the plebiscite to COMELEC's own appropriations — the region spending a national agency's money on a regional decision. This bill has the Bangsamoro Government bear the cost, and BAA 90 charges it to the Contingent Fund of the Office of the Chief Minister. Both put the cost of a regional referendum on the region.

Where this bill falls short of the enacted model is in what it leaves untouched. BAA 90 amends Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 198 — the ARMM-era statute that created the municipality under its original name — so that the renaming reaches the law the name comes from. This bill amends nothing. Sultan Mastura was itself created by an earlier statute, and renaming a municipality without touching the act that named it leaves 2 instruments disagreeing.

What the bill also omits is everything that follows a renaming. A municipality's name appears on its seal, its records, its land titles, its business permits, its road signs and every contract it is party to, and statutes that rename places normally carry a provision saying that references to the old name are read as references to the new one. This one does not, which would leave a genuine question about the continuity of instruments executed as Sultan Mastura.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 284, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The region's own tax code: 289 pages, 445 sections, 9 titles. It would govern the levy, assessment and collection of every revenue the Bangsamoro Government is entitled to.

Title II sets the regional taxes. The first of them is a 1% annual ad valorem tax on the assessed value of all real property in the region — land, buildings, machinery and improvements — with the assessed values taken from what local government units have already set. Other articles cover transfers of real property, and taxes on quarry resources taken from public lands and from the beds of seas, lakes and rivers.

Title IV deals with national taxes that have their situs in the region: capital gains, documentary stamp, donor's and estate taxes, where every taxable element sits inside the BARMM.

Title V creates a tax regime for Islamic finance. Title VII covers incentives, Title VIII creates the Bangsamoro Revenue Office under the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, and Title IX sets out the offences and penalties.

Section 11 requires the Revenue Office to run a digitalization program for tax collection. Section 8 deputizes local treasurers to collect on the region's behalf.
readings.whyProposed:
Section 2 grounds it in the autonomy the Organic Law grants. The region is entitled to levy taxes and to keep a share of what the National Government collects inside its territory, and until this passes it has no code of its own setting out how.

Section 4 is the inventory of what the region may draw on: taxes, fees and charges, the annual block grant, revenues from natural resources, 4 national taxes with situs in the region, a share in other national collections, dividends from government corporations, grants and donations, loans and official development assistance, shares in public utility revenues, and quarry taxes.
whoIsAffected: Every property owner in the region, who would pay a 1% regional tax on assessed value.
Anyone transferring real property, and anyone extracting sand, gravel or stone from public lands or waters.
Islamic finance institutions and their customers, whose transactions get a defined tax treatment.
Local treasurers, deputized to collect regional taxes.
The National Government, whose 4 situs taxes the region would administer.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Revenue Office, under the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Deputized local treasurers and withholding agents
Shari'ah Supervisory Board, certifying which transactions are Islamic finance for tax purposes

funding.detail: The Code raises revenue rather than spending it. Section 10 provides support for local government units and deputized officers out of appropriations.

whatChanges: The region would have a single code governing every tax, fee and charge it levies.
A 1% annual regional tax on real property, on top of what local units already assess.
A Bangsamoro Revenue Office exists, with a mandate to digitalize collection.
Islamic finance transactions are taxed on a stated principle rather than case by case.
readings.insight:
Title V is the part with no equivalent anywhere else in Philippine tax law. It sets out to achieve what Section 252 calls neutral tax treatment between Islamic finance transactions and their equivalent conventional ones.

The problem it solves is structural. Islamic finance avoids interest, so a transaction that functions as a loan is often structured as a sale, a lease or a partnership — and a tax code written for conventional banking taxes a sale as a sale. The same economic act ends up taxed differently depending on whether it was arranged in a way a Muslim customer could use. Title V treats the Islamic form as equivalent to the conventional one for tax purposes, with the Shari'ah Supervisory Board certifying what qualifies.

It stops at the regional line and says so: the same neutrality for national taxes under the NIRC is left to the National Government. So a transaction could be neutral for regional tax and not for national tax, which is a gap the Code names rather than closes.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 286 as filed, the Bangsamoro Revenue Code

readings.whatItDoes:
The Ibadah Friendly Hospital Act. It would require hospitals in the region to be accredited on whether they let a patient practise their faith while being treated.

To be certified a hospital must have a place of worship, a wash area, a morgue, services for a deceased patient and a person responsible for them, and attendants and helpers. Wards must be built so that the sexes are segregated.

An Ibadah Friendly Hospital Committee runs it. A certificate issues only after the Committee has carried out an ocular inspection, and it is renewed yearly on payment of a fee. A facility that partly meets the standards gets 90 days to comply before a final decision. The Committee may cancel, suspend or revoke a certificate for breach of the Act or of its rules, and there is an appeal for an institution refused or stripped of one.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill defines ibadah at the top — an Arabic word for service or servitude, usually translated as worship, and in the plural referring to the jurisprudence of Muslim religious ritual.

The argument follows from the definition. A hospital that has nowhere to pray, no water to wash with and no way to handle a death according to religious obligation is a hospital where a Muslim patient cannot keep their practice while they are being treated. The Act makes that a thing hospitals are inspected and certified on.
whoIsAffected: Patients who need to pray, wash or observe religious obligation while in hospital.
Families of patients who die in hospital, where the Act requires the facility to provide for the deceased.
Every hospital in the region, public or private, which must seek and renew accreditation.
Women and men in wards, which must be built to segregate the sexes.
implementedBy: Ibadah Friendly Hospital Committee — standards, inspection, certification and revocation
The accreditation agency named in Section 3

funding.detail: Section 16 appropriates the amount necessary for initial implementation; no figure is stated. Section 14 makes applicants pay an accreditation fee.

whatChanges: Hospitals are accredited on religious accessibility, with an annual renewal.
A place of worship, a wash area and a morgue become conditions of certification.
Wards must be built with the sexes segregated.
readings.insight:
The bill numbers 2 consecutive sections as Section 6 and then jumps to Section 9. There is no Section 7 and no Section 8.

The 2 sixes do different jobs. The first lists the physical requirements — place of worship, wash area, morgue, attendants. The second says a facility must meet the standards in an Assessment Tool referred to but not reproduced. A hospital reading the Act to find out what it must build would get one answer from the first Section 6 and be pointed at a document it has not seen by the second.

This was checked twice at different scan resolutions, because a duplicated number is exactly the kind of thing an OCR invents. It is in the document.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes a 50-bed Bangsamoro People General Hospital in the Special Geographic Area.

This is a new hospital rather than an upgrade of an existing one.
readings.whyProposed:
The Special Geographic Area is the 63 barangays of North Cotabato that voted to join the region. Its 8 municipalities were ratified in 2024 and it has no census figures of its own in PSA's published series.

It is the one part of the region with no provincial hospital of its own, because it is not a province.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the Special Geographic Area's 8 municipalities.
The Ministry of Health, which would operate it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: A 50-bed general hospital is established in the Special Geographic Area.
readings.insight:
The Special Geographic Area is the hardest part of the region to serve and the hardest to count. It is 63 barangays that voted to transfer in, grouped into 8 municipalities ratified in 2024, and it sits inside North Cotabato rather than inside any Bangsamoro province.

That has consequences a hospital bill runs into. PSA publishes no separate census for it, so the region's own directory carries no population figure for the area at all — and the 2 parliamentary districting bills that do put a number on it disagree, at 215,433 and 214,703. A 50-bed hospital for a population nobody has counted is a reasonable guess rather than a calculation, and the bill does not pretend otherwise: it states the bed count and no catchment.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Public Petitions Act. It would give any citizen of the region the right to put a written request to Parliament on any matter of public interest, and oblige Parliament to answer it.

A petition must be in writing, notarised, signed by at least 100 registered voters of the region, and carry the lead petitioner's contact details. It goes to the Office of the Speaker, in person, by post, or through an online portal.

The deadlines are the substance. The Speaker's office acknowledges receipt within 5 working days and assigns a reference number. The Speaker refers the petition to the appropriate committee within 10 working days. The committee reviews it, holds public hearings or consultations if necessary, and reports with recommendations to Parliament within 60 days of referral. Parliament then deliberates and must give the petitioners a written response setting out what it did — or its reasons for doing nothing.

The status of every petition is to be publicly accessible on an official website, and a Public Petitions Office inside Parliament helps citizens prepare their submissions.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues that the Organic Law emphasises public participation and transparency but provides no structured mechanism for it, so there is no route by which a citizen can put something onto Parliament's agenda.

The 100-signature threshold is explained as a filter: enough to show a petition represents a genuine public interest rather than one person's grievance, and low enough that a community can meet it.
whoIsAffected: Any registered voter in the region, who gains a route onto Parliament's agenda.
Marginalised and underrepresented groups, named in the explanatory note as the intended beneficiaries.
The Office of the Speaker and every committee, which take on deadlines they can be held to.
implementedBy: Office of the Speaker — acknowledgment, reference numbers, referral
The committees of Parliament — review, hearings, report within 60 days
Public Petitions Office — assisting citizens to prepare submissions

funding.detail: The Act requires a Public Petitions Office and an online portal and tracking database. No amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: A citizen with 100 signatures can compel Parliament to consider a matter and answer in writing.
Every petition gets a reference number and a publicly trackable status.
Parliament must give reasons when it decides to do nothing.
readings.insight:
The provision that matters most is the shortest. Section 9 requires Parliament to give petitioners a written response "detailing the actions taken or reasons for inaction".

An obligation to explain a refusal is a different thing from an obligation to consider a request. Most participation mechanisms end at receipt — the petition is filed, acknowledged, and then nothing is owed. This one makes silence a reportable outcome: a committee that lets 60 days pass and a Parliament that declines to act both have to say why, in writing, to a named person.

Everything else in the Act is machinery for making that promise checkable: a reference number, a public database, published status. The bill has been in committee since 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the rulebook for how the Bangsamoro Government handles money — 79 sections across 8 titles, enacted as the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025.

It sets out the 4 phases a budget moves through and who is answerable at each: preparation and authorization, execution, financial management, and accountability. It creates a Bangsamoro Budget Coordinating Committee, requires a published statement of fiscal policy and a medium-term fiscal strategy, and makes the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management the office that issues allotments and cash allocations.

3 sections near the end are the ones a citizen can use. Section 66 requires every ministry, office and government-owned corporation to carry a transparency seal on its website listing approved budgets and targets, programs and projects, beneficiaries, implementation status, accomplishment reports, procurement plans and contracts awarded. Section 67 requires MFBM to publish a citizen-friendly summary of the appropriations act every year — the Act calls it the Bangsamoro People's Budget. Section 68 requires participatory budget mechanisms.

Title VII makes 6 things punishable: certifying funds that are not available, incurring an illegal expenditure, running an overdraft, filing a fraudulent accountability report, failing to file one at all, and misusing government funds or property.
readings.whyProposed:
A cabinet bill, filed without an explanatory note. The declaration of policy in Section 2 is the argument: that accountability, integrity and moral governance in the use of public funds are to be realized through an integrated system running from planning through to review, and that the system has to account for the region's fiscal autonomy and its asymmetrical relationship with the National Government.

What the Act is for, read off its own structure, is that the region had been running its budget on national rules and circulars rather than on a law of its own.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and agency of the Bangsamoro Government, and every Bangsamoro government-owned or controlled corporation.
Constituent local government units, to the extent their revenues and expenditures affect the region's and they fall under the full disclosure policy.
Anyone trying to find out what an office was given and what it did with it — the transparency seal and the People's Budget are addressed to them.
Officials who certify, obligate or report on public funds, who now have 6 named offences to answer to.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — allotments, cash allocations, guidelines, and the annual People's Budget
Bangsamoro Budget Coordinating Committee — the fiscal policy statement and the budget priorities framework
Bangsamoro Budget Office — monitoring compliance with the transparency seal and reporting it to Parliament and the public
Every ministry, office and corporation covered, for its own seal and its own reports

funding.detail: The Act appropriates nothing of its own. It governs how everything else is appropriated, released and accounted for.

whatChanges: The region's budget process is set by its own law rather than by national rules read across.
A transparency seal becomes a legal requirement for every ministry, office and government corporation, with the Bangsamoro Budget Office reporting on who complies.
A citizen-friendly summary of the appropriations act is required every fiscal year.
6 budget offences are named, from certifying unavailable funds to failing to submit accountability reports.
readings.insight:
It took 16 months. Filed on 19 August 2024, it did not reach third reading until 9 December 2025 — the slowest passage of the 15 approved bills read here, and the exact opposite of Bill 470, a supplemental appropriation that was filed and passed in 3 days.

The sections worth watching are 66 to 68, because they are a promise this registry can check. They require the budget call's eventual product to be published in a form an ordinary reader can use, and they put the Bangsamoro Budget Office in charge of reporting who is and is not complying. A transparency seal that exists in a statute and not on a website is a gap anyone can verify, one ministry at a time.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 325 as filed, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act

readings.whatItDoes:
Renames the municipality of Datu Blah T. Sinsuat, in Maguindanao del Norte, as the municipality of West Upi.

The change does not take effect on its own. Section 3 requires a plebiscite in the municipality itself, run and supervised by COMELEC under the Local Government Code, with the Bangsamoro Government paying for it. A majority of the votes cast decides it.

Section 4 amends Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 198, which created the municipality in the first place.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 90 on 19 May 2026.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues from the National Historical Commission's own rule: that a province, city, town or barangay may be renamed provided the new name is a reversion to an older one found to be more culturally and historically significant.

The town was carved out of North Upi, Maguindanao, by MMA Act No. 198 of 24 October 2005 and ratified by plebiscite on 15 July 2006. It has 13 barangays and, on the 2020 census, 28,243 people. The name it carries is that of Datu Blah T. Sinsuat (1908–1981), Maguindanao's delegate to the 1935 Constitutional Convention and Cotabato's lone representative to the 2nd Congress.
whoIsAffected: The 28,243 residents of the municipality, who vote on whether the change happens at all.
The 13 barangays — Kinimi, Laguitan, Lapaken, Matuber, Meti, Nalkan, Pinansaran, Pura, Resa, Sedem, Sinipak, Tambak and Tubuan.
COMELEC, which has to run the plebiscite.
Anyone holding a record, title or address under the current name.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite
Bangsamoro Government — the cost of it

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Section 3 says the expenses of the plebiscite shall be borne by the Bangsamoro Government, without putting a figure on them.

whatChanges: Subject to a plebiscite, the municipality is renamed West Upi.
MMA Act No. 198 is amended rather than repealed — the municipality it created continues, under a different name.
readings.insight:
The bill is a reversion, and says so: West Upi was part of North Upi before 2005. What the explanatory note does not say is why the present name is being set aside, and the Act does not either — it recites the man's record as a 1935 Constitutional Convention delegate and a member of the 2nd Congress, and then renames the town away from him without comment.

The plebiscite requirement is the part worth knowing. A renaming here is not a decision Parliament can make alone: 19 members signed the bill, and the 28,243 people who live there still have the last word on it.

readings.whatItDoes:
A supplemental appropriation for 2024, drawn entirely from money the Bangsamoro Government had already been given in earlier years and had not spent — unutilized prior years' appropriations sitting in the Bangsamoro Treasury.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 63, the FY 2024 Supplemental Appropriations Act, at ₱8,441,261,975.

The 15 sections set the conditions: releases go out as Special Allotment Release Orders, offices may deduct engineering and administrative overhead and administrative costs within stated caps, no obligation may be incurred without a certification that funds are available, the cash budgeting system applies, and ministries must post infrastructure project details and file financial and physical accountability reports.
readings.whyProposed:
A cabinet bill with no explanatory note. The argument is the source clause: money appropriated in earlier years and left unspent is put back to work rather than left idle in the Treasury.

That is the same mechanism the region's budget process has leaned on repeatedly — reverted and unutilized funds returning as a named source — and it is why the FY 2024 budget bill added reverted allotments to its own list of funding streams.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and agency receiving a supplemental allocation.
Contractors and suppliers on infrastructure projects funded by it, whose project details must be posted.
The Commission on Audit, whose findings ministries must report back on within 60 days.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — the Special Allotment Release Orders and the cash budgeting system
Every ministry, office and agency named in the schedule
Commission on Audit

funding.detail: ₱8,441,261,975 as enacted in BAA 63, appropriated entirely out of unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury. The bill as published online does not state a figure — see the reading below.

whatChanges: ₱8.44 billion of previously unspent appropriation is made available again for 2024.
Every peso of it comes from money already granted in earlier years, so the supplemental adds nothing to what the region was given.
readings.insight:
What the Parliament published for this bill is not the whole bill. Section 1 reads "the amounts set forth in this section is hereby appropriated" and then the page ends — the schedule the colon promises is simply not in the file. The remaining 14 sections are general provisions, and the only figures anywhere in the document are 2 references to a ₱1 million threshold in the procurement and overhead clauses.

The file name says as much: it is published as the General Provisions of the FY 2024 Supplemental. So the schedule exists and is held somewhere else. But a reader who opens the document the Parliament links from this bill's own page gets the conditions on the money and no amount, and has to go to the enacted act to learn that the figure is ₱8,441,261,975.

Bill 349, the following year's supplemental, carries its total in the first sentence and a table under it. The practice is not uniform.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 330 as published — general provisions only

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Gender and Development Code — a cabinet bill running to 149 sections.

It declares a policy of equal rights for women and men and full participation of women in political, economic, social and cultural life, and says outright that it is addressing the historical and persistent marginalisation of women and girls.

4 separate sections set out where its principles come from: the Qur'an and the Sunnah, international commitments, statutes, and local customs and traditions.

The operative part covers rights of women, violence against women in its several defined forms, trafficking, sexual harassment including online, forced marriage, and the machinery to deal with them — women and children protection desks, barangay VAW desks, rape crisis centres, survivor support groups, and protection for the service providers who handle these cases.
readings.whyProposed: A cabinet bill with no separate explanatory note. Section 2 carries the argument: that gender equality and women's empowerment are vital to sustainable development, peace and security in the region, and that comprehensive and transformative measures are needed rather than piecemeal ones.
whoIsAffected: Women and girls across the region.
Survivors of violence, who gain defined services and named desks to report to.
Barangays, which would run VAW desks.
Service providers in VAW cases, who are given protection of their own.
Every office of the Bangsamoro Government, under the Code's scope of application.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Government and all its offices, under Section 3
Local government units, through women and children protection desks and barangay VAW desks
Commission on Audit, named in connection with the judicious use of gender and development budgets

funding.detail: No single figure is stated in the text read. The Code refers to gender and development budgets and to the Commission on Audit's role in auditing their use.

whatChanges: A single regional code covers women's rights, violence against women, and the services that respond to it.
Forced marriage is defined as a form of violence against women and children.
Barangay VAW desks and rape crisis centres are required rather than optional.
readings.insight:
Section 22 is the one to read if you read only one. It provides that no person shall be forced to marry on vitiated consent, that solemnisation requires the free and prior informed consent of both parties, and that a marriage brought about by coercion, force or intimidation — or without the permission of one or both parties — is a form of violence against women and children, especially where a party is a minor.

It then grounds that in Islamic jurisprudence rather than against it: free and voluntary consent of both parties is described as part and parcel of al-ijab wal qabul, offer and acceptance, which is an essential requisite of a valid nikah.

That is the Code's whole method in one section. It has 4 separate sources-of-principle sections — Qur'an and Sunnah, international commitments, statutes, local custom — because the argument it has to win is not that forced marriage is harmful but that prohibiting it is consistent with the faith and the customs of the people it applies to. A code that could only cite CEDAW would be easier to write and easier to ignore.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 336 as filed, the Bangsamoro Gender and Development Code

readings.whatItDoes:
The region's budget for 2025 as filed: ₱96,696,791,225.73 for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government from 1 January to 31 December 2025.

Section 1 names the sources — the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, and other revenues.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 65, the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro for FY 2025, on 10 December 2024, at ₱94,411,666,856.24.
readings.whyProposed: An annual appropriations bill carries no explanatory note. Its argument is the allocation.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and special purpose fund of the Bangsamoro Government.
Constituent local government units receiving shares and support funds.
Suppliers and contractors to the regional government.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — release, guidelines and the cash budgeting system
Every ministry and office named in the expenditure program
whatChanges: The region's 2025 operations are funded at ₱94.41 billion as enacted.
The budget falls year on year: FY 2024 was ₱98.47 billion.
readings.insight:
Parliament cut it. The bill was filed on 23 October 2024 at ₱96,696,791,225.73 and ratified on 10 December 2024 at ₱94,411,666,856.24 — ₱2,285,124,369.49 removed, about 2.4%.

Set beside the other 2 money bills read here, that makes 3 outcomes from 3 measures. The 2025 budget was cut by ₱2.29 billion. The 2025 supplemental, filed 4 months later, was raised by ₱1.355 billion. The 2026 budget came out of Parliament at exactly the figure it went in at, to the centavo.

FY 2025 is also the only year in this registry where the region's budget fell. It went from ₱98.47 billion in 2024 to ₱94.41 billion in 2025 and then to ₱114.08 billion in 2026 — and the cut this bill records is part of how the fall happened.

One thing to know about finding this bill at all: the registry index still files it under "Second Reading (Committee Stage)", last updated 24 October 2024, the day after it was filed. It became law 7 weeks later. The status field is not a reliable guide to whether a measure finished.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 341 as filed, the FY 2025 appropriations bill

readings.whatItDoes:
Redraws the Bangsamoro Parliament's district map after Sulu left the region, amending Section 4 of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 58.

Sulu's exclusion vacated 7 parliamentary seats. This bill reapportions them, producing 32 single-member districts across Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Tawi-Tawi, Cotabato City and the Special Geographic Area.

It uses the 2020 census and says so: the schedule's column is headed "2020 Population" and the regional total given is 3,944,692.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note builds the chain of authority rather than arguing a policy. It runs from Section 15, Article X of the 1987 Constitution, through the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro signed on 27 March 2014 after 17 years of negotiation and armed struggle, to Republic Act No. 11054 signed on 27 July 2018.

The point of the recital is the problem: the Organic Law defines the region's territory as including Sulu, and Sulu is no longer in it. 7 seats were apportioned to a province that is gone, and the map has to be redrawn before an election can be held on it.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region, whose district is redrawn.
Candidates for the 32 district seats.
COMELEC, which has to run an election on whichever map is in force.
Sulu, whose 7 seats are redistributed to the areas that remain.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament, as the body the districts elect to

funding.detail: The title provides for appropriating funds; no amount is stated in the text read.

whatChanges: Section 4 of BAA 58 is replaced with a 32-district map.
Sulu's 7 seats are reapportioned to the remaining provinces, city and special area.
readings.insight:
This is the first of 3 bills in this registry that redraw the same 32 districts, and the only one that says which census it is counting.

Its column is headed "2020 Population" and totals 3,944,692. Bill 351, the Redistricting Act of 2025, uses the same figures and does not label them. Bill 415, the Districts Act of 2025, uses the 2024 census — 4,545,486 — and does not label those either. A reader comparing the 3 has no way to tell from 2 of them which count the seats were drawn from, except by checking the numbers against PSA, which is what was done here.

readings.whatItDoes:
The 2025 supplemental appropriation, filed at ₱9,945,000,000 out of unutilized prior years' appropriations held in the Bangsamoro Treasury.

Unlike the 2024 and 2026 supplementals, this one states its total in the first sentence and carries a schedule under it, broken down by ministry, office and agency in thousands of pesos.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 75 — at ₱11,300,000,000.
readings.whyProposed: A cabinet bill with no explanatory note. The source clause is the case: money already appropriated in earlier years and not spent is made available again rather than left in the Treasury.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and agency in the schedule.
Contractors and suppliers paid out of it.
The Bangsamoro Treasury, whose idle balances are the source.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Every ministry, office and agency named in the schedule

funding.detail: ₱9,945,000,000 as filed, out of unutilized prior years' appropriations. Enacted as BAA 75 at ₱11,300,000,000, drawn from income generated on Bureau of the Treasury investments as well as unutilized prior years' appropriations.

whatChanges: ₱11.3 billion is made available for 2025 as enacted, ₱1.355 billion more than was asked for.
The funding source widens: investment income on Treasury holdings joins unspent prior appropriations.
readings.insight:
Parliament raised it. The bill was filed on 19 February 2025 at ₱9,945,000,000 and ratified on 29 May 2025 at ₱11,300,000,000 — ₱1,355,000,000 more, an increase of about 13.6% on what the executive asked for.

The funding source changed with it. The bill draws on unutilized prior years' appropriations alone; the act adds income generated on Bureau of the Treasury investments. So between filing and enactment the supplemental grew, and part of what it grew into was a stream the bill as filed did not name.

That direction is worth noting on its own. The usual story of a budget in committee is subtraction.

readings.whatItDoes:
Upgrades the Dr. Serapio B. Montañer Jr., Al-Haj Memorial Hospital in Malabang, Lanao del Sur, to 100 beds, and requires its staffing to rise correspondingly under Civil Service rules.

The hospital stays under the Ministry of Health, which approves its organizational structure, personnel, plans and programs. Funding goes into the Ministry's own program and then into the annual appropriations act. The Ministry of Health and MFBM have 60 days from effectivity to issue implementing rules.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 80 on 20 August 2025.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes a case from load. The hospital serves the highest number of patients among the 5 Bangsamoro government-run hospitals in Lanao del Sur, in a catchment of about 1.2 million people. On the Ministry of Health's 2019 statistical report it was providing care far above its bed capacity, and over the 3 years before filing its bed occupancy rate ran at roughly 300 to 400% — without any augmentation to its maintenance and operating budget beyond PhilHealth reimbursements.

It offers general medical, pediatric and surgical services, ophthalmology, obstetrics and gynaecology, and anaesthesiology.
whoIsAffected: Patients across Lanao del Sur — the note puts the catchment at 1.2 million.
The hospital's existing doctors, nurses, midwives and support staff, whose numbers are to rise.
The Ministry of Health, which absorbs the cost into its annual program.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — administrative supervision and control, structure, staffing and programs
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — jointly responsible for the implementing rules
Civil Service Commission rules govern the staffing increase

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Section 6 requires the Ministry of Health to include implementation in its program, with the funding to be carried in the Annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: The hospital's authorized capacity under regional law becomes 100 beds.
Staffing is to increase to match, under Civil Service Commission rules.
readings.insight:
The bill contradicts itself on the one fact it turns on. Section 3 upgrades the hospital "from its present 25-bed capacity to 100". Its own explanatory note, 2 pages earlier, says the hospital "has been upgraded into level 2 with 100 authorized bed capacity since June 29, 2022 under Republic Act No. 11870" — and then cites the Ministry of Health's 2019 report describing it as "the 75 bed DSBMMH".

3 capacities for one hospital in one document: 25 in the operative section, 75 in the 2019 report, 100 under a national law passed in 2022. Nothing in the bill reconciles them.

There is a reading that holds them together — that a national law can authorize 100 beds while the hospital still operates and is funded for 25 — and it may well be the right one. But the bill does not say so. It proposes to do what it says a national law did 3 years earlier, and leaves a reader to work out why that is necessary.

This is the second time this pattern has turned up here. Bill 264 proposed raising Siasi District Hospital from 25 beds when Republic Act No. 7195 had set it at 50 in 1992.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 350, substitute bill as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Parliamentary Redistricting Act of 2025. It amends Section 4 of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 58 and reapportions the region into 32 single-member parliamentary districts.

The allocation is 4 districts to Basilan, 9 to Lanao del Sur, 5 each to Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, 4 to Tawi-Tawi, 3 to Cotabato City and 2 to the Special Geographic Area.

Each district is listed with its component cities and municipalities and a population figure for each.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 77 on 19 August 2025.
readings.whyProposed: A government bill, filed without an explanatory note. The occasion is the same one Bill 347 sets out: Sulu's departure left seats apportioned to a province no longer in the region, and the map had to be redrawn before the first parliamentary election could be held on it.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region.
Candidates for the 32 district seats.
COMELEC.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. The cost of an election under the map falls to COMELEC.

whatChanges: Section 4 of BAA 58 is replaced with a 32-district map.
readings.insight:
The population figures in this bill are the 2020 census, to the person — Basilan 426,207, Lanao del Sur 1,195,518, Maguindanao del Norte 618,421, Maguindanao del Sur 723,758, Tawi-Tawi 440,276, Cotabato City 325,079 — and the bill does not say so anywhere. Its tables are headed only "TOTAL POPULATION".

Bill 415, filed later the same year and also apportioning 32 districts, uses the 2024 census instead: the same 7 areas at 541,947, 1,368,137, 741,428, 813,243, 482,645 and 383,383. That bill does not label its figures either.

The seat allocation is identical in both. So between the 2 measures the count of people underneath the map moved by roughly 600,000, and the number of seats each area gets did not move at all.

readings.whatItDoes:
Declares the Lake Lanao Area a special management area and puts it under a management plan rather than under ordinary land use rules.

Section 4 defines the geographical coverage as the combined areas of the lake and the land around it. Section 5 makes the whole of it subject to zoning and other protective measures determined by the plan. A Lake Lanao Management Authority, created by the Act, prepares the plan through its Research and Planning Service.

Sections 7 and 8 set what the plan must contain and the minimum rules and principles its management has to follow.
readings.whyProposed:
Lake Lanao is the largest lake in Mindanao, the second largest in the Philippines, the source of the Agus River that generates a large share of Mindanao's electricity, and the ancestral home of the Maranao — whose name means people of the lake.

It is also shared: its shoreline runs through many municipalities of Lanao del Sur, which means no single local government can manage it and each has had its own rules for its own stretch.
whoIsAffected: Communities on the lake shore across Lanao del Sur.
Fisherfolk working the lake.
Municipalities whose zoning would be subordinated to the area management plan.
The Maranao, for whom the lake is ancestral.
implementedBy: Lake Lanao Management Authority — the plan and its implementation
Its Research and Planning Service, which drafts the plan

funding.detail: Figures appear in the text read at ₱5,000,000.00 and ₱500,000 in connection with specific provisions; no overall appropriation is stated in the portion read.

whatChanges: The lake and its surrounding area are managed as one unit under a single plan.
Zoning in the area is set by the management plan rather than municipality by municipality.
readings.insight:
The design decision is in Section 4: the Act covers the combined areas of the lake and its surroundings, not the water alone.

That is the difference between a measure that can work and one that cannot. What damages a lake is almost never done in the lake — it is sediment off cleared slopes, waste from settlements on the shore, and abstraction upstream. An authority with jurisdiction over the water and none over the land draining into it can measure a decline it has no power to stop.

What the bill as read does not settle is how the area plan and municipal zoning rank against each other when they conflict. Section 5 subjects the area to zoning determined under the plan; it does not say what happens to a municipal ordinance already in force that says something different.

readings.whatItDoes:
Creates a Bangsamoro Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Program and an independent commission to run it — the BTJRC, 5 members, all descendants of native inhabitants of Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago or their spouses, appointed by the Chief Minister.

The Program has 5 components: documenting human rights violations against the Bangsamoro and other indigenous peoples from the American period to the present, with a view to possible prosecution or reparation; mapping land dispossession from the Treaty of Paris in 1898 onwards; establishing the historical record; recommending institutional reforms; and keeping civil society involved throughout.

The commission writes its own rules of procedure, and is directed to keep stakeholders participating without being bound by the usual formalities of law and judicial process.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 89 on 28 January 2026, consolidated with Parliament Bill No. 25.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy grounds it in the peace process: plans and programs bilaterally agreed between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, and with the Moro National Liberation Front, as part of the Bangsamoro peace process.

Transitional justice was one of the commitments in that process. This is the measure that puts it into regional law.
whoIsAffected: People with claims of human rights violations going back to the American period.
Communities dispossessed of land since 1898.
Indigenous peoples in the region, named alongside the Bangsamoro throughout.
Civil society organizations, given a standing role in the Program.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission — design, implementation and supervision
Office of the Chief Minister — appointment of the Chair and 4 Commissioners

funding.detail: No amount is stated. Section 9 grants the commission fiscal autonomy with funding released regularly and automatically, and provides that its annual appropriation shall not be reduced below the amount it received the preceding fiscal year.

whatChanges: An independent commission on transitional justice exists in regional law, with its own rules of procedure.
Its budget carries a floor: it cannot be appropriated less than it got the year before.
The historical period opened for examination runs from 1898 for land and from the American period for human rights.
readings.insight:
Section 9 is the unusual provision. The commission's annual appropriation "shall not be reduced from the amount received in the preceding fiscal year", and the pay and benefits of its chair, commissioners, officials and employees cannot be decreased either.

That is a ratchet written into a budget line, and it is the opposite of how every other office in the region is funded — the Budget System Act enacted in the same period evaluates proposals partly on past performance against target spending, which is a mechanism for giving an office less when it underspends. This commission is exempted from that pressure by its own charter.

The reason is readable enough: a body investigating the state is worth little if the state can quietly defund it. Whether that reasoning survives contact with a year when the region's budget falls — as it did in 2025, by ₱4.06 billion — is a question the Act does not answer.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes the Salamat Excellence Award for Leadership — the SEAL Program — a recognition scheme for Local Chief Executives in the region.

It judges them across 3 domains: Accountable Leadership, Participatory Leadership and Service-Oriented Leadership. Assessment runs in levels: a first level checking eligibility and documentation, a second involving onsite validation and consultations with stakeholders to confirm what a nominee claims.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 81 on 20 August 2025.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note argues that the award institutionalizes a standard rather than handing out a prize — that naming the 3 domains and tying them to criteria sets a benchmark local executives can be measured against, and that the onsite validation stage is what keeps it from being a paper exercise.

It frames the program as the Bangsamoro Government's commitment to moral governance, accountability and inclusive development.
whoIsAffected: Local Chief Executives in the region — provincial governors, city and municipal mayors.
Residents consulted during onsite validation of a nominee's record.
The ministries that would administer and fund the award.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Government, through the offices the Act designates to run the assessment

funding.detail: The title provides for appropriating funds. No amount is stated in the text read.

whatChanges: A regional award for local executives exists in law, with named criteria and a validation stage.
readings.insight:
The interesting part is the second level of assessment. A recognition program that stops at documents rewards whoever files the best paperwork; this one requires someone to go and look, and to ask the people in the area whether the claim is true.

That is also its weak point as a transparency measure. Nothing in the bill as read requires the assessments, the validations or the consultations to be published — so the thing that makes the award credible is the thing a citizen cannot inspect.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 355 as filed, the SEAL Act of 2025

readings.whatItDoes: Creates a Bangsamoro Shari'ah Judicial and Legal Academy — a training institution for the region's Shari'ah justice system, with its own powers and functions, a Board of Trustees, a Chancellor and a Vice-Chancellor.
readings.whyProposed:
The region runs a Shari'ah court system and is building a wider Shari'ah justice system around it, and both need people trained to work in them — judges, clerks, counsel and court personnel.

An academy is the standard answer to that in the Philippine judiciary, which has the Philippine Judicial Academy for the regular courts. This is the regional equivalent for the Shari'ah side.
whoIsAffected: Shari'ah judges, court personnel and counsel.
People appearing before Shari'ah courts, who are affected by how well trained those courts are.
Students and practitioners seeking qualification in Shari'ah law.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Shari'ah Judicial and Legal Academy — through its Board of Trustees and executive officials

funding.detail: A figure of ₱50 million appears in the text read in connection with the Academy; no further detail on its basis is stated in the portion read.

whatChanges: A training institution for the Shari'ah justice system exists in regional law.
It is governed by a Board of Trustees with a Chancellor and Vice-Chancellor, on a university model rather than as a court office.
readings.insight:
The structure is the tell. An academy with a Board of Trustees, a Chancellor and a Vice-Chancellor is built like a university, not like a judicial training office attached to a court.

That matters for what it can do. A court's training arm teaches the people already in the system; an institution with academic officers can set a curriculum, confer qualifications and build a field. The Shari'ah justice system the region is standing up — see Bill 473, the Shari'ah Justice System Code, also in committee — will need more qualified people than the existing courts employ, and an academy is the only part of the plan that produces them.

readings.whatItDoes: Upgrades the Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi, from a Level 1 facility of 50 beds to a Level 2 facility of 200 beds. It stays under the Ministry of Health.
readings.whyProposed: Bongao is the capital of Tawi-Tawi and this is the province's main hospital. Tawi-Tawi is the region's most remote province — closer to Borneo than to Cotabato — which makes referral off-island slow and expensive, and makes the level the hospital is rated at the practical ceiling on what can be treated without a flight.
whoIsAffected: The 482,645 people of Tawi-Tawi, on the 2024 census.
Patients who would otherwise be referred off the island group.
The hospital's staff, whose complement would rise with the level.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: The Act provides for the cost to be included in the annual appropriations; no amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: The province's main hospital quadruples in authorised capacity, from 50 beds to 200.
It moves from Level 1 to Level 2, which changes what it is permitted to treat.
readings.insight:
The jump from Level 1 to Level 2 matters more than the beds. Level is what determines the services a hospital may offer — a Level 2 facility is required to have specialty care and intensive care that a Level 1 is not.

For a province reachable only by sea or air, that is the difference between treating a patient and moving them. Tawi-Tawi's 482,645 people are nearer to Sabah than to the regional capital, and the cost of a referral is borne by families who often cannot meet it.

This is one of 4 hospital bills in this batch and the only one that raises a facility's level rather than only its bed count.

readings.whatItDoes:
Raises the authorised bed capacity of the Wao District Hospital, in Wao, Lanao del Sur, from 50 beds to 100.

It cites Section 22, Article IX of Republic Act No. 11054 — the Organic Law provision on health — as the authority, and requires the hospital to meet the standards the Ministry of Health prescribes.
readings.whyProposed:
Wao sits at the far south-eastern corner of Lanao del Sur, on the boundary with Bukidnon and Cotabato, a long way from Marawi and from the province's other hospitals.

A district hospital in that position is the only facility within reach for its catchment, which is the standard case for raising capacity rather than building elsewhere.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Wao and the surrounding municipalities at the edge of Lanao del Sur.
The Ministry of Health, which sets the standards the upgraded hospital must meet.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: The cost is to be charged against the current year's appropriations; no amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: The hospital's authorised capacity doubles, from 50 beds to 100.
readings.insight:
This bill does the thing 2 others in this registry did not. It states the hospital's current authorised capacity as 50 beds and raises it to 100, and the figure it starts from is the figure the hospital actually holds.

Bill 264 proposed raising Siasi District Hospital from 25 beds when Republic Act No. 7195 had set it at 50 in 1992. Bill 350 proposed raising the Montañer hospital from 25 when its own explanatory note said a national law had authorised 100 in 2022. Both were drafted as though the earlier law had not happened.

Wao's bill cites the Organic Law as its authority and names a starting figure nothing contradicts. Checking the other hospital bills in this batch for the same defect turned up none — so what looked like a pattern across the region's hospital legislation is 2 bills, not a habit.

readings.whatItDoes:
Creates a Bangsamoro Identification System — a regional ID — to be established by the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government together with the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology office.

The stated purpose is a reliable and secure means of identification for Bangsamoro citizens, to promote good governance and to make access to government services easier, including health, livelihood and social benefits.
readings.whyProposed:
Section 2 ties it to service delivery: the policy is equitable access to basic services such as health, education and social welfare, and an ID system is presented as the means of reaching them.

The practical case is that people in the region are often unable to prove who they are to the satisfaction of an agency — a problem that falls hardest on those with the least contact with the state and the greatest need of it.
whoIsAffected: Anyone in the region who cannot currently prove their identity to a government office.
Ministries delivering health, livelihood and social benefits.
MILG and the Bangsamoro ICT office, which would build and run it.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology office

funding.detail: The title provides for funds. No amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: A regional identification system exists, run by MILG with the region's ICT office.
readings.insight:
An identification system is a register of people, and a register of people is the most sensitive thing a government builds. The bill as filed states what the system is for and who builds it.

What the copy read does not establish is the part that decides whether it is safe: what data is collected, who may query it, how long records are kept, what happens to them when someone dies or leaves, and what a person can do if the record about them is wrong. Those are the provisions a reader should look for, and this reading cannot say whether they are in the full text.

The Philippine national ID system under Republic Act No. 11055 already covers residents of the region, so a second register raises a question the bill does not answer in what was read: what this one does that the national one does not, and whether a person has to be in both.

readings.whatItDoes:
Renames the Buluan District Hospital, in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur, as the Maguindanao del Sur Provincial Hospital.

The cost — signage, administrative adjustments — is charged against the Ministry of Health's appropriations, and the hospital's continued operation and maintenance under the new name goes into the annual appropriations act.
readings.whyProposed:
Section 2 gives the rationale in the Act itself: the new name reflects the hospital's expanded role and its commitment to serving the entire province, and acknowledges the administrative and geographical reconfigurations that created the province.

Maguindanao was divided into del Norte and del Sur in 2022. A district hospital named after one municipality became the principal hospital of a province that did not exist when it was named.
whoIsAffected: The 813,243 people of Maguindanao del Sur, on the 2024 census.
The hospital's staff and patients.
The Ministry of Health, which carries the cost.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: Charged against the Ministry of Health's appropriations, with continuing operation and maintenance to be carried in the annual General Appropriations Act. No amount is stated.

whatChanges: The hospital is renamed to match the province it now serves.
readings.insight:
This is the division of Maguindanao working its way through the region's institutions 3 years after the fact.

The province of Maguindanao del Sur was ratified in 2022. Its hospital still carries the name of the municipality it sits in, which was accurate when it was a district hospital in an undivided province and is not now. The same reconfiguration is visible in the parliamentary districting bills, which reapportion seats across del Norte and del Sur as separate provinces, and in the local government directory, which lists them separately with their own figures.

A renaming bill is the smallest of those adjustments and the easiest to overlook. It is also the one that changes what is written on the building people actually go to.

readings.whatItDoes:
Institutionalises the Panglima Sugala Community Hospital in Panglima Sugala, Tawi-Tawi, as a 10-bed infirmary hospital under the Ministry of Health.

It also provides for the hospital's services, facilities and bed capacity to be increased as warranted.
readings.whyProposed:
Panglima Sugala is a municipality of Tawi-Tawi, in the island group furthest from the regional capital. The hospital exists; what it lacks is a legal basis of its own, which is what determines whether it gets a plantilla, a budget line and a place in the Ministry's own structure.

Institutionalising an existing facility is a different act from building one: it converts something being run to something being funded.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Panglima Sugala and the nearby islands.
The hospital's existing staff, whose positions would be regularised under the Ministry.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: An existing community hospital gains a statutory basis as a 10-bed infirmary under the Ministry of Health.
Its capacity may be raised later without a fresh Act.
readings.insight:
10 beds is the smallest facility in this batch by a wide margin — against 50 for the new hospital in the Special Geographic Area and 200 for Bongao and for the proposed children's hospital in Cotabato City.

That is not a measure of ambition. An infirmary in an island municipality is the only health facility within a boat ride for the people it serves, and the point of this bill is not its size but its status: a hospital run without a statute is a hospital that can be defunded without repealing anything.

The provision allowing its capacity to be raised as warranted is what keeps it from needing to come back to Parliament to grow — which, on the evidence of the other hospital bills here, is a journey that takes years.

readings.whatItDoes:
Removes the "None of the Above" option from the ballot in Bangsamoro elections, by deleting that clause from Section 14, Article VII of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 35, the Bangsamoro Electoral Code of 2023.

The amended section leaves the ballot carrying the candidates' names and their photographs or logos, and keeps COMELEC's duty, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, to make sure voters know who is running.

Section 2 orders the immediate revision of the ballots for the 13 October 2025 parliamentary elections so that none of them carries the option.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 87 on 28 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note sets out a specific failure. Under BAA 35 as enacted, if the NOTA or abstain vote took the majority, the candidate placing second would be proclaimed the winner.

The note says COMELEC urged Parliament to amend the provision, and that proclaiming a second-place candidate is constitutionally impermissible — citing the Supreme Court in Datu Pax Ali Mangudadatu v. Commission on Elections, G.R. Nos. 260219 and 260231, June 2025.

The consequence it warns of is concrete: left unamended, the provision risked seats going unfilled in the region's first parliamentary elections.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the 13 October 2025 parliamentary elections, whose ballot changes.
Candidates, who can no longer lose a seat to an abstention count.
COMELEC and the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which had to reprint ballots.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office — revision of the official ballots

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. The cost of revising and reprinting ballots falls to COMELEC.

whatChanges: The NOTA option is deleted from the Bangsamoro ballot.
Ballots for the October 2025 elections had to be revised before the vote.
A seat can no longer be won by the second-placed candidate because abstentions outnumbered the leader.
readings.insight:
This is the Electoral Code's own design being withdrawn 2 years after it was passed, and the reason given is that it could not lawfully be made to work.

The NOTA provision was in BAA 35 as ratified on 8 March 2023. The defect was not that voters might reject every candidate — it was what the Code said should happen next: the runner-up takes the seat. The explanatory note's position, attributed to the Supreme Court, is that a second-placer cannot be proclaimed at all, which leaves the provision with no lawful outcome and a live risk of empty seats at the region's first election.
