So the option went rather than the consequence. Nothing in the bill replaces it with a different answer to a majority rejecting the field — a runoff, a fresh election, a vacancy. The ballot simply stops asking.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes a children's hospital in Cotabato City, authorised to operate at 200 beds, dedicated to children's care and under the Ministry of Health.

The Act requires a development plan covering the hospital's goals, its bed capacity and its services, and the explanatory note says the design allows for expansion and new wings.
readings.whyProposed:
The region has no hospital dedicated to children. Paediatric cases are handled in general hospitals alongside adults, by staff whose training is not specific to them.

Cotabato City is the regional centre and the most reachable point for the mainland provinces, which is the case for putting it there.
whoIsAffected: Children across the region, and the families who currently travel for paediatric care.
General hospitals, which carry paediatric load now.
The Ministry of Health, which would operate it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed.

whatChanges: A 200-bed children's hospital is established in Cotabato City.
A development plan is required, stating capacity and services.
readings.insight:
200 beds would make this the joint-largest facility proposed in this batch, alongside the Bongao upgrade, and the only one in the region dedicated to a single group of patients.

The explanatory note is written in a register unusual for a filed bill — it describes a building "where every corridor" carries a purpose, and asks its own question about whether 200 beds will be enough before answering that the plan allows for expansion.

What the copy read does not establish is the catchment the figure was drawn from. A children's hospital in Cotabato City would serve a region whose population the Parliament's own bills state variously as 3,944,692 and 4,545,486, depending on which census the drafter used — and roughly a third of that population is under 15. Neither the bill nor its note says which number 200 beds was sized against.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Parliamentary Districts Act of 2025 — one of 2 bills under that exact title.

It apportions the region into 32 single-member parliamentary districts on population and geographical area, each as far as practicable contiguous, compact and adjacent, and each with a population of at least 100,000.

Its schedule uses the 2024 census: Basilan 541,947, Lanao del Sur 1,368,137, Maguindanao del Norte 741,428, Maguindanao del Sur 813,243, Tawi-Tawi 482,645, Cotabato City 383,383 and the Special Geographic Area 214,703.

It was filed on 28 October 2025 by MP Mohammad S. Yacob with some 30 other members and co-authors. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
Section 2 declares the policy as equitable representation of the region's constituents in the apportionment of parliamentary districts.

The occasion is the one 3 other bills in this registry address: Sulu's exclusion from the region left seats apportioned to a province no longer in it, and the map had to be settled before the first parliamentary election.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region.
Candidates for the 32 district seats.
COMELEC.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee; the measure that became law on the same subject is Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86.
readings.insight:
This bill and Bill 415 carry the same short title, the same declaration of policy, the same criteria including the 100,000 floor, the same 32 districts, and the same 7 province populations — 541,947, 1,368,137, 741,428, 813,243, 482,645, 383,383 and 214,703, the 2024 census, summing to 4,545,486 in both.

They are not the same bill. This one was filed on 28 October 2025 by MP Mohammad S. Yacob, with around 30 members as authors and co-authors — among them MP Mohagher Iqbal and DFL Atty. Raissa Jajurie. Bill 415 was filed 13 days later, on 10 November, by MP Naguib G. Sinarimbo with 9 others. Bill 415 passed and became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86 on 12 January 2026. This one has not moved out of committee.

So the earlier bill, with 3 times the signatures, stopped; the later one with the same text became law. The registry records both and nothing in either document explains the relationship between them.

With Bills 347 and 351 that makes 4 measures redrawing the same 32 districts inside a single year, 2 counting the region at 3,944,692 and 2 at 4,545,486.

readings.whatItDoes:
The region's budget for 2026: ₱114,077,644,141.90 for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government from 1 January to 31 December 2026.

Section 1 names the sources — the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, collections on regional taxes, fees and charges, and unutilized prior years' appropriations.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 85, the FY 2026 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, with the total unchanged.
readings.whyProposed: An annual appropriations bill carries no explanatory note. Its argument is the allocation.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and special purpose fund of the Bangsamoro Government.
Constituent local government units receiving shares and support funds.
Suppliers and contractors to the regional government.
Members of Parliament, whose own constituency funds are line items in it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management — release, guidelines and the cash budgeting system
Every ministry and office named in the expenditure program

funding.detail: ₱114,077,644,141.90 for fiscal year 2026, from the annual block grant, other National Government subsidies, the region's share of national taxes collected in its territory, regional collections, and unutilized prior years' appropriations.

whatChanges: The region's 2026 operations are funded at ₱114.08 billion, the largest appropriation in its history.
₱800,000,000 is set aside for a Parliament Building.
₱480,000,000 goes to the Constituency Servicing Program, at ₱6,000,000 per Member of Parliament.
readings.insight:
The figure in Section 1 and the figure in the enacted act agree to the centavo — ₱114,077,644,141.90 filed, ₱114,077,644,141.90 in BAA 85. Parliament moved money within the budget and did not change its size.

The trajectory is the story. FY 2024 was ₱98.47 billion, FY 2025 fell to ₱94.41 billion, and FY 2026 rises to ₱114.08 billion — a drop of ₱4.06 billion followed by a jump of ₱19.67 billion, almost 21% in a single year.

4 of Parliament's own lines are stated outright: ₱480,000,000 for constituency servicing at ₱6,000,000 per member, ₱20,000,000 for a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum, ₱40,000,000 for a Parliament Learning Program, and ₱800,000,000 for a Parliament Building. The first of those divides to exactly 80 members — ₱480,000,000 at ₱6,000,000 each — and 80 is what the Electoral Code's own composition rule produces: BAA 35 sets Parliament at 50% party representatives and fixes their number at 40, which puts the chamber at 80, of which 40% is the 32 district seats the redistricting bills draw. The budget line, the Code and the district map all agree.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 410 as filed, the FY 2026 Bangsamoro Expenditure Program

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Parliamentary Districts Act of 2025. It apportions the region into 32 single-member parliamentary districts.

Section 3 sets the criteria: districts are apportioned on population and geographical area, each as far as practicable contiguous, compact and adjacent, and each with a population of at least 100,000.

The schedule gives a regional population of 4,545,486 and divides it 4 ways to Basilan, 9 to Lanao del Sur, 5 each to the 2 Maguindanaos, 4 to Tawi-Tawi, 3 to Cotabato City and 2 to the Special Geographic Area.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86 on 12 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed:
The declared policy in Section 2 is equitable representation of the region's inhabitants in the apportionment of parliamentary districts.

The occasion is the same as for Bills 347 and 351: the region's districts had to be settled before it could elect a parliament, and Sulu's exclusion had unsettled them.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region.
Candidates for the 32 district seats.
COMELEC.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament
whatChanges: 32 single-member districts are created, with a minimum population of 100,000 each.
The apportionment is stated against a regional population of 4,545,486.
readings.insight:
This bill counts the region at 4,545,486 and the schedule adds up to exactly that. Every province figure in it is the 2024 census to the person.

Bill 351, apportioning the same 32 districts earlier the same year, counts the region at 3,944,692 — the 2020 census, also to the person. Neither bill says which census it is using; only Bill 347, the earliest of the 3, labels its column.

600,000 people appear between one bill and the next, and the seat allocation does not move: 4, 9, 5, 5, 4, 3, 2 in both. On these figures the 100,000-per-district floor in Section 3 is comfortably met everywhere, so the newer count changes nothing about who gets what. It is worth knowing anyway, because the 2 bills cannot both be describing the region as it stands, and a reader comparing them has nothing in either document to tell them which is current.

readings.whatItDoes:
Amends the Bangsamoro Electoral Code, BAA 35, in several places at once. It was enacted, with changes, as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 88 on 28 January 2026.

As filed it lowers the share of the vote a regional political party needs before it can take any seats, from 4% to 2%, in both of the sections that carry the threshold — Section 9 on party representatives and Section 12(a) on how the seats are allocated. The act as signed sets it at 2.5%.

It changes what it takes to form a party: at least 5,000 resident registered voters, distributed across the region, with provincial and city chapters in every province and city and municipal chapters in a majority of the municipalities of each province.

As filed it also lowers the share of a party's nominees who must be women, from 30% to 20%. That change was not adopted. Section 3 of the enacted act keeps the requirement at 30% and expressly retains it.

It repeals the third paragraph of Section 17, sets out a process of certification, and revokes all certifications previously issued.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes one argument: that a high electoral threshold stifles political diversity and keeps smaller, community-rooted parties out of Parliament, and that lowering it lets the composition of the Parliament reflect voter preferences more fully.

It also argues that a regional party should be an organic institution grown from its communities rather than a name on a ballot, which is the case for the chapter requirements.

The note does not mention the change to the women's nomination requirement.
whoIsAffected: Smaller regional political parties, which can now win seats on 2% of the vote instead of 4%.
Women seeking nomination: the guaranteed share of a party's nominees falls from 30% to 20%.
Anyone forming a party, who must now show 5,000 members and a chapter structure across the region.
Parties already certified, whose certifications are revoked and must be sought again.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections — registration, certification and seat allocation
Bangsamoro Electoral Office
whatChanges: The party-representation threshold falls from 4% to 2.5% of the valid votes cast — the bill asked for 2%.
The minimum share of women among a party's nominees stays at 30%: the bill proposed 20% and Parliament did not adopt it.
A party needs at least 5,000 members and chapters in every province and city, plus a majority of municipalities in each province.
All previously issued certifications are revoked and must be sought again.
readings.insight:
2 thresholds move in this bill and the explanatory note argues for one of them.

The case it makes is for lowering the party threshold from 4% to 2%, so that smaller parties can win representation. That is what the note is about from first line to last. The same bill also amends Section 9(b) of the Electoral Code so that parties must ensure at least 20% of their nominees are women, where BAA 35 as ratified requires 30%. The note does not mention it.

The 30% was not incidental to the Code. When BAA 35 passed on 8 March 2023 by 64 votes to none, MP Alih cited the 30% women requirement in party representation as an example of asymmetry made real — a system built for the region rather than copied from the national one. MP Basman argued the Code cemented women's participation in practical terms. MP Alamia and MP Maglangit both voted for it while putting on record that they wanted women's representation to go further than the Code provided.

Parliament did not take the cut. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 88, signed on 28 January 2026, keeps the figure at 30% and says so expressly, and it settles the party threshold at 2.5% rather than the 2% the bill asked for. Both numbers in the enacted act sit where the chamber put them, not where the bill did — which is the clearest illustration in this registry of why a bill and the act it becomes have to be read as 2 different documents.

readFrom.label: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 35, enacted text — the figures this bill amends
Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 88, enacted text — what Parliament actually passed

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area — Kadayangan, Kapalawan, Ligawasan, Malidegao, Nabalawag, Old Kaabakan, Pahamuddin and Tugunan — and treats them as one development and administrative area rather than 8 separate towns, under the direct supervision of the Chief Minister. The body that runs it, the Special Geographic Area Development Authority, already existed in interim form under the Bangsamoro Administrative Code; this gives it a governing board, a staff structure, defined powers, and money of its own.

The logic of the thing is in its definition of "SGA-wide services": services whose impact crosses town boundaries, or that cost so much no single municipality could provide them. 5 are named — development planning; flood control and sewerage; rural, zoning and land use planning and shelter; health and sanitation, environmental protection and pollution control; and public safety, including disaster preparedness and relief for floods, fires and earthquakes. A sixth is open-ended: anything else the Chief Minister may delegate pursuant to a law.

The money is the part that carries furthest. Section 10 authorises ₱500 million for initial operation, then hands the Authority a fixed 5% of all revenue the Bangsamoro Government collects, every year, on top of whatever the annual appropriations act gives it. It may also levy fines and charge fees for services it renders.
readings.whyProposed: The bill's own policy section makes the argument: the Special Geographic Area needs to be treated as a special development and administrative area, and certain basic services affecting it are more efficiently planned, supervised and coordinated area-wide than town by town. These are the 8 municipalities constituted after the 2019 plebiscite in which 63 barangays of North Cotabato voted to join the Bangsamoro — new units, sharing a marshland basin, with problems that stop at no boundary. An interim Authority was already operating; this puts it on a permanent footing and funds it.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 8 SGA municipalities, for whom flood control, drainage, land use, shelter, health and sanitation, and disaster response become one authority's responsibility rather than 8.

The mayors and councils of those municipalities, whose autonomy over purely local matters is expressly preserved twice in the text, and whose consent SGADA needs before it delivers basic services in their town — but whose development plans must now fit SGADA's master plan.
Employees of the interim SGADA, who keep their duties, salaries and allowances until formally notified of a change, and who are owed 1¼ month's salary for every year of service if displaced.
Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies, whose strategic plans for the area are framed by SGADA's master plan and whose plans route through the planning authority for integration.
Every Bangsamoro taxpayer, because the 5% annual share is drawn from region-wide revenue while the services are delivered in 8 municipalities.
implementedBy: Special Geographic Area Development Authority (SGADA), under the direct supervision of the Chief Minister

The Special Geographic Area Board — the SGADA Chairperson, the Minister of the Interior and Local Government, the Minister of Finance and Budget and Management, the Bangsamoro Director General of BPDA, and the President of the SGA League of Mayors
An Executive Director and 3 Deputy Executive Directors for finance and administration, planning, and operations, all appointed by the Chief Minister
The 8 component local government units, which carry out much of the implementation
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, which integrates SGADA's plans into the Bangsamoro Development Plan
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, and the Commission on Audit, over the transfer of the interim body's assets and liabilities

funding.detail: ₱500,000,000 authorised for initial operation, with annual expenditures and capital outlays thereafter provided in the General Appropriations Act. On top of that the Authority takes a fixed 5% annually of all revenue collection of the Bangsamoro Government, and is empowered to levy fines and impose fees and charges for services rendered. The 5% share is the unusual term: it is a standing claim on regional revenue rather than a sum voted each year, and the text sets no ceiling and no expiry on it.

whatChanges: The 8 SGA municipalities become a single special development and administrative area under the Chief Minister's direct supervision.
The interim Authority becomes a permanent one with a governing board, an Executive Director, 3 deputies and a staffing pattern.
Area-wide flood control, land use, shelter, health and sanitation, pollution control and disaster response acquire one accountable office.
SGADA's master plan becomes the framework that both Bangsamoro ministry plans and the 8 LGU development plans must fit.
The Authority gains ₱500 million to start and a standing 5% of annual Bangsamoro revenue thereafter.
The Authority may contract, enter memoranda of agreement, and deal directly with foreign assistance agencies for grants and financing.
Local autonomy over purely local matters is preserved in terms, and SGADA needs an LGU's consent before delivering basic services there.
readings.insight:
3 things are worth watching, and none of them is the stated purpose.

The first is the 5%. Almost every other appropriation in the registry is a sum voted for a purpose; this is a permanent slice of regional revenue assigned to one authority serving 8 of the region's municipalities, with no ceiling and no sunset in the filed text. Whether that is proportionate is a political question, but it is the provision that will still be doing work in 10 years.

The second is who wrote it. Parliament's own member profile records the principal author, MP Butch P. Malang, as Administrator of the Special Geographic Area and Development Authority since 2022 — the body this bill expands, staffs and funds. The rulebook requires a member to take no part in proceedings on a measure where they hold a conflict of interest or stand to gain or lose financially. Whether that rule was engaged here is not something this registry can determine, and nothing in the published record suggests it was raised; the fact is stated because a reader weighing the bill deserves to know it.

The third is the paperwork. Parliament's index carries this enactment twice — as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 93 and again as No. 94, same title, same ratification date of 16 July 2026, both tracing back to Bill 431. The bill's own history line on the index closes with 'BAA No. 93', which points to 93 as the operative number and 94 as an indexing artefact. Anyone citing it should quote the date and the title as well as a number.

There is a fourth thing, and it is the reason this reading is of the bill rather than the law. Parliament has not published the signed text of this enactment. Its act pages carry no attachment, and the same is true of the 2 other acts ratified alongside it (BAA 92 and 94) — the 3 most recent acts on the index are all text-less as of this capture. So the filed bill is currently the only readable version of this law.

One drafting note on top of that: the filed copy runs Section 8 straight into Section 10. There is no Section 9.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 431, copy as filed, received 19 January 2026

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Da'wah Activities Act of 2026. It establishes a Bangsamoro Da'wah Center and creates a Bangsamoro Da'wah Council to oversee it.

The Act defines Da'wah as activities aimed at capacitating individuals in ethical communication and in cultural and values-based education consistent with Bangsamoro identity, and Da'wah workers as the people trained to carry them out.

It provides for the Center to be established progressively, sets qualifications for its trainers, and makes rules for the management of endowments intended for the welfare of Bangsamoro communities.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy cites Section 20, Article X of the 1987 Constitution and the Organic Law, and states the Bangsamoro Government's policy of promoting moral, cultural and social development anchored on the values, traditions and identity of the Bangsamoro people.

2 aims are named: developing competent and well-equipped Da'wah workers, and ensuring that endowments meant for the welfare of Bangsamoro communities are managed with transparency and accountability.
whoIsAffected: Da'wah workers, who gain a training institution and a qualification standard.
Communities that are the beneficiaries of endowments the Act brings under management rules.
Donors to those endowments.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Da'wah Center — the implementing body
Bangsamoro Da'wah Council — oversight, powers and functions under Section 7

funding.detail: Section 12 appropriates the amount necessary for initial implementation; no figure is stated in the text read.

whatChanges: A Da'wah Center and Council exist in regional law.
Endowments intended for community welfare come under stated management rules.
Trainers must meet qualifications set by the Act.
readings.insight:
The endowment provisions are the part with the widest reach. Religious endowments in the region have historically been held and administered informally, and a statute that sets rules for their management — and says plainly that the purpose is transparency and accountability — reaches further than the training program the Act is named for.

What the bill as read does not do is say who may inspect those accounts, or whether anything about them is published. The Act asks for transparency in the management of the funds; it does not make the funds transparent to anyone outside the Council.

readings.whatItDoes:
A supplemental appropriation for 2026, drawn out of unutilized prior years' appropriations held in the Bangsamoro Treasury.

It was enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 91, the FY 2026 Supplemental Appropriations Act, at ₱16,830,171,595 — releasable and obligable until 30 June 2028.

The 15 sections are the same general provisions the 2024 supplemental carried: releases by Special Allotment Release Order, caps on engineering and administrative overhead and on administrative costs, a certification of available funds before any obligation, the cash budgeting system, infrastructure project disclosure, and accountability reports.
readings.whyProposed: A supplemental bill with no explanatory note. The source clause is the case: appropriations from earlier years that went unspent are made available again rather than left idle in the Treasury.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry, office and agency receiving a supplemental allocation.
Contractors and suppliers on projects funded by it.
The Commission on Audit, whose findings ministries must report on within 60 days.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Every ministry, office and agency in the schedule
Commission on Audit

funding.detail: ₱16,830,171,595 as enacted in BAA 91, entirely out of unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, releasable and obligable until 30 June 2028. The bill as published online states no figure.

whatChanges: ₱16.83 billion of previously unspent appropriation is made available again, with a window running to mid-2028.
It is the largest of the region's 3 supplementals — twice the 2024 figure.
readings.insight:
3 days. Filed on 18 May 2026, referred to the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management on 19 May, and on 20 May the committee report was adopted and the bill passed second and third reading in the same sitting. ₱16.83 billion, from filing to final passage, inside a working week.

The document the Parliament publishes for it does not say so. As with the 2024 supplemental, Section 1 reads "the amounts set forth in this section are hereby appropriated" and the schedule the colon promises is not in the file — 14 sections of general provisions follow and the only figures anywhere are 2 references to a ₱1 million threshold. Unlike the 2024 file, which is named as the general provisions and so tells a reader it is a part, nothing here signals that anything is missing.

So the one document a citizen can reach from this bill's own page gives the conditions attached to ₱16.83 billion and not the amount, not the recipients, and not a single line of what it buys. For that they have to find the enacted act.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 470 as published — general provisions, no schedule

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Tawi-Tawi Maritime School, located somewhere in the province of Tawi-Tawi, under the supervision and control of the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, working with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and the maritime authorities.

The school would offer 2 degree programs, the Bachelor of Science in Marine Transportation and the Bachelor of Science in Marine Engineering, and certificate and short courses in basic safety training, the seafarers rating course, fishery technology, and vessel operations and maintenance. It is headed by a Director appointed by MBHTE. Instructors must hold a MARINA certificate of competency, have maritime experience, and hold a bachelor's degree in maritime education or a related field, meeting CHED and MARINA standards. Non-teaching staff are listed down to the librarian and maintenance personnel, hired under Civil Service rules.

The whole bill runs to 14 sections over 3 pages. MBHTE writes the implementing rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 16 April 2025 by MP John Anthony L. Lim, read on first reading on 22 April 2025 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 27 May 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The declaration of policy in Section 2 is the only statement of purpose: to promote maritime education and training, especially in the island provinces, to support the maritime industry, and to improve the economic condition of the people of Tawi-Tawi and neighbouring island communities.
whoIsAffected: Young people in Tawi-Tawi and neighbouring islands who want to become deck officers, marine engineers or rated seafarers without leaving the province.
Fisherfolk and boat operators, who could take short courses in fishery technology and vessel maintenance.
MBHTE, which would run a degree-granting maritime school directly.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, in coordination
Commission on Higher Education and Maritime Industry Authority, as standard-setters

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 8 puts the cost of establishing and running the school into the annual Bangsamoro budget under MBHTE, with grants, donations and the school's own income as additional sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, Tawi-Tawi gets a public maritime school offering 2 bachelor's degrees and short courses.
MBHTE becomes responsible for staffing it, setting its policies and monitoring it against educational and maritime standards.
readings.insight:
The filed copy names a single author, MP John Anthony L. Lim, and is signed by him alone. Parliament's bills index credits the bill to 18 principal authors and 23 co-authors, 41 members in all. None of the other 40 names appears on the document.

The bill does not say where in Tawi-Tawi the school would sit, what it would cost, or how a school under a ministry would be authorised to grant degrees regulated by CHED and MARINA beyond saying it will meet their standards. Those are the questions a committee would have to settle, and the index records no movement since the referral of 27 May 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Motorcycles-For-Hire Act. It brings habal-habal and motorcycle taxis, including those booked through apps, into the law: every motorcycle carrying passengers or goods for hire in the region would be recognised as a common carrier, owing passengers extraordinary diligence and presumed negligent when a passenger or third party is killed or injured. App-based transportation network companies carry the same liability.

Every motorcycle-for-hire must register with the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, which sets vehicle standards and may require brackets, top boxes, luggage carriers and speed limiters or monitoring devices. Where an app company operates, franchises are issued by the Bangsamoro Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board, which may allow an operator to sign up with multiple apps. Where none operates, the town issues the franchise, the motorcycle may only run inside that town, and the town decides how many units to allow. No franchise is issued without insurance for death or injury to rider, passenger or third parties.

Riders need a professional driver's licence under MOTC guidelines, must attend recurring safety and road courtesy training, and must wear helmets along with their passengers. Riders who are not already covered by labour law get a written contract, just compensation, safe working conditions, the right to organise and negotiate, and social protection benefits under an arrangement with the operator or app company. The Ministry of Labor and Employment writes the rules on contracts and keeps a registry of riders, operators and app companies.

It was filed on 23 April 2025 by MP Romeo K. Sema, read on first reading on 20 May 2025 and referred to the Committee on Transportation and Communications on 17 June 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says motorcycles-for-hire are often the most practical transport in both growing towns and remote places, cites a WR Numero study that 45% of Filipinos use habal-habal, 14% regularly, and argues that the trade is a main livelihood for young and low-skilled workers who have no health insurance, accident benefits or retirement security.

It grounds the bill in Section 38 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which lets the Bangsamoro Government grant regional franchises for land transport, and reads the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code as requiring MOTC guidelines before towns can regulate small public vehicles.
whoIsAffected: Habal-habal and motor taxi riders, who would need a professional licence and training but gain a contract and benefits.
Operators, who must register, insure and franchise each unit.
App-based ride and delivery companies operating in the region, which become liable as common carriers.
Passengers, who gain insurance coverage and a carrier's legal duty of care.
implementedBy: Ministry of Transportation and Communications
Bangsamoro Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board
Ministry of Labor and Employment
Local government units, where no app company operates

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. Costs fall on operators through registration, franchising and insurance, and on the ministries' existing budgets.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, motorcycle taxis become a legal, franchised mode of public transport in the region.
Every unit would need registration, a franchise and insurance, and every rider a professional licence.
Riders outside the Labor Code gain written contracts, the right to organise and social protection.
readings.insight:
The note's legal footing is cited to the wrong document. Footnote 5 sources Section 480 of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code to "Parliament Bill No. 58". The Local Governance Code was Bill 30, enacted as BAA 49 on 28 September 2023. Bill 58 is MP Sema's own Magna Carta for Workers in the Informal Economy, which has sat at first reading since 17 October 2022. The quoted provision also covers tricycles and non-motorised bancas, not motorcycles, which is the note's own point: the gap is what the bill is meant to fill.

2 section headings in the copy filed are swapped. "Statutory Benefits of Riders" sits above the sections on registration, standards and franchising, and "Regulation of Motorcycles-for-Hires" sits above the rights of riders. Section 7 also has vehicle standards recommended by a "Ministry of Tourism, Investment and Trade", where the regional ministry is the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism.

Section 14 refers to the Bangsamoro Labor and Employment Code as if it existed. When this bill was filed it was still Bill 59, also principal-authored by MP Sema. It was passed as BAA 82 on 12 November 2025, so the reference now points at a real law. This bill itself waited more than a year between first reading and its committee referral.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Integrated Bangsamoro Greening Program Act of 2025. It sets up a region-wide reforestation and land restoration program run by the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, aimed first at denuded forestland, then production and protection forests, mangroves and coastal greenbelts, ancestral domains with free, prior and informed consent, civil and military reservations, urban greening sites, watersheds, ecoparks, and areas identified in the normalization and decommissioning process.

It creates 3 bodies: a Technical Steering Committee chaired by MENRE with MAFAR and MILG as co-chairs, a Greening Technical Secretariat in MENRE's Forest Management Services Office, and an Inter-Ministerial Oversight Board of COA, BPDA and accredited civil society that holds annual public hearings and reports to Parliament. It declares an annual tree-growing festival, BARMMULA, on the first Friday of June.

Decommissioned MILF and MNLF combatants run through the bill: they sit on the steering committee, are deployed as nursery and forest protection workers, are prioritised for the family-based greening model, and may be offered site development contracts. There is a buy-back scheme for farm and forest produce with price ceilings and COA audits, scholarships from the Ministry of Science and Technology for participants' children, a 10-year strategic plan reviewed every 3 years, independent audits every 3 years, an annual State of the Forests report, and an optional Greening Trust Fund.

It was filed on 4 June 2025 by MP Alindatu K. Pagayao, read on first reading on 10 November 2025 and referred to the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 30 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 sets out the reasoning: sustainable forest management is treated as a strategy for ecological resilience and for peace, forestlands are called environmental and socio-political assets in areas affected by conflict, and the program is to support the reintegration of decommissioned combatants.
whoIsAffected: Communities near denuded forests, mangroves and watersheds, which would organise into greening committees and manage sites.
Decommissioned MILF and MNLF combatants and their communities, given priority as workers, contractors and beneficiaries.
Children of program participants, eligible for science scholarships with a return-service obligation.
Indigenous peoples, whose ancestral domains are covered only with free, prior and informed consent.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, as co-chairs
Inter-Ministerial Oversight Board of COA, BPDA and accredited civil society

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 15 charges the first year to MENRE's existing budget and later years to the regular appropriations of the ministries concerned, with official development assistance, climate finance, public-private partnerships and corporate social responsibility as further sources. Section 16 lets MENRE set up a Greening Trust Fund.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region has a statutory greening program with its own committee, secretariat and oversight board.
A phased plan must be ready within 60 days and implementing rules within 60 days.
The first Friday of June becomes the BARMMULA tree-growing festival.
MENRE must publish an annual State of the Forests report.
readings.insight:
The title says the bill appropriates funds, and it does not. Section 15 charges the program to whatever MENRE already has "as appropriated" and pushes later years into regular ministry budgets. No figure appears anywhere in the 20 sections, so the scale of the program is left entirely to future budgets.

Some of the detail reads as carried over from elsewhere. Section 10 reports results against the Bangsamoro Development Plan and the "Global Development Goals", where the usual name is the Sustainable Development Goals. The scholarship clause, attached to a greening program, lists mining engineering and geology among the priority courses. The closing line reads "Adopted", the word used for resolutions, rather than "Approved".

The bill sat for more than 5 months between filing on 4 June 2025 and first reading on 10 November 2025. A narrower earlier measure, Bill 244 requiring 4Ps beneficiaries to plant fruit-bearing trees, has been at first reading since 19 September 2023.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Right-of-Way Indemnity Act of 2025. It requires every regional infrastructure project, whatever its funding source or implementing agency, to include payment to affected property owners in its approved program of work, so that the cost of land is budgeted with the project instead of being settled afterwards.

It adopts the modes of acquisition in the national Right-of-Way Act, Republic Act No. 10752: donation, negotiated sale, expropriation or any other lawful mode. For a negotiated sale, Section 7 sets the offer: on agricultural land, the current market value of crops and trees; for new right-of-way sites, the current market value or the zonal value of the land, whichever is lower. Where a road right-of-way is already part of a subdivision or development plan, nothing more is paid.

The Ministry of Public Works reports to Parliament within 1 year and every year after on funds paid and properties compensated, writes the rules within 90 days, and every 5 years the Chief Minister convenes an independent panel to review the law. Transactions with a signed compensation agreement before the law takes effect are excluded.

It was filed on 13 June 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, read on first reading on 18 June 2025 and referred to the Committee on Public Works and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 20 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note starts from the constitutional rule that private property may not be taken for public use without just compensation, and argues that slow payment is what stalls projects. It cites BPDA figures that more than 60% of infrastructure projects scheduled for 2021 to 2023 were delayed, with right-of-way among the top 3 causes, a 2022 Ministry of Public Works review finding at least ₱1.2 billion of projects delayed by unresolved claims, and a 2023 field assessment in which over 70% of affected landowners in Maguindanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur were hesitant to allow access because of uncertain payment timelines.

The note says the bill is patterned on House Bill No. 183 of the 19th Congress.
whoIsAffected: Landowners whose property is needed for regional roads, bridges, power lines, water systems and public buildings.
Farmers on agricultural land, compensated for crops and trees.
Every ministry, office, government corporation and state college that builds regional infrastructure.
Contractors and communities waiting on stalled projects.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works
Every Bangsamoro implementing agency for infrastructure
Office of the Chief Minister, for the 5-year review

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 puts the cost in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, and Section 5 requires each project's indemnity to be costed in its program of work.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, no regional infrastructure project could be approved without right-of-way payment in its program of work.
Offers for new sites would be capped at the lower of market value and zonal value.
Parliament would receive an annual account of indemnity paid and properties affected.
readings.insight:
The note and the text pull in different directions on price. The note says just compensation means "not only the fair market value of the property but also prompt payment". Section 7 offers market value or zonal value, whichever is lower, which by construction can only be equal to market value or below it. Section 8 then preserves the owner's right to just compensation under the Constitution, so an owner offered less can still go to court, which is the delay the bill sets out to avoid.

Section 7 also pays for land, crops and trees, and nothing else. Section 3 defines the property affected as the land, the structures and improvements on it, and the crops and trees. Houses and other structures are in the definition and missing from the offer.

The note itself is unsure what is being bought. It says indemnity "does not transfer ownership" and is compensation solely for use, then the bill provides for acquisition by sale and expropriation, which do.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BARMM Special Education and Development Act. It requires at least 1 Special Education and Development Center in the provincial centre of every province in the region, and at least 1 extension centre in island municipalities and far-flung areas where travel is a barrier.

The centres are resource centres for children and youth with special needs, defined as children with disabilities under 18 and youth with disabilities aged 15 to 30. They train teachers, non-teaching staff, parents and administrators, supply schools with learning materials, orient families on children's rights, and arrange auxiliary aids. MBHTE hires the staff and gives them scholarships, training grants, allowances and exchange programs, and the Minister negotiates with the private sector and medical groups on running the centres.

Provinces may use part of their Special Education Fund to build centres and train parents and teachers. A tax deduction and loan scheme for private partners is to be drafted with the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management and the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. MBHTE must carry a separate budget line for these learners.

It was filed on 24 June 2025 by MP Abrar J. Hataman, read on first reading on 26 June 2025 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 30 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the constitutional duty to make quality education accessible to all, and argues that special education in the country, despite the treaties and laws adopted, has not reached children with disabilities, least of all indigenous children in rural areas, where schools lack budget, curriculum guides, materials and facilities. It asks the Bangsamoro Government and local governments to provide a legal framework and back it with intervention, with a centre in every province and extension centres in far-flung areas.
whoIsAffected: Children and youth with disabilities, and gifted children, in every province of the region.
Their parents and caregivers, who gain training and information on placement options.
Public school teachers and administrators, who would receive special education training from the centres.
Provincial governments, which may draw on their Special Education Fund for buildings and training.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Provincial governments
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for the private-sector incentive scheme

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 14 tells the MBHTE Minister to include implementation in the ministry's programs and the General Appropriations Act, with a separate line item for these learners. Provinces may add from their Special Education Fund.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every province must have at least 1 special education centre, with extension centres in island and remote areas.
MBHTE's budget would carry a separate line for children and youth with special needs.
readings.insight:
This is the 2nd of 3 bills on special education centres, each at a different scale. Bill 255, filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan in October 2023, wants 1 centre per municipality or city and has not moved past first reading. This one wants 1 per province. Bill 386, filed a month after this one, proposes hubs and says so in terms, contrasting itself with Bill 255. Bill 386 and this bill were sent to the same 2 committees 3 days apart, on 27 and 30 April 2026, so the committee has the choice in front of it.

Section 15 gives MBHTE 7 days from effectivity to issue guidelines for creating and running the centres, and has it do so "through the approval of" the national Department of Education,, and names the national disability council 2 ways: the National Council for Disability Affairs in Section 13 and the National Council for the Welfare of Disabled Persons in Section 15. A regional ministry needing a national department's approval to implement a regional law is a drafting choice the committee may want to revisit. The information campaign in Section 13 is assigned in part to the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, and the law takes effect on publication in 2 national newspapers rather than in the region.

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants a special hardship allowance of 25% of monthly salary to public school teachers in Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, paid for 10 months of every fiscal year and released quarterly.

Section 3 lists who qualifies: all elementary and secondary teachers in the 3 island provinces; teachers in hardship posts as measured by a Hardship Index scored from 0 to 1; multigrade teachers in pure multigrade schools; mobile teachers and Alternative Learning System coordinators handling classes; and school heads in hardship posts or pure multigrade schools.

An interim budget for 2025 is to come proportionately from the savings of the Bangsamoro Government, the Department of Education and MBHTE, and afterwards from the annual Bangsamoro appropriations. The bill has 7 sections.

It was filed on 24 June 2025 by MP Abrar J. Hataman, read on first reading on 26 June 2025 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 27 January 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says teachers in the island provinces work through geographic isolation, lack of resources and socio-economic constraints, sometimes at risk to their lives, and that a hardship allowance would recognise that and give them the compensation they deserve. It asks for more investment in infrastructure and allowances for teachers in remote areas.
whoIsAffected: Public school teachers in Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, every one of whom would qualify under Section 3(a).
Multigrade teachers, mobile teachers, ALS coordinators and school heads in hardship posts.
Teachers in Sulu, named in the bill though the province is no longer in the region.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Department of Education, consulted on the rules
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, for the annual appropriation

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The allowance is 25% of monthly salary for 10 months a year. For 2025 it would come proportionately from savings of the Bangsamoro Government, the Department of Education and MBHTE, and from 2026 from the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every public school teacher in the island provinces would receive 25% more pay for 10 months of each year.
Teachers in hardship posts and multigrade schools would be covered by name.
readings.insight:
Section 3 makes the Hardship Index irrelevant. Paragraph (a) covers all elementary and secondary teachers in the 3 provinces, so paragraphs (b) to (e), for hardship posts, multigrade schools and mobile teachers, add no one who is not already in. The index the bill carefully defines, from transport time to violence to poverty, decides nothing: a teacher in a provincial capital and a teacher on a remote island get the same 25%. The definitions section also says "at least" 25%, while Section 3 fixes it at 25%.

Sulu is in the title. The bill was filed on 24 June 2025, months after the Supreme Court removed Sulu from the Bangsamoro in 2024, so a regional appropriation would be paying teachers in a province outside the region's jurisdiction.

The funding and rules sections reach past the region. The 2025 interim budget is to come partly from Department of Education savings, which the Parliament cannot appropriate, and the implementing rules are to be issued by "the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao" without naming a ministry. The 2025 interim budget was also overtaken by events: the bill was not referred to committee until 27 January 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Public Cemetery Act. It requires every local government in the region to set aside at least 3 hectares of land for every 1,000 people for a public cemetery, written into its Comprehensive Land Use Plan or zoning ordinance and approved by its Sanggunian. At least 25% of the land must be reserved for non-Muslim residents.

Local governments build, maintain and run the cemeteries, following design, sanitation and safety standards and Islamic burial rites. Overall control and supervision rests with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. Towns may ask MENRE for help finding suitable land and may accept donated land, with recognition and tax incentives for donors.

A town that has not complied within 3 years faces administrative sanctions, including possible loss of access to regional assistance programs. MILG writes the rules with the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', the environment ministry and the Ministry of Health.

It was filed on 24 June 2025 by MPs Suharto S. Esmael, Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, Matarul M. Estino and Amiroddin Y. Gayak, read on first reading on 21 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Local Government on 23 July 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 3 gives the purpose: suitable public land for burial, in recognition of the distinct religious beliefs and burial customs of the Bangsamoro people, with cultural sensitivity and mutual respect.
whoIsAffected: Families who cannot afford private burial plots, in every town in the region.
Non-Muslim residents, guaranteed at least 25% of each cemetery.
Mayors and Sanggunians, who must find, zone and fund the land or face sanctions after 3 years.
Landowners who might donate land in exchange for incentives.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Every city and municipality in the region
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and Ministry of Health, on the rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 sources the cost from MILG's annual budget, with Bangsamoro Government subsidies, local funds and donations as supplementary sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every town must zone land for a public cemetery at 3 hectares per 1,000 people within 3 years.
A quarter of every public cemetery would be reserved for non-Muslims.
MILG gains the power to sanction towns that do not comply.
readings.insight:
The land requirement is 15 times what an earlier bill on the same subject asked. Bill 67, filed by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil in September 2022, set 2,000 square metres per 1,000 people with 20% for non-Muslims. This bill sets 3 hectares, which is 30,000 square metres, with 25%. Applied to Cotabato City's 2024 census population of 383,383, it would require about 1,150 hectares of cemetery. The 2 bills were referred to the same committee a day apart, on 22 and 23 July 2025.

The author lists do not match. The copy filed names Amiroddin Y. Gayak among the 4 authors; Parliament's index credits Abdullah E. Gayak instead, whose member profile gives his term as ending in February 2025, months before this bill was filed. The copy's co-author line also names MP Matarul M. Estino a second time and lists both "Amir A. Ahmad" and "Ahmad Amir A. Balindong".

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Bangsamoro Enterprise Support Corporation, a government-owned corporation that lends to micro, small and medium enterprises on Shari'ah-compliant terms, attached to the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism. Its head office is in Cotabato City, with provincial offices in Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Sur, Tawi-Tawi and the Special Geographic Area.

Financing must be free of interest, use structures such as murabaha, ijara, mudarabah, tawarruq and qard hasan, and avoid haram industries. The Corporation may also train borrowers, incubate start-ups, keep an MSME database, help with halal certification and export, and act as the regional arm of the national Small Business Corporation under an agreement.

It has an authorised capital of ₱500,000,000, partly subscribed and paid by the Bangsamoro Government, and an operating budget of ₱90,000,000 in the next appropriations act. An 11-member board is chaired by the Trade Minister and includes the Corporation's President, the Finance Minister, the Bangsamoro Grand Mufti, 5 government representatives named by the Chief Minister and 2 private shareholders. A Shari'ah Advisory Council of Islamic jurists checks compliance. Until the board is formed, the ministry acts for the Corporation.

It was filed on 7 July 2025 by MPs Romeo K. Sema, Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Saripuddin D. Jikiri and Randolph C. Parcasio, read on first reading on 24 July 2025, and after an authorship speech was referred to the Committee on Trade, Investment, and Tourism on 10 November 2025. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says small businesses are 99.59% of establishments nationally, employ over 62.4% of the workforce and contribute 36% of GDP, but in the region they lack finance, markets and business services, made worse by conflict, isolation and poverty. National lenders such as the Small Business Corporation do not offer the Shari'ah-compliant products the majority of the population would use, and the note cites a finding that the region has the fewest registered enterprises per capita of any region.

It presents the Corporation as a regional counterpart to the Small Business Corporation, tailored to Bangsamoro culture and religion, and as a peacebuilding measure as much as an economic one.
whoIsAffected: Micro, small and medium enterprises and cooperatives in the region, especially those that avoid interest-bearing loans.
Women entrepreneurs, youth-led businesses, displaced people and conflict-affected communities, named as priorities.
The Small Business Corporation, whose programs the new body may administer in the region.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Enterprise Support Corporation
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Shari'ah Advisory Council

funding.detail: Authorised capital stock of ₱500,000,000, partially subscribed and paid by the Bangsamoro Government out of unappropriated funds in the Bangsamoro Treasury, and ₱90,000,000 for operating expenses in the next Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region gets its own Islamic financing corporation for small business, with ₱500,000,000 in authorised capital.
Provincial offices would open in 4 provinces and the Special Geographic Area.
The Trade Minister would run it in the interim.
readings.insight:
Section 8 contradicts itself. Paragraph (b) lists murabaha (cost-plus), ijara (leasing) and mudarabah (profit-sharing), all of which return more to the financier than was advanced. Paragraph (e) then says repayment "shall be limited to the principal amount", which would rule them out and leave only the benevolent loan, qard hasan. The same paragraph says no interest shall be collected "by SB Corp.", the national corporation, not this one.

The copy has leftovers from a different draft. The board includes the President of the "Bangsamoro Enterprise Corporation"; Section 15 sets the salary of "the Administrator", an office the bill never creates, at Salary Grade 28; and Section 21 calls the bill "this Decree". The board also reserves 2 seats for private shareholders, though only the Bangsamoro Government is named as a subscriber.

Maguindanao del Norte is missing from the list of provincial offices. Section 4 names Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Sur, Tawi-Tawi and the Special Geographic Area, and puts the head office in Cotabato City, an independent city that is not part of the province.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Sports Institute Act of 2025. It establishes a Bangsamoro Sports Institute under the Bangsamoro Sports Commission, created by BAA 12, as the region's main hub for training, sports education and athlete development, a venue for events, and a centre for coach, referee and official certification.

The Commission's Chairperson appoints the Institute's officials, and the Commission owns its land and facilities for the Bangsamoro Government. The Institute coordinates with the Philippine Sports Institute and the Philippine Sports Commission, sets accreditation standards for coaches and partner institutions, promotes indigenous sports and traditional martial arts, and is to promote Islamic values through sport. The Institute writes its own implementing rules within 30 days.

It creates a Bangsamoro Sports Development Fund to pay for operations, facilities, scholarships, personnel and equipment.

It was filed on 7 July 2025 by MPs Alindatu K. Pagayao, Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., Muhammad Nadzir S. Ebil and Adzfar H. Usman, read on first reading on 24 July 2025, and after an authorship speech was referred to the Committee on Rules on 10 November 2025. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 borrows the national policy of developing sport for international and Olympic competitiveness through a national training facility, then adds the Bangsamoro aims of youth development, social cohesion, regional identity and peace. Section 4 cites the Constitution's sports provision, Section 20 of Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and BAA 10, which created the Bangsamoro Youth Commission.
whoIsAffected: Athletes resident in the region, current and aspiring, who compete regionally, nationally or internationally.
Coaches, referees and officials, who would be trained and accredited by the Institute.
Practitioners of indigenous games and traditional martial arts.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
Bangsamoro Sports Institute
Philippine Sports Commission and Philippine Sports Institute, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 creates a Bangsamoro Sports Development Fund and lists 4 sources: national appropriations through the Philippine Sports Commission, special development assistance for the region, the Bangsamoro block grant and Special Development Fund, and grants and donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the Sports Commission gains a training institute and a dedicated development fund.
Coaches and officials in the region would have a regional accreditation system.
readings.insight:
The first funding source is not one the Parliament controls. Section 12 lists national appropriations "through the Philippine Sports Commission" first; a regional law cannot direct the national budget. The bill also names no site, no size and no figure, so it does not say where the Institute would be or what it would cost.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Rules, not to a sports or education committee, on 10 November 2025. Other sports facility bills have gone elsewhere: Bill 413 on sports complexes in Cotabato City and Lamitan City went to Public Works and Finance. A closer sibling, Bill 313 for a Bangsamoro Sports Training Center, filed by MP Suharto S. Esmael in June 2024, has not been read on first reading.

The co-author line is the same 8 names in the same order as on Bill 362, MP Pagayao's greening bill filed a month earlier, which is why MP Muhammad Nadzir S. Ebil appears on this copy as both an author and a co-author.

readings.whatItDoes:
A regional public-private partnership law, the "BARMM PPP Act", letting the Bangsamoro Government contract private companies to finance, design, build, operate and maintain infrastructure and development projects, and setting the procedure for doing it.

The Chief Minister approves every PPP Project and the Bangsamoro Economic Development Council (BEDC) confirms it. For each project the Chief Minister forms an ad hoc PPP Selection Committee of BARMM officials, headed by someone at director level or above, which runs the bidding. Projects can be solicited, through single-stage or 2-stage public bidding, or unsolicited, where a private company proposes the project, negotiates terms within 60 days, receives Original Proponent Status and then faces a comparative challenge in which it has 30 days to match any better offer. If the BEDC does not act within 30 days on a project put to it, the project is deemed confirmed.

The bill covers joint ventures, including mudarabah and musharakah arrangements, toll operations, leases and the full menu of build-operate-transfer variants. Government subsidy is capped at 50% of the Project Cost, and the government's share in a joint venture at 50%. A private partner given a franchise for a facility gets it automatically on signing, and the franchise may be extended up to 50 years in total. Projects of local government units and national agencies are excluded, as are ordinary procurement under Republic Act No. 9184. The national PPP Code and procurement law apply where the bill is silent.

It was filed on 28 August 2024 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao with 9 other principal authors on the copy filed, read on first reading on 16 September 2024, and remains in committee, where the Committee on Ways and Means last acted on it on 24 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the national PPP Code, Republic Act No. 11966, covers local government units but not the region, so the Bangsamoro Government cannot use it to enter PPPs of its own. It presents a regional law as the same kind of regionalisation the Parliament did with the Local Government Code in BAA 49, and says a regional approval process would remove the need for endorsement from the national PPP Center for local projects.

The note also says a similar bill was filed earlier but was based on the old Build-Operate-Transfer law, Republic Act No. 6957 as amended by Republic Act No. 7718, which has since been repealed. It ties the measure to the Bangsamoro Government's 12-point Priority Agenda and the region's need for ports, roads, flood control and power.
whoIsAffected: Private companies, Filipino or foreign-owned, that would bid for or propose regional infrastructure and development projects.
Users of facilities built this way, who could be charged tolls, fares, fees and rentals set in the contract.
The Chief Minister and the BEDC, who would approve and confirm projects without any role for Parliament.
Bangsamoro taxpayers, whose government could pay subsidies of up to 50% of a Project Cost and carry contingent liabilities.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, which approves projects and forms a PPP Selection Committee for each
Bangsamoro Economic Development Council, which confirms projects and sets the monitoring framework

funding.detail: Section 28 appropriates ₱25,000,000 to carry out the Act without naming the fund it comes from. After that, the amounts needed go into the annual budget of BARMM.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, the regional government could enter PPP contracts on its own authority, approved by the Chief Minister and confirmed by the BEDC.
Private companies could propose projects unprompted and keep a right to match any rival offer.
Only government support paid with national funds would still need national (NEDA) approval.
readings.insight:
The explanatory note cites the national PPP Code as "R.A. No. 11966, s. 1991". The PPP Code is a 2023 law. 1991 is the year of the Local Government Code, which the note cites in its next paragraph, so the year seems to have been copied from the wrong line. The note also says R.A. No. 11966 does not reach the region, yet Section 30 of the bill makes that same Code apply wherever the bill is silent. The region's FY 2025 budget, BAA 65, already places PPP receipts under R.A. No. 11966.

The text still carries traces of where it was adapted from. Section 5 says "for purposes of this Code" in a bill that calls itself an Act. Section 10(c) limits unsolicited proposals to projects on "the list of PPP Projects referred to in Section 10", which is the section doing the referring; the list is in Section 6. Section 11(f) requires the region to tell "the PPP Center" about a takeover, but the bill never says which PPP Center it means.

The bill gives the approval power to the Chief Minister and lets the BEDC's silence for 30 days count as confirmation. Parliament has no role in approving a project, a subsidy or a franchise of up to 50 years. Bill 343, filed 3 months later by MP Ampatuan with MPs Midtimbang, Ambolodto and Utto among its co-authors, all 4 of them principal authors here, would create a separate PPP framework under a new infrastructure authority, and neither bill mentions the other.

readings.whatItDoes:
This rewrites 1 section of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 53, the act creating the Municipality of Nuling out of 19 barangays of the Municipality of Sultan Kudarat in Maguindanao del Norte.

The new Section 5 would hold the plebiscite on Nuling's creation in the barangays that would form the new municipality and "in the entire Municipality of Sultan Kudarat", within 60 days after approval of the Act. Nuling would come into existence only if a majority of votes cast approve it. Nothing else in BAA 53 changes: not the barangays, not the seat at Pinaring, not the appointed first officials, and not the ₱2.5 million a month in assistance.

It was filed on 9 September 2024 by the Government of the Day, read on first reading on 16 September 2024, and has been in committee since 19 September 2024.
readings.whyProposed:
In August 2024 the Supreme Court, in G.R. Nos. 271741 and 271972 (Datu Sajid S. Sinsuat et al. v. Hon. Ahod Balawag Ebrahim), struck down Section 5 of BAA 53 because it let only the voters of the barangays forming the new municipality vote in the plebiscite. The explanatory note says the Court ruled that voters of both the new and the mother municipality must be included.

The note gives Article 10, Section 10 of the Constitution as the basis. The same case and the same date, 20 August 2024, appear in the notes to Bills 331, 332 and 333.
whoIsAffected: Voters of the whole Municipality of Sultan Kudarat, who would vote on losing 19 barangays.
Residents of the 19 barangays that would form Nuling, who would no longer decide alone.
The Commission on Elections, which would run the plebiscite on the wider basis.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts the plebiscite
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee, so BAA 53 still has the Section 5 the Supreme Court struck down.
If enacted, the whole Municipality of Sultan Kudarat would vote on Nuling's creation, not just the 19 barangays leaving it.
readings.insight:
Of the 3 bills filed together on 9 September 2024, this is the only one still pending. Bills 332 and 333 make the same change to the acts creating Datu Sinsuat Balabaran and Sheik Abas Hamza. The registry records them as the origin bills of BAA 70 and BAA 71, both passed on 12 December 2024. Nothing comparable has passed for Nuling, so BAA 53 still contains the plebiscite clause the Supreme Court struck down, and Nuling's plebiscite clause is still in the form the Court rejected.

The explanatory note gets the geography wrong. It speaks of "the new and mother Municipality of Nuling in the Province of Sultan Kudarat". Nuling is the new municipality, its mother is the Municipality of Sultan Kudarat, and both are in Maguindanao del Norte. The operative text gets this right and names "the entire Municipality of Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao Del Norte". The title calls the amended law "Bangsamoro Act No. 53", and Section 1 calls it "Bangsamoro Autonomous Act No. 53". Its correct name is Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 53.

readings.whatItDoes:
This rewrites 1 section of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 54, the act creating the Municipality of Datu Sinsuat Balabaran out of 13 barangays of Datu Odin Sinsuat in Maguindanao del Norte.

As filed, the new Section 5 would hold the plebiscite in the barangays forming the new municipality and "in the entire Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat", within 60 days after approval of the Act, with creation depending on a majority of the votes cast. The rest of BAA 54 is unchanged.

It was filed on 9 September 2024 by the Government of the Day and read on first reading on 16 September 2024. Parliament's bills index still lists it in committee as of 19 September 2024. The registry record of BAA 70, passed on 12 December 2024 and approved on 20 December 2024, names this bill as its origin.
readings.whyProposed:
In August 2024 the Supreme Court, in G.R. Nos. 271741 and 271972 (Datu Sajid S. Sinsuat et al. v. Hon. Ahod Balawag Ebrahim), struck down Section 5 of BAA 54 because it let only the voters of the barangays forming the new municipality vote in the plebiscite. The explanatory note says the Court ruled that voters of both the new and the mother municipality must be included.

The note gives Article 10, Section 10 of the Constitution as the basis. The same case and the same date, 20 August 2024, appear in the notes to Bills 331, 332 and 333.
whoIsAffected: Voters of the whole of Datu Odin Sinsuat, which would lose 13 barangays to this act and 10 more to BAA 55.
Residents of the 13 barangays that would form Datu Sinsuat Balabaran.
The Commission on Elections, which runs the plebiscite.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts the plebiscite
whatChanges: The change has been made, as BAA 70. Parliament's bills index has not been updated and still shows this bill in committee.
The plebiscite on Datu Sinsuat Balabaran is no longer limited to the barangays that would leave Datu Odin Sinsuat.
readings.insight:
The bill as filed and the act that came from it say different things. This copy names the mother municipality and holds the vote "in the entire Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat". BAA 70 instead holds it "in the political units directly affected", the Organic Law's own general wording, and does not say which units those are. The filed version answered the question the Supreme Court raised. The enacted version leaves the answer to interpretation.

Both versions keep the 60-day period running from "the approval of the Act" without saying which act: BAA 54, approved in December 2023, or the amendment. Parliament's bills index still shows this bill in committee as of 19 September 2024, nearly 3 months before the act it became was passed, so a reader using the index alone would think the bill had stalled.

The text of all 3 bills in the set is the same except for the names.

readings.whatItDoes:
This rewrites 1 section of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 55, the act creating the Municipality of Sheik Abas Hamza out of 10 barangays of Datu Odin Sinsuat in Maguindanao del Norte.

As filed, the new Section 5 would hold the plebiscite in the barangays forming the new municipality and "in the entire municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat", within 60 days after approval of the Act, with creation depending on a majority of the votes cast. The rest of BAA 55 is unchanged.

It was filed on 9 September 2024 by the Government of the Day and read on first reading on 16 September 2024. Parliament's bills index still lists it in committee as of 19 September 2024. The registry record of BAA 71, passed on 12 December 2024 and approved on 20 December 2024, names this bill as its origin.
readings.whyProposed:
In August 2024 the Supreme Court, in G.R. Nos. 271741 and 271972 (Datu Sajid S. Sinsuat et al. v. Hon. Ahod Balawag Ebrahim), struck down Section 5 of BAA 55 because it let only the voters of the barangays forming the new municipality vote in the plebiscite. The explanatory note says the Court ruled that voters of both the new and the mother municipality must be included.

The note gives Article 10, Section 10 of the Constitution as the basis. The same case and the same date, 20 August 2024, appear in the notes to Bills 331, 332 and 333.
whoIsAffected: Voters of the whole of Datu Odin Sinsuat, the mother municipality.
Residents of the 10 barangays that would form Sheik Abas Hamza.
The Commission on Elections, which runs the plebiscite.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, which conducts the plebiscite
whatChanges: The change has been made, as BAA 71. Parliament's bills index has not been updated and still shows this bill in committee.
The plebiscite on Sheik Abas Hamza is no longer limited to the barangays that would leave Datu Odin Sinsuat.
readings.insight:
Bills 332 and 333 both name the same mother municipality, Datu Odin Sinsuat. If both were enacted as filed, every voter in Datu Odin Sinsuat would face 2 separate plebiscites on losing 23 barangays in total, each within 60 days. Neither bill mentions the other, and neither says whether the 2 votes would be held together.

As with its twin, the enacted version differs from the copy filed. BAA 71 drops the named municipality and uses "the political units directly affected". The bills index still shows this bill in committee as of 19 September 2024, though the registry names it as the origin of BAA 71. The third bill in the set, Bill 331 for Nuling, was filed the same day with the same text and has not moved since it reached committee.

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets up a Bangsamoro Neurodevelopmental Disorder and Special Needs Support Program, run by the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Social Services and Development with the education ministry. It would offer free developmental screening and diagnosis in public health centres and hospitals; subsidised occupational, speech and behavioural therapy; medical coverage through the regional health system together with PhilHealth; early intervention for children under 6 years; mental health support for children and their families; and training for health workers and caregivers.

The bill names 5 neurodevelopmental disorders: autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, intellectual disability, specific learning disorders such as dyslexia, and communication disorders. The education ministry would expand Special Education, place children in regular classes with individualised education plans where appropriate, set up SPED Centers "in every province, city and districts", and offer scholarships to SPED teachers. The Ministry of Health, with local governments, would build Special Needs Care Centers in every congressional district in the provinces. The social services ministry would give financial help to low-income families, and the 3 ministries would keep a regional database of diagnosed children.

It was filed on 15 October 2024 by MP Suharto S. Esmael, read on first reading on 17 October 2024, and remains in committee, where it was last acted on 20 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The reasons given are in the declaration of policy: these children should have access to education, health care and social services, and inclusive policies are needed for social justice in the region. The purposes listed in Section 3 are early diagnosis, accessible therapy, better inclusive education, regional care centres, and support for families.
whoIsAffected: Children with autism, ADHD, intellectual disability, learning or communication disorders and other special needs, and their families.
Low-income families, who would receive financial help for therapy, schooling and medical costs.
SPED teachers, who would be offered scholarships and training.
Public health centres and hospitals, which would provide free screening.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Ministry of Social Services and Development
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The money needed would go into the annual budget, and the government may accept donations and grants. The title says the bill appropriates funds, but no amount is given.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, developmental screening and diagnosis would be free in public facilities across the region.
3 new kinds of facility would be set up: SPED Centers, Special Needs Care Centers and the Regional Centers named in the purposes.
readings.insight:
The bill gives 3 different rules for where facilities go. Section 3 promises Regional Centers for Special Needs Care "in each province and city".
