Section 7 calls for SPED Centers "in every province, city and districts". Section 8 calls for Special Needs Care Centers "in every congressional district in the provinces", which leaves Cotabato City out. The bill never counts how many centres any of these rules would produce, and gives no amount to build them.

Bill 354, filed 6 months later by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, would create a single Bangsamoro center for children with autism, also under the Ministry of Health. MP Ampatuan is a co-author of this bill, and MP Esmael is a co-author of Bill 354. The 2 bills went to different committees: this one to Health and to Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities, and Bill 354 to Social Services and Finance. Neither bill mentions the other.

readings.whatItDoes:
The "Bangsamoro Infrastructure and Connectivity Development Act of 2024" would create the Bangsamoro Infrastructure and Connectivity Development Authority (BICDA). It would be an independent body to plan, coordinate, implement and monitor infrastructure across the region, run by a Board of Directors from the regional government, the private sector and national agencies. The Chief Minister would appoint the Board, subject to Parliament's approval.

The Authority would write a Bangsamoro Infrastructure Development Plan listing priority projects, timelines, funding sources and responsible agencies. National agencies may implement projects in the region based on that plan. It would manage a Bangsamoro Infrastructure Fund, funded by the regional budget, grants, PPP proceeds and other lawful sources, and would build a PPP framework with incentives, tax benefits and simpler rules. Priority goes to roads and bridges, ports and airports, digital connectivity, water and sanitation, and energy. All projects must include climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction.

The Authority would report to Parliament every year, and a panel of experts appointed by the Chief Minister would review the Act every 5 years. It was filed on 4 December 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, read on first reading on 23 January 2025, and remains in committee, where it was last acted on 17 June 2026.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note relies on the Organic Law's grant of authority over public works and infrastructure in Article V. It describes decades of underdevelopment and conflict that left the region with poor infrastructure, weak connectivity and underdeveloped transport.

It describes the bill as a legal framework for planning, investing in and building infrastructure in a coordinated way, in line with the Bangsamoro Development Plan and national priorities. It gives no figures on what infrastructure is missing.
whoIsAffected: The Ministry of Public Works, whose planning and implementation role the new Authority would partly duplicate, though the Ministry would write the rules.
Private investors, who would be offered incentives, tax benefits and simpler rules under a PPP framework.
Local government units, which must take part in planning and monitoring projects in their areas.
Communities in remote and underserved areas, named as priorities for power, water and roads.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Infrastructure and Connectivity Development Authority, a new independent body
Ministry of Public Works, which issues the implementing rules within 60 days
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources, and Energy, on environmental compliance

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The initial cost is charged to the Contingent Fund, and later costs go into the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. The new Bangsamoro Infrastructure Fund draws on appropriations, grants, PPP proceeds and other lawful sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, a new authority separate from the Ministry of Public Works would plan and carry out regional infrastructure.
A dedicated infrastructure fund would be created, managed by that authority.
Parliament would confirm the authority's board and receive an annual report.
readings.insight:
The bill sets up an authority to plan and build infrastructure, but the implementing rules would be written by the Ministry of Public Works, the agency it would overlap with most. The bill does not say how the 2 would divide the work. It also leaves out how many members the Board has and how seats are split among the regional government, the private sector and national agencies. Section 5 refers to "the objectives mentioned in Section 4", but the objectives are in Section 3.

The PPP provisions overlap with Bill 329, filed 3 months earlier, which sets out a full PPP procedure through the Chief Minister, the BEDC and project-by-project selection committees. This bill instead tells the new Authority to create its own PPP framework with tax benefits. MP Ampatuan and 3 of this bill's co-authors on the copy filed, MPs Tawakal B. Midtimbang, Suharto M. Ambolodto and Bassir D. Utto, are principal authors of Bill 329. Neither bill mentions the other. The bill reached committee on 17 June 2026, about 18 months after it was filed.

readings.whatItDoes:
The "BARMM Trade and Tourism Center Development Act of 2025" would build Trade and Tourism Centers in 5 places: Cotabato City, Lamitan City in Basilan, Marawi City in Lanao del Sur, Jolo in Sulu, and Bongao in Tawi-Tawi. The Ministry of Trade, Investments, and Tourism would choose the exact sites and would own and run the centres.

Each centre would have a business and investment centre, a trade exhibition hall, a tourism and cultural pavilion, a training and innovation hub, and a marketplace. Each design must reflect the culture and heritage of its province. Hotels and other commercial space could be added through public-private partnerships. Local contractors, workers and materials get priority.

The Ministry would review progress every year, and the Bangsamoro Board of Investments would track jobs, business growth and tourism. It was filed on 12 February 2025 by MP John Anthony L. Lim, read on first reading on 17 February 2025, and remains in committee, where it was last acted on 19 November 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The declaration of policy calls the centres hubs for trade, investment and tourism promotion in the region's main economic and cultural centres, built to bring the most local economic benefit.
whoIsAffected: Businesses, investors and tourism operators in the 5 host towns and cities.
Local contractors, workers and suppliers, who get priority in construction.
LGUs and private owners, who might donate land for the sites.
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Investments, and Tourism
Bangsamoro Board of Investments, which monitors economic impact

funding.detail: An initial ₱20 million for architectural and engineering design, master plans and feasibility studies. Land acquisition and construction come from annual or supplemental appropriations, with no amount stated. Later expansion may draw on PPPs, grants, soft loans and national programmes.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, the trade and tourism ministry would design and build 5 centres, with ₱20 million for design.
Land and construction would compete for funding in later budgets.
readings.insight:
One of the 5 sites is Jolo, Sulu. The Supreme Court removed Sulu from the Bangsamoro in 2024, and this bill was filed in February 2025, after that ruling. As filed, it directs a regional ministry to buy land and build a centre in a province outside the region. Other bills in this registry from the same period have had to deal with Sulu's exit, and this one does not mention it.

The only figure in the bill is ₱20 million for design across the 5 centres. Land and construction, which cost far more, have no amount and are left to future budgets. Of the 5 provinces left in the region, Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur get no centre of their own; Cotabato City is the closest.

readings.whatItDoes:
The "BARMM Water Safety in Schools Act" would require every public and private school below college level in the region to provide safe drinking water and working sanitation. This includes madrasah and alternative learning centres. Schools could meet this with filtration units, potable water tanks, piped connections or other approved systems, and toilets and handwashing stations would be maintained from each school's Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE).

The education ministry would add water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) lessons to the curriculum, and every school would run its own WASH programme. A BARMM WASH Monitoring Board, made up of representatives of the Ministry of Health and the education ministry, would set standards, inspect schools, provide technical help and training, and report every year. The bill is meant to adapt the Department of Education's WASH in Schools (WinS) programme to the region.

It was filed on 18 February 2025 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 15 April 2025, and remains in committee, where it was last acted on 15 December 2025.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says many schools in the region lack basic WASH facilities, and that this leads to waterborne illness and absences. It cites WHO data that absences can rise by up to 25% in such schools. It says that as of 2020 only 56% of urban and 28% of rural households in the region had piped water or an improved water source, and 52% had basic sanitation. It says a 2021 WinS assessment found only half of the region's schools met minimum WASH standards.

It notes that girls miss school when toilets lack privacy, especially during menstruation, and that WinS-compliant schools report up to 30% fewer absences. It bases the bill on the Constitution's provisions on health and education and on the Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Students in public and private schools, madrasah and alternative learning centres, especially girls.
School heads, who must meet the water standards and pay for upkeep from MOOE.
Private schools, which the bill covers in full.
implementedBy: BARMM WASH Monitoring Board, made up of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Ministry of Health, which writes the implementing rules within 60 days
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which allocates the first funds

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial funds come from the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro as allocated by the finance ministry, and later funds from the budgets of the health and education ministries. Toilet and handwashing upkeep is charged to each school's MOOE.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, safe drinking water and working sanitation would be a legal requirement for every school below college level.
WASH lessons would become part of the curriculum, including in madrasah.
readings.insight:
The bill covers private schools but pays for upkeep through "each institution's MOOE". MOOE is the operating allocation in a public school's budget, and the bill does not say where a private school's upkeep money would come from or who pays for its compliance.

The note's figures are not all sourced. The PSA household figures have no footnote. The 2021 WinS assessment is footnoted to a UNICEF review dated 2018, which could not report a 2021 finding. The 30% fall in absences has no source at all.

The author lists differ. The note page of the copy filed names 11 co-authors, including MPs Suwaib L. Oranon, Mohammad Kelie Antao, Tawakal Midtimbang, Mudjib Abu, Bassir Utto, Nabil Tan, John Anthony L. Lim and Kadil Sinolinding, Jr. None of those 8 appear among the 23 co-authors in Parliament's bills index. The page with the bill text names only 3.

readings.whatItDoes:
The "Bangsamoro Autism Center Act of 2025" would create a Bangsamoro Center for Autism Spectrum Disorder, a clinic for diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation under the Ministry of Health. Indigent children would get diagnosis and rehabilitation free. The centre would also provide referrals and counselling, vocational training for adults with ASD, physical and occupational therapy, social and psycho-social programmes, and school-based behavioural and skills programmes. Its staff would include physical, occupational and speech therapists, social workers and support staff.

Within 1 year the Ministry of Health and the education ministry would give Parliament a 10-year strategic plan, covering how common ASD is among the region's children and how it affects schooling. The Ministry of Health would also issue rules against forcing cures, vaccines or therapies on people with ASD, and, with the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office, rules to protect their medical records. It would report to Parliament every year, and an expert panel would review the Act every 5 years.

It was filed on 14 April 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan with 7 other principal authors, read on first reading on 21 April 2025, and has been in committee since 28 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note relies on the Constitution's provisions on the right to health and affordable care, and on the Organic Law's health provisions. It describes ASD using the US National Institute of Mental Health, the DSM-5 and the WHO, which estimates that about 1 in 100 children worldwide has autism. It cites Department of Health figures, as reported by the Philippine News Agency, of about 500,000 recorded cases in 2008, roughly doubling to 1 million a decade later.

It says therapy costs ₱500 to ₱1,500 an hour, which poor families cannot afford, and that early intervention improves outcomes. A footnote says the bill is based on Norjannah P. Mohammad's entry in a 2024 bill-drafting contest run by the offices of MPs Ampatuan, Loong, Ismael and Mitmug.
whoIsAffected: Children with ASD and their families, especially indigent families, who would get free diagnosis and rehabilitation.
Adults with ASD, offered vocational training.
Physical, occupational and speech therapists and social workers, who would staff the centre.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which supervises the centre and sets its structure
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, which prepares the 10-year strategic plan with the Ministry of Health
Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office, which advises on confidentiality rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The money needed to set up the centre would be included in the annual appropriations and submitted to Parliament.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill remains in committee.
If enacted, the region would have a public autism centre offering free services to indigent children.
Forced cures, vaccines and therapies on people with ASD would be barred by Ministry of Health rules.
readings.insight:
The bill never says where the centre would be. It creates 1 centre for the whole region and leaves its location, and the size of its staff, to the Ministry of Health and the implementing rules. The note describes free evaluations and therapy, but the text promises free services only to indigent children.

Bill 338, filed 6 months earlier by MP Suharto S. Esmael, also covers autism and is broader. It calls for care centres in every congressional district and free screening in public health facilities. MP Ampatuan co-authored Bill 338 and MP Esmael co-authors this one. The 2 bills went to different committees, and neither mentions the other. Parliament's bills index lists MP Khalid M. Hadji Abdullah as both a principal author and a co-author of this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Dignity and Welfare of Women Deprived of Liberty in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region Act of 2025. It sets out the rights of women held in jails, detention centres and correctional facilities in the region: protection from abuse with confidential reporting channels, privacy, communication with counsel, family and religious advisers including conjugal visits, adequate food and water, accommodation separate from men, hygiene products, health care equal to the community's, freedom of religion, and access to education and work.

Much of it is written for Muslim detainees. Food must be halal, cooked with separate utensils, and Muslim women may be assigned to the kitchen. Uniforms must allow the hijab, prayer areas must be designated, and any search that requires removing clothing covering the awrah, including the hijab, may only be done by a female officer in private. Denying food, water or communication as punishment is barred.

Pregnant women may not be restrained during examinations, labour or right after birth, except for security. Mothers may keep infants with them until the child is 1 year old, and pregnant women, nursing mothers and those with infants may not be put in solitary confinement. Male staff must announce themselves, may not search women except in emergencies, and may not enter areas where women may be undressed. In provincial jails, the women's section must be run and watched, including CCTV, by female staff, at ratios of 1 female custodial officer to 7 detainees and 1 female reformation officer to 24.

It was filed on 12 December 2025 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, read on first reading on 17 December 2025, and after an authorship speech on 20 January 2026 was referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities on 21 April 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites Section 12, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which directs the Parliament to protect the fundamental rights of women, and the Magna Carta of Women, which counts women in detention among women in especially difficult circumstances. It says the bill follows the UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules) and the UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners (the Bangkok Rules), both adopted by the UN General Assembly.

It also grounds the bill in Islamic principles of upholding the dignity of women, and says it hopes to improve conditions for children born to mothers in detention.
whoIsAffected: Women held in provincial jails, BJMP-run jails and other detention facilities in the region, especially Muslim women.
Pregnant detainees, nursing mothers and their infants up to 1 year old.
Provincial governments, which would have to hire enough female jail staff to meet the 1:7 and 1:24 ratios.
Male jail staff, whose access to women's areas would be restricted.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, which monitors compliance and writes the rules
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, over provincial jails
Bangsamoro Women Commission, Ministry of Social Services and Development, Ministry of Health and Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education

funding.detail: ₱5,000,000 to each of the 6 agencies named in Section 9 for the first year, ₱30,000,000 in all. No source for the first-year money is named. After that, the amounts go into each agency's annual appropriation.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, women's sections of provincial jails would have to be run by female staff at set ratios.
Halal food, hijab-compatible uniforms, prayer areas and female-only strip searches would become rights in law.
Infants could stay with their detained mothers until age 1.
readings.insight:
The copy filed names itself twice. The explanatory note calls it the "Women Deprived of Liberty in the Bangsamoro Region Act of 2024"; Section 1 calls it the "Dignity and Welfare of Women Deprived of Liberty in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region Act of 2025". The bill was filed in December 2025, so the note appears to come from an earlier draft.

The reach of the bill is narrower than its definitions. Section 3 counts municipal, city and district jails run by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology as covered facilities, but the binding staffing rules in Sections 7 and 8 apply only to provincial jails, and the regional ministries are told only to "coordinate" with the BJMP, a national bureau. Most of the rights in Section 4 are addressed to "jail and correctional facilities" in general, without saying who enforces them in a BJMP jail.

The bill sat 3 months between its authorship speech, when it was deferred, and its referral to committee on 21 April 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Blood Services Act of 2025. It makes the Ministry of Health the lead agency for voluntary blood donation in the region and creates a Bangsamoro Blood Center under the ministry to recruit and screen donors and to collect, test, store and issue blood. The Center keeps a single Bangsamoro Blood Donors Registry under the Data Privacy Act.

The ministry would run public education campaigns with the Philippine Red Cross, train government employees, and build a network of blood facilities in every province, city and municipality. MBHTE would add blood donation to school lessons. In areas without blood banks, government hospitals, rural health units, health centres and barangays must keep a list of willing donors by blood type, the "walking blood donor" system. Provinces, cities, towns and hospitals may set up their own blood facilities, funded mainly from their own revenues.

All donated blood must be tested for transfusion-transmissible infections, and donors who test reactive must be told confidentially and offered counselling. Donors get a free donor card and may receive certificates or tokens; government employees may get compensatory time off. Facilities charging more than allowed fees face suspension or loss of permits.

It was filed on 12 December 2025 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, read on first reading on 17 December 2025, and after an authorship speech on 20 January 2026 was referred to the Committee on Health and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 15 July 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites a 32% shortage in the region's blood supply reported by the Regional Health Office as of June 2025, drawn from a Bangsamoro Information Office report of 10 July 2025. It says shortages delay surgeries, raise risks for patients and can cost lives, and cites Surah 5:32 of the Qur'an, that saving a life is like saving all of mankind.

The note says the bill would reduce reliance on paid blood sources, extend donation to areas without blood banks through the walking blood donor system, and build public awareness.
whoIsAffected: Patients needing transfusions, especially in areas without blood banks.
Voluntary donors, who would get a donor card and, if government employees, possible time off.
Hospitals, rural health units, health centres and barangays in underserved areas, which must keep donor lists.
Blood facilities, which would face sanctions for overcharging.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health and the Bangsamoro Blood Center
Philippine Red Cross local chapters, in coordination
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, for school lessons

funding.detail: An initial appropriation of ₱50,000,000, with no source named. After that, the cost goes into the Ministry of Health's budget in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. Local blood facilities would be funded mainly from local revenues.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have its own Blood Center and a single donor registry.
Health facilities in areas without blood banks would have to keep standing lists of donors by blood type.
Testing of all donated blood for transmissible infections would become a regional legal requirement.
readings.insight:
An earlier bill on the same subject never moved. Bill 311, filed by MP Suharto S. Esmael on 10 June 2024 to establish a Bangsamoro Blood Services Center, has not been read on first reading. MP Esmael is a co-author of this bill.

The copy filed is not consistent in its names. The note promises a "Bangsamoro Blood Services Program"; Section 6 creates a "Bangsamoro Voluntary Blood Services Program". The policy section calls the network the "Bangsamoro Blood Transfusion Service Network (BBTSN)"; Section 4 calls it the "Bangsamoro Blood Transfusion Network (BBTN)". Section 4(e) and 4(g) both tell facilities in underserved areas to use walking blood donors.

The bill waited almost 6 months between its authorship speech on 20 January 2026 and its referral on 15 July 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Buy Bangsamoro Act of 2025. It requires every regional ministry, office and agency, local government, state university and college and government corporation operating exclusively in the region to give preference, as far as national procurement law allows, to goods made in the region and to community groups that can deliver simple infrastructure and services.

At the start of each fiscal year, each procuring entity must identify which programs and projects suit Negotiated Procurement-Community Participation, a method under the national Government Procurement Act (Republic Act 12009) that lets government buy directly from organised or unorganised community groups, and direct purchase of farm and fishery products under the Sagip Saka Act. Those projects are tagged in procurement plans. Where the conditions are met, the Bids and Awards Committee must recommend community participation, or explain in writing why not. Direct purchases need supplier listing, documented price checks against farm-gate or retail benchmarks, and audit trails.

Simple infrastructure projects are capped at ₱5,000,000 or the GPPB limit. CSEA, MTIT, MAFAR, MILG, MOLE and MIPA must run training for community suppliers. Competitive bidding stays the default method.

It was filed on 12 December 2025 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, read on first reading on 17 December 2025, deferred on 20 January 2026, and referred to the Committee on Rules on 16 July 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says restrictive procurement rules, limited market access and trade monopolies keep local farmers, fisherfolk and small producers out of government purchasing. Selling directly to government would give them steady income and fair prices, cut out middlemen, reduce post-harvest losses and support food security.

It proposes negotiated procurement through community participation, already allowed under procurement rules, as the way to do this, with communities acting as suppliers or contractors.
whoIsAffected: Farmers, fisherfolk, cooperatives and community groups in the region who could sell directly to government.
Regional ministries, local governments, SUCs and GOCCs, which must tag suitable projects and justify not using community participation.
Middlemen and larger suppliers who now win these contracts.
implementedBy: Every procuring entity in the region and its Bids and Awards Committee
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which writes the rules with the GPPB
CSEA, MTIT, MAFAR, MILG, MOLE and MIPA, for supplier training
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every regional procuring entity would have to tag projects fit for community participation in its annual plans.
A Bids and Awards Committee that chooses another method for a tagged project would have to put its reasons on file.
readings.insight:
The bill adds a planning duty, not a new procurement power. Section 4 limits it to what is "consistent with existing national procurement laws", Section 6 says nothing displaces competitive bidding as the default, and Section 9 repeats that it must be read consistently with national law. What it would actually change is the paperwork: the annual tagging of projects and a written reason whenever community participation is passed over.

Section 3(g) sets 2 ceilings for simple infrastructure: ₱5,000,000, and whatever maximum the GPPB guidelines prescribe "as amended". If the national guidelines change, the 2 figures will disagree. The rules are to be written by MFBM "in coordination with GPPB", a national body. The policy section also speaks of other countries learning about Bangsamoro industries, which the bill does not take up.

It was filed the same day as Bills 422 and 423, by the same author with the same 6 co-authors on the copy, and like them sat until mid-2026 before referral, here to the Committee on Rules rather than a trade or finance committee.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Licensure Examination Assistance Act of 2025. Its title creates the Bangsamoro Licensure Examination Assistance Program (B-LEAP); its body creates a Bangsamoro Professional Examination Review Subsidy Program under the Office of the Chief Minister, to help residents of the region prepare for PRC licensure examinations and the Bar.

The Program may pay all or part of review centre fees, give a transport, lodging and meal allowance set in the rules, and help buy review books, with more support for orphans, persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and low-income examinees. It covers residents qualified to take any PRC examination or the Bar, including those studying or working outside the region who can prove permanent residency. Applicants must show residency, eligibility to sit the exam, financial need, and swear the money is for review only.

A Board chaired by the Office of the Chief Minister, with the Ministers of Education, Social Services and Finance and the Bangsamoro Youth Commission Chairperson, runs the Program, accredits review centres and reports yearly to Parliament. Successful examinees are encouraged, not required, to give 60 hours of community service within 1 year.

It was filed on 5 January 2026 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, read on first reading on 19 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Rules and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 26 January 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the right to education in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Constitution, and Sections 13 and 16 of Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law. It says the region needs more licensed teachers, nurses, engineers, social workers and lawyers, and that review fees, materials, transport and lodging keep qualified but poor examinees from taking licensure and Bar examinations.

It describes the Program as an investment in human capital, so that poverty no longer stops Bangsamoro graduates from entering the professions.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region preparing for PRC licensure examinations or the Bar, especially low-income examinees.
Orphans, persons with disabilities and indigenous peoples, who get priority support.
Review centres, which would need Board accreditation to take part.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Professional Examination Review Subsidy Board
MBHTE, MSSD, MFBM and the Bangsamoro Youth Commission, as Board members

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The first year is to be charged to the Contingent Fund, and later years to the Office of the Chief Minister's budget in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, low-income examinees could get review fees, allowances and materials paid.
Examinees from the region living elsewhere could apply if they prove permanent residency.
readings.insight:
The program in the title is not the program in the bill. "B-LEAP" appears only in the title; Section 3 creates the "Bangsamoro Professional Examination Review Subsidy Program", and the explanatory note uses that name too. Section 7 is headed "Bangsamoro Professional Review Subsidy Board" but creates the "Bangsamoro Professional Examination Review Subsidy Board". The Board is chaired by "the Office of the Chief Minister", an office rather than a person, and Section 9 requires the Chairperson to be present for a quorum.

There is no return service. Section 11 only encourages 60 hours of community service and says it shall not be a condition of the subsidy. Bill 428, filed a week later, ties graduate scholarships for teachers to 1 year of service for each year funded.

The short title says 2025, though the bill was filed on 5 January 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Amanah Chain Act of 2025, or A-CHAIN Act. It makes a blockchain ledger, the Amanah Chain, the official public record of the region's budget allocations, releases, procurement, project milestones and disbursements, with a public Transparency Portal for non-confidential entries.

Every ministry, office and agency, province, city, municipality and barangay must connect its budget, allotment, disbursement, procurement, project and audit records to the system and name A-CHAIN compliance officers. Failing to upload required records is an administrative offence. Records are verified by "validator nodes" such as the Bangsamoro Treasury Office, COA-BARMM, universities and civil society groups. "Smart Amanah Contracts" would trigger fund releases or procurement steps automatically once requirements are met.

MFBM leads, BICTO builds and runs the system, and COA-BARMM uses it for audits. It starts as a pilot in 1 infrastructure ministry, 1 social service ministry, 1 province and 1 city or municipality. The rules are due within 90 days.

It was filed on 9 January 2026 by MP Jaafar Apollo Mikhail L. Matalam, read on first reading on 19 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Ways and Means on 21 April 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the scale of public spending in the region needs records that are verifiable, traceable and resistant to manipulation, and ties this to Amanah, the trust placed in officials to manage public resources. It says a blockchain ledger would track every peso from appropriation to audit, record procurement and contract milestones, keep disbursement trails, and open non-confidential records to the public in real time.

The note says the measure is not a copy of any national proposal, though it was inspired by the national demand to confront corruption.
whoIsAffected: Every regional ministry, office and agency, and every province, city, municipality and barangay, which must upload records.
Officials who fail to upload, who would face administrative liability.
Citizens, researchers and civil society, who would get a public portal.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office
Commission on Audit, BARMM office

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 10 names the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act, the block grant, the Special Development Fund and other lawful sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, a pilot ledger would start in 2 ministries, 1 province and 1 town.
All regional and local offices would eventually have to put their budget and procurement records on it, with penalties for not uploading.
readings.insight:
The copy filed has a missing section. Section 7 lists only MFBM's duties; the next items are numbered 8.1 to 8.4 under no Section 8 heading, covering BICTO, the Commission on Audit, all ministries and LGUs, and the public portal. Section 9 follows.

The bill assigns duties to the Commission on Audit, a constitutional body that a regional law does not direct, and names COA-BARMM as a validator node. It also makes upload mandatory for every barangay while setting no timetable beyond a pilot in 4 units, and puts no figure on what building and running the system would cost.

It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, which handles revenue, rather than the finance committee that handles spending, 3 months after first reading. The short title says 2025, though the bill was filed on 9 January 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The MBHTE Teachers Graduate Scholarship Act. It creates a scholarship program for permanent or regular MBHTE teachers, in basic, higher, technical-vocational or madaris education, to take master's or doctorate degrees in fields related to what they teach.

Applicants need at least 2 years of satisfactory service, admission to an accredited school, a field tied to their teaching, and no pending administrative or criminal case. MBHTE sets priority fields, which may include STEM, teacher education and leadership, madaris and Islamic education, special and inclusive education, technical-vocational education and ICT. Benefits may cover tuition and fees, a monthly or semestral allowance, book and thesis support and other necessary expenses, selected through a merit-based committee.

Scholars owe 1 year of service to MBHTE for every year of scholarship, and may be posted to underserved areas. A scholar who quits the program or skips return service without justifiable cause must refund all benefits and may face civil service sanctions.

It was filed on 12 January 2026 by MP Adzfar H. Usman, read on first reading on 19 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 26 January 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the Bangsamoro Education Code already recognises scholarships and support for teachers, but no law puts that into a structured graduate program. It proposes master's and doctorate grants with return service so the benefit stays in the region's schools, to raise teaching quality and fill gaps in specialised fields.
whoIsAffected: Permanent and regular MBHTE teachers with at least 2 years of service.
Schools in priority and underserved areas, where scholars may be deployed.
Contract and volunteer teachers, who are not eligible.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The first year is charged to current appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government, subject to available funds, and later years to the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, MBHTE teachers could get paid graduate study in exchange for 1 year of service per year funded.
Scholars who default would have to refund what they received.
readings.insight:
The bill leaves almost every number to MBHTE. It sets no cap on scholars, no allowance rate, no limit on years of support and no budget; benefits are "as may be determined" by the ministry, the 2-year service minimum can be waived "unless otherwise determined by MBHTE", and even the 1-for-1 return service can be changed in the rules. Its firm terms are the eligibility list and the refund on breach.

Only permanent or regular teachers qualify. Bill 461, filed in 2026 to absorb and regularise MBHTE volunteer teachers, deals with the group this bill leaves out. The copy filed names MP Usman alone; the registry lists 20 co-authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Housing and Human Settlement Development Act of 2026. It makes the Ministry of Human Settlements and Development the region's central housing authority and gives it power to issue permits for housing construction, renovation and occupancy, directly or with local governments, to inspect housing projects, to set price ceilings for economic and socialized housing, to run its own housing loan programs under Islamic finance rules, to partner with developers and to take donations.

It covers all housing in the region, public and private: socialized, economic and public housing, resettlement sites, private subdivisions and condominiums, and the building or renovation of any home. No major renovation or structural alteration of any residential building may be done without MHSD approval. MHSD sets building and safety standards, may limit occupancy to prevent overcrowding, and can issue violation notices, fine, revoke permits and order illegal works demolished at the owner's cost.

Public housing must be allocated by published rules that put low-income families and internally displaced persons first, with subleasing and unauthorised transfer barred. Projects should respect extended-family living and, where practicable, provide prayer spaces and qibla orientation. MHSD keeps a registry of projects, occupancy and permits.

It was filed on 16 January 2026 by MPs Romeo K. Sema, Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Saripuddin D. Jikiri and Nurredha I. Misuari, read on first reading on 19 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Human Settlements and Development on 26 January 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the region faces housing problems from conflict displacement, rapid urbanisation, disasters and unregulated building, and that housing efforts are fragmented, with inconsistent standards and wasted resources. It quotes Section 9, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which directs the Parliament to pass a law creating a housing and human settlements agency for the homeless and victims of conflict.

It presents the bill as fulfilling that mandate by strengthening MHSD and setting building, safety and occupancy standards drawn from international practice and Islamic values.
whoIsAffected: Every household that builds, renovates or occupies a home in the region, which would need MHSD approval for major works.
Low-income families and internally displaced persons, given priority for public housing.
Private developers of subdivisions and condominiums.
Local governments, which would share permitting with MHSD.
implementedBy: Ministry of Human Settlements and Development
Local government units, in coordination

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. It has no appropriations section; MHSD may solicit and receive donations and grants.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, any major renovation of a home in the region would need MHSD's prior approval.
MHSD could fine, revoke permits and order demolition of illegal building works.
Public housing allocation would follow published rules that prioritise low-income and displaced families.
readings.insight:
The bill does not create the agency its note says the Organic Law requires. It designates the existing ministry instead. An earlier bill tried the other route: Bill 92, filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan on 29 September 2022 to create a Bangsamoro Housing Office, was read on first reading on 22 December 2022 and has not moved. MP Ampatuan is a co-author of this bill.

The new powers reach every home in the region, but nothing pays for them. Section 9 requires MHSD approval before any major renovation of any residential building, Section 6 lets MHSD issue construction and occupancy permits, and Section 11 says its permit actions are "without prejudice to permits and clearances issued by other competent authorities", which suggests a builder could need both. The bill has no appropriations clause.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Mujahideen Orphaned Development and Empowerment (MODE) Act of 2026. It establishes an Orphanage Village and Learning Center in the Municipality of Nabalawag, Special Geographic Area, for orphans of mujahideen parents: MILF or MNLF members who died in the armed struggle as combatants or supporters, and civilians who sympathised with the Bangsamoro cause and met similar fates.

The Center would give shelter, food, clothing and health care, formal and non-formal education, technical-vocational and livelihood training, psychosocial counselling and an Islamic unit. Beneficiaries are indigent orphans aged 6 to 30, living in any Bangsamoro community inside the region or elsewhere in Mindanao, acknowledged by MSSD as needing residential care.

MSSD and MBHTE oversee it jointly. A Board of Trustees chaired by MSSD, with MBHTE as associate chair, includes MPW, MHSD, MAFAR, MOLE, MOST, 2 civil society representatives and 2 from the Ulama Council. An Executive Director runs it with teachers, child welfare specialists and social workers.

It was filed on 19 January 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao, read on first reading on 26 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 21 April 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says many children lost one or both parents, combatants or civilians who supported the Bangsamoro struggle, and now face poverty, neglect, interrupted schooling and trauma. It calls helping them a legal and moral obligation and an investment in peace that would break the cycle of poverty and prevent renewed violence.

It cites the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and says funding will come from the regional budget with support from local governments, NGOs and international agencies.
whoIsAffected: Indigent orphans aged 6 to 30 of MILF, MNLF or civilian parents who died in the conflict.
Orphans living in Bangsamoro communities outside the region, elsewhere in Mindanao.
Nabalawag, where the Center would be built.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Board of Trustees of the Center

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs come from current appropriations of MSSD and other ministries, then from the annual Bangsamoro budget, and the Center may accept grants and donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, a residential center for conflict orphans would be built in Nabalawag.
Orphans up to age 30 could receive shelter, schooling and livelihood training there.
readings.insight:
The copy filed carries a leftover name. Section 5(a) ties each learner's stay to a program agreement with "the MOVTC management", a body the bill never creates; the Center is the OVLC. Section 5 also has 2 items lettered (e).

The orphan question has been before Parliament for years. Bill 23 on reparation for orphans of war, and Bills 112 and 143 to establish Bangsamoro orphanages, all filed in 2022 and 2023, were referred together to the Social Services, Women and Youth, and Finance committees on 16 July 2025 and remain there. This bill went to Women and Youth and Finance only.

The registry data used here records the committee referral on 21 January 2026, 5 days before first reading; Parliament's own index gives 21 April 2026, which is the date used above.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Responsible Conflict Characterization Act of the Bangsamoro. It defines rido as a violent, prolonged clan feud marked by retaliation, often with deaths, property destruction or displacement, and a simple dispute as one with no violence, threats or lasting retaliation. It then bars any person, official, media organisation or entity from calling a simple dispute rido, or any similar term, in official documents, public statements or media reports.

Individuals must avoid the word when it does not apply, especially in interviews and large forums. Officials, including law enforcement officers and NGO leaders, must classify conflicts accurately in reports. Media must verify a dispute before using the term.

Willful mischaracterisation is penalised: individuals face a fine of 10,000 to 50,000 or at least 32 hours of community service; officials and media organisations face fines of 50,000 to 100,000 plus a public apology in region-wide media. Penalties start only after a 6-month awareness campaign by the Ministry of Public Order and Safety and MBHTE. The Chief Minister issues the rules within 90 days through a committee chaired by MPOS.

It was filed on 20 January 2026 by MPs Mohammad Kelie U. Antao and Suharto M. Ambolodto, read on first reading on 26 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Public Order and Safety on 21 May 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says rido, a Maranao term for violent clan conflict, is now applied to minor disagreements that involve no violence. It says this inflates the severity of disputes, makes agencies and peacebuilders divert resources from real security threats to matters that barangay or traditional mediation could handle, and dilutes the urgency of genuine clan feuds.

The bill aims to set culturally sensitive criteria for classifying conflicts and encourage accurate reporting.
whoIsAffected: Journalists and media organisations in the region, who could be fined for misusing the term.
Police, military, local officials and NGO leaders who report on local conflicts.
Members of the public who speak about disputes in interviews or public forums.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, for the awareness campaign
Office of the Chief Minister, for the rules
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, calling a non-violent dispute rido in public could bring a fine after a 6-month awareness campaign.
Officials and media found to have willfully mislabelled a dispute would also have to apologise publicly.
readings.insight:
The penalties state no currency. Section 6 sets fines of "10,000 to 50,000" and "50,000 to 100,000" without saying pesos, and does not say who decides that a mischaracterisation was willful or who collects the fine.

The cross-references are off. The unnumbered paragraph after Section 10 says penalties begin after the awareness campaign "as outlined in Section 5"; the campaign is in Section 7, and Section 5 is about who must avoid the term. Section 7 also calls the education ministry "MBSTE".

The bill would fine speech, including media reports, over the choice of a word. A related approach is in Bill 63, filed by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil in 2022 to make conflict sensitivity part of government planning, which has been with the Committee on Public Order and Safety and the Committee on Bangsamoro Justice System since 21 October 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
This would make Ramadhan flextime law for Muslim officials and employees of every regional department, bureau and agency, local government, government corporation with an original charter, and state university and college in the region, whatever their status of appointment.

The standard hours during Ramadhan would be 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and the 40-hour workweek is "deemed satisfied" through flexible or compressed arrangements as the agency head decides, without diminishing public service. Offices whose work does not fit those hours may set their own. Each agency writes its own flextime rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 20 January 2026 by MPs Tomanda D. Antok, Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., Ibrahim P. Ibay, Alindatu K. Pagayao, Butch P. Malang, Ma-Arouph B. Candao and Abdulbasit R. Benito, read on first reading on 26 January 2026 and referred to the Committee on Rules on 27 January 2026. It remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says Muslims in government fast through Ramadhan despite long working hours. Each year the Office of the Chief Minister issues a memorandum circular on Ramadhan working hours, which only repeats Section 3 of Presidential Decree No. 322 of 26 October 1973: Muslim government employees work 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. during the fast. The note says the practice should be fixed in regional law, and calls the measure fair and non-discriminatory.
whoIsAffected: Muslim officials and employees of regional offices, local governments, chartered GOCCs and SUCs in the region who fast.
Agency heads, who decide how the 40-hour week is met.
The public, whose office hours would shift during Ramadhan.
implementedBy: Every covered agency and office, through its own rules
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, Ramadhan hours of 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. would be fixed in regional law instead of an annual circular.
Agencies would no longer need the yearly memorandum to set those hours.
readings.insight:
This is a refiling of Bill 298, almost word for word. Bill 298, filed on 22 April 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua, Eddie M. Alih and Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., has the same title, explanatory note and sections, and was read on first reading on 22 May 2024 and never referred. The copy filed of this bill even keeps the closing block of the old one, a "Certified Correct" line for Secretary General Raby B. Angkal and an "Attested" line for the Speaker, now Mohammad S. Yacob in place of Pangalian M. Balindong.

2 things changed. Bill 298 gave agencies 90 days to write rules; this gives 60. And where Bill 298 added only that "the exigency of the government service shall not be affected", this one says the 40-hour workweek is "deemed satisfied" through flexible or compressed arrangements, which sits uneasily with Section 3(b), unchanged, defining flextime as hours that keep the 40-hour week.

Parliament's index page for this bill points to the title of a different measure, on monthly values formation sessions in government ministries.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Community-Based Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine Act of 2025. It sets up a region-wide rehabilitation program run by the Ministry of Health, delivered through health facilities, mobile outreach teams, home visits and tele-rehabilitation, free at the point of delivery in public facilities subject to available funds.

MOH creates a CBPRM Unit in its central office, provincial focal units in the Integrated Provincial Health Offices, and municipal focal persons where the town agrees. Each CBPRM Team has a physiatrist, a physical therapist, an occupational therapist, a speech pathologist as needed, a rehabilitation aide and a coordinator. If a town does not name a focal person or answer a request to deploy a team within 60 days, MOH may assign an acting focal officer for up to 1 year, renewable, or deploy the team itself. Services include assessment, individual care plans, therapy, assistive devices and referral to higher facilities, with priority for remote and conflict-affected areas, indigenous peoples, displaced people, stroke survivors, persons with disabilities, the elderly and children with developmental delays.

MOH reports to Parliament every year by 30 March, and the rules are due within 90 days.

It was filed on 7 July 2025 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 22 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Health and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 20 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the World Health Organization estimate that at least 1 in 3 people need rehabilitation at some point, and says the region carries a heavy load of untreated injuries, post-stroke disability, congenital impairments and war-related trauma, while services sit in a few urban tertiary hospitals. It gives the region's life expectancy as 63.2 years against a national 71.3, citing the Department of Health and the World Bank, and points to a national shortage of physiatrists and therapists.

It says local and NGO pilots of mobile and home-based care have been fragmented and unfunded, and presents the bill as implementing the Universal Health Care Act and the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities at regional level.
whoIsAffected: Persons with disabilities, stroke survivors, injured and bedridden people, and children with developmental delays, anywhere in the region.
Elderly residents with declining mobility.
Municipal health offices, which would host focal persons and teams, or see MOH act in their place after 60 days.
Barangay health workers and family caregivers, who would be trained to support therapy at home.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, through a new CBPRM Unit
Integrated Provincial Health Offices and municipal health offices
Ministry of Social Services and Development, Ministry of the Interior and Local Government and Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 15 funds the start from MOH's current appropriations, as identified in its Annual Investment Plan, and afterwards from a dedicated CBPRM line in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, MOH would run a standing rehabilitation program with teams, focal units and a central office.
Rehabilitation services in public facilities and outreach would be free at the point of delivery, subject to funds.
MOH could step into a town's role if the town does not respond within 60 days.
readings.insight:
This bill and Bill 375, the senior citizens' wellness bill, were filed by MP Dilangalen on the same day and share text. Section 18 of this bill, the repealing clause, protects "any existing program, benefit, or service for senior citizens in BARMM", word for word the clause in Bill 375, although this bill is about rehabilitation for all ages. The 2 explanatory notes also give different counts of the same group from the same 2020 Census: this one says senior citizens are 3.8% of the population, about 166,700 people; Bill 375 says 181,764, over 4%.

The 2 bills would also stand up overlapping services. Both create mobile teams and home-based care for bedridden elderly people, but this program is led by MOH and Bill 375's by MSSD, each with its own annual report to Parliament due 30 March.

A cross-reference is off. Section 12(a) says the CBPRM Unit's functions are "as provided in Section 10"; they are in Section 9. The bill waited at first reading for 10 months before its committee referral on 20 May 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Healthy Ageing and Wellness Act of 2025. It sets up a program of free health, wellness and social services for residents aged 60 and over, delivered in government facilities, barangay health stations and through outreach, subject to available resources.

The package runs from check-ups, maintenance medicines, vaccines, laboratory tests and dental care to assistive devices, nutrition therapy, mental health care, home visits, legal help with documents, palliative care and links to zakat, sadaqah and waqf support. MOH must set up at least 1 Geriatric Wellness Center in each province and chartered city, possibly inside an existing hospital or rural health unit, and field Mobile Geriatric Health Teams for remote areas. Priority goes to seniors in conflict or disaster areas, those living alone, those with disabilities, the indigent and those in isolated areas. No senior may be refused for lack of documents.

MSSD is named lead agency and keeps a Senior Citizen Health Information System. An Inter-Ministerial Oversight Committee chaired by the MSSD Minister and co-chaired by the MOH Minister meets every quarter, with 2 MPs as observers.

It was filed on 7 July 2025 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 22 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Health, the Committee on Social Services and Development and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 10 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note counts 181,764 people aged 60 and over in the region in the 2020 Census, and cites low coverage: 46% of seniors vaccinated against COVID-19 by mid-2022, 3.8% receiving comprehensive geriatric check-ups in 2021, and influenza and pneumococcal vaccination below 10%. It says the region has no Geriatric Wellness Centers, no senior health information system and no geriatric training for barangay health workers, and that care is split between health centres, local governments and civil society with no shared direction.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region aged 60 and over, especially the poor, the isolated, those living alone and those with disabilities.
Families and caregivers, who would receive training and counselling.
Local governments, which must keep a Senior Citizens Registry and are asked to add counterpart funds.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development, as lead agency
Ministry of Health, for the wellness centres and mobile teams
Inter-Ministerial Oversight Committee

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 16 charges the start to the current appropriations of MSSD and MOH, and afterwards to the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, with local counterpart funds and donor support encouraged.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every province and chartered city would have at least 1 Geriatric Wellness Center.
Senior residents would be entitled to a defined package of free services, subject to resources.
MSSD would keep a region-wide health information system on senior citizens.
readings.insight:
The bill does not settle which ministry is in charge. Section 6 makes MSSD the lead agency, and MSSD writes the rules and the budget plan, but Section 8 has MOH "establish, operate, and maintain" the centres and teams that the bill calls the program's primary implementing mechanisms, and Section 10 has MSSD build the information system while MOH writes the annual report from it. Parliament would receive 3 separate reports: MOH's annual health status report, the oversight committee's annual report and MSSD's semi-annual progress reports.

The figures do not match its companion. Bill 374, MP Dilangalen's rehabilitation bill filed the same day, puts the region's senior citizens at 3.8% of the population, about 166,700, citing the same 2020 Census that this note uses for 181,764, over 4%. Section 7 carries the heading "Priority Groups and Monitoring", repeated from Section 6, over a section that lists services.

The cover page of the explanatory note lists MP Suharto Esmael as a co-author; the bill page behind it and Parliament's index do not.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Solid Waste Management and Sanitary Landfill Phased and Clustered Compliance Act of 2025. It converts the Sub-Committee on Regional Solid Waste Management of the Regional Land Use Committee into a Bangsamoro Regional Solid Waste Management Board attached to MENRE, and requires every province, city and municipality to form its own board.

The regional board approves and monitors local plans, runs a fund, sets tipping fees and permits, and must build a phased compliance framework that sets each town's obligations by its waste volume, capacity, terrain and readiness to cluster. Neighbouring towns may share a sanitary landfill under formal agreements, sited by 9 criteria including room for 5 years of waste, and host towns get incentives. Towns may charge waste fees approved by the board. Prohibited acts and fines are those of Republic Act 9003. Within 90 days MENRE issues an updated regional plan with milestones toward full compliance by 2030.

It was filed on 16 July 2025 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan, read on first reading on 24 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 19 November 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 states the purpose: a systematic mechanism for disposing of solid waste that protects health and the environment, keeps primary responsibility with local governments while adding cooperation from other levels and the private sector, and makes public participation part of waste planning.
whoIsAffected: Every city and municipality in the region, which must have a sanitary landfill under Republic Act 9003 and BAA 49.
Towns that agree to host a shared landfill, and the towns that use it.
Households and businesses, who could be charged waste fees.
Small recyclers, for whom the board must develop safety nets and alternative livelihoods.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Regional Solid Waste Management Board
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy
Provincial, city and municipal solid waste management boards

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 18 creates a Bangsamoro Solid Waste Management Fund from fines, permit fees, donations and grants and from the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, to be used only to help local governments comply and never for salaries.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have a standing solid waste board and boards in every province and town.
Towns could meet the landfill requirement by sharing a site with neighbours.
MENRE would set 2030 as the target year for full compliance.
readings.insight:
Parts of the bill refer to bodies it does not create. The Fund in Section 18 is "to be administered by the Commission", and its sources include permits "issued by the Department"; the bill has no commission or department, and Section 5 gives management of the Fund to the Board. Section 6 has the Board's chairman and vice-chairman preside and lets agency heads send representatives, but no section says who sits on the Board.

Section 12 says the waste fees "shall be used to pay the actual costs incurred by the LGU in collecting the local fees", which read literally covers only the cost of collecting the fee, not of running a landfill.

The same 5 MPs, Sumagayan, Rashdi T. Adiong, Ahmad Amir A. Balindong, Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim and Alirakim T. Munder, are named on the copy of Bill 389, the single-use plastics ban filed 3 weeks later, which leans on this kind of local enforcement.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Barangay Officials Death and Disability Benefit Act of 2025. It gives a one-time payment of ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000 to the heirs of a covered official who dies in office, or to an official who becomes permanently disabled. Covered are the Punong Barangay, kagawads, the barangay secretary and treasurer, the SK chairperson and the Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representative. There is no age limit, and the exact amount is set by MFBM by position and, for disability, by severity.

Payments come from a Barangay Officials Benefit Investment Fund, seeded with at least ₱100,000,000 and managed by the Bangsamoro Treasury Office in Shari'ah-compliant instruments such as sukuk. The principal must stay intact; only returns are spent, partly on contributions to a Takaful operator chosen by competitive procurement. If returns fall short, the Bangsamoro Government must top up. Claims go to MILG for eligibility, then to the Treasury Office for approval. MILG and MFBM write the rules within 3 months.

It was filed on 22 July 2025 by MP Naguib G. Sinarimbo, read on first reading on 24 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Local Government, the Committee on Social Services and Development and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 11 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says barangay officials and SK chairpersons are front-line public servants who work for small honoraria rather than salaries and, unlike other government workers, have no life insurance or survivorship benefit, so their families are left with nothing when they die or are disabled, sometimes from violence in conflict areas. It presents the investment fund and Takaful cover as a sustainable, Shari'ah-compliant way to pay, grounded in the Islamic principle of mutual help, and argues the benefit will draw capable people into barangay and youth posts.
whoIsAffected: Families of barangay officials and SK chairpersons in the region who die in office.
Barangay officials who become permanently disabled.
Barangay secretaries, treasurers and Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representatives, also covered.
A Takaful operator, which would manage the contribution fund under contract.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Bangsamoro Treasury Office

funding.detail: An initial seed fund of not less than ₱100,000,000 from the Bangsamoro Government's annual budget, held as the Barangay Officials Benefit Investment Fund. Only investment returns are paid out, with supplementary Bangsamoro Government funds if returns are insufficient. Benefits run from ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000 per claim.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, heirs of covered officials who die in office would receive ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000.
The Treasury Office would manage a permanent ₱100,000,000 Islamic investment fund.
readings.insight:
The model was reused a month later. Bill 392, filed on 15 August 2025 by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., a co-author of this bill, gives one-time death benefits to families of BIAF shaheed through a "BIAF Shaheed Benefit Investment Fund" and remains at first reading in Parliament's index.

The principal-intact rule does not cap the cost. Section 10 says only returns may be spent, then obliges the Bangsamoro Government to cover any shortfall, so the real ceiling is the number of claims times up to ₱1,000,000. The bill states no estimate of how many officials it covers or how many claims to expect.

The coverage is wider than the title, which names barangay officials and SK chairpersons; Section 4 adds appointed secretaries and treasurers and the IP representative. And Section 2 promises disability assistance only to "the concerned Barangay Official", leaving it unclear whether a disabled SK chairperson qualifies, although Section 5 covers "any covered Barangay Official".

readings.whatItDoes:
The Comprehensive SPEd Service and Support Centers Act of 2025. It has MBHTE set up Comprehensive SPED Service and Support Centers "in strategic locations per province and city" for children with disabilities aged 0 to 18, each offering diagnosis, schooling, therapy, psychosocial and family support, built to universal design standards.

Each centre runs mobile outreach units, keeps a SPED Information and Referral System on enrolled and unenrolled children, runs early detection with barangay health and daycare workers, and organises a council of parent leaders. Centres also do research and adapt curriculum to indigenous and faith traditions, plan for continuity in conflict and disaster, and run transition-to-work programs with MOLE. MBHTE must sign agreements with MOH, MSSD, MIPA, MOLE and MILG, may promote barangay satellite points feeding the centres, and offers scholarships and certification for SPED staff. A monitoring board of civil society, disabled persons' organisations, academics and faith groups oversees compliance.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema, Saripuddin D. Jikiri and Haron M. Abas, read on first reading on 27 October 2025 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 27 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites a 2020 Philippine Statistics Authority report of more than 33,000 children with functional difficulties in the region, and says existing SPED centres are concentrated in urban areas and uneven in quality, leaving children in isolated, conflict-affected and indigenous communities out. It contrasts the bill with Bill 255, which mandates 1 SPED centre per municipality, and proposes instead a hub-and-spoke model in which centres are regional hubs for diagnostics, therapy, teacher training, family support and curriculum work, citing published research on culturally responsive, interagency approaches.
whoIsAffected: Children with disabilities aged 0 to 18, including out-of-school, indigenous and displaced children and those in isolated areas.
Parents and caregivers, through the parent leaders' councils and family support.
SPED teachers, therapists and paraprofessionals, offered scholarships and certification.
Local governments, asked for ordinances, counterpart funds and SPED focal persons.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education

Ministry of Health, Ministry of Social Services and Development, Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, Ministry of Labor and Employment and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, under agreements
SPED Services Monitoring and Accountability Board

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 21 charges the cost to the appropriations of MBHTE, MSSD, MOH and other ministries under the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, and Section 20 requires dedicated funds for assistive technology without naming a figure.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, MBHTE would set up multi-service SPED centres across the provinces and cities, each with mobile outreach units.
The region would have a single information and referral system on children with disabilities.
readings.insight:
This is the 3rd of 3 bills on special education centres, each at a different scale. Bill 255, filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan in October 2023, wants 1 centre per municipality or city and has not moved past first reading. Bill 367, filed by MP Abrar J. Hataman in June 2025, wants 1 per province. This bill's note sets itself against Bill 255 with a hub-and-spoke model, but Section 5 places centres "in strategic locations per province and city", which lands close to Bill 367's scale plus the cities. This bill and Bill 367 were referred to the same 2 committees 3 days apart, on 27 and 30 April 2026.

The closing sections are garbled in the copy filed. Section 22 gives MBHTE 120 days to issue rules, then runs on into the separability clause ("from the effectivity of this Act is declared unconstitutional or invalid"); Section 23 is the separability clause again; Section 24 is headed "Effectivity — Repealing Clause" and Section 25 is the effectivity clause.

Parliament's index lists MP Haron M. Abas as a 6th principal author. The copy filed names 5 and has signature lines for them only.

readings.whatItDoes:
It creates an Administrative and Finance Division in 4 offices under the Office of the Chief Minister: the Office for Settler Communities, the Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office, the Bangsamoro Information Office and the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'. Each division has 6 standard sections: administrative, supply and property procurement, cash, accounting, budget, and management and audit. The Bangsamoro Human Resource and Development Office and MFBM help set positions and qualification standards.

It also grants the 4 offices fiscal autonomy: their appropriations are released automatically and regularly and cannot fall below the previous year's, subject to budget and audit rules. The Chief Minister, through MFBM and BHRDO, writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 5 August 2025 by MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and Susana S. Anayatin, read on first reading on 27 October 2025 and referred to the Committee on Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 10 November 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says 11 offices sit directly under the Office of the Chief Minister and 4 already have fiscal autonomy, while these offices depend on other OCM units for administrative and financial work, causing delays, low budget utilisation and late payments to suppliers. It describes each office's mandate and says its own division would let it disburse, procure and implement programs on time while staying under OCM supervision.
whoIsAffected: Staff and programs of the 4 offices, which would handle their own procurement, cash and accounts.
Settler communities, digital government users, the public receiving government information, and those served by the Darul-Ifta'.
Other OCM units that now process these offices' transactions.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Bangsamoro Human Resource and Development Office

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 7 funds the start from the covered agencies' existing appropriations and later from the annual Bangsamoro budget. Section 6 guarantees each office no less than the previous year's appropriation.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the 4 offices would each gain a 6-section administrative and finance division.
Their budgets could not be cut below the previous year's and would be released automatically.
readings.insight:
The note's arithmetic does not add up. It says 11 offices are under the Chief Minister and 4 have fiscal autonomy, then calls "the remaining 5" without autonomy and names 4. Take 4 from 11 and 7 remain.

MP Susana S. Anayatin, a principal author, signs the note and the bill as "Executive Director, Office for Settler Communities", one of the 4 offices that would gain a budget floor. The note also says the measure "amends the Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13" to create the Darul-Ifta' division, but the bill has no amending section; it relies on its general repealing clause.

Fiscal autonomy for the settlers' office was proposed before. Bill 309, filed in June 2024 with MP Mitmug among its principal authors, would rename the office and give it fiscal autonomy, and has not moved past first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Single-Use Plastics Regulation Act of 2025. After a 1-year transition, it bans the manufacture, import, distribution, sale and use of single-use plastics in the region, including plastic bags, straws, stirrers, cutlery, cups, lids, thin film, sachets and styrofoam containers, and goods pre-packaged in them. It applies to businesses, public institutions and individual consumers.

Exemptions cover medical, pharmaceutical and sanitary uses, products with no certified alternative (by MENRE certificate of up to 12 months), and disaster relief, with a recovery plan due to MENRE within 30 days. Manufacturers, importers and distributors must register take-back plans with MENRE, aligned with the national Extended Producer Responsibility law, and no business permit is issued without one. Every province, city, municipality and barangay must pass an ordinance adopting the ban within the transition, and enforces it.

Penalties are a warning and compliance seminar for a first offence, a fine of up to ₱2,000 for a second, and up to ₱5,000 and/or a business permit suspension of up to 30 days after that. MENRE must prepare a Just Transition Plan for affected workers and businesses within 6 months.

It was filed on 8 August 2025 by MP Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim, read on first reading on 10 November 2025 and referred to the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy on 28 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says single-use plastics clog the region's rivers, coasts and uplands, citing global plastic production above 400 million metric tons a year, national data that plastic bags are the most common single-use plastic, and DENR's list of the most problematic items. It grounds the ban in the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology, Republic Act 9003 and the Organic Law, and points to Davao City and Palanan as places where local bans have worked with education and enforcement.
whoIsAffected: Shops, food businesses, markets and manufacturers that use or sell single-use plastic.
Consumers, who are covered by the ban on use.
Micro, small and medium enterprises, offered possible subsidies, tax relief and transition support.
Every local government in the region, which must legislate and enforce the ban.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy
Every province, city, municipality and barangay
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for local compliance

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 17 charges the start to the current appropriations of MENRE and MILG, and afterwards to the concerned agencies' budgets in the Bangsamoro appropriations act.
