whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, single-use plastics would be banned across the region after 1 year, with exemptions.
Plastic producers would need a registered take-back plan to get or renew a business permit.
Every local government would have to pass a matching ordinance within 1 year.
readings.insight:
The schedule contradicts itself. Section 7 bans straws, stirrers, cutlery and thin-film bags within the "first 6 months", but Section 5 makes nothing unlawful until the transition period ends, and Section 20 says the prohibitions and penalties are enforceable "only upon the lapse of the one (1)-year transition period".

An earlier, narrower bill is still pending. Bill 248, filed by MPs Amilbahar S. Mawallil and Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. in October 2023, would regulate rather than ban single-use plastics and has not moved past first reading. This bill's 5 MPs are the same group named on Bill 378, the solid waste and sanitary landfill bill filed 3 weeks earlier.

The ban reaches further than most local ordinances it cites as models: it covers sachets and goods pre-packaged in single-use plastic, and individual use, though the penalties top out at ₱5,000.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Timely Salary Release Act of 2025. When a scheduled payday falls on a Saturday, Sunday or declared non-working holiday, the government office must release salaries on the last working day before it.

It covers regular, contractual and casual employees of the Bangsamoro Government, its ministries, offices and agencies, local governments and government-owned or controlled corporations in the region, however they are paid. Private employers are expressly excluded. MFBM and the Civil Service Commission's regional office write the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 15 August 2025 by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., read on first reading on 10 November 2025 and referred to the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 20 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says national and regional rules require timely pay but do not provide for early release when payday falls on a non-working day, so employees wait until the next working day for money that should already be theirs, often when weekend and holiday needs arise.
whoIsAffected: Regular, contractual and casual employees of the Bangsamoro Government and its agencies.
Employees of local governments and government corporations in the region.
Payroll and cash offices, which would have to pay earlier.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Civil Service Commission, BARMM regional office
Every covered government office

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. It changes only when salaries already budgeted are released.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, a payday on a weekend or holiday would move to the last working day before it.
The rule would apply to local governments and government corporations, not only regional offices.
readings.insight:
It is a 9-section bill with a single operative rule, Section 5, and no penalty, sanction or remedy if an office pays late anyway. It still waited 6 months between first reading on 10 November 2025 and its committee referral on 20 May 2026.

The coverage goes beyond the offices whose payrolls MFBM controls: local governments and government corporations pay from their own funds, and the bill does not say how the rule applies to them. A related, older measure on late pay is Bill 41, filed by the Government of the Day in 2022, which would create a buffer fund to pay personnel of nationally funded programs on time and has been in committee since 27 September 2022.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Datu Saudi Ampatuan Municipal Hospital Act of 2025. It establishes a Level I general hospital with 25 beds in the Municipality of Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur, under the administrative supervision and control of the Ministry of Health, which approves its structure, staff and plans. The hospital is to integrate the Universal Health Care Act into its operations, and MOH writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 15 August 2025 by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., read on first reading on 10 November 2025 and referred to the Committee on Health and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 11 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 restates the general policy of comprehensive health services and a general hospital system able to respond to emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases. Nothing in the copy describes Datu Saudi Ampatuan's population, its distance to the nearest hospital or any existing facility.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Datu Saudi Ampatuan and neighbouring towns in Maguindanao del Sur.
The Ministry of Health, which would build, staff and run the hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 tells MOH to include the hospital in its program, funded through the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, Datu Saudi Ampatuan would have a 25-bed Level I hospital run by MOH.
readings.insight:
The repealing clause names a different hospital. Section 9 repeals laws "regarding the construction, establishment and operations of the Gambar Municipal Hospital", which appears nowhere else in the bill; the copy was adapted from another hospital bill. Section 3 writes the size as "twenty (25)", and Section 5 calls the facility an "upgraded hospital" though the bill creates a new one.

The 25-bed size matches what Parliament has settled on when it passes municipal hospital bills: BAA 66 cut South Ubian's request from 50 beds to 25, BAA 76 did the same for Sibutu, and BAA 67 turned Pura's requested infirmary of 10 to 15 beds into a hospital of at least 25. The bill gives no population or need figures to support even that, unlike the hospital bills that compute a bed shortage from census data.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Assistance for Inclusive Development Act of 2025, or Bangsamoro Aid. It sets up a Bangsamoro Development Assistance Plan for Bangsamoro people living outside the region: water and electricity, small infrastructure such as roads, clinics, madaris and housing, education and scholarships, health and social welfare, livelihood, cultural programs and local government capacity. Disaster aid is excluded.

A Bangsamoro Development Assistance and Management Council, chaired by the Chief Minister with 14 ministers, the heads of the planning authority, the cultural heritage, women and youth commissions, and representatives of donors, NGOs and the communities, designates areas: Bangsamoro Populated Communities (at least 2 adjacent barangays dominated by Bangsamoro people), Bangsamoro Populated Areas (1 or more municipalities) and Specially Designated Areas. The existing Office for Other Bangsamoro Communities is its secretariat and must recommend areas within 120 days. The Council approves projects and may promote sister-city ties between towns inside and outside the region.

A Bangsamoro Aid Fund starts with ₱100,000,000 from the Office of the Chief Minister, and each concerned ministry must afterwards set aside at least 5% of its approved budget for these areas.

It was filed on 26 August 2025 by MPs Hussein P. Muñoz, Omar Yasser C. Sema, Abdullah G. Macapaar, Suharto S. Esmael, Said M. Shiek, Matarul M. Estino, Amiroddin Y. Gayak, Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Faizal G. Karon and Bai Ali S. Karon, read on first reading on 10 November 2025 and referred to the Committee on Social Services and Development and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 20 January 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note quotes Article VI, Section 12 of the Organic Law, under which the national government protects Bangsamoro communities outside the region and the Bangsamoro Government, with local governments and national agencies, shall assist their economic, social and cultural development. It also cites the Constitution's social justice provision, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code and the peace agreements, and says much remains to be done for Bangsamoro people beyond the region's borders.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro people and communities outside the region, once designated by the Council.
Every concerned ministry, which must reserve at least 5% of its budget for those areas.
Local governments outside the region where the communities live, as partners.
The Office for Other Bangsamoro Communities, which becomes the Council's permanent secretariat.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Development Assistance and Management Council
Office for Other Bangsamoro Communities
Concerned Bangsamoro ministries and offices

funding.detail: An initial ₱100,000,000 for a Bangsamoro Aid Fund, sourced from the Office of the Chief Minister. Afterwards, regular budgets from the concerned ministries, at least 5% of each ministry's approved budget, plus possible national, donor and private funds managed by the Council.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, regional funds could be spent on projects in Bangsamoro communities outside the region.
Each concerned ministry would carry a 5% minimum allocation for those communities.
3 sub-paragraphs of BAA 13 would be repealed.
readings.insight:
The 5% floor is the bill's largest commitment, and it is open-ended. Section 12 requires "not less than 5%" of the approved budget of each "concerned" ministry for areas outside the region, without saying which ministries are concerned. The Council alone lists 14 ministries, so the floor could reach a large share of the regional budget, against an initial fund of ₱100,000,000.

The note builds on Section 8, Paragraph D of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code as a foundation, and Section 17 then expressly repeals sub-paragraphs b, c and d of that same paragraph, without saying what they provide or why they go.

The copy's header reads "Second Regular Session"; Parliament's index places the bill in the Fourth Regular Session, as filed in August 2025. The Council list also abbreviates the Bangsamoro Women Commission as "BMC".

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Values Formation Act. Every ministry, office and agency of the Bangsamoro Government must hold an Islamic Values Formation Session once a month, lasting at least 2 hours, on a day each office chooses to suit its work.

The Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' supplies the facilitators, keeps a Values Formation Module adaptable to each office, and makes sure sessions follow Shari'ah, moral governance and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code. Before sessions begin, it runs a needs assessment survey that at least 10% of each office's workforce must answer, and the results set the topics.

Each office's HR officer or Personnel Development Committee writes the sessions into the annual HR Development Plan and records attendance in employees' HRD records. Attending at least 1 session a year counts as the mandatory HRD intervention under the Civil Service Code. Offices report quarterly to the Darul-Ifta' and the "BHRO", and the Darul-Ifta' sends an annual report to the Chief Minister. The bill has 10 sections.

It was filed on 20 January 2026 by MP Tawakal B. Midtimbang and 8 other MPs, read on first reading on 26 January 2026, and taken up on second reading in plenary, where after an authorship speech it was deferred on 27 January 2026. Parliament's index records no later action.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 gives the purpose: to promote moral governance and strengthen the ethical foundations of public service, citing Section 3 of Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and Article 101 of the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code, BAA 17, and recognising the importance of Islamic values and ethical guidance in developing the workforce.
whoIsAffected: Every employee of the Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies, who would be offered a 2-hour session every month.
HR officers and Personnel Development Committees, who must plan, record and report the sessions.
The Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', which must staff sessions across the whole bureaucracy.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'
Every ministry, office and agency of the Bangsamoro Government

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. The copy filed has no funding section.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was deferred on second reading on 27 January 2026 and has not moved since.
If enacted, every office would hold a 2-hour Islamic values session each month.
1 session a year would satisfy each employee's mandatory HRD intervention under the Civil Service Code.
The Darul-Ifta' would gain a standing role in civil service training.
readings.insight:
This bill moved fast, then stopped. It was filed on 20 January 2026, read on first reading 6 days later and in plenary the next day, 27 January 2026, with no committee referral recorded in Parliament's index. It was deferred there and has not moved since.

The obligation is lighter than the title suggests. Offices must hold a session every month, but Section 6 says attending 1 a year meets an employee's mandatory HRD intervention. That matches what BAA 17 already allows: Article 101 of the Civil Service Code says HRD interventions "may include Islamic values formation trainings" and requires at least 1 planned intervention a year. What the bill adds is the monthly schedule and the Darul-Ifta's role.

The copy has loose ends. The short title is the "Bangsamoro Values Formation Act of 2025", though it was filed in 2026. Section 7 sends reports to a "BHRO" the bill never defines. The co-author line on the copy names 8 MPs, while Parliament's index lists 17.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Job Portal Act of 2026. Every vacant position authorised to be filled in the Bangsamoro ministries, chartered corporations, state universities and colleges and local governments must be published in the Bangsamoro Job Portal and posted in at least 3 conspicuous places: for 10 calendar days in regional agencies and at least 15 in local governments.

No recruitment, selection or appointment may happen until the post is open for applications on the Portal. Each listing must give the position title, salary grade, qualification standards, plantilla item number, duties, requirements and deadline, and display the total number of applicants. Confidential, policy-determining, highly technical, coterminous and some reappointment posts are exempt, as are posts filled by existing staff in a reorganisation.

An appointment made without Portal posting may be disapproved or invalidated, and officials who fail to post or help get around the rule face administrative charges under the Civil Service Code. The Office of the Chief Minister runs the Portal, writes the rules within 90 days and receives ₱3,000,000 for initial operations.

It was filed on 4 February 2026 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and 8 other MPs, read on first reading on 21 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Labor and Employment on 30 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 gives the purpose: efficiency, transparency and equal opportunity in recruitment and hiring, consistent with the aspiration for a responsive and effective bureaucracy.
whoIsAffected: Job seekers, who would see every covered vacancy in one place, with the number of applicants shown.
HR officers, boards of chartered corporations and mayors and governors, who become personally responsible for posting.
Appointees whose appointment skipped the Portal, who could see it invalidated.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
HR officers of every ministry, office, agency, corporation and local government

funding.detail: ₱3,000,000 for the initial operations of the Office of the Chief Minister for the Portal, with no source named. Later costs go into the OCM's annual budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, no covered post could be filled until it had been listed on the Portal.
Listings would have to show how many people have applied.
Appointments made without Portal posting could be invalidated, and officials disciplined.
readings.insight:
Most of this is already law. The Bangsamoro Civil Service Code, BAA 17, already requires vacancies to be published in the Bangsamoro Job Portal and posted in 3 conspicuous places, for at least 10 calendar days in regional agencies and 15 in local governments. Section 3 of the bill cites that very provision, Article 26 of the Code, and repeats it.

What is new is narrower: the bar on recruiting before a post is on the Portal, the requirement to show the number of applicants, the threat of invalidation and discipline, naming the Office of the Chief Minister as the Portal's keeper, and the ₱3,000,000.

The copy has small slips. It expands "SUCs" as "Schools, Universities, and Colleges", where the Code covers state universities and colleges, and Section 9 tells the OCM to ensure compliance with "this Section" rather than this Act.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Commission on Early Childhood Care and Development as the region's policy, regulatory and oversight body for services to children from conception to 5 years old. It has a Chairman and 4 Commissioners appointed by the Chief Minister for 3-year terms, renewable once, each with at least a master's degree and 10 years in the field. The Chairman holds the rank of a Minister.

All powers, personnel, assets and funds directly and exclusively tied to early childhood care in MSSD, MBHTE, the Ministry of Health, MILG, MFBM and local governments transfer to the Commission. It accredits Child Development Centers, certifies Child Development Teachers and Workers, runs technical panels, and is advised by a board chaired by the Chief Minister. Its Chairman would also chair the boards of all regional and local educational institutions and Child Development Centers in the region.

A Bangsamoro Early Childhood Care and Development Fund of ₱200,000,000 is split 40% to centers, 30% to teachers and workers, 15% to nutrition, health and protection, 10% to research and monitoring and 5% to operations, plus ₱20,000,000 for start-up. A Transitory Body chaired by the head of MSSD writes the rules within 3 months.

It was filed on 23 February 2026 by MP Tomanda D. Antok and 7 other MPs, read on first reading on 21 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities on 21 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the region has the country's highest stunting rate at 34.3%, highest anemia prevalence at 16.9% and most severe household food insecurity at 48.2%, and functional literacy of 64.7%, falling to 32.7% in Tawi-Tawi. About 44% of children aged 3 to 5 are in no early childhood program; there are 1,903 functional Child Development Centers against 9,042 needed, 2,732 Child Development Workers against 18,084 needed, and nearly 700 barangays with no center.

It blames split responsibility, with health covering ages 0 to 2, social services 3 to 4 and education 5 to 6, and says a single regional commission is needed to carry out the national ECCD System Act, Republic Act 12199 of 2025, in a culturally sensitive and faith-responsive way.
whoIsAffected: Children from conception to age 5 and their parents.
Child Development Teachers and Workers, whose posts, training and certification would move to the Commission.
Staff of MSSD, MBHTE, the Ministry of Health and local governments working on early childhood, who would be transferred.
Schools and centers whose governing boards the Commission Chairman would chair.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission on Early Childhood Care and Development
Transitory Body chaired by the head of MSSD
MSSD, MBHTE, MOH, MILG and MFBM, which hand over their early childhood functions

funding.detail: ₱200,000,000 as seed capital for the Bangsamoro Early Childhood Care and Development Fund from the annual block grant, and ₱20,000,000 from unappropriated funds in the Regional Treasury for the Commission's initial operation. MBHTE's current early childhood appropriations transfer to the Commission; later costs go into the annual appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, early childhood programs now spread across ministries would move to a single commission.
A ₱200,000,000 fund would be split by fixed shares, 40% of it for Child Development Centers.
Staff working on early childhood in several ministries and local governments would be transferred.
readings.insight:
Section 20 reaches far beyond early childhood. It makes the Commission Chairman chair of the Board of Regents or Trustees of "all Bangsamoro regional and local educational institutions". That would collide with laws already in force: BAA 40, for one, makes the Minister of Science and Technology chair of the Bangsamoro Science High School System's Board of Trustees.

The note and the text do not line up. The note spends a paragraph on licensure and accreditation trouble for teacher education graduates and lists "clarify accreditation, certification, and licensure pathways" as an aim, but no section deals with it. The fund is also sourced 2 ways: Section 12 says Bangsamoro Government appropriations, Section 21 says the annual block grant.

Other details are loose. Children aged 5 to 8 are to be served with the national Department of Education under Republic Act 10533, not MBHTE. The Transitory Body includes the chair of a Parliament committee. The bill takes effect "upon its approval", with no publication. MP Alindatu K. Pagayao is named as both a principal author and a co-author on the copy.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Magna Carta of Persons with Disabilities in the Bangsamoro, an 80-section code. Title II sets out rights to life, equality, legal capacity, liberty, freedom from torture and vilification, privacy, family, education, health, work, social protection and political participation. Title III turns them into duties: accessible public buildings and evacuation centers, sign language interpreters in courts, inclusive schooling, a rehabilitation center in government provincial hospitals and an accessible sports complex in each province.

At least 1% of appointive posts in every ministry and local government is reserved for persons with disabilities, and proof of compliance, or an explanation, must be filed before funds are released. MSSD would pay a Disability Support Allowance of ₱2,000 a month, phased in over 3 stages: children and people with significant disabilities first, then those on low incomes, then everyone after 6 years.

A Bangsamoro Committee on Disability Affairs, chaired by MSSD under the Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council, sets policy, with a new Persons with Disabilities Division in MSSD as its secretariat. The Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission becomes the PWD Ombud. Discrimination is punishable by fines of ₱100,000 to ₱500,000 and prison terms of up to 12 years, and non-residents who offend may be declared persona non grata.

It was filed on 30 March 2026 by the Government of the Day, read on first reading on 22 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities on 28 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 cites Section 23 of Article IX and Section 2(r) of Article V of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and commits the government to the full and equal enjoyment of rights by persons with disabilities, their dignity and autonomy, and their integration into society. The copy is signed by Raissa H. Jajurie as Minister of Social Services and Development.
whoIsAffected: Persons with disabilities in the region, who would gain enforceable rights and a ₱2,000 monthly allowance once phased in.
Every ministry and local government, which must reserve 1% of posts or explain why not before funds are released.
Families and carers, who face serious illegal detention penalties for locking away or chaining a relative with disability.
Businesses and individuals, who face fines and imprisonment for discrimination or denying access.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Bangsamoro Committee on Disability Affairs
Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, as PWD Ombud

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed, although the title says "providing funds therefor". The Disability Support Allowance is ₱2,000 a month per person, with MSSD to identify the fund requirement; Section 75 says funds for the ID system go to MSSD in later fiscal years. The PWD Facilities Strengthening Fund and the research fund are created with no amount.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, persons with disabilities would receive ₱2,000 a month, starting with children and those with significant disabilities.
1% of government posts would be reserved for persons with disabilities.
Discrimination, vilification and forced seclusion would become crimes with prison terms.
readings.insight:
The 1% hiring quota has a built-in exit. Section 45 makes proof of compliance a condition for the release of funds, but lets an office submit "an explanation or justification" instead, and leaves it to the new Committee to decide what explanations are acceptable. How binding the quota is depends on rules not yet written.

The allowance is the costliest promise and the least costed. At ₱2,000 a month it is ₱24,000 a year per person, it replaces existing regional support for persons with disabilities, and it is indexed to inflation every 3 years, yet the bill has no appropriation section and no estimate of how many people would qualify.

The penalties are heavy for a regional law. Discrimination can bring up to 12 years on a repeat offence, vilification 6 to 12 years, and a non-resident offender can be declared persona non grata, a sanction the bill does not define.

readings.whatItDoes:
This amends BAA 40, the Bangsamoro Science High School System Act of 2023. The Chairperson of the Board of Trustees, the Minister of Science and Technology, would appoint all officials and personnel of the System, including unique positions, and would appoint the 2 private sector trustees subject to Board confirmation.

The Executive Committee would be made up of all Campus Directors and headed by a Bangsamoro Executive Director appointed by the Board. While there is only 1 campus, the Campus Director, the department heads and other senior faculty form it instead. The amended sections also restyle the posts as "Bangsamoro Campus Director" and "Bangsamoro Executive Director".

A new Section 12 exempts faculty from any civil service examination or regulation as a requirement for appointment; the Board sets its own criteria, such as competitive examinations. The bill has 9 sections.

It was filed on 31 March 2026 by MP Suharto S. Esmael, read on first reading on 22 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws, the Committee on Science and Technology and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 29 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note, and the text gives no reason for the changes.
whoIsAffected: Teachers at the Bangsamoro Science High School, who could be hired without civil service eligibility.
Applicants for staff posts, who would be appointed by the Minister of Science and Technology as Board Chairperson.
The Board of Trustees, which would lose the appointment power to its Chairperson.
implementedBy: Ministry of Science and Technology
Board of Trustees of the Bangsamoro Science High School System

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The title says "providing funds therefor", but no section appropriates anything.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the Minister of Science and Technology would appoint all staff of the System.
Science high school faculty would no longer need civil service eligibility to be appointed.
readings.insight:
The title promises more than the text delivers. It lists Sections 6, 7, 8, 10 and 11 of BAA 40 as amended, but the body never touches Section 11, which gives each Campus Director a fixed 4-year term removable only for just cause. It also says "providing funds therefor", and appropriates nothing.

The real change is in who hires. Under BAA 40 the Board sets policy on appointment and promotion; this bill gives the Chairperson alone power to appoint everyone, and adds the civil service exemption for faculty. Together they would let 1 official hire faculty outside the civil service eligibility rules.

The effectivity clause refers to the "Official Gazette" rather than the Bangsamoro Gazette, and the new Section 12 calls the System the "BSH System".

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Transportation and Communications Code, a 118-section code in 13 books. It makes the Ministry of Transportation and Communications the region's main policy, regulatory and quasi-judicial authority over transport and communications operating exclusively within the region, and recognises 7 sectoral offices: a Land Transportation Office, a Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board, a Maritime Industry Authority, a Ports Management Authority, a Civil Aviation Authority for landside airport operations, a Civil Aeronautics Board and a Telecommunications Commission.

It sets rules for driver's licences, vehicle registration and roadworthiness, franchises and fares, vessel registration, compulsory maritime insurance, manning and safety, ports and private wharves, and courier and ticketing businesses. Traditional wooden-hull vessels get a "Safety Upgrade, Not Shutdown" transition: a registry, interim authority to operate and help to upgrade before non-compliant boats are phased out.

The Ministry and its offices get fiscal autonomy, and the Maritime Industry Authority keeps 50% of its regulatory revenue in a BMARINA Trust Fund. Violations bring fines, suspension, revocation and detention of vehicles or vessels, with fine amounts left to the rules. The Ministry writes the rules within 180 days and prepares a Transportation and Communications Master Plan.

It was filed on 13 April 2026 by MP Romeo K. Sema and 8 other MPs, read on first reading on 22 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Transportation and Communications on 27 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the lack of a unified regulatory framework has fragmented authority and hampered services, and that a code is needed to institutionalise the Ministry and its sectoral offices and define their powers. It quotes Sections 38 and 39 of Article XIII of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which give the region authority over regional transport and telecommunications franchises, registration and quasi-judicial powers.

It also calls transport and communications income-generating sectors, and says the Ministry needs ways to generate, retain and reinvest revenue in regulation, safety and modernisation.
whoIsAffected: Drivers, vehicle owners and public utility operators running routes within the region.
Boat owners and passengers in island and coastal communities, including traditional wooden-hull vessels.
Port and wharf operators, regional airlines, telecommunications utilities, couriers and ticket sellers operating only within the region.
implementedBy: Ministry of Transportation and Communications
Its 7 sectoral offices, from the Land Transportation Office to the Telecommunications Commission

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. The Maritime Industry Authority would retain 50% of its regulatory revenue in a BMARINA Trust Fund, its use subject to legislative appropriation, and the Ministry may charge fees.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have its own licensing, franchising and safety rules for transport within its borders.
Existing permits would stay valid until they expire.
Unregistered vessels would become unauthorised after a transition period.
readings.insight:
The title says the bill amends "relevant provisions" of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, but no section of the text names or amends any provision of it. The Code is written as a new law alongside BAA 13, with a general repealing clause.

The appeals route contradicts itself. Section 106 says the Minister's decision on appeal "shall be final within the executive branch"; Section 107 then allows an appeal to the Chief Minister. Section 18 also gives the Civil Aviation Authority the alternative name Bangsamoro Airport Authority, abbreviated "BAA", the same abbreviation used for every Bangsamoro Autonomy Act.

There is a sibling on maritime safety. Bill 440, filed on 11 March 2026 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan and others, would create a separate Bangsamoro Maritime Safety Office; it was read on first reading the same day as this bill, 22 April 2026. Both give vessel inspection and safety to a regional body, and they are not reconciled.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Maternal Wellness and Safe Pregnancy Act of 2026. Every pregnant woman in the region would be entitled to a Maternal Wellness Package: free prenatal checkups and screening, vitamins and iron-folic acid, nutrition support, mental health screening and counselling, health education, facility-based delivery, postnatal care, and referral and emergency transport, especially in geographically isolated areas. The Ministry of Health would also build or upgrade barangay birthing facilities.

Barangay Health Workers would be required to help pregnant women and new mothers with PhilHealth: checking membership, enrolling indigent women, preparing and filing claim documents, tracking claims and appealing denials. Every barangay must set up a Barangay PhilHealth Facilitation Desk run by trained health workers, claims documents must be completed within 5 working days of delivery where feasible, and no mother may be discharged without being offered this help.

Health workers doing claims work would get extra honoraria, transport allowance and supplies, subject to available funds. A grievance mechanism covers illegal fees, discrimination and withheld documents. The bill has 23 sections.

It was filed on 13 April 2026 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and 22 other MPs, read on first reading on 28 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities, the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management and the Committee on Health on 18 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Sections 2 and 3 give the purpose: to reduce preventable maternal and newborn illness and death, increase early prenatal checkups and facility births, cut out-of-pocket costs through better use of PhilHealth, and make sure no eligible mother loses benefits because of paperwork, distance or administrative barriers.
whoIsAffected: Pregnant women and new mothers, especially in geographically isolated areas.
Barangay Health Workers, who would take on PhilHealth claims work.
Barangays, each required to run a PhilHealth Facilitation Desk.
Midwives, nurses and rural health units, who would supervise and be trained.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Barangay Health Workers under rural health units
MSSD, MILG and MIPA, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Costs are charged against current Ministry of Health appropriations and then the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, with an optional line item for health worker training and incentives, claims desks, and digitisation.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every barangay would need a PhilHealth Facilitation Desk.
Health workers would be required to help mothers file PhilHealth maternity claims.
Pregnant women would be entitled to a defined package of free prenatal and postnatal care.
readings.insight:
The bill puts mandatory duties on volunteers. Section 4 defines a Barangay Health Worker as a "trained volunteer", yet Section 10 says all of them "shall" verify membership, file papers and track claims, and the extra pay in Section 15 is "subject to availability of funds". The duties are fixed; the support is optional.

It was referred to the Finance committee with no figure to examine: the copy names no amount and draws on the Health Ministry's current budget.

The author list on this copy is close to the one on Bill 453, MP Dumama-Alba's waste bill filed 3 days later: 21 of the 23 names are the same. Part of the monitoring section is illegible in the copy, and its section number cannot be read.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Asthma Care Act of 2026. The Minister of Health would give grants to public and non-profit groups for asthma and respiratory projects in low-income communities: screening and referral, information and education, and workshops for parents, teachers, coaches and school nurses.

Screening is to happen in hospitals and clinics and also in schools, daycare centres, community centres, public housing, convenience stores and cash assistance offices. Information must be in the language and cultural context of those it is meant for, and cover symptoms, prevention, medication such as carrying an inhaler, and treatment plans that let asthmatic children play sport. Grantees must be community-based organisations or involve one substantially. The Minister may also contract a region-wide media campaign focused on children.

The Minister reports on how many people were screened and referred and how well the projects worked. The bill has 10 sections.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 27 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Health on 18 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the Constitution's right to health and says that according to the World Health Organization 12% of a Philippine population of 90 million have asthma, about 1 in 10 Filipinos, and 98% of them lack proper treatment. It says asthma kills about 1,000 people a day worldwide and affects up to 339 million, with low- and middle-income countries hit hardest. Asthma has no cure but can be managed, and the government should provide more accessible treatment for those living in poverty.
whoIsAffected: Low-income families and children with asthma or other respiratory problems.
Community-based and non-profit organisations, which could apply for grants.
Schools, daycare centres and community centres, which become screening and education sites.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 has the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management add the cost to the Ministry of Health's budget in the first year, and to its annual appropriations after.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the Ministry of Health could fund community groups to screen and educate on asthma.
Screening would reach schools, daycare centres and cash assistance offices.
readings.insight:
The text does not fit the Bangsamoro government. Section 4 says grant applications go to "the Secretary", in a form "the Secretary" decides, though the bill defines only the Minister. It refers to paragraphs "(B)(1)" and "(B)(2)" that are lettered (a) and (b), Section 6 provides pay for "newly established positions" when none are created, and Section 7 has rules written with "the Institutions", which are never named.

The explanatory note gives no figures for the region, only national and global ones. The copy is headed "Third Regular Session", though it was filed in the fourth, and it ends with an "Adopted" block certified by the Secretary General and attested by the Speaker, as if passed.

The same is true of Bill 452, filed by MP Dilangalen the same day: same session heading, same adoption block, and the same 12 co-authors in the same order on the copy. Parliament's index lists 29 co-authors for this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Children's Information Office Act. It creates a Bangsamoro Children's Information Office attached to the Office of the Chief Minister and headed by an Executive Director the Chief Minister appoints, to build and run a Bangsamoro Children's Integrated Database System linking child records held by MOH, MSSD and MBHTE.

The system gives each child a reference number linked to PhilSys and civil registry identifiers, keeps a limited profile of registration, health, nutrition, schooling and welfare data, shares data between agencies, and sends alerts and referrals when a child misses a service such as a vaccination. Agencies stay the custodians of their own data. It may not be used for profiling or surveillance, and law enforcement access needs a court order.

An Inter-Agency Steering Committee oversees it, and a Data Protection Review Board audits it. The rollout is a pilot in the first year, and the Office reports to Parliament every year. The bill has 20 sections.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 18 May 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 18 June 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says a child's records start in the Ministry of Health with newborn screening and immunisation, move to MSSD if the child is vulnerable, and then to MBHTE's Bangsamoro Education Management Information System, and are not linked, so no one sees the whole picture. It warns that each ministry's own digital projects risk creating new silos and ties the bill to the Enhanced 12-Point Priority Agenda's e-governance commitment.

It places the Office under the Chief Minister to give it the authority to compel ministries to cooperate, neutrality between sectors, and a signal of priority.
whoIsAffected: Every child in the region, who would have a linked record across health, welfare and schooling.
Parents and guardians, whose consent and data rights the bill addresses.
MOH, MSSD, MBHTE and local governments, which must share data under common standards.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Children's Information Office
Office of the Chief Minister
Inter-Agency Steering Committee of MSSD, MOH, MBHTE and PSA-BARMM

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed, although the title says "appropriating funds therefor". Initial costs come from available funds of the Bangsamoro Government, then the annual appropriations act; the Office must prepare a budget projection covering at least 5 years.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, a new office under the Chief Minister would link children's records across ministries.
Ministries would get alerts when a child misses a service.
Children's data would get a dedicated oversight board.
readings.insight:
The rollout timeline does not add up. Section 9 sets a 5-year rollout period, then requires full deployment by the end of the third year.

Section 2 grounds a children's bill in the Magna Carta of Women, Republic Act 9710, alongside the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The Data Protection Review Board is called independent, but its members include representatives of the very office it audits, and the bill does not say who appoints them.

The copy is headed "Third Regular Session", though it was filed in the fourth, and ends with an "Adopted" block certified by the Secretary General and attested by the Speaker. Bill 449, MP Dilangalen's asthma bill filed the same day, has the same heading, block and 12 co-authors on the copy; Parliament's index lists 28 co-authors for this one.

readings.whatItDoes:
The May Ayuda sa Basura Act of BARMM. It sets up a region-wide trash-to-cash program in every province, city, municipality and barangay: residents bring segregated recyclable waste to community collection points and receive ayuda credits based on type, weight and quality, redeemable for cash, food packs, utility subsidies, school supplies or digital vouchers. Low-income households, displaced people and informal waste workers come first.

The program is run by the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy with MSSD, MILG and MBHTE, which is to put environmental and Islamic stewardship education into school curricula. Local governments set up Materials Recovery Facilities and collection points. Mosques, madaris and ulama are encouraged to preach stewardship, amanah and khalifa in khutbah and join clean-up drives.

Improperly sorted waste earns no credit, local governments may penalise failure to segregate, and repeat violators can be given environmental community service. MENRE tracks volumes and impact and reports yearly to Parliament. The bill has 15 sections.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and 23 other MPs, read on first reading on 29 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, the Committee on Labor and Employment and the Committee on Local Government on 18 June 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says poor waste disposal causes flooding, pollution and damage to natural resources, and that the Islamic principles of amanah, trust, and khalifa, stewardship, make protecting the environment a duty. It presents the program as turning waste into economic opportunity, with financial incentives for segregation and recycling that also reinforce discipline, cooperation and stewardship.
whoIsAffected: Residents, especially low-income households and displaced families, who could trade sorted waste for cash or goods.
Informal waste workers, named as priority beneficiaries.
Local governments, which must run collection points and recovery facilities.
Mosques, madaris and religious leaders, invited to promote the program.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy
MSSD, MILG and MBHTE
Local governments

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 initially, charged against the Contingent Fund of the Office of the Chief Minister, then such sums as needed in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, residents could exchange segregated recyclables for cash, food packs or vouchers.
Every local government would need collection points and recovery facilities.
Failure to segregate could bring local penalties and community service.
readings.insight:
The bill sets no prices. Section 6 says a "standardized system shall be developed" to value waste, without saying who develops it or what it pays, so the ₱50,000,000 cannot be checked against any expected volume. That money comes from the Chief Minister's Contingent Fund, yet the bill went to the environment, labor and local government committees, not to Finance.

It is the third waste bill in the registry. Bill 378, MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan's bill on solid waste incentives and sanitary landfills, has been in committee since 19 November 2025, and Bill 305, MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen's waste workers' welfare bill, has sat at first reading since June 2024.

The author list is close to the one on Bill 448, MP Dumama-Alba's maternal health bill filed 3 days earlier: 21 of its 24 names are the same.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Consumers Act of 2025. It lists 8 consumer rights, among them safety, information (including halal certification and expiry dates), choice, redress, a healthy environment, and privacy and data protection. It also lists 6 duties of consumers, such as avoiding panic buying and reporting violations.

It creates a Bangsamoro Consumer Protection Council under the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism. The Trade Minister chairs it and the Health Minister is co-chair. The other members are the ministers for agriculture, science and technology, and finance; 1 representative each from the Bangsamoro Women Commission, the Bangsamoro Youth Commission and the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'; 2 from accredited consumer organisations; and 1 from business. The Council sets standards for labelling, packaging, weights and measures, price tags and advertising. It also opens complaint desks in every province and city, investigates complaints and recommends cases against violators.

It bans 7 practices: deceptive sales, selling hazardous or expired goods, hoarding and profiteering, unfair trade practices such as bait-and-switch, refusing to honour warranties, online fraud, and tampering with weights and measures. Administrative fines run from ₱5,000 to ₱500,000, and offenders can also lose their business licence or have goods confiscated. Wilful and repeated violations carry 1 month to 5 years in prison.

It was filed on 10 October 2025 by MP Susana S. Anayatin and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Trade, Investment, and Tourism and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 19 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says consumers in the region face false product claims and fake discounts, expired food, counterfeit medicines, uncertified electrical devices and goods falsely sold as halal, hoarding and profiteering in rice and fuel, and online fraud. These are the same problems the national Consumer Act (Republic Act No. 7394) addresses, but the note says they are worse in the region because it has no regional way to enforce the rules, educate consumers or get redress.

It also points to the growth of online trade and demand for halal, eco-friendly and locally produced goods as reasons for a regional framework.
whoIsAffected: Shoppers in the region, who would have a regional body to complain to.
Traders, market vendors and online sellers, who would face fines of up to ₱500,000 and the loss of their licence.
Consumer organisations, which would get 2 seats on the Council.
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Bangsamoro Consumer Protection Council

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 10 charges the initial cost to the current appropriations of the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, with later amounts in the annual Bangsamoro budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have its own consumer protection council, with complaint desks in every province and city.
Regional fines and prison terms would apply to hoarding, false advertising, online fraud and tampered scales.
readings.insight: The Council is a board of ministers and sector representatives. The bill gives it no staff, secretariat or budget of its own, yet expects it to staff complaint desks in every province and city and to hold hearings.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Drug Dependent Treatment and Rehabilitation Centers Act of 2025. It establishes 1 government-owned and government-run treatment and rehabilitation centre in every province of the region. The Ministry of Health runs, staffs and regulates them, working with the Ministry of Public Order and Safety, the Ministry of Social Services and Development, the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and local governments.

Each centre must offer residential and out-patient treatment, detoxification and medical care, psychological, psychiatric and spiritual counselling, skills and livelihood training, and family support and aftercare. Centres take voluntary admissions and referrals from courts, police, local governments and community programs. Residents of the host province get priority. PDEA and BJMP must share lists of people arrested and found positive for drugs. The Darul-Ifta' and the Bangsamoro Endowment, Call and Guidance Center may run spiritual programs.

The ministries must also build community-based rehabilitation programs in every province, city and town. The ministries have 90 days to write the rules.

It was filed on 14 October 2025 by MP Butch P. Malang and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Health and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 15 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says drug dependence remains a public health and social problem in the region. National treatment facilities exist in other regions, but the region has no fully operational government-owned centres in its provinces. It says existing efforts such as Balay Silangan are reformation facilities that do not meet the medical, psychological and reintegration needs of drug dependents.

It cites the Constitution's health provisions and Section 22, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: People dependent on drugs and their families, in every province.
People arrested and found positive for drugs, who could be referred to the centres.
Barangay and provincial anti-drug abuse councils, which would handle referral and monitoring.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Ministry of Social Services and Development and Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, with PDEA and BJMP

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 7 charges construction to the Bangsamoro Government's annual appropriations and puts running costs in the Ministry of Health's annual budget. National assistance, international donors and public-private partnerships are allowed as extra sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every province would get a government drug treatment and rehabilitation centre run by the Ministry of Health.
Every town would be expected to run a community-based rehabilitation program.
readings.insight:
The bill commits to a building in every province but gives no site, bed count, staffing numbers or cost. It does not say how many centres that means, or when they must open.

The author lists do not match. The copy filed names 15 co-authors, while Parliament's index lists 36. Section 5 also assigns duties to the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, which are national agencies, and does not say how those duties would be secured, for example through an agreement.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BTA Gratuity Fund Act. It creates a fund to pay a one-time gratuity to employees of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority who are separated from service when the transition period ends. It covers permanent, contractual and co-terminous staff, including those on contracts of service or job orders, who are in service at the end of the transition and have at least 1 year of continuous service.

The gratuity is 1 month's salary for every year of government service, at the highest monthly basic salary the employee received. A fraction of 6 months or more counts as a full year. The human resource unit decides who qualifies, in coordination with the Civil Service Commission for BARMM, based on service records and performance evaluations. The Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management administers the fund and has 60 days to write the rules.

Recipients cannot claim other separation or retirement benefits for the same service. They cannot take a plantilla or permanent post in the Bangsamoro Government, the National Government or a government corporation for 5 years unless they refund the gratuity. Consultancy, contractual, co-terminous and temporary work is still allowed.

It was filed on 28 October 2025 by MP Susana S. Anayatin and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. It was referred to the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 16 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says many BTA staff will lose their jobs when the transition ends, not by choice but because the government is being reorganised into a regular one. It presents the gratuity as compensation and humanitarian help, not an incentive.

It cites a precedent. When ARMM was dissolved in 2019, an initial ₱500 million was set aside for gratuity and separation benefits for ARMM staff, computed under Section 10, Article XVI of the Bangsamoro Organic Law at 100%, 150% or 200% of monthly basic salary per year of service, depending on length of service.
whoIsAffected: BTA employees who are not absorbed into the regular Bangsamoro Government after the transition.
Contractual and job-order workers, who are covered on the same terms as permanent staff.
Recipients, who would be barred from permanent government posts for 5 years unless they refund the gratuity.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Civil Service Commission for BARMM, with the human resource management unit

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 8 takes the initial cost from available Bangsamoro Government funds, including unobligated balances, with later amounts in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, separated BTA staff would receive 1 month's salary for every year of government service.
Recipients would face a 5-year bar on permanent government jobs unless they pay the money back.
readings.insight:
The bill pays less than the precedent its note relies on. The note cites the ARMM formula of 100%, 150% or 200% of monthly salary per year depending on length of service. Section 6 pays a flat 1 month per year to everyone. Under the ARMM formula, someone with 10 years of service would get 20 months; under this bill, 10.

Section 6 also counts "every year of government service", not years at the BTA, which has existed only since 2019. A long-serving official who joined the BTA late would be paid for a whole career. Section 3 defines the gratuity as "not as a matter of right or demandable claim", while Section 6 fixes the amount anyone who qualifies would get.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BARMM Children Involved in Armed Conflict Protection and Rehabilitation Act of 2025. It requires the Ministry of Social Services and Development to set up at least 4 civilian-run residential facilities for children involved in armed conflict, by cluster, subject to a needs assessment and funds. The clusters are Maguindanao (serving Maguindanao del Sur and del Norte), Lanao ("Lanao del Sur A and Lanao del Sur B"), Basilan and Tawi-Tawi. The ministry may add satellite centres and mobile psychosocial teams. The facilities must be kept apart from jails and from Bahay Pag-asa centres for children in conflict with the law.

Each facility must provide shelter, health and mental health care, schooling or the Alternative Learning System, peace education, legal aid, family tracing and reunification, livelihood links, and at least 12 months of aftercare after discharge. Custody belongs only to civilian social welfare offices. Soldiers or police holding a child must hand them over within 24 hours, or 72 hours for reasons beyond their control. No tactical interrogation or intelligence debriefing may take place inside a facility, and children may not be shown to the media or used for propaganda.

An inter-agency committee chaired by the ministry coordinates the work. MSSD must report to Parliament every year and commission an outside evaluation at least every 3 years. Within 60 days, any agency holding such children must list them and turn them over.

It was filed on 28 October 2025 by MP Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim and read on first reading on 11 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 29 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says Republic Act No. 11188 treats children involved in armed conflict as victims entitled to rescue, rehabilitation and reintegration. MSSD runs case management and psychosocial programs, but the region has no dedicated facilities for these children. They cannot be placed in Bahay Pag-asa or other juvenile justice centres because the legal frameworks differ and they risk being traumatised again.

It says this gap weakens the handover from security forces to civilian authorities, delays rehabilitation planning and strains local social services.
whoIsAffected: Children rescued from, surrendered by or found with armed groups in the region.
Soldiers and police, who would have 24 hours to hand such children to civilian social workers.
Families of these children, through tracing, reunification and aftercare.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
BARMM Inter-Agency Committee on Children Involved in Armed Conflict
Local social welfare offices and Local Councils for the Protection of Children

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 13 pays for the start from available current appropriations or a supplemental appropriation, released by MFBM, with later amounts in MSSD's budget in the annual appropriations act. Grants and donations are allowed.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have at least 4 dedicated centres for children involved in armed conflict.
Security forces would have to give up custody of such children within 24 hours, or 72 hours for valid reasons.
readings.insight:
The title promises "a regional facility", but Section 5 requires at least 4. The cluster list covers Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi. It does not mention Cotabato City or the Special Geographic Area, both part of the region, and it splits Lanao into "Lanao del Sur A and Lanao del Sur B" without saying what those are.

The author lists do not match. The copy filed names 5 co-authors, while Parliament's index lists 15.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Board of Investments Act of 2025, amending BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code. Its stated purpose is to create new plantilla positions at the Board of Investments and give it a new staffing pattern. It keeps the Board attached to the Office of the Chief Minister for policy coordination, and recognises it as an investment promotion agency under the CREATE MORE Act, Republic Act No. 12066, overseen by the Fiscal Incentives Review Board.

The Board of Governors would have the BBOI Chairperson as chair, the Trade Minister as vice-chair, the Finance and Agriculture Ministers, and 2 member-governors. The Chief Minister appoints the Chair and the 2 governors to fixed 6-year terms. The Board Secretary VI also becomes a voting member, on a fixed 6-year term. Below the Board sit an Executive Director and 3 divisions: Evaluation and Incentives, Promotion and Aftercare, and Administrative.

The Board would register enterprises and decide disputes within 30 days, with appeal to the Chief Minister. It could subpoena witnesses, cite for contempt and grant immunity from prosecution, and would prepare the Regional Investment Priorities Plan for the national Strategic Investment Priorities Plan. Section 18 lists the incentives it may grant: a 4 to 7 year income tax holiday, then 10 years of a 5% special tax on gross income or 5 years of enhanced deductions, duty and VAT exemptions, and 2 extra years of tax holiday in areas recovering from conflict or disaster. The sitting Chair and 2 governors would be reappointed, and MFBM would have to release the Board's budget automatically.

It was filed on 30 October 2025 by MPs John Anthony L. Lim, Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., Nabil A. Tan, Jose I. Lorena and Baintan A. Ampatuan and read on first reading on 10 November 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 15 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note traces the Board to the Regional Board of Investments, the first national office devolved to ARMM, by Executive Order No. 458 of 1991. It argues the Board still matters because it is the only regional agency national authorities recognise as able to grant incentives on national taxes and customs duties. Its Regional Investment Priorities Plan goes to the President with the national plan, a privilege the note says no other region has. Section 8, Article XII of the Bangsamoro Organic Law keeps that arrangement, and BAA 13 renamed the office and changed its board on 3 December 2020.

The note also says registering with the Board is how companies become regional taxpayers, whose taxes the region shares once their incentives expire. It does not explain why new positions are needed or how many.
whoIsAffected: Investors seeking tax incentives for projects in the region.
Staff of the Board of Investments, whose current posts and benefits are protected.
The current Chair and 2 governors, who would be reappointed for the rest of their terms.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Board of Investments
Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 23 puts the cost in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations, with any extra from available funds or supplementary appropriations. Section 24 requires MFBM to release the Board's approved budget automatically.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the Board would have fixed 6-year terms for its Chair and governors and a voting Board Secretary.
The Board would gain new plantilla positions and 3 divisions under an Executive Director.
readings.insight:
The positions in the bill's title are not in the copy filed. Section 7 says the new positions "are spelled out in the attached Organizational Chart", but the 12-page copy ends at the author's signature, with no chart. No number of positions, salary grade or cost appears anywhere. The 3-page explanatory note is about the Board's power over tax incentives and does not mention staffing.

Section 5 gives the Board Secretary, a staff post, a full vote on the Board alongside ministers and appointed governors. The cover page says "Fourth Regular Session" and the body says "Third Regular Session".

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Grand Athletic Act of 2025. It establishes Bangsamoro Grand Athletic and Sports Complexes in Cotabato City and Lamitan City. They would be the main training centres for athletes, coaches and other sports staff in the 2 cities and nearby towns. The policy section says the facilities should meet international standards.

The Bangsamoro Sports Commission, created by BAA 12, must write a sustainability plan for the complexes. The plan covers use and management, maintenance and repair, income-earning activities to help cover costs, and waste management, and must be updated at least every 5 years. Every 5 years an independent panel named by the Chief Minister reviews how the law is working. The Commission has 60 days to write the rules.

It was filed on 3 November 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and read on first reading on 10 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Public Works and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 29 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the Constitution and Sections 13 and 20, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law on youth and sports, the World Health Organization on exercise and disease, and the Olympic gold medals of Hidilyn Diaz and Carlos Yulo. It says the region has no dedicated athletic and sports centre.

It presents the complexes as an investment in peacebuilding, giving young people in a conflict-affected region a constructive outlet and a place to train for local and international competition.
whoIsAffected: Athletes, coaches and sports officials in and around Cotabato City and Lamitan City.
Young people in the 2 cities and nearby towns.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
Ministry of Public Works, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 charges the initial cost to the Contingent Fund, with later amounts in the Sports Commission's annual budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, Cotabato City and Lamitan City would each be named the site of a regional sports complex.
readings.insight:
The bill names 2 cities but no site, land area, list of facilities or cost, and it gives no agency the job of building anything. The Sports Commission writes a sustainability plan and "may coordinate" with the Ministry of Public Works. The initial cost falls on the Contingent Fund, which is meant for unforeseen expenses.

A later bill on the same subject does give a figure. Bill 467, filed on 5 May 2026 by MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., would build a single Bangsamoro Sports Complex with ₱1,000,000,000 for construction and equipment, but names no location. It was referred to the same 2 committees. Bills 313 (a sports training centre, 2024) and 377 (a Bangsamoro Sports Institute) cover similar ground.

The co-author line on the copy, 10 names, is identical to the one on Bill 414, MP Ampatuan's education bill filed the same day.

readings.whatItDoes:
The College Education Bridging Fund Act of 2025. It creates a College Education Bridging Fund under the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education. The fund gives extra financial help to students from low-income families, meaning households counted as poor or near-poor under the Philippine Statistics Authority's poverty threshold.

A qualified student is a resident of the region who has finished third year at an accredited college or university, public or private, inside or outside the region. Incoming fourth-year students who cannot enrol for lack of money, and scholars who need help with non-tuition costs, are covered. The money can pay for transport, board and lodging, books and supplies, internet and devices, food, and other academic costs. Priority goes to students from poor and conflict-affected communities, indigenous peoples, orphans, persons with disabilities, and those in courses tied to regional priorities.

Each student is entitled to at least ₱50,000. The ministry's Higher Education Department runs the fund and reports to Parliament every year. It writes the rules with MFBM within 90 days.

It was filed on 3 November 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and read on first reading on 10 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 27 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the Philippine Statistics Authority's 2023 Labor Force Survey: only 9.6% of people in the region aged 25 and over have finished college, against 24.9% nationally, and over 50% of the population was below the poverty line as of 2021. Free tuition under Republic Act No. 10931 helps, but students still drop out over transport, lodging, food, books and internet.

It describes the fund as a supplement for students who have finished at least third year and are at risk of dropping out, and cites Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law on scholarships for the poor.
whoIsAffected: Fourth-year college students from poor and near-poor families resident in the region.
Scholars whose existing grants do not cover living costs.
Indigenous, orphaned and disabled students, and those from conflict-affected areas, who get priority.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, through its Higher Education Department
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, on the rules

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 for initial implementation, charged against the Contingent Fund of the Bangsamoro Government. Later amounts go in the ministry's annual budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, final-year college students from poor families could get at least ₱50,000 each for living and study costs.
readings.insight:
The figures cap the program at 1,000 students. With at least ₱50,000 per student, the initial ₱50,000,000 covers no more than 1,000 grants.

The fund helps students finish, not start. Section 2 speaks of students "accessing and completing" college, but Section 3 limits eligibility to those who have already finished third year, so only students in their final year can apply. Section 3 also defines the fund as covering tuition, but tuition is not among the allowable uses in Section 6.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Zero Billing Hospitalization for Expired Patients Act. When a patient dies in a hospital owned or run by the Bangsamoro Government through the Ministry of Health, the hospital must at once issue a Zero Billing Certificate. The certificate waives every charge: room and board, professional fees, laboratory and imaging, medicines and supplies, emergency, intensive care and surgery. It applies whatever the cause of death, length of stay or the family's income. The body and the medical records may not be held back for payment.

The hospital prepares the certificate within 24 hours of death and sends a monthly report to the Ministry of Health for audit and reimbursement. Hospitals that comply get priority for regional health subsidies and capital outlay, performance-based grants and recognition. Staff who hold back a body or demand payment face administrative sanctions, including suspension or dismissal. Hospitals that repeatedly violate the law can lose their incentives. The Ministry of Health and MFBM have 90 days to write the rules.

It was filed on 27 November 2025 by MP Suharto S. Esmael and read on first reading on 9 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Social Services and Development, on Health, and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 11 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 3 gives the purpose: no family should carry the cost of a relative's hospital stay when the patient dies in a government hospital. It presents this as compassion and moral governance, saying that "care does not end at death".
whoIsAffected: Families of patients who die in Bangsamoro Government hospitals.
Government hospitals, which would give up these bills and wait for reimbursement.
Hospital billing and records staff, who face sanctions for demanding payment.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Government hospitals in the region
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, on the rules

funding.detail: ₱250,000,000 for initial implementation, charged against the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. Later amounts go in the Ministry of Health's budget in the annual appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, families would owe nothing when a patient dies in a Bangsamoro Government hospital.
Hospitals could no longer hold a body until the bill is paid.
readings.insight:
The bill does not say how the ₱250,000,000 would reach hospitals or how much a hospital would be paid back per case. It also does not mention PhilHealth, so it is unclear whether hospitals should still claim PhilHealth benefits before the region pays the rest.

Its definitions do not agree. Section 4 defines a deceased patient as one who dies "while admitted or undergoing emergency treatment", but Section 5 limits coverage to patients who die "while admitted". The numbering also breaks: after Section 13 the copy goes back to a second Section 10 (Repealing Clause) and a second Section 11 (Effectivity).

readings.whatItDoes:
The Salamat Hashim Boarding Madrasah Act of 2025. It establishes a public boarding madrasah under the public madrasah system set up by Title VII of the Bangsamoro Education Code, BAA 18. The school would offer full-time residential schooling for Grades 7 to 12. It would teach the K-12 curriculum alongside Qur'anic studies, Hadith, Fiqh, Aqidah, Akhlaq, Arabic and leadership formation. Its site must be owned, leased or held in usufruct by the Bangsamoro Government.

Non-Muslim students may enrol, take Alternative Values Education instead of Islamic studies, and cannot be made to take part in religious rites. At least 60% of students must come from underserved areas, be in the top 10 of their class and pass a competitive entrance test. Teachers of secular subjects need not be of any particular religion.

The Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education supervises the school and keeps control of its budget, hiring and procurement. A Board of Trustees chaired by the Minister only recommends policy. Its members are representatives of a state college, a civil society group and the Darul-Ifta', an education expert and the chair of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, with the school's director as non-voting secretary. A Salamat Hashim Scholarship Fund would pay for graduates' further studies.

It was filed on 11 December 2025 by MPs Abdulbasit R. Benito and Omar Yasser C. Sema and read on first reading on 15 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 17 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the Bangsamoro Organic Law's education mandate, the Bangsamoro Education Code's provisions on Islamic education and madaris, and the Bangsamoro Development Plan 2023 to 2028. It describes a school that combines secular and Islamic learning to raise morally upright, academically capable young people who will contribute to peacebuilding.

It says the school would favour high-performing learners from underserved communities, admit non-Muslim students, and honour the legacy of Salamat Hashim.
whoIsAffected: High-performing Grade 7 to 12 learners from underserved areas, who fill at least 60% of places.
Non-Muslim students, who may enrol without religious instruction.
Graduates, who could draw on the Salamat Hashim Scholarship Fund for further study.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Salamat Hashim Boarding Madrasah Board of Trustees

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 charges the initial cost to the ministry's current appropriations, with later amounts in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. The Scholarship Fund may accept donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the region would have a public boarding madrasah for Grades 7 to 12 and a scholarship fund for its graduates.
readings.insight:
The bill does not say where the school would be, how many students it would take or what it would cost. It requires only that the Bangsamoro Government own, lease or hold the site in usufruct. The file Parliament published is labelled "Enhanced", a revised version of the filed copy.

It would add to the measures named after the MILF's founding chairman. BAA 60 declared his burial site a memorial, BAA 81 created the Salamat Excellence Award for Leadership program, and Bill 335 would declare his house in Camp Abubakar a historical place.

The author lists do not match. The copy filed names 13 co-authors, including MP Suharto Esmael. Parliament's index lists 25 co-authors and does not include him.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Quarantine Act of 2025.
