It creates a Bangsamoro Bureau of Quarantine under the administrative supervision of the Ministry of Health, headed by a Director III appointed by the Chief Minister. The Bureau would inspect vessels and aircraft at the region's ports of entry and exit, along with their cargo, passengers and crew, and issue quarantine certificates and bills of health. It could require doctors and hospitals to report diseases, order contact tracing, quarantine and isolation, and recommend local lockdowns to the Chief Minister.

With the Health Minister's approval, the Director could issue rules against public health emergencies of international concern. These could include inspections, fumigation, vaccination for international travel, medical checks of foreigners for immigration, and destruction of infected animals or goods. Immunisation of arriving passengers could be made mandatory. Foreign ships and aircraft would need a quarantine clearance before customs clearance, both arriving and leaving. The Bureau would run quarantine stations and could recommend banning hazardous cargo.

Violators face fines of ₱10,000 to ₱50,000, up to 1 year in prison, or both. Vessels and aircraft face fines of ₱100,000 to ₱500,000. The Bureau keeps at least 50% of its income, coordinates with the Department of Health and the national Bureau of Quarantine through the Intergovernmental Relations Body, and builds a Quarantine Management Information System under the Data Privacy Act.

It was filed on 12 December 2025 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and read on first reading on 15 December 2025. It was referred to the Committees on Health and on Finance, Budget, and Management, entered the committee stage on 17 December 2025, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says COVID-19 exposed gaps in the region's ability to detect and respond to new infectious diseases at airports, seaports and land borders. It says the region has no statutory quarantine agency, which slows responses and undermines compliance with the World Health Organization's International Health Regulations. It cites Section 2(rr), Article V of the Bangsamoro Organic Law as giving the region authority over quarantine regulations.

It also grounds quarantine in Islamic teaching, quoting the hadith on plague in Sahih al-Bukhari 5728.
whoIsAffected: Travellers, crews and shippers arriving at or leaving the region's seaports and airports.
Doctors and hospitals, who would have to report diseases to the Bureau.
People exposed to communicable diseases, who could be ordered into quarantine or isolation.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Bureau of Quarantine
Ministry of Health
Department of Health and the national Bureau of Quarantine, in coordination

funding.detail: ₱15,000,000 initial funding for the Bureau's operation, with no source named. Later amounts go in the annual appropriations act. Section 10 also lets the Bureau use at least 50% of the income it earns.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, ships and aircraft from abroad would need a regional quarantine clearance before customs clearance.
A regional bureau could order quarantine, isolation and contact tracing and recommend local lockdowns.
readings.insight:
The bill gives the regional Bureau powers the national Bureau of Quarantine already exercises at the same ports, and it does not say how the 2 would divide the work. It says only that they coordinate. Some wording points outward from the region: Section 3 extends the Bureau's authority to vessels "of the army and navy", and Section 7 speaks of keeping diseases out of "the country".

The numbering skips Section 4: the copy goes from the section creating the Bureau to Section 5. The copy filed names 6 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 21.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Comprehensive Children Social Security Act. It creates a Children Social Security Registry, a digital database meant to hold every child aged 0 to 17 in the region, run by the Ministry of Social Services and Development with local civil registrars, the Ministry of Health and the BARMM Statistics Office.

Every child born in the region would have to be registered within 5 days of birth, ideally at the hospital or clinic where the child is born. Children born before the registry exists, and children born elsewhere but raised in the region, would be registered within 5 months of the law taking effect. At birth the registry records the child's name, birthplace, sex, ethnicity, parents, the household's water, food, toilet and income situation, and newborn screening results; later it adds medical, school, welfare and disability records and any record of delinquency. Each registered child gets a unique social security number, a registration certificate and an Integrated Social Security Card, which makes the child eligible for health, education, nutrition and welfare services until age 18.

Registration desks would be set up in every birthing centre, clinic and hospital, with registration centres, mobile units, and help desks run by the Local Councils for the Protection of Children in every municipality and barangay. Falsifying entries, tampering with the system and disclosing a child's data without consent are penalised. Parents who do not register a child face no penalty. A minister whose agency fails to serve children the registry shows are in need must explain to the Chief Minister and may face administrative sanctions.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, read on first reading on 23 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Social Services and Development and the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities on 28 April 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region's children have been "invisible" to the state through neglect and conflict, and that fragmented, ad hoc welfare projects cannot reach them. A single secure registry, it argues, would let the government find children in remote island provinces and the Special Geographic Area, target nutrition, education and protection to them, and intervene in abuse, neglect and child labour early. It calls the bill "the Foundational Social Contract of the Bangsamoro".
whoIsAffected: Every child aged 0 to 17 in the region, and every child born there, who would be entered in the registry.
Parents and guardians, who create the child's account and upload the documents.
Hospitals, clinics and birthing centres, which would host registration desks and register newborns within 5 days.
Ministries that serve children, whose ministers must answer for gaps the registry reveals.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Local Civil Registry Offices, Ministry of Health, BARMM Statistics Office and MBHTE, through a coordination body
Local Councils for the Protection of Children, running help desks

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 24 says the Parliament shall ensure adequate funds based on a projection of the registry's needs, sourced from existing BARMM appropriations or from grants and pledges from local and international organisations. The title says it appropriates funds; the text appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every child in the region would get a registry number and an Integrated Social Security Card.
Newborns would have to be registered within 5 days of birth, and all other children within 5 months of the law taking effect.
Ministries would be answerable to the Chief Minister for service gaps the registry shows.
readings.insight:
Despite its name, the bill creates no social security benefit. There are no contributions, no cash grant and no pension: what it builds is a registry and an ID card that make a child "eligible" for services that already exist or that other laws must fund. Section 15 lists vaccinations, scholarships, feeding programs and cash assistance as things registered children may access, without saying who pays.

The copy filed has drafting gaps. Definition (d), "Children Social Security Registry", is a heading with nothing after it; the term is defined later as (i). The definition of a child adds that "the bill extends protections to unborn children as well", which reads as a note to the drafter. Section 26 punishes the violations "enumerated in Section 22", but the violations are in Section 25; Section 22 is about monitoring. Section 13 assigns tasks to an "SSDO" the bill never defines.

Bill 452, filed the same day by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, would create a Bangsamoro Children's Information Office and a Children's Integrated Database System. The 2 bills would each build a region-wide children's database and were sent to different lead committees.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Liguasan Inland Fisheries Enterprise (LIFE) Act of 2026. It sets up a program under the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform for small-scale fisherfolk in the part of Liguasan Marsh that lies in Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area. The program supplies fish cages for native species, nets with legal mesh sizes to replace fine-mesh nets, and community fish landing centres, ice plants and cold storage. A Blue Finance Support Mechanism would offer low-interest loans timed to fishers' seasonal income.

Every municipal fisher in the marsh must register in the FishR system to get support or access to fishing areas. The bill restates prohibitions from the national Fisheries Code, including electrofishing, explosives, poison and nets below 3 cm mesh, with penalties from fines of ₱2,000 to ₱20,000 up to 10 years in prison, and permanent bans for repeat offenders.

An Inter-Agency Management Council for Liguasan Marsh, chaired by the MAFAR Minister with the MENRE Minister as co-chair, would set management zones and keep a registry of fishers and boats. Each town would field a Bantay Pawas task force of local patrol volunteers under the Municipal Agricultural Officer and the MENRO, with an honorarium, insurance and equipment paid by the town.

It was filed on 20 April 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao, read on first reading on 20 May 2026 and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Fisheries, and Agrarian Reform on 17 June 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the marsh is one of the largest and most biodiverse wetlands in the country and a livelihood for many small fishers, but that overfishing, electrofishing and fine-mesh nets are depleting it despite the national Fisheries Code, as amended by Republic Act 10654. Without organised support, it says, fishers are stuck at subsistence income. The bill aims to organise them into cooperatives, give them credit and market access, and back local enforcement.
whoIsAffected: Small-scale fisherfolk in the BARMM portion of Liguasan Marsh, who must register in FishR to receive support or fish.
Anyone using electrofishing gear, explosives, poison or fine-mesh nets in the marsh.
Towns around the marsh, which must run and pay the Bantay Pawas patrols.
implementedBy: Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform
Inter-Agency Management Council for Liguasan Marsh
Municipal governments, through the Bantay Pawas task forces

funding.detail: ₱100,000,000 in initial funding, drawn from the Special Development Fund of the BARMM, the Office of the Interim Chief Minister and MAFAR. After that, funding is to be included in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, fishing in the marsh would require FishR registration.
Fishers would get cages, legal nets, cold storage and low-interest loans through a ₱100,000,000 program.
A new inter-agency council and town-level patrol task forces would police the marsh.
readings.insight:
This is the second bill to create a management body for Liguasan Marsh. Bill 310, filed by MP Ali B. Sangki in June 2024, would create a Liguasan Marsh Management Commission; it was read on first reading on 24 June 2024 and the registry shows no movement since. This bill does not mention it and sets up a different body, an inter-agency council under MAFAR.

The penalties contradict each other. Section 16(a) punishes the actual use of electrofishing devices with 6 months in prison and a ₱5,000 fine for a first offence; Section 16(b) punishes anyone using explosives, toxic substances "as well as electrofishing devices" with 5 to 10 years. Paragraphs (i) and (j) say the same thing about altering protected areas twice.

The copy filed is uneven in other ways. Section 12 stops mid-sentence after "business plan development". The task force is called the "Bantay Pawas Task Force (BWTF)", then "BPTF", then the "Pawas Watch Taskforce". The marsh is spelled Ligawasan in some sections and Liguasan in others. The copy names 6 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 25.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Integrated Qur'an Recitation and Adaptation (IQRA) Education System Act of 2026. It requires every MBHTE-accredited tahfidz institution, a school centred on memorising the Qur'an, to adopt a curriculum that adds life skills, technical-vocational training and civic education to recitation and memorisation.

The curriculum has 4 parts: Qur'an recitation, memorisation and applied understanding, open from age 6; and a TESDA technical-vocational track, a life skills pathway and civic education modules, open only from age 15. To graduate, a learner must finish at least 2 short TESDA courses, personal development and leadership training, and the civic modules. Completers receive an MBHTE diploma, an MBHTE certificate for life skills and civics, and a TESDA National Certificate.

The Bangsamoro Government would provide scholarships and stipends, teacher training and incentives, classrooms and workshops subject to funds, health and nutrition programs, and links to employers. Tahfidz institutions that want this support must apply for accreditation with MBHTE's Directorate General for Madaris Education and fully adopt the system within 2 years.

It was filed on 20 April 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao, read on first reading on 20 May 2026 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 21 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region's tahfidz institutions preserve a deep tradition of Qur'an memorisation but leave graduates without the skills to work and take part in civic life. The IQRA system would produce graduates who are "not only spiritually engaged but also skilled" to contribute to development, peacebuilding and political stability. It cites the Constitution, the Enhanced Basic Education Act, the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the Bangsamoro Education Code, and argues these make the system exempt from the constitutional separation of church and state.
whoIsAffected: Learners in tahfidz institutions, who would take TESDA and civics modules from age 15.
Tahfidz institutions, which must seek MBHTE accreditation and adopt the system within 2 years to receive government support.
Tahfidz teachers, who would receive training and incentives.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, through the Directorate General for Madaris Education
Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, for training and certificates
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', in designing the system

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs are charged to MBHTE's current appropriations; afterwards the amounts are to be included in the annual Bangsamoro Expenditure Program.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, accredited tahfidz institutions would have to teach vocational, life skills and civics modules alongside the Qur'an.
Graduates would leave with an MBHTE diploma and a TESDA National Certificate.
Unaccredited tahfidz centres would receive no government support until they apply and adopt the system.
readings.insight:
The mandate is circular. The bill defines a tahfidz institution as one already accredited by MBHTE and applies only to those, so centres that are not accredited are untouched unless they choose to seek support. Section 10 then points them to the support "outlined in Section 8", but Section 8 is about diplomas; the support is in Section 9.

Section 9 promises nutrition programs for students "in Grades 1 through 6", a grade structure the IQRA curriculum does not use: it is organised by age, with modules opening at 6 and at 15.

MP Antao filed Bill 458, on support systems to preserve traditional madaris, the same day. The registry shows it read on first reading on 19 May 2026 with no committee recorded. The copy of this bill names 6 co-authors, the same 6 as on his Liguasan Marsh bill, Bill 456; Parliament's index lists 24.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Volunteer Teacher Absorption and Regularization Act of 2026. It sets rules for moving volunteer teachers in the region's public schools, people who teach without a permanent appointment, into paid MBHTE positions.

Licensed volunteer teachers with at least 3 years of continuous service get preference for existing plantilla positions, and first consideration when a post opens at their own school. Non-licensed volunteers who took the Licensure Examination for Teachers and scored a general average of at least 70% may be appointed as para-teachers where licensed teachers are lacking, renewable each year. Those who do not qualify may be hired on contract of service at no less than 80% of a Teacher I entry salary.

A Licensure Support Program would help non-licensed volunteers with review and exam subsidies. Ranking would use a points system counting years of service, performance, hardship posting, training and local language, with extra points for applicants from the community who speak the learners' mother tongue.

It was filed on 22 April 2026 by MP Abrar J. Hataman, read on first reading on 30 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education on 18 May 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says volunteer teachers have been "the unheralded backbone" of public education in remote, island and conflict-affected schools, often paid only small honoraria by parent-teacher associations, towns or donors. It presents regularisation as recognition of their years of service and a correction of "structural injustice".
whoIsAffected: Volunteer teachers in the region's public schools, licensed and unlicensed.
Schools in remote and conflict-affected areas that depend on them.
Applicants for teaching posts, who would compete under a points system favouring local hires.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Civil Service Commission and Professional Regulation Commission, on qualifications

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs come from MBHTE's existing appropriations; afterwards from the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, subject to the limit on personal services under the Bangsamoro Organic Law.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, licensed volunteers with 3 years' service would get preference for plantilla posts.
Unlicensed volunteers would get para-teacher posts or contracts at no less than 80% of Teacher I pay.
MBHTE would run a licensure support program.
readings.insight:
Section 9 tells MBHTE to adopt the ranking system "in the IRR", but the bill has no section on implementing rules: no deadline and no agency named to write them. The points system that decides who is absorbed is left without a legal starting point.

The para-teacher rule pulls 2 ways. Section 6 says qualifying para-teachers "shall be absorbed into available plantilla positions", then that their appointment is renewable yearly on performance, which is how a contract works, not a plantilla post. And a non-licensed volunteer is defined as a degree holder who has not passed the licensure exam, but only those who have already taken it and scored 70% or more can become para-teachers; those who have never sat it go straight to contract of service.

The copy filed ends with "Adopted," and a "Certified correct" line for Secretary General Raby B. Angkal, the form used for measures the Parliament has passed. It was filed the same day as MP Hataman's Bill 462 with the same 11 co-authors on its cover; Parliament's index lists 29 for this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Aftercare Support for Children in Conflict with the Law Act. It establishes a Bangsamoro Aftercare Support System for children who have been released from detention or residential facilities, diverted from court, or discharged from rehabilitation, building on the aftercare duty in the national Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, Republic Act 9344.

Aftercare would be mandatory for at least 6 months, extendable. It covers counselling and mental health care, return to school or alternative learning, vocational training and job placement, family mediation and parenting sessions, community reintegration with barangays and religious leaders, and values and spiritual formation.

The Ministry of Social Services and Development leads, sets standards and runs a CICL Information and Monitoring System with regular reports to the Parliament. An Inter-Agency Committee on CICL Aftercare brings in MILG, MBHTE, the Ministry of Public Order and Safety, the Ministry of Health, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, local governments and civil society. Towns deliver services at community level, involve their Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children, budget for CICL programs and keep a registry of children in aftercare.

It was filed on 22 April 2026 by MP Abrar J. Hataman, read on first reading on 30 April 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities on 18 June 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says children in conflict with the law are often driven by poverty, lack of schooling, family instability and the effects of conflict, and that although national law requires aftercare, many in the region are released with no psychosocial, educational or livelihood support, so the gains of rehabilitation are lost and reoffending stays high. It frames aftercare in Islamic terms of rahmah, adl and islah: compassion, justice and reform.
whoIsAffected: Children in conflict with the law after release, diversion or discharge, who would receive at least 6 months of aftercare.
Their families, through mediation, parenting sessions and counselling.
Local governments and barangay child protection councils, which must deliver services and keep a registry.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Inter-Agency Committee on CICL Aftercare
Local government units and Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs are charged to the current appropriations of MSSD and other concerned ministries; afterwards to the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. Towns are told to allocate funds for CICL programs consistent with existing laws.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, aftercare of at least 6 months would become mandatory for every child released, diverted or discharged.
MSSD would track each child's progress in a regional monitoring system and report to the Parliament.
readings.insight:
Section 4 extends the law to Bangsamoro children in conflict with the law "within and outside" the region. A regional law and regional agencies cannot deliver services or bind local governments outside BARMM, and the bill names no partner outside the region.

The copy filed is loosely assembled. The enacting clause reads "Be it ordained", the wording for an ordinance. Section 3, the definitions, holds 2 items lettered (e) and then turns into principles: compassion, non-discrimination and child participation. The explanatory note is placed after the bill text, numbered as pages 1 and 2 while the text begins on page 3.

It was filed the same day as MP Hataman's Bill 461, on volunteer teachers, with the same 11 co-authors on its cover; Parliament's index lists 19. Bill 406, filed in October 2025, would create a regional facility for children involved in armed conflict and sits with the same committee.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Bahay Kanlungan for Women and Children Act. It requires a Bahay Kanlungan, a one-stop centre for women and children who are victims of violence, abuse, exploitation and discrimination, in every city and municipality in the region.

Each town provides the land and, with the Ministry of Social Services and Development, designs and runs the centre. The centre offers medical, police, medico-legal, legal and psychological help, case management for offenders, and a reception area, counselling room, medical room, interview room with a one-way mirror and recorder, records room and play area. The mayor appoints an Executive Director at no less than Salary Grade 21, a registered social worker at Salary Grade 12 and 2 administrative officers at Salary Grade 11, with a psychologist, medico-legal officer, police officer and lawyer on honoraria.

Each centre keeps a database of gender-based violence cases. Publishing a victim's name, address or other identifying details without consent carries criminal, civil and administrative liability. Centres may take donations from domestic and international sources.

It was filed on 29 April 2026 by MP Alirakim T. Munder, read on first reading on 19 May 2026 and referred to the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 16 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says violence against women and children remains widespread in the region and goes underreported, partly because of maratabat, a sense of family honour that discourages survivors from seeking help. Survivors must go from police to hospital to social worker to prosecutor, which causes distress and delay. The bill would put shelter and services under one culturally sensitive roof in every town, in line with Islamic principles of adl and rahmah.
whoIsAffected: Women and children who are victims of violence, abuse, trafficking or exploitation, in every town.
Mayors and municipal councils, which must provide land, appoint staff and help fund the centre.
Police, doctors and lawyers detailed to the centres.
implementedBy: City and municipal governments
Ministry of Social Services and Development
Ministry of Health and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, as funding sources

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 16 charges the centres' personnel, operating and equipment costs to MSSD's social protection subsidy program, the Ministry of Health's gender-based violence and health emergency fund, MILG's support fund for provincial LGUs, and the city or municipal budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, every city and municipality would have to establish and staff a one-stop centre for victims of violence.
Each centre would have an Executive Director at Salary Grade 21 or above, a social worker and 2 administrative officers.
Identifying a victim publicly without consent would become punishable.
readings.insight:
The bill is named for a shelter but builds no beds. The explanatory note promises "24/7 temporary shelter", rescue operations, education and reintegration; the list of required facilities in Section 8 is a reception area, counselling room, medical room, interview room, records room and play area, with no sleeping quarters. The definition of Bahay Kanlungan points to any shelter or willing household instead.

Section 15 makes centre staff the secretariat of a "Council" the bill never creates. The declaration of policy speaks of "the State" protecting the family, in the language of national law, and the bill has no implementing rules section.

It is the third bill in 2 years for women's centres. Bill 301, filed in April 2024, would create a haven and rehabilitation centre for women victims of gender-based violence, and Bill 382, filed in July 2025, a Bangsamoro Women's Welfare Center in every province and major hospital; the registry shows both read on first reading and not moved since. This one goes further, to every city and municipality.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Sports Complex Act of 2026. It establishes a "state-of-the-art and highly scientific" regional sports complex to serve as the main venue for training, competitions and events in the region, run by the Bangsamoro Sports Commission created by BAA 12.

Section 7 lists 22 facilities, among them an administration building, an athletes' and coaches' dormitory, baseball, softball and football fields, a covered swimming and diving pool, a gymnastics centre, a bowling centre, a track oval, tennis and volleyball courts, guest villas, a medical clinic and a prayer room, and 31 sports from aquatics and arnis to wushu. The Chief Minister appoints an Administrator with at least 5 years of sports administration experience to run it day to day.

The Commission reports quarterly to the Parliament on construction until the complex is finished, and writes the rules within 60 days with MBHTE, the finance, public works, transport and health ministries and the Bangsamoro Youth Commission.

It was filed on 5 May 2026 by MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., read on first reading on 19 May 2026 and referred to the Committee on Public Works and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 15 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region lacks modern, centralised venues, so promising athletes are recruited by institutions outside the region and end up representing other regions. It points to the annual BARMAA Meet, where events have had to be scattered across schools, covered courts and open fields with problems of water, electricity, sanitation, locker rooms, medical stations and billeting. A permanent complex, it argues, would also let the region host the Palarong Pambansa and national events and bring tourism and jobs.
whoIsAffected: Athletes, coaches and officials in the region, including BARMAA Meet delegations.
The Bangsamoro Sports Commission, which would run the complex.
Whichever city or town is chosen as the site, which the bill does not name.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
Bangsamoro Sports Complex Administrator, appointed by the Chief Minister
Ministry of Public Works and Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, among the ministries consulted on the rules

funding.detail: ₱1,000,000,000 for construction, facilities and equipment, to be included in the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. Personnel, coaches, maintenance and operating costs afterwards go into the Sports Commission's annual budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, ₱1,000,000,000 would go to building a single regional sports complex.
The Sports Commission would gain a facility to run and an Administrator appointed by the Chief Minister.
readings.insight:
The bill sets a ₱1,000,000,000 price but no place. It does not name a city, a province or a site, or say who chooses one. Bill 413, filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan in November 2025, would build sports complexes in named locations, Cotabato City and Lamitan City, and went to the same 2 committees in April 2026.

Section 8 requires quarterly reports to the Chairperson of the "Committee of Youth and Sports Development". Parliament's committee list has no such committee; the bill itself sits with Public Works and Finance. The list of 31 sports names Lawn Tennis twice, at items 19 and 25.

The copy is marked "First Regular Session" on the explanatory note and "Second Regular Session" on the bill, and ends with a "Certified Correct" block for Secretary General Raby B. Angkal and an "Attested by" block for Speaker Mohammad S. Yacob, the form used for measures the Parliament has passed.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Sustainable Forest Management Code, a 95-section code for the region's forest lands. MENRE's Forest Management Service would delineate permanent forest boundaries within 5 years, sub-classify forest land into protection and production forest, and prepare a Bangsamoro Forest Land Use Plan within 1 year. Commercial logging is banned in protection forests, and naturally growing trees in production forests may not be commercially cut. Mangroves, 20 m strips along rivers, ridge tops, watershed reservations and natural forest patches are kept as forest land even below 18% slope.

Forest use would run through Forest Management Agreements of 25 years, renewable once, for plantations, agroforestry, ecotourism, restoration and special uses, with priority in tenure for resident organisations, then MILF and MNLF communities, then indigenous peoples, then existing DENR agreement holders. MNLF and MILF camps are prioritised as forest economic areas. Ecotourism holders pay 5% of zonal value a year. The bill writes a full staffing table for the Forest Management Service into the text, sets up a framework for carbon markets, asks the national government to hand watershed management from NAPOCOR to the region within 1 year, and creates a Waqf fund from confiscated products, carbon revenue and donations.

Every town must form a Forest Protection Council and set aside a forest nursery fund from its 20% development fund. Illegal occupation or destruction of forest land carries 6 to 8 years and ₱50,000 to ₱200,000, kaingin 8 to 12 years, and offences in protected areas ₱200,000 to ₱1,000,000. Informants get 20% of auction proceeds. A Bangsamoro Forestry Adjudication Board would hear forestry cases.

It was filed on 9 June 2026 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan, read on first reading on 18 June 2026 and referred to the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy on 13 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region had 340,796 hectares of forest in 2010 and 344,416 hectares in 2020, providing climate regulation, water, soil, habitat and livelihoods, and that forest covers 35% to 43% of land in Lanao del Sur, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi. Deforestation, weak institutions, poverty, displacement and climate change threaten it. The Code is meant to set clear, equitable rules for use and access, support community and indigenous forest enterprises, strengthen enforcement, and create a fund for reforestation, framed throughout in the Islamic ideas of khilafah (stewardship) and amanah (trust).
whoIsAffected: Communities, indigenous peoples, settlers and MILF and MNLF communities living in or near forest land, who get priority for tenure.
Anyone who occupies, burns or cuts in forest land without a permit, facing up to 12 years in prison.
Every city and municipality, which must form a Forest Protection Council, run nurseries and set up a tree park or communal forest.
Investors in plantations, wood industries and carbon projects.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, through its Forest Management Service
Bangsamoro Forestry Adjudication Board
City and municipal governments, through Forest Protection Councils

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 79 has MENRE allocate funds in the annual regional budget and lists other sources: national appropriations, shares of national wealth, 10% of LGU development funds, trust funds, carbon credits, fines and fees, and bonds and loans from the World Bank and Asian Development Bank with the Parliament's approval.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, forest boundaries would be fixed on the ground within 5 years and a forest land use plan prepared within 1 year.
Commercial logging would be banned in protection forests and natural forests.
Forestry cases would go to a new regional adjudication board, and every town would need a Forest Protection Council.
readings.insight:
The same 5 MPs filed Bill 442 on 23 March 2026, 11 weeks earlier, to create a Bangsamoro Environmental Adjudication Board. This Code creates a separate Bangsamoro Forestry Adjudication Board of its own and does not mention the other. Section 88 sends "all cases" under the Code to that board, yet the Code's offences carry prison terms of up to 12 years, and Section 86 tells citizens to sue "in the proper court".

The copy filed is still a working draft. The definitions of ancestral domain and ancestral land end with the note "(use the BIPA definition)". The title says Code of 2026; Section 1 and the explanatory note say 2025. The fund for forest programs is called the Sustainable Forest Development Fund, the Sustainable Forest Management Fund, the Waqf, and the "Waqf or Trust Fund". Section 61 refers to incentives "under Section 31", which is about institutional linkages; the incentives are in Section 42. Section 62 leaves export guidelines to "the Secretary", and Section 89 consults a "BFMC" the Code never defines.

Section 42 lists as an incentive that the holder "has the no right to transfer" its rights, against Section 11, which allows transfer after 5 years with the Minister's written authority. The explanatory note counts Sulu among the region's most forested provinces, though Sulu has not been part of the region since 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Hajj Revolving Fund Act of 2026. It creates a ₱1,000,000,000 Hajj Revolving Fund that the Bangsamoro Pilgrimage Authority can draw on to pay Hajj costs in advance, such as reserving slot allocations, hotels and accommodation, and that is replenished when pilgrims pay their fees.

The Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management releases money from the Fund only for this purpose and only on the Authority's request. The Authority supervises the Fund, collects pilgrims' payments, and must ensure amounts are reimbursed immediately once pilgrims pay. The Finance Minister certifies that advances have been replenished. The bill states that pilgrims remain responsible for their own fees and that the government is not taking them on.

The Authority reports annually on releases and repayments to the ministry, the Office of the Chief Minister and the Parliament's finance committee within 2 months after each Hajj. Allocations for the same purpose in earlier regional budgets lapse when the Act takes effect and revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury.

It was filed on 7 July 2026 by the Government of the Day, read on first reading on 13 July 2026 and referred to the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 14 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the Hajj is a pillar of Islam of deep significance to much of the region's population, and that a revolving fund for advance payment of essential fees and charges would let the Pilgrimage Authority plan logistics and services and run a smooth, well-managed pilgrimage. It describes the fund as a sign of the region's "readiness to undertake the Hajj administration and supervision".
whoIsAffected: Pilgrims from the region, whose slots and lodging would be booked in advance and who must repay through the Authority.
The Bangsamoro Pilgrimage Authority, which would manage and account for the Fund.
The Bangsamoro Treasury, which puts up ₱1,000,000,000 and absorbs any amount pilgrims do not repay.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Pilgrimage Authority
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management

funding.detail: ₱1,000,000,000 is appropriated as the revolving fund. The copy filed does not say from which source the amount is drawn.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, the Pilgrimage Authority would have ₱1,000,000,000 to pay Hajj slots and hotels ahead of pilgrims' payments.
Past budget allocations for the same purpose would revert to the Treasury.
readings.insight:
The Fund sits uneasily with the law that created the Pilgrimage Authority. Section 45 of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, BAA 13, limits the Authority's collections to mutawiff and passporting or processing fees, gives pilgrims free choice of travel agencies and of where to buy logistics, and says they may in no case be forced to buy these from the Authority. This bill has the Authority paying hotels and accommodation in advance and collecting the cost from pilgrims, and it does not amend BAA 13.

The bill sets no cap per pilgrim, no deadline for repayment and no consequence if a pilgrim does not pay; it only tells the Authority to "provide a mechanism". For scale, the 2026 supplemental budget, BAA 91, gave the Authority ₱76,020,000; the Fund is about 13 times that.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Shari'ah Justice System Code. It adds to Presidential Decree 1083, the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, in 5 areas: Shari'ah civil actions, Islamic commercial contracts, divorce by mutual agreement, ta'zir offences, and mediation and arbitration. It applies mainly to Muslims in the region, and to non-Muslims and companies that agree in writing to Shari'ah court jurisdiction; once they do, they cannot back out on grounds of religion.

It restates the jurisdiction of the Shari'ah Circuit and District Courts as written in the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and extends to those courts any national law or Supreme Court rule that benefits first and second level courts. It makes breach of Shari'ah-compliant contracts, breach of sulh settlements, false halal claims, abuse of trust, waqf disputes and disputes over murabahah, ijarah, sukuk, takaful and similar contracts actionable. It adds mubara'at, divorce by mutual agreement, confirmed by a Shari'ah court after a mandatory joint hearing.

It defines 7 ta'zir offences: disturbing the adhan or congregational prayer, false halal labelling, cheating on weights and measures, vandalising mosques, madaris, waqf property or Islamic cemeteries, fraudulent use of conversion to Islam, unlawful elopement of minors, and overcharging or misrepresentation by Shari'ah counselors. It requires mediation, sulh or customary reconciliation before suit wherever practicable, and lets Shari'ah courts constitute Agama Arbitration Councils.

It was filed on 8 July 2026 by MPs Romeo K. Sema, Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Saripuddin D. Jikiri and Nurredha I. Misuari, read on first reading on 14 July 2026 and referred to the Committee on Bangsamoro Justice System and the Committee on Finance, Budget, and Management on 15 July 2026, and remains in committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says that for more than 4 decades since PD 1083 was enacted in 1977, Shari'ah in the Philippines has stayed confined to personal status and family law, with no framework for civil obligations, Islamic commerce, ta'zir offences or Shari'ah-based dispute resolution. Article X of the Bangsamoro Organic Law gives the Parliament power to legislate on these, and Section 20 calls for conciliation and mediation; the Code is meant to use that power while staying consistent with the Constitution and PD 1083.
whoIsAffected: Muslims in the region with civil, commercial or family disputes, who would gain new causes of action and divorce by mutual agreement.
Non-Muslims and companies that sign contracts choosing Shari'ah law, who would be bound to Shari'ah court jurisdiction.
Traders, food sellers and halal certifiers, exposed to the halal and weights and measures offences.
Shari'ah counselors, mediators, ulama and customary adjudicators.
implementedBy: Shari'ah Circuit and District Courts
Agama Arbitration Councils and accredited mediators
Ministries and offices to be named in the implementing rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 38 says the Parliament shall appropriate such funds as may be necessary and the Office of the Chief Minister shall release them. The title says it appropriates funds; the text appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill is in committee.
If enacted, Muslim couples could dissolve a marriage by mutual agreement confirmed in a Shari'ah court.
False halal claims, rigged scales and vandalism of Islamic institutions would become regional offences.
Parties would have to try mediation or sulh before suing, wherever practicable.
readings.insight:
Most of the new offences carry no penalty. Sections 18 to 23, on disturbing prayer, false halal claims, rigged scales, vandalism, fraudulent conversion and elopement of minors, each end "shall be liable under this section" without saying liable to what. Section 20 adds that "the same penalty" applies to deceptive market practices, but no penalty has been set. Only Section 24, on Shari'ah counselors, fixes one: up to 30 days in prison, a fine of up to ₱50,000, or both.

Much of the Code repeats existing law. Sections 7 and 9 copy word for word the Shari'ah court jurisdiction already set in Sections 5 and 6 of Article X of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which the explanatory note also quotes. The Books run from VII straight to IX; there is no Book VIII.

It is the second Shari'ah justice measure in committee. Bill 363, filed in June 2025, would create a Bangsamoro Shari'ah Judicial and Legal Academy to train the people this Code would rely on.

readings.whatItDoes:
Grants civil service eligibility to Bangsamoro government workers on job order, contract of service, casual or contractual status who have given at least 10 years of continuous and efficient service. Once eligible, they would be entitled to permanent appointment to their present positions, or to other positions the eligibility qualifies them for, as the Civil Service Commission determines.

The whole operative text is 5 short sections. The Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission writes the implementing rules within 90 days, consistent with the merit and fitness principle.

It was filed on 27 January 2025 by MP Marjanie S. Macasalong and read on first reading on 10 February 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, a little over 18 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note rests on the Bangsamoro Organic Law's provision for a regional civil service based on merit, fitness and equal opportunity. It argues that long-serving workers in non-permanent posts have earned job security and a path to advancement, and that granting eligibility would help the government keep experienced people who know their roles and their communities.
whoIsAffected: Job order, contract of service, casual and contractual workers in the Bangsamoro government with 10 or more years of continuous service.
Ministries and offices that would have to convert these workers to permanent appointments.
Applicants who earn eligibility by examination, who would compete with a new group of eligibles.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission, which issues the implementing rules
Civil Service Commission, which determines the positions the eligibility qualifies a worker for

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. No amount is stated in the copy filed, although permanent appointments would carry salary and benefit costs.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, 10 years of continuous non-permanent service would itself confer civil service eligibility.
Workers who qualify would be entitled to permanent appointment, subject to the Civil Service Commission.
readings.insight:
The same idea has been pending since 2022. Bill 56, filed on 26 September 2022 by MP Romeo K. Sema, provides for civil service eligibility and permanent appointment for casual and contractual employees of the Bangsamoro government. It was read on first reading on 17 October 2022 and the index records no referral since. Parliament's index lists MP Sema as a co-author of this bill. Neither has reached a committee.

Section 1 has a tension in its first line. It covers employees "holding career civil service positions appointed under job order, contract of service, casual or contractual status". Job order and contract of service engagements are not appointments to positions at all, so as drafted the section may cover fewer people than the title and note suggest. The note also speaks of a "total" of 10 years, while Section 1 requires 10 years of "continuous" service, which would exclude anyone whose contract had a gap.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes the Shariff Kabunsuan Shrine in Barangay Kalanganan 2, Cotabato City, as a historical and cultural landmark, a centre for Islamic studies and research, and a tourist destination.

The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage would govern and administer it. The structure of its governing body and its detailed powers are left to the implementing rules, which the Commission writes within 90 days with the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism. The shrine may enter contracts, receive donations and grants, and set rules for its use.

It was filed on 13 May 2025 by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and read on first reading on 20 May 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 15 months later.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the shrine would recognise Shariff Kabunsuan's arrival and his introduction of Islam to this part of Mindanao, and serve as a centre for cultural preservation, historical education and the promotion of peace. It adds that it would be a landmark for cultural tourism.

Section 2 cites the Constitution, the National Cultural Heritage Act of 2009 and Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law as its legal bases.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Barangay Kalanganan 2 and Cotabato City, where the shrine would stand.
Visitors and researchers of Bangsamoro and Islamic history.
The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which would run it.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, in drafting the implementing rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 9 says the funds shall be provided in the annual appropriations for public works, with disbursement by the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, a shrine to Shariff Kabunsuan would exist in regional law at Kalanganan 2, under the heritage commission.
readings.insight:
The bill establishes the shrine but says almost nothing about it. There is no site description, no land area, no statement of who owns the land, and no figure for its cost. Even the composition of the body that would run it is left to the implementing rules.

The author lists differ. The copy filed names 6 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 15.

readings.whatItDoes:
Creates the Bangsamoro State University, a public higher education institution seated in the Municipality of Kabuntalan, Maguindanao del Norte. It would offer technical-vocational, undergraduate and graduate programs, including law, public administration, health sciences and engineering, and could open branches or extension campuses.

A Board of Regents runs it, chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, with the university president as vice chair. Members include the chair of Parliament's education committee, the BPDA Director General, the Minister of Science and Technology, the Mayor of Kabuntalan, and elected faculty, student and non-teaching representatives. The president serves 5-year terms. Within 120 days the university must submit a 5-year development plan, undergo a management audit and start at least 4 degree-granting units. Donations to it are exempt from donor's tax.

It was filed on 26 May 2025 by MPs Baintan A. Ampatuan, Tomanda D. Antok, Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., Sittie Fahanie S. Uy-Oyod and Khalid M. Hadji Abdullah, and read on first reading on 29 May 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, about 14 months later.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note builds a case from enrolment data. It says BARMM's elementary completion rate was 54% against a national 94% in 2017, and that only 1 in 10 children who start primary school finishes Grade 10 on time. Citing EDCOM II through a newspaper column, it puts the region's higher education participation rate at 18.7% and its higher education attrition at 93.4%, against 39% nationally.

It concludes that a state university is needed to give Bangsamoro students easier access to higher education.
whoIsAffected: Students in the region seeking college, graduate and technical-vocational education.
Kabuntalan, Maguindanao del Norte, which would host the main campus.
MBHTE, which chairs the board and carries the budget.
implementedBy: Board of Regents of the Bangsamoro State University
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, on the development plan and rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 21 charges initial implementation to the Contingent Fund, and later years to MBHTE's budget under the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the region would have its own chartered state university, seated in Kabuntalan.
MBHTE would report to Parliament within 6 months and every year after.
readings.insight:
Parts of the charter read as carried over from a national state university template. Section 9 says the "Director General for Higher Education" presides when the chair is absent, but no such officer sits on the board. Section 10 says the president's 5-year term "shall not adversely affect the term of the incumbent President", and starts the search committee 6 months before "the incumbent President" leaves. A university created by this act would have no incumbent.

The choice of Kabuntalan is stated but not explained. Neither the note nor the text says why the seat goes there or what facilities exist. Another higher education bill is already in committee: Bill 274, which converts Upi Agricultural School into a university, was referred to the education and finance committees on 15 December 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
Makes a dedicated subject on Bangsamoro history mandatory in the secondary curriculum of all public and private schools in the region, covering both Junior High School and Senior High School.

MBHTE would develop the program, consult historians, and produce primers, textbooks and other materials. The subject must cover liberation movements and revolutions, the pursuit of self-determination, the histories of the Sultanates and other indigenous institutions, and "factual, verifiable narratives". Teachers must have knowledge or qualifications in Bangsamoro history, and MBHTE must train them and set up a research unit. Every 5 years an independent panel appointed by the Chief Minister would review implementation.

It was filed on 26 May 2025 by MPs Baintan A. Ampatuan, Don Mustapha A. Loong, Rasul E. Ismael and Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., and read on first reading on 29 May 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, about 14 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the Organic Law's duty to preserve the history and heritage of the Bangsamoro people and their Sultanates, naming Sulu, Maguindanao, Kabuntalan, Buayan, the Royal House of Ranao and the Iranun, as well as non-Moro Indigenous Peoples. It argues that knowing the history of the struggle for self-determination is essential to understanding the region today.
whoIsAffected: Secondary students in every public and private school in the region.
Teachers assigned to the subject, who would need the required background and training.
Private schools, which would have to add the subject.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
An independent review panel appointed by the Chief Minister every 5 years

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 says funds shall be included in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations, submitted by MBHTE.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, Bangsamoro history would become a required subject in every secondary school in the region.
readings.insight:
A footnote on the first page says the bill is patterned on an entry by Marinelle Diocolano Veruen in a 2024 Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of the 4 principal authors. A contest entry becoming a filed bill is unusual, and the copy credits it openly.

The title and the text describe different measures. The title speaks of integrating "basic knowledge" of Bangsamoro history into the existing curriculum. Sections 3 and 5 require a separate, dedicated, mandatory subject in secondary education, which Section 4 defines as 4 years of Junior High School and 2 of Senior High School. A dedicated subject needs its own time slot and teachers. The Bangsamoro Education Code, BAA 18, already carries the region's education framework, and the bill does not say how it fits with it.

readings.whatItDoes:
Creates a BARMM Health Benefit Program giving every Bangsamoro government employee HMO coverage, including dental and medical care, through licensed HMO providers. Coverage reaches permanent, contractual, temporary, job order and casual personnel once they have worked 6 months.

Employees may enrol dependents, including a spouse, children below 21, disabled children and parents aged 60 or above with low income, under a voluntary scheme the employee pays for in part or in full. The Ministry of Health leads, with MFBM, each office's human resource unit and the Insurance Commission. MFBM and the Ministry of Health issue rules within 60 days after consulting employee unions.

It was filed on 23 June 2025 by MP Abrar J. Hataman and read on first reading on 26 June 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 14 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that public servants face the same health problems as the people they serve, and that HMO coverage would spare them high out-of-pocket costs. It says the program would improve morale and productivity, reduce absences due to illness, and help the regional government attract and keep competent staff.
whoIsAffected: All Bangsamoro government employees, including job order and casual workers, after 6 months of service.
Their dependents, if the employee opts to enrol and pay for them.
Licensed HMO providers that would contract with the program.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Human resource offices of each ministry and office, with the Insurance Commission

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 8 funds Fiscal Year 2025 from the savings of the Bangsamoro Government, and later years through the annual appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, every regional government employee with 6 months of service would be entitled to HMO coverage paid by the government.
readings.insight:
The funding clause has expired on the calendar. Section 8 pays for the first year from Fiscal Year 2025 savings. The bill was read on first reading in June 2025 and had not reached a committee by August 2026, so that year has passed, and the bill names no source for the year it would actually start.

The program has 2 names under 1 acronym. Section 4 creates the "BARMM Health Benefit Program (BHBP)"; Section 5 entitles employees to the "Bangsamoro Health Benefit Package (BHBP)". The copy filed names MP Hataman alone; Parliament's index lists 11 co-authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
Renames the Municipality of South Upi in Maguindanao del Sur as "Teduray Municipality". The change takes effect only if a majority of votes cast approve it in a plebiscite held within 90 days, run by the Bangsamoro Electoral Office with the Commission on Elections.

On ratification, every regional law, issuance, map and document referring to South Upi would be read as referring to Teduray Municipality. The plebiscite is paid from available Bangsamoro Government funds, which the town may augment.

It was filed on 23 July 2025 by MPs Froilyn T. Mendoza and Tawakal B. Midtimbang and read on first reading on 20 August 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 12 months later.
readings.whyProposed: There is no separate explanatory note; the preamble gives the reasons. It says South Upi, created by Presidential Decree No. 1011 of 22 September 1976, is predominantly inhabited by the Teduray Indigenous People, and that the new name reflects their aspirations for cultural recognition, historical justice and self-determination. It cites the Organic Law and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
whoIsAffected: Residents and voters of South Upi, who would decide in the plebiscite.
The Teduray people, whose name the municipality would carry.
Government offices that would update records and maps.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Electoral Office, with the Commission on Elections, for the plebiscite
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for implementing rules and dissemination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The plebiscite is charged to the Bangsamoro Government's available funds, with optional augmentation from the municipality.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted and ratified, South Upi would become Teduray Municipality.
readings.insight:
A neighbouring rename has already gone through. Bill 328, which renamed Datu Blah T. Sinsuat as West Upi, was filed in August 2024 and enacted as BAA 90 in May 2026, also subject to a plebiscite. Bill 284, renaming Sultan Mastura as Subpangen, has been in the Committee on Local Government since 18 June 2024. This bill has not yet reached a committee.

The copy filed is loosely drafted. It uses a Book, Chapter and Article structure in which Section 1 appears 3 times. It names the ministry that writes the rules as the "Ministry of Local Government" in one section and the "Ministry of Interior and Local Government" in the next. The authors differ too. The copy filed names MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr. and MP Bai Ali S. Karon as co-authors; Parliament's index lists MP Sinolinding as a principal author and does not list MP Karon.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes the "Doctors of the Soul" program, which would accredit Ulama, Ustadhs, Ustadhas and other faith-based counsellors to give psycho-spiritual support within government services. The Ministry of Social Services and Development leads, sets up a dedicated unit and keeps a Regional Registry of accredited counsellors.

A Doctors of the Soul Accreditation Board, with the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' as authority on Islamic qualifications, would issue guidelines within 90 days: minimum Islamic education, basic mental health and psychosocial support training, character references and examinations, with accreditation renewable every 3 years. MSSD, MBHTE and the Ministry of Health must deploy accredited counsellors in social programs, schools and hospitals, and local governments are encouraged to. Engagement may be through plantilla positions, contracts or volunteer agreements.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema and Saripuddin D. Jikiri, and read on first reading on 20 August 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 12 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that communities in the region have long turned to religious and Indigenous spiritual leaders for mental, emotional and moral guidance, without formal recognition or support. It grounds the bill in the Organic Law's provisions on moral governance and social services, in the Maqasid al-Shari'ah, and in the principle of rahmah. It says the bill does this "without creating additional bureaucratic layers".
whoIsAffected: Ulama, Ustadhs and Ustadhas who seek accreditation and paid or volunteer engagement.
People using government social, school and health services, who would meet these counsellors.
Priests, pastors and Indigenous spiritual leaders, who are named in the policy.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development, lead agency
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', on Islamic qualifications
Ministry of Health and MBHTE, which deploy counsellors

funding.detail: The title says it appropriates funds, but no appropriation section appears in the copy filed. Section 8 tells ministries and local governments to put the engagement of counsellors in their annual plans.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, accredited religious counsellors would be placed in regional social, school and health services.
readings.insight:
The copy filed is incomplete. It has 11 pages. Page 10 ends at Section 10(a), and page 11 begins at Section 17, the effectivity clause. Sections 10(b) to 16 are missing, including whatever the bill says about welfare benefits, honoraria and funding, which are the "welfare" half of its title.

The bill is broader in its title than in its text. The title and Section 2 include Indigenous spiritual leaders, priests and pastors. But the Accreditation Board covers "Ulama, Ustadhs, Ustadhas, and similarly qualified faith-based counselors", requires minimum Islamic educational qualifications, and Section 9 frames every duty in Islamic terms, including khutbah. As written, a priest or an Indigenous elder has no evident route to accreditation. The note also says it adds no bureaucratic layers, while the text creates a working group, an accreditation board and a dedicated unit in MSSD.

readings.whatItDoes:
Establishes a Bangsamoro Women's Welfare Center to provide prenatal, postnatal, family planning, reproductive health and mental health services to women, integrating Islamic teachings with modern medicine.

The Center would have 4 divisions: medical services, mental health, community outreach, and Islamic guidance and spiritual care. It would employ obstetricians, paediatricians, psychiatrists, nurses, midwives, counsellors and Islamic scholars. Services listed include ultrasound, immunisation, breastfeeding support, contraception including IUDs, screening for breast cancer and diabetes, and post-abortion care. The Ministry of Health issues the rules.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema and Saripuddin D. Jikiri, and read on first reading on 20 August 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 12 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says women in the region face acute barriers to care, that maternal mortality in BARMM is above the national average, and, citing BPDA, that no hospital in the region has a dedicated institution for women's health. It proposes a centre that is culturally appropriate and grounded in Islamic values, and quotes Qur'an 31:14 on maternal care.
whoIsAffected: Pregnant and postpartum women in the region.
Women needing mental health care, family planning or care after violence.
The Ministry of Health and MSSD, which carry the initial cost.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Ministry of Social Services and Development, for initial funding

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 17 charges initial implementation to the current appropriations of the Ministry of Health and/or MSSD, with later years in the annual budget. Section 14 adds grants and private donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, a women's health centre combining medical and Islamic spiritual care would exist in regional law.
readings.insight:
The title promises a centre "in every province and major hospital"; the text establishes one. Section 6 says the Center "shall be established within" BARMM "to serve as the primary health institution", in the singular, and no provision mentions provinces or hospitals. The text also refers to a "Board of Trustees" in Section 16 that it never creates, calls the Center an "Institute" in Section 14, and has 2 sections numbered 8.

The note's figures do not agree with each other. Page 1 gives the global target as fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. Page 2 says the Philippine rate of 24.5 is "higher than the global target of less than 20". On the first target, 24.5 is well within it.

This is 1 of 6 bills the same 5 MPs filed on 28 July 2025, Bills 381 to 386. Only Bill 386 had reached a committee by August 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Creates a Social Equity Investment Fund, a non-lapsing revolving trust fund that would buy equity in enterprises in the region and allocate non-transferable shares, with dividend rights, to vulnerable groups: widows and orphans of conflict, persons with disabilities, displaced people, survivors of gender-based violence and Indigenous Peoples.

MSSD manages it under an Inter-Ministerial Social Equity Investment Board chaired by the Minister of Social Services and Development, with the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' advising on Shari'ah compliance. Capital would come from appropriations, grants, zakat, waqf and other Islamic social finance, corporate social responsibility contributions and public-private co-investment. Misusing fund money or rigging allocations would carry fines of ₱500,000 to ₱5,000,000 and 6 to 12 years in prison for private persons.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema and Saripuddin D. Jikiri, and read on first reading on 19 August 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 12 months later.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites a 2022 poverty incidence of 35.9% in BARMM against 18.7% nationally, and argues that current programs are aid-driven and short-term. It proposes giving the poor a direct ownership stake in enterprises, through a Shari'ah-compliant vehicle, and cites the Maharlika Investment Fund Act as a national precedent that does not fit the region's context.
whoIsAffected: Vulnerable groups who would receive non-transferable shares and dividends.
Enterprises in the region that take investment from the fund.
Private companies asked to contribute through corporate social responsibility.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development, fund manager
Inter-Ministerial Social Equity Investment Board
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', on Shari'ah compliance

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 20 charges initial implementation to MSSD's current appropriations, with later years in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, a regional fund would hold equity in enterprises on behalf of vulnerable groups and pay them dividends.
readings.insight:
The incentives the bill is built around are not in it. The note promises CSR tax credits and Shari'ah-compliant investment certifications. Section 13, "Incentives for Participating Enterprises", opens by saying enterprises "shall be entitled to incentives" which "may include", and then lists 3 obligations: comply with the equity mandate, integrate community development, submit audited reports. Section 14, "Obligations", repeats the same 3 items word for word.

Other drafting gaps are checkable on the page. Section 20 is headed "Separability Clause" but contains the appropriation text, so the bill has no separability clause. Chapter VI is missing between Chapters V and VII. The note and Section 6 name a "Bangsamoro Commission on Audit", which does not exist; Section 13 says "Commission on Audit - BARMM".

readings.whatItDoes:
Sets up a regional peace and public safety framework built around an Integrated Community Defense System that links the regional government, the police, the AFP, local governments and civil society, with councils at regional, provincial, city, municipal and barangay level. The Regional ICDS Council is chaired by the Chief Minister, convened by MILG, with the Ministry of Public Order and Safety as secretariat.

All business establishments, public buildings, terminals, ports and high-traffic areas designated by MILG must install CCTV meeting minimum specifications, including 30 days of storage. Failure to install carries fines of ₱25,000 to ₱100,000; tampering with cameras carries 6 months to 2 years in prison. At least 5% of the annual development budget of the regional government and every local government would go to peace and order programs. A Task Force Peace and Security - BARMM under MILG would run training and awareness campaigns, modelled on Task Force Davao.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema and Saripuddin D. Jikiri, and read on first reading on 19 August 2025. Parliament's index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral, so it has not moved since first reading, almost 12 months later.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites a run of violent incidents: a clash in Sumisip, Basilan, in January 2025; the BIFF occupation of the Datu Paglas market in 2021; the killing of a municipal election officer in Datu Odin Sinsuat in March 2025; and at least 26 deaths in Cotabato City and Maguindanao between February and March 2025 despite a gun ban. It points to private armed groups, rido and poor coordination between the AFP, the police and local actors.

It argues that a single framework combining modern security tools with culturally sensitive, community-based approaches is needed.
whoIsAffected: Business owners and public facilities that would have to install and maintain CCTV.
Local governments, which would have to set aside at least 5% of their development budget.
Residents, asked under the Culture of Security to report suspicious activity.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Bangsamoro ICT Office, with the Ministry of Science and Technology, on CCTV standards

funding.detail: No separate appropriation. Section 19 requires at least 5% of the annual development budget of the regional government and all local governments to go to peace and order and public safety programs.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, CCTV would become mandatory for designated establishments, with fines for non-compliance.
At least 5% of every development budget in the region would be earmarked for peace and order.
readings.insight:
Section 10, "Composition of the ICDS", opens with a sentence about childbirth: "Postnatal care shall focus on ensuring the full recovery of mothers after childbirth, providing necessary medical care, emotional support, and guidance for new mothers." That is the opening of Section 9 of Bill 382, the women's welfare centre bill, which the same 5 MPs filed the same day. It was carried into a security bill and not removed.

The acronym BPOC means 3 different things. Section 5 defines it as the Bangsamoro Peace and Order Council, the regional body. Section 10 uses it for Barangay Peace and Order Committees. Sections 20 and 25 refer to a "Barangay Peace and Order Council (BPOC)", and make it the body with which MILG writes the implementing rules. Section 12 also says the Regional ICDS Council is composed of the agencies listed "under Section 12", which is itself; the list is in Section 10.

A narrower bill on the same ground came later. Bill 436, filed in January 2026, would set up a security data and information management body, and is also unreferred.

readings.whatItDoes:
It declares Tawi-Tawi the Seaweed Capital of the Philippines. That declaration, in Section 5, is the only operative provision. It rests on Tawi-Tawi being the major producer of Eucheuma and Kappaphycus seaweeds, the main sources of carrageenan, and the biggest contributor to the country's seaweed exports.

Sections 2 to 4 are statements of fact rather than rules: seaweed farming is the main livelihood of thousands of coastal families, the industry has helped lift the province out of the 20 poorest in the country, and the Agal-Agal Festival, held each year on the province's founding anniversary on 25 September, is the country's main seaweed festival. The bill creates no office, program or duty and spends nothing. The whole text runs to 8 sections over 2 pages.

It was filed on 3 October 2022 with MP Eddie M. Alih first among 45 principal authors, was read on first reading on 24 January 2023, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 1 cites the Bangsamoro Organic Law's mandate to promote economic prosperity and culture, and its provision that regional fisheries policy should support small farmers and marginal fisherfolk. Section 5 gives the reasons for the title: recognising Tawi-Tawi's output and export share, supporting the province's economy, and promoting its culture and traditions.
whoIsAffected: Seaweed farming families in Tawi-Tawi, whose industry would carry the title.
The provincial government and the Agal-Agal Festival, which could use the designation in promotion.
implementedBy: No agency is named. The bill is a declaration only.
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, Tawi-Tawi would be declared the Seaweed Capital of the Philippines in regional law.
No program, office, incentive or funding would follow from the declaration itself.
readings.insight:
The filed copy is signed by MP Eddie M. Alih alone, though it lists 46 names as introducers. One of them, MP Aida M. Silongan, appears twice in that list, which is why Parliament's index counts 45 principal authors. The index also credits 21 co-authors where the copy names 14.

The declaration is the least demanding of 3 seaweed bills filed in the first months of this Parliament, and none of them has moved. MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil, a principal author here, filed Bill 80, incentivising seaweed farming, and Bill 86, creating a Seaweed Industry Development Authority, both on 27 September 2022. Bill 86 was read on first reading on 22 December 2022 and Bill 80 on 19 January 2023, and like this one neither shows a committee referral in the index. As of October 2026 this bill has sat at first reading for 3 years and 8 months.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Political Party Subsidy Act. It creates a Bangsamoro Political Party Subsidy Fund to pay regional political parties, including sectoral parties and organisations, for party development and campaign spending.
