Section 19 appropriates ₱100,000,000 from the Bangsamoro treasury on approval and ₱100,000,000 every year after, administered by the Commission on Elections through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office.

Each year's fund is split 4 ways: 10% to COMELEC for monitoring and voter education, 60% to parties by their seats in Parliament, 25% to parties by the local posts they hold, from governor down to municipal council, and 5% to sectoral parties with sectoral seats in Parliament. In a non-election year the money may only go to party development and activities the Electoral Code requires; in an election year 75% goes to campaigning and 25% to party development. Parties qualify through accreditation judged on political representation, organisational strength and track record.

Parties must keep separate accounts, submit to Commission on Audit examination, publish their officials' statements of assets and liabilities and disclose contributions and spending. A party that fails to comply loses its share, which reverts to the Bangsamoro treasury. COMELEC and COA must report to Parliament by 30 June each year.

It was filed on 6 March 2024 by MP Tarhata M. Maglangit with 6 other principal authors, read on first reading on 20 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 gives the reasoning: political parties are the essence of participatory democracy, and public funding would reduce the influence of private money on elections and, through elections, on public policy, levelling the field among candidates and parties.
whoIsAffected: Regional political parties and sectoral organisations, which could receive a share of ₱100,000,000 a year.
Candidates of accredited parties, whose campaign travel, staff and materials the fund could pay for.
Voters, who would get annual published reports on how parties used public money.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office
Commission on Audit
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, on release guidelines

funding.detail: Section 19 appropriates ₱100,000,000 from the funds of the Bangsamoro treasury not otherwise appropriated, effective on approval, and ₱100,000,000 every year after.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, regional parties would receive public money each year, distributed by seats held.
Parties taking the subsidy would face separate accounts, COA audits and public disclosure.
COMELEC would receive 10% of the fund for monitoring and voter education in the region.
readings.insight:
Most of the fund was written to be shared by results that did not yet exist. Section 10 distributes 60% by seats won "in the most recent regional elections" and 5% by sectoral seats in Parliament. When the bill was filed, the Parliament was still the appointed Bangsamoro Transition Authority and no regional parliamentary election had been held. The 25% tied to governors, mayors and local councils also counts seats won "in the most recent regional elections", though those posts are not filled in the parliamentary elections the Bangsamoro Electoral Code governs.

The drafting has loose ends. Section 4(g) extends the disclosure duty to "accredited national political parties" in a bill that otherwise funds only regional ones. Section 8 says a party "accredited in accordance with Section 9" may apply for accreditation, which is circular. "The Commission" is used throughout and never defined, though the context points to COMELEC.

The filed copy names 4 co-sponsors; Parliament's index credits 15 co-authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Book Excellence Act. It sets up a Bangsamoro Book Excellence Recognition and Incentive Committee under the Office of the Chief Minister to recognise and reward Bangsamoro authors of published books judged excellent. Only Bangsamoro people as defined in the Organic Law qualify. Fiction and non-fiction count, including novels, short stories, poetry, history, science, law and academic works, in print or electronic form; theses and dissertations do not.

The committee is chaired by the Senior Minister, with the Minister of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education as vice-chairperson and representatives of the Office of the Chief Minister, Parliament's education committee, 6 other regional bodies, 2 literary organisations, the academe and the publishing industry. It writes its own manual and standard of excellence, receives and screens submitted books, and decides how much each author is awarded. It also runs workshops for aspiring authors, gives feedback to those not recognised, and promotes Bangsamoro literature. The first awards fall in the year after the implementing rules take effect, then every 3 years.

It was filed on 7 March 2024 by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, read on first reading on 20 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that writing preserves a people's stories and that books by Bangsamoro authors can do for the region what Jose Rizal's novels did for the Filipino nation. It says the BARMM is history in the making and that without authors to document it, the history of the Bangsamoro people would be lost, and presents the bill as a tribute to the sacrifices authors make in pursuit of truth.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro authors of published books, who could submit their work for recognition and an award.
Aspiring writers, through the committee's workshops and feedback.
Schools, libraries and literary groups the committee would partner with.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, on the implementing rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 puts the cost in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the region would hold a book awards cycle every 3 years with cash or other incentives for authors.
A new committee under the Office of the Chief Minister would set the standards and the size of each award.
readings.insight:
The bill never says what the incentive is or how large it can be. Section 6 leaves the committee to "determine the amount of incentives", and no figure, cap or form of reward appears anywhere in the 15 sections. Parliament would be funding a prize it has not sized.

The committee's make-up does not hold together. Section 7 names the Minister of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education as vice-chairperson, then says the representative of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage "shall serve as the vice-chairperson" too. It seats representatives of the environment and agriculture ministries on a literary jury, then requires every member to have a proven track record in literature.

The filed copy names 33 co-authors; Parliament's index credits 45.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Agri-fishery Workers Social Protection Act of 2024. It creates a Bangsamoro Agri-fishery Workers Social Protection Board, attached to the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and chaired by its Minister, with the labour, interior, science and social services ministers and 5 representatives of farmers, fisherfolk and their organisations. The Board writes a social protection agenda covering basic services, redistribution of resources, sustainable use of natural resources and a say in decisions. A new Social Protection Bureau in MAFAR serves as its secretariat.

Farmers, fisherfolk and farm labourers would register in person at centres in every town and city a year after the law takes effect. The registry would hold personal data including religion, tribal affiliation and blood type, along with a photograph and a full set of fingerprints, and each worker gets a free Social Protection ID that counts as proof of identity in regional offices. MAFAR would enrol registered workers with the Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation, PhilHealth and the Social Security System and pay their contributions for the first year, after which workers pay their own.

The bill also sets rules for Community Savings Groups of 15 to 25 members, accredited by MAFAR provincial offices for 3 years at a time and given start-up kits. An independent panel reviews the law every 10 years.

It was filed on 25 March 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Don Mustapha A. Loong and Rasul E. Ismael, read on first reading on 20 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the constitutional duty to protect labour and the Organic Law's call to support small farmers and marginal fisherfolk. It argues that growth must not come at the expense of agri-fishery workers who earn little, work long hours in hazardous conditions and lack basic benefits, and that income support, crop insurance, health coverage, microfinance and training would reduce their vulnerability and raise production.

A footnote says the bill is patterned on an entry by Jamal R. Pandapatan in a 2023 Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of the 4 principal authors.
whoIsAffected: Farmers, fisherfolk and farm labourers, who would register, receive an ID and be enrolled in crop, health and social insurance.
Farmer and fisherfolk organisations, which would nominate Board members.
Community savings groups, which could seek accreditation and support from MAFAR.
implementedBy: Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, through a new Social Protection Bureau
Bangsamoro Agri-fishery Workers Social Protection Board

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Article VIII charges the first year to the contingency fund of the Office of the Chief Minister and later years to the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. MAFAR would carry 1 year of each registered worker's insurance contributions, which the bill does not cost.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, MAFAR gains a Social Protection Bureau and an attached policy Board.
Agri-fishery workers would register with biometrics and receive a Social Protection ID.
MAFAR would pay 1 year of crop insurance, PhilHealth and SSS contributions for registered workers.
readings.insight:
This is one of 3 bills the same 4 MPs filed on 25 March 2024 that each carry a footnote saying the text is patterned on an entry in their own 2023 drafting contest. Bill 290 on a regional laboratory and Bill 291 on agri-fishery lessons in schools are the others. All 3 were read on first reading in May 2024 and none has been referred to a committee.

The copy does not settle what it is creating. The title calls the new office the Bureau of Social Protection (BSP); Article III calls it the Social Protection Bureau (MAFAR-SPB). The explanatory note's title says "Framework" where the bill's says "Program". The registry would collect religion, tribal affiliation and fingerprints, and the bill limits that only by a reference to the Data Privacy Act.

The Bureau would sit inside MAFAR, which Bill 102 proposes to split into 3 bodies. That bill reached committee in November 2025; this one is still at first reading after 2 years and 4 months.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Diagnostic and Clinical Laboratory Act of 2024. It establishes a Bangsamoro Diagnostic and Clinical Laboratory under the administrative supervision of the Ministry of Health, which decides its organisational structure. The laboratory would do the annual diagnostic examinations of all employees of Bangsamoro ministries and offices, and serve as the referral laboratory for tests that hospitals and laboratories in the region cannot do.

At minimum it is staffed by a pathologist, medical technologists registered with the Professional Regulation Commission, and support staff. It integrates the Universal Health Care Act into its operations. The Ministry of Health writes the rules within 60 days and reports to Parliament every year, and an independent panel reviews the law every 10 years.

It was filed on 25 March 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan with MPs Don Mustapha A. Loong, Rasul E. Ismael and Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., read on first reading on 20 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the constitutional right to health and the Organic Law's call for a general hospital system. It says early detection leads to better outcomes, and that many special tests ordered by doctors in the region are not available there, so specimens are sent to the Southern Philippines Medical Center in Davao City or the Philippine General Hospital in Manila. A regional laboratory with complete special tests would let doctors diagnose patients in time.

A footnote says the bill is patterned on an entry by Abdulnawaf M. Daud in a 2023 Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of the 4 principal authors.
whoIsAffected: Patients whose specimens are now sent to Davao City or Manila for special tests.
Employees of Bangsamoro ministries and offices, who would have their annual examinations there.
Hospitals and doctors in the region, who would gain a referral laboratory.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 puts construction, equipment, supplies, personnel and other costs in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the region would have its own referral laboratory for special tests under the Ministry of Health.
Annual examinations of Bangsamoro government employees would be done there.
readings.insight:
The bill does not say where the laboratory would be. Section 5 establishes it "in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region" and nothing more: no city, no hospital it would sit beside, no list of tests, no cost. For a facility whose case rests on distance from Davao City and Manila, its own location is the first thing a committee would have to decide.

It is one of 3 bills the same 4 MPs filed on 25 March 2024 that each carry a footnote saying the text is patterned on an entry in their own 2023 drafting contest; Bills 289 and 291 are the others. None of the 3 has been referred to a committee in the 2 years and 4 months since first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Basic Agri-Fishery Knowledge Act of 2024. It makes Basic Agri-fishery Knowledge a mandatory subject in all public and private elementary and secondary schools in the region, covering cultivating land, planting and growing crops, fishing and raising animals. The Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education integrates it into the existing curriculum, working with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform.

The subject must be taught by someone with knowledge and expertise in agriculture and fishery, given continuing training. A unit within MBHTE keeps the content under review. MBHTE writes the rules within 60 days and reports to Parliament every year, and an independent panel reviews the law every 10 years.

It was filed on 25 March 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan with MPs Don Mustapha A. Loong, Rasul E. Ismael and Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., read on first reading on 21 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the Organic Law's treatment of agriculture as a key development strategy and a 2019 statement by then Agriculture Secretary Emmanuel F. Pinol that the region could become a major food producer, with about 100,000 hectares suited to high-value crops and the potential to produce at least 3 million metric tons of paddy rice a year. It argues that teaching every pupil the basics of farming and fishing would plant interest in the sector early.

A footnote says the bill is patterned on an entry by Nor-Alejah P. Anarig in a 2023 Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of the 4 principal authors.
whoIsAffected: Elementary and secondary pupils in public and private schools, who would take a new required subject.
Teachers, who would need agriculture and fishery expertise to teach it.
MBHTE, which must fit the subject into the existing curriculum.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 provides only that "the funds necessary for the establishment of playgrounds" be included in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, every elementary and secondary school in the region would teach Basic Agri-fishery Knowledge.
MBHTE would set up a unit to keep the subject's content under review.
readings.insight:
The appropriations clause funds the wrong thing. Section 11 reads: "The funds necessary for the establishment of playgrounds shall be included in the General Appropriation Act of the Bangsamoro." Nothing in this bill establishes a playground. MP Ampatuan is the principal author of Bill 50, which requires a children's playground in every school and was referred to committee on 16 July 2025, and the clause reads as carried over from that kind of text. As filed, the curriculum bill has no clause funding the curriculum.

It is one of 3 bills the same 4 MPs filed on 25 March 2024 from entries in their own 2023 drafting contest; Bills 289 and 290 are the others. 2 other curriculum mandates sit at the same stage: Bill 171, on Bangsamoro and indigenous culture in secondary schools, at first reading since 21 June 2023, and Bill 360, on Bangsamoro history, since 29 May 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Economic Empowerment of Former Bangsamoro Women Combatants Act of 2024. It covers women members of the armed forces of the MILF and the MNLF, certified by their peace panels or authorities, whose membership dates from no later than 27 March 2014, the signing date of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. They must have taken up roles in peace and development and consent to the programs. Coverage extends to Bangsamoro communities outside the region with significant numbers of former women combatants.

Section 5 lists 15 kinds of program: civic sessions, entrepreneurial training with Mindanao State University, Cotabato State University and the University of Southern Mindanao, skills training, livelihood assistance with seed capital and tools, access to land and farm inputs, business incubation, preferably Shari'ah-compliant finance, market linkages and trade fairs, business continuity planning, job placement, social insurance, a voice in policy, psychosocial support, and monitoring.

The Office of the Chief Minister leads, with 10 named ministries and offices. A Coordinating Council chaired by the Office of the Chief Minister, with at least 3 former women combatants each from the MILF and MNLF, meets every quarter, oversees a grievance mechanism and reports yearly to the Chief Minister.

It was filed on 1 April 2024 by MP Diamila D. Ramos with MPs Eddie M. Alih and Suharto M. Ambolodto, read on first reading on 21 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says women served in the Bangsamoro struggle as fighters, medics, intelligence officers, political commissars and support personnel, and that many now struggle to build new livelihoods. It grounds the bill in the Organic Law's commitments to social justice and gender-responsiveness and in the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, and presents it as part of the normalization process under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.
whoIsAffected: Former women combatants of the MILF and MNLF certified by their organisations, inside and outside the region.
Their families and communities, through livelihood, psychosocial and reintegration support.
Partner universities, banks, cooperatives and training institutions.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, as lead agency
Bangsamoro Women Commission, MSSD, MBHTE, MAFAR, MOLE, MTIT and other ministries
Peace, Security and Reconciliation Office, on the implementing rules

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 charges the first year, including setting up the Coordinating Council, to the Contingent Fund of the Bangsamoro Government, and later years to the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro. Section 12 lets the Council accept donations and grants.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, former women combatants would have a statutory claim to a package of livelihood, training, finance and social protection programs.
A Coordinating Council with MILF and MNLF women members would oversee the programs and a grievance mechanism.
readings.insight:
The implementing rules are assigned to an office the operative text never mentions. Section 13 gives the Peace, Security and Reconciliation Office 60 days to write them, but the PSRO appears otherwise only in footnote 8, which describes it as created by the Chief Minister's Executive Order No. 08 of 2022. Section 6 makes the Office of the Chief Minister the lead agency, and the Coordinating Council is chaired by the OCM. Footnote 7 also explains the justice provision as Section 4(m); it is Section 5(m).

The bill names 15 programs and no figure for any of them. The filed copy lists 12 co-authors; Parliament's index credits 28.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Financial Assistance for Senior Citizens Act. The Ministry of Social Services and Development would pay ₱2,000 a month to every senior citizen in the region registered under the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, to buy maintenance medicines.

To qualify, a senior must be a bona fide resident, a registered senior citizen, and apply with a prescription for maintenance medication issued within the last 6 months. Approved beneficiaries get a monthly support card that can be used at any public or private pharmacy, only for prescribed medicines, vitamins and supplements, on a prescription no older than 6 months. The support cannot be transferred and unused amounts cannot be converted to cash. MSSD writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 4 April 2024 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Hamid U. Malik, read on first reading on 21 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the Organic Law requires the Bangsamoro Government to deliver responsive health programs, including for senior citizens who have contributed to the region's development, and that older people struggle with the cost of maintenance medicines. A monthly cash aid would ease that burden and improve their health and longevity.
whoIsAffected: Registered senior citizens in the region with a prescription for maintenance medicines.
Public and private pharmacies, where the support card would be used.
MSSD, which would process applications and issue cards.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, in coordination

funding.detail: No amount is stated for the program as a whole. Section 3 fixes the benefit at ₱2,000 a month per senior, and Section 7 puts the cost in MSSD's budget in the appropriations act for the year after enactment.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, every registered senior with a maintenance prescription would receive ₱2,000 a month on a card for medicines.
The aid would be usable at private as well as public pharmacies.
readings.insight:
The benefit is fixed and the cost is not. ₱2,000 a month is ₱24,000 a year per senior, with no income test and no cap on the number of beneficiaries, and the copy filed gives no estimate of how many registered seniors the region has or what the program would cost.

The same 4 MPs filed this bill, Bill 294 on medical assistance for indigent patients and Bill 295 on a GIS bureau on 4 April 2024. Bills 293 and 294 share their appropriations, implementing rules, separability and repealing clauses word for word and both run through MSSD, yet they disagree on vitamins: this bill pays for vitamins and supplements, while Bill 294 expressly excludes them. MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, a principal author here, filed Bill 375, a community-based health program for seniors, which reached committee on 10 December 2025. This bill has not moved in 2 years and 4 months.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Medical Assistance Program for Indigent Patients Act. The Ministry of Social Services and Development would run a program paying for indigent residents confined in public and private hospitals: hospitalisation, medicines, implants, common laboratory tests, diagnostic imaging, postpartum complications and assistive devices. Immunisation, birthing and vitamins or supplements not related to treatment are excluded.

Applicants prove residency with a government ID and financial need with an income tax return, pay slip or other proof of income, plus certificates of indigency from MSSD and from their barangay. Every hospital in the region must host a Social Services Desk staffed by MSSD medical social workers, with a special lane for senior citizens and persons with disabilities, and an MSSD representative at each desk approves requests. MSSD monitors the program with client satisfaction surveys and writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 4 April 2024 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Hamid U. Malik, read on first reading on 21 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says many indigent patients have to use private hospitals for specialised treatment or services public hospitals lack, and cannot afford them. A targeted program with clear eligibility, a fund mechanism and oversight would bridge that gap and ensure no one is left behind.
whoIsAffected: Indigent residents confined in public or private hospitals in the region.
Every hospital in the region, which must host an MSSD desk.
Senior citizens and persons with disabilities, who get a special lane at each desk.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 8 puts the cost in MSSD's budget in the appropriations act for the year after enactment.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, indigent patients could have hospital bills, medicines and tests paid through MSSD.
Every hospital in the region would host an MSSD Social Services Desk with medical social workers.
readings.insight:
The bill sets no ceiling on what a patient can receive and no total for the program. It covers any illness, in private as well as public hospitals, and leaves the money to MSSD's future budgets.

It was filed the same day by the same 4 MPs as Bill 293 on senior citizens' medicines, and the 2 bills share their closing clauses word for word. They part on one point: Bill 293 pays for vitamins and supplements, this one excludes them. The special lane for seniors and persons with disabilities overlaps Bill 151, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan's bill for help desks for them in hospitals, which was referred to committee on 17 July 2025. This bill has not moved in 2 years and 4 months.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Geographic Information System Act of 2023. It amends the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, BAA 13, to add a Geographic Information System Bureau to the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, as the central mapping unit of the regional government. The bureau has 4 divisions: mapping and geodesy, hydrography, resource data analysis, and geospatial information systems.

It would research remote sensing such as satellite imagery and airborne radar, produce and update base maps, keep the central repository of natural resource data, set up a region-wide geodetic network of control points, run hydrographic and coastal surveys for nautical charts, and provide photogrammetry and cartographic services. BPDA must use GIS in formulating, monitoring and evaluating the regional government's development projects and set data-sharing standards, and must prepare a Bangsamoro Spatial Development Framework consistent with the National Spatial Strategy. BPDA writes the rules within 6 months.

It was filed on 4 April 2024 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Hamid U. Malik, read on first reading on 21 May 2024, and has not moved since. Parliament's index records no committee referral.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says mandating GIS in the planning, execution and oversight of development projects would allow precise resource allocation and data-driven decisions, and that a GIS bureau within BPDA would build and share geospatial data and expertise, supporting transparency and sustainable development.
whoIsAffected: BPDA, which gains a 4th bureau and a duty to use GIS in all development projects.
Ministries and local governments, which would work to BPDA's GIS standards and use its maps.
Mariners and fisherfolk, through hydrographic surveys and nautical charts.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed, and the bill has no appropriations clause.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, BPDA would gain a Geographic Information System Bureau with 4 divisions.
Every regional development project would have to be planned and monitored using GIS.
BPDA would prepare a Bangsamoro Spatial Development Framework.
readings.insight:
The amendment adds a bureau without adding a director. Section 4 rewrites Section 41 of BAA 13 to list the new bureau as item 4, but leaves untouched the sentence above it: BPDA is headed by a Director General "assisted by a Deputy Director General and 3 Bureau Directors." BAA 6, the 2019 planning act that created BPDA, gives it 3 bureaus, and this bill does not amend BAA 6 at all.

The short title calls it the Act "of 2023", though it was filed on 4 April 2024. One division is to maintain "ENR databases", an abbreviation for environment and natural resources the bill never defines, and the bill has no appropriations clause though it creates a bureau with 4 divisions.

It was filed the same day by the same 4 MPs as Bills 293 and 294, and like them has sat at first reading for 2 years and 4 months.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Environment, Culture, and Opportunity (ECO) Tourism Villages Act of BARMM. It would have the region build tourism villages that combine eco-friendly practice, cultural display and local business, open to all the region's peoples; the bill names the Bajau, B'laan, Dulangan Manobo, Higaonon, Iranun, Lambangian, Maguindanaon, Maranao, Sama, Tausug, Teduray and Yakan, and lets a single village carry several cultures.

Government builds some villages; corporations, cooperatives, partnerships and sole proprietorships may build others once registered with the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism. Private builders must be local: a sole proprietor must live in the city or municipality where the village goes up, and any other entity must be majority-owned by its residents. Every approved village, public or private, is exempt for 10 years from taxes and duties imposed by BARMM.

Section 9 sets the money and the deadline: at least ₱10,000,000 per province or city from the regional budget, for government-built villages only, and at least 1 village built in each province or city within 1 year of effectivity. The trade ministry runs the program, with a Provincial or City Board in each province or city chaired by its provincial director and a dedicated window in each provincial office.

It was filed on 19 August 2024 by MP John Anthony L. Lim, with 13 co-authors, and read on first reading on 27 August 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The declaration of policy is the only statement of purpose: sustainable development, cultural preservation and community engagement across the region's local government units, organised around the 3 words of its acronym.
whoIsAffected: The region's peoples, whose crafts, performances and festivals the villages are meant to carry.
Local businesses and cooperatives, which may build villages and take a 10-year exemption from regional taxes.
Each province and city, which would receive at least ₱10,000,000 for a government-built village.
Investors from outside a town, who are shut out unless residents hold the majority.
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, with overall authority and a dedicated window in each provincial office
Provincial or City Boards for ECO Tourism Villages, chaired by the ministry's provincial director
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the cultural heritage commission, for environmental and cultural oversight

funding.detail: At least ₱10,000,000 per province or city from the regional government's annual budget, for villages built by government only. Private and cooperative villages get no grant but share the 10-year exemption from BARMM taxes and duties, a cost in revenue the bill does not estimate.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, every province and city would get at least 1 government-built tourism village within 1 year.
Approved villages, public or private, would pay no BARMM taxes or duties for 10 years.
Private villages would have to be locally owned: by a resident, or majority-owned by residents.
readings.insight:
The title promises villages "in all local government units"; the body delivers far fewer. Section 9 requires at least 1 village per province or city and funds them at that level, ₱10,000,000 each. A region with dozens of municipalities would get one village for each province and city, not one for each town.

The residency rule is the provision with most bite. A sole proprietor must live in the municipality where the village is built, and a corporation must be majority-owned by its residents, so the 10-year tax holiday can only go to local money. That is a choice, and a reader should see it plainly: it keeps outside investors from capturing the incentive, and it also keeps out any investor large enough to build without a grant.

The bill sits among several tourism measures at first reading. Bill 13, creating a Ministry of Tourism, and Bill 280, a tourism framework, have both stood at first reading since 2022 and 2024, with no committee referral in the index.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Martyred Mujahideen Act. It would give the families of mujahideen and mujahidat who died before they could be decommissioned the support that decommissioned combatants receive.

The benefits are listed rather than priced: monthly financial aid for the family's lifetime, adjusted for inflation; a scholarship program for the children covering tuition, supplies and ancillary costs; free healthcare in public hospitals with psychological counselling; a quota of public-sector jobs for qualified dependents and incentives for private employers who hire them; housing grants, subsidised loans or land for a home; legal assistance; and annual commemorations. "Family" covers the spouse, children and dependent relatives up to the 3rd civil degree.

A Martyred Mujahideen Assistance Fund holds the money. The Office of the Chief Minister runs the program through a dedicated task force and writes the rules, and an independent body evaluates it. Fraudulent claims are punished under the Revised Penal Code.

It was filed on 22 August 2024 by 10 principal authors led by MP Michael E. Midtimbang and read on first reading on 29 August 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that many combatants died during the struggle and so were never decommissioned, and that their families are therefore "deprived of the government benefits afforded to other mujahideen or mujahidat or combatants who have undergone documented decommissioning". The bill is meant to close that gap.
whoIsAffected: Spouses, children and dependent relatives up to the 3rd civil degree of combatants who died before decommissioning.
Children of those combatants, who would get scholarships.
Public employers, which would hold a quota of jobs for dependents.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which would run the task force.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, through a dedicated task force, and as rule-maker
An independent evaluation body, which the bill says shall be constituted without saying by whom

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 13 says the money "shall be appropriated from the national budget", with donations, grants and international aid as extra sources.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, families of combatants who died before decommissioning would get a lifetime monthly allowance, at a rate the bill does not set.
Their children would get scholarships, and the families free public healthcare and counselling.
A quota of public jobs would be reserved for qualified dependents.
readings.insight:
The funding clause points at a budget this Parliament does not write. Section 13 charges everything to "the national budget" (confirmed on the page image). A regional act can appropriate regional money; it cannot appropriate Congress's. As filed, the bill creates a fund and a lifetime entitlement and names no source the Bangsamoro Government controls.

Read it beside BAA 57, enacted in February 2024. That act pays ₱7,000 a month to surviving mujahideen who meet its tests, and its benefit is lifetime and non-transferable: it stops at death and does not pass to a family. This bill addresses the people that design leaves out, the families of those who died. It also leaves out what BAA 57 had to define: there is no monthly amount, no definition of decommissioning or of which forces count, and no rule for proving that someone died in the line of duty.

A later bill takes up part of the same ground. Bill 392, filed in August 2025, would pay a one-time death benefit to the families of Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces shaheed, and it too stands at first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Ghazali Jaafar Memorial Site Act of 2024. It would declare the grave of Hajji Salik B. Abu, known as Ghazali Jaafar, in Sitio Tapuken, Pigcalagan, Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, a Bangsamoro Memorial Site. The title describes him as vice chair for political affairs of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and chairman of the expanded Bangsamoro Transition Commission.

At least 1,000 square meters is set aside, with exact boundaries left to a management board. The site is to be preserved and reconstructed when necessary to keep its original form, and it joins the region's recognised tourism and heritage sites.

The board is chaired by the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage and seats the education, public works, and trade and tourism ministries, the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' and a representative of the family. It writes the rules within 90 days. ₱5,000,000 is appropriated to start.

It was filed on 22 August 2024 by MP Susana S. Anayatin, with 27 co-authors, and read on first reading on 29 August 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The bill rests on the description of Ghazali Jaafar in its own title and on its declaration of the site as a memorial.
whoIsAffected: The family of Ghazali Jaafar, which gets a seat on the board.
Residents of Pigcalagan, Sultan Kudarat, where the site is.
The cultural heritage commission and 3 ministries, which sit on the board.
implementedBy: Ghazali Jaafar Memorial Site Management Board, chaired by the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, Ministry of Public Works, Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, and the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' as members

funding.detail: ₱5,000,000 initial appropriation, with later funds carried in the annual appropriations of the ministries, offices and agencies concerned.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, the grave would become a protected memorial site of at least 1,000 square meters.
A management board including the family would run it, with ₱5,000,000 to begin.
readings.insight:
This bill is BAA 60 with a different name in it. BAA 60, enacted on 23 July 2024 from the cabinet's Bill 36, declared the burial site of Sheikh Salamat Hashim and Alim Abdul Aziz Mimbantas in Butig a Bangsamoro Memorial Site, and its design is the one here: at least 1,000 square meters, boundaries left to a board, preservation and reconstruction in the original form, a board chaired by the cultural heritage commission with education, public works, tourism and the Darul-Ifta', a family representative, and ₱5,000,000 to begin. Bill 327 was filed a month after that act passed.

The copy carries a numbering slip: there are 2 sections numbered 5, one on recognition as a heritage site and one creating the board (confirmed on the page image). It also spells the name 2 ways, "Ghazali" throughout but "Gazali Jaafar Memorial Site" in the title.

The same man is the subject of Bill 236, a 50-bed Ghazali Jaafar General Hospital in Cotabato City. That bill was read on first reading in September 2023 and was not referred to committee until 11 December 2025. On the index, Bill 327 has not yet reached that step.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Mental Wellness and Family Week Act of BARMM. It would declare the first 7 days of Shawwal each year, the week that begins with Eid'l Fitr, as Mental Wellness and Family Week.

Ministries, agencies and offices are encouraged to mark it, with 4 themes: mental health awareness from an Islamic perspective, the family as the cornerstone of Islamic society, balancing family and work, and long-term well-being. Section 4 lets each ministry or office declare 1 or more of those days non-working for its own staff, and run programs or seminars.

Each ministry funds its own activities from its budget. The Bangsamoro Government issues guidelines within 90 days, and the week is to coordinate with National Mental Health Month in October and World Mental Health Day on 10 October.

It was filed on 17 September 2024 by MP Baileng S. Mantawil, with 26 co-authors, and read on first reading on 18 September 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the days after Ramadan are a natural time to rest the mind and rebuild family life after the demands of fasting, and that the national observances in October do not reflect the region's religious and cultural context. The week is meant to treat mental health and family "from an Islamic viewpoint, with a focus on work-life balance".
whoIsAffected: Employees of regional ministries and offices, who may get extra days off at their office's discretion.
Families in the region, the intended audience of the week's programs.
Private-sector workers, whom the bill does not cover.
implementedBy: Each ministry and office of the Bangsamoro Government, for its own observance and budget
The Bangsamoro Government, for guidelines within 90 days

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 5 has each ministry and office set aside "an appropriate portion" of its own budget for the week's activities.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, the first 7 days of Shawwal would become an official observance.
Each regional office could give its staff 1 or more of those days off, at its own discretion.
readings.insight:
The non-working days are left to each office. Section 4 lets a ministry give its staff 1 or more days off in the week; it does not set a day for everyone. 2 offices in the same building could keep different calendars, and the bill says nothing about private employers or about pay. Under BAA 39, the holidays act, the first of those days, Eid'l Fitr, is already a regular holiday, so the bill's real effect falls on days 2 to 7.

It is one of several mental health bills that have not moved. Bill 193 (a Bangsamoro Council for Mental Health) has been at first reading since June 2023, Bill 307 (support for teachers) is still only filed, and Bill 344 (a Bangsamoro Office on Mental Health) has been at first reading since January 2025. This one adds an observance week to a region that does not yet have the office or council those bills propose.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Sheikh Salamat Hashim Bangsamoro Historical Places and Landmarks Act. It would declare 2 places historical landmarks and part of the region's primary cultural heritage: the house of Sheikh Salamat Hashim in Camp Abubakar, and the Islamic Center in Buliok, Pagalungan, Maguindanao del Sur. The bill says both served as his headquarters in leading the Bangsamoro struggle.

Ownership does not change. The house stays with the family or its registered owner; the Islamic Center stays with whoever holds it lawfully, or, if no one does, the local government. Custody goes to the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which gets the right of first refusal if either property is sold, and may match any offer.

The commission is given strong powers: an ex parte cease and desist order when a site is in danger of destruction or major alteration, lifted only after notice and hearing; a compulsory repair order to a private owner who lets a site decay, with the commission doing the work at the owner's cost if the owner fails to act within 30 to 45 days; and inspection at any time. The public may visit, and fees may be charged for upkeep.

It was filed on 20 September 2024 by MPs Akmad I. Abas, Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., Abdullah B. Hashim and Hashemi N. Dilangalen, and read on first reading on 26 September 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note argues that marking the places where the struggle was conceived and directed helps later generations understand it, and that the house and the Islamic Center, "where he used to maintain and operate his abode and command post", deserve recognition. It asks for their restoration, renovation and upkeep.
whoIsAffected: The family of Sheikh Salamat Hashim, who keep the house but must allow visits, inspection and repair orders.
Whoever holds the Islamic Center in Buliok.
The local governments where the sites are, which must care for them and report to the commission.
Visitors, who gain a right of access, subject to fees.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, with custody, first refusal, cease and desist and repair powers
The local government units where the 2 sites lie

funding.detail: The title says "providing funds therefor", but the copy filed has no appropriations section and names no amount. The only money it mentions is visitor fees and repairs charged to a defaulting owner.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, the 2 sites would become protected historical landmarks under the cultural heritage commission.
The commission could stop work on them ex parte and order a private owner to repair them.
The commission would have first claim to buy either property if it is ever sold.
readings.insight:
Parliament has already legislated for the same man and the same camp. BAA 60, enacted in July 2024, made Sheikh Salamat Hashim's burial site in Butig a memorial site, and BAA 61, enacted in August 2024, put a memorial marker and eco-park in Camp Abubakar. This bill, filed a month later, adds his house in the same camp and the Islamic Center in Buliok. It does not refer to either act or say how its house sits within the eco-park's grounds.

The title promises funding the text does not give. There is no appropriations section; the restoration, renovation and upkeep the explanatory note asks for would have to come from fees, from the commission's own budget, or from the owner under a repair order. The copy also does not say which municipality the Camp Abubakar house is in, though it names Pagalungan for the Islamic Center.

The powers are borrowed from heritage law and are strong for a private home. The commission may halt activity ex parte and charge repairs to the owner, and the house belongs to the family. The bill offsets that with the family keeping ownership and with a hearing before any stop order is lifted.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Waqf Act. It would give Islamic endowments, waqf, a legal framework and a regulator: a 5-member Bangsamoro Waqf Commission attached to the Office of the Chief Minister.

A waqf is a permanent dedication of property for religious, charitable or educational purposes, or for the founder's family. The bill sets the rules. The founder must be of legal age and sound mind, own the property and not be insolvent. The property must be immovable, inside the region, free of liens, and capable of income or community benefit. A waqf made to cheat creditors or deprive heirs is void, and one made during a final illness may not exceed 1/3 of the estate. The deed must be written, name a manager (mutawalli) and carry 2 witnesses. Registration is annotated on the land title, and once registered the waqf cannot be revoked.

The Commission registers waqf and managers, keeps a registry of properties, issues advisory opinions, trains managers, and arbitrates disputes, with appeal to the Shari'ah courts. Properties worth more than ₱5,000,000 must be run by a registered waqf corporation. No waqf property may be sold or mortgaged without the Commission's approval. Registered properties used exclusively for religious, charitable or educational purposes are exempt from taxes within the Parliament's taxing powers.

It was filed on 26 September 2024 by 8 principal authors including MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari and Tarhata M. Maglangit, and read on first reading on 14 October 2024. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says waqf already exists in the region informally: mosques, madrasahs and other buildings stand on waqf land, but there is no data on how many, no central body to support them, and no way to know whether founders' intentions are being honoured. It cites Article V, Section 2 of the Organic Law, which gives the region authority over Islamic banking and finance, as covering social finance such as waqf and zakat.
whoIsAffected: Muslims who wish to endow property, who gain a registered, enforceable form.
Mosques, madrasahs and others already on informal waqf land.
Managers of waqf property, who must file annual reports and can be removed for misuse.
Heirs and creditors, protected against endowments meant to defeat them.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Waqf Commission, 5 members appointed by the Chief Minister, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Waqf Academy, a unit inside the Commission for education
Shari'ah Circuit and District Courts, on appeal from the Commission's arbitration

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 33 draws the cost from the Bangsamoro Special Development Fund while it lasts, then from the annual General Appropriations Act. Tax exemptions on registered properties are an unpriced cost in revenue.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, waqf would become a registered legal form, annotated on land titles and irrevocable once registered.
A Waqf Commission would keep a public registry and approve any sale or mortgage of waqf property.
Registered waqf used only for religious, charitable or educational purposes would be exempt from regional taxes.
readings.insight:
The cover page says "Second Regular Session" (confirmed on the page image), but the Parliament's index places the bill in the third regular session, and the receiving stamp is dated 26 September 2024. It reads like a draft prepared in an earlier session and filed later. Parliament's index also lists 22 co-authors; the copy filed names 15 co-sponsors.

The definitions and the rules do not quite agree on who can be a founder. Section 3 defines waqf as an endowment "made by a Muslim", while Section 7, which lists what a founder must be, does not mention faith. And Section 26 creates a 5-member Commission without saying how its chairperson is chosen, though Section 27 refers to one.

The Commission would issue advisory opinions, which the bill calls fatwa, on waqf. The bill does not mention the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta', the body that other enacted acts, such as BAA 39 on holidays, rely on for religious rulings. A committee would need to decide which body has the last word on whether a waqf is valid under Shari'ah.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Solar Energy Promotion and Accessibility Act. The title speaks of micro-grids; the text goes much further.

It sets a target that within 3 years, at least 50% of the electricity used by public institutions in the region, including schools, hospitals and government buildings, must come from solar. It has the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy build micro-grid solar systems in remote communities, first in areas off the main grid, chosen by energy need, location, solar potential and sustainability, and designed to be maintained by local governments and residents.

A Solar Power Incentive Program would offer tax reductions to solar investors, subsidies for households and small businesses installing panels, and a revolving fund for solar projects in communities with little electricity. The Ministry of Science and Technology would promote solar research. A monitoring body reports each year to the Chief Minister and Parliament.

It was filed on 15 October 2024 by MP Suharto S. Esmael and read on first reading on 17 October 2024, the same day as his Bill 340. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The declaration of policy names the aims: a continuous and economic energy supply, renewable sources, lower emissions, and better lives in far-flung and underserved areas.
whoIsAffected: Remote and off-grid communities, first in line for micro-grids.
Schools, hospitals and government offices, which would have to draw half their power from solar within 3 years.
Households and small businesses, eligible for installation subsidies.
Solar investors, eligible for tax reductions.
implementedBy: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, as lead implementer and builder of micro-grids
Ministry of Science and Technology, for research
Ministry of Public Works and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, in coordination and rule-making

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 charges the cost to the annual appropriations of the Bangsamoro Government. The subsidies, revolving fund and tax reductions are unpriced.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, public institutions would have 3 years to source at least 50% of their electricity from solar.
Off-grid communities would get micro-grid solar systems built by the environment and energy ministry.
Households and small businesses could get subsidies for panels.
readings.insight:
The 50% target is the largest commitment and has no money attached. Every school, hospital and government building in the region would have to source half its power from solar within 3 years, and the bill names no amount, no schedule and no audit of current use. The rule-making clause also trails off: Section 11 lists 4 ministries "and" then nothing (confirmed on the page image).

The region already has several solar bills that have not moved. Bill 79 (solar for government offices) and Bill 239 (solar-powered water systems) have been at first reading since 2023, and Bill 68 (solar in socialised housing) was read in November 2022 and referred to committee only on 22 July 2025. Bill 263, on rural electrification, was referred in April 2026. A committee taking up energy would find this bill's public-institution target overlapping with Bill 79's.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Restroom Handheld Bidet Sprayer Act. It would require handheld bidets in the public restrooms of malls, hospitals, cinemas, restaurants, cafes, inns, hotels, airports, terminals, gasoline stations and similar establishments open to the public across the region.

The Ministry of Health leads, with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government; the health ministry writes the guidelines, and both monitor compliance and maintenance. Existing establishments have 90 days from approval to comply.

Penalties begin with a warning and a 30-day grace period to repair a non-working bidet. After that, private establishments pay ₱5,000 to ₱10,000 for a first violation, ₱15,000 to ₱25,000 for a second, and ₱30,000 to ₱50,000 plus suspension of operations until compliance for any later one. Fines fall on owners, operators or managing officers. Government offices face administrative sanctions against the head of office: warning, reprimand or suspension.

It was filed on 15 October 2024 by MP Suharto S. Esmael and read on first reading on 17 October 2024, together with his Bill 339. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The declaration of policy cites health and sanitation, and the people's right to good health and social services.
whoIsAffected: Owners and operators of malls, restaurants, hotels, terminals, gasoline stations and similar places, who must install and maintain bidets.
Heads of government offices, who face sanction if their restrooms do not comply.
The public using these restrooms.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, as lead agency and writer of guidelines
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, in enforcement and monitoring

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. Installation costs fall on the establishments; the copy filed says nothing about funding inspection, or about installation in government buildings.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, covered establishments would have 90 days to install bidets in public restrooms.
Repeat violators could pay up to ₱50,000 and be suspended until they comply.
readings.insight:
The penalty clause is written for broken bidets more than for missing ones. The 30-day grace period in Section 6 is for repair of a bidet found "non-operative and non-compliant"; the bill does not say what happens to an establishment that never installed one, other than through the general fines. Suspension of operations for a third violation is a heavy sanction for a gasoline station or a cafe.

The copy names the second agency as the "Ministry of Internal and Local Government" (confirmed on the page image), which is not the ministry's name; the companion Bill 339, filed the same day by the same author, gets it right as the Ministry of Interior and Local Government. The 2 copies carry an identical list of 13 co-authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Economic Zone Act of 2025. It would put the Bangsamoro Economic Zone Authority (BEZA), already created under the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, on its own statute as an investment promotion agency, as the national CREATE MORE Act (Republic Act No. 12066) now recognises it.

It names 8 areas for economic zones: parts of Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and Tawi-Tawi; Lamitan and Basilan; Marawi and Lanao del Sur; the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area; and any private industrial estate that applies. The Chief Minister proclaims each zone on BEZA's recommendation. Zones, including the existing Polloc Freeport and Ecozone, are run as autonomous customs territories. BEZA gets a Director General with a 6-year term, 4 deputy directors, a 10-member board chaired by the trade minister, power to borrow and issue bonds, eminent domain with the Chief Minister's concurrence, and exclusive control of public land inside a zone.

Section 30 sets the tax regime: apart from real property tax on developers' land, businesses in a zone pay no national or local taxes and instead pay 5% of gross revenue, of which 3% goes to the regional government, 1% to the host municipalities and cities, and 1% to a development fund for the host province. It repeals MMA Act No. 154, the ARMM economic zone law of 2003, and the Administrative Code clause giving the ports authority control of ports in economic zones.

It was filed on 3 December 2024 by MP Marjanie S. Macasalong and read on first reading on 23 January 2025. Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 2 sets out the basis instead: the Organic Law lets the region create economic zones and a BEZA with powers like the Philippine Economic Zone Authority's, and Section 16(L) of the CREATE MORE Act lists BEZA among the country's investment promotion agencies. Section 3 states the aims: streamlined investment, incentives, infrastructure, regional trade linkages within a halal ecosystem, and environmental standards.
whoIsAffected: Businesses that register in a zone, which would trade most taxes for a 5% levy on gross revenue.
Host municipalities and cities, which receive 1% of zone gross revenue, and host provinces, which get a 1% development fund.
Landholders near or inside a zone, subject to eminent domain, with disturbance compensation and agrarian reform benefits for those displaced.
Workers in zones, with labour standards no lower than the Labor Code and a multipartite industrial peace body.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Economic Zone Authority, attached to the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, headed by a Director General
BEZA Board of 10, chaired by the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Chief Minister, who proclaims each zone; Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which keeps an incentives database

funding.detail: ₱29,000,000 for personal services, sourced from the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, and ₱63,000,000 for initial operations, sourced from the Office of the Chief Minister; thereafter through the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. Section 30 has BEZA keep in trust 20% of the 5% gross revenue levy for its first 5 years of remittances.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, BEZA would be governed by its own act instead of the Administrative Code alone.
Zone businesses would pay 5% of gross revenue in place of most national and local taxes.
MMA Act No. 154 would be repealed and ports in zones would pass from the ports authority to BEZA.
readings.insight:
The tax arithmetic is the bill's core and it is internally consistent: 3% to the region, 1% to the host towns and 1% to a provincial development fund make 5%, and BEZA keeps 20% of that 5% for its first 5 years. What the text does not settle is the reach of the region's power to waive national taxes. Section 30 says no national taxes are imposed in a zone, while Section 4 quotes the Organic Law's own limit that regional tax exemptions "shall not diminish national revenues". A committee would have to reconcile those.

This is the second BEZA bill to stop at first reading. Bill 83, creating the Authority, was filed by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil in September 2022 and read in January 2023, and has not moved since. Bill 342 assumes the Authority already exists under BAA 13 and cites its existing staffing notices.

The cover says "Second Regular Session" (confirmed on the page image), though the receiving stamp is 3 December 2024 and the index places it in the third session; the short title is dated 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Mental Health Act of 2024. It would create a Bangsamoro Office on Mental Health, attached to the Ministry of Health, as the region's principal body for mental health policy, planning, regulation and services.

The Office is headed by an Executive Director with a deputy. It writes a regional mental health care system and a development plan, builds research and data systems, and runs a Mental Health and Well-Being Program covering services, preventive care, education campaigns and staff training, with the aim of removing stigma.

One mental health center is to be set up in each province, supervised by the ministry through the Office with local governments. Each is headed by a Registered Guidance Counselor and staffed with a Guidance Associate, who needs a relevant bachelor's degree, 200 hours of supervised practicum and 12 units of behavioural science. An independent panel appointed by the Chief Minister reviews the Act every 5 years.

It was filed on 4 December 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, with 25 co-authors, and read on first reading on 23 January 2025 (the date in Parliament's index; the registry summary gives 4 December 2024). Parliament's bills index, as captured on 15 August 2026, records no committee referral and no later step.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the constitutional and Organic Law right to health, the WHO definition of mental health, and national figures: at least 3.6 million Filipinos with mental, neurological and substance use disorders according to the Department of Health; fewer than 1 mental health worker per 100,000 Filipinos; a 57.3% rise in the suicide rate in 2020, with 4,892 cases; and 17,884 suicide-related calls to the National Center for Mental Health hotline since 2019. It argues that stigma and the lack of public institutions make the problem worse in the region.
whoIsAffected: People in the region needing mental health care, who would get a center in each province.
Families who isolate members with psychological conditions, a pattern the note names.
Guidance counselors and graduates in psychology, social work and allied fields, who would staff the centers.
The Ministry of Health, which gains an attached office.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Office on Mental Health, attached to the Ministry of Health, headed by an Executive Director
Ministry of Health, supervising the provincial centers and issuing the implementing rules within 60 days
Local government units, in collaboration on the centers

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial implementation is charged to the Contingent Fund, and later funding goes into the Ministry of Health's budget in the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not left first reading.
If enacted, the region would have a dedicated mental health office attached to the Ministry of Health.
Each province would get a mental health center headed by a registered guidance counselor.
The Act would be reviewed by independent experts every 5 years.
readings.insight:
The centers are built around counselling, not clinical care. Each is headed by a Registered Guidance Counselor with a Guidance Associate, and the bill names no psychiatrist, psychologist or nurse, though Section 5 asks the Office to meet "psychiatric, neurologic, and psychosocial needs". The text also uses 2 names for its body: Section 3 creates the "Bangsamoro Office on Mental Health", while Section 9 makes the "Ministry of Health - Mental Health Office" the program's central body. And both the Office (Section 13) and the ministry (Section 17) are told to write the rules.

The explanatory note opens with the Constitution's clause on the youth, though nothing in the bill is limited to young people.

It is one of several mental health bills waiting at first reading. Bill 193, a Bangsamoro Council for Mental Health, has been there since June 2023; Bill 334, a Mental Wellness and Family Week, since September 2024. 2 bodies built for the same job are proposed, and neither has reached a committee.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Emergency Runway Act. It would have the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, with the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority and local governments, plan emergency runways placed strategically in the provinces of the region, and present the plan to the Bangsamoro Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council for vetting.

The runways are meant for aircraft used in disaster response, humanitarian aid and evacuation. The ministry sets the building criteria, which at least require a strategic location, facilities for loading and unloading supplies and personnel, compliance with existing regulations, and a design that can withstand hazards such as earthquakes. Once built, the runways would be managed by a "Bangsamoro Airport Authority" under the ministry, working with the local governments. The ministry writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 4 April 2024 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Hamid U. Malik, read on first reading on 22 May 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says disasters from natural hazards and conflict have become more frequent, and that the COVID-19 pandemic showed the region still lacks resilience, with no commercial flights during transport restrictions. Emergency runways in every province would close logistical gaps by carrying humanitarian aid, emergency supplies and relief staff, and could be used for evacuations.
whoIsAffected: Communities in provinces hit by disasters, who would be reached by air.
Humanitarian and relief workers moving people and supplies.
Local governments, which help plan the runways and take part in running them.
implementedBy: Ministry of Transportation and Communications
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
Bangsamoro Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 makes the cost of building, maintaining and running the runways part of the annual appropriations of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the transport ministry would have to plan an emergency runway system for the provinces.
Runways would be built and run for disaster response, not commercial flights.
readings.insight:
The copy filed calls itself the "Bangsamoro Emergency Runway Act of 2023", though it was received on 4 April 2024. It does not say how many runways, where, or at what cost; all of that is left to a plan the ministry has yet to write.

Section 5 hands the runways to a "Bangsamoro Airport Authority (BAA) of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications". The bill does not create that body, and no Bangsamoro Autonomy Act in the registry does either. Its abbreviation is also the one the region uses for its own laws.

The same 4 MPs filed Bill 297, on risk assessments for development projects, the same day. Both were read on 22 May 2024 and neither has gone to a committee since.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Comprehensive Risk Assessment and Disaster-Resilient Development Act. Before any development project in the region is approved, the office proposing it would have to carry out a comprehensive risk assessment: the natural and man-made hazards in the project area, how vulnerable the communities, infrastructure and ecosystems there are, how the hazards could affect the project, and how resilient the project is.

It covers Parliament, the ministries, agencies, commissions and boards of the Bangsamoro Government, and its government-owned corporations. Offices must work with civil society, the academe and local communities, and fold their findings into their budget proposals. The Bangsamoro Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council advises on the assessments, checks that their findings are acted on, builds them into the regional disaster plan, which is to be updated every 3 years, and sets up a regional information system holding hazard and climate data. The council writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 4 April 2024 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil with MPs Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Hamid U. Malik, read on first reading on 22 May 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says risk reduction has to be part of how government projects are planned and budgeted, so that growth does not come at the cost of people's safety as disaster and climate risks grow. It points to the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which requires a regional disaster risk reduction and management plan, and says a required risk assessment would make development projects in the region safer and more resilient.
whoIsAffected: Ministries, agencies, commissions and government corporations, which must assess risk before a project is approved.
Communities near planned projects, which the assessments must look at and consult.
The regional disaster council, which takes on new monitoring and data duties.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council
Every office of the Bangsamoro Government proposing a project

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. Offices would carry out assessments within their own budgets and fold the findings into their budget proposals.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, no regional development project could be approved without a prior risk assessment.
The regional disaster plan would be updated every 3 years with the assessments' findings.
A regional database of hazard and climate data would be set up.
readings.insight:
The bill says what an assessment must contain but not what happens when it finds a project unsafe. No one is named to review an assessment before approval, no project can be stopped on its findings, and no penalty is set for skipping it.

Its coverage in Section 4 is the regional government only. Local governments, which approve and build much of the region's infrastructure, are not listed.

It was filed the same day by the same 4 MPs as Bill 296, the emergency runway bill, and both have sat at first reading since 22 May 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
This would make Ramadhan flextime law for Muslim officials and employees of every regional department, bureau and agency, local government, government corporation with an original charter, and state university and college in the region, whatever their status of appointment.

Each Ramadhan, offices adopt flextime suited to their work. The standard is 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., provided "the exigency of the government service shall not be affected". Offices whose work does not suit those hours may set their own, as long as public service stays effective. Flextime is defined as flexible hours that still meet the 40-hour workweek. Every covered agency writes its own flextime rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 22 April 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua, Eddie M. Alih and Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., read on first reading on 22 May 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says Muslims in government keep the Ramadhan fast despite long working hours. Each year the Office of the Chief Minister issues a memorandum circular on Ramadhan working hours, which only repeats Section 3 of Presidential Decree No. 322 of 26 October 1973: Muslim government employees work 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. during the fast. The note says the practice should be fixed in regional law to avoid that yearly repetition, and calls the measure fair, inclusive and non-discriminatory.
whoIsAffected: Muslim officials and employees of regional offices, local governments, chartered GOCCs and SUCs in the region who fast.
Agency heads, who adapt the hours to their office's work.
The public, whose office hours would shift during Ramadhan.
implementedBy: Every covered agency and office, through its own rules
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, Ramadhan hours of 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. would be fixed in regional law instead of an annual circular.
Agencies would have 90 days to issue their own flextime rules.
readings.insight:
This bill was refiled almost word for word as Bill 434 on 20 January 2026, with the same title, explanatory note and sections. The refiled version gives agencies 60 days instead of 90 to write rules, and replaces the proviso that service must not be affected with a line saying the 40-hour workweek is "deemed satisfied" through flexible or compressed arrangements.

The 2 bills went different ways. Bill 434 was referred to the Committee on Rules on 27 January 2026. This one, read on first reading on 22 May 2024, was never referred to a committee.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Autonomy and Heritage Museum Act of 2024. It would set up a museum that exhibits only the history of the Bangsamoro struggle toward autonomy.

The collection is to include books on the political groups that fought for self-determination, the original signed Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Bangsamoro Organic Law, photo galleries of leaders of the struggle and of Bangsamoro military camps and other significant places, unserviceable firearms used by Bangsamoro combatants, lists of Mujahideen and Mujahidat who fought and who died, and photos of the members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and executive officials. Mujahideen and Mujahidat are defined as members of the MILF and MNLF certified by the chair of their central committee. The museum is to be guarded at all times by at least 2 guards in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces tiger uniform. The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage writes the rules.

It was filed on 30 April 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua and Eddie M. Alih, read on first reading on 22 May 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says cultural preservation covers both tangible and intangible heritage, and that the Bangsamoro Organic Law requires the regional government to preserve the history, culture and heritage of the Bangsamoro people.
