A dedicated museum would preserve and display the artifacts, documents and stories of the struggle for self-determination, honor those who gave their lives to it, and help all Filipinos understand it.
whoIsAffected: Former MILF and MNLF fighters, whose names and roles the museum would record.
Families of those who died in the struggle.
Students, visitors and researchers.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 for initial implementation, charged against the annual appropriation of the Bangsamoro Government. After that, operating funds go into the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro under the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the region would have a museum devoted to the history of its autonomy struggle.
Official lists of Mujahideen and Mujahidat would be put on public display.
readings.insight:
The bill says what the museum must show but not where it stands, who runs it, or who decides what goes in. It names no site, no building and no curator or board; the heritage commission funds it and writes the rules, but no section puts it in charge.

It is the second museum bill at first reading. Bill 64, which would establish a Bangsamoro Museum with its own museum board, has been at first reading since 21 November 2022. Neither bill has gone to a committee.

The museum is "exclusively" for the history toward autonomy, and the people it honors are defined through MILF and MNLF certification. Bills 300 and 301, by the same 2 MPs, were filed the same day.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Physical Fitness Act of 2024. Every ministry, office and agency of the Bangsamoro Government would be enjoined to hold physical conditioning activities every week for its employees, whatever their status of appointment.

The activity lasts at least 30 minutes on Friday afternoon, preferably at 4:30 p.m., as long as service is not interrupted. A skeleton workforce stays in the office to keep services running. Offices that cannot use that slot may set their own schedule. Agency heads write the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 30 April 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua and Eddie M. Alih, read on first reading on 22 May 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says regular exercise improves physical and mental health, and cites research that for mild to moderate depression it can work as well as medication or therapy. It points to the Bangsamoro Organic Law's promise to protect the right to health and to Republic Act No. 11036, the Mental Health Act. Employees work at least 40 hours a week and are too tired to make time for exercise, so the bill would build it into the work week.
whoIsAffected: Employees of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies.
Skeleton staff who stay at their posts during the activity.
The public, if Friday afternoon service is thinned.
implementedBy: Heads of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, regional offices would hold a weekly fitness session of at least 30 minutes, usually on Friday afternoon.
readings.insight:
The bill is softer than its policy section. Section 2 says offices "shall conduct" weekly fitness activities; Section 5, the operative clause, only says they are "enjoined" to, and lets any office move the time. No one reports on whether it happens.

The copy filed runs on past its own signatures: its last 2 pages are the cover and explanatory note of Bill 301, the haven bill for victims of gender-based violence filed by the same 2 MPs the same day.

It covers only the regional government's employees, not local governments.

readings.whatItDoes:
This would set up a haven and rehabilitation center as a temporary shelter for victims of gender-based violence, defined as harm done to a person because of their sex, gender, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Any victim may stay, with free meals and toiletries, for 30 days if the abuse left them unable to do their daily work for at least 30 days; 15 days if they have minor injuries and psychological trauma; and 7 days if they have no physical injury but serious psychological trauma. Residents would have access to skills training. The Ministry of Social Services and Development writes the rules and the Bangsamoro Women's Commission has visitorial power over the centers.

Anyone who enters without authority and disrupts residents faces a reprimand and a fine of ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a first offense, 7 days to 1 month in prison and ₱1,001 to ₱1,500 for a second, and 1 month and 1 day to 3 months and ₱1,501 to ₱2,000 for a third.

It was filed on 30 April 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua and Eddie M. Alih, read on first reading on 18 June 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says violence against women persists despite the Magna Carta of Women, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004 and the Bangsamoro Organic Law. It cites the 2022 National Demographic and Health Survey, in which 17.5% of Filipino women aged 15 to 49 reported violence by an intimate partner, and 2021 counts of 8,399 physical violence cases, 1,791 rapes and 1,505 acts of lasciviousness. It says many women stay with abusers because they depend on them and have nowhere to go, and a shelter with skills training gives them somewhere safe and a way to support themselves.
whoIsAffected: Victims of gender-based violence, mostly women, who need a safe place to stay.
People who enter a center without permission, who face fines and jail.
Regional agencies, whose gender and development budgets would help pay for it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
Bangsamoro Women's Commission

funding.detail: ₱100,000,000 for initial implementation, charged against the annual appropriation of the Bangsamoro Government. After that, operating funds go into the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro under MSSD. Agencies' gender and development budgets, at least 5% of their total, may also be used.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, victims of gender-based violence could stay at a shelter for 7 to 30 days with free meals.
Entering a center without authority and disturbing residents would be punishable.
readings.insight:
The bill appropriates ₱100,000,000 but does not say how many centers there would be, where, or who runs them day to day. Its title speaks of "women", while its definition and Section 4 cover "any victim".

The copy filed numbers 2 sections as Section 6, one for implementing rules and one for penalties. The stay periods also run the wrong way for some victims: someone with serious psychological trauma and no injury gets 7 days, less than someone with minor injuries.

Later bills take up the same need with a wider reach. Bill 466, filed on 29 April 2026, would put a Bahay Kanlungan one-stop center for women and children in every city and municipality and is in committee; Bill 382 would place a women's welfare center in every province and major hospital.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Eid'l Fitr Act of 2024. It would make Eid'l Fitr a 2-day holiday across the whole region. If the new moon is sighted on the evening of the 29th day of Ramadhan, the 2 days that follow, the 1st and 2nd of Shawwal, are holidays. If it is not sighted, the 2 days after the 30th day of Ramadhan are.

Its policy section says the shifting date of Eid should not disrupt business in government or the private sector, and that the regional government should fix the number of days by the Hijri calendar.

It was filed on 13 May 2024 by MP Jamel B. Macacua, read on first reading on 18 June 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says Eid'l Fitr is one of the most important festivals in Islam. Presidential Decree No. 1083 makes it an official Muslim holiday, but because the date depends on moonsighting, the celebration sometimes does not match the national holiday, and employees have to report to work on Eid. It cites Section 5, Article VII of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which lets Parliament declare Bangsamoro holidays.
whoIsAffected: Workers and employers across the region, public and private.
Muslim employees who now sometimes have to work on Eid.
implementedBy: No agency is named in the copy filed; holidays under BAA 39 are proclaimed by the Chief Minister
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, Eid'l Fitr would be 2 days off across the region instead of 1.
readings.insight:
The region already had a law on this when the bill was filed. BAA 39, the Bangsamoro Holidays Act, approved on 17 August 2023, makes Eid'l Fitr on 1 Shawwal a regular non-working holiday and has its date set each year on the Grand Mufti's recommendation. The bill cites only Presidential Decree No. 1083, and does not say whether it amends BAA 39.

The note and the text disagree on the days. The note says the bill would make the last day of Ramadhan and the first day of Shawwal holidays; Section 4 makes them the 1st and 2nd of Shawwal. And the copy filed has 2 sections numbered 4, then jumps to Section 7.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Lawyer and Shariah Counsellor for the People of the Bangsamoro Region Act. It would set up a Bangsamoro Legal and Shariah Scholarship and Return Service Program for students taking a Juris Doctor or Bachelor of Laws degree at state universities and colleges, or at private schools in areas with none. Scholars get free tuition and fees, monthly living and lodging allowances, book allowances, and bar review and bar exam fees. A scholar who fails the bar on the first try pays for later attempts.

A separate program helps Shari'ah bar examinees with a daily allowance during the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos' training seminar, books, the exam fee, and travel and lodging, for up to 2 attempts. Applicants must be Filipino citizens, with preference for BARMM residents.

Scholars must take the bar within 1 year of finishing, and within 5 years of admission to the bar give 5 years of return service in courts, the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, regional ministries, the Public Attorney's Office or other legal aid offices. Those who find no government post within 3 years may repay the scholarship or do an alternative program. Refusing return service means repaying twice the cost. The Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office sets the number of scholars every 3 years and writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao with 11 other principal authors; Parliament's index does not give a legible filing date. It was read on first reading on 18 June 2024 and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says marginalized communities in the region struggle to get justice because of poverty and language barriers, and often face discrimination and lack representation. A scholarship tied to return service would build a pool of lawyers who understand those communities, and support for Shari'ah bar examinees would strengthen the Shari'ah justice system.
whoIsAffected: Law students, especially from the BARMM, who could study for free.
Shari'ah bar examinees, who could have their exam costs covered.
Poor and marginalized people who need legal help, served by scholars on return service.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, through its Shari'ah training seminar
Law schools in the region

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 says the cost goes in the annual General Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, the region would pay for law school and bar exams in return for 5 years of government legal service.
Shari'ah bar examinees could get their costs covered for up to 2 attempts.
readings.insight:
The section numbering in the copy filed is broken, and it reaches into the substance. There are 2 sections numbered 5 and 2 numbered 7. Section 5(e) says return service is "provided under Section 8", but Section 8 is the alternative to return service; the return service itself is in the second Section 7. Section 10 calls the program the "LSRS Program" rather than the BLSSRS.

The second Section 7 also has an unfinished sentence: "If the scholar fails to obtain a passing grade in the Bar Exam within 5 years ... Provided, That", with no main clause.

It follows the model of Bill 61, a general scholarship and return service program for deserving students in the region, which has sat at first reading since 21 November 2022.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Waste Workers' Health and Welfare Act of 2024. It would have the Ministry of Labor and Employment and the Civil Service Commission set up a health and welfare program for waste workers: anyone who collects, transports, processes or disposes of solid waste, including garbage collectors, waste pickers, recyclers and landfill and dumpsite workers.

Workers would register to be covered. The program gives free yearly check-ups, vaccinations and hospitalization help with the Ministry of Health; regular safety training; free personal protective equipment from employers or agencies, which is mandatory; help getting scholarships for workers and their dependents; and low-interest loans for housing, emergencies or livelihood through qualified financial institutions. The rules are due within 60 days.

It was filed on 17 May 2024 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 18 June 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the Constitution and the Labor Code on humane working conditions. It says waste workers are among the lowest paid in the country, some earning as little as ₱2,000 a month, and are exposed to musculoskeletal injuries, eye trauma, skin disease and stomach illness, and in incinerator plants to heavy metals and dioxins. The program would give them health care, protective equipment, training and financial help.
whoIsAffected: Garbage collectors, waste pickers, recyclers and landfill and dumpsite workers in the region.
Employers and agencies, which must give protective equipment for free.
Workers' dependents, who could get educational help.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment
Civil Service Commission
Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 5 draws funding from the annual General Appropriations Act and lets MOLE and the CSC accept grants and donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, registered waste workers would get free check-ups, vaccinations and protective equipment.
Waste workers could borrow at low interest through the labor ministry.
readings.insight:
The program is co-run by the Civil Service Commission, which deals with government employees, though most of the people it covers, waste pickers and recyclers, work informally or for private haulers. The bill does not say who registers them or how an informal worker without an employer gets the free equipment.

It is the earliest of 3 waste bills in the registry. Bill 378 on solid waste boards and shared landfills has been in committee since 19 November 2025, and Bill 453, the trash-to-cash program filed in April 2026, names informal waste workers as priority beneficiaries. This one has sat at first reading since 18 June 2024.

The copy filed is marked "Enhanced" by hand, and lists MP Amilbahar Mawallil as a co-author; Parliament's index does not.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Special Emergency Leave Act of 2024. Every worker in the region, public or private, with at least 1 year of service would get 5 days of paid special emergency leave a year when directly affected by a natural calamity or disaster. It is separate from other leave credits, can be taken in a row or spread out, cannot be carried over or converted to cash, and is lost if not claimed in time.

The grounds are being stranded with no safe transport, falling ill because of the calamity, caring for affected immediate family, or urgently repairing a damaged home. The leave depends on a state of calamity declared by the President or the local sanggunian under Republic Act 10121, but an employer may grant it without one on proof or verified news reports. Employees must notify the employer within 24 hours. Government workers who serve during calamities are excluded, as are businesses with fewer than 10 workers and any the labor minister exempts. The Ministry of Labor and Employment writes the rules.

It was filed on 17 May 2024 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, read on first reading on 19 June 2024, and has not been referred to a committee.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the Philippines faced 80 disasters from natural causes in 2021, affecting over 20.5 million people and causing about ₱60.6 billion in losses, and that the region itself was put under a state of calamity for widespread flooding in 2022 on top of displacement from armed conflict. A 5-day leave, separate from vacation and sick leave and with full pay, would let affected workers deal with the crisis.
whoIsAffected: Workers in the region, public and private, with at least 1 year of service.
Employers, who pay for the leave and judge eligibility.
Workers in businesses with fewer than 10 employees, who are left out.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment
Heads of offices and employers

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. Employers and government offices would bear the cost of the paid leave.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not been referred to a committee.
If enacted, workers hit by a calamity could take 5 paid days off without using their leave credits.
readings.insight:
The deadlines in Section 7 do not fit together. Workers must use the leave "within 10 days from the date when the natural calamity or disaster occurred, but no later than 6 months after", which sets 2 different limits. Section 6 adds a third, notice to the employer within 24 hours, which a worker stranded by a typhoon may not manage.

The leave hangs on a declaration by the President or a local sanggunian. Nothing is said about a calamity declared at the regional level.

Leave bills from the same months moved faster. Bills 270 and 281 on bereavement leave were consolidated into BAA 72, approved on 3 March 2025; this bill has sat at first reading since 19 June 2024.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would have the Bangsamoro Government help Mujahideen correct or change entries in their civil register records: births, deaths, marriages, divorces, changes of name and the other entries kept by local civil registrars, the Civil Registrar General, Philippine consulates and the Shari'ah district and circuit registrars. A Mujahideen is defined as a member of the MILF or MNLF as attested by their Central Committees.

The help is administrative, legal and financial, including filing petitions and representing beneficiaries before courts and quasi-judicial bodies. The Office of the Chief Minister would set up an ad hoc office, under its full control, to screen, guide, assist and represent applicants. The programme would run for 5 years only unless a new law extends it, and the OCM would issue rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 24 May 2024 by MP Abdullah B. Hashim with 24 co-authors named on the copy filed, and read on first reading on 24 June 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The only stated purpose is the policy section: to ensure necessities and equal opportunities, promote social justice, and devise mechanisms to integrate Bangsamoro Mujahideen into civilian life.
whoIsAffected: MILF and MNLF members whose birth, marriage or other civil records carry wrong or inconsistent entries.
Local civil registrars and Shari'ah registrars, who would receive the petitions.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which would staff and run the ad hoc office.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister, through an ad hoc office

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The cost would be included in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister, and later in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, Mujahideen could get free legal and administrative help, including court representation, to correct their civil records for 5 years.
readings.insight:
The bill sets up a new ad hoc office inside the Office of the Chief Minister, although one already exists there for this population. BAA 57, which came from Bill 44 and was approved in March 2024, created the Office of the Bangsamoro Mujahideen Under Special Circumstance inside the OCM, which keeps a register of qualifying Mujahideen. The bill does not mention it.

Section 4 says the bill covers corrections under "Republic Act No. 9084 as amended by Republic Act No. 10172". Republic Act No. 10172 amended Republic Act No. 9048, the law that lets civil registrars correct clerical errors without going to court. The 9084 in the copy filed looks like a transposition of 9048.

readings.whatItDoes:
It is a settlers' rights law and a reorganisation of the Office for Settler Communities in 1 bill. It defines Settlers as people who migrated to and are domiciled in the region and are neither Bangsamoro nor indigenous peoples. It says Shari'ah law applies to a Settler only if they submit to a Shari'ah court voluntarily, that laws contrary to Settlers' cultural and religious beliefs do not apply to them, and that no Torrens title issued by the National Government will be invalidated. It reserves 2 of the sectoral seats in Parliament for Settlers and asks for equitable Settler representation in local councils and peace and order councils.

The office would be renamed the Office of Settlers' Affairs and given fiscal autonomy: its budget could not fall below the previous year's and MFBM would release it automatically. A separate Settlers' Empowerment Fund equal to 5% of the previous year's Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act would be managed by the Office of the Chief Minister on the office's recommendation. The office would get a Technical Division, an Administrative and Finance Division, and 9 field offices.

It was filed on 3 June 2024 by MPs Rasul E. Ismael, Amilbahar S. Mawallil and Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., and read on first reading on 24 June 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has not moved past first reading in more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says some people, Bangsamoro and Settlers alike, wrongly believe that land owned by Settlers now belongs to the Bangsamoro Government under the Organic Law and can be taken from them, so Settlers' rights need to be written into law. It says the office has struggled under its current setup and needs fiscal autonomy, a full administrative and finance division and more staff.

On the name, the note argues that the Organic Law's "office for settler communities" is a description, not a proper name, and that only natural or juridical persons hold rights, so the law should speak of "Settlers", capitalised, rather than "settler communities".
whoIsAffected: Settlers living in the region, who would gain a written list of rights and reserved seats.
Staff of the Office for Settler Communities, which would be renamed, enlarged and given its own budget powers.
Local councils and peace and order councils, which would have to seat Settler representatives.
Every other budget line, since 5% of the previous year's budget would go to the Settlers' Empowerment Fund.
implementedBy: Office of Settlers' Affairs, now the Office for Settler Communities
Office of the Chief Minister, which manages the Settlers' Empowerment Fund
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management

funding.detail: A Settlers' Empowerment Fund equal to 5% of the previous year's General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, separate from the office's own budget, which could not be reduced below the previous year's.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading, and the office keeps its current name and place under the Office of the Chief Minister.
If enacted, 2 of Parliament's sectoral seats would be reserved for Settlers.
The office would be renamed the Office of Settlers' Affairs, gain fiscal autonomy and open 9 field offices.
5% of the previous year's regional budget would be set aside each year for Settler projects.
readings.insight:
The Settlers' Empowerment Fund is the largest figure in the bill and the note does not mention it. At 5% of the FY 2024 budget of ₱98.47 billion in BAA 56, it would come to about ₱4.9 billion a year, on top of the office's own budget. Footnote 23 shows that an earlier draft gave the 5% to the office itself.

The copy filed was received on 3 June 2024, but its short title is the "Settlers' Rights and Welfare Act of 2023" and its header says "Second Regular Session". One of the 9 field offices is in "The Province of Jolo". There is no such province: Jolo is a town in Sulu. Sulu has since left the region, a change BAA 65 writes into its general provisions.

The idea of fiscal autonomy for this office came back in Bill 387, filed in August 2025 with MP Mitmug again a principal author. That bill gives fiscal autonomy to 4 offices including this one, has no 5% fund, and was referred to committee in November 2025. This bill has stayed at first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would create a Liguasan Marsh Management Commission under the Office of the Chief Minister to manage and conserve the marsh's resources and to harmonise the national laws that apply there, from the protected areas law and the Fisheries Code to the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act. The commission would have 3 commissioners, for operations, finance and administration, and planning, and would be headed by an Executive Director appointed by the Chief Minister, with a staff of at least 25.

A management board chaired by the Minister of Environment and Natural Resources, with the Governor of Maguindanao as vice chair, 6 other officials and 2 private members, would set policy, approve business and gas exploration permits, and issue rules. The commission would lead climate adaptation planning for the Cotabato River Basin, set up an Area Growth Centre for former combatants and indigenous communities, court investors including sovereign wealth funds in the Middle East, and could recommend that the Chief Minister ask Malacañang for an executive order to open the marsh's natural resources to exploration.

It was filed on 4 June 2024 by MP Ali B. Sangki and read on first reading on 24 June 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. The policy section cites Section 3, Article XIII of the Organic Law on a comprehensive framework for sustainable development, and the creation section cites Section 9, Article XIII, which transfers to the Bangsamoro Government the management of protected areas already defined by the National Government.
whoIsAffected: Farmers, fishers and indigenous communities living in and around the Liguasan Marsh.
Former combatants, who would be among the intended beneficiaries of the Area Growth Centre.
Businesses and gas exploration interests, which would need permits approved by the board.
Local governments around the Cotabato River Basin, which the commission would coordinate.
implementedBy: Liguasan Marsh Management Commission, under the Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, whose minister chairs the board

funding.detail: ₱150,000,000 for initial organisation and operation, from unappropriated funds or any other funds of the Bangsamoro Government. The Executive Director would be paid ₱750,000 a year and each commissioner ₱660,000 a year.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, a new commission with a ₱150,000,000 start-up fund would regulate business and exploration in the Liguasan Marsh.
Permits for business, gas exploration, eco-tourism and fisheries in the marsh would go through its board.
readings.insight:
The copy filed reads like an older draft. It was received on 4 June 2024, but Section 1 calls it the "LigMarsh Act of 2021". Its board is vice-chaired by "The Provincial Governor of Maguindanao", a single province that no longer exists; Bill 309, filed the day before, already lists Maguindanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte as separate provinces.

The leadership does not fit together. Section 3 gives the commission 3 commissioners, Article II puts an Executive Director and a Deputy Executive Director at its head, and the board includes a "Director General of the Commission". The bill says nothing about how these roles relate. It is also as much an investment bill as a conservation bill: next to its conservation aims, it gives the commission the job of attracting investment in energy and recommending an executive order to open the marsh to exploration.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would turn the current ₱3,000 monthly honorarium of barangay health workers into law and add a year-end assistance equal to 1 month's honorarium. A worker who has served at least 15 years and stops serving at 60 or later would receive special financial assistance of at least half the monthly honorarium for every year of service.

Beneficiaries are barangay health workers registered with their city or municipal health board and already receiving regional benefits. The Ministry of Health would keep a regional register and issue rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 10 June 2024 by MP Suharto S. Esmael and read on first reading on 15 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Its policy section adopts the policy of Republic Act No. 7883, the Barangay Health Workers' Benefits and Incentives Act of 1995, and calls barangay health workers frontliners of primary health care whose work is a property right under the Constitution.
whoIsAffected: Registered barangay health workers, who would get a guaranteed ₱3,000 a month plus a year-end payment.
Long-serving workers retiring at 60 or later, who would receive a lump sum based on years served.
The Ministry of Health and local health boards, which would keep the registers.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Provincial and city health offices

funding.detail: No total is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 declares the current ₱3,000 monthly honorarium "appropriated and institutionalized" but names no sum or source for the year-end and retirement assistance.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading, and the honorarium depends on each year's budget.
If enacted, the ₱3,000 monthly honorarium would become a legal entitlement, with a 13th payment each year.
Workers with at least 15 years of service would receive half a month's honorarium for each year when they stop serving at 60 or later.
readings.insight:
The service requirement is written as "at least ten (15) years", so the copy filed gives 2 different figures for the same rule.

The money already flows without the law. BAA 63, the supplemental budget approved in October 2024, carries a Barangay Health Workers Program of ₱124,560,000 under health. This bill would make the payment a right instead of a yearly budget decision, but its appropriation clause names only a monthly rate and not a total. A broader bill for public health workers, Bill 237, has been at first reading since September 2023.

readings.whatItDoes:
Every official document issued by a Bangsamoro ministry, office or agency would have to carry a QR code with security features set by the issuing office. Documents bearing the code would be recognised as true and correct once the receiving office has checked those security features.

The Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office would train the ICT staff of every agency in creating codes, securing them and checking authenticity, and would issue rules within 90 days. Violations would be prosecuted as falsification under Articles 171 and 172 of the Revised Penal Code.

It was filed on 11 June 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua and Eddie M. Alih and read on first reading on 15 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says QR codes are already used by government agencies to verify IDs and give access to forms, and that adopting them would make services efficient and in line with global standards, align with the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000, and provide a secure way to verify documents. It also argues that fewer physical copies would save paper and cut carbon emissions, citing the right to a balanced ecology in the Constitution and the Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Every Bangsamoro ministry, office and agency, which would have to put QR codes on its documents.
People who submit government documents, who could have them verified by scan.
ICT staff in each agency, who would need BICTO training.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Information and Communications Technology Office
All Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing and has no funding section.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, all official Bangsamoro documents would carry a QR code with security features.
A document with a verified QR code would be accepted as true and correct without separate certification.
readings.insight:
The title promises that photocopies bearing the QR code will be recognised as "certified true and correct", but the operative text never mentions photocopies. Section 6 only says official documents bearing QR codes are true and correct once their security features are checked.

The section numbers run 1 to 9 and then start again at 7, 8 and 9 for the separability, repealing and effectivity clauses, so the copy filed has 2 sections each numbered 7, 8 and 9. It also has no funding section, although every agency would need new security features and training.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would ban the sale and use of all firecrackers and pyrotechnic devices in the region. That covers everything from the bawang and the kwitis to sparklers, luces, fountains and paper caps for toy guns. It would also be unlawful to induce, direct or allow a minor to use them.

Fines would be ₱10,000 for a first offence, ₱30,000 for a second and ₱50,000 for a third and later offences, without prejudice to prosecution under the Revised Penal Code and the Civil Code. The Philippine National Police would enforce the ban and keep records. A panel of experts named by the Chief Minister would review the law every 5 years, and the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government would issue rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 18 June 2024 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and read on first reading on 15 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says national regulation under Republic Act No. 7183 and Executive Order No. 28 of 2017 has not stopped the injuries. It cites Department of Health figures of 609 fireworks-related injuries in 2023, up 98% from 307 in 2022, and 442 as of 2 January 2024.

It also cites the air pollution from fireworks, including a study of Metro Manila's 2019 New Year that found fine particulate matter peaking at 383.9 µg/m³, above Philippine, US and WHO standards.
whoIsAffected: Anyone in the region who sells or uses firecrackers or sparklers, including at New Year.
Parents and adults who let minors use them.
Vendors and stores that sell pyrotechnics.
The PNP and MILG, which would enforce the ban and write its rules.
implementedBy: Philippine National Police
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The first year would be charged to the Contingent Fund, and later years to the MILG budget in the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading, and national rules under Republic Act No. 7183 still apply.
If enacted, all sale and use of firecrackers and pyrotechnics in the region would be banned, with fines from ₱10,000 to ₱50,000.
readings.insight:
This is a total ban, not regulation. The list of banned items is copied from Section 2 of Republic Act No. 7183, as the bill's own footnote says, but that law regulates these items, while this bill prohibits all of them. There is no exemption for licensed community displays, and even sparklers and paper caps are covered. The ban reaches sale and use but not manufacture or possession.

The note's injury figures add up: 609 against 307 is a 98% rise. Enforcement is given to the PNP, a national agency, while the money goes to the MILG.

readings.whatItDoes:
Every civil society organisation operating in the region would have to register with a Bangsamoro Civil Society Organizations Registry under the Office of the Cabinet Secretary. Registered CSOs could also apply for accreditation, which would be based on their governance, finances, programmes and impact.

Accredited CSOs would have the right to take part in planning and monitoring government programmes, to access public information, and to receive financial and technical support. The Bangsamoro Government would set up a fund for grants to accredited CSOs, provide training, and publish an annual report on the state of civil society. CSOs would have to report regularly and operate without discrimination. The Office of the Cabinet Secretary would issue rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 11 July 2024 by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema and read on first reading on 23 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says CSOs promote community participation and advocate for marginalised groups, but should meet high standards of accountability and transparency. It says many CSOs lack capacity and funding, and that a legal framework would formalise their role, set up registration and accreditation, and give them capacity-building and financial support.
whoIsAffected: Every civil society organisation operating in the region, which would have to register.
Accredited CSOs, which could get government grants and a role in planning.
The Office of the Cabinet Secretary, which would run the registry and monitoring.
implementedBy: Office of the Cabinet Secretary

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 10 creates a fund for grants to accredited CSOs but names neither a sum nor a source.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, all CSOs operating in the region would have to register with a new registry.
Accredited CSOs would become eligible for a regional grants fund.
readings.insight:
Registration would be mandatory, as Section 5 says all CSOs operating in the region "shall register", but the bill sets no penalty and does not say what happens to a group that does not register. Its tax incentives clause grants nothing new: it refers only to exemptions already in existing laws.

A second CSO bill followed. Bill 399, filed on 11 September 2025, would institutionalise CSO engagement and create a Bangsamoro CSO Coordinating Office. It too has not moved past first reading.

The copy filed is headed "Second Regular Session", although it was filed in July 2024, which Parliament's index places in the third regular session. Bill 321, filed by MP Sema the same day, has the same header.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would establish a Bangsamoro Legislative Academy to train Members of Parliament and parliamentary staff and to research legislative practice. The Academy would run orientation for new members, continuing courses on legislative drafting, procedure and governance, and workshops on policy issues, and would publish its research.

A Board of Trustees chaired by the Speaker would govern it. The board would also include the Deputy Speakers, the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, a Civil Service Commission representative, 2 academics and 2 civil society representatives. The board would appoint a Director General for a 3-year term, renewable once, and the Academy would have 3 divisions and report to Parliament every year.

It was filed on 11 July 2024 by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema and read on first reading on 23 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says autonomy brings the responsibility of writing laws suited to the region, and that Members and staff need training in legislative process, parliamentary procedure and policy analysis to do it well. It argues that a dedicated academy offering training, research and partnerships would improve oversight of the executive and support evidence-based laws.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, especially newly elected ones, who would receive orientation and training.
Parliamentary staff, who would get continuing education in drafting and procedure.
Academic and civil society partners, who would sit on the board.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Legislative Academy, under a Board of Trustees chaired by the Speaker
Bangsamoro Parliament

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 in initial funding from the current appropriations of the Bangsamoro Parliament, then the annual budget of the Parliament. The Academy may also accept grants and donations.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, Parliament would have a ₱10,000,000 training academy for its Members and staff, governed by a board chaired by the Speaker.
readings.insight:
The Academy would be Parliament training itself with its own money. The ₱10,000,000 start-up fund comes from Parliament's own appropriations, and the board is chaired by the Speaker and includes the Deputy Speakers. The author was himself a Deputy Speaker when he signed the bill.

Like Bill 319, filed the same day by the same author, the copy filed is headed "Second Regular Session", although it was received on 11 July 2024, in what Parliament's index records as the third regular session.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would require the Ministry of Transportation and Communication and the Ministry of Public Works, with local governments, to identify and build a bike route network connecting every local government unit in the region, starting as soon as the law takes effect. The routes would be designed for safety, accessibility and connectivity for cyclists of all ages and abilities. The definitions also cover skates, skateboards and push scooters.

MOTC would run public awareness and safety education campaigns and monitor how the network is used, how safe it is, and its effect on congestion and health. MOTC would issue rules within 60 days with MPW and MILG.

It was filed on 17 July 2024 by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and 7 other principal authors and read on first reading on 24 July 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the Organic Law's mandate to protect the right to health. It says cycling cuts emissions and congestion and improves health, but that a lack of safe, connected routes keeps people from using bicycles. A network linking urban and rural areas would make cycling safer, encourage commuting by bicycle and support tourism.
whoIsAffected: Cyclists and users of other non-motorised vehicles in the region.
Local governments, which would help plan the routes through their areas.
MOTC and MPW, which would build and run the network out of existing budgets.
implementedBy: Ministry of Transportation and Communication
Ministry of Public Works
Local government units

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs would come from the existing appropriations of MOTC and MPW, and later costs from their budgets in the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, MOTC and MPW would have to plan and build bike routes connecting every local government unit in the region.
readings.insight:
The bill asks for a network linking every local government unit in the region but sets no deadline, no standard for what counts as a bike route, and no amount. It would be paid for out of what MOTC and MPW already have.

The co-authors line on the copy filed is blank. Parliament's index lists 14 co-authors, one of whom, MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, is also among the 8 principal authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
It would let permanent officials and employees of the Bangsamoro Government turn good performance ratings into extra leave. An employee rated at least Very Satisfactory for 2 successive rating periods could convert that into up to 3 days of service leave a year.

The leave must be converted in the year after the rating and used within the year of conversion, all at once, and only after the employee has taken mandatory leave. It cannot be added to leave credits used to compute terminal leave, and it travels with the employee on transfer within the Bangsamoro Government. The Civil Service Commission for BARMM would issue rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 5 August 2024 by MPs Jamel B. Macacua and Michael E. Midtimbang and read on first reading on 19 August 2024. Parliament's index records no committee referral and no later step, so it has sat at first reading for more than 2 years.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note cites the Constitution's call to strengthen the merit and reward system and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code's call to promote morale, and argues that high morale raises productivity and retention. It says the bill takes inspiration from PNP Circular No. 009 of 4 September 2007, which lets police convert medals into service credit and leave.
whoIsAffected: Permanent officials and employees of the Bangsamoro Government with consistently Very Satisfactory ratings.
Human resource offices, which would track and transfer the new service credits.
The Civil Service Commission for BARMM, which would write the rules.
implementedBy: Civil Service Commission for BARMM
Human resource offices of Bangsamoro ministries and agencies
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has not moved since first reading.
If enacted, permanent employees with 2 successive Very Satisfactory ratings could earn up to 3 extra days of leave a year.
readings.insight:
The bill does not contain the points system in its title. The note describes points earned for performance, targets, training and conduct, but the operative text has no points at all: it converts 2 successive Very Satisfactory ratings into at most 3 days of leave.

The borrowing from the police circular shows. Section 5(d) bars adding the credits to the terminal leave benefits "of retiring PNP personnel", though the bill covers Bangsamoro civil servants. Section 5(c) says unused leave is "deemed converted", while 5(e) says unused credits are forfeited, and Section 6 gives the commission "60 upon its effectivity" without saying 60 of what.

Other leave bills moved further. Bills 276 and 282, on moral recovery leave and pilgrimage leave, have since been approved by Parliament. This one has not moved since first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
It amends Section 5 of the Bangsamoro Bereavement Leave Act of 2025, BAA 72, the definition of immediate family whose death entitles an employee to the act's 7 days of paid bereavement leave a year. 2 kinds of relative are added: legitimate or illegitimate ascendants, including but not limited to grandparents, and legitimate or illegitimate descendants, including but not limited to grandchildren.

The rest of the list is kept as it is: legitimate spouse or spouses, biological or adoptive parents or legal guardians, legitimate parents-in-law, biological or adoptive children or legal wards, and full-blood siblings. The number of leave days does not change, and the employer may still ask for a death certificate, obituary or proof of relationship.

It was filed on 28 April 2026 by MP Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim, with MPs Amenodin U. Sumagayan, Rashdi T. Adiong, Ahmad Amir A. Balindong and Alirakim T. Munder as co-authors in the copy filed, and was read on first reading on 30 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the current definition does not match how families in the region live: grandparents often take on the role of parents, and grandchildren grow up depending on them, so losing one weighs as much as losing a parent, spouse or child. It adds that leave should not depend on legitimacy of birth.

The note stresses that the amendment adds no leave days and no burden on employers, keeps the documentation safeguard, and stays consistent with civil service leave rules.
whoIsAffected: Employees in the region whose grandparent, grandchild or other ascendant or descendant dies.
Employees whose relatives in that line are illegitimate, who would be covered on the same terms.
Public and private employers, who would grant the same 7 days for more deaths; small and micro enterprises remain exempt under BAA 72.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment
Civil Service Commission for the BARMM, for public employees

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. The leave is paid by each employer, as under BAA 72.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the death of a grandparent or grandchild would qualify for bereavement leave.
Illegitimate ascendants and descendants would count on the same terms as legitimate ones.
The entitlement would stay at 7 days a year.
readings.insight:
Because ascendants and descendants are "not limited to" grandparents and grandchildren, the amended list would reach great-grandparents and great-grandchildren, while siblings stay limited to full blood. A half-brother or half-sister would still not count. Parents-in-law also stay limited to legitimate ones, even as the bill drops the legitimacy test for relatives in the direct line.

The lettering in the copy filed runs from a) to f) and then repeats e) for full-blood siblings. The bill comes 14 months after BAA 72 was approved on 3 March 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Youth Information Desk Act. It would set up a Youth Desk in barangay halls, municipal halls and city halls as a single point of information and referral for young people aged 15 to 30, the range taken from Republic Act 8044. The desks would coordinate the youth programs of national agencies, local governments and private groups and give information on scholarships, jobs, medical, psychological and legal assistance, PWD benefits, training, civil service and licensure exam applications, and SSS.

The Punong Barangay provides the space, tables, chairs and logbook and designates the SK chair or a member, or the kagawad in charge of youth affairs where there is no SK chair. Mayors provide an area in the municipal or city hall and put the Municipal or City Youth Development Officer in charge. Desks open 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM and 1:00 PM to 5:00 PM, Monday to Friday, while each desk's social media page and hotline must be available 24/7. Municipal and city desks keep a database open to the barangay desks, and quarterly reports go up to the youth development officer and then to the Bangsamoro Youth Commission, which, with the Liga ng mga Barangay and the SK Federation, gives administrative and technical help.

It was filed on 29 April 2026 by MP Alirakim T. Munder, with 8 co-authors named in the copy filed and 20 listed in Parliament's index, and was read on first reading on 18 May 2026. The index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says many young people, especially from marginalized sectors, do not know about or cannot reach the government programs meant for them, and that an accessible, institutional link between youth and those programs is needed. The desks are meant to be the first stop for information, assistance and referrals on scholarships, jobs and livelihood, and medical, legal and counseling services.
whoIsAffected: Young people aged 15 to 30 who live in or stay in the region.
Punong barangays, SK chairs and members, and barangay kagawads, who would staff the barangay desks.
Mayors and municipal and city youth development officers, who would run the municipal and city desks.
The Bangsamoro Youth Commission, which would receive quarterly reports.
implementedBy: Barangay, municipal and city governments
Bangsamoro Youth Commission

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed, and the bill has no appropriations section. Barangays, municipalities and cities would supply the space, furniture and materials themselves.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, every barangay, municipal and city hall would host a Youth Desk open on weekdays.
Each desk would need a social media page and a hotline available 24/7.
Desk activity would be reported quarterly, ending with the Bangsamoro Youth Commission.
readings.insight:
The title and Section 2 speak of a desk in every city and municipality, but Section 6 also puts one in every barangay hall, and the explanatory note speaks of every barangay and municipality. Barangays in fact get the most detailed duties. Section 4 refers to services "indicated on Section 4 (2) of this Ordinance", which suggests the text was adapted from a local ordinance, and Section 10, headed "Support from the LGU", is about support from the Bangsamoro Government.

Every desk, down to the barangay, must keep a hotline and social media page available 24/7, though desks are staffed only in weekday office hours and no one is named to answer outside them. The bill sets no deadline for setting up the desks and no consequence for a local government that does not.

readings.whatItDoes:
It deletes Section 45(g) of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code, BAA 49, the region's anti-dynasty rule for local elections. That paragraph disqualifies anyone related within the 2nd civil degree of consanguinity or affinity, whether full or half blood, legitimate or illegitimate, including spouses, to an incumbent local official running in the same election from running for a position in the same province, city, municipality or barangay.

It also deletes the final paragraph of Section 45, which sets additional disqualifications for Sangguniang Kabataan candidates. It changes nothing else.

It was filed on 12 May 2026 by MPs Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim, Amenodin U. Sumagayan, Alirakim T. Munder, Rashdi T. Adiong, Jose I. Lorena and Naguib G. Sinarimbo, with 5 co-authors listed in Parliament's index, and was read on first reading on 21 May 2026. The index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note calls Section 45(g) the first regional attempt in the Philippines to define and regulate political dynasties, but argues that Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution leaves that definition to a national law that Congress has never passed. It says a disqualification applied only in the region risks violating equal protection under Article III, Section 1, that a regional law cannot contravene national law on qualifications for elective office, and that the provision has been challenged in petitions before the Supreme Court.

The note also calls on Congress to pass an anti-dynasty law that would apply uniformly, including in the region.
whoIsAffected: Spouses and close relatives of incumbent local officials, who would no longer be barred from running in the same locality.
Voters in every province, city, municipality and barangay in the region.
Sangguniang Kabataan candidates, whose additional disqualifications would be removed.
implementedBy: No agency is named; the bill only deletes provisions of BAA 49.
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the anti-dynasty bar in Section 45(g) would be removed before it ever applied.
The additional disqualifications for Sangguniang Kabataan candidates would also go.
readings.insight:
The rule being deleted has not yet applied to any election. Section 595 of the Code says Section 45(g) applies only from the May 2028 elections, so the bill would remove it before any candidate is disqualified under it. The bill does not amend Section 595, which would be left referring to a paragraph that no longer exists.

It is one of a pair. The same 6 MPs filed Bill 469 the same day to delete the companion rule in the Bangsamoro Electoral Code, which bars parties from nominating related candidates; the 2 explanatory notes make the same 4-point case in nearly the same words. The note mentions petitions before the Supreme Court but names no case.

readings.whatItDoes:
It deletes Section 9(d), Article III of the Bangsamoro Electoral Code, BAA 35. As the explanatory note describes it, that paragraph prohibits regional political parties from nominating candidates who are related within the 2nd civil degree of consanguinity or affinity, a rule meant to keep political dynasties out of the Bangsamoro Parliament. The bill changes nothing else.

It was filed on 12 May 2026 by MPs Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim, Amenodin U. Sumagayan, Alirakim T. Munder, Rashdi T. Adiong, Jose I. Lorena and Naguib G. Sinarimbo, and was read on first reading on 21 May 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note calls Section 9(d) a pioneering regional effort against political dynasties but argues that Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution leaves their definition to a national law that Congress has not passed. It says a rule applied only in the region risks violating equal protection under Article III, Section 1, and that a regional law cannot override national laws on electoral qualifications.

It says deleting the paragraph is not an abandonment of the fight against dynasties, and calls on Congress to pass a national anti-dynasty law.
whoIsAffected: Regional political parties, which could nominate relatives on the same list.
Candidates related to other nominees of their party.
Voters in the region's parliamentary elections.
implementedBy: No agency is named; the bill only deletes a provision of BAA 35.
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, parties would no longer be barred from nominating candidates related to each other within the 2nd civil degree.
readings.insight:
Parliament reopened this same section less than 4 months earlier and left the paragraph in place. Section 3 of BAA 88, passed on 28 January 2026 and approved on 11 February 2026, restated Section 9 of Article III, kept paragraph (b) on women nominees, and marked paragraphs (a), (c), (d) and (e) "x x x", unchanged. MPs Rakim, Munder, Sumagayan and Adiong, 4 of the 6 authors here, were also principal authors of Bill 419, which became BAA 88.

It is one of a pair: the same 6 MPs filed Bill 468 the same day to delete the matching anti-dynasty rule for local elections in the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code.

readings.whatItDoes:
It amends Section 3, Chapter 1, Title XVI of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, BAA 13, on the make-up of the Bangsamoro Women Commission. The Commission stays at 7 Commissioners: 5 representing Basilan including Lamitan City, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Lanao del Sur including Marawi City, and Maguindanao including Cotabato City and the 63 barangays of the Special Geographic Area, one of whom is Chairperson. The other 2, now the heads of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the Office for Settler Communities sitting ex officio, become regular Commissioners for non-Moro Indigenous Peoples women and for settler women.

The Chief Minister would appoint them in their personal capacity from shortlists of at least 3 nominees, submitted by the Ministry for the Indigenous Peoples seat and by the Office for the settler seat. They would have the same rank, tenure, pay and security of tenure as the other Commissioners and would not represent the offices that nominated them. The Chief Minister has 90 days from effectivity to appoint them; the ex officio Commissioners stay until they take office. The Commission, with the Office of the Chief Minister, the Ministry and the Office, writes the rules within 60 days.

It was filed on 15 July 2026 by MPs Susana S. Anayatin and Froilyn T. Mendoza and was read on first reading on 16 July 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says that tying the 2 seats to executive posts, whose holders serve at the Chief Minister's trust and confidence, weakens continuity, independence and the steady voice of Indigenous Peoples women and settler women on the Commission. It lists 5 reasons for the change: proper budgeting of the seats as Personal Services without burdening the 2 offices, full-time attention to the work, a stable mandate not dependent on executive appointments, better program implementation, and the inclusive governance principles of Republic Act 11054.
whoIsAffected: Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples women and settler women, who would get dedicated full-time Commissioners.
The Minister of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the head of the Office for Settler Communities, who would lose their ex officio seats and gain the right to submit shortlists.
The Bangsamoro Women Commission, which would have 7 regular Commissioners.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Women Commission
Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and Office for Settler Communities, for nominations

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The explanatory note expects the 2 seats to be paid as Personal Services of the Commission, but the bill has no appropriation clause.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the 2 sectoral seats would be filled by appointed women serving fixed terms instead of agency heads.
The Chief Minister would have 90 days to appoint them from shortlists of at least 3.
readings.insight:
The principal author signs the explanatory note both as Member of Parliament and as Executive Director of the Office for Settler Communities in the Office of the Chief Minister. Under the current law, as the note describes it, the head of that office sits on the Commission ex officio, so the bill would end a seat attached to her own post and give her office the shortlist from which the settler women's Commissioner is chosen.

Parliament's own bills index lists number 474 twice: once for this bill, and once, with the authors Lim and Yacob, for the Halal Development Authority bill that is also listed as Bill 475.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Halal Development Authority Act of 2026. It creates the Bangsamoro Halal Development Authority, a non-stock, non-profit public regulatory body attached to the Office of the Chief Minister for policy coordination. The Authority would issue, suspend, revoke and renew halal certificates in the region, run a Bangsamoro Halal Certification System, set standards consistent with Shari'ah and international halal standards, inspect and audit certified establishments, accredit halal auditors and inspectors, keep a Bangsamoro Halal Registry, and investigate complaints of fraudulent halal claims.

A Shari'ah Advisory Council of Islamic scholars nominated by the Bangsamoro Darul Ifta and appointed by the Chief Minister would advise it, and the Authority could not issue standards or certificates inconsistent with the Council's rulings. No one could hold out a product or service as "Bangsamoro Halal Certified" without the Authority's certificate. Fees may only recover costs. Prohibited acts include unauthorized use of the Bangsamoro Halal Mark, falsified or expired certificates, false claims of certification and obstructing inspectors; after due process the Authority may warn, suspend or revoke, fine ₱10,000 to ₱500,000, and permanently disqualify repeat offenders. Rules are due within 120 days.

It was filed on 16 July 2026 by MPs John Anthony L. Lim and Mohammad S. Yacob and was read on first reading the same day. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region, Muslim-majority and inside the BIMP-EAGA growth area, is placed to become the country's halal hub, yet has no institution mainly responsible for halal certification, monitoring and enforcement, which hurts consumer confidence and market access for local businesses. It cites Malaysia's halal authority as the model and stresses that the Authority would be non-profit, with fees limited to the cost of its services.
whoIsAffected: Businesses that want to sell products or services as Bangsamoro Halal Certified, which would need the Authority's certificate and inspections.
Consumers relying on halal marks.
Halal auditors and inspectors, who would need the Authority's accreditation.
The Bangsamoro Darul Ifta, which would nominate the Shari'ah Advisory Council.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Halal Development Authority
Shari'ah Advisory Council
Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial costs are charged to the current appropriations of the Office of the Chief Minister, and later sums go in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. Fees collected may only cover the cost of services.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill was read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the region would have its own halal certification body and a Bangsamoro Halal Mark.
Using the mark or claiming Bangsamoro halal certification without a certificate could bring a fine of up to ₱500,000.
readings.insight:
The bill creates an Authority but never says who runs it. There is no head, no board, no qualifications or terms and no staffing; Sections 10 and 12 let "the Authority" suspend certificates and fine up to ₱500,000 without naming who decides. Even the Shari'ah Advisory Council has no set number of members.

It does not make certification compulsory: Section 7 bars only the claim "Bangsamoro Halal Certified" without the Authority's certificate, and the bill says nothing about halal certificates from other bodies. 3 earlier halal bills are still pending and go unmentioned: Bill 10 (2022), requiring Muslim restaurants to be certified, and Bill 60 (2022), against misrepresenting food as halal, both in committee, and Bill 268 (2023), the Halal Consumers Act, read on first reading. Parliament's index lists this bill twice, as 474 and 475.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Halal Festival Act. It makes the Bangsamoro Halal Festival a yearly event, held in the month of Shawwal right after Ramadan or on a nearby date set by the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism with the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'. Activities may include halal trade and investment fairs, sale of halal-certified goods, Islamic cultural performances, seminars on halal standards, business matching and culinary competitions. Section 2-A declares the festival a cultural, economic and tourism event that establishes no religion, and the bill states that it declares no holiday; any non-working day would need a separate proclamation by the Chief Minister.

It goes beyond the festival. MTIT must promote halal certification and give incentives to enterprises seeking it, and the Bangsamoro Government would offer fiscal incentives (tax incentives, certification subsidies, concessional and Islamic financing) and non-fiscal ones (training, priority in trade fairs and procurement, branding, and support for halal industrial zones, slaughterhouses and cold chains). It creates a Bangsamoro Halal Council chaired by the Trade Minister, with 5 other ministers, the Darul-Ifta', halal certifiers and private sector members, as the main policy body for the halal industry. Falsely presenting a product as halal-certified to join the festival leads to disqualification from the festival and other government programs.

It was filed on 11 March 2026 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan, MP Rashdi T. Adiong, MP Ahmad Amir A. Balindong, MP Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim and MP Alirakim T. Munder, and read on first reading on 30 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region's cultural, religious and economic life is rooted in Islamic principles, including halal standards in food, trade and lifestyle, and that the Bangsamoro Organic Law gives the region powers over culture, tourism, trade and industry, and Islamic banking. A yearly festival would showcase halal-certified products, promote local entrepreneurs, encourage tourism and give MSMEs, farmers and fisherfolk in the halal value chain institutional support.
whoIsAffected: Halal producers, MSMEs, cooperatives, farmers and fisherfolk, who would get a yearly showcase and access to incentives.
Businesses that falsely claim halal certification, who could be barred from the festival and other government programs.
Visitors and the public, as a yearly event in the month after Ramadan.
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, as lead agency
Bangsamoro Halal Council
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' and recognized halal certifying bodies

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 8 charges initial costs to MTIT's current appropriations and later costs to the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act. Section 8-A lets MTIT set up a Bangsamoro Halal Festival Fund that may take grants, donations, sponsorships and official development assistance.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the region would hold an official halal festival every Shawwal.
A Bangsamoro Halal Council would become the main policy body for the halal industry, and MTIT would run a halal incentives program.
readings.insight:
The title and the explanatory note are about a festival, but the bill also creates a standing Bangsamoro Halal Council to make policy for the whole halal industry, an incentives program with tax incentives and duty exemptions, and a halal export policy. A reader of the title alone would miss most of it.

It is not the only bill to build a halal body. Bill 475, filed on 16 July 2026 by MP John Anthony L. Lim and MP Mohammad S. Yacob, would create a Bangsamoro Halal Development Authority over halal certification and enforcement. MP Yacob is a co-author of this bill. Neither the Council here nor the Authority there is reconciled with the other. The copy filed names 8 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 13.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Environmental Adjudication Board Act. It creates a quasi-judicial board, attached to the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy for policy coordination only, with original and exclusive administrative jurisdiction over violations of Bangsamoro environmental laws: pollution control, solid waste and sanitation, inland waters, forest management, wildlife and biodiversity, and compliance requirements of Bangsamoro agencies. It can issue cease-and-desist and closure orders, fine, suspend or revoke permits, order rehabilitation, subpoena and cite for contempt, and recommend criminal or civil cases. It has no jurisdiction over crimes, and violations of national laws such as the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act and Solid Waste Act go to DENR and the national Pollution Adjudication Board.

The board has a chairperson and 4 members appointed by the Chief Minister on the MENRE Minister's recommendation and confirmed by Parliament, each with at least 10 years of relevant experience and 5 years' residence in the region, for single 6-year terms. Fines run from ₱5,000 to ₱50,000 for minor violations and ₱50,000 to ₱200,000 a day for serious ones; grave violations carry up to ₱200,000 a day plus permanent cancellation of permits or closure. Second offences draw at least 50% of the maximum fine, and 2 prior final findings within 5 years make an offender habitual. Communities may opt for customary dispute resolution under the board's supervision. Decisions are appealable to the courts.

It was filed on 23 March 2026 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan, MP Rashdi T. Adiong, MP Ahmad Amir A. Balindong, MP Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim and MP Alirakim T. Munder, and read on first reading on 27 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region has no quasi-judicial body to adjudicate violations of Bangsamoro environmental laws, which leaves gaps and delays in enforcement. The board is meant to give the region a local, accessible way to sanction violators while respecting the national Pollution Adjudication Board and the courts' jurisdiction over crimes. The note says fines are calibrated to the ceilings in the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act, and that a sunset and review clause answers concerns about overreach.
whoIsAffected: Businesses and operators holding Bangsamoro environmental permits, who could face fines, suspension or closure.
Communities affected by pollution, dumping or illegal resource extraction, who would have a regional body to bring cases to.
Indigenous and Moro communities that choose customary dispute resolution.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Environmental Adjudication Board
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 12 charges initial costs to MENRE's current appropriations and later costs to the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, violations of Bangsamoro environmental rules would be heard by a regional board instead of only by national bodies.
Serious violators could be fined up to ₱200,000 for each day a violation continues.
readings.insight:
The same 5 MPs filed Bill 471, the Bangsamoro Sustainable Forest Management Code, on 9 June 2026, 11 weeks later. This bill gives the environmental board original and exclusive jurisdiction over forest management, wildlife and biodiversity cases; the Forest Code creates a separate Bangsamoro Forestry Adjudication Board for forestry cases and does not mention this one. If both passed, 2 regional boards would claim the same cases.

Section 16 is headed "Sunset and Periodic Review Clause", and the explanatory note presents it as a sunset clause, but it sets no end date. It orders a review within 5 years and then says the board's powers "shall remain in force" unless Parliament acts. The penalty matrix also tops out at the same ₱200,000 a day for serious and grave violations, so a grave violation can draw no higher fine than a serious one. The copy filed names no co-authors; Parliament's index lists 16.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Basic Utilities Assistance Act. It creates a Bangsamoro Basic Utilities Assistance Office, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister and headed by an Executive Director, to run a monthly subsidy for the electricity and water bills of indigent households.

A household qualifies if it is a bona fide resident of the region (at least 6 months), is classified as indigent under Ministry of Social Services and Development criteria, has its own residential meter in a household member's name, and stays within the consumption threshold the office sets. The subsidy is up to ₱1,000 a month for electricity and ₱300 a month for water, and a household whose bill goes above those amounts loses the subsidy for that month. Businesses, offices, mixed-use and shared or sub-metered connections are excluded, and calamity victims get priority. Beneficiaries apply to the office for an endorsement letter, the utility deducts the subsidy from the bill, and the office reimburses the utility.

It was filed on 31 March 2026 by MP Suharto S. Esmael, and read on first reading on 28 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Section 4 states the purpose: to reduce household poverty and ensure dignified living by helping indigent households pay for basic electricity and water, which Section 5 calls essential services rather than commodities.
whoIsAffected: Indigent households with their own residential electricity or water meter, who could get up to ₱1,300 a month off their bills.
Electric cooperatives and water utilities, which would deduct subsidies and claim reimbursement, and face sanctions if they refuse.
Households on shared or sub-metered connections, which are excluded.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Basic Utilities Assistance Office, under the Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Social Services and Development, for indigency
Electric cooperatives and water utilities

funding.detail: Section 14 appropriates not less than ₱50,000,000 for the first year from the Contingency Fund or other available funds; later amounts go in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act. Section 15 gives the office fiscal autonomy, with yearly funding never lower than the year before.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, qualified indigent households would get up to ₱1,000 a month on electricity and ₱300 a month on water.
A new office under the Chief Minister would screen applicants and reimburse utilities.
readings.insight:
The first-year money is small against the promise. At the full ₱1,300 a month for electricity and water, ₱50,000,000 covers about 3,200 households for 12 months, before paying the new office's staff. Section 15 then guarantees that the office's budget never falls below the previous year's, a protection usually given to constitutional bodies, not to an office attached to the Chief Minister.

The rules on the amount pull 2 ways. The last paragraph of Section 7 says the assistance covers "the total billing amount for the basic consumption", while Section 8 caps it at ₱1,000 and ₱300 and drops a household for the month if its bill goes over those figures. The copy filed has 2 sections numbered 18, the repealing clause and the effectivity clause.

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets one framework for regional franchises, concessions, and leases and permits over agricultural and forest land.
