Regional franchises for public utilities or services may be granted only by a law of Parliament, and concessions are to be awarded by competitive public selection as a rule. Every grant must state its term, area, performance standards, safeguards, fees or revenue share, and grounds for revocation. Franchises, concessions and agricultural leases run up to 25 years.

It empowers the Chief Minister to grant leases over agricultural lands and permits for agro-industrial and plantation projects, with limits: no lease over land with unresolved tenure disputes, none that displaces farmers, agrarian reform beneficiaries or customary users without due process, a maximum area per entity to be set in the rules, and public consultation for large leases. The Chief Minister may also grant forest management permits, from community-based agreements to sustainable forest resource licenses, but none that allow clear-cutting. A public Regional Franchises and Concessions Registry would list every grant with maps, fees and beneficial owners, and all existing grants must be reviewed within 1 year.

It was filed on 6 April 2026 by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and MP Eduard U. Guerra, and read on first reading on 27 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Its declaration of policy says it aims for transparent, accountable governance over franchises and concessions, sustainable use of agricultural and forest land, respect for indigenous and Bangsamoro communities' customary land use, and safeguards against land grabbing, illegal logging and corruption.
whoIsAffected: Investors and companies seeking agricultural leases, plantations, forest permits or regional franchises.
Farmers, agrarian reform beneficiaries and indigenous communities on land that could be leased, who get protection from displacement and priority as lessees.
Holders of existing franchises, leases and permits, which would be reviewed within 1 year.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, for forest matters
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform, for agricultural land

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing and has no funding section. Section 26 lets the Bangsamoro Government charge application fees, rentals, royalties and penalties.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the Chief Minister would grant agricultural leases and forest management permits under one set of rules.
Every franchise, lease and permit would be published in a public registry with maps and beneficial owners.
readings.insight:
Many key numbers are left blank or to the rules. The short title in Section 1 ends "Act of ____" with the year left blank. The maximum lease area per entity, the size of lease that triggers public consultation, and the share of revenue for environmental funds, communities and enforcement are all left to the implementing rules or to "a portion". Section 9 allows minor or ancillary franchises without a law "as authorized under this Act", but no section defines those classes.

It overlaps with Bill 471, the Bangsamoro Sustainable Forest Management Code filed on 9 June 2026, which sets up its own system of 25-year Forest Management Agreements and puts MENRE's Forest Management Service in charge of forest lands. Here the forest management grants are the Chief Minister's. The copy filed names 17 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 26.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Resilient Infrastructure and Safe Facilities Act. Every public building and lifeline facility owned, funded or maintained by the Bangsamoro Government or its local governments, including schools, hospitals, offices, markets, bridges, roads, ports, evacuation centres and water systems, must undergo a structural safety audit every 5 years or right after a major disaster, whichever comes first. Facilities that pass get a Resilience Certificate; deficient ones are prioritised for retrofitting, subject to funds. New construction and post-disaster rebuilding must meet resilience standards, and private and religious buildings may join voluntarily.

It creates a Resilience and Safety Unit inside the Ministry of Public Works, staffed from existing offices, to set standards, run the audits, accredit private engineers, keep a Regional Infrastructure Risk Database and train engineers. The MILG would build resilience into local building permits, BARMM READi would supply hazard data, and MENRE would align standards with climate policy. MPW must report to Parliament every year by 30 March.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, and read on first reading on 19 May 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note points to the disasters of late 2025: a magnitude 6.9 earthquake in northern Cebu on 30 September 2025 that killed at least 72 people, twin earthquakes in Davao Oriental on 10 October 2025, and flooding from Tropical Storm Fengshen (Ramil). The region faces the same hazards, and many of its schools, hospitals and bridges were built before modern safety codes.

It says MPW, MILG and MENRE already run programs on resilience, but these are administrative, not institutionalised. The bill would make them permanent without creating a new agency.
whoIsAffected: Pupils, patients and staff in public schools, hospitals and offices, whose buildings would be audited every 5 years.
Local governments, which would build resilience criteria into building permits and retrofit deficient facilities.
Private engineers and consulting firms, which could be accredited to carry out audits.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works, through a new Resilience and Safety Unit
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
BARMM READi

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 13 funds the start from MPW's current appropriations, and later costs from a dedicated program in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, every public building and lifeline facility would be audited at least every 5 years and after major disasters.
Deficient facilities would be listed for retrofitting, and safe ones would carry a Resilience Certificate.
readings.insight:
The title says the bill appropriates funds, but it appropriates nothing. Retrofitting is "subject to funding availability", so the audits are mandatory while the repairs they find are not.

The copy filed was received on 16 April 2026, in the Fourth Regular Session, but its header reads "Third Regular Session", and the explanatory note calls it the Act "of 2025". It ends with "Adopted.", a "Certified correct" line for Secretary General Raby B. Angkal and an attestation by Speaker Mohammad S. Yacob, the form used for measures Parliament has passed, though it has only been read on first reading. MP Dilangalen filed Bill 451, on a disaster volunteer corps, the same day with the same 12 co-authors on its cover; Parliament's index lists 22 for this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Disaster Volunteer Corps Act of 2026. It creates a corps of trained, accredited volunteers for disaster response, relief, evacuation, medical and psychosocial help, and peace and displacement emergencies, under BARMM READi and the policy direction of the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. Volunteer units would sit in provincial, city, municipal and barangay disaster risk reduction offices, and a Bangsamoro Disaster Volunteer Unit inside READi, headed by a Chief Volunteer Officer, would keep the registry and run training and deployment.

Only accredited volunteers may join official operations. Training covers first aid, search and rescue, evacuation, fire safety, emergency communication and psychosocial first aid, and leads to a card and certificate valid for 3 years. People with at least 2 years of past volunteer service may be accredited on validation. Accredited volunteers get protective equipment, group accident insurance, medical and death benefits as MILG decides, freedom from civil liability for good-faith acts, psychosocial support, and a service record that may count for government jobs or scholarships, all subject to funds.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, and read on first reading on 18 May 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says BARMM READi, set up by Executive Order No. 12 of 2019, coordinates disaster response, but no law recognises, protects or mobilises citizen volunteers. Volunteer groups often help in relief and rescue, yet remain unaccredited, untrained and uninsured. The note frames volunteerism as a civic and moral duty grounded in Islamic values of service and generosity and in traditions of mutual aid.
whoIsAffected: Volunteers and volunteer groups in disaster and displacement response, who would need accreditation to join official operations.
Accredited volunteers, who would get insurance, safety gear and protection from civil suits for good-faith acts.
Local disaster risk reduction offices, which would host volunteer units.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, through BARMM READi
Bangsamoro Disaster Volunteer Unit, within BARMM READi
Local disaster risk reduction and management offices

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 16 funds the start from MILG's current appropriations, and later costs from the BARMM READi program in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, disaster volunteers would be registered, trained and accredited by BARMM READi, with cards valid for 3 years.
Accredited volunteers would be insured during official operations.
readings.insight:
The explanatory note promises 2 things the bill does not contain. It says the measure "creates a Bangsamoro Disaster Volunteer Support Fund" for training, logistics and insurance, and that it lets the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission count long volunteer service as eligibility for government posts. The operative text has no such fund, funding instead from MILG's existing budget, and mentions the Civil Service Commission only for staffing and the implementing rules.

Like Bill 450, filed by MP Dilangalen the same day, the copy filed is headed "Third Regular Session" and ends with "Adopted." and the Secretary General's and Speaker's attestation. The cover names 12 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 27. Bill 4, filed in September 2022 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan to build a wider volunteerism framework, has been in committee since 16 July 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Comprehensive Gun Control and Regulation Act. It sets regional rules around firearm licensing while leaving the Chief of the Philippine National Police as the sole licensing authority under Republic Act No. 10591. Applicants must be at least 21, earn an income, and pass psychiatric and drug tests, police and NBI clearances, and a gun safety and values seminar with Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' modules. No person or entity may hold more than 2 registered firearms, and every firearm in the region, including the Special Geographic Area, must be registered.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety leads, through a Bangsamoro Firearms Office and an inter-agency committee co-chaired with the police regional office that keeps a Firearms Information Management System. There would be a 12-month amnesty for registering loose firearms, a "Guns-to-Plowshares" program trading surrendered guns for farm kits, livestock, power tillers or college scholarships, and mobile units for the 8 SGA municipalities. During a rido the committee may suspend carry permits and require guns to be deposited until a peace covenant is signed. Using a firearm in a rido brings lifetime revocation; failing to report a transfer or change of address, a fine of up to ₱5,000.

It was filed on 16 April 2026 by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, and read on first reading on 23 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites at least 85 shooting incidents in the first 2 months of 2025, 759 violent incidents between October 2024 and May 2025, an estimated 7,343 loose firearms held by armed groups, and independent monitoring by Climate Conflict Action Asia that places 70% of the country's election hotspots in the region. It says the decommissioning track of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro lacks a framework for how weapons are handed in.

It also presents the bill as a regional safeguard against a March 2024 change in national rules under RA 10591 allowing civilians to own semi-automatic rifles.
whoIsAffected: Gun owners and applicants in the region, who would face a 2-firearm limit and extra seminars and checks.
Holders of loose firearms, who would have 12 months to register them.
Families in rido, whose carry permits could be suspended and guns held until a settlement.
Former combatants going through decommissioning.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety, through a Bangsamoro Firearms Office
Philippine National Police, which keeps licensing power
Bangsamoro Inter-Agency Coordinating and Monitoring Committee

funding.detail: The title says it appropriates funds, but the copy filed has no appropriations section and states no amount.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, no person or entity in the region could hold more than 2 registered firearms.
Loose firearms could be registered under a 12-month amnesty, and surrendered guns traded for livelihood packages.
readings.insight:
The copy filed is out of order. Section 17 is followed by Sections 22 to 24, then 18 to 21, then 25. There are 2 Articles V and 2 Sections 32. Several provisions appear twice in different words: the one-stop shop (assigned to the inter-agency committee in Section 9 and to MPOS in Section 10), the licensing protocols (Sections 10 and 18), inherited and heritage firearms (Sections 11 and 21), and support for decommissioning (Sections 15 and 25). The header reads "Second Regular Session", though the bill was received in April 2026.

The amnesty sits uneasily with the rest. Section 20 lets holders of loose firearms register "without facing criminal prosecution for illegal possession", while Section 5 leaves licensing to the national police and Section 28 sends possession of loose firearms to prosecution under RA 10591, a national law. Section 6 covers government agencies and law enforcement, so the 2-firearm cap in Section 17 reads as applying to them too, though the next paragraph has government offices file firearm inventories.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Special Geographic Area (SGA) History Month Act. It makes February SGA History Month and 14 February a special non-working holiday in the SGA, marking the day in 2019 when the Commission on Elections announced that 63 barangays of North Cotabato had voted to join the region. It honours the MILF, allied MNLF factions, the Mujahideen and Mujahidat, volunteers and residents who took part.

The Special Geographic Area Development Authority would lead the month's events with the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the MILG and MBHTE. The Commission would document SGA history, map cultural resources across the 63 barangays, and run a search for a single "Father or Mother of SGA", picked by the Chief Minister from 3 nominees and recommended to Parliament. MBHTE would prepare learning materials, possibly a non-credit course or a half-day seminar, and in-school programs every 14 February. When the SGA becomes a province, the provincial government must keep the observance.

It was filed on 20 April 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao, and read on first reading on 29 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note recalls the 2-part plebiscite of January and February 2019, after which 63 barangays from Aleosan, Carmen, Kabacan, Midsayap, Pigcawayan and Pikit joined the region, and the COMELEC proclamation of 14 February 2019. It says the month would honour those who worked for self-determination, celebrate the progress of the 8 new SGA municipalities, and ensure that a future SGA province keeps remembering the event.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the SGA's 8 municipalities, who would get a special non-working holiday on 14 February.
Schools in the SGA, which would hold programs and lessons on SGA history.
The SGA Development Authority and the 8 municipal governments, which would organise and help fund the month.
implementedBy: Special Geographic Area Development Authority
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education and Ministry of the Interior and Local Government

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 13 draws on the yearly appropriations of the Office of the Chief Minister and the SGA Development Authority, contributions from the 8 SGA municipalities, and later the future provincial government.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, 14 February would be a special non-working holiday in the SGA and February its history month.
One person would be named "Father or Mother of SGA" permanently.
readings.insight:
The day has 2 names. Section 5, the section that creates it, calls 14 February "SGA Incorporation and Unity Day"; Section 3, Section 7 and the explanatory note call it "SGA Commemorative Existence Day". The holiday is declared directly in the bill, which does not refer to BAA 39, the region's law on holidays.

The 8 municipalities the bill names, from Kadayangan to Tugunan, are those created by BAA 41 to 48 in 2023. Since filing, BAA 93 (from Bill 431, passed on 16 July 2026) has expanded the SGA Development Authority's powers; this bill assumes the Authority will later become a provincial government. MP Antao filed Bills 458 and 459 the same day; all 3 covers carry the same 6 co-authors, while Parliament's index lists 11 for this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Traditional Madaris Preservation and Sustainability Act of 2026. It covers traditional madaris, defined as community-based, privately run, non-formal weekend schools teaching classical Islamic studies, that are registered with and accredited by MBHTE. A Traditional Madaris Support Council, co-chaired by MBHTE's Directorate General for Madaris Education and the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, with 2 members each from ulama organisations, prominent madaris and civil society, would design and oversee their programs.

Registered and accredited madaris would get yearly grants for upkeep of facilities, a monthly stipend for asatidz (teachers), teacher training in livelihood, environmental and health subjects, and free tuition for students. Historic madaris buildings would be preserved, and their history and old curricula shown in a heritage museum. Madaris keep control of their curriculum and religious direction. Diplomas from unaccredited madaris would be "non-credit" unless they teach the curriculum MBHTE requires.

It was filed on 20 April 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao, and read on first reading on 19 May 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the traditional madrasah has long been a pillar of moral guidance, religious instruction and community life, and educated leaders such as the late MILF Amir Ustadz Salamat Hashim. It warns that modernisation, poverty, shifting education policy and lack of funding put many madaris at risk of decline, and proposes funding and institutional support to keep them going and to align them with the region's education goals.
whoIsAffected: Traditional weekend madaris that register with MBHTE, which would get grants and their students free tuition.
Asatidz in those madaris, who would get a monthly stipend and training.
Madaris that do not register, whose diplomas would be treated as non-credit.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, through the Directorate General for Madaris Education
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
Traditional Madaris Support Council

funding.detail: Section 13 sets initial funding of ₱50,000,000 from the appropriations of MBHTE and the Commission and other resources the Chief Minister directs, then ₱100,000,000 a year from the Bangsamoro budget for a Traditional Madrasah Development Fund.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, accredited traditional madaris would get yearly grants and their teachers a monthly stipend.
A Traditional Madrasah Development Fund would get ₱100,000,000 a year.
readings.insight:
The bill defines traditional madaris as weekend schools that run on Saturdays and Sundays, yet seats on its Council go to administrators of the 2 most prominent madaris "offering academic programs preferably from kindergarten to College", which are not weekend schools. The same schools are called "Conservative Weekend Madaris" in Section 3 and "Traditional Weekend Madaris" in Section 5. Section 9 brands unaccredited madaris' diplomas "non-credit", then accepts them if the school follows the MBHTE curriculum, while Sections 8 and 11 promise madaris their own curriculum.

It is one of several madaris funding bills. Bill 142, by MP Jaafar Apollo Mikhail L. Matalam, a co-author here, would create a Madaris Education Fund Assistance and has been in committee since 17 July 2025; Bill 167 from 2023 would pay madaris teachers at least ₱2,000 a month. MP Antao filed Bill 459, on Qur'an memorisation schools, the same day; the cover of each names the same 6 co-authors, while Parliament's index lists 18 for this bill.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Inclusive Digital Education Act (IDEA) of 2026. It sets up a Digital Learning Access Program to bring digital learning into basic, madrasah, Alternative Learning System and higher education, with priority for remote, indigenous and conflict-affected areas. MBHTE would build a single Bangsamoro Learning Management System that works online and offline, carries madaris and Islamic content, and supports mother tongue instruction.

The Bangsamoro Government would expand internet access in all public schools and set up school ICT centres and community digital learning hubs. MBHTE would train teachers in digital teaching, ALS facilitators and madrasah teachers, and school heads. Content must follow gender and development, indigenous education, Islamic values and peace education principles. MBHTE and the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority would assess results every year and report to Parliament.

It was filed on 22 April 2026 by MP Abrar J. Hataman, and read on first reading on 28 April 2026. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region still struggles to deliver equal, quality education in isolated, conflict-affected and poor areas, and that the COVID-19 pandemic showed how many learners lacked connectivity and devices. MBHTE has named digital transformation a key strategy, but gaps remain in infrastructure, devices, teacher skills and culturally relevant materials. The bill would put MBHTE's digital education agenda into law.
whoIsAffected: Learners in public schools, madaris and ALS, especially in remote and conflict-affected areas.
Teachers, ALS facilitators and school heads, who would get digital teaching training.
Communities that would host digital learning hubs.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, for monitoring

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 11 charges initial costs to MBHTE's current appropriations and later costs to the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act, with grants and donations allowed.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, MBHTE would run a single regional learning platform usable offline.
Public schools would be targeted for internet connection and ICT centres, with no deadline set.
readings.insight:
The bill puts existing MBHTE policy into law but sets no numbers: no deadline for connecting "all public schools", no count of hubs or devices, no budget, and no new office. Its main enforceable duty is the annual report to Parliament.

The copy filed ends with "Adopted," and the Secretary General's and Speaker's attestation, the form used for measures Parliament has passed, like MP Hataman's Bill 461 filed the same day. The cover names 11 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 22. Bill 185, filed in May 2023 by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and others on digital literacy and ICT skills training, was read on first reading on 26 June 2023 and has not moved since.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BARMM Water Sustainability Act of 2025. It sets up a regional Water Sustainability Framework, to be drawn up by MILG, the Ministry of Public Works, MOST, MENRE and MAFAR with community representatives, setting annual targets, budget needs and performance indicators. Priority goes to areas with low access to potable water: new and upgraded Level II and Level III piped systems, rehabilitation and expansion of existing ones, and Level I wells or pumps where only those are feasible.

A Water Sustainability Board of the 5 ministries, at least 3 community representatives and 1 water cooperative representative would set regional water policy, manage a BARMM Water Sustainability Fund, promote community water cooperatives and create a technical committee of experts. The Board must also set up a monitoring system with a public scorecard, a water conflict resolution committee with the Ministry of Justice, and rules recognising customary water governance and gender inclusion. One target is cutting the share of untreated wastewater by 50%. The Board writes the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 28 July 2025 by MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Romeo K. Sema and Saripuddin D. Jikiri, and read on first reading on 19 August 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says many communities in the region still lack safe water. It cites BPDA data that only 33.8% of households had safe drinking water on their premises in 2020, and a 2022 figure of 80.2% with at least basic drinking water against a national average of 97%. It blames conflict, displacement, aging and damaged facilities, climate change, and a water sector split across more than 30 government agencies, and says the region has no water framework of its own.

It presents the Board, water cooperatives and partnerships with universities and indigenous leaders as the fix, and frames water access as both a human right and an Islamic duty of stewardship.
whoIsAffected: Households in areas with low access to potable water, which get priority for new and improved systems.
Communities that would form water cooperatives to run local systems.
Local governments, which would coordinate through MILG and could earn performance-based incentives.
Women, indigenous peoples and other marginalized groups, guaranteed seats on the Board.
implementedBy: Water Sustainability Board
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, Ministry of Public Works and Ministry of Science and Technology
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 21 puts the cost in the annual budgets of the concerned ministries and the Bangsamoro Government, with official development assistance and grants as extra sources. Section 14 creates a BARMM Water Sustainability Fund of annual appropriations, grants and private contributions.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, a Water Sustainability Board would set regional water policy and manage a dedicated fund.
Communities could form water cooperatives with Board training, technical help and financing.
Water disputes between users or local governments would go to a new mediation committee.
readings.insight:
Section 10 swaps 2 ministries' jobs. Under the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy it lists farm duties: sustainable agricultural practice, water use in agriculture and fisheries, and outreach to farmers and fisherfolk. Under the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform it lists environmental policy and ecosystem conservation. The copy filed also calls the Board "WBS" in Sections 12, 13 and 22 after defining it as WSB.

The bill says it supports a "Bangsamoro Safe and Drinking Water Act of 2022". No Bangsamoro Autonomy Act by that name appears in the registry. The nearest measure is Bill 89, a clean and safe drinking water bill filed on 27 September 2022, which has not moved past first reading. The Board has no named chair, and its funding power in Section 9 has no amount behind it.

readings.whatItDoes:
It establishes a regional science high school in Lamitan City, Basilan, to be called the Lamitan Regional Science High School. The school would teach advanced science, mathematics and technology to gifted learners and serve as a centre of excellence in STEM for the region.

It would run under the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, in coordination with DepEd and DOST, and follow the national regional science high school curriculum and admission rules in DECS Order No. 69, s. 1993. Lamitan City must provide the land. MBHTE writes the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 8 August 2025 by MP Abrar J. Hataman and read on first reading on 27 October 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the region has only 1 regional science high school, Amir Bara Lidasan National High School in Parang, Maguindanao, converted in 1996. Gifted learners from the island provinces such as Basilan stay in regular high schools because Parang is too far and too costly to reach. A school in Basilan would remove that barrier.

It grounds the bill in the Constitution's right to quality education, the Science Act of 1958, DECS Orders 69 (1993) and 44 (1995), and Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Gifted secondary learners in Basilan and the island provinces.
Lamitan City, which must donate the land.
MBHTE, which would staff, run and fund the school.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
City Government of Lamitan, for the land

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 charges start-up and operation to the Bangsamoro appropriations act, and later years to MBHTE's annual budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, Basilan would get a regional science high school in Lamitan City under MBHTE.
Lamitan City would have to provide the site.
readings.insight:
The bill uses 2 names for the school. Its title and explanatory note call it the Basilan Science High School; Sections 1 and 3 name it the Lamitan Regional Science High School.

The bill does not mention the region's own science school law. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 40 of 2023 set up the Bangsamoro Science High School System under the Ministry of Science and Technology, to Philippine Science High School standards, with campuses in different locations in the region. This bill would instead create a stand-alone school under MBHTE on the national DECS curriculum, so the region would run science high schools on 2 separate models.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BIAF Shaheed Benefit Act of 2025. It pays a one-time benefit to the surviving spouse, children or parents of Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces fighters who died in combat or war-related operations before the signing of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. The amount depends on rank: ₱100,000 for senior commanders, ₱75,000 for mid-level commanders, ₱50,000 for squad leaders and specialized units, ₱30,000 for regular fighters and ₱20,000 for auxiliary personnel such as messengers and medics.

MPOS, with the Office of the Chief Minister and the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, keeps an official list of recognised shaheed, based on records, MILF certification and community validation. Families claim through MPOS, which endorses to the Bangsamoro Treasury Office for payment. Claims must be filed within 10 years of the implementing rules.

MFBM would set up a BIAF Shaheed Benefit Investment Fund with ₱100,000,000 seed money, half reserved for Shari'ah-compliant investment such as sukuk. The fund runs for 15 years, after which any balance returns to the Treasury. MFBM and MPOS write the rules within 3 months.

It was filed on 15 August 2025 by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr. and read on first reading on 10 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says BIAF fighters made the ultimate sacrifice in the struggle for self-determination and peace, and their families still bear the weight of it. The benefit is meant as a tangible expression of the Bangsamoro Government's recognition and gratitude, and the investment fund as a sustainable, Shari'ah-compliant way to keep the program going.
whoIsAffected: Surviving spouses, children and parents of BIAF fighters killed before the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.
The MILF, whose certification is one basis for recognition as shaheed.
MPOS, which would verify each death and rank and keep the official list.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Bangsamoro Treasury Office

funding.detail: An initial seed fund of ₱100,000,000 from the Bangsamoro Government's annual budget for the BIAF Shaheed Benefit Investment Fund, with more allocated yearly as MFBM decides. 50% of the seed fund is reserved for investment. Benefits run from ₱20,000 to ₱100,000 per Shaheed.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, families of recognised BIAF shaheed could claim ₱20,000 to ₱100,000 once.
MPOS would keep an official, yearly updated list of recognised shaheed.
readings.insight:
It borrows the investment-fund model of Bill 379, the barangay officials' death benefit bill filed 3 weeks earlier, of which MP Kadatuan is a co-author. Both funds start at ₱100,000,000. Here, though, only 50% of the seed is reserved for investment; Bill 379 keeps the whole principal intact. The bill does not say how the other ₱50,000,000 is to be used, and the benefits are far smaller: ₱20,000 to ₱100,000, against ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000 in Bill 379.

The bill gives no estimate of how many shaheed families would qualify, so there is no way to tell from it whether ₱100,000,000 is enough or too much. The copy filed names 10 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 23.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Matanog District Hospital Act of 2025. It converts the World Assembly of Muslim Youth (WAMY) clinic in Matanog, Maguindanao del Norte, into a Level I government hospital with a 10-bed capacity, to be called the Matanog District Hospital.

The hospital must offer at least general medical and minor surgical care, emergency and outpatient care, maternal and child health, isolation, basic laboratory and diagnostic services, and a pharmacy. The Ministry of Health assigns a medical officer, nurses, midwives, a pharmacist, medical and radiologic technologists and support staff, and has 60 days to issue guidelines.

It was filed on 19 August 2025 by MPs Abdulraof A. Macacua and Butch P. Malang and read on first reading on 10 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says Matanog, a town of 8 barangays that are mostly geographically isolated, has long struggled to reach health care. Residents travel to hospitals in Malabang, Parang or Cotabato City. The WAMY clinic has filled part of the gap, but the note says temporary solutions are no longer enough.

It says a Level I hospital typically serves 10,000 to 30,000 people, and Matanog had 41,146 residents in the 2024 census, up from 36,034 in 2020, so it qualifies. It also expects jobs for health workers, lower maternal and child deaths, and relief for distant hospitals.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Matanog and neighbouring upland barangays.
Patients now sent to hospitals in Malabang, Parang or Cotabato City.
The WAMY clinic and its staff, whose facility would become a government hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 6 puts the cost in the Bangsamoro appropriations act for the year after enactment and every year after.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, Matanog would have a 10-bed Level I government hospital run by the Ministry of Health.
The WAMY clinic would become a public facility.
readings.insight:
The bill converts a clinic that, by the note's own account, was set up by the World Assembly of Muslim Youth as humanitarian outreach. It contains no provision on transferring the building or land to the government, no agreement with WAMY, and no budget for conversion or equipment.

The principal author is Abdulraof A. Macacua, who as Chief Minister approved Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 87 on 11 February 2026. The copy filed names 9 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 32. The note's population of 41,146 matches the figure given for Matanog in the district table of Bill 403.

readings.whatItDoes:
It amends Article VII, Section 14 of the Bangsamoro Electoral Code (Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 35) on the official ballot. The ballot would keep its "None of the Above" option, but the bill adds that votes for it are for statistical and policy guidance only. They would not count in deciding the winning candidate, and could not be a ground for declaring a failure of election, which stays limited to the grounds in Section 6 of the Omnibus Election Code.

It was filed on 28 August 2025 by MPs Randolph C. Parcasio, Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Nurredha I. Misuari, Saripuddin D. Jikiri, Romeo K. Sema, Nabil A. Tan and Jose I. Lorena, and read on first reading on 10 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note says the Electoral Code puts "None of the Above" on the ballot but never says what the votes mean. If it wins a plurality, there could be an electoral vacuum or a failure of election on grounds the law does not allow, and COMELEC could face charges of grave abuse of discretion. It warns that counting those votes in the party-list share would either leave seats empty or turn rejections into support for parties.

It argues for keeping the option, with limits, because it gives voters a lawful way to reject all candidates and so cuts the number of blank ballots open to tampering.
whoIsAffected: Voters in Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.
Candidates and regional political parties, whose seat count would not be affected by these votes.
COMELEC and the Bangsamoro Electoral Office.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office
whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
The provision it amends has since been changed by Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 87, which removed the option altogether.
If enacted as filed, "None of the Above" votes would be counted for statistics only.
readings.insight:
Parliament went the other way. Bill 396, filed on 3 September 2025, 6 days after this one, removed "None of the Above" from the ballot entirely by amending the same Section 14. It was approved on third reading on 28 January 2026 and became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 87, approved by the Chief Minister on 11 February 2026. This bill would now amend a provision that no longer contains the option it sets out to keep.

MP Nabil A. Tan is a principal author of both bills. The copy filed names 1 co-author, MP Hatimil E. Hassan; Parliament's index lists 6.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Ramadhan Bonus Act of 2025. It makes a yearly Ramadhan Bonus of at least ₱10,000 a legal entitlement for qualified officials and employees of the Bangsamoro Government's ministries, offices and agencies, released in time for Ramadhan.

Contract of service and job order workers are covered, subject to the implementing rules. Excluded are those absent without leave, and consultants, experts, apprentices, student laborers and institutional contract of service workers who are not part of the government's organic manpower. MFBM writes the rules within 30 days and may issue yearly guidelines.

It was filed on 9 September 2025 by MPs Susana S. Anayatin, Hashemi N. Dilangalen and Ibrahim P. Ibay, and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the Bangsamoro Government has granted a Ramadhan allowance for 3 consecutive years, under Parliament Resolutions 323 (2023), 441 (2024) and 530 (2025). It has eased the cost of living for government workers and honoured the meaning of Ramadhan. The bill would make the grant permanent at not less than ₱10,000 a year, to support morale and productivity.
whoIsAffected: Officials and employees of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies.
Contract of service and job order workers, covered subject to the implementing rules.
Consultants, apprentices and institutional contract workers, who are excluded.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management

funding.detail: No total is stated in the copy filed. Each qualified employee gets at least ₱10,000 a year, charged against the appropriate funds in the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, the Ramadhan Bonus would no longer depend on a yearly Parliament resolution.
Each qualified worker would get at least ₱10,000 every year.
readings.insight:
The copy filed has no Section 8. The numbering runs from Section 7, on the implementing rules, straight to Section 9, the separability clause.

The bill sets a floor of ₱10,000 but no ceiling, and gives no headcount or total cost, though it would add a permanent yearly charge on the budget. The title says "all employees", but Section 5 excludes several groups, and Section 4 leaves contract of service and job order coverage to rules MFBM has not yet written. The copy filed names 14 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 26.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Civil Society Organizations Engagement and Empowerment Act of 2025. It creates a Bangsamoro CSO Coordinating Office under the Office of the Chief Minister, headed by an Executive Director, with divisions for policy, programs, monitoring, legal, finance, communications and provincial community liaison.

The office would keep a consolidated CSO registry, issue standard accreditation guidelines for ministries and local governments, map CSOs every 3 years with yearly updates, run an online portal and train staff. Every ministry and agency must consult accredited CSOs and fund programs for their engagement. CSOs convicted of misusing funds, ghost projects or falsification lose accreditation permanently, and officials who conspire face liability under existing law. A CSO Grievance Committee, chaired by the Chief Minister, would hear disputes. The Office of the Chief Minister writes the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 11 September 2025 by MP Abdulbasit R. Benito and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note cites the Constitution, Article IX, Section 10 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, the Local Government Code and the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code (BAA 49). It relies on a 2023 Asia Foundation mapping study that found CSO engagement with the Bangsamoro Government fragmented, sector-specific and inconsistent, and recommended a central office.

It says the bill came out of inception meetings, focus groups, sectoral and regional consultations and workshops, with technical help from Parliament's Policy Research and Legal Services, and points to OECD, World Bank and Open Government Partnership evidence that structured participation raises trust and improves services.
whoIsAffected: Civil society, people's and faith-based organizations working with the Bangsamoro Government.
Every ministry and agency, which must consult accredited CSOs and fund CSO programs.
Local governments, which would follow the office's accreditation guidelines.
Officials who conspire in CSO fraud.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro CSO Coordinating Office
Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: ₱50,000,000 is appropriated from the Contingent Fund for the office's initial operating expenses. After that, its budget goes in the Bangsamoro appropriations act. It may also accept donations and grants.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, a single office would handle CSO accreditation and liaison across the regional government.
Every ministry would be required to consult accredited CSOs and budget for CSO engagement.
readings.insight:
Section 13 asks for the annual report "not later than 31st of January of each preceding year", covering the previous calendar year. A report on the past year cannot be due in the year before it, so the timing has to be fixed in drafting.

The Grievance Committee is called independent, but 6 of its 9 members are the Chief Minister, the office's own director and 4 ministry representatives, against 3 CSO members. An earlier CSO bill is still pending: Bill 319, filed by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema on 11 July 2024, has not moved past first reading. The copy filed names 12 co-authors; Parliament's index lists 22.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Trust Fund for Development Continuity Act of 2025. It creates a trust fund under MFBM to hold development money that has been obligated but not spent by the end of the fiscal year, so it is not lost. Sources include unspent block grant, Special Development Fund and national subsidy balances, grants and donations, and Shari'ah-compliant investment earnings.

Retained funds may be carried over for up to 2 more fiscal years, under a memorandum of agreement with DBM, COA and the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board, with extensions by Parliament. They may pay for delayed projects, priority sectors, contingency reserves and peacebuilding, but not salaries, debt or political activity. The total held may not exceed 5% of the regional budget without a special law.

A Management Board chaired by the Minister of Finance, Budget and Management, with the BPDA Director General, the chair of Parliament's finance committee, a non-voting COA representative and 1 CSO member, would govern the fund. It must report yearly to Parliament, publish data online and undergo a third-party audit every 3 years.

It was filed on 18 September 2025 by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says that because of bureaucratic delays, procurement bottlenecks and limited absorptive capacity, large parts of the region's development allocations go unspent each year and revert to the national treasury, breaking development continuity. A dedicated trust fund would allow retention, carryover and multi-year programming of committed funds. It cites the fiscal autonomy guaranteed in Article XII, Section 15 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Ministries and agencies with delayed development projects.
Communities waiting on unfinished projects, which could keep their funding.
Parliament, whose finance committee chair would sit on the Board.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
BTFDC Management Board
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority

funding.detail: ₱500,000,000 is appropriated to set up the fund, charged against the Continuing Appropriation Fund for the current year. Later amounts go in the yearly Bangsamoro appropriations act. Total holdings are capped at 5% of the regional budget.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, obligated but unspent development money could be kept for up to 2 more years.
A Management Board would publish fund use and report to Parliament every year.
readings.insight:
The bill cannot stop reversion on its own terms. Section 7 makes every carryover subject to a memorandum of agreement with DBM, COA and the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board, which are national bodies, so the mechanism the note promises depends on national consent the bill cannot compel.

Section 7 also contradicts itself on extensions. One paragraph allows a single extension of at most 1 fiscal year by Parliament resolution; the next allows the 2-year period to be extended by Parliament with no limit stated. The same section refers to a "BTFDC Governing Board", while Section 8 creates a "Management Board". The copy filed lists no co-authors; Parliament's index names 7.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Parliamentary Redistricting Act of 2025. It divides the region into 32 single-member parliamentary districts, each with at least 100,000 people as far as practicable, in contiguous, compact territory, on a stated regional population of 4,545,489.

Basilan gets 4 districts, Lanao del Sur 9, Maguindanao del Norte 5, Maguindanao del Sur 5, Tawi-Tawi 4, the Special Geographic Area 2 and Cotabato City 3, with every town or barangay and its population listed. It would take effect immediately on publication.

It was filed on 24 October 2025 by MPs Suharto M. Ambolodto, Baintan A. Ampatuan, Amenodin U. Sumagayan, Ishak V. Mastura, Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim, Rashdi T. Adiong and Alirakim T. Munder. It was read on first reading on 27 October 2025, deferred on 28 October 2025 and referred to the Committees on Rules and on Local Government on 30 October 2025. It was archived on 12 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Its declaration of policy says only that Parliament must ensure equitable representation of the region's inhabitants in apportioning districts.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region, whose parliamentary district would be redrawn.
Candidates for district seats.
COMELEC and the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which would apply the map.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office
whatChanges: Nothing. The bill was archived on 12 January 2026 and will not become law.
The region's districts are set by Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86, from Bill 415, passed the same day.
readings.insight:
This bill is closed. On 12 January 2026, in Special Session No. 8, Parliament adopted Committee Report No. 196 on Bills 403, 407, 408, 411, 415 and 416, all district bills, approved Bill 415 on third reading, and archived this one the same day. Bill 415 became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86, which keeps the same 32 seats and the same split by province as this bill, with different groupings inside them. This bill's short title is also the same as that of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 77, the 2025 redistricting law it would have replaced.

The arithmetic in the copy filed does not quite add up. In Cotabato City, the barangays listed under the 1st District sum to 138,537, not the stated 138,628, and those under the 3rd District sum to 141,583, not 141,492. The 7 provincial totals add up to 4,545,486, 3 fewer than the regional population stated.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Sitio Mekir Peace Sanctuary and Safe Evacuation Center Act. It declares Sitio Mekir in Barangay Lamud, South Upi, Maguindanao del Sur, a peace sanctuary and safe evacuation centre for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples during armed hostilities. The site is to be respected as a demilitarized, neutral area, free of armed operations, and a humanitarian protection zone for displaced indigenous people.

The Office of the Chief Minister and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs implement it, with MPOS, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, MSSD and local governments, and with the Teduray and Lambangian traditional structure, the Kemamal Keadatan. MIPA sets up monitoring and writes the rules within 90 days.

It was filed on 27 October 2025 by MP Froilyn T. Mendoza and read on first reading on 13 November 2025. Parliament's index records no committee referral, and it has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The copy filed has no explanatory note. Its declaration of policy recognises the ancestral domain of the Teduray and Lambangian tribes and their right to peace, safety and self-governance during armed conflict and emergencies, citing the Constitution, the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 and the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Teduray and Lambangian communities in South Upi and nearby areas displaced by fighting.
Women, children and elders, named as the main people the sanctuary protects.
Security forces and armed groups, which would be barred from operating in the area.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister and Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs
Ministry of Public Order and Safety and Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission
Ministry of Social Services and Development and the South Upi local government

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Section 7 charges the start to available funds of the concerned ministries, and later costs to their budgets in the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved since.
If enacted, Sitio Mekir would be a legally declared neutral zone and evacuation site for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples.
MIPA would monitor compliance with humanitarian and cultural protection standards.
readings.insight:
Parliament's index and the registry record the filing date a year late. The receiving stamp on the copy filed reads 27 October 2025, which fits its first reading on 13 November 2025.

The bill declares the site demilitarized but does not say how that would bind the national armed forces or armed groups, set the site's boundaries, or provide any facilities for an evacuation centre. The copy filed leaves the co-author line blank, while Parliament's index lists 15. MP Mendoza also filed Bill 380 on 23 July 2025, to rename South Upi "Teduray Municipality"; it has not moved past first reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
It is 1 of 3 bills in this registry carrying the short title Bangsamoro Parliamentary Districts Act of 2025, with Bills 407 and 415. It apportions the region into 32 single-member parliamentary districts on population and geographical area, each as far as practicable contiguous, compact and adjacent, and each with at least 100,000 people.

Its schedule counts the region at 4,545,486: Basilan 4 districts (541,947), Lanao del Sur 9 (1,368,137), Maguindanao del Norte 5 (741,428), Maguindanao del Sur 5 (813,243), Tawi-Tawi 4 (482,645), the Special Geographic Area 2 (214,703) and Cotabato City 3 (383,383).

Its final provisions go further than the map. If Sulu rejoins the region, Congress may allocate it at least 7 district seats. The Omnibus Election Code applies where the bill is silent, and COMELEC is told to issue guidelines and provide the funding.

It was filed on 28 October 2025 by MP Romeo K. Sema with MPs Abdulkarim T. Misuari, Randolph C. Parcasio, Saripuddin D. Jikiri and Nurredha I. Misuari, read on first reading on 29 October and referred to the Committees on Rules and Local Government on 30 October 2025. On 12 January 2026, at Special Session No. 8, Parliament adopted Committee Report No. 196 on Bills 403, 407, 408, 411, 415 and 416, passed Bill 415 as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86, and archived this bill the same day.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note traces the problem through the courts. Province of Sulu v. Medialdea (9 September 2024) took Sulu out of the region and left the BAA 58 map out of step with it. Lanang T. Ali v. COMELEC (30 September 2025) struck down BAA 77 and ordered the Parliament to set the districts for the first regular election by 30 October 2025.

The bill's stated aims are equitable representation, a map aligned with the latest population and geographic data, compliance with both rulings, and readiness for the first parliamentary election.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region, whose district it would have fixed.
Candidates for the 32 district seats.
The people of Sulu, whose possible return the bill leaves to Congress.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing. Section 6 tells COMELEC to provide the funding needed to implement it.

whatChanges: Nothing. The bill was archived on 12 January 2026; the district map in force is the one in Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86, enacted from Bill 415.
Had it passed, any seats for a returning Sulu would have been for Congress to allocate, at no fewer than 7.
readings.insight:
The explanatory note calls BAA 77 "the Bangsamoro Electoral Code of 2023". It is not. BAA 77 is the Bangsamoro Parliamentary Redistricting Act of 2025, ratified on 19 August 2025; the Electoral Code is BAA 35, ratified on 8 March 2023.

Section 5 brings back the feature the courts objected to. It lets Congress allocate at least 7 seats to Sulu if it rejoins, which is the clause BAA 77 carried. Bill 411's explanatory note, written a week later, lists among the Supreme Court's reasons for striking down BAA 77 that it gave Congress powers the Organic Law assigns to the Parliament and imposed a fixed minimum of 7 seats. BAA 86, the act that passed, has no such clause.

The numbering also slips. There are 2 sections numbered 6 (Suppletory Laws and the Separability Clause), and Sections 3 and 4 carry the same heading, "Criteria in the Apportionment of Parliamentary Districts".

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Parliamentary Redistricting Act of 2025. It apportions the region into 32 single-member districts against a stated 2024 population of 4,545,489: 5 for Basilan, 4 for Tawi-Tawi, 9 for Lanao del Sur, 5 each for Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, 3 for Cotabato City, and a single Lone District of 214,703 for the Special Geographic Area.

Section 2 lists 5 guiding principles: legal compliance, equitable representation including indigenous peoples and geographically isolated communities, contiguity and compactness with regard to natural features and cultural ties, open consultation, and inclusivity. Section 3 repeats the Organic Law's tests of contiguous, compact and adjacent territory and at least 100,000 people per district, both "as far as practicable".

3 districts fall below 100,000: Basilan's 3rd (Tuburan, Hadji Mohammad Ajul, Akbar) at 90,744, Basilan's 4th (Tipo-Tipo, Al-Barka, Ungkaya Pukan) at 94,093, and Maguindanao del Norte's 5th (Talitay, Northern Kabuntalan, Kabuntalan) at 81,945.

It was filed on 3 November 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan with MPs Jose I. Lorena, Khalid M. Hadji Abdullah and Sittie Fahanie S. Uy-Oyod, read on first reading on 10 November and referred to the Committees on Rules and Local Government on 11 November 2025. It was archived on 12 January 2026, at Special Session No. 8, when Parliament adopted Committee Report No. 196 on this and 5 other districting bills and passed Bill 415 as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note sets out the Supreme Court's decision of 30 September 2025 striking down BAA 77 on 5 grounds, among them that it broke the contiguity requirement, gave Congress powers that belong to the Parliament and fixed a minimum of 7 seats. It records the Court's order to set the districts by 30 October 2025 and to hold the election no later than 31 March 2026.

It then defends its own exceptions. Basilan's island geography, with a municipality separated from the mainland, makes strict contiguity and population balance impracticable. Maguindanao del Norte's 5th District, at 81,945, is justified by contiguity, compactness and the distinct cultural and historical identity of its communities.
whoIsAffected: Every voter in the region.
Basilan, which would get 5 seats instead of the 4 it has under BAA 86.
The Special Geographic Area, which would vote as 1 district instead of 2.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament
whatChanges: Nothing. The bill was archived on 12 January 2026; the map in force is Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86.
Had it passed, Basilan would have had 5 districts and the Special Geographic Area 1.
readings.insight:
The bill was filed on 3 November 2025, 4 days after the 30 October 2025 deadline its own explanatory note cites.

Its headline figure does not match its own tables. The schedule states the 2024 regional population as 4,545,489, but the 7 area totals it lists (541,947, 482,645, 1,368,137, 741,428, 813,243, 383,383 and 214,703) add up to 4,545,486, the figure every other districting bill of that season uses.

The seat split is the real difference. It gives Basilan a 5th seat, defending 2 Basilan districts under 100,000 as a matter of geography. It also folds the Special Geographic Area, at 214,703 enough for 2 districts on the 100,000 floor, back into a single Lone District. That was the BAA 58 arrangement that BAA 77 and BAA 86 both split in 2, and that Bill 416, filed 8 days later, proposed splitting. The note explains the Basilan and Maguindanao del Norte exceptions but says nothing about the Special Geographic Area.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Cotabato Airport Modernization Act of 2025. It orders the upgrade of the Cotabato Airport in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, to take more commercial and domestic flights and better handle passengers, cargo and logistics.

The lead agency is the Bangsamoro Airport Authority, working with the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines and the Department of Transportation. It plans, designs, builds and maintains the airport to CAAP and ICAO standards. Within 90 days it submits a Modernization and Development Plan to Parliament and the Chief Minister, covering runways, taxiways and aprons, terminals and cargo facilities, navigation and safety equipment, access roads and parking, green infrastructure, accessibility, and monitoring. Implementing rules come within 60 days, with the Ministry of Transportation and Communications.

Section 9 restates that the National Government continues to fund airport maintenance, including at Cotabato, under the Organic Law.

It was filed on 3 November 2025 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, with 28 co-authors in Parliament's index. It was read on first reading on 10 December 2025 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note calls Awang the region's only Class 1 major domestic airport, about 8 km from Cotabato City. Passenger traffic was 295,801 in 2022, up 83% on 2021. It recalls the closure of 22 June 2023 for runway and terminal work, which sent travellers to Davao or General Santos until commercial flights resumed on 1 October 2023.

It adds Cotabato City's 2022 output of ₱72 billion and the region's 7.5% growth in 2021, and argues that modernisation would cut logistics costs, support disaster response and serve communities moving out of conflict.
whoIsAffected: Air travellers in Cotabato City and the surrounding provinces.
Businesses shipping cargo through the airport.
Communities near the airport in Datu Odin Sinsuat.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Airport Authority
Ministry of Transportation and Communications
Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The initial cost goes into the General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro for the year after enactment, then into annual appropriations, with national grants, loans, official development assistance or public-private partnerships also allowed.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, a modernisation plan for the airport would be due within 90 days.
readings.insight:
The bill rests everything on a Bangsamoro Airport Authority but does not create one, and no Bangsamoro Autonomy Act in this registry does either. The name turns up in other bills: Bill 296 (2024) puts emergency runways under a "Bangsamoro Airport Authority (BAA) of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications", and Bill 447 (April 2026) uses it as another name for its Civil Aviation Authority. Each uses the abbreviation "BAA", the same one used for every Bangsamoro Autonomy Act.

The division of labour is also left open. Section 5 has the regional body plan, build and maintain the airport, while Section 9 and the Organic Law provision quoted in the note leave maintenance of existing airports with the National Government. The bill does not say who pays for what.

The copy filed names 10 co-authors; Parliament's index credits 28.

readings.whatItDoes:
This divides the Special Geographic Area, the 63 former North Cotabato barangays that joined the region in the 2019 plebiscite, into 2 parliamentary districts with 1 seat each.

The First District is Pahamuddin, Kadayangan, Nabalawag and Tugunan; the Second is Malidegao, Ligawasan, Kapalawan and Old Kaabakan. Section 2 says that in the present term 2 of the appointed members are assigned to the seats, and afterwards each district is represented by a member who is elected or "chosen through political party selection".

The annexes give 2020 figures by barangay: the First District covers 289.39 sq km, 103,233 people and ₱120.66 million in annual income; the Second covers 515.89 sq km, 112,210 people and ₱125.17 million.

It was filed on 11 November 2025 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao with MPs Suwaib L. Oranon, Tawakal B. Midtimbang and Mudjib C. Abu. It was read on first reading on 18 November and referred to the Committees on Local Government and Rules on 19 November 2025. It was archived on 12 January 2026, at Special Session No. 8, when Parliament adopted Committee Report No. 196 on 6 districting bills and passed Bill 415 as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86.
readings.whyProposed:
The introductory note quotes the Organic Law: Article VII, Section 7(b) on district seats, Section 10 on redistricting and its 100,000 floor, and Article XVI, Section 4 on the transition authority's duty to set districts.

It argues that 2 representatives would carry the area's concerns to the Parliament, assist constituents, "act as lobbyists for local interest groups" and speed up its development.
whoIsAffected: About 215,000 people in the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area.
Candidates for the area's district seats.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections
Bangsamoro Parliament
whatChanges: Nothing from this bill, which was archived on 12 January 2026.
The split it proposes is in force anyway: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 86 gives the Special Geographic Area the same 2 districts.
readings.insight:
The bill was archived but its substance became law. BAA 86, enacted from Bill 415 on the day this bill was archived, divides the Special Geographic Area into exactly these 2 groups of 4 municipalities.

It is a refiling. Bill 122, filed on 22 November 2022 by MP Antao with MPs Mohagher M. Iqbal, Lanang T. Ali Jr. and Aida M. Silongan, carries the same title and the same 34 and 29 barangay split. It was read on first reading on 21 March 2023 and went no further. Section 2's arrangement for "the present term", where appointed members fill the seats, dates from that earlier transition.

The note says the First District has 33 barangays and the Second 29, which makes 62, not 63. Annex 1 lists 34 barangays for the First District, numbered 1 to 34, which brings the total to 63. The annexes are also by barangay and by the old North Cotabato towns of origin, while Sections 3 and 4 name the 8 new municipalities, and the copy does not show how one maps onto the other.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Higher Education Act of 2025. It creates the Bangsamoro Commission on Higher Education, separate from the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education and attached to the Office of the Chief Minister for administrative supervision only. It would cover public and private higher education institutions and degree programs in non-chartered public post-secondary schools.

The Chief Minister appoints a Chairman and 4 Commissioners for 4 years, renewable once. Each must hold an earned doctorate and have 10 years in higher education, and they rank as a Minister and Deputy or Assistant Ministers. The ministry's higher education programs, budgets, personnel and assets move to the Commission, whose Chairman also chairs the boards of new regional colleges and all non-chartered public institutions. A Board of Advisers chaired by the Chief Minister meets at least once a year.

A Higher Education Development Fund gets ₱500,000,000 in seed capital and ₱50,000,000 for start-up, plus a standing share every year: 5% of the annual block grant, 10% of the Special Development Fund and 10% of regional natural-resource revenues. It pays for scholarships and loans, research, salary subsidies for private school staff, review and convention centres, and help for institutions damaged in the 2017 Marawi siege.

It was filed on 21 November 2025 by MP Tomanda D. Antok with 7 other principal authors and 17 co-authors. It was read on first reading on 9 December 2025 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note invokes Article IX, Sections 16 to 20 of the Organic Law and models the Commission on the national arrangement, where CHED sits apart from DepEd under the Office of the President. It says the Commission would represent the region on CHED, the UniFAST board and PEAC, supervise private colleges, and take over the ministry's higher education functions. Those would include jurisdiction over local colleges, the Bangsamoro Regional Institute for Higher Islamic Studies and state universities in the region.
whoIsAffected: Students and staff of public and private colleges and universities in the region.
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education personnel in higher education, who would transfer to the Commission.
Private school teachers and staff, eligible for salary subsidies from the Fund.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission on Higher Education
Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education

funding.detail: ₱500,000,000 in seed capital "from the 2020 annual block grant" and ₱50,000,000 from unappropriated funds in the Regional Treasury for start-up (Section 22), then annual appropriations. The Fund would also take 5% of the annual block grant, 10% of the Special Development Fund and 10% of regional natural-resource revenues every year.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, higher education would leave the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education for a separate commission.
A fixed share of the block grant would be earmarked for higher education every year.
readings.insight:
The money is drawn from a year that has passed. Section 22 charges the ₱500,000,000 seed capital to "the 2020 annual block grant" in a bill filed in November 2025.

Other references point to the wrong place. Section 10(l) refers to the Fund "as described in Section 10"; it is in Section 12. Section 24 has the implementing rules written by "the transitory body created under Section 25", but Section 25 is the repealing clause and the body is created in Section 23. Section 10(m) opens offices in "Maguindanao", a province since divided in 2. The title says the bill amends Book VI, Title II of the Administrative Code, and Section 4 defines a Ministry of Basic and Technical Education "established as a result of the amendment" by this Act, but no section amends the Code.

There are 2 earlier proposals on the same subject. Bill 16, filed on 19 September 2022 by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and others, would create the same commission with a chair, 4 commissioners and a development fund, paid from existing higher education appropriations; it has not moved past first reading. Bill 47, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan's split of the ministry into 4 agencies including a Bangsamoro Commission on Higher Education and Development, was referred to committee on 20 November 2025, the day before this bill was filed.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Agriculture and Fishery School Act of 2026. It creates a Bangsamoro Agriculture and Fishery School in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, on land the Bangsamoro Government allocates within its Government Center there.

The School gives technical-vocational education in agriculture, fisheries, aquaculture, agribusiness and allied fields, and serves as a training, research and extension centre for farmers, fisherfolk, cooperatives and youth groups. It works under the policy supervision and academic oversight of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, with technical guidance and extension links from the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform. Its programs need ministry approval. Implementing rules are due within 90 days.

It was filed on 5 January 2026 by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan; the copy names 3 co-authors and Parliament's index lists 21. It was read on first reading on 19 January 2026 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note points to a slowing economy. In its Table 1, regional growth falls from 6.6% in 2022 to 4.3% in 2023 and 2.7% in 2024, while agriculture, forestry and fishing go from 3.5% to 2.7% to a contraction of 4.2%. In its Table 2 the sector employs 57.8% of workers in 2019 and 58.4% in the first quarter of 2020.

It says existing schools, the Upi Agricultural School and MSU-Maguindanao, serve only their own localities. Parang, as the seat of government, is a catchment for the Iranun towns of Matanog, Barira, Buldon and Sultan Mastura and for neighbouring Lanao del Sur.
whoIsAffected: Young people in farming and fishing communities around Parang and the Iranun towns.
Farmers, fisherfolk and cooperatives, as users of its training and extension services.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. The initial cost is charged to the Contingent Fund, then to the annual General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, a new agri-fishery school would be set up inside the Government Center in Parang.
readings.insight:
The explanatory note misreads its own table. It says agriculture, forestry and fishing is "the second largest source of employment after services", but its Table 2 shows the sector at 57.8% and 58.4% of employment against 35.5% for services, so it is the largest by a wide margin. Those employment figures are also from 2019 and early 2020, used to describe a contraction in 2024.

The school is thinly specified. The copy sets no head, governing board, enrolment, staffing or cost, and leaves the Contingent Fund, which is meant for unforeseen expenses, to pay for start-up.

It also does not mention the region's existing training body. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 59 (17 July 2024, from Bill 39) created the Bangsamoro Agriculture and Fisheries Training Institute to train farmers, fisherfolk and extension workers, which overlaps with the training and extension role given to this school.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Community-based Agricultural Crop Enterprise Development Act of 2026. It sets up a Regional Agricultural Enterprise Development Council, chaired by the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform with the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism as vice chair. The other members are representatives of the finance, environment and science ministries and the Cooperatives Authority, 2 small-farmer representatives per province, 1 cooperative, 1 academic and 1 planning expert from BPDA.

Working with local governments, the Council picks the priority crops for each municipality and writes a Regional Agricultural Enterprise Development Plan. A Bangsamoro Farming Enterprise Support Program offers training (including halal-compliant practice), low-interest loans and start-up grants, farm-to-market roads, irrigation and post-harvest facilities, buyer linkages and research.

Priority goes to marginalised farmers, women, indigenous communities and people affected by conflict who own or rent long-term between 0.5 and 3 hectares and belong to an association or cooperative. The Ministry monitors the program and reports every year to the Chief Minister and Parliament.

It was filed on 20 January 2026 by MP Mohammad Kelie U. Antao; the copy names 5 co-authors and Parliament's index lists 14. It was read on first reading on 26 January 2026 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note lists fragmented land use, low productivity, poor market access, climate risk and a "disorganized community value chain" as the sector's problems. It quotes Agriculture Secretary Francisco P. Tiu Laurel Jr. at a September 2024 forum in Manila.

It argues that crop zoning and value-chain farming together would let small farmers move from subsistence to community-managed enterprises, in line with the Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act and the Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Small farmers on 0.5 to 3 hectares who belong to an association or cooperative.
Farmers' cooperatives and associations, and the local governments that work with them.
implementedBy: Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform
Regional Agricultural Enterprise Development Council

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Start-up comes from the current appropriations of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and cooperating offices, with further amounts in the General Appropriations Act for the Bangsamoro.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, a regional council would set priority crops for each municipality and run a support program for small farmers.
readings.insight:
The bill promises loans, start-up grants, farm-to-market roads and irrigation, but states no amount. It draws on the agriculture ministry's existing budget.
