The key definition is written twice. Section 5(e) defines small farmers in 2 slightly different wordings, one after the other; both limit them to conflict-affected households on no more than 3 hectares. Section 12 then adds a 0.5-hectare minimum the definition does not have.

The structure has loose ends: 2 parts are numbered Article IV, the lettering in Section 9 restarts partway through, and there is no repealing clause. The "research findings" cited in the explanatory note are a single website article.

readings.whatItDoes:
The BIPOSSDIM Act of 2026. It creates the Bangsamoro Integrated Public Order and Safety, and Security Data and Information Management Coordinating Body, attached to the Ministry of Public Order and Safety, to collect, consolidate, analyse and share data on peace and order, crime, disasters and security.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety chairs it and the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government is associate chair. The other members are the health and social services ministries; NICA, the PNP and the AFP in the region; a "Philippine Statistics Office"; the regional ICT office; BPDA; and the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission. The Body builds a secure shared database, standardises collection, ensures data privacy compliance and reports to the Chief Minister. Data is classed as public or exclusive, the latter open only to members and others the Body recognises. Rules are due within 60 days, written with the National Privacy Commission.

It was filed on 22 January 2026 by MPs Mohammad Kelie U. Antao and Butch P. Malang; the copy names 4 co-authors and Parliament's index lists 15. It was read on first reading on 26 January 2026 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: The explanatory note says the region has many agencies working on peace, order and security but no centralised, integrated data system, and that this slows and weakens decisions. The Body would be a central point for sharing, a secure real-time database, a way to respond faster to incidents and disasters, and a source of accurate public safety information.
whoIsAffected: Regional ministries, police, military and intelligence offices that would share data.
Local governments, as both suppliers and users of the data.
People whose personal data would be held, under the Data Privacy Act.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Initial funds come from the current year's appropriations, then from the annual "Bangsamoro Appropriations Act (BAA)".

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, the region would have a single coordinating body and database for public order and security data.
readings.insight:
The copy is a rough draft. The acronym appears 3 ways: BIPOSSDIM in the title, BISPOSSDIM in both definitions of "Authorized User", and DIPOSSDIM in Sections 5 and 6. "Authorized User" is defined twice in a row, and Sections 5 and 6 say the same thing in different words. Section 10 makes the Ministry secretariat of "the Taskforce", a body the bill never creates, and the bill moves from Article I and Article II to "Chapter II". It also abbreviates the appropriations act as "BAA", the abbreviation used for every Bangsamoro Autonomy Act.

The gaps that matter are about control. 3 of the listed members are national security agencies (NICA, the PNP and the AFP), but no provision says how a regional act obliges them to share. The bill does not say who decides what is "exclusive", and it sets no penalty for misusing security or personal data. It also lists a "Philippine Statistics Office", where other bills in this registry cite the Philippine Statistics Authority.

readings.whatItDoes:
Renames the Tamparan District Hospital, in Tamparan, Lanao del Sur, as the Lanao del Sur Provincial Hospital. The short title is the Lanao del Sur Provincial Hospital Act of 2026.

That is all it does. The 6 sections set a title, a policy statement, the renaming, and the usual separability, repealing and effectivity clauses. Nothing changes the hospital's bed capacity, service level, staff or budget.

It was filed on 6 March 2026 by MPs Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr. and Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., with 7 co-authors in Parliament's index. It was read on first reading on 21 April 2026 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed: There is no explanatory note in the copy filed. Section 2 cites Article IX, Section 22 of the Organic Law on comprehensive health services and a general hospital system, but says nothing about why this hospital, or why the name.
whoIsAffected: Patients and staff of the Tamparan District Hospital.
Residents of Lanao del Sur.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: The bill appropriates nothing and has no funding provision.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, only the hospital's name would change.
readings.insight:
A renaming is not an upgrade, and this bill does only the first. A district hospital would carry a provincial name with nothing else changed. Compare Bill 246, enacted as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 73 on 19 May 2025, which converted the Iranon District Hospital in Parang into a 200-bed provincial hospital, with staffing and a deadline.

Its closest sibling is Bill 372, filed on 24 June 2025 with MP Sinolinding among its principal authors, which would rename the Buluan District Hospital as the Maguindanao del Sur Provincial Hospital. That bill at least charges the cost of signage and adjustments to the Ministry of Health; this one names no source. Bill 372 was referred to the Health and Finance committees on 11 December 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Maritime Safety and Security Act. It creates a Bangsamoro Maritime Safety Office under the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, a civilian body headed by a Chief Marine Safety Officer whom the Chief Minister appoints for 3 years, with a 10-grade rank structure of officers and inspectors.

The Office inspects municipal and inter-island vessels in Bangsamoro waters for passenger loading and manifests, life-saving equipment, capacity limits and compliance with safety advisories, and inspects ports, wharves and landing sites. It runs route risk assessments and post-incident surveys, may set up pre-departure checks, keeps a Maritime Safety Database and coordinates incident response. It may issue deficiency notices and compliance orders and recommend suspension of local operating clearances. Overloading, missing safety equipment, false manifests and ignoring advisories are prohibited, subject to administrative fines, suspension or temporary bans; criminal cases go to national authorities.

Its limits are written in. It may not register or certify vessels, make arrests, re-certify vessels already certified, charge duplicate fees, or run search and rescue without the Philippine Coast Guard.

It was filed on 11 March 2026 by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan with MPs Rashdi T. Adiong, Ahmad Amir A. Balindong, Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim and Alirakim T. Munder. It was read on first reading on 22 April 2026 and has not moved since.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note describes the region as maritime, with island communities that depend on sea transport, and cites overloading, poor safety equipment and weak manifests behind recent incidents across the country. The Coast Guard and MARINA keep primary jurisdiction, it says, but there is a regional gap in local monitoring, pre-departure checks, risk surveys and incident records.

It stresses that the Office is not an armed force, has no arrest powers, does not register or certify vessels, and does not duplicate MARINA, BMARINA or the Coast Guard.
whoIsAffected: Boat operators and passengers on municipal and inter-island routes.
Port, wharf and landing site operators under regional jurisdiction.
Coastal and island communities that rely on sea transport.
implementedBy: Ministry of Transportation and Communications
Bangsamoro Maritime Safety Office

funding.detail: No amount is stated in the copy filed. Funds are to be included in the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act. The bill provides for fines but leaves their amounts unstated.

whatChanges: Nothing yet. The bill has been read on first reading and has not moved.
If enacted, vessels on regional routes could face a regional safety inspection and pre-departure check in addition to national certification.
readings.insight:
It overlaps with Bill 447. That bill, the Bangsamoro Transportation and Communications Code filed on 13 April 2026 by MP Romeo K. Sema, gives vessel safety, manning and inspection to a Maritime Industry Authority (BMARINA) under the same Ministry, and it was read on first reading on 22 April 2026, the same day as this bill. Both give vessel inspection and safety to a regional body, and neither mentions the other. This bill leaves registration and certification to BMARINA but creates a second office for safety inspection alongside it.

The name says more than the text. The short title calls it a "Safety and Security Act", while Section 4 rules out any armed or paramilitary role and any arrest powers.

The explanatory note in the copy filed stops mid-sentence, at "It also establishes a", and the next page begins the bill itself.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to authorize, as a special and time-bound measure, the zero-tariff direct importation of rice from Sabah, Malaysia, for the Province of Tawi-Tawi only. The stated aims are lower rice prices, food security and relief for Tawi-Tawi households.

It asks that the authority come with national government regulatory safeguards and reasonable limits on volume, duration and destination, but it does not set those limits itself. Copies go to the Office of the President, the concerned national agencies and the Provincial Government of Tawi-Tawi.

Authored by MP John Anthony L. Lim and 58 others. Adopted on 19 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed: Tawi-Tawi is an island province far from the country's rice-producing areas. Its rice comes from Zamboanga City and other distant ports, and shipping, fuel and handling costs push up the landed price. Sabah is closer than any mainland supply point, and Tawi-Tawi sits inside the BIMP-EAGA cross-border cooperation area. The resolution points to Section 1608 of the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act, which lets the President modify import duties on the recommendation of the Economy and Development Council, and to Executive Order No. 105 (s. 2025). It states plainly that it does not recognize or legitimize informal or unauthorized trade.
whoIsAffected: Households in Tawi-Tawi, particularly low-income families, who pay the landed price of shipped-in rice.
Rice traders and importers who could bring rice directly from Sabah if the President allowed it.
implementedBy: Office of the President
Concerned national government agencies
Provincial Government of Tawi-Tawi
whatChanges: Nothing changes unless the President acts. Tariff changes are a national power under the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act; the resolution is a request.
Copies are sent to the Office of the President, the concerned national agencies and the Tawi-Tawi provincial government.
readings.insight: The resolution asks for limits on volume, duration and destination but names no figure for any of them, and gives no current rice price or price gap to show the hardship it describes. It is the only adopted resolution in the index on rice imports. It carried 59 principal authors. The page header carries its proposed number, P.P. Res. No. 780.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament rewrites Sections 1 and 2 of Rule XXIX of its own rules (Resolution No. 268) so that committee and sub-committee meetings, hearings and public consultations can be live streamed on the BTA website and official social media, not only floor sessions.

The new Section 1 sets up closed-circuit viewing of floor, committee, sub-committee and public proceedings in every Member's office. The new Section 2 has Parliament run a system for broadcasting, recording and live streaming, distribute broadcasts to news media, store recordings and caption them. Accredited broadcasters may get access. Recordings are released only on request and with the Speaker's approval, and coverage may not be used for political purposes, in commercial advertising, or with commercial sponsorship outside bona fide news and public affairs programs.

The text also sets out a Section 3 listing 5 grounds for going into executive session without broadcast: public order and safety, witness protection, an ongoing criminal or administrative investigation, sensitive personal data, and executive privilege invoked by the Chief Minister. The Secretary General is told to secure the proceedings and archive the recordings. Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 27 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law (Section 24, Article VII) assures public access to the proceedings of Parliament and its committees, and the Constitution recognizes the right to information on matters of public concern. Under the existing rules, only official recordings by the Committee Secretariat or Media Division were allowed in committee, unless the chair gave permission. The authors argue that committee meetings held without live streaming limit public participation and can let contentious provisions through without scrutiny, and that streaming reaches a wide audience at little cost.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament and committee chairs, whose committee work can now be broadcast.
The public and news media, who can watch committee hearings and consultations without attending.
Witnesses and resource persons, who are covered by the new exceptions.
implementedBy: Secretary General of the Parliament
Speaker of the Parliament

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It does not price the streaming, captioning or archiving system it requires.

whatChanges: This binds Parliament itself: it amends Rule XXIX of the rules of procedure, so committee proceedings are presumptively open to broadcast.
Executive session without broadcast is limited to the 5 listed grounds.
Access to stored recordings still runs through the Speaker's approval, on request.
readings.insight: This is an internal-rules resolution, so unlike most it has force: it changes how Parliament's own committees operate. The open question is practice. The rule lets proceedings be streamed and requires a system, but sets no date for it, and stored recordings remain available only when the Speaker approves a request. Section 6 of Rule XIII, which limits recording to the Secretariat or Media Division unless the chair permits, is quoted in the preamble but is not itself amended. The page header carries its proposed number, P.P. Res. No. 777.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes all of its parliamentary and statutory committees to keep holding meetings, hearings and consultations while the Second BTA Parliament is in mandatory adjournment. The authority takes effect on adoption and stays in force until amended or repealed. Copies go to the committees for reference.

Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. Adopted on 28 January 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The Fourth Regular Session was set to adjourn sine die on 29 January 2026 under Resolution No. 560. Committees still had priority codes before them, the Bangsamoro Revenue Code among them, plus other bills and resolutions, and the authors wanted that work to continue during the break.
whoIsAffected: Parliamentary and statutory committees, which may keep meeting while plenary is adjourned.
People with business before the committees, including those following the Bangsamoro Revenue Code.
implementedBy: Parliamentary and statutory committees of the BTA Parliament
whatChanges: Committees may hold meetings, hearings and consultations during the adjournment, with no end date other than amendment or repeal.
readings.insight: This is the 4th such authority in the index, after Resolutions No. 324 (2023), No. 443 (2024) and No. 539 (2025). Resolution No. 539 also named the Bangsamoro Revenue Code as pending in committee in February 2025; it is named again here nearly a year later, and the repo's act index lists no Revenue Code. The adopted page is dated 28 January 2026, a day after the 27 January date in Parliament's index, and its footer reads "Parliament Resolution No. 565", a slip carried over from another document; both are visible on the page image. The header gives the proposed number, P.P. Res. No. 791.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament sets its session calendar for the rest of the transition period. It sits in 4-day blocks: 20 to 23 April, 27 to 30 April, 11 to 14 May, 18 to 21 May, 25 to 28 May, 8 to 11 June, 15 to 18 June, 22 to 25 June and 13 to 16 July 2026, then 5 to 8 October, 12 to 15 October and 19 to 22 October 2026. It resumes on 26 October 2026 and goes into mandatory adjournment on 29 October 2026.

Authored by MP John Anthony L. Lim. Adopted on 20 April 2026, the first day of the calendar it sets.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 12317 moved the first regular Bangsamoro elections to 14 September 2026, extending the transition period and the BTA's term. Parliament needed a calendar for the added months.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, whose sitting days are fixed by it.
Anyone tracking when bills can move on the floor before the transition ends.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It binds Parliament's own schedule: 13 sitting blocks from 20 April to 29 October 2026, ending in mandatory adjournment.
readings.insight: The calendar leaves a gap from 16 July to 5 October 2026 with no sessions, which spans the 14 September 2026 election date. Sessions then resume for most of October, after the elections, before the mandatory adjournment on 29 October. It follows earlier calendars for this session, Resolutions No. 538 and No. 560, the latter of which had the session adjourn sine die on 29 January 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament formally recognizes and commends Amenah F. Pangandaman for her service as Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management and for her contributions to the Bangsamoro region, and orders that a copy be presented to her.

Authored by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and 8 others. Adopted on 21 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: Pangandaman, from Marawi City, was DBM Secretary from 2022 to 2025, the first Muslim Filipina to hold the post, and co-chaired the Intergovernmental Relations Body. The resolution credits her with activating all 7 intergovernmental relations mechanisms within 1 year, finishing the IGRB Manual of Operations in under 4 months, a Hajj agreement between the NCMF and the Bangsamoro Pilgrimage Authority, a PRC office in the region, and the transfer of LTO functions to the Bangsamoro Ministry of Transportation and Communications. It also cites public financial management training reaching at least 500 participants, funding for Marawi siege victim compensation under Republic Act No. 11696, and her work on the Women, Peace and Security agenda.
whoIsAffected: Former Secretary Amenah F. Pangandaman.
whatChanges: Nothing beyond the record: a copy of the resolution is presented to Pangandaman.
readings.insight: Parliament first congratulated Pangandaman in Resolution No. 274 (October 2022), on her confirmation as DBM Secretary; this one marks her departure. The achievements listed are the resolution's own claims and are not independently documented in it.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua to identify, acquire and establish a parking facility near, but outside, the Bangsamoro Government Center in Cotabato City, so internal spaces can be redeveloped.

It also urges him to buy or otherwise lawfully acquire a suitable parcel of land; have ministries run feasibility studies, site assessments, valuation and due diligence in line with procurement and audit rules; gradually clear parking inside the Government Center and build pedestrian walkways, covered walkways and safe access corridors; and adopt traffic management measures for the new facility. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and other concerned offices.

Authored by MP Alindatu K. Pagayao and 45 others. Adopted on 22 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: Parking inside the Government Center cannot hold the growing number of government and private vehicles of officials, employees and the public, causing congestion on internal roads, gates and nearby streets. Parked vehicles also take up space that could hold walkways and other improvements. Moving parking to a separate site nearby would free that space.
whoIsAffected: Officials, employees and members of the public who use the Bangsamoro Government Center.
Owners of land near the Government Center, if a parcel is bought.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministries and offices the Chief Minister assigns to the feasibility studies and acquisition

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing and names no amount or fund source for buying land or building the facility.

whatChanges: It gives Parliament's backing for a land purchase by the executive, but the money would still have to come through a budget.
No site, size, cost or deadline is fixed.
readings.insight: The resolution authorizes a land acquisition without naming a site, a budget or a deadline, and asks for no report back to Parliament. The executive already handles government property; what Parliament adds here is its endorsement, signed by 46 principal authors.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government and the national Department of the Interior and Local Government, through the Bureau of Fire Protection, to set up municipal fire stations in the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister, the MILG and other concerned agencies.

Authored by MP Butch P. Malang. Adopted on 23 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The Special Geographic Area is made up of 63 barangays from Cotabato Province that joined the region in the 2019 plebiscite and were organized into 8 municipalities in 2023. According to the resolution, none of these municipalities has a fully operational fire station, leaving lives and property exposed as population and development grow.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area.
The Bureau of Fire Protection, which would staff and equip the stations.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Department of the Interior and Local Government
Bureau of Fire Protection
whatChanges: Nothing binding: it is a request to a regional ministry and a national bureau, with copies sent to the Chief Minister's office and the MILG.
readings.insight: The request sets no deadline, no number of personnel or trucks, and no funding source, and asks for no report back. The Special Geographic Area has come up before for basic services: Resolution No. 195 (2021) urged the regional finance ministry to fund hospitals in each province and the Special Geographic Areas.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges strict enforcement in the region of Republic Act No. 11361, the Anti-Obstruction of Power Lines Act. It asks the DPWH, with the Ministry of Public Works, to lead enforcement with NGCP, local governments and the region's electric cooperatives; to run regular right-of-way inspections and clear vegetation and illegal structures under power lines, with PNP or AFP help where security is needed; and to build obstruction control into all power infrastructure programs.

It asks NGCP and every electric cooperative and distribution utility in the region to submit right-of-way clearing programs, obstruction risk maps and maintenance schedules to the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, which is to oversee enforcement and recommend further measures. Local governments are enjoined to issue notices of violation, help with clearing and pass supporting ordinances. Copies go to all of these offices and the DENR.

Authored by MP Amenodin U. Sumagayan and 4 others. Adopted on 23 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: At a hearing of the Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy on 11 February 2026, NGCP and other stakeholders said vegetation and structures along transmission corridors are among the main causes of unstable supply and the low voltage behind frequent outages in Lanao del Sur, particularly the Basak area. The resolution says the same obstructions occur in the areas of the Maguindanao, Tawi-Tawi and Basilan electric cooperatives and the Cotabato Light and Power Company, and that clearing them is a cheap, fast fix while longer-term rehabilitation is under way.
whoIsAffected: Households, schools, clinics and businesses hit by outages, particularly in Lanao del Sur.
Owners of structures, trees and crops inside power line right-of-way clearances.
NGCP and the region's electric cooperatives and distribution utilities.
implementedBy: Department of Public Works and Highways
Ministry of Public Works
Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy
National Grid Corporation of the Philippines
BARMM-based electric cooperatives and power distribution utilities
Provincial and municipal local governments
Philippine National Police
Armed Forces of the Philippines
whatChanges: Nothing new is made illegal; Republic Act No. 11361 already applies. The resolution asks for it to be enforced.
Utilities are asked to file clearing programs, risk maps and maintenance schedules with the MENRE, which gives the regional ministry a monitoring role if they comply.
readings.insight: Most of the offices named, including the DPWH, NGCP, PNP and AFP, are national bodies Parliament cannot direct. The most concrete ask is the filing of clearing programs and risk maps with the MENRE, but no deadline is set and no report to Parliament is required. Unusually, the resolution grows out of a dated committee hearing, on 11 February 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament congratulates and welcomes Mel Senen S. Sarmiento on his appointment as Secretary of the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, and expresses continued support for his leadership of the Bangsamoro peace process. A copy is to be presented to him.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 29 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: Sarmiento takes over OPAPRU while normalization programs continue and the region prepares for elections. The resolution notes he was Secretary of the Interior and Local Government and a Member of the House of Representatives, and credits his predecessor, Carlito G. Galvez Jr., with laying the foundation for the current peace work.
whoIsAffected: Secretary Mel Senen S. Sarmiento of OPAPRU.
whatChanges: Nothing beyond the record: a copy of the resolution is presented to Sarmiento.
readings.insight: Adopted the same day, by the same author, as Resolution No. 574, which thanks the outgoing OPAPRU Secretary, Galvez. The 2 resolutions mark the handover between them.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses gratitude and formal recognition to Carlito G. Galvez Jr., former Secretary of the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, for his service to peace and for his part in establishing and strengthening the Bangsamoro region. A copy is to be presented to him.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 29 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: Galvez, a retired AFP general, became Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process in December 2018 under President Rodrigo Roa Duterte and was kept on as OPAPRU Secretary under President Marcos, overseeing the change from OPAPP to OPAPRU. The resolution quotes his message at the region's anniversary on 21 January 2026 and credits him with sustaining the peace process as his tenure ends.
whoIsAffected: Former OPAPRU Secretary Carlito G. Galvez Jr.
whatChanges: Nothing beyond the record: a copy of the resolution is presented to Galvez.
readings.insight: About 11 months earlier, in Resolution No. 548 (29 May 2025), Parliament urged President Marcos to keep Galvez in the post. This resolution marks his exit, and was adopted alongside Resolution No. 573 welcoming his successor, Mel Senen S. Sarmiento.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament declares its full support for Fatwa No. 07, Series of 2026, of the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' on the employment of Bangsamoro women as overseas workers. It urges the Ministry of Labor and Employment and the Bangsamoro Women Commission to integrate the fatwa into regional labor policies and pre-departure orientation, and directs the Ministry of Social Services and Development and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform to prioritize and expand community-based livelihood programs as local alternatives. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister, the Darul-Ifta' and all relevant ministries.

Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 29 April 2026.
readings.whyProposed: On 7 April 2026 the Darul-Ifta' issued Fatwa No. 07, which, as the resolution describes it, holds that Muslim women should not travel for work without a mahram, a male guardian. Women are not barred from working, but travelling alone for work is impermissible unless there is a compelling necessity, read strictly. The resolution cites Department of Migrant Workers figures of about 8,126 documented deployments from the region in the first quarter of 2025, most of them women in domestic and elementary work, and reports that women abroad without a mahram are more exposed to abuse, trafficking and illegal recruitment. It says poverty and lack of local jobs push women abroad.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro women who work or plan to work overseas, and their families.
Pre-departure orientation programs and regional labor policy.
Families who would rely on expanded local livelihood programs.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment
Bangsamoro Women Commission
Ministry of Social Services and Development
Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'
whatChanges: Parliament's endorsement gives the fatwa political weight but does not make it law; a fatwa is religious guidance.
Regional ministries are asked to fold it into labor policy and pre-departure orientation, and to expand livelihood programs, with no deadline or report required.
readings.insight: Adopted 22 days after the fatwa was issued. The resolution asks regional ministries to integrate the fatwa into labor policy but does not say how that would work with overseas deployment, which national agencies such as the Department of Migrant Workers regulate. The only figure it offers is the 8,126 deployments in a single quarter of 2025, which shows the scale of the question.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament states its full support for Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua's decision to change the leadership of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, and frames it as moral governance and a fight against corruption in education. It calls on the Chief Minister and MBHTE leadership to carry out urgent education interventions.

It resolves to strengthen Parliament's oversight of MBHTE and other ministries through inquiries, budget hearings and review of COA reports, and authorizes its committees to review the MBHTE budget for coming years and recommend realigning unspent and unobligated funds to classrooms, learning materials and teacher hiring. It pledges cooperation with the Chief Minister's concurrent leadership of MBHTE and asks the public to support the move. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and MBHTE.

Authored by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr. and 40 others. Adopted on 19 May 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution lists EDCOM 2 and other figures: functional illiteracy of 38.3%, the highest in the country; a shortage of 13,237 classrooms; 9,599 unfilled teaching positions and 36,773 unmigrated ARMM teaching items; 277,817 learners without textbooks, 567,946 without armchairs and 757,379 without learning kits; and higher education enrolment of 18.7%. It cites a COA special audit finding ₱16,068,000 in liquidated damages not imposed for a 520-day delay in armchair deliveries, 53 contracts worth nearly ₱1,950,000,000 awarded despite defects, and 73 disbursement vouchers above ₱2,200,000,000 processed without procurement documents. It says the minister, a co-terminous appointee, refused to resign after more than a year of messages from the Chief Minister and that MBHTE leadership withheld documents from the Blue Ribbon Committee.
whoIsAffected: Learners and teachers in the region's schools.
MBHTE, now led concurrently by the Chief Minister.
Parliament's committees, given a mandate to review MBHTE's budget.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Committees of the BTA Parliament

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It authorizes committees to recommend realigning unspent and unobligated MBHTE funds toward classrooms, learning materials and teacher hiring, without naming an amount.

whatChanges: The removal itself is the Chief Minister's act; the resolution supports it but does not effect it.
It sets an internal task: Parliament's committees are authorized to review future MBHTE budgets and recommend realignments.
No deadline or specific intervention is required of MBHTE.
readings.insight: The resolution does not name the minister who was replaced. Its most checkable content is the COA findings it quotes, and the part within Parliament's own power is the oversight it gives Parliament's own committees. Education reporting has been asked for before: in February 2025 Resolutions No. 532 and No. 533 requested MBHTE reports to Parliament, including on textbook availability. In June 2025, Resolution No. 552 backed the Chief Minister's call for courtesy resignations of all ministers.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament declares strong support for Senate Bill No. 1903 by Senator Joseph Victor G. Ejercito, which would create the Mindanao Railways Authority, and urges the Senate and the House of Representatives to prioritize and pass it. It encourages the Bangsamoro Government, through its ministries, to work with national agencies so the region's priorities are built into planning of the Mindanao Railways System. Copies go to the Senate, the House, the Office of the President, the DOTr and the Mindanao Development Authority.

Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and MP Rasul E. Ismael. Adopted on 21 May 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The bill would create the Mindanao Railways Authority, attached to the Department of Transportation, as the agency responsible for planning, building, running and regulating railways in Mindanao, amending Republic Act No. 4156 as amended by Republic Act No. 6366. The authors argue a Mindanao-wide railway would cut transport costs, move farm goods, and widen access to markets, schools and services in the Bangsamoro region, and that a dedicated authority gives the project continuity.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro communities along or near a future Mindanao railway line.
Regional ministries asked to coordinate on railway planning.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
House of Representatives
Department of Transportation
Bangsamoro Government ministries and offices
whatChanges: Nothing binding: Congress decides on the bill. The resolution adds the BTA Parliament's voice and sends copies to Congress, the President, the DOTr and the Mindanao Development Authority.
readings.insight: A support resolution for a national bill. The repo does not track Senate bills, so it holds no record of whether Senate Bill No. 1903 has moved. The resolution names no railway route or station in the Bangsamoro region; it asks only that the region's interests be integrated into planning.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses full support and confidence in the leadership of Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua and reaffirms its commitment to moral governance and the fight against graft and corruption. It backs his leadership in preparing for an orderly and credible first Bangsamoro parliamentary elections in 2026, and commits Parliament to work with the Office of the Chief Minister, ministries, local governments, the National Government and other stakeholders. Copies go to the Chief Minister and concerned offices.

Authored by MP Romeo K. Sema and 47 others. Adopted on 17 June 2026.
readings.whyProposed: The preamble credits the Chief Minister with promoting unity across political and sectoral lines, stressing moral governance and the protection of public funds, responding to emergencies, recommitting to the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, and strengthening ties with local governments, the National Government and international partners. It describes the period as critical and says the government's success depends on stability. It cites no specific event, figure or decision.
whoIsAffected: Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua.
whatChanges: Nothing beyond a statement of confidence. It directs no office and changes no rule.
readings.insight: A vote of confidence signed by 48 principal authors. It is the latest of several adopted resolutions backing Macacua's actions: Resolution No. 552 (June 2025) on his call for courtesy resignations of all ministers and Resolution No. 576 (May 2026) on his change of MBHTE leadership. Like the preamble, the resolution gives no particular reason for being adopted when it was. The page header carries its proposed number, P.P. Res. No. 816.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Ministry of Public Works, the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority and all other concerned ministries and agencies to prepare and submit the provincial and municipal priority development projects of the region's local governments for funding by the national government.

Copies go to the Ministry of Public Works, the Planning and Development Authority and the other ministries and agencies for their information and appropriate action. Adopted on 17 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law makes the national government responsible for funding national roads, bridges, water supply, flood control and irrigation in the region, and Section 23 of Article XII promises additional national funds for 5 years after ratification for development projects, including provincial and municipal roads, following a plan drawn up by the Bangsamoro Government. The resolution says that 5-year window is nearing its end with no notable projects to show for it, and stresses that this money is separate from the block grant.
whoIsAffected: Provincial and municipal governments whose road and infrastructure projects would be put forward for national funding.
The Ministry of Public Works and the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, named to do the preparatory work.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
Other concerned BARMM ministries and agencies
whatChanges: Copies are sent to the Ministry of Public Works, the Planning and Development Authority and other ministries.
The resolution uses the word 'direct', but it sets no deadline, no list of projects and no reporting back to Parliament.
readings.insight:
The occasion is a deadline. The Organic Law was ratified on 21 January 2019, so the 5-year special development fund in Section 23 of Article XII ran to about January 2024; this resolution, adopted in October 2024, says the window is closing and nothing significant has come of it. It does not say how much money was at stake or whether any project list was ever submitted.

It is one of 10 resolutions in this stretch (504 to 533) filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan alone, and the same fund is cited again in Resolution 526, adopted in February 2025, which asks for a 15-year infrastructure plan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament respectfully requests the House of Representatives and the Senate to extend the transition period again, from 2025 to 2028, postponing the region's first regular parliamentary election.

The stated reasons are to leave time to resolve the legal issues affecting the election, to widen the participation of political parties, to let voters understand the new parliamentary system, and to let the Bangsamoro Government keep its socio-economic momentum. Copies go to the House, the Senate and the Commission on Elections. Adopted on 22 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: On 9 September 2024, 6 weeks earlier, the Supreme Court in Province of Sulu v. Medialdea upheld the Organic Law but ruled Sulu out of the region. The resolution says this unsettled the enacted Bangsamoro laws on the composition of Parliament, the 7 district seats reserved for Sulu, and voting and candidacy rights. It adds that a challenge to the Bangsamoro Electoral Code was pending in the Supreme Court, that only 3 of 16 political parties seeking registration had been accredited by COMELEC as of 2 October 2024, and that a survey by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance found most likely voters knew little or nothing of the new voting system. It cites regional growth of 4.3% in 2023 and poverty incidence falling from 52.6% in 2018 to 23.5% in 2023 as the momentum to protect.
whoIsAffected: Voters of the region, whose first parliamentary election would be postponed.
The 80 appointed members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, whose term would run on.
Political parties preparing for the first election.
implementedBy: House of Representatives
Senate of the Philippines
Commission on Elections (copy furnished)
whatChanges: Only Congress can move the election date; the resolution is a request to it.
Copies are furnished to the House, the Senate and COMELEC.
readings.insight:
Congress did postpone, but not to 2028. Republic Act No. 12123, signed on 19 February 2025, moved the election only to 13 October 2025. That date also failed: on 1 October 2025 the Supreme Court voided BAA 77, the redistricting act passed after Sulu's exclusion, and held that no election could proceed without a valid districting law. Republic Act No. 12317 then set the first election for 14 September 2026. So the region did not get the 2028 date asked for here, but it did not vote in 2025 either.

This was Parliament's second such request. Resolution 93, adopted in November 2020, asked Congress to extend the transition to 30 June 2025, which Republic Act No. 11593 did. The figure on poverty is worth reading carefully: the drop from 52.6% to 23.5% is 29.1 percentage points, which the resolution calls an 'almost 30%' reduction rate. The resolution has 13 principal authors, led by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament encourages the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education to consider providing free hygiene kits, especially free sanitary napkins, in the comfort rooms of all public high schools in the region.

A copy goes to the Ministry for consideration and appropriate action. Adopted on 22 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution describes 'period poverty', a lack of access to menstrual products, hygiene facilities and education, which it says affects an estimated 500 million people worldwide. Students without products on hand may leave school early or miss classes, and poor menstrual hygiene can lead to infection. It ties the request to the Ministry's 12-point agenda, which includes comprehensive health and nutrition programs in schools.
whoIsAffected: Menstruating students in public high schools in the region.
The Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, which would have to supply and stock the kits.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
whatChanges: A copy goes to the Ministry. 'Encourage to consider' is the softest form a request can take; nothing is required.
readings.insight: The operative clause is narrower than the argument for it. The WHEREAS clauses ask the Ministry to plan free menstrual products in all public school comfort rooms; the RESOLVED clause limits the request to public high schools. No cost estimate, number of schools or number of students is given, and the resolution names no funding source. It is the only adopted resolution in the index on hygiene kits or sanitary products. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses support for the motions filed with the Supreme Court by the Bangsamoro Attorney-General's Office and by individuals asking the Court to reconsider its ruling excluding Sulu from the region.

A copy goes to the Supreme Court for consideration and appropriate action. Adopted on 23 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: On 9 September 2024 the Supreme Court ruled in Province of Sulu v. Medialdea that the Organic Law is constitutional but that Sulu is not part of the region, because the province voted against ratification; the region received the decision on 16 September. On 1 October the Bangsamoro Attorney-General's Office moved to intervene and for partial reconsideration, arguing the region was never a party to the case. Deputy Speaker Laisa M. Alamia filed a similar motion on 17 October, and MP Don Arbison Loong and others on 18 October. Their filing said the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management allocated over ₱4,500,000,000 in 2024 for 7,872 positions in Sulu's ministries and offices. 9 MPs gave privilege speeches on the ruling between 16 and 19 September 2024.
whoIsAffected: The people and province of Sulu.
Bangsamoro government employees in Sulu, put by the resolution at 7,872 positions.
The Bangsamoro Government, whose territory, budget and parliamentary seats the ruling changed.
implementedBy: Supreme Court (copy furnished)
whatChanges: The resolution adds no legal weight to the motions; it records Parliament's position and sends it to the Court.
Nothing is asked of any Bangsamoro office.
readings.insight:
The motions failed. The Supreme Court denied the motions for reconsideration with finality on 26 November 2024, about a month after this resolution, and Sulu's exclusion became final. The consequences ran through the rest of the transition: the 7 Sulu seats had to be redistributed, BAA 77 attempted that and was voided by the Court in October 2025, and Resolution 546 in May 2025 asked the Intergovernmental Relations Body to work out the budgetary transition for Sulu.

The resolution was adopted the day after Resolution 505, which asked Congress to postpone the election partly because of the same ruling. It has 9 principal authors, led by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses support for the immediate passage of Senate Bill No. 2817, which would strengthen the independence of the Commission on Elections by amending the Omnibus Election Code, with the stated aim of strengthening COMELEC's field offices, including the Bangsamoro Electoral Office.

Copies go to the Office of the Senate President, the House of Representatives and the Office of the Chief Minister. Adopted on 23 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: COMELEC can only appoint civil service employees to positions Congress creates, so it has filled its growing workload with contractual and job-order workers who are paid less than their tasks warrant. The House passed House Bill No. 10579 to strengthen COMELEC field offices, and on 11 September 2024 3 Senate committees submitted Committee Report No. 318 recommending the substitute Senate Bill No. 2817, which would create positions, reclassify existing ones and upgrade salaries.
whoIsAffected: COMELEC field personnel, including contractual and job-order workers.
The Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which the title names.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
House of Representatives
Office of the Chief Minister (copy furnished)
whatChanges: A statement of support sent to Congress; it has no effect on the bill's progress.
readings.insight: The Bangsamoro Electoral Office appears only in the title and the RESOLVED clause. None of the WHEREAS clauses say what the bill would do for the Bangsamoro office in particular, how many positions it has, or how the region's first parliamentary election would strain it. The repo has no record of what became of Senate Bill No. 2817. Filed by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Mindanao Development Authority to brief it on the status of the Mindanao River Basin Master Plan, especially the priority development programs and projects it identified.

A copy goes to the Authority for its information. Adopted on 23 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Mindanao River Basin covers 21,503 square kilometres across Regions X, XII and the Bangsamoro region, and the resolution calls it the country's largest. A master plan was prepared by Woodfield Consultants from 2010 to 2012 with the support of national agencies, and was endorsed by the 3 regional development councils, including the planning board of the former ARMM. Executive Order No. 50 of 2011 moved the work of the presidential task force on the basin to regular agencies, including the Mindanao Development Authority. Parliament says it needs to be updated so it can support the plan with policy and legislation.
whoIsAffected: Communities along the Mindanao River Basin in the region, which the plan's flood control and watershed components would cover.
The Mindanao Development Authority, asked to report.
implementedBy: Mindanao Development Authority
whatChanges: A request for a briefing from a national agency. The copy is sent 'for information', not for action, and no date is set.
readings.insight: The plan is more than a decade old: drafted between 2010 and 2012 and endorsed by the planning board of an ARMM that no longer exists. The resolution does not say what has or has not been implemented, which is the point of asking. It is the only adopted resolution in the index on the river basin, and the repo holds no record of a reply. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament respectfully requests the Government Service Insurance System to open branches or extension offices in different areas of the region, and asks the Bangsamoro Government to put the proposal on the agenda of the Intergovernmental Relations Body so GSIS acts on it.

A copy goes to GSIS for consideration and appropriate action. The document is dated 24 October 2024; Parliament's index lists 23 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: GSIS insures government workers and offers loans and retirement, life and disability benefits. As of 18 January 2022, according to the resolution, only 1 of its 42 branch offices was in the region, in Cotabato City. The Bangsamoro Government has offices in all 6 provinces and local governments employ their own staff, all GSIS members, and the resolution names the employees of Lanao del Sur, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Basilan and Maguindanao del Sur as needing closer service.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro government and local government employees who must travel to Cotabato City for GSIS transactions.
Government pensioners in the region.
implementedBy: Government Service Insurance System
Bangsamoro Government, through the Intergovernmental Relations Body
whatChanges: A request to a national corporation, plus a request that the Bangsamoro Government raise it in the Intergovernmental Relations Body.
No number or location of offices is specified.
readings.insight:
The key figure, 1 branch out of 42, is dated January 2022, nearly 3 years before adoption, and the resolution does not say whether that had changed. It also lists Sulu among the provinces needing service, though the Supreme Court had excluded Sulu from the region the month before. The resolution drew broad support, with 35 authors led by MP Susana S. Anayatin, and is the only adopted resolution in the index about GSIS.

The adoption date printed on the document, 24 October 2024 (checked on the page image), is a day later than the 23 October 2024 in Parliament's index.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board to include the rehabilitation and upgrading of the Narciso Ramos Highway, within the region, on its priority agenda.

A copy goes to the Board for consideration and appropriate action. The document is dated 24 October 2024; Parliament's index lists 23 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The 154-km Narciso Ramos Highway links the region to the rest of Mindanao and carries goods from production areas to markets. As a national road, its repair falls to the national Department of Public Works and Highways under Section 37 of Article XIII of the Organic Law. The Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board coordinates national and Bangsamoro infrastructure plans, and both the DPWH Secretary and the Bangsamoro Minister of Public Works sit on it, so Parliament sees it as the place for a joint decision.
whoIsAffected: Travellers and freight moving along the Narciso Ramos Highway.
Producers who rely on the road to reach markets.
implementedBy: Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board
whatChanges: A request to put an item on the Board's agenda. It sets no budget, timeline or scope of work.
readings.insight:
The resolution names the road's length but not its condition, the stretch inside the region, or a cost. It set a pattern: Resolution 558, adopted in August 2025, uses the same wording to ask the same Board to prioritise the Awang–Upi–South Upi–Lebak Highway. It has 23 authors, led by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

As with Resolution 510, the date on the document, 24 October 2024 (checked on the page image), differs by a day from Parliament's index.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Supreme Court and the Legal Education Board to consider adding to the Clinical Legal Education Program a provision requiring law students to give free legal assistance to barangay officials implementing the Katarungang Pambarangay Law.

A copy goes to both bodies. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The barangay justice system, set up under Presidential Decree No. 1508 in 1978 and carried into the Local Government Code of 1991, settles disputes in the community before they reach court. It is run by the barangay chair and Lupon members chosen for integrity and standing, not legal training. The resolution argues that law students, already required by Legal Education Board Memorandum Order No. 23 of 2020 to take clinical legal education, could help them with questions of law, and links this to settling rido, the recurring clan feuds that have troubled the region.
whoIsAffected: Barangay chairs and Lupon members handling disputes.
Law students, who would take on the required service.
Disputing parties in barangays, including families in rido.
implementedBy: Supreme Court of the Philippines
Legal Education Board
whatChanges: A request to national bodies over which Parliament has no authority. Only the Supreme Court and the Legal Education Board can change the program.
readings.insight: The proposal would apply wherever the program applies, which is nationwide; the resolution does not limit it to law schools in the region or say how many there are. It was one of 14 resolutions Parliament adopted on 23 January 2025. Filed by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Government of the Day to activate the Shari'ah Public Assistance Office at once.

A copy goes to Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim for his consideration and approval. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA 13) created the Shari'ah Public Assistance Office, headed by a director with 2 counselors who are members of the Shari'ah Bar, to give free legal help to poor litigants in each Shari'ah judicial district, and attached it to the Office of the Chief Minister until a ministry is assigned. The resolution says poor constituents still cannot afford a Shari'ah counselor to appear for them in the Shari'ah courts.
whoIsAffected: Poor and indigent litigants in the Shari'ah courts.
Shari'ah counselors who would staff the office.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A request to the executive to staff and operate an office that the law already created. It does not set a deadline or fund it.
readings.insight: The office already exists on paper. The Administrative Code was passed on 28 October 2020, so by this resolution the office had gone more than 4 years without being activated. The resolution does not say why, nor what it would cost. It was adopted the same day as Resolutions 516 and 517, also on the Shari'ah justice system. Filed by MP Baileng S. Mantawil.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its gratitude for the return of supervision over the Public Attorney's Offices in Maguindanao, Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi to the Public Attorney's Office regional office for the Bangsamoro region. It calls on the Public Attorney's Office to make the handover smooth.

A copy goes to the Office of the Chief Public Attorney. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: In 2009 the Public Attorney's Offices in Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi were moved under the Zamboanga Peninsula regional office, and in 2015 Maguindanao went to the SOCCSKSARGEN regional office, leaving only Lanao del Sur under the regional office for the autonomous region. After letters dated 8 February 2024 from the Budget Secretary and a Justice Undersecretary, the Public Attorney's Office issued Office Order No. 22 of 2024 restoring the 4 provinces to the Bangsamoro regional office. The resolution praises Chief Public Attorney Persida V. Rueda-Acosta, in office since 2001.
whoIsAffected: Indigent clients of the Public Attorney's Office in Maguindanao, Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi.
Public attorneys in those provincial offices, who change regional supervisors.
implementedBy: Public Attorney's Office
whatChanges: A thank-you for a change already made by Office Order No. 22 of 2024, plus a call to carry out the handover smoothly.
readings.insight: The restoration came first and the thanks later: the Office Order followed letters from February 2024, and the resolution was adopted almost a year after them. It also thanks the agency for returning Sulu's office to Bangsamoro supervision, and lists Sulu as part of the region, although the Supreme Court's exclusion of Sulu had become final in November 2024, 2 months before adoption. The resolution does not address what that means for the Sulu office. Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament respectfully requests the Department of Justice to restore the National Bureau of Investigation's regional office in the Bangsamoro region to its original coverage and to set up NBI district offices in every province, including the Special Geographic Area.

Copies go to the Secretary of Justice, the NBI Director and the Intergovernmental Relations Body. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The NBI Reorganization and Modernization Act (Republic Act No. 10867) requires a regional office in every region and a district office in every province. But under Department of Justice Circular No. 046 of 27 July 2012, the NBI office for the region was cut back to Cotabato City and Maguindanao, and even then without Datu Paglas, Buluan, Pagalungan and Datu Montawal. The resolution says the other provinces are left without ready access to the bureau.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Lanao del Sur, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi and the Special Geographic Area, outside the NBI regional office's current coverage.
Crime victims and complainants who need the bureau's investigative help.
implementedBy: Department of Justice
National Bureau of Investigation
Intergovernmental Relations Body (copy furnished)
whatChanges: A request to a national department; the NBI's offices are set by the Department of Justice, not by Parliament.
readings.insight: The resolution rests on a concrete gap between law and practice: Republic Act No. 10867 calls for a district office in every province, while a 2012 circular limited the regional office to Cotabato City and part of Maguindanao. It does not say where those other provinces are served from now. It sits alongside Resolution 514, adopted the same day, which thanks the Public Attorney's Office for a similar return of provincial offices to regional supervision. Filed by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., through the Judicial and Bar Council, to appoint judges to the vacant Shari'ah District Courts established under the Code of Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree No. 1083).

Copies go to the Office of the President and the Judicial and Bar Council. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Presidential Decree No. 1083 created 5 Shari'ah judicial districts, each with 1 district court and 1 judge: Sulu; Tawi-Tawi; Basilan with the Zamboanga provinces and cities; the Lanao provinces with Iligan and Marawi; and Maguindanao, North Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat and Cotabato City. The resolution says that as of June 2021 only 2 of the 5 courts had a judge, and that it was the same person, acting in the 5th; the Supreme Court's website showed the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th courts' presiding judges as vacant. Unfilled courts clog dockets and, the resolution warns, push litigants toward settling disputes outside the law.
whoIsAffected: Litigants with cases before the Shari'ah District Courts, mostly on Muslim personal and family law.
Shari'ah lawyers and counselors appearing before those courts.
implementedBy: Office of the President
Judicial and Bar Council
whatChanges: A request to the President. Lower court judges are appointed by the President from Judicial and Bar Council shortlists; Parliament has no role.
readings.insight: By the resolution's own count, 4 of the 5 Shari'ah District Courts had no presiding judge, and the one sitting judge was also acting in a second district. The resolution does not say how many cases are pending. Parliament had raised the Shari'ah courts before: Resolution 177 in 2021 asked Congress for more Shari'a courts, and Resolutions 457 and 458 in May 2024 asked for a pre-judicature program for Shari'ah judgeship applicants and for the organisation of the Shari'ah High Court. Resolution 517, adopted the same day, addresses the supply of qualified candidates. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Bangsamoro Government, through Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim, to set up a Juris Doctor bridging program, as a scholarship grant, to prepare graduates of kulliyah, Islamic colleges abroad and in the region, for law practice and for appointment as judges in the region's Shari'ah courts.

A copy goes to the Chief Minister for consideration and appropriate action. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law requires judges of the Shari'ah circuit, district and high courts to have passed the Philippine Bar. The ulama, religious scholars, are trained in Islamic law but generally lack a Philippine law degree, so they cannot qualify. A bridging program would let them meet the Bar requirement.
whoIsAffected: Ulama with kulliyah degrees from schools abroad or in the region.
The Shari'ah courts, which need qualified judges.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: The resolution asks for a program 'as a scholarship grant' but names no amount and no source. It appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: A request to the executive to design and fund a scholarship program. No size, cost or partner school is named.
readings.insight: This is the supply side of Resolution 516, adopted the same day, which asks for judges in 4 vacant Shari'ah District Courts. 516 needs candidates; 517 points out that the obvious candidates, Islamic scholars, are barred by the Philippine Bar requirement. Neither resolution gives numbers on how many ulama might apply. Filed by MP Suharto S. Esmael.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requires all ministries and offices of the region, through the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, to submit to Parliament an annual accomplishment report for each year from 2019 to 2024.

Copies go to all ministries and offices. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: More than 5 years after the region replaced the ARMM, its ministries and offices have achieved a good deal, but the resolution says there are also gaps in carrying out programs and projects. It wants a record of physical and financial accomplishments for each year, in a standard format to be drawn up by the Planning and Development Authority, to guide this and future Parliaments in legislating.
whoIsAffected: Every Bangsamoro ministry and office, which must compile 6 years of reports.
Present and future members of Parliament, who would use them.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
All BARMM ministries and offices
whatChanges: Uses the word 'require', but sets no deadline and no consequence for not complying.
The Planning and Development Authority is to devise the report format.
readings.insight: The request covers 6 years at once, 2019 to 2024, which says something on its own: Parliament did not already have annual accomplishment reports from the ministries it funds. The resolution sets no due date. It is one of 5 resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025 that route a reporting or planning request through the Planning and Development Authority (518, 519, 520, 523, 524), all filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council, through the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, to submit a long-term plan for the region to Parliament for its consideration.

A copy goes to the Council's secretariat and the Planning and Development Authority. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Under BAA 6, the Council evaluates and recommends short-, medium- and long-term plans for Parliament's approval. Its rules task a Regional Land Use Committee with keeping a Regional Physical Framework Plan, described as the region's long-term 'mother of all plans', with a 30-year horizon, sitting above the medium-term Bangsamoro Development Plan and the provincial plans. Provinces were updating their framework plans and the second Bangsamoro Development Plan was being finalised, and the resolution wants the long-term plan on top of them.
whoIsAffected: The Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council and its Regional Land Use Committee.
Provincial and local governments, whose plans are meant to align with the regional one.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
whatChanges: A request for a plan to come to Parliament; no deadline is set.
readings.insight: The resolution asks for a document whose existence it never confirms: it does not say whether a Regional Physical Framework Plan had been drafted, or when. It closes its case with a long quotation from the American planner Daniel Burnham, 'Make no little plans'. It is one of 5 planning and reporting resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025 and filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority to enhance, update and maintain its online database of programs and projects.

A copy goes to the Authority for information and appropriate consideration. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Authority's database, the resolution says, was developed in 2023 and needs improving and regular updating. A current database would guide planning, budgeting and monitoring, show the public which projects are funded by national, regional and local governments, and help shape legislation.
whoIsAffected: The public, who would be able to look up projects.
The Planning and Development Authority, which maintains the database.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
whatChanges: An exhortation to an office. It sets no standard, no update frequency and no deadline.
readings.insight: The resolution does not name the database, give its address, or say what is wrong with it beyond needing an update. It is one of 5 planning and reporting resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025 and filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament encourages everyone in the region to observe and commemorate Bangsamoro Foundation Day every year.

Copies go to all ministries and offices. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Administrative Code proclaims 21 January, the date the Organic Law was ratified in 2019, as Bangsamoro Foundation Day and a non-working holiday. The resolution's WHEREAS clauses go further than the resolution itself: private entities are to organise or support events and display commemorative symbols, and ministries, offices and local governments are to hold special activities and fly the regional flag.
whoIsAffected: All residents of the region, public and private.
whatChanges: An encouragement only. The holiday already exists under the Administrative Code; this adds no obligation.
readings.insight: Adopted on 23 January 2025, 2 days after that year's Foundation Day. The same day Parliament adopted 2 more resolutions tied to the anniversary: Resolution 522 on an inter-agency sports festival and Resolution 525 on tree planting every 21 January. Filed by MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament supports the Bangsamoro Government, through the Bangsamoro Sports Commission, in improving and continuing the inter-government agency sports festival held during the region's annual founding anniversary.

A copy goes to the Bangsamoro Sports Commission. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution says a sports festival during the anniversary brings employees of different ministries and agencies together, promotes health and teamwork, and gives workers something to look forward to. It suggests events such as basketball, volleyball, football, athletics and traditional games.
whoIsAffected: Employees of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
whatChanges: An expression of support; no budget, schedule or rules for the festival are set.
readings.insight: One of 3 resolutions on the region's founding anniversary adopted on 23 January 2025, 2 days after the anniversary itself (with 521 and 525). Filed by MP Jamel B. Macacua, MP Eddie M. Alih, MP Hamid U. Malik and MP Michael E. Midtimbang.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requires the Office of the Chief Minister, through the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, to update the Bangsamoro Transition Plan 2019-2022 and submit it for Parliament's consideration and approval.

Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and the Authority. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law requires the interim Chief Minister to submit a transition plan for the bureaucracy within the first 60 days, for the Transition Authority to approve. Parliament approved it on 17 June 2019 through Resolution No. 12. Since then the transition was extended to 30 June 2025 by Republic Act No. 11593 and a new set of 80 members was appointed in August 2022. The resolution says the plan should be updated to set the Transition Authority's road map and deliverables for the extended period.
whoIsAffected: The Office of the Chief Minister and the Planning and Development Authority, asked to rewrite the plan.
Members of Parliament, who would approve it.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
whatChanges: Requests a revised plan for Parliament's approval. No deadline is given.
readings.insight: The timing is the story. The extension the plan was meant to cover began in 2022; this resolution asking for the updated plan came in January 2025, with about 5 months left before the 30 June 2025 end date it cites. That end date then moved: Republic Act No. 12123 in February 2025 and Republic Act No. 12317 later pushed the first election to September 2026, with the Transition Authority continuing until then. The resolution is one of 5 planning and reporting resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025 and filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council, through the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, to prepare and submit to the national government a comprehensive performance report of the Bangsamoro Government covering 2019 to 2022 and 2023 to 2024.

A copy goes to the Office of the Chief Minister to guide ministries, agencies and offices. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law requires the Transition Authority, on its dissolution, to report on the transition to Parliament, the House, the Senate and the President. The first Transition Authority served from 19 February 2019 to 10 August 2022 and a second set of 80 members was appointed in August 2022. The resolution wants the first period documented, with gains by sector, laws passed, and the main implementation problems, and the report sent by the Chief Minister to the President, the Senate President and the Speaker of the House.
whoIsAffected: The national government and the public, the intended readers.
Every ministry, agency and office, which would supply the data.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A request to produce a report for the national government. It names who prepares and who submits it, but no deadline.
readings.insight: This and Resolution 518, adopted the same day, ask for overlapping material: 518 wants annual accomplishment reports for 2019 to 2024 sent to Parliament, 524 wants a performance report for the same years sent to Manila. The resolution also explicitly asks that implementation problems be reported, not only achievements. It is one of 5 planning and reporting resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025 and filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges Bangsamoro ministries, agencies, offices and local governments to hold a tree-planting activity every 21 January as part of Bangsamoro Foundation Day, in line with the Arbor Day Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10176), and encourages schools, NGOs and private businesses in the region to take part.

Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister, all ministries and offices, local governments, schools, NGO networks and private establishments. Adopted on 23 January 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution cites repeated states of calamity: flooding from August to October 2022, Typhoon Paeng in October 2022 (followed by a national 6-month state of calamity in the region and 3 other regions), and El Niño in April 2024. It argues trees reduce flooding and erosion, cites the Qur'an and Sunnah on stewardship of the earth, and says designating 21 January as tree-planting day ties environmental care to the region's founding.
whoIsAffected: Ministries, offices and local governments asked to hold the activity.
Communities exposed to flooding and drought.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro ministries, agencies and offices
Local government units

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It notes that the Arbor Day Act already requires local governments to allocate a budget for tree planting.

whatChanges: Asks for a yearly event on a fixed date; it creates no obligation and names no number of trees or target area.
readings.insight: The Arbor Day Act already requires local governments to set a day for tree planting and to budget for it, which this resolution does not change; what it adds is a suggested date. It is one of 3 Foundation Day resolutions adopted on 23 January 2025, 2 days after the 2025 Foundation Day (with 521 and 522), and the only adopted resolution in the index on tree planting. Filed by MP Diamila D. Ramos.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council and the Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board to jointly prepare a long-term Infrastructure Development Plan and Investment Program for the 15 years from 2023 to 2038.

Copies go to the Council and the Board. Adopted on 10 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution says the former ARMM was left out of Mindanao's development, receiving the smallest infrastructure budget in the country at ₱900,000,000 a year and ranking lowest on infrastructure development. The Organic Law makes the national government fund national roads, bridges, water, flood control and irrigation, gave 5 years of additional national funds for development projects, and provides that after 20 years certain regional tax revenues and natural resource shares will be deducted from the block grant. A long-term plan, coordinated by the Planning and Development Authority, would list projects at each stage, split funding between national and regional sources, and go to NEDA for inclusion in national plans.
whoIsAffected: Communities in the region awaiting roads, water and flood control.
The Council, the Board and the Planning and Development Authority, which would produce the plan.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Economic and Development Council
Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
whatChanges: A request for a joint plan; no deadline is set and the resolution allocates no money.
readings.insight: The plan's 15 years start in 2023, nearly 2 years before the resolution was adopted, so part of the planning period had already passed. The ₱900,000,000 annual figure for ARMM is given without a year or source. The resolution returns to Section 23 of Article XII of the Organic Law, the 5-year additional development fund, which Resolution 504 had said in October 2024 produced no notable projects. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Philippine National Police and other authorities in the region to act at once and investigate the killing of Baiwan Banog Angan in Sitio Kukor, Barangay Mantao, Datu Hoffer, Maguindanao del Sur.

A copy goes to the PNP and other relevant authorities. Adopted on 11 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Baiwan Banog Angan, a non-Moro Indigenous Peoples leader of the Menubu Dulangan tribe, went fishing in the river with Cita Manguda Angan at about 1:00 PM. Armed men sent Cita home; gunfire followed and Baiwan was killed. The resolution says the attackers allegedly abused him and made him dig his own grave before shooting him. Parliament condemns the killing and wants the perpetrators brought to court.
whoIsAffected: The family of Baiwan Banog Angan.
The Menubu Dulangan community in Maguindanao del Sur.
implementedBy: Philippine National Police
whatChanges: A call on the police to investigate. It asks for no report back to Parliament.
readings.insight: The adopted text dates the killing 7 December 2027, which is after the resolution's own adoption date of 11 February 2025; the error is on the signed document, confirmed on the page image, and the resolution gives no other date. It is shorter than the other killing resolutions adopted the same day (528 and 529): no list of demands and no request for a progress report. One of a long line of resolutions condemning killings in and around the region. Filed by MP Froilyn T. Mendoza.

readings.whatItDoes:
