The resolution points to the Special Development Fund under the Organic Law (₱5,000,000,000 a year for 10 years) and to about ₱500,000,000 the Office of the Chief Minister has set aside for the Marawi Rehabilitation Program.
whoIsAffected: Displaced Marawi families living in temporary shelters on leased private land, at least 1,419 of them served eviction notices
Private landowners in Sagonsongan, Boganga, Dulay, Patani and Rorugagus
The Office of the Chief Minister and the Marawi City government
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Relevant government agencies, unnamed

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It urges the Government of the Day to provide "the required funding" for a 2-year lease extension without estimating what that costs; its WHEREAS clauses cite the roughly ₱500,000,000 Marawi Rehabilitation Program allocation of the Office of the Chief Minister.

whatChanges: A request reaches the Office of the Chief Minister to fund a 2-year extension of the shelter leases.
No amount, deadline or report back to Parliament is set.
readings.insight:
The resolution arrived late against its own facts. The leases expired in early 2023, the eviction date it cites was 15 October 2023, and it was adopted on 17 July 2024, 9 months after that date, still citing 2023 reporting. The text also dates the Marawi mayor's assurance that there would be no evictions to "October 12, 2022" while calling it recent and placing it after the October 2023 notices; the page image confirms the year is printed as 2022.

Marawi is one of the most repeated subjects in the Parliament's resolutions, from compensation for siege victims (Resolutions 14, 33, 151, 156 and 216) to the return of displaced residents (179). Judging by the titles in the index, this is the only one aimed at the land under the temporary shelters, and it names no cost for the extension it asks the regional government to pay for.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the new Shari'ah counselors-at-law who passed the 2024 Shari'ah Bar Examinations, and presents the resolution to the passers for their information.

Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba. Adopted on 23 July 2024, a week after the results came out.
readings.whyProposed: Shari'ah is one of the pillars of the region's justice system under the Organic Law, and a successful examinee earns the title counselor-at-law. The Supreme Court held the first digitalized and regionalized Shari'ah Bar on 28 April and 2 May 2024, at the University of the Philippines Diliman and Ateneo de Davao University. Of 853 examinees, 183 passed, 21.45%, as announced on 16 July 2024 by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh, the exam's chairperson; Supreme Court B.M. No. 4248 approved the formal title Shari'ah Counselor-at-Law.
whoIsAffected: The 183 passers of the 2024 Shari'ah Bar Examinations
whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a commendation sent to the passers.
readings.insight:
The figures check: 183 of 853 is 21.45%. The resolution names no individual passer.

It sits among several Shari'ah-justice measures of 2023 and 2024. Resolution 326 (March 2023) asked the Supreme Court to form a committee on integrating the Shari'ah bar, and Resolution 488, adopted a month after this one, commended the national law creating 3 new Shari'ah judicial districts.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education to include in its programs awareness-raising on the Anti-Hazing Act of 2018 for higher education institutions in the region, and forwards the resolution to the Ministry for information and appropriate action.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 23 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 11053 bans hazing and punishes it as a crime. It was passed after the 2017 hazing death of University of Santo Tomas law student Horacio "Atio" Castillo III, and hazing deaths continued afterwards: the resolution cites Adamson University student John Matthew Salilig, whose body was found in a shallow grave in Imus, Cavite, on 28 February 2023. The resolution argues that hazing persists partly because people do not know the law's prohibitions, and proposes information campaigns, seminars and orientations for college and graduate students.
whoIsAffected: College and graduate students in the region's higher education institutions
Fraternities, sororities and other campus organizations
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
whatChanges: A request reaches the Ministry to add anti-hazing awareness to its programs for higher education institutions.
No deadline, budget or report is attached.
readings.insight: Both cases the resolution cites happened outside the region, in Manila and Cavite. It gives no figure or incident for hazing at Bangsamoro campuses, so the text never shows how big the problem it targets is in the region. It is the only adopted resolution on hazing in the index.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament formally asks the House of Representatives to keep the present 3 Chancellor-Regents on the Mindanao State University Board of Regents in House Bill No. 969, "An Act Strengthening the Mindanao State University and Appropriating Funds Therefor", and forwards the resolution to the House for its consideration.

Filed by MP Eddie M. Alih and 18 others. Adopted on 23 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Under Republic Act No. 1387 as modified in 1986, the MSU Board of Regents has 15 members, 11 of them ex officio, including the chancellors of MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology, MSU General Santos and MSU Tawi-Tawi. House Bill No. 969, filed by Rep. Rufus B. Rodriguez on 1 July 2022 and referred to the House Committee on Higher and Technical Education on 27 July 2022, would replace them with 1 Chancellor-Regent elected by all MSU chancellors for a 1-year term, on a board chaired by the CHED Chairperson. The resolution argues that the 3 chancellors speak for distinct regions and cultural groups (Northern Mindanao, the island provinces of Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, and Southern Mindanao) and that 1 regent cannot.
whoIsAffected: The MSU campuses at Iligan, General Santos and Tawi-Tawi, whose chancellors now sit on the Board
The MSU system's governance
implementedBy: House of Representatives
whatChanges: A statement of Parliament's position goes to the House of Representatives for its consideration.
Parliament has no vote on the bill, so the resolution binds no one.
readings.insight:
The resolution targets a single clause, Section 12(h), in a bill filed 2 years earlier, and backs the existing board over the proposed one. The repository holds no record of what happened to House Bill No. 969 afterwards.

Most MSU entries in the index are commendations. Resolution 501, adopted 3 months later, took MSU's side again, this time against a Legal Education Board order closing its College of Law.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Department of Education to speed up the drafting of the implementing rules and regulations of Republic Act No. 11650, the national law on inclusion and services for learners with disabilities, and presents the resolution to the DepEd Central Office for information.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 23 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 11650, signed on 11 March 2022, requires schools to admit learners with disabilities and to provide them with inclusive services. Section 32 gave DepEd 90 days from effectivity to issue the implementing rules, and required the rules and a roadmap to reach Congress within 6 months and 1 year. The resolution says the rules had still not been released, leaving unclear how schools will identify learners with special needs and who is accountable for discrimination. It cites DSWD Listahanan data from 2019 that an estimated 60% of Filipino children with disabilities were out of school, and Section 59 of the Bangsamoro Education Code, which already provides for inclusive education.
whoIsAffected: Learners with disabilities and their parents
Public and private schools
implementedBy: Department of Education
whatChanges: A request reaches the national Department of Education, sent for information only.
Nothing in the region changes. The Bangsamoro Education Code already sets its own inclusive-education framework.
readings.insight:
By the resolution's own reckoning the deadline was long past: 90 days from a law signed in March 2022, against an adoption date of July 2024, more than 2 years later. Parliament has no authority over DepEd and sent the request "for information".

It is the second resolution on this law. Resolution 372 (20 July 2023) asked the region's own education ministry to explain the law to teachers and administrators.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education to allow religion to be taught to children in public elementary and secondary schools in the region during regular class hours, and forwards the resolution to the Ministry for information and appropriate action.

Filed by MP Susana S. Anayatin. Adopted on 23 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The 1987 Constitution (Article XIV, Section 3(3)) allows religion to be taught in public schools during class hours if parents or guardians opt in writing. The instructors must be designated or approved by the children's religious authorities, at no additional cost to the government. DepEd Order No. 49, s. 2009 sets out how this works and provides sanctions for principals, school heads and teachers who violate it. In its WHEREAS clauses the resolution "advises" the Ministry to promote such teaching without discrimination between religions, with parental consent, and to discipline school officials who willfully violate the order.
whoIsAffected: Children in public elementary and secondary schools and their parents
School principals, heads and teachers
Religious instructors
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
whatChanges: A request reaches the Ministry to allow religious instruction in class hours on the terms the Constitution already sets.
No new rule is made. The arrangement already exists under the Constitution and DepEd Order No. 49, s. 2009.
readings.insight: The resolution asks the Ministry to allow something the Constitution already permits and a 2009 national order already regulates. It names no school, division or incident where religious instruction was refused, so the text does not show what practice it is correcting. The disciplinary point appears only in a WHEREAS clause; the RESOLVED clause just says "allow".

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim and the Ministry of Science and Technology, led by Minister and Member of Parliament Engr. Aida M. Silongan, for the Bangsamoro Assistance for Science Education (BASE) and similar scholarships. It also congratulates the first BASE batch (2020), who graduated in academic year 2023-2024, some with Latin honors.

It names 19 graduates with honors: 2 summa cum laude (Aiman A. Candidato, BS Biology, MSU-Marawi, and Schweitzer Quero, BS Forestry, Tawi-Tawi State College), 4 magna cum laude and 13 cum laude, from Cotabato City (3), Maguindanao (1), Lanao del Sur (6), Basilan (1), Sulu (1) and Tawi-Tawi (7). Copies go to the Chief Minister, the Ministry and the honor graduates. Filed by MP Baileng S. Mantawil, MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and MP Mary Ann M. Arnado. Adopted on 25 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The first cohort of the Ministry's flagship science scholarship had graduated, and several of them with honors. The resolution records the program's reach: 714 BASE scholars across the first 4 batches, 208 on BASE MERIT, 444 on the Mujahideen/Mujahidat Assistance for Science Education scholarship, and 400 with the BASE scholarship. A BASE grant pays ₱80,000 per scholar per year.
whoIsAffected: The 19 BASE graduates with Latin honors
BASE and other Ministry of Science and Technology scholars

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It records the BASE benefit as ₱80,000 per scholar per year.

whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a commendation, with copies sent to the officials and graduates named.
readings.insight:
The Parliament is commending a ministry headed by one of its own sitting Members. Minister Silongan is not among the 3 authors.

The scholarship figures do not reconcile as printed: 714 BASE scholars across 4 batches, and separately 400 "with the BASE scholarship", with no explanation of how the 2 numbers relate. The resolution lists who graduated with honors but not how many of the first batch graduated at all, so a completion rate cannot be worked out from it.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the concerned ministries, offices and agencies, the Philippine National Police and the Philippine Army to protect the residents and property of Barangays Kusiong, Linek, Mompong and Badak in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, and nearby areas against armed attacks and harassment by an unidentified group. It also urges them to protect the rights of the displaced and to give them assistance.

The resolution is forwarded to those bodies for information and appropriate consideration. Filed by MP Susana S. Anayatin. Adopted on 25 July 2024.
readings.whyProposed: On 24 July 2024 armed conflict broke out in the coastal barangays of Datu Odin Sinsuat, forcing residents to flee their homes. The resolution asks for tighter security, relocation options and assistance for the displaced.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Kusiong, Linek, Mompong and Badak, Datu Odin Sinsuat, and those displaced from them
implementedBy: Philippine National Police
Philippine Army
Concerned Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies, unnamed
whatChanges: An appeal reaches the police, the army and unnamed regional agencies.
No ministry is named, and no report or deadline is set.
readings.insight:
Parliament adopted this a day after the fighting began, which is fast for a resolution. That speed shows in the text: it has a single factual WHEREAS clause, no casualty or displacement figures, and no named ministry.

Datu Odin Sinsuat comes back in later resolutions. Resolution 544 (April 2025) condemned the killing of the town's COMELEC election officer and her husband.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament condemns the killing of South Upi Vice Mayor Roldan M. Benito and his companion Weng Marcos, and the wounding of others, and urges the Bangsamoro Government's concerned agencies to investigate immediately, thoroughly and impartially.

It also says the Special Investigation Task Group organized by the Philippine National Police should be directed to investigate the killing and report to Parliament through the Committee on Public Order and Safety. Copies go to the Task Group, Police Regional Office BAR and the South Upi Municipal Police Station "for information and compliance". The resolution consolidates 2 proposed resolutions, P.P. Res. Nos. 615 and 616. Filed by MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., MP Michael E. Midtimbang and MP Froilyn T. Mendoza. Adopted on 19 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: On 2 August 2024 an ambush in Sitio Linao, Barangay Pandan, South Upi, Maguindanao del Sur, killed the Vice Mayor and Weng Marcos and wounded the barangay chairperson of Pandan and others. Benito was a non-Moro Indigenous Peoples leader of the Téduray community who defended their ancestral domain, the fusaka inged. The resolution calls the killing the latest in an unexplained series in the region.
whoIsAffected: The families of Roldan M. Benito and Weng Marcos and those wounded
The Téduray community of South Upi
implementedBy: PNP Special Investigation Task Group
Police Regional Office BAR
South Upi Municipal Police Station
Bangsamoro Government agencies concerned with public order
whatChanges: A request reaches the police to investigate, along with a request for a report to Parliament's Committee on Public Order and Safety.
No deadline is set for that report.
readings.insight:
Unlike most condemnations, this one asks for a report back to a named committee of Parliament. The body it "directs", though, is a national police task group that Parliament does not command, and no deadline is attached.

The resolution itself calls this the latest in a series, and the index bears that out. Earlier condemnations of killings include Resolutions 387 (Dr. Marivic Tello), 434 (the ambush of Dr. Sharmaine Ceballos Barroquillo) and 450 (Christhia Angela Aragoncillo). Resolution 276 (October 2022) had already ordered the same committee to inquire into the series of killings in Maguindanao, Pikit and the Special Geographic Area.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament congratulates and commends Mohammad Nur Casib of the Philippine Science High School-Central Mindanao Campus. At the 1st International Nuclear Science Olympiad he won gold, was the highest scorer and was named Nuclear Ambassador.

The resolution is presented to his family and his school. It consolidates 3 proposed resolutions, P.P. Res. Nos. 617, 619 and 621. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, MP Suharto S. Esmael, MP Aida M. Silongan, MP Amroussi A. Macatanong, MP Marjanie S. Macasalong and MP Diamila D. Ramos. Adopted on 19 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Philippines hosted the first International Nuclear Science Olympiad from 1 to 6 August 2024 at New Clark City, with 55 contenders, 27 team leaders and 14 observers from 14 Asia-Pacific countries. As a member of the Philippine team, Casib won gold and special awards for the highest points in both the experimental and theoretical exams, and took the top overall score.
whoIsAffected: Mohammad Nur Casib, his family and the Philippine Science High School-Central Mindanao Campus
whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a commendation presented to the honoree's family and school.
readings.insight: It is the second time Parliament has honored the same student. Resolution 389 (15 August 2023) congratulated Mohammad Nur Guma-os Casib of Lanao del Sur for a bronze medal at the International Chemistry Olympiad in Zurich. 3 separate proposed resolutions were filed for this single achievement. 3 days later Resolution 494 moved commendations out of the resolution process and into a speech slot in plenary.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament congratulates and commends gymnast Carlos Edriel Poquiz Yulo for winning 2 gold medals at the 2024 Paris Olympics, and the other Filipino medalists, and presents the resolution to them.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 19 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Yulo, 24, from Malate, Manila, won the men's floor exercise and the vault on 3 and 4 August 2024, averaging 15.166 on vault (15.433 and 14.800), and became the country's first double Olympic gold medalist. Boxers Nesthy Petecio and Aira Villegas won bronze in the women's 57-kg and 50-kg divisions, and the 4 medals made the Philippines the best Southeast Asian team for the second Games in a row. The resolution lists Yulo's earlier world, Asian, SEA Games and World Cup medals.
whoIsAffected: Carlos Edriel Poquiz Yulo, Nesthy Petecio and Aira Villegas
whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a commendation presented to the medalists.
readings.insight: None of the 3 honorees has a Bangsamoro connection stated in the text. The resolution says itself that the Parliament "has frequently recognized outstanding Filipino athletes", and it has: Resolutions 144 and 148 (August 2021) honored the Tokyo medalists, Petecio among them, so she has now been commended twice.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recognizes the contributions of the late Commissioner Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic to the Bangsamoro people and conveys its deepest condolences to his family, to whom the resolution is presented.

Filed by MP Diamila D. Ramos. Adopted on 20 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Marohomsalic, born on 21 July 1955 in Lumba-Bayabao, Lanao del Sur, died on 6 July 2024 at the Philippine Heart Center. The resolution traces a long public career. At 33, in 1988, he sat on the Regional Consultative Commission that drafted the first ARMM Organic Act (Republic Act No. 6734). He became a Commissioner on Human Rights in 1994. He held national posts in the Integrated Bar from 2007 to 2017 and founded the Muslim Legal Assistance Foundation in 2005. He sat on the panel of independent lawyers that helped draft parts of the Bangsamoro Basic Law in 2014. He intervened before the Supreme Court to defend both the 2008 Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain and, in January 2019, the Bangsamoro Organic Law. He became a Commissioner of the National Amnesty Commission on 20 February 2023. His books include "Aristocrats of the Malay Race" (2001) and the novel "Maratabat".
whoIsAffected: The family of the late Commissioner Nasser A. Marohomsalic
whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a tribute and condolence presented to the family.
readings.insight:
Unusually for a condolence resolution, this one records the deceased's work on the legal foundations of the region: the first Organic Act's drafting commission, the panel that helped draft the Bangsamoro Basic Law, and 2 Supreme Court defenses of the peace agreements.

2 days later Resolution 492 commended his daughter, Atty. Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic, for her admission as counsel before the International Criminal Court, an achievement this resolution already mentions.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., the Senate and the House of Representatives for enacting Republic Act No. 12018, which amends Articles 138, 147 and 150 of the Code of Muslim Personal Laws to create 3 more Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 more Shari'ah circuit courts. The resolution is presented to the Office of the President, the Senate and the House.

Filed by MP Diamila D. Ramos and 59 others. Adopted on 20 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Shari'ah courts under Presidential Decree No. 1083 (1977) sat only in certain Mindanao provinces and cities, so Muslims elsewhere had no access to them. The new law came from Senate Bill No. 2594 (approved by the Senate on 12 August 2024) and House Bill No. 8257 (approved on 14 August 2023). The 6th district covers Bukidnon, Misamis Oriental, Misamis Occidental, Camiguin, Cagayan de Oro and the Davao and Caraga regions. The 7th covers Western, Eastern and Central Visayas. The 8th covers Metro Manila, the Cordillera and the Luzon regions down to MIMAROPA. Circuit courts rise from 51 to 63: 5 new in the 6th district, 3 in the 7th and 4 in the 8th.
whoIsAffected: Muslim Filipinos living outside the existing Shari'ah court areas
Shari'ah counselors-at-law, whose courts of practice expand
whatChanges: Nothing changes because of the resolution. The courts were created by the national law it commends.
readings.insight: The arithmetic is consistent: 5, 3 and 4 make the 12 new circuit courts, and 51 plus 12 gives 63. 60 Members signed it as authors. The resolution follows Resolution 477, which a month earlier commended the 2024 Shari'ah Bar passers, who will practice before these courts.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts a dress code for its Members. During regular or special sessions, men wear the Barong Tagalog or a coat and tie; women wear a Filipina dress or modest business attire; and traditional Filipino dress, including modest traditional Bangsamoro attire, is allowed for all. Parliament provides robes, which are compulsory in plenary sessions, and Members must wear their issued Parliament pins. The Speaker may order a different dress code for a particular occasion.

Violations are punished in steps. A first offense brings a written notice from the Office of the Speaker. On a second, the Member is considered absent, and any action they raise in plenary has no effect and is not recorded. A third offense is referred to the Committee on Ethics and Privileges. That Committee oversees the code, settles disputes and reviews it periodically. The code takes effect immediately and stays in force until replaced. Filed by MP Hatimil E. Hassan and 13 others. Adopted on 21 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law lets Parliament adopt its own rules, and the Rules (Adopted Resolution No. 268) already require decorum and conduct that reflects the honor of the Parliament. The authors argue that clear attire standards are part of upholding that dignity, and cite the duty of public officials under Republic Act No. 6713 to live modestly.
whoIsAffected: Members of the Parliament
implementedBy: Committee on Ethics and Privileges
Office of the Speaker

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It says parliamentary robes "shall be provided by the Parliament" without stating a cost.

whatChanges: Binding on Members from adoption: a prescribed session attire, compulsory robes in plenary, and Parliament pins.
A graduated sanction: a written notice, then being marked absent with the Member's floor actions voided, then referral to the Ethics Committee.
readings.insight:
This one has teeth because it binds Parliament itself. The second-offense penalty goes beyond dress: a Member marked absent loses the effect of anything they raise on the floor that day, so a dress violation can cost them their participation in that sitting.

It was adopted together with Resolution 491, the companion code for staff and visitors. The authors are the same, except that MP Eddie M. Alih signed this one and not that one.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts an "Efficient Use of Paper Rule". It applies to Parliament, its committees and offices, and to every Bangsamoro ministry, office and agency when they write or submit to Parliament. Bills, resolutions, reports and letters must be single-spaced with 1.5 spaces between paragraphs, in 12-point type, printed on both sides of legal-size paper (13 by 8.5 inches). Formal correspondence uses A4. Margins are fixed at 1.5 inches left, 1.2 top and 1.0 right and bottom, and every page must be numbered.

Documents are filed in 2 original copies only, plus a PDF e-mailed to the receiving office. Members no longer receive individual printed copies of session materials. Only printed copies of the Order of Business are provided in the session hall, everything else is e-mailed, and Members print what they need themselves. The rule takes effect immediately. Filed by MP Mary Ann M. Arnado. Adopted on 21 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The WHEREAS clauses argue the environmental case against paper: they say paper use has grown 400% in 40 years and that over 2,000,000 trees are cut every day to supply it, without citing a source, and they point to the pollution from pulp and paper mills. The Bangsamoro Government should cut its own use as a first step on climate change.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament and the Secretariat
Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies that submit documents to Parliament
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Parliament and its Secretariat
Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies submitting to Parliament
whatChanges: Binding format and filing rules for documents submitted to Parliament: 2 originals plus a PDF.
An end to individual printed packets for Members at sessions.
readings.insight:
This is a working rule rather than a request, and it reaches the executive too: ministries must follow its format when they submit to Parliament. It sets no penalty for non-compliance.

It sits awkwardly with Resolution 494, adopted the next day, which rewrote the Order of Business rule to say that each Member "shall be furnished with a printed copy of the Order of Business". This rule says only that printed copies of the Order of Business will be available in the session hall.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts a dress code for parliamentary staff and visitors during sessions. They must wear formal, business, smart-casual or modest cultural attire. The Secretariat, legislative pages and security staff wear their uniforms with visible identification cards, and Members' staff and visitors, caterers included, get temporary visible IDs. The code bans 10 kinds of clothing: distressed jeans, slippers, noisy footwear, miniskirts or shorts above the knee, plunging necklines, neon colors, caps or hats other than religious or cultural headwear, sleeveless garments, leggings, and clothing with offensive text or images.

Anyone who does not comply is refused entry to the session hall. The Office of the Secretary-General may allow a seasonal dress code in the hottest months, staff with heat-sensitive medical conditions may apply for exemptions with a medical certificate, and Parliament is to consult health professionals on heat-appropriate wear. The Office of the Secretary-General, the Protocol and Decorum Division and the Sergeant-at-Arms enforce it. The code takes effect immediately and stays in force until replaced. Filed by MP Hatimil E. Hassan and 12 others. Adopted on 21 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Rules let the Speaker protect Parliament from annoyance by non-Members and remove them from the plenary. The authors argue that the dignity of the Parliament calls for clear attire standards for everyone present in the building during sessions, not just Members.
whoIsAffected: Parliamentary staff, including Members' staff
Visitors and caterers present during sessions
implementedBy: Office of the Secretary-General
Protocol and Decorum Division
Sergeant-at-Arms
whatChanges: Binding attire rules and a list of 10 banned items for anyone in the session hall.
Denial of entry as the only sanction, with seasonal and medical exceptions.
readings.insight:
The 2 dress codes adopted that day treat insiders and outsiders differently. Members (Resolution 489) get a warning first and graduated penalties; staff and visitors are simply refused entry. The staff code also builds in a hot-season relaxation and medical exemptions, which the Members' code does not.

The text calls the required IDs "Anti-Red Tape Authority (ARTA) identification cards" without explaining why a national agency's name is attached to the Parliament's passes.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends and congratulates Atty. Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic on her admission as counsel before the International Criminal Court, which makes her the first Bangsamoro, the first Filipina and the 5th Filipino lawyer on the list. The resolution is to be presented to her personally or by mail.

Filed by MP Khalid M. Hadji Abdullah. Adopted on 22 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Counsel must be admitted to the ICC's list before they can represent defendants, victims or witnesses, and admission depends on experience and litigation skill. According to the resolution, as of early 2024 only 4 Filipino lawyers had been admitted: Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, Charles Janzen Chua and Herminio Harry L. Roque. Marohomsalic is a Meranao lawyer from Lanao del Sur and a member of the Integrated Bar's Lanao del Sur chapter.
whoIsAffected: Atty. Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic
whatChanges: Nothing outside Parliament changes. The resolution is a commendation presented to the honoree.
readings.insight: 2 days earlier, Resolution 487 mourned her father, Commissioner Nasser A. Marohomsalic, and already mentioned her ICC admission in its WHEREAS clauses. This resolution was adopted the same day as Resolution 494, which moved such commendations into a speech slot in plenary.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament resolves to adhere to Executive Order No. 64, s. 2024, the President's order updating the salary schedule for civilian government personnel and authorizing an additional allowance. The resolution is furnished to all persons and entities concerned for their information.

Filed by MP Ubaida C. Pacasem and MP Jose I. Lorena. Adopted on 22 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: President Marcos Jr. issued Executive Order No. 64 on 2 August 2024. It raises salaries and adds a medical allowance for civilian personnel in all branches and in local governments, but excludes military and uniformed personnel and contract-of-service and job-order workers. DBM's National Budget Circular No. 594 covers the first tranche. Under the Organic Law, the region follows the national compensation system of Republic Act No. 6758, and its Personal Services spending may not exceed 45% of its total revenue. The resolution points to the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund in the 2024 Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act for salary deficiencies, and says the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management shall issue guidelines for the first tranche.
whoIsAffected: Civilian personnel of the Bangsamoro Government
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. Its WHEREAS clauses point to the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund of the 2024 Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act for salary deficiencies, without estimating the cost, and recall the 45% ceiling on Personal Services spending.

whatChanges: Parliament puts on record that the region follows the national salary update of Executive Order No. 64.
The guidelines are left to the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, which is named only in a WHEREAS clause and given no deadline.
readings.insight: The operative clause says only "to adhere"; it directs no one. The practical work, the guidelines and the payments, rests with the finance ministry, which appears only in the WHEREAS clauses. The resolution raises the 45% ceiling on Personal Services spending but gives no estimate of what the increase costs or how close the region is to that ceiling. It was adopted 20 days after the executive order.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends Rule VIII of its Rules (Adopted Resolution No. 268) to set a fixed slot in each session for recognitions, commendations and condolences. The daily Order of Business now has a new item for "Recognitions, Commendations, Memorials, and Messages and Communications", right after the approval of the previous journal. A Chief Minister's Hour follows the roll call on the first Wednesday of every quarter.

Members who want to give a recognition or commendation notify the Floor Leader's office at least 3 calendar days before the session and get at most 3 minutes to speak. The Floor Leader may move to amend the Order of Business to fit in requests made before a session starts. The Order of Business is posted on the Parliament's website and e-mailed to Members, as far as practicable 3 calendar days ahead. The amendment takes effect immediately. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and 14 others. Adopted on 22 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Many of the resolutions Members filed honored achievements or offered condolences, and each one went through the full process of interpellation and amendment in plenary. The authors call that time-consuming, and propose giving Members speaking time "rather than having the members file it as a resolution".
whoIsAffected: Members of the Parliament
The Floor Leader and the Secretariat, who manage the Order of Business
implementedBy: Office of the Floor Leader
Secretariat of the Parliament
whatChanges: A binding change to Parliament's own Rules: a standing slot in the Order of Business for recognitions and condolences, with 3-minute speeches on 3 days' notice.
A quarterly Chief Minister's Hour is written into the Order of Business.
readings.insight:
This rule worked, and the index shows it. In the 12 months before it, 47 of the 102 adopted resolutions open as congratulations, commendations, recognitions or condolences. Of the 84 adopted after it, through June 2026, only 4 do (Resolutions 561, 569, 573 and 574), and all 4 honor national officials involved in the peace process or intergovernmental relations. Commendations of student achievers, athletes and board passers stopped altogether.

The rule did not ban such resolutions; it gave Members another way to do the same thing. A small drafting gap: the heading of Section 2 mentions extending condolences, but its text covers only recognition and commendation.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Office of the Secretary-General to set up a picture gallery of the Members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament and display it in a conspicuous place in the Parliament building. Copies go to all Members, ministers, deputy ministers and the Office of the Chief Minister for information.

Filed by MP Suharto S. Esmael and 7 others. Adopted on 28 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The authors want to mark the transition period in the Parliament's history and honor its Members' contributions. They cite the 5 priority codes the Parliament enacted: the Administrative Code (BAA 13), the Civil Service Code (BAA 17), the Education Code (BAA 18), the Electoral Code (BAA 35) and the Local Governance Code (BAA 49). They also praise the working relationship among Members regardless of affiliation.
whoIsAffected: Members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
The Office of the Secretary-General
implementedBy: Office of the Secretary-General

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing and does not state what the gallery would cost.

whatChanges: A request to Parliament's own Secretariat to create and display a gallery of Members' pictures.
No deadline or cost is set.
readings.insight: It is a resolution by Members about honoring Members, addressed to their own Secretariat. Unlike most requests adopted around the same time, it is one Parliament can carry out itself. It sets no budget or timeline.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Office of the Secretary-General to devise a mechanism for tracking how the ministries, offices, local governments and other stakeholders concerned implement the resolutions Parliament adopts, and to report that status to Parliament every quarter.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 28 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: According to the BARMM Government's website, the Parliament had adopted 444 resolutions as of 29 February 2024, with hundreds more pending. There was no institutional way to know whether any of them were acted on. The authors do not want measures "with noble intentions" to stay stuck on paper.
whoIsAffected: The Office of the Secretary-General
Ministries, offices, local governments and others addressed by adopted resolutions
implementedBy: Office of the Secretary-General
whatChanges: A standing duty for Parliament's Secretariat: build a tracking mechanism and report quarterly on implementation of adopted resolutions.
No deadline is set for building the mechanism, and the offices being tracked are not required to answer.
readings.insight:
The figure checks against the index: Resolution 444 was adopted on 29 February 2024. The resolution names a real gap. Requests adopted in the same months, like Resolutions 476, 478, 497, 498, 502 and 503 go out with no deadline, no reporting duty and no follow-up.

The direction binds Parliament's own Secretariat and sets a quarterly cadence. It does not oblige the ministries or local governments to report anything, and it gives the Secretariat no date by which the mechanism must exist.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Civil Service Commission's BARMM regional office to devise a way to give everyone the opportunity to take the Civil Service Examination, and forwards the resolution to it for information.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 28 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The exam is given twice a year, applications must be filed in person, and filing closes once a field office's quota is reached. The pandemic cut testing-room capacity in a region that already had few test centers. At a Committee on Rules meeting on 8 April 2024 Parliament learned that the region gets fewer exam slots than other regions, and that CSC-BARMM is classed as a "small organization" with limited capacity. The resolution argues that a new autonomous government needs thousands of eligible civil servants. It suggests more testing centers, priority for local residents, a review of the CSC's structure in the region and more exam slots for BARMM.
whoIsAffected: People working in or seeking jobs with the Bangsamoro Government who lack civil service eligibility
CSC-BARMM
implementedBy: Civil Service Commission - BARMM
whatChanges: A request reaches CSC-BARMM, sent for information only.
No deadline or report is set.
readings.insight: The central complaint, that the region gets fewer exam slots than other regions, is stated without numbers, so the gap cannot be measured from the text. The fixes it lists, such as more slots and a bigger regional office, are decisions for the Civil Service Commission nationally rather than the regional office it writes to. The resolution itself acknowledges the Commission is an independent constitutional body.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges all government ministries, offices and agencies in the region, including local governments, to set up lactation stations in their offices for women employees and clients, as Republic Act No. 10028, the Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act of 2009, requires. It calls on the Ministry of Health to give technical help so that the stations meet the law's standards.

The resolution is furnished to all government agencies and offices in BARMM "for their information, compliance, and necessary action". Filed by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen. Adopted on 28 August 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Breastfeeding protects infant health, the Shari'ah recommends a 2-year lactation period, and the resolution cites government data that 45% of the region's children under 5 were stunted as of 2023, one of the highest rates in the country. Republic Act No. 10028 already requires lactation stations in government offices and other establishments. The resolution notes that the 5% Gender and Development budget may be used to build and maintain them.
whoIsAffected: Women employees and clients of government offices in the region who are nursing
Ministries, offices, agencies and local governments
implementedBy: All Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies
Local government units
Ministry of Health

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It notes that the 5% Gender and Development budget may be allocated to build, repair and maintain lactation stations.

whatChanges: An appeal to every government office in the region to comply with an existing national law, and a request to the Ministry of Health for technical help.
No deadline, inventory or report is required.
readings.insight: Lactation stations are already a legal requirement under a 2009 national law, so the resolution urges compliance rather than creating anything new. It does not say how many offices lack a station. On 14 October 2024 Resolution 500 made the companion request for child-minding centers in government workplaces.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the 19th Congress to pass a law creating a province, to be named Kutawato, out of the 8 municipalities of the Special Geographic Area: Pahamuddin, Kadayangan, Nabalawag, Old Kaabakan, Kapalawan, Malidegao, Tugunan and Ligawasan. The resolution goes to the Speaker of the House and the Senate President, with copies to the Office of the President and the Philippine Congress-Bangsamoro Parliament Forum.

Filed by MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr. and 12 others. Adopted in special session on 27 September 2024.
readings.whyProposed: 63 barangays of Carmen, Kabacan, Midsayap, Pigcawayan, Pikit and Aleosan in Cotabato province voted to join the region in the plebiscite of 6 February 2019. Parliament organized them into 8 municipalities through BAA Nos. 41 to 48 (17 August 2023), voters ratified them on 13 April 2024, and the Chief Minister appointed officers-in-charge on 13 July 2024. Having left Cotabato province, the area could not vote for a House member, governor or provincial board in 2022, and it has no province to supervise its towns. Under Section 461 of the Local Government Code, a new province needs an average annual income of ₱20,000,000 plus either 2,000 km² of territory or 250,000 people. The 8 towns have ₱282,609,928 in income, 814.7555 km² and 215,433 people. The resolution concedes they miss some requirements, and cites Biliran and Dinagat Islands as provinces Congress created below the thresholds.
whoIsAffected: The 215,433 residents of the 8 Special Geographic Area municipalities
Cotabato province, from which the area came
implementedBy: Congress of the Philippines
whatChanges: A request reaches Congress, which alone can create a province.
Nothing changes unless Congress passes a law and the province is ratified in a plebiscite.
readings.insight:
By the resolution's own figures, the area clears the income test by a wide margin, 14 times the minimum, but meets neither alternative. Its land area is about 41% of the 2,000 km² required and its population about 86% of the 250,000. The case therefore rests on the Biliran and Dinagat precedents, the second of which the Supreme Court upheld in Navarro v. Ermita.

The population figure, 215,433, is the same one BAA 58 used to place the whole Special Geographic Area in a single parliamentary district.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament encourages the ministries, agencies and offices in the region to set up child-minding centers in their workplaces or somewhere easy to reach from them, and forwards the resolution to all of them, local governments included, for information.

Filed by MP Abdullah B. Hashim. Adopted on 14 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 11861, the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act, recognizes how hard it is for solo parents to balance work and child care. Its revised implementing rules have DOLE and the Civil Service Commission promote child-minding centers. National agencies with more than 300 employees, and private employers with 200 or more, may set up free centers for employees' children aged 7 and below, with priority for solo parents. The resolution argues that such centers improve performance, reduce absenteeism, and could also give clients a safe place for their children while they do business in government offices.
whoIsAffected: Government employees in the region with children aged 7 and below, solo parents first
Clients who bring children to government offices
implementedBy: Bangsamoro ministries, agencies and offices
Local government units
whatChanges: Encouragement only, sent for information; no office is required to do anything.
No deadline, budget or report is set.
readings.insight: "Encourage" is the weakest verb in the Parliament's range, and the national rules it cites are permissive too: agencies "may" set up centers. The resolution gives no count of Bangsamoro offices large enough to meet the 300-employee mark. It follows Resolution 498 (28 August 2024) on lactation stations, another measure about government offices as workplaces for parents.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its strong support for the Mindanao State University College of Law continuing to provide legal education to the Bangsamoro people, and forwards the resolution to the Supreme Court, the Senate, the House of Representatives, the Legal Education Board and the MSU Board of Regents.

Filed by MP Marjanie S. Macasalong and 19 others. Adopted on 15 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Legal Education Board, citing non-compliance with its requirements, issued Resolution No. 231-18 cancelling the accreditation of the MSU College of Law and ordering its program closed on all campuses from academic year 2025-2026. MSU argues that the Board has no jurisdiction over it. The college was created by the MSU Board of Regents in 1981 under the university charter, 12 years before Republic Act No. 7662 created the Board in 1993. That law covered only law schools then under the education department, and its legislative record shows chartered state universities were not meant to be covered. The resolution cites the Board's own 10-year report, which shows the college produced 422 lawyers from 2011 to 2020, the most of any law school in the region.
whoIsAffected: Students and prospective students of the MSU College of Law, especially those who cannot study elsewhere
The MSU system and its Board of Regents
The Legal Education Board
whatChanges: A statement of support reaches the courts, Congress, the Legal Education Board and the MSU Board of Regents.
It asks none of them to do anything specific and binds no one.
readings.insight:
Parliament takes a side in a jurisdictional dispute between a national regulator and a chartered university without asking any party to act. It sets out MSU's legal argument in full but does not engage with the compliance findings behind the Board's order.

The college is a familiar name in the index. Resolutions 243 (June 2022) and 337 (May 2023) commended it, alongside Notre Dame University, for producing 94 and then 46 new Bangsamoro lawyers.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Office of the Chief Minister and the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education to devise a mechanism that rewards families with at least 3 high school or college students, so that the students finish their schooling. The resolution is forwarded to both offices for information.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 15 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: According to a World Bank article the resolution cites, only 1 in 10 students in BARMM who start primary school complete junior high school on time, and out-of-school youth and adults make up 45%, double the national average. CHED figures show 42,709 students in the region's state universities and colleges getting free higher education in academic year 2020-2021. Tertiary Education Subsidy grantees grew from 10,965 in 2018-2019 to 17,967 in 2019-2020 and 19,876 in 2021-2022. The authors argue that, on top of scholarships, families with several children in school need an incentive to keep sending them.
whoIsAffected: Families with 3 or more children in high school or college in the region
The Office of the Chief Minister and the education ministry
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing and does not say what the incentive would be or cost.

whatChanges: A request to the Chief Minister's office and the education ministry to design an incentive, sent for information.
No form, amount, deadline or report is specified.
readings.insight: The only eligibility rule is a headcount: 3 or more students in BARMM institutions. The WHEREAS clauses say the aim is to help families facing "significant financial challenges", but there is no income test, so as written a well-off family with 3 students would qualify and a poor family with 2 would not. Its newest figure is from academic year 2021-2022, 2 years before adoption.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Madaris Education arm of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education to set up a Madrasah and Markadz Database Management System, and furnishes the resolution to the Ministry's Director General for Madaris Education for consideration and appropriate action.

Filed by MP Abdullah E. Gayak, MP Romeo K. Sema and MP Eddie M. Alih. Adopted on 15 October 2024.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law tells Parliament to develop and strengthen the Madaris system. The resolution describes the database as a tool to list every madrasah with its students and asatidz and to monitor its progress. It would encourage unregistered madaris to register so they qualify for priority assistance and quality programs, and serve as a base for research. The authors add that monitoring would help prevent madaris being misused to foster violent extremism.
whoIsAffected: Madaris in the region, especially unregistered ones
Madrasah students and asatidz
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education - Madaris Education
whatChanges: A request to the Ministry's Madaris office to build a registry and monitoring database.
No deadline, budget or report is set.
readings.insight:
The text is unclear whether the system already exists. The WHEREAS clauses describe it in the present tense (it "is designed", it "includes" lists of madaris, students and asatidz), while the RESOLVED clause urges the Ministry to establish it. It gives no count of registered or unregistered madaris.

Its justification contrasts with an earlier stance. In Resolution 94 (November 2020) the Parliament asked the Armed Forces to be careful in their statements about the madaris, warning that such statements could alienate Muslims. This resolution itself cites preventing the misuse of madaris for violent extremism as a reason for monitoring them.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education (MBHTE) to require that notices of government-funded education scholarships be posted in designated prominent areas of every academic institution in the region. A copy goes to the MBHTE for information and appropriate action.

The resolution sets no deadline, prescribes no format for the notices and does not list which scholarships are covered beyond 'government-funded'. Adopted on 13 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Scholarship announcements, the resolution says, mostly circulate on social media, so students in remote areas with little or no internet access miss them and funds may not reach their intended beneficiaries. It cites the Bangsamoro Education Code (BAA 18): Section 9's principle that those who have less in life should receive more in educational opportunities, and Section 14, which lets the MBHTE Minister issue the rules needed to carry out the ministry's programs. Filed by MP Jamel B. Macacua.
whoIsAffected: Students across the region, especially in areas with limited internet access
Schools, colleges and other academic institutions that would have to post the notices
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
whatChanges: Nothing binding: the resolution asks the MBHTE to issue a posting requirement, which only the ministry can do under Section 14 of BAA 18.
A copy is sent to the MBHTE for appropriate action.
readings.insight:
The fix requested is cheap and specific: a physical notice in every school alongside online announcements. Whether it happens depends entirely on the MBHTE issuing a rule, and the resolution gives no deadline and asks for no report back. A WHEREAS clause speaks of students 'within post-secondary educational institutions' while the RESOLVED clause covers 'all academic institutions', so the intended reach is not fully settled in the text.

Filed on 30 August 2024 as Proposed Resolution No. 629, it was adopted on Committee Report No. 105 of the Committee on Basic, Higher, and Technical Education about 5 months later.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Government of the Philippines and Moro Islamic Liberation Front peace implementing panels to fast-track the deployment of the Joint Peace and Security Team, especially in areas where peace and order are disturbed. The resolution is forwarded to both panels for information and appropriate action.

Adopted on 13 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The trigger was an attack in Talayan, Maguindanao del Sur. On the night of 26 July 2023 armed men stormed a Teduray tribal enclave in Sitio Nunagen, on the border of Barangays Blanting and Marader, burning houses and the tribal worship hall. At least 114 non-Moro Teduray fled and were temporarily relocated to Barangay Biarong, South Upi, leaving their livestock and harvestable rice and corn behind. The resolution cites the Organic Law's commitment to the rights of non-Moro indigenous peoples. Filed by MP Ramon A. Piang Sr., MP Eddie M. Alih and MP Albakil D. Jikiri.
whoIsAffected: The displaced Teduray community of Sitio Nunagen, Talayan
Communities in areas where peace and order are disturbed
implementedBy: Government of the Philippines peace implementing panel
Moro Islamic Liberation Front peace implementing panel
whatChanges: No binding effect: it asks the 2 peace panels to speed up a deployment that they control.
Copies go to both panels.
readings.insight:
The proposal began narrower and more concrete. Proposed Resolution No. 412, filed on 15 September 2023, asked the Inter-Agency Task Force and the Joint Peace Security Task Force to set up a joint military station at Sitio Nunagen itself. It was adopted 17 months later 'as amended', on Committee Report No. 129, in a general form that names no place: deploy the Joint Peace and Security Team wherever peace and order are disturbed.

By adoption the attack was more than 18 months old. The community that prompted the resolution appears only in its WHEREAS clauses, and the text does not say whether the 114 displaced Teduray had returned home.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament honors and pays tribute to former Senator Dr. Santanina 'Nina' Tillah Rasul for her contributions to women's empowerment, the peace process and autonomy. It encourages the MBHTE, the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and other relevant offices to continue her advocacy against adult illiteracy through targeted literacy programs.

Copies go to her family as an expression of condolence, and to the 2 ministries and other offices for appropriate consideration and action. Adopted on 17 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Senator Rasul, born in Siasi, Sulu on 14 September 1930, died on 28 November 2024 at 94. The resolution records her as the first Muslim woman in the Philippine Senate (1987 to 1995) and the first Muslim senator re-elected; sponsor of laws including Republic Act No. 6949, declaring 8 March National Women's Day, and Republic Act No. 7165, creating the Literacy Coordinating Council; a member of the government panel that negotiated the peace agreement with the MNLF; and founder in 1991 of the Magbassa Kita Foundation, whose Literacy for Peace and Development program reached over 67,000 neo-literate adults in 4 years, 85% of them women. It ties the tribute to the region's literacy gap: a basic literacy rate of 78.7% in the 2019 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey, the lowest of any region, against a national average of 94%. Filed by MP Diamila D. Ramos, MP Eddie M. Alih, MP Hatimil E. Hassan and MP Susana S. Anayatin.
whoIsAffected: Senator Rasul's family
Adults in the region who cannot read or write
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education
Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs
whatChanges: A tribute entered in Parliament's record and a copy sent to the family.
An encouragement, not a direction, to the MBHTE and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs to sustain literacy programs; no target or funding is attached.
readings.insight:
A tribute with a policy tail. The figure carrying it is the 78.7% basic literacy rate, which the resolution places last among all regions. The WHEREAS clauses also say roughly 1/3 of adults in the region cannot read or write, a larger gap than the 78.7% rate implies; the resolution cites no source for that figure, and the 2 may measure different age groups.

Filed on 10 December 2024 as Proposed Resolution No. 659 and adopted without committee referral. The ministries are encouraged rather than directed, and nothing is asked of them by a date.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament approves the choice of Barangay Sarmiento in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, as the site of the Bangsamoro Government Center, as identified by the Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government (CESG) in its Resolution No. 001, Series of 2024.

It adds 2 conditions: Parliament will continue its oversight of BAA 37, the Seat of Government Act of 2023, and the CESG is to consult Parliament on every major step in developing the site. A copy goes to the CESG. Adopted on 17 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: BAA 37, enacted on 19 June 2023, moved the seat of government to Parang and, under Section 5, made the CESG's choice of a specific site subject to Parliament's approval. The CESG, chaired by the Senior Minister, chose Barangay Sarmiento on 7 March 2024; the Office of the Senior Minister endorsed the choice to the Speaker on 22 March 2024, and the Ministry of Interior and Local Government held a community consultation in Sarmiento on 26 April 2024. The resolution says the selection was unanimous. Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba and 40 others.
whoIsAffected: Barangay Sarmiento and the Municipality of Parang
Bangsamoro ministries and offices that would move to the new center
Cotabato City, home of the present government center
implementedBy: Committee on the Establishment of the Seat of Government
whatChanges: This one has legal effect: Section 5 of BAA 37 made Parliament's approval a condition of the site choice, and this resolution supplies it.
The CESG is to consult Parliament on every major step of site development.
Parliament records that its oversight of BAA 37 continues.
readings.insight:
Unlike most resolutions, this completes a legal step. It was slow to arrive: the CESG chose Sarmiento on 7 March 2024 and Proposed Resolution No. 565, carrying 41 principal authors, was filed on 6 May 2024, but it sat with the Committee on Rules until Committee Report No. 131 was adopted on 17 February 2025, more than 9 months later, though the resolution itself calls Parliament's immediate action 'imperative'.

The approval names a barangay, not a parcel, budget or timetable. 14 months later, Resolution No. 570 (22 April 2026) authorized the Chief Minister to acquire a parking facility near the existing Bangsamoro Government Center in Cotabato City to free up space inside it, so the government was still investing in the old center.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts its calendar for the Fourth Regular Session of the Second Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament. The session opens on 8 April 2025, then sits in 14 blocks of Monday-to-Thursday sittings from mid-April, generally in the 3rd and 4th weeks of each month, and ends with mandatory adjournment on 29 October 2025. The calendar has 29 numbered entries.

Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Parliament's rules (BTA Resolution No. 268) require regular sessions to follow an annual calendar and plenary sittings to run Monday to Thursday in the 3rd and 4th weeks of the month. The resolution notes that Congress had approved the consolidated Senate Bill No. 2942 and House Bill No. 11144 resetting the first regional elections to 13 October 2025, with interim members serving until their successors are elected; the enrolled bill had gone to the President on 10 February 2025. Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, MP Raissa H. Jajurie, MP Mary Ann M. Arnado and MP Jose I. Lorena.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament
Parliament's secretariat and the public following its sittings
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: Binding on Parliament: it fixes when plenary sittings begin and end in the 2025 session.
Mandatory adjournment on 29 October 2025 falls 16 days after the 13 October 2025 election date the resolution cites.
readings.insight:
The calendar was built around an election that did not happen. It ran the session to 29 October 2025, just after the 13 October 2025 election set by the consolidated bills, which became Republic Act No. 12123. On 30 September 2025 the Supreme Court held that election could not proceed without a valid districting law, and Resolution No. 560 (28 October 2025) extended this calendar to a mandatory adjournment on 29 January 2026; Resolution No. 568 (20 April 2026) later set a calendar for the rest of the transition.

It follows the same pattern as the Second BTA Parliament's earlier session calendars, Resolution Nos. 265, 336 and 442.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes all its parliamentary and statutory committees to hold meetings, hearings and consultations during the recess of the Second Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament. The authority takes effect on adoption and stays in force until amended or repealed. Copies go to the committees for reference.

Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Third Regular Session was to adjourn sine die on 20 February 2025 under Memorandum Order No. 0225-544, Series of 2025, with the Bangsamoro Revenue Code, the Bangsamoro Gender and Development Code and other bills and resolutions still pending in committee. Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, MP Raissa H. Jajurie, MP Mary Ann M. Arnado and MP Jose I. Lorena.
whoIsAffected: Parliament's committees and their members
Ministries and stakeholders called to committee hearings during the recess
implementedBy: Parliamentary and statutory committees of the BTA Parliament
whatChanges: Binding on Parliament: committees may keep working between the 3rd and 4th regular sessions.
It has no expiry date; it stays in force until amended or repealed.
readings.insight:
Routine housekeeping, adopted in the same words for the 3rd year running: Resolution No. 324 (21 March 2023) and Resolution No. 443 (29 February 2024) gave the same authority before earlier recesses.

The 2 codes it names as the reason for working through the recess were still not law more than a year later: neither a Bangsamoro Revenue Code nor a Gender and Development Code appears among the acts in the registry, which runs to BAA 94 of July 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests all food establishments in the region to display prominently at their entrance whether or not they serve pork and pork by-products. Copies go to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Tourism, the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos and the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' for information and appropriate action.

Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution acknowledges there is no law requiring restaurants to label pork dishes, and leans on the broader aims of the Food Safety Act of 2013 (Republic Act No. 10611) and on the Philippines' recognition as an emerging Muslim-friendly destination and halal hub. It gives 2 figures for the Muslim population: about 6% of Filipinos per the Philippine Statistics Authority, and 10%, or 12,000,000 people, per the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, most of them in the region. Filed by MP Suharto S. Esmael.
whoIsAffected: Restaurants and other food businesses in the region
Muslim diners and others who avoid pork
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Tourism
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'
whatChanges: Nothing enforceable: it is a request to private businesses, with no penalty and no agency told to enforce it.
Copies go to 3 offices for appropriate action.
readings.insight:
Parliament adopted 2 resolutions on the same point the same day. This one (Proposed Resolution No. 568, filed 8 May 2024) asks for a sign at the entrance; Resolution No. 541 (Proposed Resolution No. 537, filed 7 March 2024) asks for 'No Pork' or 'With Pork' signs on menus and display counters. Both went through the Committee on Trade, Investment and Tourism, came out as separate committee reports (Nos. 106 and 107), and were adopted separately rather than consolidated.

The resolution states its own limit: no law requires pork labelling, and a request cannot create that requirement.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges all food establishments in the Bangsamoro region to display either 'No Pork' or 'With Pork' signage on their menus and food display counters. Copies go to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Tourism, the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos and the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' for information and appropriate action.

Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution grounds the request in Section 30, Article XIII of the Organic Law, which directs the Bangsamoro Government to run a halal awareness campaign and Parliament to strengthen halal policy by law. It notes that Islam, Judaism and some Christian denominations such as the Seventh-day Adventists restrict pork, that there have been 'many instances' of Muslims eating pork by mistake leading to 'unfortunate incidents and squabbles', and that about 91.28% of the region's population is Muslim. Filed by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong.
whoIsAffected: Restaurants and other food businesses in the region
Muslim diners and others who avoid pork
implementedBy: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Tourism
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'
whatChanges: Nothing enforceable: an appeal to private businesses with no penalty or enforcing agency.
Copies go to 3 offices for appropriate action.
readings.insight:
The twin of Resolution No. 540, adopted the same day: this one wants signs on menus and display counters, that one at the entrance. Filed 2 months apart (this one as Proposed Resolution No. 537 on 7 March 2024), they were reported out separately by the Committee on Trade, Investment and Tourism and never consolidated, so a restaurant is asked to do both.

The resolution cites Section 30 of the Organic Law, which tells Parliament to strengthen halal policy by enacting laws; it chose a non-binding urging instead.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament condemns the raid that killed 7 members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, expresses deep concern over reported excessive force and violation of the victims' rights, and calls on 'higher authorities' to conduct a fair, impartial and speedy investigation, carried out transparently with public findings, to hold those responsible accountable.

It requests the immediate return of the International Monitoring Team to the region, and calls on all parties to use the established mechanisms, namely the Coordinating Committee on the Cessation of Hostilities, the Ad Hoc Joint Action Group and the peace panel, when apprehending MILF members suspected of crimes. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister, OPAPRU, the Commission on Human Rights and other agencies. Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: On 18 June 2023 a raid in Barangay Damawato, Datu Paglas, Maguindanao del Sur left 7 MILF members dead of gunshot wounds: Nasser Yousef M. Husain, 34; Norjihad M. Husain, 29; Nasrullah Mamay Singkala, 38; Ivan Pumpugay, 18; Izrael Laguiab, 41; Morsid Madidis, 50; and Mama Kakim, 53. Reports said they were handcuffed and killed in different places, including a mosque. They had already applied for amnesty, and the raid took place during the decommissioning and normalization track of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. Filed by MP Baileng S. Mantawil and MP Mary Ann M. Arnado.
whoIsAffected: The families of the 7 men killed
MILF members in the normalization process and awaiting amnesty
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
Commission on Human Rights
whatChanges: No binding effect; it names no investigating agency, calling only on 'higher authorities'.
A formal request for the International Monitoring Team's return, sent to the Chief Minister, OPAPRU and the Commission on Human Rights.
readings.insight:
Filed the day after the raid, as Proposed Resolution No. 310 on 19 June 2023, and adopted 20 months later. The Committee on Public Order and Safety's report (No. 127) was approved on 13 February 2025, the measure was deferred that same day, and it passed on 18 February. A call for a 'speedy' investigation arrived long after the moment it was written for, and the text was not updated to say what had happened in the meantime.

The amnesty detail links it to Resolution No. 561 (13 November 2025), which asked the President to speed up safe conduct passes for MILF and MNLF amnesty applicants, citing about 3,000 applications and 27 passes approved and issued.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Ministry of Public Order and Safety (MPOS) to formulate a regional reintegration program for rebel returnees and other armed groups returning to the fold of the law, and to submit it to the Office of the Chief Minister. A copy goes to the MPOS for information and appropriate action.

Adopted on 18 February 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Most members of armed groups in Sulu and elsewhere in the region, the resolution says, have abandoned violent extremism and surrendered, but there is no program for them beyond one-time assistance a local government may give on surrender. Existing programs, such as Kapayapaan sa Pamayanan and initiatives of the Ministry of Social Services and Development, TESDA and the MILG, serve mainly MILF members and to some extent MNLF members. It points to OPAPRU's push for Localized Peace Engagement and to Proclamation Nos. 1090 and 1091 of 2021 granting amnesty to MNLF and MILF combatants. Filed by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong.
whoIsAffected: Surrenderees and former members of armed and violent extremist groups, especially in Sulu
Communities they return to
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A request to the MPOS to draft a program; there is no deadline, no funding and no requirement to report to Parliament.
Any program would go to the Chief Minister, not to Parliament.
readings.insight:
The original proposal was explicit about its target. Proposed Resolution No. 331, filed on 21 June 2023, sought a program for rebel returnees 'including the armed supporters and sympathizers of the Abu Sayyaf and other terrorist groups'; the adopted text drops the Abu Sayyaf reference for 'other armed groups'. It waited 8 months to be referred to the Committee on Public Order and Safety and 20 months to be adopted; like Resolution No. 542, its committee report was approved and then deferred on 13 February 2025 before passing on 18 February.

The gap it describes is stated without numbers: the resolution does not say how many people have surrendered, or where.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament condemns in the strongest terms the killing of COMELEC Municipal Election Officer Bai Maceda Lidasan-Abo of Datu Odin Sinsuat and her husband Jojo Olea Abo. It calls on the Philippine National Police, the National Bureau of Investigation, the local government of Datu Odin Sinsuat and other authorities to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation, apprehend the perpetrators and take measures to protect government workers and civilians.

Copies go to the PNP, COMELEC, the Ministry of Public Order and Safety, the Datu Odin Sinsuat local chief executive and other agencies. Adopted on 15 April 2025.
readings.whyProposed: On 26 March 2025 the couple were ambushed in Barangay Makir, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, on the way to her post. Citing the provincial police director, the resolution says gunmen riding in tandem fired in broad daylight, shattering the vehicle's windows. Lidasan-Abo had served COMELEC as a Municipal Election Officer for 28 years. Filed by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr., MP Kadil M. Sinolinding Jr., MP Abdulwahab M. Pak, MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, MP Abdulkarim T. Misuari and MP Michael E. Midtimbang.
whoIsAffected: The families of Bai Maceda Lidasan-Abo and Jojo Olea Abo
Election officers and other government workers in the region
implementedBy: Philippine National Police
National Bureau of Investigation
Local Government Unit of Datu Odin Sinsuat
whatChanges: No binding effect on the national police or the NBI; it records Parliament's condemnation and a call to investigate.
Copies go to the PNP, COMELEC, the Ministry of Public Order and Safety and the municipal chief executive.
readings.insight:
Filed on 14 April 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 690 and adopted the next day, 20 days after the killing. It was one of 2 fatal ambushes in Datu Odin Sinsuat within 9 days in March 2025 to reach Parliament: lawyer Junisa Kimamao was killed in the same municipality on 17 March, and Resolution No. 545 followed a week after this one.

The victim ran elections in a municipality of a region then preparing for its first parliamentary election. The resolution states no motive and asks for no report back.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament strongly condemns the attack that killed lawyer Junisa Kimamao and wounded lawyer Ibrahim Pendatu. It urges the PNP, the NBI, the local government of Datu Odin Sinsuat and other authorities to conduct a thorough, transparent and impartial investigation, and to step up protection of legal professionals and justice workers in the region.

It also directs Parliament's Committee on Public Order and Safety and Committee on Local Government to jointly investigate, in aid of legislation, this attack and other similar killings in the same municipality. Copies go to the PNP, the NBI, the Ministry of Public Order and Safety and the Datu Odin Sinsuat local chief executive. Adopted on 22 April 2025.
readings.whyProposed: On 17 March 2025, the resolution says, 2 gunmen on a motorcycle shot Kimamao and her fiancé Pendatu as they drove along the highway in Barangay Awang, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte. Kimamao died and Pendatu was critically injured. Filed by MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr. and 8 others.
whoIsAffected: The families of Atty. Kimamao and Atty. Pendatu
Lawyers and justice workers in the region
Residents of Datu Odin Sinsuat
implementedBy: Committee on Public Order and Safety
Committee on Local Government
Philippine National Police
National Bureau of Investigation
whatChanges: The binding part is internal: 2 Parliament committees are directed to hold a joint inquiry in aid of legislation.
The call on the PNP, NBI and local government to investigate has no binding force.
readings.insight:
Unlike most condemnation resolutions, this one gives Parliament's own committees work: a joint inquiry into this attack and 'other similar incidents of killings in the same municipality'. A week earlier Resolution No. 544 had condemned the 26 March 2025 ambush of Datu Odin Sinsuat's COMELEC election officer and her husband, 9 days after this attack. No committee report on the directed inquiry appears in the registry's committee records.

Filed on 15 April 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 700 and adopted a week later without committee referral.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Intergovernmental Relations Body (IGRB) to do 4 things on Sulu's transition out of the region: release timely and accurate information on the status and direction of transition plans; study the fiscal, administrative and employment effects; invite stakeholders, especially affected Tausug employees and community representatives, into discussions and planning; and ensure Tausug concerns are reflected in decisions on public employment, fiscal allocations and service delivery.

Copies go to the IGRB, the Office of the President, the Department of Budget and Management and other offices. Adopted on 20 May 2025, the date on the signed text; the Parliament's adopted-resolution index lists 21 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Following the Supreme Court decision of 9 September 2024 and its resolution of 26 November 2024, Sulu is leaving the Bangsamoro region. The resolution says Tausug public servants and residents have had no clear guidance from the IGRB or the national government on salaries, services and the programs the Bangsamoro Government ran in Sulu, and that provincial offices in Sulu have reportedly been left out of budget planning for Fiscal Year 2026, risking exclusion from both the national and the regional budget. It also asks the IGRB chairman for the membership of the IGRB's Technical Working Group on Sulu. Filed by MP Nabil A. Tan.
whoIsAffected: Government workers in Sulu, especially Tausug employees of the Bangsamoro Government
Sulu residents who depend on regional programs and services
Provincial offices and agencies operating in Sulu
