implementedBy: Intergovernmental Relations Body
whatChanges: No binding effect on the IGRB, a joint national-regional body that Parliament does not control.
Copies go to the IGRB, the Office of the President and the DBM.
readings.insight:
Filed on 19 May 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 709 and adopted the next day. Its premise, that the IGRB was not communicating on Sulu, got worse rather than better: Resolution No. 564, adopted 7 months later, says the IGRB had formed a Technical Working Group on Sulu's transfer to Region IX under its national co-chair, DBM Secretary Amenah Pangandaman, but that her resignation left the chair vacant and the IGRB stopped convening, delaying Sulu's transition.

It follows Resolution No. 507 (23 October 2024), which supported motions before the Supreme Court against Sulu's exclusion; this one accepts the exclusion and turns to its consequences. The signed text and the proposed-resolution history both give 20 May 2025; the 21 May date in the adopted index appears to be an error.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. to include as priority legislation the creation of a Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Regional Office for the Bangsamoro region and 5 new District Engineering Offices. Copies go to the Office of the President, the Senate, the House of Representatives, the DPWH, the Chief Minister and the Ministry of Public Works.

Adopted on 21 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Under Section 37, Article XIII of the Organic Law, national roads, bridges, flood control and similar works in the region are funded and implemented by the national government. The resolution says that without a DPWH regional office inside the region these projects are run from offices outside it, causing delays, misaligned priorities, confusion over responsibility and slow emergency repairs. Senate Bill No. 2756 proposes the regional office and 5 district engineering offices, which the resolution says would reach remote mainland municipalities, the island provinces and the Special Geographic Area. Filed by MP Hashemi N. Dilangalen, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, MP Zulfikar-Ali S. Bayam and MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr.
whoIsAffected: Communities served by national roads, bridges and flood control in the region
The island provinces, remote mainland municipalities and the Special Geographic Area
The Ministry of Public Works, which would coordinate with the new office
implementedBy: Office of the President
Congress of the Philippines
Department of Public Works and Highways
whatChanges: No binding effect: it asks the President to prioritize a national bill; only Congress can create the office.
Copies go to both houses of Congress, the DPWH and the regional government.
readings.insight:
The ask was softened on the floor. As filed on 16 May 2025 (Proposed Resolution No. 706) it appealed to the President to certify Senate Bill No. 2756 as urgent; it was deferred on 19 May and adopted 'as amended' on 21 May as a request to list the measure as priority legislation. A WHEREAS clause still speaks of 'certifying this proposed measure as urgent', a leftover of the original.

Parliament had asked before: Resolution No. 346 (21 June 2023) supported the President's call to create DPWH district engineering offices and a regional office for the region. The registry does not record what became of Senate Bill No. 2756.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends Secretary Carlito G. Galvez Jr., Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, for his commitment to peace and reconciliation, and urges President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to retain him in the post to preserve continuity in peacebuilding in the region. Copies go to the Office of the President, OPAPRU, the MNLF Central Committee and other agencies.

Adopted on 29 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The President had asked Cabinet officials for courtesy resignations to evaluate performance, and Galvez complied. The resolution credits him with moving forward the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the Moro National Liberation Front, including making the MNLF Peace Implementing Committee operational, and with OPAPRU's support for transitional justice and development programs. It cites a 26 May 2025 statement of support from the MNLF Central Committee, issued by Ustadz Abdulkarim Tan Misuari as Vice Chairman and Acting Chairman. Filed by MP Abdulkarim T. Misuari, MP Randolph C. Parcasio, MP Romeo K. Sema, MP Nurredha I. Misuari and MP Saripuddin D. Jikiri.
whoIsAffected: Secretary Carlito G. Galvez Jr.
The MNLF and MILF peace tracks overseen by OPAPRU
implementedBy: Office of the President
whatChanges: No binding effect: the appointment is the President's alone.
Copies go to the Office of the President and OPAPRU.
readings.insight:
Filed on 28 May 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 717 and adopted the next day, paired with Resolution No. 549, a same-day resolution by the same 5 authors backing Secretary Antonio Ernesto F. Lagdameo Jr. The MNLF statement it cites came from Ustadz Abdulkarim Tan Misuari; the lead author is MP Abdulkarim T. Misuari.

It is one of a series on Galvez: Parliament thanked the President for appointing him in Resolution No. 280 (22 November 2022) and for reappointing him in Resolution No. 363 (17 July 2023), and in Resolution No. 574 (29 April 2026) thanked him as 'former Secretary' of OPAPRU.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses full support for Secretary Antonio Ernesto F. Lagdameo Jr., Special Assistant to the President, recognizes his role in the region's peace and governance framework, and urges President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to retain him. Copies go to the Office of the President, the Office of the Special Assistant to the President and other agencies.

Adopted on 29 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Like Resolution No. 548, it responds to the President's call for Cabinet courtesy resignations. It describes Lagdameo as a bridge between the Office of the President and the region's stakeholders, who has enabled high-level engagements, aligned national priorities with regional aspirations and supported both the MNLF and the MILF. Filed by MP Abdulkarim T. Misuari, MP Randolph C. Parcasio, MP Romeo K. Sema, MP Nurredha I. Misuari and MP Saripuddin D. Jikiri.
whoIsAffected: Secretary Antonio Ernesto F. Lagdameo Jr.
implementedBy: Office of the President
whatChanges: No binding effect: the appointment is the President's alone.
Copies go to the Office of the President and the Office of the Special Assistant to the President.
readings.insight:
Filed on 28 May 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 718 and adopted the next day alongside the matching Galvez resolution by the same 5 authors. Its WHEREAS clauses are general; it names no specific program or agreement Lagdameo advanced.

Parliament came back to him 7 months later: Resolution No. 564 (17 December 2025), with 50 principal authors, endorsed Lagdameo as the national government's co-chair of the Intergovernmental Relations Body after that post fell vacant.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Ministry of Health to intensify its program for eliminating tuberculosis in the region, and forwards the resolution to the ministry for information and immediate action. The WHEREAS clauses also encourage the ministry to run a multi-platform public education campaign on TB control and treatment.

Adopted on 29 May 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution cites national figures: 612,000 TB cases reported in 2023, about 549 per 100,000 people, up from 439 per 100,000 in 2022, as reported by Health Secretary Ted Herbosa; and Department of Health statements on World TB Day 2024 that about 70 Filipinos die of TB daily and that the Philippines accounts for 7% of global cases. It says the region and the Cordillera lag behind in TB treatment enrollment. The national framework is Republic Act No. 10767, the Comprehensive Tuberculosis Elimination Plan Act of 2016. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and 14 others.
whoIsAffected: People with TB in the region and their households
Health workers running TB detection and treatment
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
whatChanges: Phrased as a direction, but it sets no target, deadline, budget or reporting requirement.
The resolution is forwarded to the Ministry of Health.
readings.insight:
Every figure in the resolution is national or global; the only statement about the region is that it lags in treatment enrollment, with no regional case count, incidence rate or treatment success rate. The national figures also come from different series: 549 per 100,000 in 2023 and 439 in 2022 sit beside an estimated 650 per 100,000 in 2021 and 554 the year before, so they cannot be read as 1 trend.

Filed on 14 June 2024 as Proposed Resolution No. 596 and adopted on the Committee on Health's report (No. 138) almost a year later. 'Directing' a ministry is firmer language than most resolutions use, but with no measure attached Parliament has nothing to check the result against.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses full support for Chief Minister Abdulraof 'Sammy Gambar' A. Macacua's call for the courtesy resignation of all ministers, deputy ministers and heads of offices and agencies of the Bangsamoro Government. It affirms support for his reform agenda and urges all officials concerned to heed the call. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and all ministries, offices and agencies.

Adopted on 25 June 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Chief Minister directed all appointed or designated ministers, deputy ministers and heads of offices to submit unqualified courtesy resignations on 30 June 2025, 'in light of serious and grave complaints brought to him', to promote efficiency and integrity and to allow a reorganization at the tail end of the transition. The resolution grounds this in Section 32, Article VII of the Organic Law, which gives the Chief Minister the power to appoint heads of ministries and offices, and in the moral governance provisions of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code and Civil Service Code. Filed by MP Paisalin P. Tago and 39 others.
whoIsAffected: Ministers, deputy ministers and heads of Bangsamoro offices and agencies
The Chief Minister
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: No legal effect: the resignations rest on the Chief Minister's own appointing power, which needs no approval from Parliament.
A political signal of support, copied to every ministry and office.
readings.insight:
Filed and adopted on the same day, 25 June 2025, as Proposed Resolution No. 736 with 40 principal authors and no committee referral, 5 days before the resignations were due. The resolution cites 'serious and grave complaints' as the reason but does not say what they were or against whom.

A month earlier the President's own Cabinet courtesy-resignation call had prompted Resolution Nos. 548 and 549 urging that 2 national officials be retained; this time Parliament backed the call itself.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Government to reconstitute and convene the Bangsamoro Council of Leaders, in light of the 2025 national and local elections and the appointment of a new Chief Minister, under Section 9, Article VI of the Organic Law and Sections 3 and 4, Book II of the Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA 13). The reconstitution is to be done in full consultation with stakeholders and sectors. A copy goes to the Office of the Chief Minister.

Adopted on 17 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Council of Leaders advises the Chief Minister and is made up of elected and appointed officials and sectoral representatives. The 2025 elections changed the roster of elected officials who sit on it, and Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua was appointed before those elections. The resolution quotes his post-election call to move forward 'united in purpose, grounded in the principles of moral governance'. Filed by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr., MP Ishak V. Mastura and MP Kitem D. Kadatuan Jr.
whoIsAffected: Members of the Bangsamoro Council of Leaders, including newly elected local officials
The Chief Minister, whom the council advises
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A request to the executive, with no deadline or report back.
A copy goes to the Office of the Chief Minister.
readings.insight:
The resolution does not say when the council last met or whether it had met at all under the new Chief Minister, which would be the useful fact. Filed on 19 May 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 710, it was adopted 2 months later without committee referral; the filed title referred to the 'prior' appointment of a new Chief Minister, the adopted one to the 'recent' appointment.

No other adopted resolution in the registry asks for the Council of Leaders to be convened.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Office of the Chief Minister and the Office of the Parliament Speaker to jointly set up a Technical Working Group to prepare the documents needed for an orderly turnover from the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament to the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament. The group would include representatives of the 2 offices, the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority and other offices they choose. Copies go to both offices and others concerned.

Adopted on 17 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed: With the first parliamentary elections then set for October 2025 under Republic Act No. 12123, the resolution argues that handing over powers, functions, assets and liabilities needs documentation, inventory and transition planning, especially as several offices and ministries had yet to complete their staffing, systems and programs. It describes the BTA as managing a budget of roughly ₱75,000,000,000 to ₱90,000,000,000 a year. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.
whoIsAffected: The incoming first elected Bangsamoro Parliament
Ministries and offices whose programs, assets and records would be handed over
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Office of the Parliament Speaker
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority
whatChanges: A request; it does not itself create the working group or set it a deadline.
Copies go to the Chief Minister's and the Speaker's offices.
readings.insight:
The budget figure understates what is being handed over. The General Appropriations Acts of the Bangsamoro in the registry's budget data total ₱98,467,200,000 for 2024 and ₱94,411,666,856.24 for 2025, both above the top of the range the resolution gives, and that is the whole regional government's budget rather than the Parliament's.

The October 2025 election it planned for was stopped by the Supreme Court on 30 September 2025 and later reset, most recently to 14 September 2026 under Republic Act No. 12317, so the turnover moved back about a year. Filed on 26 May 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 713 and adopted without committee referral.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts rules for accounting and liquidating 2 allocations held for each Member: the Constituency Servicing Program (CSP) and Financial Assistance/Subsidy (FAS). Liquidation follows applicable accounting and auditing rules and is done through 'Liquidation by Way of Certification'. The Office of the Speaker is to issue guidelines and forms, and each Member must keep documentary evidence of payments and disbursements, ready for inspection and audit by the Commission on Audit.

The rules stay in effect until revoked by the Members. A copy goes to the Office of the Speaker. Adopted on 22 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro funds a CSP for each Member, released on written request to the Finance Services, and a separate FAS appropriation under the BTA. The resolution states there were no guidelines on how either is used or liquidated, and argues that the distinct nature of Parliament's legislative, oversight and constituency work calls for tailored mechanisms. Filed by MP Khalid M. Hadji Abdullah and 37 others.
whoIsAffected: Every Member of Parliament holding CSP and FAS allocations
Constituents who receive assistance funded from these allocations
The Commission on Audit, which audits the spending
implementedBy: Office of the Speaker of the Parliament

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It governs how already-appropriated CSP and FAS funds are liquidated. For scale, the 2025 General Appropriations Act sets the CSP at ₱288,000,000 in all, ₱3,600,000 per Member, and the 2026 act at ₱480,000,000, ₱6,000,000 per Member; the resolution names no FAS amount.

whatChanges: Binding on Parliament: it sets how Members liquidate their CSP and FAS allocations.
Members liquidate by certification and keep the supporting documents themselves, available to the Commission on Audit when needed.
The Speaker's office must issue the forms and guidelines.
readings.insight:
One of the few resolutions here with real force, and it applies to the Members who voted for it. It took 6 deferrals: filed on 23 June 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 733 with 38 principal authors, deferred on 23, 24, 25 and 26 June and 17 and 21 July, and adopted on 22 July 2025. By its own account there were no guidelines on the use or liquidation of these funds until then.

The sums grew after the rule was set: the CSP was ₱3,600,000 per Member in the 2025 budget and ₱6,000,000 per Member in the 2026 budget. 'Liquidation by Way of Certification' is not defined in the text; the details were left to the Speaker's guidelines.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD) to brief Parliament on the status of trafficking in persons in the region and on the programs and initiatives the ministry is running against it. The resolution is forwarded to the MSSD.

Adopted on 24 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution draws on national and global data: the 2018 Global Slavery Index, which it says ranked the Philippines 12th in the Asia-Pacific for modern slavery; a case of 13 minors, including a 2-month-old baby, trafficked by relatives and rescued by the NBI; and the July 2022 US Trafficking in Persons Report, which kept the Philippines at Tier 1 for 7 consecutive years and counted 1,802 victims identified from April 2021 to March 2022, up from 1,534 in 2020. It argues that updates on trafficking in the region would inform policy and program evaluation. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.
whoIsAffected: Victims of trafficking and people at risk in the region, including overseas job applicants
The MSSD, which must report
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: The MSSD is directed to report to Parliament, but no deadline, format or hearing is set.
The resolution is forwarded to the MSSD.
readings.insight:
The resolution contains no regional figure at all, which is the point of the request. But its evidence was old by adoption: filed on 22 May 2023 as Proposed Resolution No. 263 and adopted on Committee Report No. 147 on 24 July 2025, 26 months later, it still leans on a 2018 index and a report covering April 2021 to March 2022.

It was adopted the same day as Resolution No. 557, another request by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan for an MSSD briefing, on orphanages. Neither sets a date for the briefing.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Social Services and Development to brief Parliament on the status of orphanages in the region. The resolution is forwarded to the MSSD.

Adopted on 24 July 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Citing a study by The Asia Foundation, 'Children of War', the resolution says there are no orphanages or shelters in the region accredited by the Department of Social Welfare and Development, and that many Muslim orphans handled by the DSWD in Mindanao are sent to orphanages in Manila. It invokes Section 14, Article IX of the Organic Law on protecting children, 'especially orphans of tender age', and argues for a centralized, updated database of orphanages to be shared with Parliament. Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan.
whoIsAffected: Orphaned, abandoned and neglected children in the region
Orphanages and shelters operating in the region
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: A request for information, with no deadline.
The database argued for in the WHEREAS clauses is not part of what is resolved.
readings.insight:
The WHEREAS clauses make the case for a regional database of orphanages, but the RESOLVED clause asks only for a status briefing, so the database is never actually requested. The resolution does not date The Asia Foundation study it relies on.

Filed on 9 October 2023 as Proposed Resolution No. 429 and adopted 21 months later on Committee Report No. 148, the same day as Resolution No. 556 on trafficking, both by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Parliament had raised a related concern early on: Resolution No. 43 (18 October 2019) called for a bureau for orphans and widows who are victims of war and violence.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board to put the immediate rehabilitation and upgrading of the 67.9-kilometer Awang–Upi–South Upi–Lebak Highway on its priority agenda, taking into account the road's deteriorated condition and its importance to the region. Copies go to the board and the Ministry of Public Works.

Adopted on 20 August 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The highway is described as a major arterial road linking municipalities in the region, now badly deteriorated, posing safety risks and limiting trade and access to services. Its repair falls to the national DPWH under Section 37, Article XIII of the Organic Law, while the board, which includes the DPWH Secretary and the Minister of Public Works, coordinates national and Bangsamoro infrastructure plans under Section 6, Article VI. Filed by MP Ramon A. Piang Sr., MP Eddie M. Alih and MP Hatimil E. Hassan.
whoIsAffected: Motorists and residents along the Awang–Upi–South Upi–Lebak corridor
Traders moving goods along the route
implementedBy: Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board
Ministry of Public Works
whatChanges: No binding effect; the board sets its own agenda.
Copies go to the board and the Ministry of Public Works but not to the DPWH, which the resolution says is responsible for the repairs.
readings.insight:
Same template, different road: Resolution No. 511 (23 October 2024) asked the same board to prioritize the Narciso Ramos Highway. Neither names a cost, a funding source or a timeline. This one was filed on 20 February 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 687 and adopted 6 months later on the Committee on Public Works' report (No. 156).

The resolution says the national DPWH is responsible for the road, yet sends it no copy; it reaches the department only through the DPWH Secretary's seat on the board.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the national Department of Public Works and Highways to fast-track the renovation of the Quirino Bridge in Cotabato City, and states that the department, through Secretary Manuel M. Bonoan and its regional offices, shall do so to ensure safe and reliable routes. Copies go to the Office of the President, the DPWH Secretary, the DPWH regional office for SOCCSKSARGEN and the Cotabato City mayor.

Adopted on 20 August 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Built in the 1950s by the United States Bureau of Public Roads and the Philippine Public Works, the bridge links key parts of Cotabato City and is described as a historic landmark. The resolution says its structure has significantly deteriorated despite earlier maintenance, causing frequent traffic disruptions, overloading alternative routes and slowing emergency response, and that it remains under the national DPWH because of its national importance and funding scope. Filed by MP Abdulbasit R. Benito.
whoIsAffected: Motorists, pedestrians and businesses in Cotabato City and nearby municipalities
Emergency services that use the crossing
implementedBy: Department of Public Works and Highways
DPWH Regional Office for SOCCSKSARGEN
whatChanges: No binding effect on a national department, despite the RESOLVED clause's 'shall'.
Copies go to the President, the DPWH and the city.
readings.insight:
The 2nd RESOLVED clause is written as a command, that the DPWH 'shall fast-track' the work, but a regional parliament's resolution cannot bind a national department. The text gives no figure for the bridge's condition, no renovation cost or schedule, and does not say what earlier maintenance was done.

The copy to the SOCCSKSARGEN regional office shows the arrangement Resolution No. 547 complained of 3 months earlier: national works in the region run from an office outside it. Parliament had made a general version of this request in Resolution No. 425 (15 January 2024) on national highways and bridges. Filed on 22 April 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 702.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends the Resolution No. 538 calendar to extend the Fourth Regular Session past its 29 October 2025 end. The new schedule adjourns on 30 October 2025, resumes for sitting weeks from 10, 17 and 24 November, 1, 8 and 15 December 2025 and 19 and 26 January 2026, and sets mandatory adjournment on 29 January 2026.

Adopted on 28 October 2025.
readings.whyProposed: On 30 September 2025 the Supreme Court held that the 13 October 2025 parliamentary election under Republic Act No. 12123 could not proceed because there was no valid law apportioning the 32 parliamentary districts, and directed COMELEC to hold the election no later than 31 March 2026. Resolution No. 538 had set sine die adjournment for 29 October 2025 while key measures, including priority legislation required by the Organic Law, were still pending. Filed by MP Sha Elijah B. Dumama-Alba, MP Raissa H. Jajurie, MP Jose I. Lorena, MP Randolph C. Parcasio, MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and MP Suharto S. Esmael.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament
Pending bills, including the districting law the Supreme Court found missing
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: Binding on Parliament: the session runs 3 months longer, to 29 January 2026.
Adds 8 sitting weeks between November 2025 and January 2026.
readings.insight:
Adopted the day before the old calendar would have closed the session. The extension gave Parliament room to pass the districting law the Supreme Court said was missing: BAA 86, apportioning the district seats, carries a ratification date of 12 January 2026 in the registry, before the new 29 January adjournment. The resolution itself names no specific measure.

Filed on 7 October 2025 as Proposed Resolution No. 759 and 'adopted with amendments' 3 weeks later. On 20 April 2026 Resolution No. 568 set a calendar for the remainder of the transition period.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament thanks President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. for issuing Memorandum Order No. 36, Series of 2025, which it says affirms the government's commitment to protect the rights and security of qualified MILF and MNLF members under the amnesty program. It requests the President to direct the National Amnesty Commission to expedite the issuance of Safe Conduct Passes under that order to qualified MILF and MNLF amnesty applicants.

Copies go to the President and the National Amnesty Commission. Adopted on 13 November 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Proclamation Nos. 405 and 406, signed on 22 November 2023, granted amnesty to MILF and MNLF members, and Executive Order No. 47 tasked the National Amnesty Commission with processing applications. The resolution cites the commission's own figures: about 3,000 people have applied, 90% of them requesting a Safe Conduct Pass, but only 140 applications are under review and 27 have been approved and issued. At a ceremony in Cotabato City on 11 June 2025, 25 passes were issued, 7 to MILF members and 2 to MNLF members. Filed by MP Dan S. Asnawie and 6 others.
whoIsAffected: MILF and MNLF members with pending amnesty applications
The National Amnesty Commission
implementedBy: Office of the President
National Amnesty Commission
whatChanges: A request to the President; no binding effect on the commission.
Copies go to the Office of the President and the National Amnesty Commission.
readings.insight:
The figures make the case: of roughly 2,700 applicants seeking a Safe Conduct Pass (90% of about 3,000), 27 had been issued, about 1%. The resolution does not explain what Memorandum Order No. 36 provides beyond the passes, and of the 25 passes issued in June 2025 it accounts for only 9 as going to MILF or MNLF members.

The filed version asked for something else. Proposed Resolution No. 627, filed on 28 August 2024, requested the President to hold in abeyance the serving of arrest warrants on MILF and MNLF leaders and members pending decisions on their amnesty applications; 14 months later it was adopted as this commendation and safe-conduct request. Resolution No. 542, earlier in 2025, concerned 7 MILF members with pending amnesty applications killed in a 2023 raid.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes the Speaker to establish an Association of Former Members of the Parliament (AFMP) as a formal platform for former parliamentarians, to enhance governance, community engagement and the preservation of the region's legislative heritage. The association is placed under the Office of the Speaker with 1 room and 1 secretariat.

Adopted on 17 November 2025.
readings.whyProposed: Former Members, the resolution argues, carry experience that could keep serving the region through advice, mentorship, community service and the documentation of Parliament's legislative history. It points to associations of former members in the United Kingdom, New South Wales and Canada. Filed by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr.
whoIsAffected: Former Members of the Bangsamoro Parliament
The Office of the Speaker, which houses the association
implementedBy: Office of the Speaker

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It assigns the association 1 room and 1 secretariat under the Office of the Speaker but names no cost or funding source.

whatChanges: Binding inside Parliament: it creates the association and gives it space and staff under the Speaker.
Membership rules, eligibility and functions are left undefined.
readings.insight:
Adopted before the region's first parliamentary election, the association would in practice serve former members of the appointed transition authority. The text does not define who qualifies, how members join or what the association may do beyond its broad aims.

As filed on 15 October 2024 (Proposed Resolution No. 644), it 'requested the Bangsamoro Parliament' to set up the association; the adopted version, 13 months later on a Committee on Rules report (No. 162), authorizes the Speaker instead and adds the room and secretariat.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office to file the appropriate pleading asking the Supreme Court to decide the pending cases on the first BARMM parliamentary election before 30 March 2026, the date COMELEC set for it. The resolution goes to the Attorney General 'in the most expeditious manner', and to the House of Representatives and the Senate for information.

Adopted on 15 December 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The Supreme Court's decision of 30 September 2025 in Ali v. BTA Parliament and Macapaar v. COMELEC struck down the earlier districting laws and ordered elections by 31 March 2026; COMELEC Resolution No. 11181 of 19 November 2025 set 30 March 2026, with candidacy filing on 5 to 9 January 2026, while the BTA had yet to pass a new districting law. The resolution lists 3 other pending cases: G.R. No. 267368, filed 14 June 2023 against the Bangsamoro Electoral Code (BAA 35); G.R. No. 277012, filed 20 February 2024 by the ISAMA Party over registration rules for regional parties; and G.R. No. E-00158, filed 9 July 2025 against Republic Act No. 12123. It also cites Senate Bill No. 1587, filed 9 December 2025 to fix the election on 30 March 2026, and an MILF statement the same day that the 120-day bar on altering precincts before an election made a 30 March election legally impossible. Filed by MP Ishak V. Mastura and 7 others.
whoIsAffected: Voters and candidates in the first Bangsamoro parliamentary election
Parties to the pending Supreme Court cases
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office
whatChanges: A request to the region's own legal office, which, the resolution says, was already set to file a motion for early resolution.
Copies go to both houses of Congress.
readings.insight:
As filed on 3 December 2025 (Proposed Resolution No. 772), this urged the Supreme Court itself to decide the cases; the adopted version redirects the request to the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office, which a WHEREAS clause says had already filed a Motion for Partial Reconsideration on 21 October 2025 and was to file a Motion for Early Resolution.

The registry records what followed. BAA 86, apportioning the district seats, is dated 12 January 2026, 77 days before 30 March and inside the 120-day window the resolution warned about. COMELEC announced on 28 January 2026 that it was deferring the 30 March election, and Republic Act No. 12317 reset it to 14 September 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recommends the immediate designation of the national government's chair of the Intergovernmental Relations Body (IGRB), and endorses Special Assistant to the President Antonio Ernesto F. Lagdameo Jr., described as a Mindanaoan and an active IGRB participant since the start of the Marcos administration, as the national government's co-chair. The resolution goes to the Office of the President through Executive Secretary Ralph Recto.

Adopted on 17 December 2025.
readings.whyProposed: The IGRB, created under Section 2, Article VI of the Organic Law to resolve national-regional issues through regular consultation, had been co-chaired on the national side by DBM Secretary Amenah Pangandaman, under whom it formed a Technical Working Group on Sulu's transition to Region IX. Her resignation from the DBM left the chair vacant, and the resolution says the vacancy stopped the IGRB from convening and delayed many intergovernmental issues, including Sulu's transition. Filed by MP Jose I. Lorena and 49 others.
whoIsAffected: The Bangsamoro Government in its dealings with the national government
Sulu's government workers and residents awaiting the transition
Secretary Antonio Ernesto F. Lagdameo Jr.
implementedBy: Office of the President
whatChanges: A recommendation and endorsement; the designation is the President's to make.
Sent to the Office of the President through the Executive Secretary.
readings.insight:
This consolidates 2 proposals filed and adopted on the same day, 17 December 2025: Proposed Resolution No. 774, a 4-author recommendation to fill the chair, and No. 775, a 47-author request to name Lagdameo. 7 months earlier Resolution No. 549 had urged the President to keep Lagdameo in his post, and Resolution No. 546 had complained that the IGRB was not giving out information on Sulu.

The IGRB's stall is Parliament's own explanation here for the Sulu delay. Resolution No. 569 (21 April 2026) later commended Pangandaman as former IGRB co-chair; the registry does not show whether Lagdameo was designated.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends its own rules (Resolution No. 6) to create a Chief Minister's Hour. A new item, Chief Minister's Hour (Wednesday), is added to the daily Order of Business right after the roll call. The Order of Business is to be posted on the websites of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and the Bangsamoro Government and, as far as practicable, emailed to Members at least 3 days before session.

Rule XVIII is rewritten. At the start of each regular session the Chief Minister delivers a general policy speech, and selected Cabinet members may discuss their ministries. Once a month, on a Wednesday and in open session, the Chief Minister or a Cabinet Minister reports on the accomplishments and status of the Bangsamoro Government without interruption; Members may then ask clarificatory questions on matters covered by the report.

Authored by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and 28 others. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law gives the region a parliamentary form of government. The authors argue that, in such a system, the Government of the Day should have regular chances, through the Chief Minister, to report to Parliament, answer questions on its operations and clarify issues.
whoIsAffected: The Chief Minister and Cabinet Ministers, who gain a monthly reporting slot on the floor.
Members of Parliament, who may question the report.
The public, who can follow the report in open session.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: This is an internal-rules resolution, so it has force inside Parliament: the Order of Business and Rule XVIII now read as amended.
It puts a monthly report by the Chief Minister or a Cabinet Minister into the rules, but sets no consequence if no report is given.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: Consolidated Proposed Resolution No. 87 approved as a simple resolution; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 31.
readings.insight: Members' questions are limited to clarificatory questions on matters covered by the report, so the hour is a report with questions, not an open interpellation. The rule also requires the Order of Business to be posted on the BTA's website, yet Resolution 40, adopted 26 days later, says the BTA had no website of its own and relied on the BARMM site run from the Office of the Chief Minister. Resolutions 29, 31 and 32, all amending the rules, were adopted the same day.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends Rule IV, Section 1 and Rule VI, Section 4 of its rules (Resolution No. 6) so that a Deputy Majority Floor Leader and a Deputy Minority Floor Leader are also elected.

Members who voted for the Speaker form the Majority and all others the Minority. Members appointed after the Speaker's election choose a side by oral or written manifestation to the Speaker. The Majority and the Minority each elect their own floor leader and deputies from among their members.

Authored by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The rules named only the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and the 2 floor leaders as officers, and nothing allowed another Member to stand in when a floor leader was absent. The authors wanted to avoid disruption on the floor and keep the Majority and Minority continuously represented in all committees.
whoIsAffected: The Majority and Minority blocs, who each elect a deputy floor leader.
Members appointed after the Speaker's election, who now have a set way to join a bloc.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: The rules now provide for 2 deputy floor leaders; this binds Parliament.
It also writes down how late-appointed Members choose the Majority or the Minority.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong asked whether the deputy floor leader positions must be created before members are elected; the Chair said the positions were already created, and MP Adiong said he had no objection.
30 August 2019: Adopted as a simple resolution; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 32.
readings.insight: Despite the title's reference to an election in the Parliament, the deputies are chosen by each bloc from among its own members, not by the whole house. The resolution also adds a rule the title does not mention: how Members appointed after the Speaker's election join a bloc. It was 1 of 3 rules amendments adopted on 30 August 2019, with Resolutions 29 and 31.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses support for House Bills No. 3543, 3418 and 3922, which seek a law giving monetary compensation for the losses suffered by the people of Marawi. It prays that Congress consolidate the bills and enact them swiftly, and sends the resolution to the Speaker of the House of Representatives for appropriate action.

Authored by MPs Eddie M. Alih, Hamid Aminoddin D. Barra, Paisalin P. Tago, Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong and Anna Tarhata S. Basman. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law lists reparations, including just compensation and relocation, as part of transitional justice. The resolution recounts the toll of the Marawi Siege of May to October 2017: more than 1,000 dead, 98% of the city's population displaced, 95% of structures in the 4 square kilometre main battle area heavily damaged or collapsed, 3,152 buildings completely destroyed and 2,145 more partly to heavily damaged. Where compensation cannot come from the offender, it says, the state should provide it.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Marawi who lost family, homes or property in the 2017 siege.
implementedBy: House of Representatives
whatChanges: Nothing changes unless Congress acts; the resolution is an expression of support.
A copy goes to the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong proposed adding House Bill Nos. 3428 and 3922 to the sixth Whereas clause; the author accepted, but MP Adiong later withdrew it and moved to drop the clause naming bill authors.
30 August 2019: MP Paisalin Tago objected that commending congressmen for filing a bill is inappropriate since it is their duty, and warned of setting a precedent.
30 August 2019: MP Eddie Alih defended recognizing congressmen whose bills help Marawi siege victims and moved for division of the house if the objection stood.
30 August 2019: MP Hamid Aminoddin Barra proposed rewording the title to 'expressing support to the filing' so the body would not be commending the filer.
30 August 2019: MP Alzad Sattar said members should first ask what the people have felt from the BTA's work in 6 months, saying his inbox is full of complaints.
30 August 2019: Speaker Ali Pangalian Balindong moved approval subject to style without naming the House bill authors; MP Paisalin Tago subscribed and the motion carried.

30 August 2019: Approved subject to style on motion of Speaker Ali Pangalian Balindong, without naming the House bill authors; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 33, retitled as expressing support for House Bills 3543, 3418 and 3922.
readings.insight: Parliament pressed this issue repeatedly. Resolution 14 (26 June 2019) had already backed a compensation law for Butig, Piagapo and Marawi. Resolutions 151 and 156 (September 2021) asked the Senate to move its bill; Resolution 216 (17 February 2022) appealed to President Duterte to sign Senate Bill No. 2420 and House Bill No. 9925, the Marawi Siege Victims Compensation Act; and Resolution 308 (24 January 2023) thanked President Marcos for constituting the Marawi Compensation Board. The 3 House bills named here were not the numbers that reached the President.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament realigns the 2019 Personnel Services allotment of the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly's assemblymen and their co-terminus staff to pay the 5 staff of each BTA Member for July 2019. Copies go to the Civil Service Commission and the Commission on Audit.

Authored by MPs Eduard U. Guerra and Ubaida C. Pacasem. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Elected ARMM officials sat in the BTA only until noon of 30 June 2019, but the 2019 General Appropriations Act still carried Personnel Services money for them and their 6 co-terminus staff each. The Department of Budget and Management approved 5 staff positions per BTA Member, an Executive Assistant VI, 2 legislative officers (VI and V), an Executive Assistant III and an Executive Assistant II, funded only from 1 August 2019. Members had already hired staff and used them in sessions and committee work before then.
whoIsAffected: Staff of BTA Members who worked in July 2019 before their positions were funded.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
Civil Service Commission
Commission on Audit

funding.detail: No amount is named. The resolution redirects the 2019 General Appropriations Act Personnel Services allotment for the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly's assemblymen and co-terminus staff to July 2019 pay for BTA Members' staff.

whatChanges: It authorizes, on Parliament's side, the use of leftover RLA personnel money for 1 month of BTA staff pay.
Copies go to the Civil Service Commission and the Commission on Audit, which can examine the realignment.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: MP Omar Yasser Sema objected to approval subject to style because funding already allotted to an office cannot be realigned by mere resolution.
30 August 2019: MP Baintan Ampatuan suggested retitling it as a resolution authorizing use of personal services funds for BTA staff, noting a bill is needed to realign.
30 August 2019: Approved subject to style; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 34.
readings.insight: The resolution gives no peso figure for the realignment or for July salaries, so the amount moved cannot be checked from the text. It is 1 of 3 resolutions spending money left over from the abolished Regional Legislative Assembly: Resolution 9 used ₱63,000,000 of it for BTA operating expenses in March and April 2019, and Resolution 53 used ₱8,485,158 for staff year-end bonuses.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Ministry of Health to brief the Bangsamoro Transition Authority on the health situation of the region, particularly in light of the dengue outbreaks being declared around the country. The resolution is forwarded to the Ministry of Health.

Authored by MPs Abraham T. Burahan and Paisalin P. Tago. Adopted on 18 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Several provinces had declared dengue outbreaks in the preceding days. The authors want the public to know the extent of dengue and other diseases so they can prevent and prepare for it, and want Parliament informed so it can recommend action to the Ministry and the Chief Minister, including more funds for contingencies.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region exposed to dengue and other outbreaks.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
whatChanges: It is a request for a briefing; it sets no date, format or follow-up.
A copy goes to the Ministry of Health.
deliberation: 18 September 2019: Deputy Minister Zul Qarneyn M. Abas reported 2,516 suspected dengue cases from 1 January to 13 August, about twice the same period last year, with 22 deaths and a 0.9% case fatality rate.
18 September 2019: MP Laisa Alamia asked for the provincial breakdown; MP Abas cited Maguindanao 985, Lanao del Sur 712 and Marawi 407, and agreed fresh-water areas are most affected.
18 September 2019: MP Laisa Alamia asked the Ministry of Health to study the causes of the 22 deaths; MP Abas said the deaths were in hospitals from complications.
18 September 2019: On the dengue vaccine, MP Abas said many academic doctors do not recommend it and that 200 plus policemen vaccinated through DOH-ARMM are being monitored, with no deaths reported.

18 September 2019: MP Omar Yasser Sema asked about readiness and funding; MP Abas said many programs are unfunded and gave 16 billion as the ideal initial figure, which could be toned down (the journal later refers to it as 16 million pesos).
18 September 2019: MP Musa Diamla asked the Ministry of Health to include completion and operation of the unfinished Marawi City Public Hospital in its plans.

18 September 2019: Taken up in the Business for the Day with a dengue briefing by Deputy Minister of Health Zul Qarneyn M. Abas; the journal records no separate vote, but the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 35 of session 16.
readings.insight: The resolution cites no dengue case count for the region; the need for data is the point of the request. Nearly 4 years later Parliament asked again: Resolution 383 (14 August 2023) directed the Ministry of Health, in aid of legislation, to report on dengue cases, deaths and prevention measures in the region.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Department of the Interior and Local Government, through the regional Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, to clarify Memorandum Circular No. 2019-121 on clearing roads of illegal structures. It poses 4 questions: what area the circular covers; how it treats titled lot owners; whether the clearing amounts to road widening, entitling owners to just compensation; and whether local executives, rather than the Department of Public Works and Highways, may demolish structures within 15 meters of the centre of a national highway.

Copies go to the DILG Secretary, the DPWH Secretary and the BARMM Minister of the Interior and Local Government. Authored by MP Sittie Shahara I. Mastura. Adopted on 20 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: After President Duterte's 2019 State of the Nation Address, the DILG issued the circular on 29 July 2019 giving local executives 60 days to show results, requiring weekly reports and warning of administrative cases for non-compliance. Some local executives treated 15 meters from the centre of national highways as right of way and removed everything in it. Titled owners argue that this is taking property without just compensation, that the circular does not mention a 15 meter measurement, and that clearing national highways is the DPWH's job.
whoIsAffected: Titled lot owners along national highways whose structures were removed or threatened.
Local chief executives facing administrative cases if they did not comply and lawsuits if they did.
implementedBy: Department of the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Department of Public Works and Highways
whatChanges: It asks a national department for an interpretation; it cannot stop any clearing operation.
Copies go to the DILG, the DPWH and the regional interior ministry.
deliberation: 19 September 2019: MP Sittie Shahara I. Mastura said some local chief executives were widening roads, treating 15 meters from the highway center as right of way, which requires compensation.
19 September 2019: The Majority Floor Leader cited DILG Secretary Año that Memorandum Circular 2019-121 covers only road obstructions and not road widening.
19 September 2019: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan asked whether the circular was officially received by the BARMM or only circulated on Facebook, saying the BARMM is not bound otherwise.
19 September 2019: MP Suharto M. Ambolodto asked that a Committee on Local Government look into acts already done in good faith by local officials.
19 September 2019: Adopted subject to style on motion of MP Laisa Alamia; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 36.
readings.insight: The resolution sets out the lot owners' arguments in detail but takes no position of its own beyond asking for clarification, and names no town, case or count of structures removed. It also asks for nothing to be paused while the answer is awaited, even though the circular's 60 day reporting window was running.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament states its strong objection to House Resolution No. 333, which calls for creating a national Department of Public Works and Highways office in the Bangsamoro region. Copies go to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and all members of Congress from the region.

Authored by MPs Paisalin P. Tago, Abraham T. Burahan, Jose I. Lorena, Nabil A. Tan, Omar Yasser C. Sema and Eddie M. Alih. Adopted on 20 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Public works and infrastructure is among the powers the Organic Law gives the Bangsamoro Government (Article V, Section 2). The authors argue the House resolution is unnecessary because Article XIII, Section 37 already says the National Government funds and implements national roads, bridges, water, flood control and irrigation in the region, and that disputes belong in the Intergovernmental Relations Body and the Intergovernmental Infrastructure Development Board.
whoIsAffected: The regional Ministry of Public Works and the national DPWH, whose roles in the region were in question.
implementedBy: House of Representatives
whatChanges: It is a statement of objection; it has no effect on the House resolution itself.
Copies go to the House Speaker and the region's members of Congress.
deliberation: 19 September 2019: MP Paisalin P. Tago said House Resolution No. 333 was unnecessary because the BOL already provides the Intergovernmental Relations mechanism, and the BTA must protect autonomy.

19 September 2019: MP Jose I. Lorena called it an anathema to meaningful autonomy contrary to Section 6, Article VI and Section 37, Article XIII of RA 11054, and said he would go to court against any such law.

19 September 2019: Deputy Speaker Hatimil E. Hassan noted RA 11054 created a Ministry of Public Works without Highways and that the 2020 national budget has more than ₱5 billion for highways in the BARMM.
19 September 2019: MP Don Mustapha A. Loong argued the national DPWH must have offices in the region because the BOL makes it responsible for the 992 kilometers of national roads.
19 September 2019: MP Laisa M. Alamia noted the resolution did not follow the 3-day notice rule and cited Disomangcop v. Datumanong on DPWH field offices.
19 September 2019: OIC Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua read a text from Congressman Mujiv Hataman saying the House authors were allies, proposed a meeting first, and later abstained.

19 September 2019: Nominal vote: 40 in favor, 9 against, 7 abstentions. Division of the house by standing, not a name-by-name roll. The first count was 41 in favor and 10 against; after MP Romeo K. Sema and OIC Chief Minister Abdulraof A. Macacua said they had abstained, a second count gave 40 in favor, 9 against and 7 abstentions. The Speaker did not vote. No names are recorded.
19 September 2019: After a division of the house by standing vote, approved 40 in favor, 9 against, 7 abstentions on a second count; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 37.
readings.insight: Parliament's position later shifted. Resolution 346 (21 June 2023) supported President Marcos's call to create DPWH district engineering offices and a DPWH regional office for the region, the kind of national presence this resolution objected to in 2019. Later resolutions such as 425 (15 January 2024) and 559 (20 August 2025) asked the national DPWH directly for repairs in the region.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples to cease and desist from conducting delineation processes in the territory of the Bangsamoro region.

Authored by MP Akmad I. Abas and 38 others. Adopted on 25 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Teduray had applied to the NCIP for certificates of ancestral domain title, and the NCIP had begun delineating the claim in Talayan, Sharif Aguak, Guindulungan and Datu Odin Sinsuat in Maguindanao. The authors argue that the Organic Law gives the Bangsamoro Government authority over ancestral domain and cadastral surveys, and requires a regional ministry for indigenous peoples, so the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, not the NCIP, has authority in the region.
whoIsAffected: Teduray communities whose ancestral domain application was being processed by the NCIP.
Residents and landholders in the 4 Maguindanao towns covered by the delineation.
implementedBy: National Commission on Indigenous Peoples
whatChanges: It is an urging; the NCIP is a national body and the resolution cannot order it.
It names no recipient for copies.
deliberation: 25 September 2019: The Majority Floor Leader said the NCIP Region XII survey covers 201,880 hectares, 80% of Maguindanao, and that only the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs has jurisdiction in the BARMM.

25 September 2019: MP Romeo C. Saliga, for the non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, said approval would deny them ancestral domain rights under the Constitution, IPRA and RA 11054, and moved that the NCIP and claimants be invited to explain.
25 September 2019: MP Romeo C. Saliga said titled and government properties, roughly 50%, would be excluded from the 201,880 hectares, leaving far less for the ancestral domain.
25 September 2019: MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu agreed with the proponents but suggested softening the word 'protesting' in the title, and joined as co-author.

25 September 2019: MP Jamel D. Macaraya and MP Maisara D. Latiph said the NCIP move runs against the BOL and should go through the Intergovernmental Relations Body, Latiph citing the 200,000 hectares involved.
25 September 2019: Approved on motion of the Majority Floor Leader, with the minority interposing no objection; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 38.
readings.insight: The title also asks the NCIP to stop proceedings to issue ancestral domain titles, but the operative clause asks only that delineation stop. The adopted text prints the same WHEREAS clause, that the NCIP has no power to delineate or issue titles in the region, twice in a row. The question was settled in regional law 5 years later: the Bangsamoro Indigenous Peoples' Act (BAA 64, ratified 10 December 2024) requires pending NCIP ancestral domain applications, naming the Téduray Lambangian claim, to be turned over to the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs within 90 days.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Philippine Statistics Authority to prioritize the rollout of the Philippine Identification System (Republic Act No. 11055) in the Bangsamoro region, and says the PSA and the BTA shall work together on it.

Copies go to the PSA Director-General, the National Security Adviser, the Secretary of National Defense, the Secretary of the Interior and Local Government, the Chairman of the Commission on Elections and the head of PhilHealth. Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 25 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The authors want a single identification system for residents of the region to simplify public and private transactions, curb fraud and red tape, and strengthen internal security. They cite recent bombings in Sultan Kudarat and Sulu that the security sector attributed to foreign and local terrorists.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region who need to register for the national ID.
implementedBy: Philippine Statistics Authority
whatChanges: It asks a national agency to move the region up its rollout schedule; it cannot require it.
Copies go to 6 national offices, from the PSA to the defense and security officials.
deliberation: 25 September 2019: MP Omar Yasser C. Sema said many people had come to his office for affidavits to prove their identity and urgently need official IDs, particularly in Cotabato City.
25 September 2019: MP Omar Yasser C. Sema cited 3 bombings involving foreign nationals and said PSA IDs would also help identify voters under the Electoral Code being drafted.
25 September 2019: Approved with no interpellation after co-authors were added in the period of amendments; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 39.
readings.insight: The case is made mainly on security grounds, and the copy list leans that way too, with the National Security Adviser and the Secretary of National Defense on it. The clause that the PSA and BTA 'shall work together' names no mechanism, office or timetable. It is the only adopted resolution in the index about the national ID.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls for the urgent establishment of an official website for the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, maintained by its own Information and Communication Technology Unit, to inform the public of developments in Parliament and serve as an official online source of information, consistent with full disclosure, transparency and good governance.

Authored by MP Laisa M. Alamia and 22 others. Adopted on 25 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: As of 18 September 2019 the BTA had handled 15 proposed bills, 101 resolutions, 6 committee reports and 15 journals, plus calendars and procurement, none easily accessible to the public. The only official website was the BARMM site run by the ICT Office under the Office of the Chief Minister, which covered executive work. Members themselves got documents from the Secretary-General only on request. The authors cite the constitutional policy of full public disclosure and the spread of fake news.
whoIsAffected: The public, who had no official online source for Parliament's work.
Members of Parliament, who relied on documents released on request.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It is a call addressed to Parliament itself, but it names no office to deliver it, no deadline and no budget.
deliberation: 25 September 2019: MP Don Mustapha A. Loong said an official BTA website would spare members trips to the Secretary-General's office for copies of resolutions, bills and session schedules.
25 September 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong asked whether a budget is needed; MP Loong said no, it would be charged to the Secretary-General's Management Information System Unit.

25 September 2019: MP Jose I. Lorena urged allocating funds to keep up with information technology; MP Loong declined to set a precedent of budget items in a simple resolution, pointing to the 2020 budget.
25 September 2019: MP Nabil A. Tan asked whether the BTA has expert technicians; MP Loong said the hardware is procured and the website is 80% done.
25 September 2019: MP Saffrullah M. Dipatuan said the BARMM must communicate its accomplishments after 7 months and asked to co-author.
25 September 2019: Approved after interpellation; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 40.
readings.insight: A month earlier, Resolution 31 had already required the Order of Business to be posted on the BTA's website, which this resolution says did not exist. The BTA's website was later set up: the adopted resolutions read for this registry are published on parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph, and Resolution 566 (27 January 2026) extended live streaming on the BTA official website to committee hearings.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament creates a Special Committee on Marawi Recovery, Reconstruction, and Rehabilitation (the Special Committee on Marawi) to gather data on and monitor the rebuilding of Marawi City and recommend what the Bangsamoro Government should do. It has a Chair, a Vice-Chair and members as the rules allow, confirmed in plenary.

The committee may invite national, regional and local agencies, NGOs, development partners and experts, and issue subpoenas for testimony and documents in accordance with law. It may hold consultations, field interviews, surveys and inspections, must report periodically to Parliament, especially on aid reaching residents, and must make its hearings and reports public. BARMM ministries and offices must cooperate when asked. Its Chair requests a budget from the Speaker, and it exists until Parliament dissolves it.

Authored by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and 39 others. Adopted on 26 September 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Almost 2 years had passed since the President declared Marawi liberated on 17 October 2017, and the rebuilding was led by national agencies through Task Force Bangon Marawi. Under Article VI, Section 13 of the Organic Law, the Marawi rehabilitation program stays nationally funded, but the Bangsamoro Government may add supplemental funding. The authors argue any such help must rest on accurate information, which the public also has a right to.
whoIsAffected: Residents and displaced families of Marawi City.
National, regional and local agencies involved in the rebuilding, which may be invited or subpoenaed.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
BARMM ministries and offices

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. The committee's Chair is to request from the Speaker whatever budget its work requires.

whatChanges: It creates a standing special committee inside Parliament, with subpoena powers to be used in accordance with law.
BARMM ministries and offices are required to cooperate; national agencies can be invited or subpoenaed but not directed.
readings.insight: The committee has no end date and no set reporting schedule beyond 'periodic' reports. Its job is to inform supplemental regional help, since the Organic Law leaves Marawi's rehabilitation to national funding. Marawi stayed on Parliament's agenda: Resolution 52 (29 November 2019) opposed new military camps in the city, and Resolutions 179 (2021) and 476 (2024) took up the displaced residents.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Health to conduct an intensive education and immunization campaign across the Bangsamoro region to contain and eradicate the polio outbreak.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and 6 others. Adopted on 17 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Philippines had been polio-free since October 2000, with the last case in 1993. On 19 September 2019 the Department of Health confirmed polio in an unvaccinated 3-year-old girl from Lanao del Sur, then a 5-year-old boy in Laguna, and environmental samples in Manila and Davao tested positive. Children under 1 year need 3 doses of oral polio vaccine and 1 dose of inactivated vaccine. Some Muslim parents refuse or hesitate to vaccinate, and the resolution notes the Ministry may use a fatwa on immunization to address their concerns.
whoIsAffected: Children under 5 in the region, the group most at risk.
Parents, including Muslim parents hesitant about vaccination.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
whatChanges: It urges the Ministry of Health; it sets no target, deadline or reporting requirement.
It names no recipient for copies.
readings.insight: The resolution speaks directly to vaccine hesitancy among Muslim parents and suggests a religious ruling as a tool, a point specific to the region. 6 weeks later, after 2 more cases were confirmed in Maguindanao, Parliament went further with Resolution 51, asking for a region-wide state of calamity.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament resolves to work for the creation of a Bureau for orphans and widows who are victims of war and violence. The resolution says the Bureau would sit directly under the 'Ministry of Social Welfare' and provide basic services, including access to education and sports, nutritional supplements, hygiene and sanitation, and psychological and mental health support, and help reintegrate them into the mainstream.

Authored by MP Susana S. Anayatin. Adopted on 18 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Past conflicts in the former ARMM displaced countless families. The authors say children and widows of war carry trauma, lack access to education, food and shelter, and are vulnerable to violent extremism. They cite the Constitution's provisions on youth and women and the Organic Law's duties toward children, especially orphans of tender age, and toward women.
whoIsAffected: Children orphaned by war and violence.
Women widowed by war and violence.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: A resolution cannot create a government bureau; Parliament only commits to 'endeavor' for one.
It names no bill, budget or deadline, and no copy goes to the ministry.
readings.insight: The bureau is placed under a 'Ministry of Social Welfare', a name the region's social services ministry does not carry; later resolutions call it the Ministry of Social Services and Development. The resolution gives no count of orphans or widows. Parliament returned to the subject in Resolution 557 (24 July 2025), asking that ministry to report on the status of orphanages in the region.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament resolves that the Bangsamoro Transition Authority shall either end its sessions or go into recess a reasonable time before Friday Jumu'ah prayers, so Members can go to the mosque.

Authored by MPs Datu Tucao O. Mastura, Sittie Shahara I. Mastura and Ibrahim D. Ali. Adopted on 18 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Friday sessions had been running into the time for congregational prayer, and Members did not want to disrupt floor proceedings by leaving. Most Members are Muslims, and the resolution quotes Surah 62, verses 9 and 10, which call believers to leave off business for the Friday prayer.
whoIsAffected: Muslim Members of Parliament and staff who attend Friday prayers.
Anyone following or taking part in Friday sessions.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It sets a practice for Parliament's own Friday sessions.
readings.insight: The rule leaves 'a reasonable time' undefined and sets no hour. Unlike Resolutions 31 and 32, it does not amend the written rules in Resolution No. 6, so it stands as a separate standing resolution.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament resolves that in the 2020 budget all sub-regions of the Bangsamoro region will have an equitable share, for an inclusive fiscal policy consistent with the Organic Law and the principle behind the block grant.

Authored by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and 11 others. Adopted on 24 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management was holding technical budget hearings for 2020 anchored on the Interim Chief Minister's 12-point priority agenda. The authors want the 2020 fiscal framework to spread growth across the southwestern, north central and south central sub-regions, improving access to education, health, housing and jobs, and propose that equitable allocation be based on the representation of communities by congressional districts in the provinces.
whoIsAffected: Provinces and communities in each of the 3 sub-regions.
Ministries preparing their 2020 budget proposals.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management
whatChanges: It is a statement of Parliament's sense; the budget itself had to come as a law.
It names no recipient for copies and sets no formula.
readings.insight: The resolution names a basis for sharing, congressional district representation, but gives no formula, shares or peso figures, so whether the 2020 budget met it cannot be judged from the text. Parliament ratified that budget, the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act for FY 2020 (BAA 3), 36 days later on 29 November 2019.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its deepest condolences to the family of former Senate President Aquilino 'Nene' Pimentel Jr., who died on 20 October 2019, and acknowledges with gratitude his support and contributions to the Bangsamoro.

Authored by MP Ahod Balawag Ebrahim. Adopted on 24 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Pimentel served 17 years in the Senate and was Senate President from 2000 to 2001. He was jailed several times under martial law, authored Republic Act No. 6734, the law that preceded the Bangsamoro region, was called the father of the Local Government Code, and openly supported the creation of the Bangsamoro Government in congressional hearings.
whoIsAffected: The Pimentel family.
whatChanges: None beyond the record; it is an expression of condolence.
readings.insight: Adopted 4 days after his death. Its sole author was the Interim Chief Minister. In December 2022 Parliament thanked Senator Aquilino 'Koko' Pimentel III for disaster relief in Resolution 287.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration to look into the plight of distressed overseas Filipino workers from the Bangsamoro region, learn their conditions and help them obtain the help and benefits due to them from the national or regional government. It asks OWWA to give Parliament official data on distressed workers from the region, their current conditions and the assistance already given.

Copies go to the OWWA Administrator and the Minister of Labor and Employment. Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 24 October 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Many residents of the region work overseas, most of them women, and a number are poorly paid, abused or illegally recruited, returning as distressed workers. Reports from non-government organizations counted 52 cases of distressed workers from the region in 2017 and 2018 and 92 in 2019. The resolution cites Republic Act No. 10801, which makes OWWA a principal agency for the welfare of overseas workers.
whoIsAffected: Distressed overseas workers from the region, mostly women, and their families.
implementedBy: Overseas Workers Welfare Administration
Ministry of Labor and Employment
whatChanges: It asks a national agency for action and for data; no deadline is set for either.
Copies go to the OWWA Administrator and the regional labor minister.
readings.insight: The case figures come from NGOs, not government, which is why the resolution asks OWWA for official data. Parliament later legislated on the subject itself: the Overseas Bangsamoro Workers Act of 2020 (BAA 19) was ratified on 17 June 2021.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament gives full support to the Bangsamoro Children's Declaration, and resolves that laws passed by Parliament and programs of the Bangsamoro Government shall ensure that children's rights are promoted, protected and fulfilled.

The Declaration, written by children of the region, asks for good schools with complete facilities, freedom from poverty and hunger, lasting peace and an end to war and rido, officials who do their duties and avoid corruption, support for parents to care for their children, and for children to be listened to.

Authored by MP Akmad I. Abas and 75 others. Adopted on 20 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The occasion is the 30th anniversary of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by the Philippines and 195 other countries. The resolution cites the Constitution and the Organic Law's duties toward children, and Philippine Statistics Authority figures: 31.4% of children nationally lived below the poverty line in 2015, while the poverty rate in the autonomous region rose from 52.6% in 2006 to 63.1% in 2015.
whoIsAffected: Children in the Bangsamoro region.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
Bangsamoro Government
whatChanges: It is a statement of support and principle; it creates no program, office or budget.
readings.insight: With 76 principal authors, it carried the names of almost all of the BTA's 80 Members. The commitment that laws and programs 'shall ensure' children's rights has no mechanism or measure attached.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament formally acknowledges the turnover of 63 barangays to the Bangsamoro Government and thanks the leadership and people of North Cotabato for paving the way for their inclusion in the region.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph. Adopted on 22 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: In the second round of the Organic Law plebiscite on 6 February 2019, 63 of 67 barangays from 6 North Cotabato towns voted to join the region: 7 in Carmen, 7 in Kabacan, 13 in Midsayap, 12 in Pigcawayan, 2 in Aleosan and 22 in Pikit. They were officially turned over to the Interim Chief Minister and the regional Minister of the Interior and Local Government on 20 November 2019.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the 63 barangays.
The provincial government of North Cotabato.
whatChanges: None beyond the record; it is an acknowledgment and an expression of thanks.
readings.insight: Adopted 2 days after the turnover. The town counts in the text add up to 63. The barangays remained a distinct unit in Parliament's later work; Resolution 117 (24 March 2021) treated them alongside the provinces when asking for focal persons for an indigent database.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament creates a Committee on Bangsamoro Justice System as one of its statutory committees and resolves that its rules be amended to include it. Copies go to the Speaker, the Committees on Rules, Finance and Budget, and Accounts, and the Secretary-General.

Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema and 9 others. Adopted on 29 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Article X of the Organic Law sets up the Bangsamoro Justice System, recognizing Shari'ah, tribal justice, the regular courts and alternative dispute resolution. Section 4 gives Parliament power to legislate on Shari'ah in personal, family and property law, commercial and civil matters not covered by the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, and minor offenses. The BTA had not created a committee for this when it organized.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament working on Shari'ah and justice legislation.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It creates a new statutory committee of Parliament; this binds Parliament.
It directs that the rules be amended, but does not itself set out the committee's jurisdiction or membership.
readings.insight: This is an internal resolution with force: it adds a standing committee. The authors argue the committee is needed for Parliament to exercise its Shari'ah lawmaking power, though the text does not show that the Organic Law requires a dedicated committee. The amending text for the rules is left for later.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Interim Chief Minister, through the Interim Minister of Health, to declare the Bangsamoro region under a state of calamity because of the polio outbreak, and calls on all local government units to support and take part in the campaign to stop the spread of polio.

Authored by MPs Zul Qarneyn M. Abas and Saffrullah M. Dipatuan. Adopted on 29 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: 19 years after the country was declared polio-free, a case was confirmed in a 3-year-old girl in Lanao del Sur on 18 September 2019, after vaccine-derived poliovirus had been detected in Metro Manila and Davao City since 22 July. The Secretary of Health declared a national outbreak on 19 September 2019. In October 2 more cases were confirmed in Datu Paglas and Datu Piang, Maguindanao. Polio has no cure but is preventable by vaccination. The resolution notes that funds could come from the region's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management funds.
whoIsAffected: Children under 5 in the region.
Local government units asked to join the vaccination campaign.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Health
Local government units

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It notes that polio activities could be funded from the region's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management funds, which a calamity declaration would open up, but names no amount.

whatChanges: It asks the executive for a calamity declaration; only the Chief Minister can make one.
It names no recipient for copies.
readings.insight: Its co-author, MP Saffrullah M. Dipatuan, is the official Resolution 60 addresses 2 months later as the Minister of Health, so the request is routed in part through its own author's office. It is Parliament's 2nd polio resolution in 6 weeks, after Resolution 42.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament opposes the establishment of more military camps in the Most Affected Area of Marawi City, and appeals to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte not to push through with a planned military camp in the city. Copies go to the Office of the President, the Office of the Chief Minister, the Intergovernmental Relations Body secretariat and Task Force Bangon Marawi.

Authored by MP Paisalin P. Tago. Adopted on 29 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: On 14 October 2019 the Philippine Army announced plans for new camps in Marawi after securing writs of possession over more than 10 hectares in Barangays Caloocan East and Kapantaran. The resolution cites UNHCR figures of 73,266 people still displaced, slow rehabilitation, unresolved land claims inside military reservations, and a warning from then Senior Associate Justice Antonio Carpio about dispossession.
