It says the plan was made without consulting residents, who openly oppose it, and that terrorism is better fought through local governance, intelligence and winning public support.
whoIsAffected: Displaced residents of Marawi's Most Affected Area, especially in Caloocan East and Kapantaran.
The Philippine Army.
implementedBy: Office of the President
Philippine Army
whatChanges: It is an appeal; the decision rests with the President and the Army.
Copies go to the Office of the President, the Office of the Chief Minister, the Intergovernmental Relations Body and Task Force Bangon Marawi.
readings.insight: The resolution gives specific figures: more than 10 hectares under writs of possession and 73,266 people still displaced 2 years after the siege. Displacement stayed on Parliament's agenda: Resolution 179 (14 October 2021) backed displaced residents' call to return to the Most Affected Area, and Resolution 476 (17 July 2024) sought a 2-year extension of leases for their temporary shelters.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes using ₱8,485,158 from the unspent Personnel Services appropriation of the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly to pay the year-end bonuses and cash gifts of Members' immediate support staff, including newly hired Legislative Staff Officers assigned to committees.

Authored by MP Musa K. S. Diamla. Adopted on 29 November 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Regional Legislative Assembly's 2019 funds passed to the BTA under the Organic Law. The Department of Budget and Management had allocated ₱7,258,182 for 273 proposed support staff positions, but Members had since filled 410 positions, including committee staff, and the allocation could not cover year-end bonuses and cash gifts for all of them.
whoIsAffected: The 410 immediate support staff of Members of Parliament.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament

funding.detail: ₱8,485,158 from the unexpended Personnel Services appropriation of the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly under the 2019 General Appropriations Act, for year-end bonuses and cash gifts.

whatChanges: It authorizes, on Parliament's side, spending leftover RLA personnel funds on staff bonuses.
It names no recipient for copies.
readings.insight: Support staff positions grew from 273 to 410, or 137 more than budgeted. Spread evenly, ₱8,485,158 comes to about ₱20,696 per position. It is the 3rd resolution in 2019 to spend leftover Regional Legislative Assembly money, after Resolution 9 (₱63,000,000 for operating expenses) and Resolution 34 (July 2019 staff pay).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament extends the phase-out of accountable officers of the former ARMM, including finance officers and selected support staff, to 31 March 2020, or until all accounts are settled and annual financial and physical accomplishment reports are submitted, whichever comes first.

Ministries and offices must send the Office of the Chief Minister their list of officers to be extended, and Parliament's offices must send theirs to the Office of the Speaker, by 31 December 2019. The Chief Minister approves the list for executive offices and the Speaker for legislative offices. Their pay is charged to the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund of the FY 2020 Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.

Authored by MP Eduard U. Guerra. Adopted on 27 December 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law has the BTA schedule the gradual phase-out of the abolished ARMM offices, and the approved transition plan ended the phase-out on 31 December 2019. Ministries still had to settle accounts and submit annual financial and accomplishment reports to Parliament, the Department of Budget and Management and the Commission on Audit, which needed the officers responsible for them.
whoIsAffected: Former ARMM finance and accountable officers kept on to close the books.
Ministries and offices that must settle ARMM accounts.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Office of the Speaker
Bangsamoro ministries and offices

funding.detail: No amount is named. Salaries of the extended personnel are charged to the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund under the FY 2020 Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.

whatChanges: It keeps selected ARMM officers in service past 31 December 2019.
It sets a deadline for lists and gives the Chief Minister and the Speaker the final say on who stays.
readings.insight: Offices had 4 days, from adoption on 27 December to 31 December 2019, to submit their lists. The 3-month extension did not hold: Resolution 75 (25 June 2020) extended the phase-out further, and Resolution 95 (16 December 2020) extended it again to 30 June 2021, 18 months past the original end date.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament approves the Committee on Rules' enhancements to the BTA transition plan for 2019 to 2022.

Authored by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 27 December 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Under Article XVI, Section 6 of the Organic Law, the Interim Chief Minister submits a transition plan within the first 60 days and the BTA acts on it within 10 days. The BTA approved the plan on 17 June 2019 as Resolution No. 12, but it lacked the BTA's own organizational structure, mandates, functions and jurisdiction. The Committee on Rules filled those gaps in Committee Report No. 9, submitted in plenary on 12 December 2019.
whoIsAffected: The Parliament's own offices and staff, whose structure the enhancement covers.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It adopts the enhanced transition plan for Parliament's organization; this binds Parliament.
readings.insight: The resolution approves the changes without reproducing them; their content is in Committee Report No. 9, which is not part of the published resolution. The transition plan was revisited again more than 5 years later, when Resolution 523 (23 January 2025) required the Office of the Chief Minister, through the planning authority, to update the 2019 to 2022 plan.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls for the creation of the National Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission for the Bangsamoro (NTJRCB), as recommended in the report of the Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission (TJRC). It calls on the Inter-Cabinet Cluster Mechanism on Normalization to make the NTJRCB, and a transitional justice and reconciliation program for the whole country and not only the region, among its priorities.

Copies go to the Senate President, the Speaker of the House, the Inter-Cabinet Cluster Mechanism through its secretariat at the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, and the Office of the Chief Minister. Authored by MP Anna Tarhata S. Basman and 20 others. Adopted on 24 January 2020.
readings.whyProposed: Transitional justice is part of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. The TJRC set up under it recommended a dedicated national agency because healing cannot happen in one region alone. A bill for the NTJRCB was filed in the previous Congress but never left committee. The Organic Law lets Parliament enact a transitional justice mechanism, but only within the region. Executive Order No. 79 (s. 2019) tasked the Inter-Cabinet Cluster Mechanism with implementing the TJRC's recommendations, and recent public disputes over historical injustices, the resolution says, show the need for a national approach.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro people and other communities with grievances from the conflict.
Congress and the national agencies responsible for normalization.
implementedBy: Congress
Inter-Cabinet Cluster Mechanism on Normalization
Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
whatChanges: Nothing changes unless Congress legislates; the resolution is a call.
Copies go to both houses of Congress, the Inter-Cabinet Cluster Mechanism and the Office of the Chief Minister.
readings.insight: Parliament made the same call again in Resolution 418 (20 November 2023), urging the Senate and House leaders to prioritize the NTJRCB bill and the President to certify it as urgent; the repo does not record whether that bill passed. On the same day as this resolution, Resolution 58 asked for a regional commission; that one came through the region's own law, BAA 89, ratified on 28 January 2026.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament appeals to the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Committee to exempt all lawyers who are Members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority from the continuing legal education requirement.

Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 24 January 2020.
readings.whyProposed: Many BTA Members are lawyers who also served in the 2 Bangsamoro Transition Commissions over almost 5 years. The authors cite their heavy workload of priority legislation, setting up the bureaucracy and preparing for the first elected government in 2022. Section 3, Rule 7 of Bar Matter No. 850 allows a lawyer to file a verified request for exemption for good cause, such as disability, illness, postgraduate study abroad or proven expertise in law, and the authors argue these circumstances amount to good cause.
whoIsAffected: Lawyer-Members of the BTA.
implementedBy: Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Committee
whatChanges: It is an appeal; only the MCLE Committee, under Supreme Court rules, can grant an exemption.
It names no recipient for copies.
readings.insight: Bar Matter No. 850, as the resolution itself quotes it, provides for a verified request by the individual lawyer, while this is a collective appeal by Parliament for all its lawyer-members. Workload is not among the example grounds it quotes. The resolution does not say how many Members are lawyers.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recommends the enactment of a bill creating a Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission in the Bangsamoro region, defining its powers and functions and providing its funds.

Authored by MP Mohagher M. Iqbal and 12 others. Adopted on 24 January 2020.
readings.whyProposed: Article IX, Section 1 of the Organic Law requires Parliament, taking into account the TJRC report, to enact a transitional justice mechanism for the legitimate grievances of the Bangsamoro and indigenous peoples: historical injustice, human rights violations and marginalization through land dispossession. The authors argue the courts are too slow for grievances this numerous and serious.
whoIsAffected: Bangsamoro and indigenous peoples with grievances from the conflict and land dispossession.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: It is a recommendation to Parliament itself to pass a law; it does not create the commission.
readings.insight: The law came 6 years later. A bill was filed on 10 April 2025, and the Bangsamoro Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Act of 2025 (BAA 89) was ratified on 28 January 2026 and approved by the Chief Minister on 11 February 2026. On the same day as this resolution, Resolution 56 called for a separate national commission, which the repo does not record as created.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends MP Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong for being named among the 10 Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) of the Philippines for 2019.

Authored by MPs Susana S. Anayatin and Rasul E. Ismael. Adopted on 31 January 2020.
readings.whyProposed: MP Adiong was the spokesman during the Marawi crisis, a former Majority Floor Leader and Assemblyman of the Regional Legislative Assembly, and a sitting BTA Member. The award, organized by Junior Chamber International Philippines, was given on 13 December 2019 in Manila for his leadership and service to the Bangsamoro people.
whoIsAffected: MP Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong.
whatChanges: None beyond the record; it is a commendation.
readings.insight: A commendation of a sitting Member by 2 colleagues. It is the only TOYM resolution in the index.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the regional Ministry of Health to station a standby emergency medical assistance team at the Shariff Kabunsuan Cultural Complex during sessions of Parliament, and forwards the resolution to Minister Saffrullah M. Dipatuan.

Authored by MPs Diamila D. Ramos and Edrieza H.N. Rimbang. Adopted on 31 January 2020.
readings.whyProposed: During a session, a staff member of a Member of Parliament collapsed in the session hall and was rushed to hospital by Members and staff. The authors want emergency care and first aid on hand for Members, staff, guests and the audience, citing the region's health powers under the Organic Law.
whoIsAffected: Members, staff, guests and audiences at sessions of Parliament.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
whatChanges: It asks the Ministry of Health to provide a team; it sets no budget or schedule.
A copy goes to the Minister of Health.
readings.insight: The footer records that it consolidates 2 proposed resolutions, Nos. 181 and 184. The adopted text is dated 31 January 2020, while Parliament's index lists 30 January 2020.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament records its consensus on the appointment of Khalipha Usman Nando as Wali of the Bangsamoro Government, under Republic Act No. 11054, the Bangsamoro Organic Law. The Wali is the ceremonial head of the Bangsamoro Government, appointed by Parliament.

Parliament's index credits it to the whole house, 98 names in all. Adopted on 29 March 2019, the day of the inaugural session.
readings.whyProposed: Section 1, Article VIII of the Organic Law has Parliament appoint the Wali. The BTA had selected Nando, and the resolution lists his record: a graduate in Islamic theology of Al-Azhar University in Cairo; chairman of the Bangsamoro Consultative Assembly for 2 years; chairman of the MILF Central Committee's committee on education for 16 years; Chief Justice of the MILF Shariah Supreme Court for 14 years; a senior member of the MILF Central Committee and Jihad Executive Council; and a member of the ceasefire committee for the Eastern Cotabato region. It says he meets the qualifications in the Organic Law and has the moral ascendancy to represent the government.
whoIsAffected: Khalipha Usman Nando, named Wali.
The Bangsamoro Government, whose ceremonial head the Wali is.
whatChanges: It is the act of appointment the Organic Law assigns to Parliament: Nando is named Wali by Parliament's consensus.
deliberation: 29 March 2019: Adopted unanimously as read by the Secretary General.
readings.insight: This is Resolution No. 1, adopted at the inaugural session. Parliament returned to the same appointment twice more: Resolution No. 266 (21 September 2022) re-affirmed the consensus on Nando for the second BTA Parliament, and Resolution No. 315 (17 February 2023) expressed condolences on his death. Resolution No. 445 (13 May 2024) expressed the consensus on a successor, Muslim Masaglang Guiamaden.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its condolences on the death of Ghazali B. Jaafar, a Member of the BTA, and sends the resolution to his family.

Parliament's index credits it to the whole house, 98 names in all. Adopted on 29 March 2019, the day of the inaugural session.
readings.whyProposed: Jaafar was First Vice-Chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. President Rodrigo Roa Duterte appointed him to the BTA and he took his oath on 22 February 2019. The resolution says the overwhelming majority of Members had chosen him to be Speaker, and that he chaired the 2nd Bangsamoro Transition Authority, which crafted what became the Organic Law, Republic Act No. 11054.
whoIsAffected: The family of Ghazali B. Jaafar.
whatChanges: A copy of the resolution goes to Jaafar's family. Nothing else follows from it.
deliberation: 29 March 2019: MP Jose I. Lorena paid tribute to the late MP Ghazali B. Jaafar as the unifying leader of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission and 'a man of peace' before moving adoption.
29 March 2019: Adopted unanimously on motion of MP Jose I. Lorena.
readings.insight: Jaafar died before Parliament's first session; the resolution notes he was the majority's choice for Speaker. Resolution No. 21 (29 July 2019) is the condolence for the 2nd sitting Member to die in the BTA's first year, Abdul M. Dataya Sr.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament, by unanimous vote of the Members present, authorizes the Interim Chief Minister to ask the National Government, through the Office of the President and the Department of Budget and Management, to source funds for the transition from any available funds, as submitted by the Coordinating Team for Transition, and release them to the BTA through the Office of the Chief Minister.

Copies go to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte and the Secretary of Budget and Management. Parliament's index credits it to the whole house, 98 names in all. Adopted on 29 March 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The BTA was constituted on 22 February 2019 and elected its officers on 29 March 2019. Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law charges the cost of the transition, including organizing the BTA and its bureaucracy and hiring personnel, against available funds in the current General Appropriations Act. The resolution notes the transition period is barely 2 and a half years.
whoIsAffected: The BTA and the offices it had to set up in its first months.
Personnel to be hired for the new bureaucracy.
implementedBy: Office of the Interim Chief Minister
Office of the President
Department of Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It asks for transition funds without stating an amount.

whatChanges: The Interim Chief Minister is authorized to make the request; whether and when money is released is up to the National Government.
deliberation: 29 March 2019: MP Paisalin P. Tago argued that authorizing the Chief Minister to 'request' funds was an executive function and proposed a new title having the Chief Minister, through his Cabinet Minister, make representation with the Office of the President and DBM.
29 March 2019: MP Jose I. Lorena explained the word 'request' followed Article XVI of RA 11054, which vests legislative and executive powers in the BTA, but submitted to the amendment.
29 March 2019: Adopted subject to style, with MP Paisalin P. Tago's amendment to the title.
readings.insight: This is the 1st of several early requests for the same money. Resolution No. 4, adopted the same day, asks for the ARMM's current-year appropriations; Resolution No. 7 (22 May 2019) authorizes the Minister of Finance to deal directly with the Department of Budget and Management because the transition funds had still not been released; Resolution No. 17 (26 June 2019) asks for the ARMM's 2019 public works funds.

readings.whatItDoes:
By majority vote of the Members present, Parliament authorizes the Interim Chief Minister to ask the National Government, through President Rodrigo R. Duterte, to transfer the current-year appropriations of the defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) to the BTA. Copies go to the President and the Secretary of Budget and Management.

Parliament's index credits it to the whole house, 98 names in all. Adopted on 29 March 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The transition began with the ratification of the Organic Law; the BTA was constituted on 22 February 2019 and elected its officers on 29 March 2019. Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law provides that the current year's appropriations for the ARMM shall also be transferred to the BTA.
whoIsAffected: The BTA and its offices, which needed operating money.
Programs and personnel funded under the ARMM's 2019 budget.
implementedBy: Office of the Interim Chief Minister
Office of the President
Department of Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It names no amount for the ARMM appropriations it asks to be transferred.

whatChanges: The Interim Chief Minister is authorized to ask; the transfer itself is for the President and the Department of Budget and Management.
deliberation: 29 March 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong raised a point of inquiry on adopting Proposed Resolution No. 4 'subject to style' without stating the amendments; MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu said he did so to avoid prolonging debate.
29 March 2019: MP Irene P. Tillah pointed out that Resolutions No. 3 and 4 covered different matters: the P1.2 billion transition fund versus the transfer of the current ARMM budget.
29 March 2019: Adopted unanimously subject to style on motion of MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu.
readings.insight: Resolution No. 3, adopted the same day, carries the vote as unanimous; this one says majority, the only difference the text gives between them. The Organic Law already provides for the transfer, so the resolution asks for what the law says should happen. Resolution No. 17 (26 June 2019) came back to one part of the ARMM money, the 2019 regional public works funds, nearly 3 months later.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament creates an ad hoc Committee on Finance, Budget and Management to find the remaining unexpended funds of the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly (RLA) and draw up an expenditure program for Parliament to use them. The committee is to report to Parliament as soon as possible.

Parliament's index credits it to the whole house, 98 names in all. Adopted on 22 April 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Parliament needed to find every possible source of funds for its work. Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law transfers the ARMM's current-year appropriations to the BTA, which includes the money that had been budgeted for the RLA.
whoIsAffected: Members of the BTA, whose early operating expenses were to come from the RLA money.
Staff of the RLA, the outgoing ARMM legislature.
implementedBy: Ad hoc Committee on Finance, Budget and Management of the BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It sets up a temporary committee of Parliament and tells it to report. It binds Parliament itself.
readings.insight: The committee reported within days. Resolution No. 9, adopted 2 days later on 24 April 2019, records that the ad hoc committee met on 23 April and found ₱63,000,000 of RLA local funds in the bank, and uses it for Members' operating expenses. Resolution No. 10, the same day, sets an expenditure program for ₱1,505,358,906 of transition funds.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts its first rulebook, the Parliamentary Rules, Procedures, and Practices of the BTA, in 37 rules. It sets out the officers (Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Majority and Minority Floor Leaders), 15 statutory committees mirroring the ministries and 6 parliamentary committees (Rules; Accounts and Audit; Ways and Means; Good Government; Ethics and Privileges; and Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws), committee powers of subpoena and contempt, the kinds of bills and resolutions, question hour, privilege hour, quorum, motions, debate, discipline, broadcasting and the session hall.

Bills follow a parliamentary path: a first reading with no debate, a second reading where Parliament votes on the bill's general principles before it goes to committee, a committee stage, consideration of the committee report, and a third reading. A Swift Passage Procedure lets a bill pass in 7 working days without the committee stage, and the Chief Minister can certify an emergency bill that Parliament must act on within 24 hours. Plenary quorum is a simple majority of all Members; the rules may be amended by a majority of all Members. They take effect 15 days after publication.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 21 May 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Article VII, Section 25 and Article XVI, Section 3 of the Organic Law require the BTA to adopt its own rules. The preamble ties this to the duty to set up the basic structure of the Bangsamoro government. Its stated purposes are to find the will of the majority, preserve the rights of the minority, and keep business orderly.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, bound by the rules in every session and committee.
Ministers, resource persons and witnesses, who can be summoned and held in contempt.
The public, whose access to sessions and records the rules set.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
Secretary-General of the Parliament
Committee on Rules
whatChanges: It binds Parliament itself: every session, committee hearing, bill and resolution runs under these rules.
Committees gain subpoena and contempt powers over witnesses.
deliberation: 21 May 2019: MP Nabil A. Tan asked that amendments drafted by the Committee on Rules come back to plenary for approval; the Majority Floor Leader agreed.
21 May 2019: Approved subject to amendments to be submitted by Members to the Committee on Rules, as worded by Minority Floor Leader Laisa M. Alamia.
readings.insight: The posted copy is not the text adopted in May 2019: its header says it is as amended by Resolutions No. 27 (privilege hour), 29 (committee quorum, now 30% of members), 31 and 32, and the file is dated August 2020. It does not list Resolution No. 73 (18 June 2020), whose title says it amended Section 4 of Rule XIII to allow sessions by teleconference, and Section 4 still reads Monday to Wednesday sittings from 1:00 p.m. The rules also define a resolution as expressing the sentiment of the BTA, without creating or modifying a law. The 2nd BTA Parliament adopted new rules as Resolution No. 268 on 22 September 2022, and later amendments cite that number.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament authorizes the Minister of Finance, Eduard U. Guerra, to deal with the Department of Budget and Management and other national agencies for the immediate release of the transition funds allocated to the BTA.

Filed by MP Suharto M. Ambolodto. Adopted on 22 May 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The BTA had been working since 22 February 2019. The resolution says the transition funds appropriated by the National Government for the year had to be released urgently to keep Parliament, the ministries and other offices running.
whoIsAffected: Parliament, the ministries and the other BTA offices waiting on transition funds.
implementedBy: Minister of Finance, Bangsamoro Transition Authority
Department of Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It names no amount.

whatChanges: The Minister of Finance has Parliament's authority to negotiate the release; it does not oblige the Department of Budget and Management.
readings.insight: It is the 2nd request for the same transition money in under 2 months. On 29 March 2019, Resolution No. 3 had authorized the Interim Chief Minister to ask for it; 54 days later the funds were still unreleased and Parliament gave the Finance Minister his own mandate. No amount is named in either.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts the calendar for its First Regular Session: it sits from 29 March 2019, then in 3-day blocks starting 22 April, 20 May, 24 June, 29 July, 27 August, 23 September, 28 October, 25 November and 16 December 2019, and 27 January and 26 February 2020, with mandatory adjournment on 28 February 2020.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr., Majority Floor Leader. Adopted on 22 May 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 5, Rule VI of the BTA rules says the regular session opens every year on the 4th Friday of March and ends no later than 30 days before the next session opens. A calendar was meant to guide Members in their legislative and constituency work.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, whose sitting days it fixes.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It sets Parliament's own schedule: about 3 sitting days a month.
deliberation: 22 May 2019: Adopted unanimously on motion of the Majority Floor Leader.
readings.insight: The calendar lasted 10 weeks. Resolution No. 22 (31 July 2019) repealed it, and Resolution No. 69 (28 February 2020) repealed No. 22 in turn. Under it Parliament would have sat 34 days in the whole session: the opening day plus 11 blocks of 3 days, 9 of them starting on a Monday.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament uses ₱63,000,000 of unexpended 2019 local funds allocated to the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly (RLA) for the initial maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) of the offices of the BTA for March and April 2019.

Filed by MP Eduard U. Guerra, with all Members of the BTA as co-authors. Adopted on 24 April 2019.
readings.whyProposed: At Session No. 3 on 23 April 2019, Parliament created an ad hoc committee to plan the use of the RLA's 2019 local funds. That evening the committee found ₱63,000,000 cash in bank and agreed unanimously to spend it on Members' MOOE for March and April 2019, allocated equally to 97 Members at ₱600,000 each.
whoIsAffected: Members of the BTA, who received the MOOE allocation.
The RLA's leftover 2019 budget, redirected to the BTA.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
Ad hoc Committee on Finance, Budget and Management

funding.detail: ₱63,000,000 from the unexpended 2019 local funds of the defunct Regional Legislative Assembly, for Members' MOOE for March and April 2019; the WHEREAS clauses set it at ₱600,000 each for 97 Members.

whatChanges: It directs leftover RLA money to the BTA's own offices. It is a spending decision by Parliament for itself.
deliberation: 24 April 2019: MP Eduard U. Guerra moved to delete 'RECOMMENDING THE APPROPRIATION AND'; MP Raissa H. Jajurie, MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu, MP Suharto M. Ambolodto and MP Baintan A. Ampatuan each proposed other wording before MP Laisa M. Alamia's final title was adopted.
24 April 2019: MP Irene P. Tillah warned that amending the title also affects the body of the resolution and asked that copies be given to all Members.
24 April 2019: Adopted as amended on motion of the Majority Floor Leader.
readings.insight: The figures in the text do not add up. ₱600,000 for each of 97 Members is ₱58,200,000, not the ₱63,000,000 the resolution uses, leaving ₱4,800,000 unaccounted for in the text. The 97 also sits oddly with an 80-seat body: Resolution No. 28, which amended this one on 30 August 2019, refers to the 80 Members of the BTA. Both numbers are clear on the page image. Parliament adopted the spending the day after the ad hoc committee's first meeting.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts an expenditures program for the transition funds of the BTA in the amount of ₱1,505,358,906.

Filed by MP Eduard U. Guerra, with all Members of the BTA as co-authors. Adopted on 24 April 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law charges the initial transition funding against available funds in the current General Appropriations Act. In a letter dated 15 April 2019 to Interim Chief Minister Al-Haj Murad Ebrahim, replying to an earlier query to Executive Secretary Esmael O. Pasigan, the Department of Budget and Management gave guidance on how an initial transition fund of 1.2 billion pesos could be secured. The ad hoc committee drew up the expenditure program on that guidance.
whoIsAffected: The BTA and the ministries and offices it was setting up.
Priority programs of the BARMM in its first year.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
Office of the Interim Chief Minister
Department of Budget and Management

funding.detail: ₱1,505,358,906 in transition funds under Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law, to be charged to the 2019 General Appropriations Act. The adopted text gives no breakdown.

whatChanges: It sets Parliament's program for spending the transition fund; the money itself still depends on release by the Department of Budget and Management.
deliberation: 24 April 2019: MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu asked that the full text be flashed or distributed so Members would know its specific intent; MP Eduard U. Guerra promised hard copies.
24 April 2019: MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu said the Office of the Chief Minister should transmit the adopted resolution to the DBM.
24 April 2019: Adopted on motion of the Majority Floor Leader.
readings.insight: The headline figure is larger than the guidance it rests on. The WHEREAS clauses twice cite a Department of Budget and Management letter about 1.2 billion pesos; the program adopted is for ₱1,505,358,906, about ₱305,000,000 more, and the posted page explains neither the difference nor how the money is to be spent. Release was still pending a month later, when Resolution No. 7 (22 May 2019) sent the Minister of Finance to the department.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its condolences to the family of Abul Khayr D. Alonto, chairman of the Mindanao Development Authority, who died on 9 May 2019, and acknowledges his contributions to the Bangsamoro.

Filed by MP Laisa M. Alamia and MP Rasul E. Ismael; the text also names MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil, MP Suharto M. Ambolodto, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, with all Members as co-authors. Adopted on 22 May 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Alonto became the first Muslim chairman of the Mindanao Development Authority on 5 September 2016. After the 1968 Jabidah massacre he organized the Muslim youth group LAM ALIF that led to the founding of the Moro National Liberation Front, and he was one of its original Top 90 and its Vice-Chairman. After the 1976 Tripoli Agreement he was elected Assemblyman, served as interim head of the regional autonomous government and then Speaker of the Regional Legislative Assembly. In 1994 he was named ambassador to Nigeria and 21 African states, and in 2014 he took part in congressional deliberations on the Bangsamoro Basic Law.
whoIsAffected: The family of Abul Khayr D. Alonto.
whatChanges: The resolution records Parliament's condolences and gratitude. Nothing else follows from it.
deliberation: 22 May 2019: Deputy Speaker Hatimil E. Hassan proposed replacing 'autonomy' with the MNLF's objective of 'full independence of the Bangsamoro Homeland', saying autonomy was only accepted in negotiations in 1975.
22 May 2019: Adopted, with all Members present made co-authors.
readings.insight: It is one of 45 adopted resolutions in the index whose titles express condolences or sympathy, and the 1st for someone outside the BTA.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament approves the Transition Plan of the BTA for the transition period 2019 to 2022, without prejudice to the passage of an Administrative Code and the creation of BARMM offices.

Filed by MP Ahod Balawag Ebrahim, the Chief Minister. Adopted on 17 June 2019, at a special session.
readings.whyProposed: Section 6, Article XVI of the Organic Law requires the Chief Minister to submit, within 60 days of the transition period, a transition plan containing the proposed organizational plan and its implementation schedule. Chief Minister Ebrahim submitted the plan on 30 May 2019, and at his request Parliament held a special session on 17 June 2019 to consider it.
whoIsAffected: Ministries and offices of the BARMM, organized under the plan.
ARMM employees whose offices were to be phased out.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: It gives Parliament's approval to the Chief Minister's organizational plan for 2019 to 2022. The adopted text does not reproduce the plan.
readings.insight: The Organic Law's 60-day deadline ran from the start of the transition on 22 February 2019; the plan arrived on 30 May, 97 days in. Parliament approved enhancements to it in Resolution No. 55 (27 December 2019), and Resolution No. 523 (23 January 2025) required the Chief Minister to update the 2019 to 2022 plan, nearly 3 years after the period it covered. Resolution No. 26 later dates the plan's passage to 18 June 2019, a day after the adoption date on this page.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Secretary-General to fast-track the BTA's organizational requirements: an organizational structure and staffing pattern for the legislative arm to replace the Regional Legislative Assembly set-up; accounts with GSIS, Pag-IBIG and Land Bank; hiring paperwork; offices for Members who hold no cabinet post; and a report on the personnel, assets and liabilities taken over after 30 June 2019.

The work is to be coordinated with the chairs of the ad hoc committees on Creation of Offices and on the Administrative Code, staffing must follow national position classification and pay rules, and the structure and staffing proposal goes to the Committee on Rules by 30 June 2019. Filed by MP Laisa M. Alamia, MP Suharto M. Ambolodto, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and MP Rasul E. Ismael. Adopted on 24 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 10, Article XVI of the Organic Law has the BTA schedule the phasing out of ARMM offices. The elected RLA officials would serve until noon of 30 June 2019, but RLA personnel would stay until the BTA set a phase-out schedule, so Parliament needed its own staff structure in place.
whoIsAffected: RLA personnel awaiting a phase-out schedule.
Staff to be hired for the BTA's legislative arm.
Members without cabinet posts who needed offices.
implementedBy: Secretary-General of the BTA
Ad hoc Committee on Creation of Offices
Ad hoc Committee on Administrative Code
Committee on Rules
whatChanges: It is an instruction from Parliament to its own Secretary-General, with a deadline of 30 June 2019 for the staffing proposal, 6 days after adoption.
readings.insight: It sets a hard deadline, and a short one: 6 days. The adopted text says President Duterte signed the Organic Law on 26 July 2019, a date after the resolution's own adoption; it is printed that way on the page. The Administrative Code it was coordinating with became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, ratified on 28 October 2020.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament supports the public's call for a law compensating the victims of the armed encounters in Butig, Piagapo and Marawi City, all in Lanao del Sur, and asks Congress to act promptly on the relevant bills as soon as they are filed. Copies go to the Senate President, the Speaker of the House and the Office of the Chief Minister.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil, MP Rasul E. Ismael, MP Suharto M. Ambolodto and MP Laisa M. Alamia. Adopted on 26 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Marawi siege began in May 2017, when the Maute Group, the Abu Sayyaf Group and others inspired by Daesh tried to take the city; it was preceded by fighting in Butig in November 2016 and Piagapo in January 2017. Residents lost homes, businesses and livelihoods. Compensation bills for Marawi were filed in both houses of the 17th Congress but never got past committee before it adjourned, and none covered Butig or Piagapo. Compensation is for Congress alone to enact, but the resolution cites the Organic Law's duty to provide basic necessities and promote social justice.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Marawi City, Butig and Piagapo who lost property and livelihoods.
Members of Congress with compensation bills before them.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
House of Representatives
Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: It is an appeal to Congress; only Congress can pass the law.
deliberation: 26 June 2019: MP Omar Yasser C. Sema moved that the small group, the Majority Floor Leader and the Chief Minister be named authors; MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong said all Members should be co-authors.
26 June 2019: MP Anna Tarhata S. Basman reported a substitute drafted by a small group chaired by MP Paisalin P. Tago; adopted.
readings.insight: It began a long run. Parliament came back to Marawi compensation in Resolution No. 33 (30 August 2019, supporting House Bills No. 3543, 3418 and 3922), No. 151 and No. 156 (September 2021, urging the Senate), and No. 216 (17 February 2022, asking the President to sign Senate Bill No. 2420 and House Bill No. 9925, the Marawi Siege Victims Compensation Act). Resolution No. 308 (24 January 2023) thanked President Marcos for constituting the Marawi Compensation Board. The later titles name Marawi only; Butig and Piagapo, which this resolution singled out as left out of every bill, do not appear in them.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament confirms the membership of 8 ad hoc committees: Education Code (chaired by MP Mohagher M. Iqbal), Administrative Code (MP Jose I. Lorena), Electoral Code (MP Lanang T. Ali Jr.), Local Government Code (MP Datu Midpantao M. Midtimbang), Civil Service Code (MP Laisa M. Alamia), Internal Revenue Code (MP Anna Tarhata S. Basman), Creation of Offices (MP Baintan A. Ampatuan) and Indigenous Peoples' Affairs (MP Melanio U. Ulama). Each lists a vice-chair and members, with the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and both floor leaders as ex-officio members.

The headings give the committees 44, 40, 41, 39, 19, 23, 29 and 17 seats. Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Parliament's index dates the adoption to 26 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution has no WHEREAS clauses. The ad hoc committees were set up to draft the priority codes the Organic Law expects Parliament to pass during the transition, and to organize the new government's offices.
whoIsAffected: Members assigned to draft the priority codes.
Everyone later governed by those codes.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It confirms committee assignments inside Parliament. It binds only Parliament.
deliberation: 26 June 2019: MP Eddie M. Alih asked to leave the Ad Hoc Committee on Revenue Code for Finance; the Majority Floor Leader said the 4-committee limit applies only to the ad hoc committees.
26 June 2019: Approved as a simple resolution after the Secretary General read the members of the 8 ad hoc committees.
readings.insight: Five of these codes became law: the Administrative Code (Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, ratified 28 October 2020), the Civil Service Code (No. 17, 24 February 2021), the Education Code (No. 18, 18 May 2021), the Electoral Code (No. 35, 8 March 2023) and the Local Governance Code (No. 49, 28 September 2023). The repo's act index lists no revenue code. The page closes with 'Adopted, March 29, 2019', 3 months before the 26 June 2019 date in Parliament's index; the image confirms it. In the Creation of Offices list, MP Hussein P. Muñoz is named twice, as members 2 and 9.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament confirms the vice-chairperson and members of the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management: chaired by MP Eduard U. Guerra, with MP Ubaida C. Pacasem as vice-chair, members including MP Mohagher M. Iqbal, MP Raissa H. Jajurie and MP Jose I. Lorena, and the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and both floor leaders ex officio. The heading gives the committee 31 seats.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 26 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution has no WHEREAS clauses. The finance committee is a statutory committee under the BTA rules, with jurisdiction over the budget.
whoIsAffected: Members assigned to the finance committee.
Budget bills that pass through it.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It sets the membership of Parliament's own finance committee.
deliberation: 26 June 2019: Approved, confirming MP Ubaida C. Pacasem as vice chair of the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management.
readings.insight: The posted text is titled as confirming the vice-chairperson and membership, slightly wider than the index title. Guerra, the chair, was also the BTA's Minister of Finance (Resolution No. 7) and the author of the funding Resolutions No. 9 and No. 10, so the finance minister also chaired the committee that reviews the budget.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Department of Budget and Management to immediately release and transfer the ARMM's 2019 public works funds to the BARMM. The Secretary-General is to send the resolution to the Office of the Chief Minister, and copies go to the Department of Budget and Management, the Bangsamoro Minister of Finance and the Office of the President.

Filed by MP Jose I. Lorena. Adopted on 26 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 14, Article XVI of the Organic Law transfers the funds meant for the ARMM in the current General Appropriations Act to the BTA. The Regional Legislative Assembly had submitted the Regional Public Works Act of 2019 on 7 January 2019, and its funding was already in the 2019 General Appropriations Act. Article XVIII, Section 1 of the Organic Law keeps RLA laws in force unless inconsistent or repealed.
whoIsAffected: Communities waiting on 2019 regional public works projects.
Contractors and the BARMM's public works ministry.
implementedBy: Department of Budget and Management
Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Office of the President

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It names no amount for the 2019 public works funds.

whatChanges: It is a request to the Department of Budget and Management; the release is the department's decision.
readings.insight: It is the 4th request in 3 months for money the Organic Law already transferred, after Resolutions No. 3, No. 4 and No. 7. The Organic Law transfers ARMM appropriations to the BTA, but this resolution asks for the money to go to the BARMM through the Chief Minister rather than to the BTA.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends Major General Cirilito E. Sobejana for his support for the peace process and his commitment to peace in the Bangsamoro. Copies go to the Senate President, the Speaker of the House and the Interim Chief Minister.

Filed by MP Laisa M. Alamia, MP Suharto M. Ambolodto, MP Baintan A. Ampatuan, MP Don Mustapha A. Loong, MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and MP Rasul E. Ismael. Adopted on 26 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Sobejana had served in the Armed Forces since 1987. As a captain commanding the 1st Scout Ranger Company in Basilan he received the Medal of Valor for a fight with about 150 Abu Sayyaf members on 13 January 1995, in which he was shot twice and kept command; the resolution says only 41 soldiers have received the medal since 1935. He later commanded Joint Task Force Sulu and, from 26 May 2018, the 6th Infantry Kampilan Division, and was named Commander of the Western Mindanao Command with the rank of Lieutenant General on 28 June 2019.
whoIsAffected: Major General Cirilito E. Sobejana.
whatChanges: The resolution records Parliament's commendation and sends copies to Congress and the Interim Chief Minister.
deliberation: 26 June 2019: MP Mussolini S. Lidasan said the body should also recognize the support of the Regional Legislative Assembly.
26 June 2019: Approved as a simple resolution and adopted subject to style.
readings.insight: The page carries 2 dates: 'Adapted 23rd of July 2019 at Cotabato City' after the last clause, and 'Adopted, June 26, 2019' below it, which matches Parliament's index. It also cites Sobejana's new command as of 28 June 2019, 2 days after that adoption date. Both are visible on the page image.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls for the youth to take an active part in the Bangsamoro Government. Its 7 points: young people should join Bangsamoro leaders in their offices for training in governance; the government should invest in youth development programs; youth should be encouraged to fight corruption and demand accountability and transparency; the government should create programs for psycho-social wellness; health facilities should be asked to serve all women and young people regardless of status, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity; youth should lead an advocacy for the environment; and youth groups should promote good family relationships.

Filed by MP Narciso Co Yu Ekey. Adopted on 29 July 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Article IX, Section 13 of the Organic Law recognizes the rights of the youth. The resolution cites Presidential Decree No. 603 (the Child and Youth Welfare Code) and Republic Act No. 8044 (the Youth in Nation-Building Act), notes that today's young people are the largest generation in Philippine history, and lists the pressures they face: bullying and cyberbullying, discrimination, depression, anxiety, violence and suicide.
whoIsAffected: Young people in the Bangsamoro.
Bangsamoro offices asked to take in youth trainees.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Government

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It calls for investment in youth programs without naming an amount.

whatChanges: Nothing is mandated: the resolution says the listed actions 'may be made'. It names no office, deadline or budget.
deliberation: 29 July 2019: Approved as a simple resolution.
readings.insight: It is a statement of direction, written in permissive language, with no office, deadline or follow-up named. Even the health care point, which names sexual orientation and gender identity among the grounds, only has the government request health facilities to serve everyone.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament endorses the nomination of Court of Appeals Justice Japar B. Dimaampao to the Supreme Court and sends the resolution to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, with a copy to the Judicial and Bar Council.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and 7 others. Adopted on 29 July 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Judicial and Bar Council had opened nominations for the seat of Associate Justice Mariano C. del Castillo, retiring on 29 July 2019. Dimaampao, from Marawi City, was on the list. The resolution says he was the youngest magistrate ever appointed to the Court of Appeals, had served there about 15 years and chaired its 7th Division, and was the first Muslim Senior State Prosecutor. It cites Article VI, Section 11 of the Organic Law, which calls for Bangsamoro representation in national offices as far as practicable.
whoIsAffected: Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
Muslim Filipinos, whom the resolution says his appointment would represent.
implementedBy: Office of the President
Judicial and Bar Council
whatChanges: It is an endorsement; appointment belongs to the President from the Council's list.
deliberation: 29 July 2019: MP Omar Yasser C. Sema moved to incorporate Section 11, Article VI of RA 11054, on Bangsamoro participation in the central government, as the preamble.
29 July 2019: MP Eddie M. Alih noted the late Justice Alwahid A. Bidin was the first Filipino Muslim on the Supreme Court.
29 July 2019: Approved subject to MP Omar Yasser C. Sema's amendment; all Members made co-authors.
readings.insight: Dimaampao did not get the 2019 seat. He was appointed 2 years later, and Parliament adopted 5 resolutions on it in 2 days, Resolutions No. 157 to 161 (15 and 16 September 2021). No. 157 names him the 191st Associate Justice and the 2nd Muslim on the Court.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its sympathy and condolences on the death of its Member Abdul M. Dataya Sr., recognizes his contributions to the Bangsamoro cause, and sends the resolution to his family.

Filed by MP Susana S. Anayatin, MP Eduard U. Guerra and MP Ubaida C. Pacasem. Adopted on 29 July 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Dataya died of a heart ailment on 9 July 2019 at Davao Doctors Hospital. He chaired the MILF Ad Hoc Joint Action Group and was the United Bangsamoro Justice Party's provincial executive officer in Maguindanao. In government he had been regional director of the Regional Anti-Smuggling Action Center in Region XI and of the Economic Intelligence and Investigation Bureau in Region XII, and after retiring he served the office of the late MILF Chairman Ustadz Hashim Salamat.
whoIsAffected: The family of Abdul M. Dataya Sr.
whatChanges: A copy goes to Dataya's family. Nothing else follows from it.
deliberation: 29 July 2019: Consolidated with Proposed Resolution No. 48; all Members present made co-authors; adopted.
29 July 2019: Consolidated with Proposed Resolution No. 39 and adopted.
readings.insight: The page notes that it consolidates 2 proposals, PR 39 and PR 48. Dataya was the 2nd BTA Member mourned in the Parliament's first 4 months, after Ghazali B. Jaafar in Resolution No. 2. He had been named to 4 ad hoc committees and the finance committee in Resolutions No. 15 and No. 16.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament adopts a new calendar for the First Regular Session and repeals Resolution No. 8. Sessions move to Wednesday-to-Friday blocks, twice a month: 21 to 23 August, 28 to 30 August, 18 to 20 September, 25 to 27 September, 16 to 18 October, 23 to 25 October, 20 to 22 November, 27 to 29 November, 18 to 20 December and 25 to 27 December 2019, then 22 to 24 January, 29 to 31 January and 19 to 21 February 2020, with the last block opening 26 February and mandatory adjournment on 28 February 2020.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 31 July 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 5, Rule VI of the rules sets the regular session from the 4th Friday of March. The resolution says the new calendar would guide Members and also fast-track legislation.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, whose sitting days it fixes.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It replaces Parliament's own schedule from August 2019 to February 2020, roughly doubling the sitting blocks.
deliberation: 30 July 2019: The Chair asked whether Proposed Resolution No. 62 amends the Parliamentary Rules; MP Lanang Ali Jr. answered that Section 5, Rule VI allows a resolution defining the regular session, so it amends the earlier calendar.
30 July 2019: MP Amilbahar Mawallil asked about the 21 August resumption date falling on a holiday; MP Lanang Ali Jr. said a session day that falls on a holiday moves to the next day, 22 August.
30 July 2019: MP Laisa Alamia proposed adding a sentence that the resolution nullifies the previous calendar of session; the author accepted.
30 July 2019: Approved with an amendment from MP Laisa Alamia stating that it nullifies the previous calendar of session; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 22.
readings.insight: The new calendar has 14 sitting blocks against the 7 left under Resolution No. 8 for the same months. One block opens on 25 December 2019. The rules still set plenary sittings for Monday to Wednesday, so Resolution No. 27 moved privilege hour from Monday to Thursday to fit the new days. Resolution No. 69 (28 February 2020) repealed this calendar in turn.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls for an ad hoc Joint Body to be constituted to define the Zones of Joint Cooperation in the Sulu Sea.

Filed by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and 9 others. The page notes it consolidates proposals PR 52 and PR 55. Adopted on 31 July 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Section 18, Article XIII of the Organic Law creates Zones of Joint Cooperation in the Sulu Sea and the Moro Gulf, with coordinates to be set by an ad hoc Joint Body of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority and an equal number of Bangsamoro representatives. The law says the body shall be convened within 30 days of ratification. The resolution says the coordinates are needed for joint work on non-living resources, protection of indigenous communities' traditional fishing grounds, and equitable sharing of benefits.
whoIsAffected: Fishing communities in the Sulu Sea, including indigenous communities with traditional fishing grounds.
The national and Bangsamoro governments, which share management of the zones.
implementedBy: Department of Environment and Natural Resources
National Mapping and Resource Information Authority
Bangsamoro Government
whatChanges: It is a call, addressed to no specific office and with no deadline. It sends no copy to anyone.
deliberation: 30 July 2019: MP Laisa Alamia said the Zones of Joint Cooperation follow the 1982 UNCLOS and Section 18, Article XIII of RA 11054, and the Joint Body should have convened within 30 days of ratification.

30 July 2019: MP Omar Yasser Sema joined the MNLF members as co-authors and moved to consolidate Proposed Resolution Nos. 52 and 55 and add the Moro Gulf to the title; MP Amilbahar Mawallil, for the proponents, agreed and the motion carried.

30 July 2019: Moved for approval as a simple resolution; consolidated with Proposed Resolution No. 55, with the Moro Gulf added to the title and MNLF members and MP Sahie Udjah added as co-authors; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 23 of session 12.
readings.insight: The Organic Law's 30-day deadline for convening the body had long passed when this was adopted, more than 5 months after ratification. The resolution covers the Sulu Sea only, though the law creates zones in the Moro Gulf too. The issue was still open 4 years later: Resolution No. 370 (18 July 2023) strongly urged the Joint Body to finalize the delineation of Bangsamoro waters and the zones in both the Sulu Sea and the Moro Gulf.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the Senate and the House of Representatives for passing House Bill No. 8281, an act providing for the regulation and organization of Islamic banks, and appeals to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte to sign it into law.

Filed by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph. Adopted on 25 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Senate approved House Bill No. 8281 without changes on 3 June 2019, by 20 votes; the House had passed it on 3rd reading on 20 November 2018. It grew out of House Bill No. 492, filed by Anak Mindanao Representative Sitti Djalila A. Turabin-Hataman on 30 June 2016, and House Bill No. 3975 by Representative Gloria Macapagal Arroyo. The bill sets a legal framework for Islamic banking, aims for tax neutrality with conventional banking, and would open Shari'ah-compliant financing for small businesses in the Bangsamoro. The resolution ties it to the Organic Law's grant of power over Islamic banking and finance and to Article XII, Section 32, which has Parliament promote Islamic finance.
whoIsAffected: Muslim entrepreneurs and small businesses in the Bangsamoro without Shari'ah-compliant financing.
Banks seeking to offer Islamic banking products.
implementedBy: Office of the President
whatChanges: It is a commendation and an appeal; the signing was the President's call alone.
deliberation: 25 June 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong asked whether an author may give a sponsorship speech before referral; the Majority Floor Leader said the Rules allow it.
25 June 2019: MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong proposed deleting the call urging the President to sign, saying it is the President's prerogative and the bill lapses into law after 30 days.
25 June 2019: Speaker Ali Pangalian M. Balindong agreed it is not proper to urge the President to sign, though the body might appeal to him; MP Nabil A. Tan concurred.
25 June 2019: MP Paisalin P. Tago objected that Members did not yet know the contents of House Bill No. 8281 and that the President has deeper wisdom than the BTA.
25 June 2019: Adopted as a simple resolution subject to style on motion of MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong, with the author agreeing to drop the call urging the President to sign the bill.
readings.insight: The text says its author took part in drafting the bill, alongside the technical working group that included the Bangko Sentral, the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank and the ARMM. The repo does not record whether the President signed the bill. Al-Amanah does recur in the repo's readings of the Bangsamoro budgets: the Contingent Fund from FY 2020 to FY 2026 carries a line for the cost of acquiring Al-Amanah Islamic Bank.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament constitutes and activates 19 statutory and parliamentary committees, among them Accounts and Audit; Ways and Means; Good Government, Accountability of Public Officers and Investigation; Ethics and Privileges; Amendments, Revision and Codification of Laws; and committees for each sector from education and health to public works and public order and safety.

Filed by MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu and 8 others. Adopted on 25 June 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The rules task committees with considering bills and resolutions and reporting to the plenary, and provide for statutory and parliamentary committees.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, who take seats on the committees.
Bills and resolutions that need committee action.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It brings Parliament's permanent committee system into operation. It binds only Parliament.
deliberation: 25 June 2019: Approved as a simple resolution; the Majority Floor Leader then withdrew his separate motion to activate the committees.
readings.insight: The list omits 2 of the 21 committees in the rules: the Committee on Rules and the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, whose membership Resolution No. 16 confirmed the next day. About 2 months later, Resolution No. 29 (30 August 2019) cut the committee quorum to 30% of members so the newly active committees could meet regularly. The text cites the committee provisions as Article X of the code of procedure; in the posted rules they sit in Rule VII.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recognizes the urgent need to activate the Bangsamoro Government's Intergovernmental Relations (IGR) Body and support secretariat, asks that the Chief Minister appoint them, and asks the Bangsamoro Government to start operating the National Government-Bangsamoro Government IGR Body. It also asks the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management to fund the personnel and operating expenses of the Bangsamoro IGR Body and secretariat.

Filed by MP Eddie M. Alih and MP Abdulmuhmin A. Mujahid. Adopted on 22 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Article VI of the Organic Law creates a National Government-Bangsamoro Government Intergovernmental Relations Body to resolve issues through regular, non-adversarial consultation, with unresolved issues elevated to the President. The Transition Plan left intergovernmental relations to be set out in the Administrative Code, but issues between the 2 governments had to be resolved before they could go into it. The resolution quotes President Duterte on 25 June 2019 citing a breakdown in communication between the central government and the BTA.
whoIsAffected: The Bangsamoro and national governments, which use the body to settle disputes.
Staff of the IGR secretariat to be appointed.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution names no amount. It asks the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management to fund the personnel services and operating expenses of the Bangsamoro IGR Body and secretariat.

whatChanges: It asks the Chief Minister and the finance ministry to act; it sets no deadline and binds neither.
readings.insight: The national IGR body stayed a recurring subject. In May 2025, Resolution No. 546 urged the IGR Body to release information on Sulu's budgetary transition, and in December 2025 Resolution No. 564 recommended the immediate designation of the national government chairman of the body, more than 6 years after this call. The text says the Transition Plan passed on 18 June 2019; Resolution No. 12, which approved it, is dated 17 June 2019.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends Section 1, Rule XVII of its rules so that privilege hour is held every Thursday of regular sessions instead of Monday. Privilege hour may not be interrupted except by a point of order, a motion to adjourn, or, in exceptional cases, a question of personal or collective privilege.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 22 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The rules set privilege hour on Mondays. The new calendar of session moved sittings to Wednesday through Friday, so Monday privilege hours would no longer fall on session days.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament who use privilege hour to speak on matters of their choice.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It binds Parliament itself: privilege hour now falls on Thursdays.
readings.insight: This is the 1st amendment to the rules, 3 months after they were adopted, and the change appears in the consolidated rules posted as Resolution No. 6. The WHEREAS clause cites the new calendar as 'BTA Resolution No. 62', approved 29 July 2019 and amending 'Resolution no. 22'; the calendar actually adopted is Resolution No. 22 itself, dated 31 July 2019, which repealed Resolution No. 8.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends Resolution No. 9 to provide continuing maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) for the 80 Members of the BTA Parliament, charged against the Bangsamoro local fund and other available national funds. The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management is to prepare the computations and supporting documents, and a copy goes to the Office of the Chief Minister.

Filed by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and 10 others. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Regional Legislative Assembly had appropriated the ARMM's 2019 local funds, including MOOE for its Members, and the terms of its 24 elected officials ended on 30 June 2019. Resolution No. 9 covered BTA Members' MOOE only for March and April 2019, from ₱63,000,000 of RLA funds. The BTA needed continuing money for monthly operations and community activities.
whoIsAffected: Members of the BTA and their offices.
The Bangsamoro local fund, which carries the cost.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Office of the Chief Minister

funding.detail: No amount is stated. MOOE for the 80 Members is to be charged against the local fund of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region and other available national funds, with the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management computing the figures.

whatChanges: Members' MOOE becomes a continuing allocation rather than a one-time grant, at an amount left to the finance ministry to compute.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: Adopted as a simple resolution in view of its urgency; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 28.
readings.insight: The resolution turns a 2-month, ₱63,000,000 allotment into an open-ended one without a figure. It counts 80 Members where Resolution No. 9 divided the money among 97. Resolution No. 76 (25 June 2020) later let Members use their MOOE for assistance to constituents during the COVID-19 pandemic.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends Section 3, Rule VIII of its rules to lower the quorum for committee meetings and hearings to at least 30% of all members, including ex-officio members. The amended text then says a decision 'requires a simple.' and stops; the word 'majority' is missing.

Filed by the Committee on Rules. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: Parliament had activated its statutory and parliamentary committees and expected bills to be deliberated there. To let the committees meet regularly, it wanted a lower quorum, which it says follows the practice of other legislatures and collegial bodies.
whoIsAffected: Committee members, who can now meet with 30% present.
Bills and resolutions waiting on committee action.
implementedBy: BTA Parliament
whatChanges: It binds Parliament: committees can do business with 30% of members present, including ex-officio members.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: Adopted as a simple resolution; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 29.
readings.insight: The truncated sentence is on the page image as adopted. The consolidated rules posted as Resolution No. 6 read 'a simple majority of the members present', which is the obvious intent. The resolution does not state the old quorum it replaces. Resolutions No. 15 and No. 16 seat the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and both floor leaders ex officio on committees, so they count toward the 30%.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks Congress to allocate funds in the proposed 2020 General Appropriations Act for building the Bangsamoro Parliament, and sends the request to the Senate President and the Speaker of the House.

Filed by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and 6 others. Adopted on 30 August 2019.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law vests the powers of government in Parliament. The resolution says the 80 representatives need a venue to draft and debate laws, and that a building for Parliament and Members' offices would symbolize the authority of the Bangsamoro government. A WHEREAS clause puts the request at ₱100,000,000.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament and their staff, who needed offices and a session hall.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
House of Representatives

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It asks Congress for ₱100,000,000 in the 2020 General Appropriations Act; the figure appears only in a WHEREAS clause.

whatChanges: It is a request to Congress, which alone decides the national budget.
deliberation: 30 August 2019: MP Nabil Tan asked whether the ₱100 million would come from the block grant; MP Rasul Ismael said no, it is a Senate commitment to be charged to the 2020 GAA.

30 August 2019: MP Musa Diamla said ₱100 million may not be enough and asked that the amount follow the technical computation; the Majority Floor Leader said it was not a good idea to ask the Senate for more than it offered.
30 August 2019: MP Jose Lorena suggested asking Senator Migz Zubiri for a continuing ₱1 billion budget for the building, starting with the ₱100 million offered.
30 August 2019: Approved as a simple resolution in view of its urgency, with all Members made co-authors; the adopted index lists it as Resolution No. 30.
readings.insight: The ₱100,000,000 is the only figure, and it sits in the WHEREAS clauses, not the resolved clause. The repo's index of adopted resolutions has no later resolution on a Parliament building, so whether Congress funded it cannot be traced here.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the Commission on Elections, the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the security sector, the local government units and the voters of Maguindanao for the successful and peaceful plebiscite that divided the province into Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur. A copy goes to each of them, for information.

Authored by MP Haron M. Abas. Adopted on 27 September 2022.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 11550, signed on 27 May 2021, split the 36-town Province of Maguindanao in 2. The Constitution requires a plebiscite before a province is divided, and it was held on 17 September 2022. The resolution reports turnout of 86.93%, with 99.27% voting yes, and cites NAMFREL's report that voting, counting and canvassing were smooth and peaceful.
whoIsAffected: The Commission on Elections, the teachers of the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the security sector and local governments that ran the plebiscite.
Voters of the former Province of Maguindanao.
whatChanges: Nothing changes in law. The division itself was done by Republic Act No. 11550 and the plebiscite; this is a commendation.
Copies go to the bodies commended, for information.
deliberation: 27 September 2022: MP Lorena asked the plebiscite turnout; MP Abas (H) said 86.93% of registered voters took part, with 99.27% voting yes and 0.73% no.

27 September 2022: MP Ampatuan and MP Lorena suggested also commending those who made the plebiscite succeed, and MP Ampatuan's amendments naming COMELEC, MBHTE, the security sectors and LGUs were accepted.
27 September 2022: MP Sangki recalled that an earlier division creating Shariff Kabunsuan was struck down by the Supreme Court because the ARMM could not create provinces.
27 September 2022: Approved subject to style; the proposed index records it as adopted Resolution No. 272.
readings.insight: Adopted 10 days after the vote. It gives turnout and the yes share as percentages only, with no vote counts. Parliament commended much the same bodies in Resolution No. 462 (19 June 2024) for the plebiscite that ratified the new municipalities of the Special Geographic Area. The adopted text is marked PR32, the number of the proposal it came from.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends Mindanao State University-Main Campus in Marawi City for ranking 6th nationwide, with a passing rate of 94.85%, among schools with 10 or more examinees and at least 80% passing in the September 2022 Social Worker Licensure Examination.

The resolution is to be presented to MSU System President Atty. Basari D. Mapupuno and furnished to Prof. Soraidah B. Ali, Dean of the MSU College of Public Affairs, and Prof. Norhainah C. Abdul Aziz, Chairperson of the Social Work Department.

The index lists it as authored by all Members of Parliament (80 names). Adopted on 17 October 2022.
readings.whyProposed: The Professional Regulation Commission released the results on 27 September 2022. Of MSU's 97 examinees, 92 passed, against 2,955 of 4,723 examinees nationwide. The resolution also cites MSU's special mandate to bring Muslim Filipinos and cultural communities into national life through public education, and the placing of MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology (5th) and MSU-Main Campus (9th) among the top 10 Philippine universities in a July 2022 Webometrics-based list.
whoIsAffected: Mindanao State University-Main Campus, its College of Public Affairs and its Social Work Department.
whatChanges: Nothing changes in law. This is a commendation.
Copies go to the MSU System President, the college dean and the department chairperson.
deliberation: 17 October 2022: MP Diamila D. Ramos spoke in support, noting Mindanao State University’s 94.85% rating, with 92 of 97 examinees passing the September 2022 Social Worker Licensure Examination.
17 October 2022: MP Khalid Ma-Amor H. Hadji Abdullah asked that all Members present be added as principal authors; the Chair said Members could instead fill up the co-authorship form.
17 October 2022: Treated as a simple resolution; interpellations and amendments dispensed with and approved, subject to style.
readings.insight: The figures check: 92 of 97 is 94.85%. The national passing rate they imply is about 62.6% (2,955 of 4,723). The title says schools with 10 or more examinees, but the RESOLVED clause drops 'or more'. It is one of several commendations for licensure and civil service results in late 2022, with Resolution No. 279 (veterinary board, 8th place) and Resolution No. 295 (Career Service Professional Examination, 10th place). The adopted text is marked PR44.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament congratulates and commends Amenah F. Pangandaman on the Commission on Appointments' confirmation of her appointment as Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management. A copy is to be presented to her.

Authored by MP Eddie M. Alih and 41 others. Adopted on 17 October 2022.
readings.whyProposed: The Commission on Appointments confirmed her on 28 September 2022. The resolution describes her as the first Muslim appointed DBM Secretary and the only Muslim in President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.'s cabinet, a Meranaw whose father is from Marawi City. It lists her earlier posts: in the House and Senate, as chief of staff to Senator Edgardo J. Angara in 2007 and in Senator Loren Legarda's office, as DBM Assistant Secretary (2016 to 2018) and Undersecretary (2018), and as Assistant Governor at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.
whoIsAffected: Secretary Amenah F. Pangandaman.
whatChanges: Nothing changes in law. This is a commendation.
A copy is presented to the Secretary.
deliberation: 17 October 2022: MP Diamila D. Ramos proposed adding a whereas clause describing Secretary Pangandaman as a Maranao Bangsamoro professional and naming President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos, Jr. in the third whereas; MP Jose I. Lorena asked her to submit the amendments to the Secretariat for incorporation.
17 October 2022: Treated as a simple resolution, all Members present made authors, interpellations and amendments dispensed with, and approved, subject to style.
readings.insight: Adopted 19 days after the confirmation, with 42 authors. Parliament returned to her in Resolution No. 569 (21 April 2026), commending her as former DBM Secretary on her departure. The adopted text is marked PR47.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament extends its condolences to the family of Datu Jamael Q. Sinsuat Sr., former Barangay Chairman of Dalican, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao, who was shot dead. A copy is to be presented to the family.

Authored by MP Mohagher M. Iqbal. Adopted on 17 October 2022.
readings.whyProposed: Datu Jamael Quesada Sinsuat Sr., 55, was shot by an unidentified gunman on 30 September 2022, just after Friday prayers, near a mosque in Barangay Dalican. The resolution says he served the Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat for 18 years. He left his wife, Bai Monessa Usman-Sinsuat, and 6 children.
whoIsAffected: The family of Datu Jamael Q. Sinsuat Sr.
whatChanges: Nothing changes in law. This is a condolence.
A copy is presented to the family.
deliberation: 17 October 2022: Treated as a simple resolution; the sponsor waived his authorship speech and it was approved without interpellation or amendment.
readings.insight: The resolution names no suspect and asks no agency to investigate. On the same day Parliament adopted Resolution No. 276, which lists this killing as the 10th of the incidents behind its order for a Committee on Public Order and Safety inquiry; that resolution describes him as a former Datu Odin Sinsuat mayoral candidate. The adopted text is marked PR50.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs its Committee on Public Order and Safety to conduct an inquiry in aid of legislation into the series of killings and the state of public order in the Province of Maguindanao, the Municipality of Pikit and the Special Geographic Area, to submit a report and to recommend specific actions to normalize the situation. A copy goes to the committee chairperson for appropriate action.

Authored by MP Hussein P. Muñoz. Adopted on 17 October 2022.
readings.whyProposed: The resolution says killings and other violence in Maguindanao and the Special Geographic Area were rising and had left more than 30 people dead. It lists 10 incidents between 19 July and 30 September 2022, most in Pikit and its barangays in the Special Geographic Area, among them the ambush of Barangay Macabual Chairperson Datu Jalandoni Matalam Akas on 20 July, an ambush that killed 4 men in Barangay Manaulanan on 26 August, the shooting of Corporal Al Muiz Dima in Parang on 19 September, and the killing of Datu Jamael Sinsuat Sr. on 30 September. It cites the Bangsamoro Organic Law's provisions on peace and order and on Parliament's power to hold inquiries.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Maguindanao, Pikit and the Special Geographic Area.
Parliament's Committee on Public Order and Safety, which must hold the inquiry.
implementedBy: Committee on Public Order and Safety
whatChanges: This one binds Parliament's own committee: it must hold an inquiry, report and recommend actions.
It sets no deadline for the report and directs no agency outside Parliament.
deliberation: 17 October 2022: Treated as a simple resolution; interpellations and amendments dispensed with on motion of MP Omar Yasser C. Sema and approved, subject to style.
readings.insight: The 10 incidents it lists account for 10 dead and 5 injured; the 'more than 30' dead it cites are not itemized. One incident, the shooting of a patrolman, is placed in Poblacion, Pikit, North Cotabato rather than the Special Geographic Area. Pikit also figures in Resolution No. 207 (January 2022), on 6 civilians killed in Gokotan, and in Resolution No. 431 (January 2024) on the killing of a mother and son. The adopted text is marked PR64.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament appeals to President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to extend the period for qualified members of the MILF and MNLF to apply for amnesty. Copies go to Congress, the National Amnesty Commission, the Intergovernmental Relations Body and the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, for information.

Authored by MP Mary Ann M. Arnado, MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, MP Mohagher M. Iqbal and MP Baileng S. Mantawil. Adopted on 21 November 2022.
readings.whyProposed: Proclamations No. 1090 and No. 1091, issued on 5 February 2021, granted amnesty to MILF and MNLF members for crimes committed in pursuit of their political beliefs, and gave applicants 1 year from effectivity to file with the National Amnesty Commission.
