whatChanges: It is a call to a national agency; the resolution has no distribution clause naming who receives it.
deliberation: 26 January 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan asked for an update since the resolution was filed a year earlier; MP Rasol Y. Mitmug, Jr. said the conversion could happen within the year and the resolution would encourage Congress to pass the bill.
26 January 2021: Approved after debate (the journal prints 'No. 193' at the approval line); recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 102 of 26 January 2021.
readings.insight: The law had already ordered the conversion; what was pending was CHED's check that the college met Section 26. The resolution does not say which requirements were still unmet. By February 2024, Resolution 438 addresses the school as Cotabato State University in commending its centennial.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its deep grief and sorrow at the passing of Member of Parliament and Deputy Chief Minister Abdul Raji Sahrin on 20 January 2021. Copies go to his family and to media outlets in the region.

Authored by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil and 17 others. Adopted on 26 January 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Abdul 'Kong' R. Sahrin, Deputy Chief Minister for the Island Provinces, Secretary-General of the MNLF Central Committee (Sema faction) and a BTA Member, died at Zamboanga Peninsula Medical Center after a month-long battle with a brain tumour. A Tausug fighter of the MNLF's Batch 300, also known as 'Hassan Jawali' in diplomatic circles, he defended the gains of earlier peace agreements, pushed for their convergence in a new autonomy law, and believed in the oneness of the MNLF and MILF struggles.
whoIsAffected: The family of Abdul Raji Sahrin.
The Moro National Liberation Front.
whatChanges: It records Parliament's sentiment and sends a copy to the family; it directs no office to do anything.
deliberation: 26 January 2021: Consolidated with Proposed Resolution No. 378 and approved and adopted subject to style; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 103 of 26 January 2021.
26 January 2021: Consolidated with Proposed Resolution No. 376 and approved and adopted subject to style; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 103 of 26 January 2021.
readings.insight: Adopted 6 days after his death. It followed Resolution 92 (17 November 2020) on the death of MNLF Chairman Yusop H. Jikiri. Sahrin died a sitting Member of Parliament and Deputy Chief Minister.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recognises the International Day of the Girl Child and supports the advancement of girls' rights in the region. It reaffirms the region's commitment to end discrimination and violence against girls and to pursue policies for their safety, health, welfare and rights, and encourages all ministries, agencies and organisations in the region to observe the day with ceremonies and activities every year from now on. Copies go to the Bangsamoro Women Commission, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission and other agencies.

Authored by MP Bainon G. Karon. Adopted on 26 January 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The United Nations General Assembly declared 11 October the International Day of the Girl Child in 2011. The authors cite the Magna Carta of Women's protection of girl-children and the Organic Law's provision on the rights of children, and the 2020 theme, 'My voice, our equal future'.
whoIsAffected: Girls in the region.
Ministries, agencies and organisations, encouraged to hold yearly observances.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Women Commission
Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission
whatChanges: It encourages a yearly observance; it does not require one or fund it.
deliberation: 26 January 2021: The Majority Floor Leader called the resolution long overdue and said MP Raissa H. Jajurie supported it; MP Baintan A. Ampatuan and the Majority Floor Leader asked to be co-authors.
26 January 2021: Approved and adopted; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 104 of 26 January 2021.
readings.insight: Adopted 107 days after the 11 October 2020 observance it recognises. The commitments are general; the resolution names no program, target or office responsible for the yearly observance.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its highest gratitude to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for appointing Atty. Anisah B. Amanodin-Umpa as Associate Justice of the Court of Appeals, and congratulates her as the first Bangsamoro woman to sit on that court. Copies go to the President and to her.

Authored by MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong. Adopted on 27 January 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Amanodin-Umpa, from Balindong, Lanao del Sur, studied accountancy and law (cum laude) at Mindanao State University in Marawi City and passed the CPA exam in 1985 and the bar in 1990. She was Clerk of Court V at the Municipal Trial Court of Iligan from 2001 to 2009, a Regional Trial Court judge from 2009 to 2020, and a professor at the MSU College of Law. President Duterte appointed her on 22 December 2020.
whoIsAffected: Justice Anisah B. Amanodin-Umpa.
whatChanges: It is a thank-you and congratulation; it directs no one.
deliberation: 27 January 2021: MP Paisalin P. Tago said Parliament should also thank President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for appointing a Bangsamoro woman to the Court of Appeals; MP Khadafeh G. Mangudadatu suggested a separate resolution for that instead.
27 January 2021: MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil replaced the last whereas clause to call the appointment an affirmation of the Moro commitment to excellence in the judiciary; accepted.
27 January 2021: MP Paisalin P. Tago moved to retitle the resolution to express gratitude to the President and congratulate the appointee; accepted by MP Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong.
27 January 2021: MP Maisara D. Latiph added 2 whereas clauses on the equality of women and men under the 1987 Constitution and women's participation in the State; accepted.
27 January 2021: Approved; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 105 of 27 January 2021.
readings.insight: The text calls her the first Moro woman in the 84-year-old Court of Appeals. Parliament earlier endorsed Justice Japar B. Dimaampao of the same court for the Supreme Court in Resolution 20 (2019), and thanked the President for appointing him in Resolution 158 (2021).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament amends 2 committee provisions in Rule VII of its rules. The Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, with 31 Members, gets jurisdiction over income, revenues, budget preparation and appropriations for the Bangsamoro Government, including expenditure, public debt, claims, inter-governmental revenue sharing and public expenditure in general, and the scrutiny of the Government's budget and spending.

The Committee on Accounts, with 17 Members, is limited to reviewing and assessing the budget of the Bangsamoro Parliament.

Authored by MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. and 28 others. Adopted on 28 January 2021.
readings.whyProposed: At its 13 January 2021 meeting the Committee on Rules agreed to restyle the Finance committee's provision so its scrutiny role is clear. On the Speaker's proposal it also agreed to rewrite the Accounts committee's provision to avoid confusion over jurisdiction and to delete its jurisdiction over audit.
whoIsAffected: The Committee on Finance, Budget and Management and the Committee on Accounts.
Ministries, whose budgets are now scrutinised by the Finance committee alone.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament
whatChanges: This is an internal-rules resolution, so it binds Parliament: committee jurisdictions are rewritten.
The audit role that the committee previously held is deleted, and the resolution gives it to no other committee.
deliberation: 27 January 2021: MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil asked what 'Bangsamoro Government' means; MP Lanang T. Ali, Jr. said it refers to the executive authority of the BTA, and offered to change it to 'Bangsamoro Transition Authority'.

27 January 2021: MP Jose I. Lorena rejected the idea that the executive alone is the government, saying there is only one Bangsamoro Government that includes Parliament, as defined in the Administrative Code.

27 January 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan objected to dropping 'Audit' from the Committee on Accounts and Audit and asked who would review Parliament's expenditures; MP Ali said internal audit offices and the Blue Ribbon Committee cover that.

27 January 2021: MP Laisa M. Alamia likened the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management to a Public Accounts Committee and said 'audit' was dropped because the word evoked fear; MP Ali said it was too broad and confusing.

27 January 2021: MP Baintan A. Ampatuan's restated amendment limiting the Committee on Accounts to reviewing the Parliament budget was accepted, while MP Maisara D. Latiph's change was not accepted after consultation with the Speaker; MP Ali B. Sangki's proposal to retain 'budget' was accepted.

27 January 2021: MP Abdulmuhmin A. Mujahid proposed adding the expenditures of the Bangsamoro Government and raising the Finance committee from 31 to 33 members; MP Ali said the first would overlap powers and the second would go to the Committee on Rules.
27 January 2021: Committee Report No. 54 was adopted on motion of Deputy Majority Floor Leader Raissa H. Jajurie; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 106 of 28 January 2021.
readings.insight: Under the original rules this committee was the Committee on Accounts and Audit, with power to examine the income and spending plans of all ministries 'including the audit thereof'; Resolutions 96 and 100 cite that wording. After this amendment it reviews only Parliament's own budget, and no committee is named for audit.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urgently directs the Ministry of Health to brief Parliament on its assessment, plan and program for distributing COVID-19 vaccines. The resolution is forwarded to the ministry.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph and MP Abdullah B. Hashim. Adopted on 18 February 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The regional government had set aside ₱500 million for vaccine procurement, on top of ₱380 million in the Ministry of Health's COVID-19 response plan. The ministry's officer-in-charge, Dr. Ameril Usman, was reported as saying no supply agreement had been signed and the ministry was still choosing a vaccine suited to the region, including its cold-storage needs. The authors want Parliament involved early so distribution reflects a collective decision across the region's areas.
whoIsAffected: Residents awaiting COVID-19 vaccination.
The Ministry of Health.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It cites ₱500 million for vaccine procurement and ₱380 million in the Ministry of Health's COVID-19 response plan.

whatChanges: It directs a briefing but sets no date and no form for it.
deliberation: 16 February 2021: MP Suharto M. Ambolodto argued the resolution only asks the Ministry of Health for a report and should be treated as a simple resolution; after MP Zul Qarneyn M. Abas and Minority Floor Leader Laisa M. Alamia agreed, MP Lanang T. Ali, Jr. withdrew his motion to refer it to the Committee on Health.
16 February 2021: MP Omar Yasser C. Sema raised a point of order that the resolution must be approved before the Deputy Minister of Health could report; it was approved first.

16 February 2021: MP Zul Qarneyn M. Abas reported that the BARMM was about 30% ready, vaccination was projected to start in late March or early April 2021, and the ₱500,000,000 regional allocation would serve as a buffer to vaccines supplied by the DOH.

16 February 2021: MP Don Mustapha A. Loong proposed that the Bangsamoro Government fund the cost of adverse vaccine effects; MP Susana S. Anayatin said she would back a resolution creating a BARMM indemnity fund.

16 February 2021: MP Laisa M. Alamia and MP Eddie M. Alih urged more vaccination sites for island areas such as Siasi, Sumisip, Mapun and Turtle Islands; MP Abas said each province has 1 refrigerated container van, so for now there would be 1 site per province.

16 February 2021: On 18 February debate was closed and amendments dispensed with on motion of MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, and the consolidated Proposed Resolution Nos. 382 and 383 was approved; recorded in the adopted index as Resolution No. 107 of 18 February 2021.
readings.insight: The ₱380 million matches the ₱379,968,484 COVID response line for the Ministry of Health in the FY 2021 budget, BAA 15. A month later, Resolution 113 (17 March 2021) expressed full support for the national and regional vaccination plans. Cold storage, raised here as an open question, returned in Resolution 132 (June 2021), which urged the purchase of ultra-low-temperature freezers.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses gratitude, recognition and support to the Office of the President, through the Presidential Communications Operations Office and Secretary Martin Andanar, for creating Salaam TV and Salaam Radio, and calls on the Bangsamoro Government to support them as public information platforms. Copies go to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Secretary Andanar.

Authored by MP Diamila D. Ramos. Adopted on 24 February 2021.
readings.whyProposed: In his first State of the Nation Address in 2016, the President promised a state-run channel for Muslim Filipinos. Salaam TV was launched on 23 July 2017, with radio on Radyo Pilipinas 738 kHz AM in Metro Manila, and airs from 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. on PTV's digital sub-channel and cable. The authors say it fights stereotypes of the Bangsamoro but lacks support from Muslim audiences, and suggest the region's Bureau of Information and the PCOO explore collaboration.
whoIsAffected: Salaam TV and Salaam Radio.
Bangsamoro Government offices, which could use them for public information.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Government
whatChanges: It calls on the regional government to support the channel but names no office, form of support or amount.
deliberation: 24 February 2021: MP Adiong asked whether the resolution's call for content 'relevant and beneficial' meant budgetary assistance; MP Ramos answered the form of support was left to the Bangsamoro Government's discretion, such as placing ministry programs on Salaam TV and Radio.
24 February 2021: MP Tago asked what law or order created Salaam TV; MP Ramos answered it came from the President's SONA pronouncement and no Executive Order exists yet.

24 February 2021: MP Mawallil argued the second part of the resolution set a precedent of parliamentary support for every communication initiative and was vague, and urged prioritizing the Bangsamoro Information Office budget instead.

24 February 2021: MP Mangudadatu read 'support' as budgetary and asked that the resolution be committed to a committee; MP Ramos replied it had already been treated as a simple resolution and the support she sought was content production.
24 February 2021: MP Rimbang supported a Salaam TV in the BARMM but said he could not support funding it, since the block grant comes from the national government.

24 February 2021: MP Lorena moved approval subject to style; MP Adiong warned against approving measures 'subject to style', and MP Mawallil's counter-title dropping the call for support was not taken up as MP Ramos preferred MP Lorena's amendment.
24 February 2021: Approved by the Body; listed in the adopted index as Resolution No. 108.
readings.insight: The call for support is open-ended: it could mean placing public information campaigns on the channel, as the WHEREAS clauses suggest, but nothing is specified, and the copy goes only to the President and the PCOO, not to any regional office.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the Organization of Islamic Cooperation for its support of the Bangsamoro peace process, shown in Resolution No. 2/47-MM, 'On Question of Muslims in Southern Philippines'. The resolution is forwarded to Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim for information and appropriate action.

Authored by MP Ustadz Abdulmuhmin A. Mujahid and MP Hatimil E. Hassan. Adopted on 24 February 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, at its 47th session in Niamey, Niger, on 27 and 28 November 2020, adopted a resolution that commends the third-party facilitators of the agreements with the MNLF and MILF, urges full implementation of the 1996 Final Agreement and of the Framework and Comprehensive Agreements on the Bangsamoro, and asks the Philippine Government to facilitate a visit by OIC and Islamic Development Bank representatives to set up development assistance for the region.
whoIsAffected: The Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
whatChanges: It is a commendation; its only copy goes to the Chief Minister, not to the OIC.
readings.insight: The OIC itself is not on the distribution list. Parliament thanked the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers again after its 48th session, in Resolution 241 (24 March 2022).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends Al-Basher Buto, described as the first and youngest Bangsamoro international chess player, for his feats in national and international championships. It asks the Bangsamoro Government, through the Bangsamoro Sports Commission, the Bangsamoro Youth Commission or the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, to give him financial support for training and competition as a representative of the region and the country.

Copies go to the Chief Minister, the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education and the 2 commissions, for action, and to Buto. Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and 6 others. Adopted on 16 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Buto, a 10-year-old Maranao, was the only Bangsamoro player on the Philippine team at the 2020 FIDE Online World Cadets and Youth Rapid Championships. He won gold at the 13th Asian Schools Chess Championship in China and the overall crown at the 8th ASEAN Age Group Championship in Malaysia in 2017. He learned at sidewalk games in Quiapo, with no formal training beyond his uncle. His parents could not afford to go with him abroad, weak internet hurt his online games, and his father sold their house to pay for his training.
whoIsAffected: Al-Basher Buto and his family.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
Bangsamoro Youth Commission
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It asks for financial support but names no amount or fund.

whatChanges: It asks 3 offices for financial support and copies the finance ministry; it sets no amount and binds none of them.
readings.insight: Unusually for a commendation, it asks for money and copies the finance ministry. Parliament commended Buto again in Resolution 294 (21 December 2022), for earning the Candidate Master title at the 6th Eastern Asia Youth Chess Championship in Bangkok.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament directs the Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' to hold an Ulama consultation or conference on the 2021 Ramadan moon sighting, and to come up each year with a unified declaration of the first day of fasting. The resolution is forwarded to the Darul-Ifta'.

Authored by MP Ustadz Abdulmuhmin A. Mujahid. Adopted on 17 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Ramadan 2021 was expected to begin on Tuesday, 13 April. The author says disagreement over moon sighting has often split Muslim groups for lack of consultation, and that Ulama from the region's provinces and from Bangsamoro communities outside it should agree on a single schedule and declaration.
whoIsAffected: Muslims in and outside the region, who would start the fast on a common day.
The Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta' and the Ulama it would convene.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta'
whatChanges: It assigns the Darul-Ifta' a yearly task, but sets no deadline before Ramadan and no report back.
readings.insight: Adopted 27 days before the expected start of Ramadan. Parliament later gave the Darul-Ifta' other tasks: a fatwa on halal conduct of officials in Resolution 130 (June 2021) and an annual Ramadhan symposium in Resolution 402 (October 2023).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its deepest condolences and sympathy to the family of former Lanao del Sur Governor Princess Tarhata Alangadi Alonto Lucman. The resolution is sent to her family.

Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and 8 others. Adopted on 17 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Princess Tarhata died in Marawi City on 26 February 2021, at 95, of cardiac arrest. Daughter of Senator Alauya Alonto, the first Maranao senator, and wife of Congressman Haroun Al-Rashid Lucman, she was elected Lanao del Sur's first woman governor in 1971, worked on Muslim-Christian ties and the settlement of clan feuds, defied martial law, and was removed from office and exiled to Saudi Arabia in 1975. After 1986 she helped secure the release of hostages abducted in Marawi City.
whoIsAffected: The family of Princess Tarhata Alangadi Alonto Lucman.
whatChanges: It records Parliament's sentiment and sends a copy to the family; it directs no office to do anything.
readings.insight: Adopted 19 days after her death. The text presents her as an early example of Bangsamoro women in governance; Parliament commended women's achievements in Resolution 114, adopted the same day.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses full support for the national and regional (MOH-BARMM) COVID-19 vaccine deployment and vaccination plans, and urges all government units, agencies and instrumentalities in the region to cooperate fully, including through advocacy, education and information campaigns. The resolution goes to all Bangsamoro ministries.

Authored by MP Zul Qarneyn M. Abas. Adopted on 17 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Ministry of Health had adopted a BARMM Deployment and Vaccination Plan alongside the national plan, with ₱500 million allocated for vaccine procurement. The author states that the plans do not go against Islamic beliefs or the faith of other residents, and that risk communication and community engagement are needed to raise awareness.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region eligible for COVID-19 vaccines.
Ministries and local government units asked to help with campaigns.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health
Bangsamoro ministries
Local government units in the region

funding.detail: The resolution appropriates nothing. It cites ₱500 million allocated for vaccine procurement.

whatChanges: It is an expression of support and an appeal for cooperation; it assigns no specific task.
readings.insight: It came a month after Resolution 107 (18 February 2021) directed the Ministry of Health to brief Parliament on the same plan. The statement that vaccination does not conflict with Islamic belief anticipates hesitancy, which Parliament addressed more directly in Resolutions 133 (June 2021) and 212 (February 2022).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the social, economic, cultural and political achievements of women in the Bangsamoro as the region joins the International Women's Day celebration on 8 March 2021. The resolution goes to the Bangsamoro Women Commission.

Authored by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil. Adopted on 17 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The author notes the Organic Law's protection of women's rights under CEDAW, training and capacity-building on the Magna Carta of Women and CEDAW in the region, and the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, praised for its provisions on women after 17 years of negotiations.
whoIsAffected: Women in the region.
whatChanges: It is a commendation; it directs no one.
readings.insight: Adopted 9 days after International Women's Day. It names no individual women or achievements. Resolution 104 (26 January 2021) did the same for the International Day of the Girl Child.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the appropriate ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government to formulate rationalised guidelines for livelihood projects and to share databases of beneficiaries, to improve socio-economic conditions in the region. The resolution goes to Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim.

Authored by MP Edrieza H.N. Rimbang. Adopted on 24 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The author cites the 2015 Family Income and Expenditure Survey placing the former ARMM at the top of the 5 regions with the highest poverty incidence, with at least 59% of its population below the poverty threshold, and the Organic Law's social justice mandate. Streamlined processes, unified beneficiary records and shared databases would make livelihood projects run more smoothly.
whoIsAffected: Beneficiaries of livelihood projects.
Ministries and offices running them.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministries and offices running livelihood projects
whatChanges: It calls for guidelines and data sharing but names no lead ministry and sets no deadline.
readings.insight: The poverty figures are from 2015, before the region existed. It names no lead ministry. Resolution 117, adopted the same day, asked for a database of indigents to avoid duplicate relief, and Resolution 116 for monitoring of the 4Ps.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Chief Minister, through the Regional Action Committee, to regularly monitor and report on compliance with and implementation of Republic Act No. 11310, the law institutionalising the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), in the region. The Ministry of Social Services and Development is to report to the Regional Action Committee and other agencies. Copies go to Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim and the ministry.

Authored by MP Edrieza H.N. Rimbang. Adopted on 24 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The 4Ps is implemented in the region, which has the highest poverty incidence, and concerns had been raised about its implementation in various LGUs. The author cites the State's duties to free people from poverty, prioritise children's education and health, and empower women.
whoIsAffected: 4Ps beneficiary households in the region.
The Ministry of Social Services and Development.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Regional Action Committee
Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: It asks for regular reports but sets no frequency, and does not ask that they come to Parliament.
readings.insight: The 'concerns' are not described. The reports flow to the Regional Action Committee and 'other agencies'; Parliament does not list itself among those who receive them.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Chief Minister to consider designating a focal person or committee for each province, and for the 63 barangays, to build a database of Bangsamoro indigents. The aim is a consolidated list of areas where Members of Parliament can extend support, and no duplicate relief. Copies go to Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim and the Ministry of Social Services and Development.

Authored by MP Punduma B. Sani and MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. Adopted on 24 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: On 30 April 2020, the Office of the Chief Minister issued an advisory to distribute 16,000 sacks of rice equally among the 80 Members of Parliament. The authors want Members to have assigned areas so their assistance is systematic and reaches far-flung areas, and want the system reused whenever aid is needed again.
whoIsAffected: Indigent households in the region.
Members of Parliament who distribute relief.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: It asks the Chief Minister to consider designations; it does not create the database.
readings.insight: The 16,000 sacks split equally among 80 Members is 200 sacks each. The database is meant to assign Members of Parliament areas for relief they distribute themselves. Resolution 115, adopted the same day, also called for shared beneficiary databases.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government to monitor the establishment of institutional mechanisms for programs and services for persons with disabilities in the region, under Republic Act No. 7277 as amended by Republic Act No. 10070. Copies go to the ministry and the Ministry of Social Services and Development.

Authored by MP Bai Maleiha B. Candao. Adopted on 24 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 10070, approved on 6 April 2010, requires local governments to set up a Persons with Disability Affairs Office, though 4th to 6th class municipalities may designate a focal person instead, and to fund its work. The author recommends that the region ensure such mechanisms at regional and local levels, in line with the Organic Law's call for a special agency and services for persons with special needs.
whoIsAffected: Persons with disabilities in the region.
Local governments that must set up PDAOs or focal persons.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Social Services and Development
whatChanges: It asks for monitoring of an existing national requirement; it sets no deadline and asks for no report.
readings.insight: The PDAO requirement is in national law already; the resolution adds a monitor but no count of which LGUs comply. Resolution 404 (17 October 2023) returned to the same Magna Carta, calling on all offices and LGUs to comply with and monitor it.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Professional Regulation Commission to create and operate a regional office in the region, which is within its power under the PRC Modernization Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8981). Copies go to the PRC main office, the Office of the President, the Department of Labor and Employment, the Inter-Governmental Relations body and the regional Ministry of Labor and Employment.

Authored by MP Saffrullah M. Dipatuan and 42 others. Adopted on 25 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The PRC serves professionals in more than 40 regulated professions, but had no regional or even satellite office in the region, so professionals from the region had to travel to neighbouring regions to take exams, renew licences or transact. The authors say a regional office would save them money, time and effort, especially those like medical practitioners who renew every 1 or 2 years. The regional Ministry of Labor and Employment was already in talks with DOLE and its attached agencies.
whoIsAffected: Professionals and licensure examinees in the region.
implementedBy: Professional Regulation Commission
Department of Labor and Employment
Ministry of Labor and Employment
whatChanges: It urges a national commission; it cannot compel it.
readings.insight: With 43 principal authors, it carried the names of over half of the 80 Members. The repo does not record whether a PRC office was later opened in the region.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament requests the Office of the Chief Minister to authorise a Ramadhan allowance for all personnel and employees of the region, sourced from any available funds of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority. The Office of the Chief Minister sets eligibility, but contractual employees and job orders must be included. Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management for immediate action.

Authored by MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 25 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The author compares Ramadhan to Christmas, when employees receive a 13th month pay equal to 1 month's basic salary under Presidential Decree No. 852, and argues that an allowance would recognise the region's customs and keep employees motivated through the month of fasting and night prayers.
whoIsAffected: Personnel and employees of the regional government, including contractual and job-order workers.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management

funding.detail: The resolution names no amount. It asks that the allowance come from any available funds of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority.

whatChanges: It is a request; the decision and the amount rest with the Chief Minister.
readings.insight: This was the first of a yearly series: Resolution 237 (2022) authorised a Ramadhan allowance, 323 (2023) asked for inflation relief of up to ₱15,000, and 441 (2024) and 530 (2025) asked for at least ₱10,000. This first request named no amount and gave no headcount or cost.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Senate to speed up passage of Senate Bill No. 1395, which would pay monetary compensation for homes, cultural and commercial structures and other property lost or destroyed in the Main Affected Area and the Greater Marawi Area during the 2017 siege, and to match the House of Representatives' version of the same measure. The resolution is sent to the Senate for its information and immediate action.

Authored by MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong and 7 others. Adopted on 14 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The authors say the victims of the Marawi siege had waited 4 years for compensation. The House had approved House Bill No. 9925, the Marawi Compensation Act, on second reading on 31 August 2021, while Senate Bill No. 1395, referred to 3 Senate committees on 23 November 2020, was still pending at committee level as of 1 September 2021. The resolution cites the Bangon Marawi plan's estimate that ₱51.7 billion is needed for Marawi's full recovery and rehabilitation.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Marawi City who lost homes and property in the 2017 siege.
The Senate, asked to act on its bill.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
whatChanges: A request to the Senate; it binds no one.
A copy goes to the Senate for information and action.
readings.insight: Parliament adopted a second resolution on the same Senate bill the next day, Resolution 156, and had backed a compensation law since Resolution 14 (26 June 2019) and Resolution 33 (30 August 2019). Senate Bill No. 1395 is not the number that reached the President: Resolution 216 (17 February 2022) asked President Duterte to sign Senate Bill No. 2420 and House Bill No. 9925, and Resolution 308 (24 January 2023) records that Republic Act No. 11696 was approved on 13 April 2022 and thanks President Marcos for constituting the Marawi Compensation Board.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Philippine Statistics Authority to brief the Bangsamoro Transition Authority on the results of the 2020 household survey and the latest poverty statistics. Copies go to the PSA's national office and to PSA BARMM for information and appropriate consideration.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 14 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Government must deliver health, education, housing, power and water, and the authors say it needs reliable statistics to plan for them. The resolution notes that parliamentary districts must be apportioned by population, with at least 100,000 people each, and that BARMM was the fastest-growing region: from 3,781,387 in the 2015 census to 4,404,288 in the 2020 census, an annual growth rate of 3.26%, a count it says excludes Cotabato City, Isabela City and the 63 barangays in North Cotabato.
whoIsAffected: Members of Parliament, who would receive the briefing.
The PSA's national and BARMM offices.
implementedBy: Philippine Statistics Authority
PSA BARMM
whatChanges: A request to a national agency, which the BTA cannot compel.
It sets no date or form for the briefing.
readings.insight: The request has no deadline and no follow-up mechanism. The link to districting is the sharpest point in the text: the Organic Law's 100,000-per-district floor makes the census count matter for the parliamentary districts the BTA still had to draw. It is 1 of 5 resolutions by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan adopted between 14 and 22 September 2021, with Resolutions 153, 155, 156 and 168.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Office of the Chief Minister to nominate representatives of the Bangsamoro Government to the governing boards of government-owned and controlled corporations operating in the region. The resolution is sent to Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim for information and appropriate consideration.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law lists dividends from regional corporations and a share of the dividends of national corporations operating in the region among Bangsamoro revenues, as determined by the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board. Article XII, Section 32 says the Bangsamoro Government shall be represented on the boards of corporations that do a substantial part of their business in the region, with at least 1 seat. The authors say nominees are needed to fill that representation.
whoIsAffected: The Office of the Chief Minister, asked to make nominations.
Government corporations operating in the region.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A call to the Chief Minister's office; it names no corporations and sets no deadline.
A copy goes to the Chief Minister.
readings.insight: The resolution quotes Article XII, Section 33, under which the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board was to determine the Bangsamoro Government's participation in Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank and the Southern Philippines Development Authority within 6 months of the BTA's establishment. That window had long closed by September 2021, and the resolution does not say whether it was met. A week later the same author asked the Chief Minister for a report on the Southern Philippines Development Authority projects turned over to the old ARMM (Resolution 168).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends the Senate, under Senate President Vicente C. Sotto, for approving Senate Bill No. 2214 on third reading. It names the Committee on Local Government, chaired by Senator Francis N. Tolentino, Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel F. Zubiri and all senators involved. The resolution is sent to the Senate President for information.

Authored by MP Eddie M. Alih. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Senate Bill No. 2214, consolidated on 20 May 2021 from bills filed by Senators Aquilino Pimentel III and Richard Gordon, resets the first regular election of the Bangsamoro Parliament to 2025. The Senate approved it on third reading on 6 September 2021. The authors say the pandemic, lockdowns, scarce resources and security threats made the 3-year transition too short.
whoIsAffected: The Senate and the senators named.
The BTA, whose term the bill would extend.
whatChanges: A commendation; it changes nothing by itself.
A copy goes to the Senate President.
readings.insight: It is one link in a chain on the election reset: Resolution 93 (17 November 2020) asked Congress to extend the transition to 30 June 2025, Resolution 150 (26 August 2021) commended the Senate's second-reading approval, and in the following week Parliament adopted Resolutions 162, 163 and 167 on the bicameral conference, the House vote and the President's certification. Resolution 246 later records that President Duterte signed Republic Act No. 11593 on 28 October 2021.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament calls on the Office of the Chief Minister to give financial assistance to frontline healthcare workers who caught COVID-19 and needed inpatient care or hospital confinement, the amount depending on how severe their illness was. The Office of the Chief Minister, with the Ministry of Health, is to issue implementing guidelines.

Copies go to Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim, the Ministry of Health and other concerned ministries. Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: About 3,000 healthcare workers of the Ministry of Health and BARMM-READi serve on the front line, and some caught COVID-19 on the job. The authors point to the Quick Response Fund under the Office of the Chief Minister in the 2021 Bangsamoro appropriations act, and to a Supreme Court circular (OCA Circular No. 51A-2021, 28 April 2021) that grants its own personnel assistance graded by severity of illness.
whoIsAffected: Frontline healthcare workers hospitalized for COVID-19.
The Office of the Chief Minister and the Ministry of Health.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is named. The WHEREAS clauses point to the Quick Response Fund under the Office of the Chief Minister in the 2021 Bangsamoro appropriations act; the resolution itself appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: A call to the executive; the payments depend on the Chief Minister's office acting.
It asks for implementing guidelines but sets no deadline for them.
readings.insight: The resolution borrows its model from the Supreme Court, which pays its staff by severity of illness, but leaves the amounts, eligibility and timing to guidelines the executive has yet to write. It does not say how many of the roughly 3,000 frontline workers had been hospitalized.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Senate to prioritize the compensation bill for Marawi. The resolution is sent to Senate President Vicente C. Sotto for information and appropriate consideration.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: House Bill No. 9925, the proposed Marawi Compensation Act, passed the House on third and final reading on 6 September 2021. It would compensate lawful owners or possessors displaced by the 2017 fighting in Marawi City and institutionalize Task Force Bangon Marawi. The Senate's counterpart, Senate Bill No. 1395, was still awaiting action; the authors say compensation is owed given the delayed completion of the Marawi rehabilitation.
whoIsAffected: Residents displaced by the Marawi siege who lost homes and property.
The Senate.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
whatChanges: A request to the Senate; it binds no one.
A copy goes to the Senate President.
readings.insight: It repeats Resolution 151, adopted the day before by different authors, which asked the Senate to expedite the same Senate Bill No. 1395. The House bill named here, No. 9925, is the number that later reached the President with Senate Bill No. 2420 (Resolution 216, 17 February 2022). Resolution 308 records that Republic Act No. 11696 was approved on 13 April 2022.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament congratulates and commends Justice Japar B. Dimaampao on his appointment as the 191st Associate Justice of the Supreme Court and as the 2nd Muslim magistrate to serve on the Court. The resolution is sent to Justice Dimaampao.

Authored by MP Amilbahar S. Mawallil, MP Sittie Shahara I. Mastura and MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: On 14 September 2021 Malacañang released the appointment, signed by President Duterte and dated 2 July 2021. Justice Dimaampao, from Poona Bayabao and Lumba-Bayabao, Lanao del Sur, served 17 years on the Court of Appeals and was the youngest appointed to it. He follows Justice Abdulwahid Bidin of Tawi-Tawi, appointed in 1987, and may serve until 2033. The BTA had endorsed him in Resolution No. 20 (29 July 2019).
whoIsAffected: Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
whatChanges: A commendation; a copy goes to Justice Dimaampao.
readings.insight: It is the 1st of 5 resolutions on the appointment adopted on 15 and 16 September 2021 (Resolutions 157 to 161): 2 congratulate the Justice and 3 thank President Duterte. The 5 texts do not agree on details. This one dates Chief Justice Gesmundo's appointment to 5 April 2021, while Resolution 159 says 15 April 2021, and Resolution 161 says he was shortlisted 15 times where Resolutions 159 and 160 say 14.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament thanks President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for appointing Court of Appeals Justice Japar B. Dimaampao as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. The resolution is sent to the President and Justice Dimaampao.

Authored by MP Modayao M. Sacar. Adopted on 15 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The authors say the Bangsamoro had long wanted 1 of the Court's 15 seats; the last Muslim justice, Abdulwahid Bidin, was appointed in 1987. Justice Dimaampao had been shortlisted by the Judicial and Bar Council many times, and at times topped the list.
whoIsAffected: President Rodrigo Roa Duterte.
Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
whatChanges: A message of thanks; copies go to the President and the Justice.
readings.insight: It is 1 of 3 thank-you resolutions to President Duterte for the same appointment, with Resolutions 159 and 161, adopted within 2 days; 2 more (157 and 160) congratulate the Justice. This is the shortest of the 5.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its gratitude to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for appointing Justice Japar B. Dimaampao as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. The resolution is sent to the President.

Authored by MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong and 6 others. Adopted on 16 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The 1996 Final Peace Agreement and the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro both commit the National Government to Bangsamoro representation in national agencies, and Article VI, Section 11 of the Organic Law repeats this. In the Court's 120 years only 1 Bangsamoro, Justice Abdulwahid Bidin, had served. Justice Dimaampao had been shortlisted 14 times since 2010 and was sworn in on 14 September 2021 as the 191st Associate Justice, the first Meranao on the Court.
whoIsAffected: President Rodrigo Roa Duterte.
Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
whatChanges: A message of thanks; a copy goes to the President.
readings.insight: The same 7 authors filed Resolution 160, adopted the same day, congratulating the Justice; both repeat much of the same history. It is 1 of 5 resolutions on the appointment (157 to 161). It dates Chief Justice Gesmundo's appointment to 15 April 2021; Resolution 157 says 5 April 2021.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends and congratulates Justice Japar B. Dimaampao as the first Maranao and 2nd Bangsamoro appointed Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. The resolution is sent to Justice Dimaampao.

Authored by MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong and 6 others. Adopted on 16 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The 1996 Final Peace Agreement says at least 1 Supreme Court justice and 2 Court of Appeals justices should come from the autonomous region. The resolution recounts his record: a CPA at 19 in 1983, admitted to the Bar in 1987, the first Muslim senior state prosecutor, appointed to the Court of Appeals at 40 in April 2004 where he served 17 years, a law teacher and author, and 2020 chair of the Shari'ah Bar examinations committee. Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim recommended him to the President in 2019, and the BTA endorsed him in Resolution No. 20.
whoIsAffected: Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
whatChanges: A commendation; a copy goes to Justice Dimaampao.
readings.insight: It is the fullest of the 5 resolutions on the appointment (157 to 161), and it says the BTA is optimistic about having another Bangsamoro on the Court. Its figure of 14 shortlistings since 2010 matches Resolution 159 but not Resolution 161, which says 15.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses appreciation and profound gratitude to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for appointing Japar B. Dimaampao as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. The resolution is sent to the Office of the President, Justice Dimaampao and the Judicial and Bar Council.

Authored by MP Diamila D. Ramos, MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph and MP Susana S. Anayatin. Adopted on 16 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: President Duterte appointed him on 2 July 2021 and he took his oath on 14 September 2021 as the 191st Associate Justice. The authors cite 4 years as a Regional Trial Court judge in Mandaluyong City and 17 years on the Court of Appeals, and his work on Shari'a law, and say he is the 2nd Bangsamoro on the Court, 34 years after Justice Abdulwahid Bidin's appointment on 12 January 1987.
whoIsAffected: President Rodrigo Roa Duterte.
Justice Japar B. Dimaampao.
whatChanges: A message of thanks; copies go to the President, the Justice and the Judicial and Bar Council.
readings.insight: It is the 3rd thank-you to President Duterte for the same appointment in 2 days, after Resolutions 158 and 159. It says he was shortlisted 15 times, where Resolutions 159 and 160, adopted the same day, say 14.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Senate and the House of Representatives to convene a bicameral conference committee at once to reconcile Senate Bill No. 2214 and House Bill No. 10121, so a law resetting the first Bangsamoro regional elections to 2025 can be enacted quickly. The resolution is sent to both chambers for immediate action.

Authored by MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong and 6 others. Adopted on 16 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law set the first regular election for 2022. The authors say the pandemic delayed the political and normalization tracks, and that the BTA had yet to pass the Bangsamoro Electoral Code or set the parliamentary districts. The Senate passed its bill on 6 September 2021 by 15 votes to 3 with 1 abstention, and the House passed its version on 15 September 2021, differing mainly on the appointment of new BTA members.
whoIsAffected: The Senate and the House of Representatives.
The BTA, whose term the bill would extend.
Voters in the region, whose first regional election would move to 2025.
implementedBy: Senate of the Philippines
House of Representatives
whatChanges: A request to Congress; it binds no one.
Copies go to the Senate and the House.
readings.insight: It was adopted the day after the House vote. The difference it flags, on appointing new BTA members, came back: 26 days later Parliament appealed to the President to keep the incumbent members (Resolution 173). Resolution 173 records that the Senate ratified the bill on 27 September 2021, 11 days after this request, and Resolution 246 records that Republic Act No. 11593 was signed on 28 October 2021.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends and thanks the House of Representatives for approving on third and final reading House Bill No. 10121, which resets the first regular Bangsamoro elections by amending Article XVI, Section 13 of the Organic Law. The resolution is sent to the office of Senate President Vicente C. Sotto for information.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph and 13 others. Adopted on 16 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law gave the BTA a 3-year transition from 2019 and a list of tasks, among them the priority codes and the parliamentary districts. The authors say the pandemic hampered the political track, the normalization track and the transition plan, that the Bangsamoro people asked for elections to move to 2025, and that the House approved the bill on 15 September 2021.
whoIsAffected: The House of Representatives.
The BTA.
whatChanges: A commendation; it changes nothing by itself.
A copy goes to the Senate President's office.
readings.insight: The resolution commends the House but is sent only to the Senate President, not to the Speaker of the House. The same 14 authors filed Resolution 167 5 days later, thanking President Duterte for certifying the same bill as urgent.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management and the Ministry of Health to apply Department of Budget and Management Budget Circular No. 2021-2 properly in preparing the 2022 Bangsamoro appropriations act. Copies go to both ministries.

Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and 6 others. Adopted on 21 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The DBM circular, dated 25 August 2021, upgrades the salary grade of Nurse II positions and reinstates the 7-series nurse positions, effective not earlier than 1 June 2021, at the rates of the second-tranche national salary schedule. Article XII, Section 19 of the Organic Law gives health the highest budget priority and applies DBM budgeting rules to the block grant. The BTA was then preparing for its 2022 budget hearings.
whoIsAffected: Nurses employed by the Bangsamoro Government.
The finance and health ministries preparing the 2022 budget.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management
Ministry of Health

funding.detail: No amount is named. The resolution asks the 2022 budget to provide for the upgraded nurse salaries; it appropriates nothing itself.

whatChanges: An urging to 2 ministries; it does not itself change any salary.
Parliament, which passes the budget, can check whether the 2022 appropriations act carries it.
readings.insight: Unlike most requests to the executive, this one has a natural check: the 2022 Bangsamoro appropriations act, which Parliament itself had to pass. The resolution does not estimate how many nurse positions or how much money are involved.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament encourages the appropriate ministries to put up memorial gates, arches and road and gateway signs at the region's entry and exit points, so residents and visitors know the territory and its culture, traditions and laws. It names the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government and the Ministry of Public Works, working with the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism and the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, and asks that designs carry the locality's cultural heritage.

Copies go to the 4 offices. Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. Adopted on 21 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The 2019 plebiscite added areas formerly in Region 12 to the Bangsamoro. The authors say many people do not know where the region's boundaries lie, some in the newly added areas do not know they are in the Bangsamoro, and Shari'ah law and indigenous customs also apply inside the region. Gates and signs would mark the border and promote tourism and local art.
whoIsAffected: Travellers and residents at the region's borders.
The 4 offices asked to build the structures.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Public Works
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage

funding.detail: No amount or source is named for building the gates and signs. The resolution appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: An encouragement only; it identifies no specific entry points and sets no timetable.
readings.insight: The resolution asks for construction but names no sites, budget or lead office among the 4, leaving the work to whichever ministry takes it up.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, the Ministry of Public Order and Safety and the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government to support Mindanao State University and other local institutions in bringing justice to the families of slain students Zinal Omar and Hamza Rauf, and in strengthening safety across the MSU system. Copies go to the 4 offices.

Authored by MP Rasol Y. Mitmug Jr. and 6 others. Adopted on 21 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The 2 MSU students, from Taraka, Lanao del Sur and Baloi, Lanao del Norte, were shot dead by unidentified gunmen near the graduate school building on the Marawi campus on the evening of 14 September 2021. The regional police director had ordered an investigation. The authors say earlier killings at MSU remain unresolved and that students and teachers fear for their safety, and cite each office's mandate under the Education Code and the Administrative Code.
whoIsAffected: The families of Zinal Omar and Hamza Rauf.
Students and staff of Mindanao State University.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission
Ministry of Public Order and Safety
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
whatChanges: An urging to 4 offices; it sets no task, report or deadline.
readings.insight: Parliament adopted a second resolution on the same killings the next day, Resolution 169, by a different author, which condemns them and asks the Human Rights Commission to help investigate. The 2 texts name the students differently, Zinal Omar here and Omar Zinal there. Neither says what became of the earlier MSU cases they call unresolved.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament commends and thanks President Rodrigo Roa Duterte for certifying as urgent House Bill No. 10121, which resets the first regular Bangsamoro elections by amending Article XVI, Section 13 of the Organic Law. The resolution is sent to the President.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph and 13 others. Adopted on 21 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The authors recall the President's support for Bangsamoro autonomy and that he signed the Organic Law on 26 July 2018 after certifying it as urgent. They say the pandemic hampered the transition, that the Bangsamoro people asked for elections to move to 2025, and that the President certified the reset bill as necessary for immediate enactment.
whoIsAffected: President Rodrigo Roa Duterte.
whatChanges: A message of thanks; a copy goes to the President.
readings.insight: The same 14 authors had commended the House for the same bill 5 days earlier (Resolution 163). Republic Act No. 11593, resetting the election, was signed on 28 October 2021, according to Resolution 246.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Office of the Chief Minister to submit to Parliament a comprehensive report on the assets, liabilities, programs and projects the Southern Philippines Development Authority turned over to the former ARMM, now under the Bangsamoro region. The resolution is sent to Chief Minister Ahod B. Ebrahim.

Authored by MP Baintan A. Ampatuan. Adopted on 22 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Executive Order No. 142 of 1993, signed by President Ramos, transferred 5 Southern Philippines Development Authority projects to the ARMM: the Kapatiran Agro-Industrial Cooperative Settlements, the Maguindanao Integrated Development Project, the Lake Buluan Development Project, the Lake Lanao Fish Cage Project and the Integrated Marine Fisheries Development Project. The authors say their condition must be known because they may be assets or liabilities, and suggest the Chief Minister could form an inter-agency task group to assess them. The Organic Law gives local governments a preferential right to acquire any of the authority's property that is transferred or disposed of.
whoIsAffected: The Office of the Chief Minister, asked to report.
Communities around the 5 projects.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
whatChanges: A request for a report to Parliament; it sets no deadline.
A copy goes to the Chief Minister.
readings.insight: It follows Resolution 153, by the same author a week earlier, on Bangsamoro seats on the boards of government corporations, which also cites the Organic Law's 6-month deadline for settling the region's stake in the Southern Philippines Development Authority. The request names 5 projects but sets no date for the report.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament strongly condemns the killing of MSU students Omar Zinal and Hamza Rauf and asks the concerned agencies, especially the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission, to help investigate. Copies go to the Commission, the Mayor of Marawi City and MSU's main campus.

Authored by MP Punduma B. Sani. Adopted on 22 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Omar Maruhom Punag Zinal, a 3rd-year civil engineering student, and Hamza Ariong Rauf, a 3rd-year physical education student, were shot dead inside the MSU main campus on 14 September 2021. The author says it was not the first shooting on the campus and that Marawi City needs stronger security measures.
whoIsAffected: The families of the 2 students.
MSU students and staff.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission
City Government of Marawi
whatChanges: A condemnation with a request for help in the investigation; it binds no agency.
readings.insight: It follows Resolution 166, adopted the day before by different authors, which urged 4 Bangsamoro offices to support MSU on the same case. Read together they ask for the same thing twice, a day apart.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament condemns the violence, discrimination and killings reported against members of the LGBTQ+ community in Datu Piang, Maguindanao on 18 and 19 September 2021. It resolves that the Bangsamoro Government, through the Office of the Chief Minister, and all local governments in the region shall put in place concrete measures to protect everyone's rights, including those of LGBTQ+ people, across the region.

Copies go to the Office of the Chief Minister and the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. Authored by MP Susana S. Anayatin, MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph, MP Bainon G. Karon, MP Muslima A. Asmawil and MP Narciso Co Yu Ekey. Adopted on 22 September 2021.
readings.whyProposed: On the afternoon of 18 September 2021 a bomb exploded where a group reported to be LGBTQ+ was playing volleyball in Barangay Poblacion, Datu Piang, wounding 7 and killing 1. The next evening a lesbian was shot dead in her home by an unidentified gunman. The authors cite the Organic Law's guarantee of human rights and ask the government to establish whether the victims were targeted for their sexual orientation or gender identity.
whoIsAffected: LGBTQ+ people in the Bangsamoro.
The victims and their families in Datu Piang.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government
Local government units in the region
whatChanges: A condemnation, plus a directive-worded clause on protective measures that names no measure, office lead or deadline.
readings.insight: It was adopted 3 days after the second attack. Parliament took up anti-LGBTQ+ violence again 3 weeks later, condemning the public head-shaving of 6 young women in Ampatuan, Maguindanao (Resolution 176). The WHEREAS clauses ask for an investigation into motive, but the RESOLVED clauses do not direct one.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage to promote, protect and preserve the region's boat-making tradition, possibly by setting up a school of living tradition for boat making. The resolution is sent to the Commission.

Authored by MP Don Mustapha A. Loong and 6 others. Adopted on 12 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Boat making is an ancestral practice in Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, especially among the Sama, for whom the lepa serves as home, workplace and transport. The Tausug and the Yakan are tied to the sea, Maguindanao marks Shariff Kabunsuan's arrival with a fluvial parade of wooden boats, and boats remain the only inter-island transport in the island provinces. The Organic Law tasks the Commission with sustaining cultural institutions and programs.
whoIsAffected: Boat builders in Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi.
The Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
whatChanges: An urging; the school is suggested as a possibility, not required.
readings.insight: The resolution's key ask is hedged twice, urging a school that the Commission may 'possibly' develop or establish. No funding, site or timetable is named.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges the ministries, offices and the offices of Members of Parliament to adopt the Government Internship Program as a regular program and to budget for the 25% counterpart that host offices pay. The resolution is sent to the ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government.

Authored by MP Hatimil E. Hassan and 7 others. Adopted on 12 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Ministry of Labor and Employment, through its Bureau of Employment Promotion and Welfare, runs the Government Internship Program to give young people exposure to public service. Interns are paid the minimum wage, 75% by the ministry and 25% by the host office, under a 9-month memorandum of understanding. The authors say most prospective hosts could not take interns because they had no budget for their share.
whoIsAffected: Young people seeking government internships.
Ministries, offices and MPs' offices that would host interns.
implementedBy: Ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government
Offices of Members of Parliament
Ministry of Labor and Employment

funding.detail: No amount is named. Host offices are asked to budget the 25% share of each intern's minimum-wage stipend; the Ministry of Labor and Employment pays the other 75%. The resolution appropriates nothing.

whatChanges: An urging; whether any office budgets for interns is up to that office.
It applies to MPs' own offices, which Parliament can act on directly.
readings.insight: Because it covers the offices of Members of Parliament, this is one request Parliament can act on itself, through its own budget. It does not count how many interns or how much money the 25% share would take.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament appeals to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte to let the incumbent BTA members serve until 2025 by giving them primary consideration when he appoints the members for the extended transition. Copies go to the President, the Office of the Presidential Adviser for Unity, Peace and Reconciliation, the Department of National Defense and the Department of the Interior and Local Government.

Authored by MP Nabil A. Tan and 14 others. Adopted on 12 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Senate ratified the bill postponing the first regional elections on 27 September 2021; it gives the President power to appoint all 80 BTA members for the extended transition. The authors argue that new members would need time to learn the parliamentary system and could delay the priority codes, that donors and institutions had spent about 2.5 years training the incumbents, and that the current membership is balanced across provinces, sectors and the MILF and MNLF.
whoIsAffected: The 80 incumbent BTA members.
The President, who holds the sole power of appointment.
whatChanges: An appeal to the President; it cannot bind his appointments.
Copies go to the President and 3 national offices.
readings.insight: Parliament repeated the appeal in Resolution 209 (15 February 2022), then in Resolution 229 (15 March 2022) thanked President Duterte for approving his security cluster's recommendation to keep the BTA's composition as it was. Republic Act No. 11593 was signed on 28 October 2021, 16 days after this resolution, according to Resolution 246.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses its sympathy and condolences to the family of the late Mayor Mohammad-Ali 'Kits' S. Guro of Matanog, recognizing his contribution to the town's peace and development. The resolution is to be presented to his family.

Authored by MP Ubaida C. Pacasem, MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong, MP Anna Tarhata S. Basman and MP Raissa H. Jajurie. Adopted on 13 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Mayor Guro died on 2 October 2021, aged 52. A Shari'ah counselor and law graduate, he worked for DAR-ARMM and DILG-ARMM, became vice-mayor in 2010 and was elected mayor 3 times from 2013. The resolution credits his term with 73 kilometers of concrete road, electricity for 83% of Matanog's sitios, water systems for 8 barangays and the settlement of more than 30 family feuds. Matanog, once part of the MILF's Camp Abubakar, won Gender and Development awards from 2015 to 2018.
whoIsAffected: The family of Mayor Guro.
The people of Matanog.
whatChanges: A condolence; it is presented to the family.
readings.insight: It was adopted 11 days after his death. The achievements listed are the resolution's own account and are not checked against other records.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament recognizes the late Atty. Jose Luis Martin 'Chito' C. Gascon as a human rights advocate, and his role in the review of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the MNLF and the OIC's peace committee, and in the peace talks with the MILF up to the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. The resolution is to be presented to his family and to the Commission on Human Rights.

Authored by MP Susana S. Anayatin. Adopted on 13 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Gascon chaired the Commission on Human Rights from 2015, was the youngest member of the 1987 Constitutional Commission and of the 8th Congress, and helped create the Sangguniang Kabataan and pass Republic Act No. 7610 on child protection. He sat on the government's technical working group on power sharing with the MILF, was an alternate panel member, and signed the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro on 27 March 2014 as a government panel consultant. He died of COVID-19 on 9 October 2021, aged 57.
whoIsAffected: The family of Atty. Gascon.
The Commission on Human Rights.
whatChanges: A tribute; copies go to his family and the Commission on Human Rights.
readings.insight: It was adopted 4 days after his death. As printed, the text dates his Cambridge master of laws (1997) before his UP law degree (1999).

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament condemns the public shaming of 6 young women whose heads were shaved in public in Maguindanao.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph. Adopted on 14 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: On 8 June 2021 a local news outlet posted photos of 6 women in Ampatuan, Maguindanao whose heads were forcibly shaved in front of people, including men in uniform. A fact-finding report of the Bangsamoro Women Commission, quoted in the resolution, says they were punished for being LGBTQIA, taken from their homes, paraded on the town park stage and mocked, and showed signs of trauma. The authors cite the Organic Law's guarantee of human rights and a 30 June 2016 UN Human Rights Council resolution against violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
whoIsAffected: The 6 women and their families.
LGBTQ+ people in the region.
whatChanges: A condemnation only. It directs no office, asks for no investigation, and does not even send a copy to anyone.
readings.insight: It came about 4 months after the incident; the typed proposed-resolution number, PR486, is lower than those of resolutions adopted around it. The official page's web address speaks of calling on the BTA to promote adherence to the UN Human Rights Council resolution, but the adopted text keeps only the condemnation. It follows Resolution 170 (22 September 2021) on the Datu Piang attacks on LGBTQ+ people.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges Congress to create more Shari'a courts in addition to the existing ones. Copies go to Senate President Vicente C. Sotto III, House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco and the Supreme Court through the Court Administrator.

Authored by MP Paisalin P. Tago, MP Ziaur-Rahman A. Adiong, MP Omar Yasser C. Sema, MP Nabil A. Tan, MP Abraham T. Burahan and MP Jose I. Lorena. Adopted on 14 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Presidential Decree No. 1083 of 1977 set up 5 Shari'a district courts and authorized 51 Shari'a circuit courts, but only 25 circuit courts operate, serving areas meant for 51. A Supreme Court and UNDP draft report says the courts sit mostly at provincial level, requiring costly travel, and that Muslims in Metro Manila must file cases in their home provinces. Court Administrator Midas Marquez is quoted calling for courts in Manila, Taguig and Baguio City. Article X of the Organic Law widens Shari'a court jurisdiction and lets Congress create Shari'a courts outside the region where many Muslims live.
whoIsAffected: Muslims, inside and outside the region, with cases under Muslim personal law.
Congress and the Supreme Court.
implementedBy: Congress of the Philippines
Supreme Court of the Philippines
whatChanges: A request to Congress; only a national law can create courts.
readings.insight: Congress acted almost 3 years later: Resolution 488 (20 August 2024) commends the enactment of Republic Act No. 12018, which created 3 more Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 more circuit courts. Resolution 516 (23 January 2025) then asked for judges to be appointed to vacant Shari'ah district courts. The adopted text prints the same quoted paragraph from the UNDP report twice.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament urges ministries, offices, local governments and private establishments to comply with national occupational safety and health standards in workplaces. The resolution is sent to the ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government for information and guidance.

Authored by MP Romeo K. Sema. Adopted on 14 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: Republic Act No. 11058, enacted on 17 August 2018, strengthens compliance with occupational safety and health standards and penalizes violations. The Ministry of Labor and Employment considers it should apply not only to private establishments but also to government workplaces, and asks that offices assign safety and health officers. The resolution cites accidents and COVID-19 as workplace risks and a 2020 joint memorandum circular on safety and health for the private sector.
whoIsAffected: Workers in government and private workplaces in the region.
Employers, public and private.
implementedBy: Ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government
Local government units
Ministry of Labor and Employment
whatChanges: An urging to comply with a law that already binds employers; it adds no new duty.
Copies go only to Bangsamoro ministries and offices.
readings.insight: The resolution urges local governments and private establishments, but sends copies only to Bangsamoro ministries and offices. The safety-and-health officers the WHEREAS clauses ask for, and that the official page's web address still mentions, are not in the RESOLVED clause.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses full support for the call of Marawi City's internally displaced persons to return to their properties in the Most Affected Area. The resolution is sent to President Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Task Force Bangon Marawi.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph, MP Paisalin P. Tago and MP Omar Yasser C. Sema. Adopted on 14 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Marawi siege began on 23 May 2017, and displaced families had been away for 4 years and 4 months. Task Force Bangon Marawi reported that 80% of the rehabilitation was done, including the barangay complex, cultural centers, 5 mosques and roads. Many displaced residents were asking to go home, and the authors cite the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement and the Organic Law's guarantee of human rights.
whoIsAffected: Displaced residents of Marawi's Most Affected Area.
whatChanges: A statement of support; it asks no office to do anything specific.
Copies go to the President and Task Force Bangon Marawi.
readings.insight: It sits beside Parliament's resolutions on Marawi compensation (151, 156, 216). The displacement did not end soon: in Resolution 476 (17 July 2024) Parliament asked for funds to extend for 2 years the lease agreements for temporary shelters of Marawi's displaced persons.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament expresses deep appreciation to the national government for Republic Act No. 11054, the Organic Law, and for Proclamation No. 1906, which declares October Indigenous Peoples Month. It directs all ministries and offices of the region to hold suitable activities.

Authored by MP Romeo C. Saliga. Adopted on 21 October 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Philippines has an estimated 14 million to 17 million indigenous people in 110 ethno-linguistic groups, more than 100,000 of them in the Bangsamoro, mostly non-Moro indigenous peoples. The Constitution recognizes their rights, the Organic Law protects them in the region, and President Arroyo's Proclamation No. 1906 of 2009 made October Indigenous Peoples Month. A WHEREAS clause assigns the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs to lead the celebrations.
whoIsAffected: Non-Moro indigenous peoples in the region.
Bangsamoro ministries and offices.
implementedBy: Ministries and offices of the Bangsamoro Government
Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs
whatChanges: A message of appreciation, plus a direction to Bangsamoro offices to hold activities, which falls within the region's own government.
readings.insight: It was adopted on 21 October 2021, with 10 days of Indigenous Peoples Month left. The official page's web address refers to Republic Act No. 8371, while the adopted title and text credit Republic Act No. 11054.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament earnestly urges the Congress of the Philippines to concur with the proclamations of President Rodrigo Roa Duterte granting amnesty to members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) for their political offenses.

Copies go to the Office of the President and the Secretary of Justice, for information and appropriate consideration.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph. Adopted on 24 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: On 5 February 2020 President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 1090 and Proclamation No. 1091, granting amnesty to MILF and MNLF members who committed crimes under the Revised Penal Code and special penal laws in furtherance of their political beliefs. Under Section 19, Article VII of the Constitution, an amnesty needs the concurrence of a majority of all Members of Congress. The resolution ties the request to the Annex on Normalization of the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro, which commits the Government to amnesty, pardon and other processes for people charged with or convicted of offenses connected to the armed conflict, and calls amnesty an instrument of healing and reconciliation.
whoIsAffected: MILF and MNLF members charged with or convicted of crimes committed in furtherance of their political beliefs.
Congress, whose majority concurrence the amnesty proclamations need.
implementedBy: Congress of the Philippines
Office of the President
Department of Justice
whatChanges: Nothing changes unless Congress concurs; the resolution is an appeal.
Copies are sent to the Office of the President and the Secretary of Justice.
readings.insight: The resolution urges Congress but sends no copy to either chamber; it goes only to the President and the Justice Secretary. It was adopted more than a year after the 2 proclamations were issued. The amnesty question returned in later resolutions: Resolution 277 (November 2022) asked President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to extend the application period for amnesty of qualified MILF and MNLF members, and Resolution 377 (July 2023) thanked him for his commitment to grant amnesty.

readings.whatItDoes:
Parliament asks the Senate Committee on Government Corporations and Public Enterprises to give due consideration to the provisions of the Bangsamoro Organic Law (R.A. No. 11054) on the Bangsamoro Government's power over inland waters, while Senate Bills No. 90, 389 and 1015, which seek to create a Lake Lanao Development Authority, are pending. It also asks the committee to consider using the Intergovernmental Relations Body to discuss the positions of the stakeholders.

Copies go to Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim and Senate President Vicente Sotto III.

Authored by MP Maisara Dandamun Latiph and MP Lanang T. Ali Jr. Adopted on 25 March 2021.
readings.whyProposed: The Organic Law places all inland waters in the region, lakes included, under the Bangsamoro Government and says Parliament shall enact laws on their regulation, conservation and management and shall create a Bangsamoro authority and offices for specific bodies of water. The authors read the word "shall" as mandatory. They argue that the exception for waters that power generating plants, and the co-management rule for waters that supply energy outside the region, cover only the joint grant of rights over energy, not management of the lake itself. A national Lake Lanao authority would, in their view, make those provisions meaningless. They point to the Intergovernmental Relations Body and the Intergovernmental Energy Board as the forums for settling the issue.
